We propose a summary statistic defined as a weighted average of logged relative risks and demonstrate that, provided the instantaneous logged relative risk does not change sign, a bijection always exists between the WLR statistic and this weighted average logged relative risk. We further show that this bijection can be consistently estimated at each analysis under a specific shape assumption, for which we outline two potential options. Additionally, we outline the derivation of design-adjusted p-values and confidence intervals and offer guidance on applying bias-correction methods. Finally, we detail various decisions made regarding the design of the NLST interim analysis plan and the reporting of its primary endpoint results.

De novo molecule generation often faces data inefficiency, necessitating vast training datasets or extensive sampling to achieve objective optimization. This limitation is especially problematic when pairing deep generative models with the computationally intensive scoring functions (oracles) prevalent in computer-aided drug design. Consequently, recent research has prioritized enhancing sample efficiency or establishing benchmarks within this domain. This study adapts a recent sample efficiency benchmark to better align with realistic goals, specifically incorporating the quality of generated chemistry, a critical factor in small-molecule drug design. Following this adaptation, we re-evaluate all benchmarked generative models. Our findings indicate that adjusting rankings to account for molecular weight and LogP relative to training data, as well as chemical diversity, significantly alters the model hierarchy. Furthermore, we assessed a recently proposed method for improving sample efficiency, known as Augmented Hill-Climb, which emerged as the top performer when balancing sample efficiency with the chemical properties of generated molecules. These ongoing advancements in both sample efficiency and chemical desirability facilitate the routine integration of computationally expensive scoring functions within a more practical timeframe.

This brief paper outlines a concept for assisting autonomous vehicle drivers in reclaiming control following an extended period of automated driving. The central hypothesis posits that effectively communicating the location and behavior of pertinent environmental objects will enable drivers to rapidly comprehend the situational context, thereby facilitating a safe manual takeover. Building on this premise, the study proposes a research framework detailing the required components and the relevant disciplines involved.

Although pre-training has advanced significantly across various NLP tasks, effective strategies for dense retrieval still require exploration. This paper introduces RetroMAE, a retrieval-focused pre-training framework built upon the Masked Auto-Encoder (MAE) architecture. RetroMAE features three key designs: first, a unique MAE workflow where input sentences are masked differently for both encoder and decoder; the encoder generates a sentence embedding from its masked input, which is then used alongside the decoder's masked input to recover the original sentence via masked language modeling. Second, it employs an asymmetric model structure, utilizing a full-scale BERT-like transformer for the encoder and a single-layer transformer for the decoder. Third, it uses asymmetric masking ratios, applying a moderate range (15–30%) for the encoder and an aggressive range (50–70%) for the decoder. The framework is straightforward to implement and empirically competitive, delivering substantial improvements over state-of-the-art results on diverse dense retrieval benchmarks such as BEIR and MS MARCO. The source code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/staoxiao/RetroMAE to encourage further research.

We provide complete analytic solutions for all master integrals associated with the three-loop banana graph featuring four identical, non-zero masses. These outcomes are notably straightforward, with every integral formulated as a linear combination of iterated integrals of modular forms of uniform weight, corresponding to the same congruence subgroup found in the two-loop equal-mass sunrise graph. Additionally, we demonstrate how to express these results using elliptic polylogarithms evaluated at rational points.

The escalating volume of monitored data within the Industry 4.0 landscape necessitates robust and dependable anomaly detection methods. Digital Twin technologies facilitate realistic simulations of intricate machinery, making them ideal for creating synthetic datasets to support anomaly detection strategies when contrasted with actual sensor readings. This paper introduces novel weakly-supervised anomaly detection frameworks tailored for industrial environments. These frameworks leverage a Digital Twin to construct a training set that mimics normal operational states, supplemented by a limited collection of labeled anomalous measurements from real machinery. Specifically, we propose a clustering-based method named Cluster Centers (CC) and a neural architecture utilizing Siamese Autoencoders (SAE), both optimized for weakly-supervised scenarios with scarce labeled data. The efficacy of these proposed techniques is evaluated against leading state-of-the-art anomaly detection algorithms using a real-world dataset from a facility monitoring system, assessed through numerous performance metrics. Furthermore, the impact of hyper-parameters concerning feature extraction and network architecture is analyzed. Our findings indicate that the SAE-based solutions consistently and robustly outperform existing state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods across a wide range of hyper-parameter configurations on all measured performance indicators.

Deep learning advancements have significantly advanced biomedical image analysis. Given that breast cancer is the leading cause of death among women, early detection remains critical for enhancing survival rates. While medical imaging, such as ultrasound, offers a clear visual depiction of organ function, radiologists often find analyzing these scans time-consuming and difficult, which can delay diagnosis. Despite existing deep learning approaches showing promise, this article presents an efficient Residual Cross-Spatial Attention guided Inception U-Net (RCA-IUnet) model designed for tumor segmentation in breast ultrasound images. This model utilizes minimal training parameters to enhance segmentation accuracy across varying tumor sizes. The RCA-IUnet architecture combines a U-Net topology with residual inception depth-wise separable convolutions and hybrid pooling layers (incorporating both max and spectral pooling). Furthermore, cross-spatial attention filters are integrated to filter out irrelevant features and emphasize target structures. Validated on two public datasets using standard metrics, the proposed model demonstrates superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art segmentation techniques.

The $k$-sample testing problem assesses whether $k$ distinct groups of data originate from identical distributions. While Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) remains the standard for this task, it relies on rigid parametric assumptions that are frequently unsuitable. Since independence testing and $k$-sample testing are closely linked, numerous nonparametric multivariate independence tests—such as Distance Correlation (Dcorr) and the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC)—offer robust theoretical and empirical capabilities. We demonstrate that universally consistent independence tests yield universally consistent $k$-sample testing, revealing that statistics like Energy and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) are mathematically equivalent to Dcorr. Empirical evaluations across $k$-sample scenarios show that these nonparametric approaches generally surpass MANOVA, even when data follows a Gaussian distribution. Furthermore, we extend these nonparametric procedures to handle multiway and multilevel testing, highlighting a wealth of theoretically grounded and high-performing $k$-sample tests. A Python library named hyppo, containing all these independence and $k$-sample tests, can be accessed at https://hyppo.neurodata.io/.

Current planetary evolution models forecast that young giant planets begin with large radii and low densities, gradually contracting over hundreds of millions of years to reach their mature size. To date, these predictions lack empirical validation, largely because detecting and characterizing very young planets is difficult due to the intense activity of their host stars. However, recent findings of young transiting planetary systems now offer preliminary constraints on these evolutionary theories. V1298 Tau, a solar-type star estimated to be only 20 million years old, is among the youngest known hosts of transiting planets and contains a multiple system with two Neptune-sized, one Saturn-sized, and one Jupiter-sized planet. This study presents the results of a radial velocity campaign that identified two periodic signals corresponding to two of these planets. Planet b, orbiting every 24 days, has a mass of 0.64 Jupiter masses and a density comparable to giant planets in our Solar System and older exoplanets. In contrast, Planet e, with a 40-day orbital period, possesses a mass of 1.16 Jupiter masses and a density higher than that of most known giant exoplanets. This finding is surprising for such a young age and implies that some giant planets may contract more rapidly than currently expected, thereby challenging existing evolutionary models.

The potential of high-rate low-density parity check (LDPC) codes to significantly lower the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computing relies on developing efficient, fault-tolerant logical gate implementations. While transversal gates represent the most straightforward fault-tolerant operations, their application to LDPC codes has historically been overlooked. This study examines transversal gates within hypergraph product codes, a specific family of LDPC codes. Our investigation is supported by the development of a symplectic canonical basis for the logical operators of these codes, a finding that holds independent significance. We demonstrate that transversal gates can execute Hadamard operations (modulo logical SWAPs) and control-Z gates across all logical qubits in these codes. Furthermore, we show that interleaving sequences of transversal operations with error correction enables the implementation of entangling gates between any pair of logical qubits within the same code block. Consequently, we establish that transversal gates, when augmented with state injection, can serve as the foundation for universal quantum computation on LDPC codes.

This study details our investigation into the thermodynamics of SU(2) gauge theory. We utilize a Symanzik improved action to significantly minimize discretization errors and apply scaling relations to address finite volume effects near the critical temperature. The beta-function for this specific theory is calculated and subsequently employed to determine various thermodynamic observables. Our findings are then compared with earlier studies that relied exclusively on the standard Wilson action. We confirm that employing an improved action is essential for accurately and efficiently accessing the continuum thermodynamics of the theory.

Assessing the influence of climate change on future air quality remains a complex challenge within air quality research. This study utilizes an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to simulate hourly ozone (O3) levels, trained on hourly data from 2009 to 2012 (June–August) at Tehran, Iran, including temperature, solar radiation, and nitrogen monoxide and dioxide concentrations. Future climate projections, derived from the HadCM3 General Circulation Model under IPCC SRES A1B, A2, and B1 scenarios, are downscaled using the LARS-WG5 model for the periods 2015–2039 and 2040–2064, assuming constant precursor emissions. The analysis evaluates O3 metrics such as the frequency of days exceeding 1-hour (120 ppb) and 8-hour (75 ppb) standards, as well as 8-hour Air Quality Index (AQI) thresholds. Projected increases in solar radiation, decreases in precipitation, and anticipated summer temperature rises of approximately 1.2°C and 3.0°C for the first and second time periods, respectively, suggest more favorable conditions for ozone formation. Based on the 2012 violation-free summer, future exceedance days for the 8-hour O3 standard are expected to rise by roughly 4.2 days in the short term and 12.3 days in the mid-term. Conversely, using the polluted 2010 summer (with 58 exceedance days) as a baseline, projections indicate an increase of about 4.5 days in the short term and 14.1 days in the mid-term. Additionally, the frequency of "Unhealthy" and "Very Unhealthy" days according to the 8-hour AQI is also forecast to increase for both baseline scenarios.

We present examples of rank-one transformations that exhibit weak double ergodicity and rigidity—implying all their Cartesian products are conservative—yet possess a non-ergodic $2$-fold Cartesian product. Additionally, we establish conditions under which rank-one infinite measure-preserving transformations are (weakly) doubly ergodic and ensure their $k$-fold Cartesian products remain conservative. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a (weakly) doubly ergodic nonsingular group action is ergodic with isometric coefficients, proving that this property strictly implies weak measurable sensitivity.

Recently, learned image compression techniques have surpassed traditional hand-crafted approaches like BPG, largely due to learned entropy models that estimate the probability distribution of quantized latent representations. While most recent models rely on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) similar to other vision tasks, CNNs are limited by their local connectivity, which hinders their ability to model long-range dependencies—a critical factor since reducing spatial redundancy is essential for effective image compression. To address this, we introduce the Information Transformer (Informer), a novel entropy model that leverages an attention mechanism to capture both global and local information in a content-dependent manner. Experimental results demonstrate that Informer achieves superior rate-distortion performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on the Kodak and Tecnick datasets, all while avoiding the quadratic computational complexity associated with such approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/naver-ai/informer.

Large-scale network operators face requests from virtual service provider customers who require specific connectivity solutions, such as bandwidth-allocated multicast transitions. While operators aim to profit from delivering these quality-assured services, they also strive to minimize infrastructure investments or avoid them entirely. This study focuses on circuit-switched optical networks addressing repetitive multicast demands where sources and destinations are predetermined. Consequently, operators can pre-allocate corresponding trees and adjust their infrastructure to support these recurring transmissions by configuring available branching routers at specific nodes within the predefined trees. These branching nodes are opto-electronic devices capable of duplicating and retransmitting data in multiple directions; however, they are costlier and more energy-intensive than transparent nodes. The paper addresses the strategic placement of a limited number of branching routers within a multicast tree to minimize the total required bandwidth. After formally defining the problem, we present and prove the optimality of a polynomial-time algorithm. Exhaustive computations demonstrate the operational gains achieved by using this algorithm across various multicast tree construction methods. The work concludes with dimensioning guidelines and an outline of future research directions.

Frequently, we estimate a target parameter, $\psi$, under identifying conditions that include a nuisance parameter, $\theta$. Notable examples from causal inference include Inverse Probability Weighting, Marginal Structural Models, and Structural Nested Models. When deriving treatment effects from observational data, these approaches typically assume a (pooled) logistic regression model for treatment and/or censoring probabilities, estimating these parameters first. All such methods rely on unbiased estimating equations. Initially, we derive a general formula for the variance of $\psi$ when $\theta$ is estimated in a preliminary step, utilizing the Partition Inverse Formula. Subsequently, we present four findings regarding $\hat{\psi}$ estimators based on unbiased equations where the nuisance parameter $\theta$ is estimated via (partial) score equations, provided $\psi$ does not depend on $\theta$. This independence commonly occurs in causal inference when $\theta$ represents treatment probabilities, in missing data contexts where $\theta$ denotes missingness probabilities, and in measurement error scenarios where $\theta$ characterizes the error distribution. 1. Counter-intuitively, the asymptotic variance of $\hat{\psi}$ is usually smaller when $\theta$ is estimated rather than when a known $\theta$ is plugged in. 2. Neglecting the estimation of $\theta$ leads to a conservative sandwich variance estimator for $\hat{\psi}$. 3. A consistent variance estimator for $\hat{\psi}$ can be computed rapidly without resorting to bootstrapping. 4. If $\hat{\psi}$ using the true $\theta$ is efficient, the limiting variance of $\hat{\psi}$ remains unaffected by whether $\theta$ is estimated. To demonstrate these concepts, we apply observational data to estimate: 1. the comparative effect of cazabi versus colistin in patients with resistant bacterial infections, and 2. how the impact of one year of antiretroviral therapy varies based on the timing of initiation in HIV-infected individuals.

A book cover serves as its face and acts as a key attraction for readers, making its design a critical component of the publishing industry. A primary challenge in this field is encapsulating a book's thematic essence within a single image. This research investigates methods for generating book covers using artificial intelligence, grounded in the correlation between a book's summary and its cover art. Our primary motivation is leveraging text-to-image synthesis to create visuals from specific textual descriptions. We examine various existing text-to-image conversion methods and propose a framework to utilize these tools for producing covers based on book summaries. To support this, we have developed a dataset of English books comprising numerous pairs of existing summaries and their corresponding cover images. This paper details our methodology for collecting, organizing, and pre-processing this dataset for model training. Finally, we apply diverse text-to-image synthesis techniques to generate covers from these summaries and present the resulting outputs.

Longitudinal studies yield significant insights, particularly in medicine, but their full utility is hindered by the correlation between repeated measurements from the same subject. While hierarchical models effectively address this correlation for data in Euclidean space by separating intra- and inter-subject variability, medical data often resides on nonlinear manifolds. To address this, geodesic hierarchical models were initially introduced to extend linear assumptions by modeling time-induced changes along generalized straight lines within the manifold. However, this approach frequently fails to capture complex dynamics such as periodic motion or saturation effects. Consequently, we propose a hierarchical framework for manifold-valued data that incorporates higher-order trends using B\'ezier splines. We introduce a functional-based Riemannian metric to rigorously compare these shape trends, which enables efficient and straightforward computations through variational time discretization that relies solely on solving regression problems. The model's efficacy is demonstrated using longitudinal data from the osteoarthritis initiative, specifically for classifying disease progression.

We introduce DiscoSense, a benchmark designed to evaluate commonsense reasoning through the comprehension of diverse discourse connectives. In creating DiscoSense, we employ Conditional Adversarial Filtering, an enhanced version of Adversarial Filtering that utilizes conditional generation, to produce highly effective distractors. Our findings demonstrate that even state-of-the-art pre-trained language models face significant challenges on this dataset, positioning DiscoSense as an optimal resource for assessing future generations of commonsense reasoning systems.

We examine the emergence of anomalous quantum wavefunction amplitudes within a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice characterized by correlated diagonal disorder. This rogue-wave-like phenomenon arises from a dynamic interplay between localization and mobility. Ultimately, the effective correlation length of the disorder minimizes local disorder strength, thereby driving the occurrence of extreme events with significantly higher amplitudes compared to scenarios involving uncorrelated disorder. These results, applicable to a range of discrete one-dimensional systems, highlight the critical influence of randomness in generating rogue waves.

4D seismic imaging is extensively utilized in CO$_2$ sequestration initiatives to track fluid movement in subsurface volumes inaccessible to well sampling. Ideally, real-time monitoring and near-future forecasting would equip site operators with critical insights into reservoir dynamics and potential risks. However, practical constraints such as high deployment costs, limited equipment availability, and exclusion zones around surface infrastructure result in the acquisition of only sparse seismic data. This limitation creates an expanding knowledge gap over time. Since operators must comprehend fluid flow throughout the project's lifespan yet receive seismic data at only a few discrete intervals, current data availability is inadequate for fully understanding reservoir behavior. To address these challenges, we have developed spatio-temporal neural-network-based models capable of generating high-fidelity interpolated or extrapolated images efficiently. These models utilize an autoencoder architecture enhanced with a long short-term memory (LSTM) structure and a novel loss function regularized by optical flow. We validated our approach using real 4D post-stack seismic data from the Sleipner CO$_2$ sequestration field. Evaluation employed two strategies: numerically comparing our models against baseline methods using standard pixel-based metrics, and conducting a blind survey gathering 20 responses from domain experts to assess generated data quality. Both quantitative and expert evaluations confirm that our models can produce high-quality 2D/3D seismic imaging at a reasonable cost, enabling real-time monitoring and potentially near-future forecasting of CO$_2$ storage reservoirs.

We describe the diffraction-free transmission of space-time wave packets (STWPs)—a category of propagation-invariant pulsed beams—over a distance of approximately 1 km in an outdoor laser range under low-turbulence conditions. Utilizing $\approx\!100$-fs pulses (with a bandwidth of $\sim\!25$ nm) at a wavelength of $\approx\!1$ $\mu$m, we generated two STWPs: one with an initial transverse width of $\approx\!2$ mm that broadened to $\approx\!3$ mm after $\sim\!500$ m, and another expanding from $\approx\!8$ mm to $\approx\!10$ mm after 1 km. We compared the STWP propagation characteristics against Gaussian wave packets sharing the same transverse spatial width and bandwidth. Furthermore, we developed a theoretical framework that identifies the primary factors constraining STWP propagation distances and proposes strategies for extending these limits.

This paper addresses risk-sensitive sequential decision-making within Reinforcement Learning (RL). Our work offers two primary contributions. First, we propose a new, coherent metric called "composite risk," which captures the combined impact of aleatory and epistemic uncertainty throughout the learning phase. Previous research has typically examined these risks separately or merely added them together; however, we demonstrate that the additive approach is simply a specific instance of composite risk when the epistemic risk measure is substituted with an expectation. Consequently, composite risk exhibits greater sensitivity to both forms of uncertainty compared to individual or additive models. Second, we introduce SENTINEL-K, an algorithm leveraging ensemble bootstrapping and distributional RL to separately represent aleatory and epistemic uncertainty. This ensemble of K learners utilizes Follow The Regularised Leader (FTRL) to aggregate return distributions and derive the composite risk. Experimental results confirm that SENTINEL-K not only provides superior estimation of the return distribution but also achieves enhanced risk-sensitive performance relative to state-of-the-art risk-sensitive and distributional RL algorithms when utilizing composite risk estimates.

Identifying user informational needs by analyzing their history is essential for proactive information retrieval systems. To address understanding and relevance, Wikipedia offers the necessary background knowledge for intelligent systems. This study investigates how leveraging Wikipedia concepts within query context can enhance proactive retrieval from noisy text. We developed two models utilizing entity linking to connect Wikipedia topics with the relevance model. Experiments focused on retrieving podcast segments revealed a distinct relevance signal within Wikipedia concepts, showing that incorporating them into a ranking model improves precision. Additionally, we found that applying Wikipedia concepts to the background context of a query aids in disambiguation, thereby further supporting proactive information retrieval.

This study investigates the function of character patterns across three tasks: morphological analysis, lemmatization, and copy. We employ an adapted sequence-to-sequence architecture featuring a pattern-matching encoder. This encoder evaluates every possible substring of length N on the source side, utilizing the score of the highest-ranking subword to both initialize the decoder and feed the attention mechanism. Consequently, the model learns to identify which input subwords are crucial for output generation. By training models on identical source data but with different target languages, we compare the importance of subwords across tasks and their interrelationships. We introduce a similarity metric, a generalized Jaccard similarity, to assign scores to each pair of tasks operating on the same source with varying targets. Finally, we analyze the relationships between these three tasks across 12 languages, and our code is open to the public.

It has been suggested that low-mass primordial stars ($m_{\rm Pop III}\,\leq 0.8\,M_\odot$) could potentially reach the main sequence and survive to the present day within the Galaxy. However, constraints in current numerical methods limit three-dimensional (3D) simulations of disk fragmentation to merely a few thousand years post-protostar formation. To address this, we employed a modified version of the {\sc Gadget}-2 smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) code to model the non-linear collapse of gas clouds with varying initial solid-body rotation rates (defined by parameter $\beta$), utilizing a piecewise polytropic equation of state. These 3D simulations were extended until protostellar objects accreted 50$M_{\odot}$, a duration sufficient to analyze the interaction between protostars and their surrounding gas, as well as to derive the mass function, accretion rates, and long-term survival prospects. Our results indicate that protostars forming in slow-rotating parent clouds can grow massive through accretion in the absence of radiative feedback. Conversely, approximately 10–20% of those born in fast-rotating clouds ($\beta \ge 0.1$) may be ejected from their gravitationally bound clusters, potentially emerging as low-mass stars.

In generalized chiral color models, a non-universal axigluon induces flavor-changing neutral currents (FCNCs) at the tree level. We examine the phenomenological impact of axigluon exchange on new contributions to $B_{q}$ (where $q=d, s$) mixing and the associated CP asymmetries. Our analysis reveals that while $\Delta m_{B_q}$ imposes strict limits on the parameters governing $b\to q$ transitions, the precise measurement of $\sin2\beta_{J/\Psi K^0}$ further restricts the viable parameter space for $b\to d$ transitions. Furthermore, axigluon-mediated effects can amplify the like-sign dimuon charge asymmetry ${\cal A}^{b}_{s\ell}$ by an order of magnitude beyond standard model predictions. Consequently, this leads to large CP asymmetries, specifically $\sin2\beta^{J/\Psi \phi}_s$ and the difference $\sin2\beta_{J\Psi K^0}-\sin2\beta_{\phi K^0}$.

This study investigates a binary classification task utilizing a support vector machine grounded in a variational quantum-circuit model. We introduce a method to resolve the support vector machine's linear equations through $\Gamma$ matrix expansion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any arbitrary quantum state can be generated by optimizing a universal quantum circuit capable of representing an arbitrary $U(2^N)$ operation via the steepest descent algorithm. This approach may serve as a quantum analogue to Field-Programmable-Gate Arrays (FPGAs).

On a bordered surface featuring marked points, we construct a holonomy matrix by multiplying elements from the supergroup $\mathrm{OSp}(1|2)$, thereby establishing a flat $\mathrm{OSp}(1|2)$-connection. We demonstrate that these matrix expressions for arcs correspond to the super $\lambda$-length within Penner-Zeitlin's decorated super Teichm\"uller space, extending the matrix formulations previously developed by Fock-Goncharov and Musiker-Williams. Furthermore, we verify that our matrix formulas are consistent with the combinatorial formulas presented in our earlier publications. As a practical application, we apply this matrix formula to an annulus to derive novel results concerning super Fibonacci numbers.

We introduce a high-contrast imaging survey targeting intermediate-mass stars (1.75--4.5 $M_\odot$) to identify the most extreme stellar binaries, specifically those with the lowest-mass companions. Utilizing adaptive optics at the Lick and Gemini observatories, we monitored 169 stars and identified 24 candidate companions; 16 are new discoveries, and all except three are probable or confirmed physical partners. Although our survey achieved sensitivity down to the substellar limit for 75% of the sample, no companions were found below 0.3 $M_\odot$, strongly indicating that the distribution of stellar companions is cut off at a minimum mass ratio of $q_\mathrm{min} \gtrsim0.075$. When combined with data on known brown dwarf companions, our findings reveal a "low-mass companion desert" for intermediate-mass stars between $0.02\lesssim q \lesssim0.05$, a pattern that quantitatively aligns with the established brown dwarf desert around solar-type stars. We conclude that the formation mechanism for multiple systems functions in a largely scale-invariant way, preventing the creation of extremely unequal systems, likely because proto-binary components accrete the majority of their mass after initial cloud fragmentation. Similarly, the process forming "planetary" companions ($q \lesssim 0.02$) appears to scale linearly with stellar mass, potentially due to the correlation between stellar mass and protoplanetary disk properties. Finally, we predict a significant population of brown dwarf companions around low-mass stars and an increasing number of planetary-mass objects approaching $\approx 1\,M_\mathrm{Jup}$ near solar-type stars, predictions that future instrumentation improvements will be able to test.

In the scaling regime where the parameter beta scales inversely with the system size, the empirical distribution of Gaussian beta ensembles (and correspondingly, beta Laguerre ensembles) is known to converge to the probability measures defined by associated Hermite (and Laguerre) polynomials, respectively, with Gaussian fluctuations around this limit also well-documented. This work investigates a dynamical extension of these findings by examining beta Dyson's Brownian motions and beta Laguerre processes. Specifically, we derive laws of large numbers and central limit theorems for the moment processes within this same regime.

Accurately gauging consumer preferences is critical for the fashion sector, as effectively utilizing this data can significantly boost profitability. However, detecting trends in fashion remains difficult given the industry's rapid evolution, and predicting the visual appeal of new designs is particularly challenging due to a scarcity of historical data. To address this, we introduce MuQAR, a Multimodal Quasi-AutoRegressive deep learning framework composed of two components: (1) a multi-modal multi-layer perceptron that integrates categorical, visual, and textual product features, and (2) a quasi-autoregressive neural network that models the "target" time series of a product's attributes alongside the "exogenous" time series of related attributes. We leverage computer vision, image classification, and captioning techniques to automatically derive visual features and textual descriptions from images of new products. Since fashion design is initially visual, these features capture the product's unique identity without disrupting the designers' creative workflow by demanding extra manual inputs. We use the target attributes' time series as a surrogate for temporal popularity trends to overcome data limitations, while exogenous series help identify trends across interconnected attributes. Through extensive ablation studies on two large-scale fashion datasets, Mallzee and SHIFT15m, we evaluate MuQAR's effectiveness, and we test its generalizability on the Amazon Reviews: Home and Kitchen dataset. Furthermore, comparative analysis on the VISUELLE dataset demonstrates that MuQAR outperforms the current state of the art by 4.65% in WAPE and 4.8% in MAE.

As the demand for high-quality computational solutions increases across various computer-executed tasks, fields like engineering and computer graphics—which rely on meshes to address complex problems—face growing requirements. Hexahedral elements are particularly advantageous for these meshes due to their superior numerical properties; however, the accuracy of the resulting solutions hinges entirely on the quality of the constituent elements. When individual elements deform into shapes that hinder accurate computation, they are deemed invalid. To ensure users obtain precise results, the geometry of these flawed elements must be modified to meet validity criteria. This study integrates findings from two prior papers to create a workflow that scans a mesh, detects invalid elements, and adjusts their shapes accordingly to produce a functional algorithm. While this combination yields a working solution, opportunities for enhancement exist; consequently, several improvements are introduced to accelerate the process and enhance its robustness. Following rigorous testing and comparison against alternative methods, this work presents a novel, efficient, and robust approach to resolving invalid mesh configurations.

This paper presents and investigates the notion of countable strongly annihilated ideals within commutative rings, with a specific focus on rings of continuous functions. We demonstrate that a maximal ideal in $C(X)$ is countable strongly annihilated precisely when it is a real maximal $z^\circ$-ideal. Furthermore, we establish that $X$ is an almost $P$-space if and only if countable strongly annihilated ideals coincide with strongly divisible $z$-ideals, which occurs exactly when every $M_x$ is a countable strongly annihilated ideal for any $x\in X$. Additionally, we note that an almost $P$-space $X$ is Lindelöf if and only if every countable strongly annihilated ideal is fixed. Finally, we provide a negative response to a question posed by Gilmer and McAdam.

Knowledge graphs and other complex, heterogeneous dynamic networks serve as potent tools for modeling data provenance within computer systems. From a security standpoint, these attributed graphs facilitate causality analysis and tracing, enabling the investigation of diverse cyberattacks. Nevertheless, there is a significant shortage of systematic pipelines designed to transform system executions and provenance data into usable graph representations suitable for machine learning. This deficiency in instrumentation obstructs scientific progress in provenance graph machine learning by compromising reproducibility and restricting access to the data essential for techniques such as graph neural networks. To address this gap, we introduce Flurry, an end-to-end data pipeline that simulates cyberattacks, captures provenance information across multiple system and application layers, converts audit logs into data provenance graphs, and integrates this data with a framework for training deep neural models. This framework supports both preconfigured and custom-designed models for analyzing resilience in real-world systems. We demonstrate the pipeline's capabilities by processing data from various system attacks and performing anomaly detection through graph classification using existing benchmark graph representational learning frameworks. Flurry offers a rapid, customizable, extensible, and transparent solution to provide the critical data needed by cybersecurity professionals.

Network function virtualization (NFV) is a pivotal technology for advancing 5G networks, as it enhances hardware utilization flexibility and minimizes base station construction. NFV supports vast service chains tailored to user demands, consisting of sequential network functions implemented as virtual network functions (VNFs) within virtual environments via software and virtual machines. Effectively deploying virtual machines to process these VNFs rapidly upon receiving user requests poses a significant challenge for traditional algorithms on a large scale. In contrast, quantum computing offers superior computational performance due to quantum parallelism. This study constructs an integer linear programming model for the VNF scheduling problem aimed at minimizing delays, which is then converted into a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. We propose a heuristic algorithm that utilizes a quantum annealer to solve this model. Finally, we assess the computational results and investigate the feasibility of applying quantum computing to address VNF scheduling challenges.

It has long been established that the low-energy dynamics of open strings are captured by non-abelian gauge theories, mirroring how Einstein's gravity governs the low-energy effective description of closed strings. In this brief note, we examine and discuss instances where the opposite holds: specific limits of non-abelian gauge theories exhibit effective behaviors described by extended objects such as strings or branes. Our analysis is restricted to a select few examples that share common characteristics.

This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of measured cross-section data for open-strange processes, including $e^+e^- \to K^+K^-$, $e^+e^- \to K\bar{K}^{*}+c.c.$, $e^+e^- \to K^{*+}K^{*-}$, $e^+e^- \to K_1(1270)^+K^-$, $e^+e^- \to K_1(1400)^+K^-$, $e^+e^- \to K_2^{*}(1430)\bar{K}+c.c.$, and $e^+e^- \to K(1460)^+K^-$, within the context of hadron spectroscopy research. We demonstrate that light vector mesons near the 2 GeV energy scale contribute to these cross-sections, offering a novel approach to defining the light vector meson family and elucidating the nature of the $Y(2175)$.

This paper investigates the existence of random fixed points for lower semicontinuous condensing random operators acting on Banach spaces, thereby extending relevant findings found in existing literature.

Prior research indicates that addressing issues identified by static code analyzers early can significantly reduce future costs; however, developers frequently overlook these warnings for two primary reasons. First, many alerts require interpretation to confirm they represent genuine program flaws. Second, static analyzers often fail to present findings in an actionable format. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce Sorald, a new system that utilizes metaprogramming templates to modify program abstract syntax trees and propose fixes for static analysis warnings. Consequently, the developer's role shifts from interpreting and correcting issues to reviewing and approving complete solutions. Sorald currently addresses violations of 10 rules within SonarJava, one of the most prevalent static analyzers for Java. We evaluated Sorald using a dataset comprising 161 popular GitHub repositories. Our analysis demonstrates its effectiveness, successfully fixing 65% (852 out of 1,307) of the violations that met the repair preconditions. Overall, our experiments confirm that it is feasible to automatically resolve significant violations generated by SonarJava, a state-of-the-art static analyzer.

This thesis introduces a two-layer uniform facet elastic object designed for real-time simulation using physics-based modeling. It outlines a procedural algorithm for creating elastic objects via particle systems, progressing from basic one-dimensional forms to intricate two- and three-dimensional structures. The proposed double-layered model comprises inner and outer mass-spring surfaces alongside compressible internal pressure. Unlike single-layer objects, the inner layer can possess a distinct density and move in opposition to the outer layer. These unique capabilities enable a superior simulation of soft body dynamics, such as the non-uniform fluid deformation of tissue, by more closely mirroring the physical structure of real tissues. The system effectively demonstrates inertial behaviors within environments featuring gravity and collisions with walls, ceilings, and floors. Collision detection utilizes an elastic collision penalty method, while object motion is governed by Ordinary Differential Equation calculations. Furthermore, the framework allows users to interact with and deform the modeled objects, observing their real-time responses.

Numerical methods are employed to construct solutions to the Einstein constraint equations on a range of compact, orientable 3D manifolds featuring non-trivial topologies. Specifically, both straightforward constant mean curvature (CMC) solutions and more intricate non-constant mean curvature (non-CMC) solutions are calculated for example manifolds drawn from three of the eight Thurston geometrization classes. Notably, the CMC solutions identified in this study also satisfy the Yamabe problem, which seeks to transform a given geometry into one possessing constant scalar curvature.

We introduce CoMet, a new method designed to calculate group cohesion and leverage this information to enhance robot navigation within dense crowds. This approach employs a unique cohesion metric grounded in social psychology research, derived from analyzing visual cues of pedestrians captured by an RGB-D camera mounted on the robot. These cues include interpersonal proximity, relative walking speeds, group size, and member interactions. Utilizing this metric, we developed a navigation strategy that adapts to varying degrees of group cohesion as the robot traverses a crowd. Perceptual evaluations assessed the precision and recall of our cohesion metric. Furthermore, we demonstrated the algorithm's effectiveness on a Turtlebot, reporting significant improvements across multiple metrics: a 57% reduction in freezing rate, a 35.7% decrease in deviation, and a 23.2% shortening of the trajectory path.

Audio-to-score alignment (A2SA) involves synchronizing audio signals with musical notation. While recent studies highlight the advantages of Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) for frame-level alignment, this research focuses on leveraging AMT deep learning models to achieve note-level alignment. We introduce a method that combines HMM-based score-to-score alignment with AMT, demonstrating significant improvements over current state-of-the-art results. Additionally, we develop a systematic approach to utilize large datasets lacking aligned scores. Finally, we conduct extensive evaluations and comparisons across multiple datasets.

Precise measurement of cerebral blood flow (CBF) is crucial for diagnosing and evaluating various neurological conditions. Although Positron Emission Tomography (PET) using radiolabeled 15O-water is the gold standard for human CBF assessment, its widespread adoption is hindered by high costs and the requirement for onsite cyclotron production of short-lived tracers. In contrast, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers greater accessibility without exposing patients to ionizing radiation. This study introduces a convolutional encoder-decoder network enhanced with attention mechanisms to generate gold-standard 15O-water PET CBF images from multi-sequence MRI data, removing the dependency on radioactive tracers. The model utilizes common MRI sequences, including T1-weighted, T2-FLAIR, and arterial spin labeling. Training and validation were performed using 5-fold cross-validation on a cohort of 126 subjects, comprising both healthy individuals and patients with cerebrovascular diseases, who all underwent simultaneous PET/MRI scans. The findings indicate that the proposed model effectively synthesizes high-quality PET CBF maps, achieving an average SSIM of 0.924 and a PSNR of 38.8 dB, outperforming both concurrent and previous synthesis techniques. Furthermore, the clinical relevance of the algorithm was confirmed by assessing its ability to accurately identify vascular territories with abnormally low CBF. These approaches could facilitate broader and more precise CBF evaluation in larger populations who are unable to undergo PET imaging due to radiation risks, limited access, or logistical barriers.

Identifying user intent and extracting relevant slots from utterances are critical components of natural language understanding. Because these tasks are closely linked, jointly modeling them has become a standard practice in training such systems. However, limited data availability and domain-specific vocabularies present further hurdles. Recently, pre-trained contextualized language models like ELMo and BERT have transformed the landscape by enabling the training of large-scale models through minimal fine-tuning on task-specific datasets. This work builds upon BERT and RoBERTa to introduce a novel architecture. Furthermore, we propose an intent pooling attention mechanism that enhances slot filling by integrating intent distributions, word features, and token representations. Experiments on standard datasets demonstrate that our model surpasses both the existing non-BERT state-of-the-art and several robust BERT-based baselines.

A primary role of the LHC beam loss measurement system is safeguarding equipment from damage resulting from particle impacts that generate secondary showers and dissipate energy within matter. Reliability standards are adjusted based on the severity of potential consequences and the frequency of particle impact events. While enhancing reliability frequently necessitates more intricate systems, increased complexity often compromises availability; consequently, a balance must be struck between these opposing demands. This paper presents a comprehensive review of chosen concepts and solutions for the LHC system, illustrating the methodologies employed across various components, ranging from sensors and signal processing to software implementation, as well as operational and documentation requirements.

We introduce HyperNST, a neural style transfer (NST) approach designed for artistic image stylization, which integrates Hyper-networks with the StyleGAN2 framework. Our primary contribution is a novel technique for inducing style transfer parameterized within a metric space, specifically one pre-trained for style-based visual search (SBVS). We demonstrate for the first time that this space can effectively drive NST, allowing for the application and interpolation of styles derived from an SBVS system. Technically, we present a hyper-network that generates weight updates for a StyleGAN2 model pre-trained on a diverse range of artistic portraits. This method tailors style parameterization on a per-region basis by utilizing a semantic map of facial regions. We show that HyperNST surpasses state-of-the-art methods in content preservation for stylized images while maintaining strong style transfer performance.

Carbon nanotubes have recently become a subject of intense scientific investigation. Mathematically, they can be represented as quantum graphs. In this work, we examine a structure analogous to carbon nanotubes: a different quantum graph created by rolling a square lattice rather than a graphene sheet. This inherent symmetry generates specific characteristics that simplify the analysis of certain movements by establishing convenient pairs of incoming and outgoing states.

We enhance higher-order CR Sobolev inequalities on $S^{2n+1}$ assuming the vanishing of higher-order moments of the volume form. Leveraging this result, we provide a novel and direct proof for the classification of minimizers associated with CR-invariant higher-order Sobolev inequalities. Following a similar approach, we establish nearly sharp Sobolev inequalities for GJMS operators on general CR manifolds and demonstrate the existence of minimizers in $C^{2k}(N)$ for higher-order CR Yamabe-type problems whenever $Y_k(N) < Y_k(\mathbb{H}^n)$.

We will demonstrate that a smooth, quasi-projective variety $X$ possesses a holomorphically convex universal covering $\wt X$ under the conditions that (i) $\pi_1(X)$ is residually nilpotent and (ii) an admissible variation of Hodge structures exists over $X$ with a monodromy representation having a finite kernel; in both scenarios, it is assumed that the associated period mapping is proper.

This work investigates the channel coding problem within the moderate deviations regime, characterized by sub-exponential error probability decay and a rate approaching capacity slower than $O(1/\sqrt{n})$. We refine the moderate deviations findings of Altuğ and Wagner by establishing both lower and upper bounds for the third-order term in the asymptotic expansion of the maximum achievable message set size. This expansion introduces a novel metric termed channel skewness. For the binary symmetric channel and the majority of practically significant $(n, \epsilon)$ pairs—specifically where $n$ ranges from 100 to 500 and $\epsilon$ spans $[10^{-10}, 10^{-1}]]$—our approximation, which accounts for channel skewness, provides superior accuracy compared to other expansions found in existing literature.

The integration of millimeter-wave (mmWave) spectrum into consumer electronics is expected to elevate wireless communication service levels. Characterized by extensive bandwidths and multi-Gbps speeds, mmWaves are ideal for bandwidth-intensive tasks like streaming video to extended reality devices; however, these applications also demand extremely low latency, as low as 1 ms. Pinpointing these minute delays necessitates a detailed analysis of each layer within the network stack. Beginning from the foundation, this study investigates the sources of physical layer (PHY) latency in mmWave Wi-Fi networks. It introduces a novel simulation framework that transforms conventional laboratories into virtual experimental environments, thereby accelerating computations. Using a case study of the IEEE 802.11ad standard, the work demonstrates the framework's capacity to monitor PHY-level packet latency and isolate specific bottlenecks. Notably, it assesses how the number of LDPC decoding iterations influences latency within short transmission sequences.

This study leverages recent advancements in representation learning to design a neural architecture for natural language inference. Our approach mirrors the human cognitive process involved in evaluating two statements for logical consistency. By integrating variants of Long Short Term Memory (LSTM), attention mechanisms, and composable neural networks, the model executes this task. Each component of the architecture corresponds directly to a specific human function utilized during natural language inference. Furthermore, the model is fully differentiable end-to-end, allowing for training via stochastic gradient descent. When evaluated on the Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) dataset, the proposed system outperforms all previously published models in terms of accuracy.

A privacy-preserving Context-Aware Publish-Subscribe System (CA-PSS) allows a broker to align publisher content with subscriber requests based on real-time context, all while safeguarding the confidentiality of subscriptions and notifications. Similarly, a privacy-preserving Ride-Hailing Service (RHS) enables a service provider to match ride requests with drivers in a privacy-conscious manner. In this study, we expose vulnerabilities in a CA-PSS proposed by Nabeel et al. (2013), demonstrating that any system entity, including the broker, can deduce subscribers' confidential information. We also reveal flaws in the privacy-preserving RHS known as lpRide, introduced by Yu et al. (2019), showing that any rider or driver can efficiently reconstruct the secret keys of all other participants and determine any rider's location. These attacks stem from our cryptanalysis of the modified Paillier cryptosystem proposed by Nabeel et al., which serves as a foundational component for both protocols.

We provide a concise overview of leptogenesis, examining both the unflavoured and flavoured variants of the $N_2$-dominated scenario, alongside an analysis of their respective success rates. After discussing these findings and potential corrections to this basic framework, we concentrate on the flavoured case to establish the prerequisites for strong thermal leptogenesis, wherein the resulting asymmetry remains independent of initial conditions. Assuming no significant cancellations occur within the seesaw mechanism or flavoured decay parameters, we demonstrate that strong thermal leptogenesis implies a lightest neutrino mass of $m_1\gtrsim10\,\mbox{meV}$ for normal ordering and $m_1\gtrsim 3\,\mbox{meV}$ for inverted ordering. Lastly, we briefly address the utility of absolute neutrino mass scale experiments in either validating or constraining strong thermal leptogenesis.

Equation-of-state (EOS) models form the foundation of numerical simulations essential to high energy density physics, inertial confinement fusion, laboratory astrophysics, and related fields. These applications demand EOS models capable of spanning thermodynamic variable ranges far beyond those supported by available data, making uncertainty quantification (UQ) a critical issue. A primary challenge in EOS UQ is model uncertainty, which stems from the assumed functional form; this is often overlooked in favor of parameteric and data uncertainties that are simpler to quantify without breaching physical constraints. This study introduces a novel statistical EOS framework that inherently accounts for model uncertainty while strictly adhering to thermodynamic consistency. Applied to existing $B_4C$ data, the model establishes an upper limit on EOS and Hugoniot uncertainties, demonstrating that ignoring thermodynamic constraints leads to overestimation of uncertainty when data exist and underestimation when extrapolating to data-sparse regions. Furthermore, we explore potential extensions of this methodology and the utility of Gaussian Process-based models in accelerating simulations and experiments, facilitating portable uncertainty-aware EOS tables and supporting downstream tasks that incorporate uncertainty awareness.

This study addresses the challenge of establishing safety constraints and creating Run Time Assurance (RTA) mechanisms for Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) tactical autopilots equipped with neural network control systems (NNCS). Focusing on a specific scenario where an NNCS executes autonomous formation flight with RTA providing collision avoidance and geofencing guarantees, the research first employs Systems Theoretic Accident Models and Processes (STAMP). This initial phase identifies hazards, potential accidents, and safety constraints while constructing a functional block diagram for the ground station, manned flight lead, and surrogate unmanned wingman. Subsequently, Systems Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) is utilized to examine interactions among the ground station, flight lead, wingman, and the wingman's internal components, thereby pinpointing unsafe control actions, their causal scenarios, and the necessary safety requirements to mitigate risks. This work represents the inaugural application of both STAMP and STPA to a neural network control system bounded by RTA.

This study addresses a critical issue in machine learning: performance deterioration when models encounter out-of-distribution (OOD) test data. This challenge is especially prominent in medical imaging diagnostics, where systems often perform well initially but fail when applied to new hospitals or datasets. Recent research suggests that such failures occur because models learn shortcut and non-relevant features rather than generalizable ones. We propose that adversarial training can remove shortcut features, while saliency-guided training can eliminate non-relevant features; both types constitute nuisance features responsible for OOD performance drops. Based on this, we develop a novel training framework for deep neural networks designed to learn robust, generalizable features for classification and detection, ensuring consistent performance on OOD data. Experimental results, both qualitative and quantitative, using benchmark chest X-ray image datasets for classification tasks demonstrate the superior efficacy of our proposed method.

This paper establishes the monotonicity of Steklov eigenvalues on graphs, a result that extends He-Hua's findings in *Calc. Var. Partial Differential Equations* 61 (2022) to higher-order Steklov eigenvalues within the special case of trees. Furthermore, it provides positive resolutions to two specific questions raised by He-Hua in *arXiv: 2103.07696*. Leveraging this monotonicity, the study derives new estimates for Steklov eigenvalues on trees, thereby generalizing the isodiametric estimate for the first positive Steklov eigenvalues previously presented by He-Hua in *arXiv:2011.11014*.

The time evolution of an infinite two-dimensional quantum many-body lattice system can be modeled using the Suzuki-Trotter decomposition applied to infinite projected entangled pair states (iPEPS). Every Trotter step expands the bond dimension ($D$) of the tensor network, necessitating truncation via an error-minimizing method. This study moves past simplified metrics employed by full update (FU), simple update (SU), and neighborhood tensor update (NTU) schemes, instead directly maximizing the overlap between the exact iPEPS with an elevated bond dimension and the newly truncated iPEPS. This optimization occurs within the tangent space of the iPEPS variational manifold. The resulting gradient tensor update (GTU) is evaluated through simulations of a sudden transverse field quench in the 2D quantum Ising model and the associated quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism.

This work investigates the asymptotic stability of traveling wave solutions within nonlinear dispersive equations resembling Burgers' equation. While the primary focus is the Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, the findings apply more broadly. By utilizing modulation of the translation parameter alongside energy estimates, we derive a stability condition requiring the associated one-dimensional Schrödinger equation to possess precisely one negative eigenvalue, allowing a rank-one perturbation to render the operator positive semi-definite. We determine a sufficient condition for stability by counting the bound states of this Schrödinger equation, expressing it through Bargmann's integral; this integral represents the distance between the monotonicized front and its corresponding ideal shock. For the KdVB equation, we analytically confirm that the stability criterion is satisfied across an open interval of the relative dispersion parameter that encompasses all monotone fronts, with numerical experiments indicating stability extends over a wider range.

Machine learning models are widely applied to numerous real-world issues, making it crucial to ensure their behavioral correctness. Identifying effective test cases capable of exposing potential failures in these trained systems is essential for retraining them to improve accuracy. However, because failures in well-trained models are infrequent, locating these rare scenarios through exhaustive evaluation or randomized search is often prohibitively expensive and sometimes infeasible due to vast search spaces, constrained computational resources, and time limitations. This paper addresses the challenge of discovering such failure scenarios more efficiently than traditional randomized methods. Our core strategy involves partitioning the input data space into regions of high and low failure probability, utilizing insights derived from training data, real-world statistics, and domain expert knowledge. Leveraging this information, we developed a generative model designed to produce scenarios with a high probability of triggering failures. Experiments conducted in two distinct settings demonstrated that this approach accelerates failure discovery by a factor of one thousand compared to traditional randomized search.

We have derived the full set of conditions that the forward $2\to2$ scattering amplitude must satisfy within unitary and causal frameworks. These conditions rely on an infinite collection of energy-dependent parameters, termed "arcs," which are represented through dispersion relations as moments of a positive measure defined at arbitrarily high energies. We have pinpointed optimal finite subsets of these constraints that are effective for bounding Effective Field Theories (EFTs) at any specific order in the energy expansion. At tree level, these arcs correspond directly to Wilson coefficients. We have determined the criteria under which this approximation holds, highlighting apparently viable EFTs where it fails entirely. Furthermore, we examine the validity ranges regarding both couplings and energy for all scenarios. Our findings are also extended to cases involving small but finite $t$. A key outcome of this analysis is that EFTs exhibiting energy growth in the scattering amplitude faster than $E^6$ in certain regimes are incapable of UV completion.

This study establishes the viability of utilizing extensive integral field spectroscopic surveys to assess the frequency of galactic-scale outflows within the nearby Universe. By analyzing integral field data from the SAMI and Wide Field Spectrograph, we examine the characteristics of the isolated disk galaxy SDSS J090005.05+000446.7 (z = 0.05386). The integral field datasets reveal skewed line profiles that vary across the galaxy, resulting from the superposition of distinct kinematic components along the line of sight. Through spectral decomposition, we disentangle these profiles into three spatial pixel-specific components: a narrow component aligned with HII regions, a broad component indicative of shock excitation, and an intermediate component reflecting a mix of shock excitation and photoionization. These three kinematic components exhibit unique velocity fields, velocity dispersions, line ratios, and electron densities. By modeling these properties using MAPPINGS IV shock and photoionization simulations, we achieve a striking correspondence between the observational data and theoretical models. Our analysis confirms that the observed variations in emission line characteristics stem from significant galactic outflows that introduce shock excitation alongside photoionization from star formation. Specifically, interstellar shocks within these outflows shock-excite and compress the gas, accounting for the elevated line ratios, velocity dispersions, and electron densities seen in the broad component. Based on energy constraints and the absence of a powerful active galactic nucleus, we conclude that the outflows are likely driven by starburst activity. Furthermore, our findings provide a benchmark for the analytical capabilities of the SAMI Galaxy Survey when applied to large populations of galaxies.

This study examines how the COVID-19 pandemic influenced financial markets, specifically analyzing the evolution of market efficiency through two metrics: the Hurst exponent and the memory parameter of fractional Lévy-stable motion. The latter methodology integrates an alpha-stable distribution with a dependence structure for price returns within a single dynamic framework. We develop a dynamic estimation technique for these efficiency indicators that incorporates a free discount factor, optimized to produce the most accurate alpha-stable density forecasts for observed price returns. When applied to stock indices during the pandemic, the results indicate a significant decline in efficiency for US markets. Conversely, Asian and Australian indices appear less impacted, with their inefficiency during the crisis being doubtful.

Blockchain front-running occurs when unauthorized agents attempt to claim payments from a contract, a problem exacerbated by the blockchain's public transparency and network congestion. This paper draws a parallel between such payment disputes and classic ownership conflicts, akin to King Solomon's dilemma. We introduce a simultaneous reporting mechanism that resolves this dilemma using only ordinal preference data while simultaneously eliminating front-running. In both scenarios, the mechanism operates by threatening to strip ownership from all claimants and by leveraging the legitimate claimant's preference against allocations to other agents.

We introduce neutrino-transport hydrodynamic simulations of electron-capture supernovae (ECSNe) conducted in \texttt{FLASH} utilizing novel two-dimensional (2D) collapsing progenitor models. These models incorporate 2D simulations of oxygen-flame propagation up to the point of core collapse. Using six axisymmetric progenitor models with varying flame front radii at the moment of collapse, alongside a comparative simulation employing the canonical spherical n8.8 model, we observed that differences inherited from stellar evolution and flame propagation do not substantially impact the global characteristics of the neutrino-driven ECSN explosion. Specifically, the explosion energy remains consistent ($\sim1.36$-$1.48\times10^{50}$ erg), as do the mass and composition of the ejecta ($\sim0.017$-$0.018M_\odot$). However, aspherical perturbations caused by the 2D flame introduce a minor fraction ($\lesssim1.8\times10^{-3}~M_\odot$) of low-$Y_e$ ($0.35<Y_e<0.4$) material into the ejecta. At approximately 400 ms, the baryonic mass of the protoneutron star is found to be $\sim1.34~M_\odot$ for the new models and $\sim1.357~M_\odot$ for the n8.8 model; this slight discrepancy arises from updated weak-interaction rates in the evolutionary simulations. These findings highlight the nature of ECSN progenitors with strongly degenerate ONeMg cores and support the idea of a standardized explosion triggered by ONeMg core collapse. Additionally, a preliminary three-dimensional simulation yielded explosion properties compatible with the 2D results. While this study enhances our understanding of post-ONeMg core collapse ECSN explosions, further 3D simulations remain necessary.

The widespread integration of Internet-of-Things (IoT) applications has given rise to Fog computing, a paradigm that effectively leverages both mobile-edge and cloud resources. However, scheduling tasks in these environments remains difficult due to limited resources, IoT mobility, resource heterogeneity, network hierarchy, and stochastic behaviors. Existing heuristic and Reinforcement Learning methods often lack generalizability and rapid adaptability, failing to address these challenges optimally; furthermore, they cannot exploit temporal workload patterns and are restricted to centralized configurations. In contrast, Asynchronous-Advantage-Actor-Critic (A3C) learning offers quick adaptation to dynamic scenarios with minimal data, while the Residual Recurrent Neural Network (R2N2) enables fast model parameter updates. Consequently, we propose an A3C-based real-time scheduler for stochastic Edge-Cloud environments that supports decentralized learning across multiple agents simultaneously. By employing the R2N2 architecture, the model captures extensive host and task parameters alongside temporal patterns to facilitate efficient scheduling decisions. This adaptive system dynamically adjusts hyper-parameters according to specific application needs, a selection process validated through sensitivity analysis. Experimental results using real-world datasets demonstrate significant performance gains compared to state-of-the-art algorithms, achieving reductions of 14.4% in energy consumption, 7.74% in response time, 31.9% in Service-Level-Agreement violations, and 4.64% in running costs.

Cognitive processes in both human and non-human primates depend on the dynamic interaction of distributed neural networks, suggesting that cognition cannot be sustained by macroscopic brain dynamics operating near thermodynamic equilibrium. We validated this hypothesis by analyzing electrocorticography data from non-human primates in various unconscious states (sleep, and anesthesia induced by propofol, ketamine, or a combination of ketamine and medetomidine) alongside functional MRI data from humans during deep sleep and propofol anesthesia. Consistently, all reduced consciousness states exhibited dynamics closer to equilibrium than conscious wakefulness, evidenced by measures of entropy production and the curl of probability flux within phase space. These findings identify non-equilibrium macroscopic brain dynamics as a reliable indicator of consciousness, paving the way for the study of cognition and awareness using statistical mechanics methodologies.

As robotic systems grow more complex and non-expert users become more common, it is reasonable to assume that task constraints are not explicitly defined. This paper introduces a method tailored for non-experts, enabling systems to infer constraints from demonstrations to optimize autonomous controllers and avoid singularities without explicit knowledge of those constraints. By maximizing learned manipulability throughout the motion of a constrained system, the approach prevents unpredictable behavior and is applicable beyond kinematic systems. Comparative analyses with other control policies demonstrate that using demonstration-based constrained manipulability successfully avoids singularities in scenarios where alternative policies fail. Furthermore, when explicit manipulability under task constraints is unavailable, the method can infer these constraints with high accuracy, achieving errors below 10^-5 in 3DOF simulations and under 10^-2 in 7DOF real-world robotic applications.

Supervised learning forms the backbone of numerous remote sensing tasks, yet these approaches, particularly modern deep learning models, typically demand vast quantities of labeled data for training. Although satellites generate extensive datasets, the annotation process remains labor-intensive, costly, and necessitates specialized expertise. Consequently, there is a critical need for enhanced methods that function effectively with fewer labeled samples. We introduce MSMatch, the inaugural semi-supervised learning technique that rivals supervised methods in scene classification across the EuroSAT and UC Merced Land Use benchmark datasets. Our evaluation encompasses both RGB and multispectral EuroSAT imagery, supported by extensive ablation studies to pinpoint the model's essential components. The resulting neural network achieves state-of-the-art performance on EuroSAT, delivering accuracy improvements of up to 19.76% over prior methods contingent on the volume of labeled training data. Specifically, utilizing only five labeled examples per class, we attain 94.53% and 95.86% accuracy on the RGB and multispectral EuroSAT datasets, respectively. Furthermore, on the UC Merced Land Use dataset, our approach surpasses previous works by up to 5.59%, achieving 90.71% accuracy with five labeled examples. These findings demonstrate that MSMatch significantly lowers the barrier for labeled data requirements, proving highly effective with multispectral inputs and enabling applications previously hindered by data scarcity. To facilitate easy replication and rapid integration, we have made the MSMatch source code publicly available online.

We compute radiative corrections for the decay rates of the CP-odd Higgs boson $A$ across the four two-Higgs-doublet model types characterized by a softly broken discrete $Z_{2}$ symmetry. These decay branching ratios are evaluated at next-to-leading order for electroweak corrections and next-to-next-to-leading order for QCD corrections. Our study comprehensively examines how electroweak corrections influence both decay rates and branching ratios. We observe that radiative corrections significantly alter branching ratios, particularly for the $A\to Zh$ channel in the nearly alignment limit, where the couplings of the SM-like Higgs boson $h$ closely resemble those of the Standard Model. Furthermore, we present correlations between the branching ratios of $A$ and the scaling factor of the SM-like Higgs coupling, incorporating higher-order effects. Additionally, we identify distinct predictions for decay patterns based on specific Yukawa interaction types, offering a method to discriminate between these interaction types in future collider experiments.

Chirality and chiral molecules are fundamental components of contemporary chemical and biochemical sectors. The precise manipulation and subsequent separation of chiral enantiomers have long represented a challenging objective in molecular physics and chemistry, prompting the development of numerous methods over time. In this study, we theoretically show that a pair of cross-polarized terahertz (THz) pulses interacting with chiral molecules via their permanent dipole moments can induce enantioselective orientation. This orientation remains stable for extended periods, lasting orders of magnitude longer than the THz pulse duration, and we examine its dependence on temperature and pulse parameters. Such persistent orientation could improve molecular deflection in inhomogeneous electromagnetic fields, potentially enabling practical separation techniques.

This paper primarily addresses the numerical resolution of high-dimensional stochastic optimal control problems governed by fully-coupled forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) using deep learning techniques. We initially reformulate the problem as a stochastic Stackelberg differential game (a leader-follower scenario) and subsequently develop a cross-optimization (CO) method. This approach alternately optimizes the leader's and follower's cost functionals through deep neural networks. Regarding numerical validation, we apply the method to two investment-consumption examples based on stochastic recursive utility models; the outcomes from both cases confirm the efficacy of our proposed algorithm.

This study introduces the first method for automatically constructing resources dedicated to academic writing. The objective is to develop a writing assistance system capable of automatically editing texts to align more closely with academic stylistic norms. Building upon established academic datasets, such as the COCA Academic Word List, the New Academic Word List, and the Academic Collocation List, we further investigate techniques to dynamically create resources that can automatically detect informal or non-academic vocabulary and phrases. These resources are generated using flexible, domain-agnostic approaches that allow for extension across various domains and languages. We detail the evaluation of these resources within a system implementation featuring three components: informal word identification (IWI), generation of academic candidate paraphrases, and ranking of those paraphrases. To generate and rank candidates within their specific contexts, we utilized the PPDB and WordNet paraphrase databases, while the Concepts in Context (CoInCO) "All-Words" lexical substitution dataset served as the basis for both IWI and paraphrase generation experiments. Our IWI component achieved an F-1 score of 82%, a result that significantly surpasses a stratified classifier baseline. The primary contribution of this work is a domain-independent methodology for creating targeted resources designed to support writing aids.

The Dirac-Einstein framework for quark-leptons interacting with gravity is extended into a spacetime featuring chiral and dark discrete extra dimensions. Within this structure, Einstein gravity, Standard Model gauge vectors, Higgs fields, and a dark photon (massive due to a dark Higgs scalar) are unified as components of the generalized vielbein. Derived from an extended Einstein-Hilbert action, the Standard Model must meet specific conditions that successfully predict the Weinberg angle, Higgs mass, and top quark mass, aligning closely with experimental data. Because the Dirac operator, augmented by discrete derivatives, yields a non-diagonal mass matrix, it induces mixing between each quark-lepton and its Kaluza-Klein partner. This small mixing angle assigns a Stueckelberg mass to these Kaluza-Klein partners in the hundreds of TeV range, while simultaneously implying weak interactions between them and the Standard Model's gauge fields. Consequently, these Kaluza-Klein modes are viable candidates for dark matter.

We present the higher topological complexity (TC_{n}) of a fibration through two distinct approaches: the higher homotopic distance and the Schwarz genus. Subsequently, we establish several results connecting this concept to TC, TC_{n}, or the category of a topological space or fibration. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the TC_{n} of a fibration remains invariant under fiber homotopy equivalence.

We investigate the Constraint Satisfaction Problem CSP(A), where A is a structure containing addition that is first-order definable in the integers under addition and one. We demonstrate that such problems are either solvable in polynomial time or are NP-complete.

Quantum sensors are currently driving advancements in metrological sensitivity.
