Nevertheless, when measuring arbitrary signals with high precision, constraints in linear dynamic range can cause distortions during the detection of frequency, magnitude, and phase in unknown signals. This study addresses these issues by employing an advanced sensing protocol that integrates quantum phase-sensitive detection with heterodyne readout. Through both theoretical analysis and experimental validation using nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, we demonstrate the capability to detect radio signals with a 98 dB linear dynamic range, a sensitivity of 31 pT/Hz$^{1/2}$, and resolution across arbitrary frequencies. Additionally, we successfully achieved distortion-free, high-fidelity sensing of audio signals, including melodies and speech, with quantum assistance. These developed methods have the potential to expand the scope of quantum sensors for telecommunication applications, which demand high-fidelity, low-distortion performance across multiple frequency bands within compact sensing volumes.

In recent years, there has been a growing need for ransomware defense mechanisms capable of rapidly identifying and categorizing various ransomware types to enable swift response strategies. Although deep learning has demonstrated its value in automating and enabling self-learning across many fields, the scarcity of ransomware and malware samples remains a significant obstacle to developing effective deep learning solutions. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a Siamese Neural Network grounded in few-shot meta-learning, which not only detects ransomware attacks but also classifies them into specific categories. Our model leverages entropy features extracted directly from ransomware binaries to preserve fine-grained details linked to distinct ransomware signatures. These entropy features are subsequently used to train and optimize the model via a pre-trained network (such as VGG-16) within a meta-learning framework. This methodology yields more accurate weight factors than traditional feature image approaches, thereby mitigating the bias often introduced by models trained on limited datasets. Experimental results indicate that our proposed model is highly effective, achieving a weighted F1-score that surpasses 86%.

This paper presents the introduction of homogeneous mixed Herz-Morrey spaces, denoted as $M\dot{K}_{p,\vec{q}}^{\alpha,\lambda}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and examines several of their characteristics. Specifically, we investigate the boundedness of sublinear and fractional-type operators within these spaces. Notably, these findings extend to both Calderón-Zygmund operators and fractional maximal operators. Furthermore, we establish the boundedness of the commutators associated with these operators in the context of homogeneous mixed Herz-Morrey spaces.

Identity-Based signature schemes are increasingly popular, with numerous proposals emerging over the past decade. While libraries such as the Java-based JPBC and the Python-based charm-crypto offer implementations of identity-based cryptosystems, they do not cover all widely used schemes; specifically, JPBC supports only one such signature scheme, whereas charm-crypto supports three. Additionally, these libraries restrict implementations to a single pairing curve. In pairing-based cryptography, both signature size and performance (signing and verification speed) are dependent on the selected curve. Different applications prioritize either minimizing signature size or maximizing performance. This work outlines popular signature schemes and their implementation via JPBC, analyzes how varying pairing curves impact signature size and performance, and introduces two novel methods to reduce signature size that are not available in the default library configurations.

By applying a remainder theorem for field valuations, we offer a novel perspective on the norm function of global fields. We introduce the Euler totient function for such fields and restore its fundamental analytical characteristics, specifically the product formula. Furthermore, we establish the holomorphic nature of the corresponding zeta function. As an application, we derive an analogue of the Erdős, Dressler, and Bateman mean value theorem utilizing the Wiener-Ikehara theorem.

This study investigates the decays $B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ and $B^0_s \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ utilizing proton-proton collision data with an integrated luminosity of 3 fb$^{-1}$. An untagged, time-integrated amplitude analysis is conducted for $B^0_{(s)} \to (K^+\pi^-)(K^-\pi^+)$ decays within two-body invariant mass windows of 150 MeV$/c^2$ centered on the $K^{*0}$ mass. The analysis reveals a significantly higher longitudinal polarization fraction in the ${B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}}$ channel ($f_L = 0.724 \pm 0.051 \,({\rm stat}) \pm 0.016 \,({\rm syst})$) compared to the ${B^0_s\to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}}$ channel ($f_L = 0.240 \pm 0.031 \,({\rm stat}) \pm 0.025 \,({\rm syst})$). Furthermore, the ratio of branching fractions for these two decays is measured, yielding a branching fraction for ${B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}}$ of $(8.0 \pm 0.9 \,({\rm stat}) \pm 0.4 \,({\rm syst})) \times 10^{-7}$.

State estimation for legged robots navigating dynamic rigid surfaces (DRS)—defined as rigid environments moving within the world frame, such as ships, aircraft, and trains—remains a largely unexplored challenge. This study presents an invariant extended Kalman filter designed to estimate a robot's pose and velocity during DRS locomotion using standard legged robot sensors, including inertial measurement units (IMU), joint encoders, and RGB-D cameras. A primary advantage of this filter is its explicit handling of nonstationary surface-foot contact points and hybrid robot dynamics. Additionally, when IMU biases are absent, the filter meets attractive group affine and invariant observation conditions, ensuring provable convergence during deterministic continuous phases. Observability analysis was conducted to assess how DRS motion impacts state observability, while the convergence properties of the hybrid, deterministic filter system were evaluated for observable variables. Experiments featuring a Digit humanoid robot walking on a pitching treadmill confirm the filter's effectiveness under significant estimation errors and moderate DRS movement. The experimental video is available at: https://youtu.be/ScQIBFUSKzo.

This paper addresses the challenge of Conditional Human Motion Animation (cHMA). The objective involves taking a source image and a driving video to generate a new sequence of frames where the subject from the image mimics the pose transitions found in the video. Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have achieved significant success in image and video synthesis, cHMA remains difficult due to the complexity of effectively leveraging conditional guidance, such as images or poses, while maintaining high visual fidelity. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework called Quantize, Scrabble, and Craft (QS-Craft) for conditional human motion animation. Our approach introduces three distinct stages: quantize, scrabble, and craft. Notably, the QS-Craft model integrates transformer-based attention mechanisms to enhance its structure. In this setup, the driving information is encoded as a sequence of pose coordinates extracted from the video. Comprehensive experiments conducted on human motion datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

This study analyzes near-infrared spectroscopic data from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) for 45 white dwarf-main sequence (WDMS) binaries, previously identified as confirmed or candidates by optical SDSS and LAMOST surveys. Within this group, three systems are reclassified as having red giant primaries based on LAMOST data, and fourteen are identified as young stellar object contaminants in the SDSS sample. For the remaining 28 systems confirmed to have main sequence primaries, we derive orbital periods and velocity amplitude limits for fourteen of them. Seven of these systems exhibit significant velocity variations, qualifying them as post-common-envelope (PCE) binaries; four are newly classified, three are newly confirmed, and five allow for the derivation of complete orbital parameters. If verified, the newly discovered system 2M14544500+4626456 would possess the second-longest orbital period for a typical compact PCE WDMS binary ($P=15.1$ days). Beyond these seven, we also characterize the well-known PCE WDMS systems EG UMa and HZ 9 using APOGEE data. Furthermore, we examine the metallicity distribution of the WDMS sample, a parameter space rarely explored for such systems. Notably, we identify one system, 2M14244053+4929580, as extremely metal-poor (${\rm [Fe/H]}=-1.42$) compared to the rest of the near-solar sample. Additionally, our results suggest that PCE systems in this sample are, on average, more metal-rich than their wide-binary counterparts, though we caution that this small sample size may not fully represent the overall distribution of WDMS systems.

Simulating the two-way coupled interaction between a rarefied gas and colloidal particles of arbitrary shape holds significant practical value for fields such as aerospace engineering, lung drug delivery, and semiconductor manufacturing. Using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) numerical simulations, we examined how particle orientation and rarefaction levels affect drag and lift coefficients for prolate and oblate ellipsoids within a uniform ambient flow. This investigation utilized a cut-cell algorithm integrated into our DSMC solver, where the particle surface was defined analytically and microscopic gas-solid interactions were calculated precisely via a ray-tracing technique. The resulting drag and lift coefficients were employed to extend existing continuum-regime correlations into the rarefied regime, specifically targeting the transitional and free-molecular regimes. We adopted functional forms for these ellipsoidal correlations by generalizing them from spherical cases. Our results demonstrate that the derived fits can predict values outside the simulated range of the Knudsen number ($Kn$) by validating the model against $Kn$ values excluded from the fitting process, thereby achieving higher precision than current predictive models found in the literature. Ultimately, this study highlights the importance of providing new correlations for non-spherical particles, which can enhance point-particle Euler-Lagrangian simulations to address contamination issues caused by finite-size particles in advanced mechanical systems.

This study evaluates three privacy-preserving distributed learning methods: federated learning, split learning, and SplitFed, applying them to build binary classification models for tuberculosis detection via chest X-rays. The comparison focuses on classification accuracy, communication and computational overhead, and training duration. We introduce SplitFedv3, a new distributed learning architecture that outperforms both split learning and SplitFedv2 in our experiments. Additionally, we propose an alternative mini-batch training approach for split learning, which yields superior results compared to the alternate client training method where clients sequentially train the model.

This paper introduces RAPID, a joint communication and radar (JCR) system designed for next-generation IEEE 802.11ay WiFi networks in the 60 GHz band. Unlike most existing human sensing methods at millimeter-wave frequencies that rely on dedicated radars to detect the micro-Doppler effects of human movement, RAPID attains radar-grade sensing precision by adapting standard IEEE 802.11ay access points. It utilizes the IEEE 802.11ay beam training protocol to precisely localize and track multiple individuals, while extracting micro-Doppler signatures from the time-varying phase of the channel impulse response (CIR) using in-packet beam tracking fields. This approach facilitates activity recognition and person identification via IEEE 802.11ay networks without altering the standard's packet structure. RAPID was implemented on an IEEE 802.11ay-compatible FPGA platform equipped with phased antenna arrays, estimating the CIR from transmitted packet reflections. Evaluated on a large dataset of CIR measurements, the system demonstrates robustness across various environments and subjects, outperforming current state-of-the-art sub-6 GHz WiFi sensing methods. When using two access points, RAPID reliably tracks multiple subjects, achieving activity recognition and person identification accuracies of 94% and 90%, respectively.

We demonstrate that integrating $2$-sequences, whose generating functions are rational, yields $3$-sequences through the framing of these sequences. This result is achieved by extending Wolstenholme's Theorem.

In practical scenarios, it is essential for end-to-end spoken language translation models to function effectively on continuous audio streams without depending on manually provided segmentation. For online translation tasks, where translation must begin before an utterance is fully spoken, most prior research has overlooked segmentation issues. This paper evaluates various approaches to enhance model resilience against segmentation errors and compares different segmentation strategies in both offline and online contexts, reporting outcomes regarding translation quality, flicker, and latency. Results across five language pairs indicate that a simple fixed-window audio segmentation strategy can yield surprisingly strong performance under appropriate conditions.

Robots must navigate complex perceptual environments characterized by shifting viewpoints, lighting conditions, and backgrounds. Existing simulated reinforcement learning (RL) benchmarks, such as DM Control, often lack this complexity by providing visual input without such distractions, thereby hindering the transfer of high-performing methods to real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a new challenging benchmark for vision-based control by augmenting DM Control with three specific types of visual distractions: variations in background, color, and camera pose. We evaluate state-of-the-art RL algorithms within these modified settings. Our experiments reveal that current vision-based RL methods struggle significantly under distraction, with performance degrading as distraction complexity increases, indicating a critical need for new approaches to handle real-world visual intricacies. Furthermore, our findings suggest that combining multiple distraction types creates difficulties that exceed the sum of their individual impacts.

We introduce a robust learning algorithm designed to detect and resolve collisions in 3D deforming meshes. The proposed collision detector utilizes a bilevel deep autoencoder enhanced with an attention mechanism to pinpoint colliding mesh sub-parts. A numerical optimization algorithm, guided by the network, is employed to resolve penetrations. Our learned handler successfully manages collisions in unseen, high-dimensional meshes containing thousands of vertices. To ensure stable network performance across these large and novel spaces, we progressively introduce new collision data derived from inference errors. These data are automatically labeled using an analytical collision detector, enabling the progressive fine-tuning of the detection networks. We evaluated our method on complex 3D meshes from various datasets featuring different shapes and topologies, including dressed and undressed human poses, cloth simulations, and multiview-captured human hand poses. Our approach surpasses supervised learning methods, achieving $93.8-98.1\%$ accuracy relative to ground truth determined by analytical methods. Furthermore, compared to previous learning-based methods, our approach reduces the false negative rate in collision detection by $5.16\%-25.50\%$ and increases the success rate in collision handling by $9.65\%-58.91\%$.

This study computes the convex hulls formed by face-vertex incident vectors in 3-face-colorable convex polytopes. The results indicate that each such hull is a $d$-polytope containing either $d+2$ or $d+3$ vertices. By employing the Gale transform and Gale diagrams, we determine the combinatorial structure of these hulls. Furthermore, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for determining when two such convex hulls are combinatorially equivalent.

This study proves the global existence of smooth solutions for the two-dimensional (2D) compressible, isentropic, irrotational Euler equations governing Chaplygin gases, utilizing short pulse initial data originally proposed by Christodoulou. This work addresses Majda's conjecture regarding the absence of shock wave formation from smooth initial data in multi-dimensional nonlinear symmetric systems that are entirely linearly degenerate. Our analytical approach relies on two key components: demonstrating the positivity of the inverse foliation density near the outermost conic surface over all time and resolving a global Goursat problem within this outermost cone. To address challenges arising from the slower decay rate of 2D wave equation solutions and the magnitude of the solution itself, we develop novel auxiliary energy functionals. Furthermore, the methodologies and findings presented herein are applicable to general 2D quasilinear wave equations that satisfy corresponding null conditions when subjected to short pulse initial data.

Reservoir computing offers a machine learning method for creating surrogate models of dynamical systems, achieving this with fewer trainable parameters and less training data compared to other methods. A simplified variant, called next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), further streamlines the process by eliminating many algorithmic hyperparameters to automatically identify high-performing traditional reservoir computers. This study examines a difficult scenario involving a dynamical system with multiple co-existing attractors and disparate time scales. By comparing NGRC and traditional reservoir computing using metrics that assess the geometry of both the true and predicted attractors, we analyzed a four-dimensional system. Results show that NGRC requires approximately 1.7 times less training data, needs $10^3$ times less warm-up time, involves fewer hyperparameters, and achieves roughly 100 times greater accuracy in predicting co-existing attractor characteristics than traditional reservoir computing. Additionally, the method successfully predicts the basin of attraction with high precision. These findings reinforce the superior learning capabilities of this new algorithm for modeling dynamical systems.

This study investigates the dynamical entropy of dense gluonic states arising in high-energy proton-proton collisions by employing phenomenological models of the unintegrated gluon distribution. Transverse momentum probability distributions are calculated as a function of rapidity, yielding the dynamical entropy density within the rapidity range pertinent to Large Hadron Collider operations. The total entropy density for the dense system is derived as a function of rapidity evolution, defined by $\Delta Y = Y-Y_0$ relative to an initial rapidity $Y_0$. Furthermore, the analysis examines theoretical uncertainties and compares the findings with related methods found in existing literature.

This work introduces a neural-symbolic integration approach designed for abstract concept explanation and interactive learning. By combining neural-symbolic integration with explanation capabilities, we enable domain experts and users to understand the data-driven decision-making processes within large neural models. These models are queried through a symbolic logic language, allowing user interaction to validate or reject revisions to the neural model via logic-based constraints that can be distilled into the model's architecture. We demonstrate this methodology using the Logic Tensor Network framework in conjunction with Concept Activation Vectors, applying it to a Convolutional Neural Network.

In a connected graph $G$, two vertices $u$ and $v$ are said to be doubly resolved by a pair $x, y \in V(G)$ if the inequality $d(v, x) - d(u, x) \neq d(v, y) - d(u, y)$ holds. A set $W$ of vertices in $G$ constitutes a doubly resolving set if, for every pair of distinct vertices in $G$, there exists a pair within $W$ that doubly resolves them. The parameter $\psi(G)$ denotes the minimum size of such a doubly resolving set for $G$. This paper explores the properties of doubly resolving sets within graphs. It establishes an upper bound for $\psi(G)$ based on the graph's order and diameter. Furthermore, the value of $\psi(G)$ is calculated for several significant graph types, and all graphs of order $n$ satisfying the condition $\psi(G) = n-1$ are fully characterized.

This study introduces a bias-reduced estimator for the mean absolute deviation parameter within a median regression framework. To address the conventional lack of smoothness typically required for general bias reduction, a specific workaround is implemented. The validity of this bias correction is established through a local asymptotic normality property and a Bahadur-Kiefer representation. Although the methodology is formulated under a classical asymptotic regime, simulation results indicate its effectiveness extends to high-dimensional contexts as well.

Capturing information from patient-physician interactions is crucial for medical conversation summarization, as these summaries facilitate physician hand-offs and support future care. However, creating high-quality summaries is often labor-intensive and demands specialized domain knowledge. While modern pre-trained NLP models like PEGASUS have emerged as effective alternatives to human summarization—achieving state-of-the-art results on various benchmarks—many downstream applications still rely on moderately sized datasets to perform well. This study investigates two main areas: (1) the impact of dataset size on transfer learning for medical conversation summarization using PEGASUS, and (2) the efficacy of different iterative labeling strategies within low-data regimes, adapting successful approaches from classification tasks. Our findings indicate that model performance plateaus as dataset size increases and that the evaluated active-learning strategies yield equivalent results compared to simply expanding the dataset. Furthermore, we observe that naive iterative pseudo-labeling performs on par with, or slightly worse than, approaches without pseudo-labeling. This work clarifies the challenges and successes of adapting low-data classification techniques to medical summarization and offers guidance for future research. The relevant code is available at \url{https://github.com/curai/curai-research/tree/main/medical-summarization-ML4H-2021}.

Through comprehensive numerical simulations, we examined magnetization switching in a two-dimensional artificial spin ice (ASI) system composed of peanut-shaped nanomagnets. We further analyzed how external magnetic fields influence the degeneracy of magnetic states within this architecture. Our findings indicate that the switching field in this proposed ASI system is approximately one order of magnitude lower than that of conventional, highly anisotropic nanoislands, such as elliptically shaped nanomagnets. The metastable 2-in/2-out (Type II) magnetic state remains robust at remanence, and by precisely adjusting the external magnetic field, we successfully accessed other microstates corresponding to Type II configurations. This demonstrates that magnetic state degeneracy can be controlled via an appropriate magnetic field. Notably, removing nanomagnets introduces defects that disrupt magnetic charge neutrality, resulting in a 1-out/3-in or 3-out/1-in (Type III) spin state that resembles a magnetic monopole. We consider this study essential for advancing next-generation spintronic devices for future technological applications.

This work investigates the theory of projective representations for a compact quantum group $\mathbb{G}$, defined as actions of $\mathbb{G}$ on $\mathcal{B}(H)$ for a Hilbert space $H$. We demonstrate that every such projective representation is inner, meaning it arises from an $\Omega$-twisted representation associated with a unitary measurable $2$-cocycle $\Omega$ on $\mathbb{G}$. Furthermore, we establish that a projective representation is continuous—specifically, it restricts to an action on the compact operators $\mathcal{K}(H)$—if and only if the corresponding $2$-cocycle is regular; notably, this regularity holds automatically when $\mathbb{G}$ is of Kac type. These findings enable the characterization of the torsion of projective type for $\widehat{\mathbb{G}}$ via the projective representation theory of $\mathbb{G}$. For any given regular unitary $2$-cocycle $\Omega$, we examine $\Omega$-twisted actions on C$^*$-algebras, introducing deformed crossed products that yield a twisted analogue of the Baaj-Skandalis duality and a quantum adaptation of the Packer-Raeburn trick. As an application, we derive a twisted version of the Green-Julg isomorphism and construct the quantum Baum-Connes assembly map for permutation torsion-free discrete quantum groups.

Automated segmentation of vascular maps in retinal images offers significant potential for diagnosing various ocular conditions. This paper introduces a novel unsupervised approach for retinal blood vessel segmentation that integrates top-hat transformation, contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE), and 2-D Gabor wavelet filters. The process begins with preprocessing the retinal image using top-hat morphological operations followed by CLAHE to isolate blood vessel pixels amidst exudates, the optic disc, and the fovea. Subsequently, multiscale 2-D Gabor wavelet filters are applied to the enhanced image to effectively capture both thick and thin vessels across different orientations. The algorithm's performance was evaluated using the publicly available DRIVE database, which contains manually annotated images. On this dataset, the method achieved an average accuracy of 94.32% with a minimal standard deviation of 0.004. When compared to leading algorithms, our approach demonstrates superior performance in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and kappa agreement.

We examine the search for right-handed weak interaction effects within the SU(2)$_L \times$SU(2)$_R$ model, which features lepton doublets $(\nu_\ell, \ell^-)_L$ and $(N_\ell, \ell^-)_R$ ($\ell = e, \mu, \tau$). We highlight that the sole opportunity to observe such right-handed weak interaction effects lies in the rare decay $K^+ \rightarrow \pi^- \mu^+ \mu^+$.

We investigate exact support recovery in high-dimensional sparse linear regression under conditions of weak, rare, and potentially heterogeneous signals. By fixing the minimum signal magnitude at the information-theoretic optimal rate, we examine the asymptotic selection accuracy of best subset selection (BSS) and marginal screening (MS) under an independent Gaussian design. Surprisingly, despite this ideal setup, marginal screening may fail to achieve exact recovery with probability approaching one when signals are heterogeneous, whereas BSS remains model-consistent provided the minimum signal strength exceeds the information-theoretic threshold. To address BSS's computational demands, we introduce ETS (Estimate Then Screen), a surrogate two-stage algorithm combining iterative hard thresholding and gradient coordinate screening. We demonstrate that ETS matches BSS's exact asymptotic optimality regarding recovery. Finally, a simulation study compares ETS against LASSO and marginal screening; the numerical findings align with our asymptotic theory even for realistic sample sizes, dimensions, and sparsity levels.

A fundamental aspect of cognitive radar is generalization, which ensures consistent performance across a wide variety of sensing environments given that physical scene characteristics can fluctuate. This poses a significant hurdle for learning-based waveform selection methods, as transmission strategies optimal for one scenario may perform poorly in another. To mitigate this, one can strategically bias a learning algorithm by leveraging high-level structural patterns across different tracking instances, a technique known as meta-learning. This study introduces an online meta-learning framework for waveform-agile tracking, utilizing insights from prior target tracks to accelerate and improve learning in subsequent instances. By capitalizing on the inherent similarities among tracking scenes—driven by shared physical elements like target types or clutter—this approach achieves sample-efficient learning across a range of finite state target channels. We model the online waveform selection problem using Bayesian learning and establish prior-dependent performance bounds for meta-learning via PAC-Bayes theory. Furthermore, we propose a computationally tractable posterior sampling algorithm and evaluate its efficacy through simulations involving diverse scenes. Finally, we investigate both the potential performance gains and the practical challenges inherent to applying online meta-learning in waveform-agile tracking.

Conversational Text-to-Speech (TTS) focuses on generating utterances with appropriate linguistic and emotional prosody within a dialogue setting. While previous research has leveraged utterance-level dialogue history to enhance speech expressiveness, the significant influence of fine-grained, word-level context remains underexplored. To address this, we introduce FCTalker, a novel expressive conversational TTS model that simultaneously learns both fine and coarse-grained context dependencies during speech synthesis. FCTalker employs dual encoders to capture word-level and utterance-level contextual information; specifically, a dialogue BERT-based fine-grained encoder models the word-level relationships between an utterance and its history. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses all baselines, producing speech that is both more expressive and contextually appropriate. The source code is available at: https://github.com/walker-hyf/FCTalker.

The ZX-Calculus serves as a diagrammatic language for reasoning within quantum mechanics and quantum information theory, complete with an equational framework. This work centers on the language's completeness—a crucial property ensuring the equational theory fully encompasses quantum mechanics. We begin by enhancing the known-complete presentation for the Clifford fragment, a non-universal restriction, by introducing new axioms. Leveraging a back-and-forth translation system between the ZX-Calculus and a third-party complete graphical language, we demonstrate that this expanded axiomatization achieves completeness for the first approximately universal fragment, Clifford+T. Subsequently, we establish that the expressive power of this presentation, originally targeted at Clifford+T, extends to a broader class of diagrams termed "linear with Clifford+T constants." Utilizing an alternative version of the third-party language alongside an adapted translation mechanism, we prove completeness for the ZX-Calculus in its entirety, without restriction. The text concludes with a brief discussion of the added axioms and presents a complete axiomatization for a modified version of the language featuring an additional generator, thereby simplifying the presentation.

It is widely acknowledged that quantum mechanics necessitates a modification of classical propositional calculus due to its physical implications. Nevertheless, the assertion that a new quantum logic is essential for modeling propositions across all quantum theories is contested. This essay critically examines that claim by demonstrating that classical logic can be restored within a quantum framework through the lens of Bohmian mechanics. We argue that this theoretical approach offers the requisite conceptual instruments to reestablish a classical logic of experimental propositions, leveraging its distinct metaphysical structure and measurement theory. Specifically, we show that the reinstatement of a classical propositional calculus stems from the theory's primitive ontology—a point that remains underappreciated in existing literature on Bohmian mechanics. Our work seeks to address this oversight.

Using Dawn Framing Camera imagery from the Low Altitude Mapping Orbit (LAMO), we identified all surface boulders on dwarf planet Ceres exceeding 105 meters in size. Our analysis reveals that these boulders are more abundant at high latitudes and possess a maximum estimated lifetime of $150 \pm 50$ Ma, derived from crater counts. These traits differ significantly from those observed on asteroid (4) Vesta, a previous Dawn target, suggesting that Ceres' boulders are mechanically weaker. Insights into their nature stem from Ceres' complex crust, which contains abundant phyllosilicates and salts. Given that water ice is believed to exist merely meters beneath the surface, we propose that these boulders also contain ice. Additionally, the size-frequency distribution of the boulders aligns best with a Weibull distribution rather than the typical power law, a pattern also seen on Vesta, a result that remains robust despite potential size measurement errors.

This work extends the investigation of symplectically flat bundles by generalizing the concept of symplectically flat connections on symplectic manifolds to $\zeta$-flat connections on arbitrary smooth manifolds. Such connections on principal bundles correspond to maps defined by extensions of the base manifold's fundamental group into the structure group. We define functionals whose zero sets consist of symplectically flat connections and analyze their critical points, which generate new geometric flows. Additionally, we outline certain characteristic classes associated with $\zeta$-flat bundles.

We present ALMA Band 3 data observing the CO(6-5), CO(7-6), and [CI](2-1) lines in B14-65666 ("Big Three Dragons"), a luminous Lyman-Break Galaxy at $z>7$ with strong rest-frame UV, far-infrared, and [OIII] 88 $\mu$m and [CII] 158 $\mu$m emission. No detections were found for CO(6-5), CO(7-6), or [CI](2-1), with $3\sigma$ upper limits on their luminosities approximately 50 times lower than the [CII] luminosity. Utilizing three approaches—(i) [CII] luminosity combined with a [CII]-to-H$_{2}$ conversion factor derived from local metal-poor dwarfs, (ii) a dust mass and metallicity-dependent dust-to-gas ratio, and (iii) a dynamical mass estimate—we derive a molecular gas mass ($M_{\rm mol}$) of $(0.05-11)\times10^{10} M_{\rm \odot}$. This range aligns with the upper limit suggested by the non-detection of mid-$J$ CO and [CI](2-1). Despite the large uncertainty in $M_{\rm mol}$, we calculate a high molecular gas-to-stellar mass ratio ($\mu_{\rm gas}$) of $0.65-140$ and a short gas depletion time ($t_{\rm dep}$) of $2.5-550$ Myr. These values are generally consistent with previous extrapolations of $\mu_{\rm gas}$ and $t_{\rm dep}$ based on redshift, specific star formation rate, and stellar mass. The brief $t_{\rm dep}$ likely indicates a starburst phase triggered by a major merger. If no external gas accretion occurs, B14-65666 could evolve into a passive galaxy at $z\gtrsim4$. In summary, these findings underscore the challenges of drawing robust conclusions from mid-$J$ CO observations alone during the reionization epoch and encourage the use of alternative gas mass tracers.

Two papers in Information Science examine the derivatives of interval functions according to Svetoslav Markov's framework. Their authors attempted to identify the specific functions and points where these derivatives exist, but their characterization contains inaccuracies. This article highlights these errors and outlines the necessary corrections.

This study investigates frame-level audio feature learning for chord recognition via artificial neural networks. We argue that while chroma vectors contain sufficient data to model harmonic content for chord identification, conventional extractors often generate overly noisy features. Consequently, we propose a learned chroma feature extractor based on artificial neural networks, designed to encode harmonic information crucial for chord recognition while remaining robust against irrelevant interference. By feeding the network an audio spectrum with context rather than a single frame, the system can learn to selectively mitigate noise and resolve harmonic ambiguities. When compared against hand-crafted features using a simple linear frame-wise classifier across various datasets, the results demonstrate that our learned feature extractor yields superior chroma vectors for chord recognition.

This experimental investigation examines how the electrical resistance $R(T)$ of epitaxial Cr thin films evolves as quantized spin density wave domains transform with varying temperatures. Distinctive resistance noise emerges exclusively within the temperature range exhibiting hysteresis during cooling-warming cycles in $R(T)$. We suggest an analytical framework analogous to Barkhausen noise in ferromagnets, where magnetization $M(H)$ fluctuates under a swept magnetic field $H$. By mapping $M$ to $\Psi_0$ (the spin density wave order parameter) and $H$ to $T$, we extend the Preisach model to describe our findings using a random distribution of resistive hysterons. These hysterons correspond to quantized spin density wave domains characterized by varying sizes, local energies, and node counts.

We present a framework for graphical security proofs in device-independent quantum cryptography, utilizing the techniques of categorical quantum mechanics. We anticipate that this method will render some of the highly intricate proofs in quantum cryptography more accessible, aid in the discovery of novel proofs, and support automated verification. As a demonstration of our framework, we reprove a prior result in device-independent quantum cryptography: any linear randomness expansion protocol can be transformed into an unbounded randomness expansion protocol. We provide a graphical proof for this result and implement a portion of it within the Globular proof assistant.

This study introduces a 1D unsteady model designed for supersonic single-phase ejectors, conceptualizing the device as a pipe network featuring two inlets and a single outlet. By integrating a 1D gas dynamics framework within each pipe segment with a junction model to handle entrainment and mixing, the approach is calibrated and verified using steady-state experimental data to examine the choking mechanism of the mixed flow. Subsequently, the model was benchmarked against 2D URANS simulations to assess its ability to forecast ejector responses to abrupt operational shifts, which generate traveling waves. Findings indicate that the model accurately predicts both ejector performance and the longitudinal evolution of key integral parameters, such as mass flow rates and momentum, across steady and transient regimes.

Logo detection has attracted significant interest due to its extensive applications in multimedia, including copyright infringement identification, brand visibility tracking, and social media product management. This paper presents LogoDet-3K, the largest fully annotated logo detection dataset to date, featuring 3,000 logo categories, approximately 200,000 manually annotated objects, and 158,652 images. By offering broader category coverage and a more diverse range of annotated objects than existing resources, LogoDet-3K establishes a more rigorous benchmark for logo detection. We detail the dataset's collection and annotation methodologies and compare its scale and diversity with prior datasets. Additionally, we introduce Logo-Yolo, a robust baseline model that integrates Focal loss and CIoU loss into the YOLOv3 architecture to address challenges such as multi-scale objects, sample imbalance, and inconsistent bounding-box regression. On LogoDet-3K, Logo-Yolo achieves roughly a 4% performance gain over YOLOv3 and outperforms several other reported deep detection models. Further evaluations on three additional datasets confirm the method's effectiveness and the dataset's superior generalization capabilities for detection and retrieval tasks. To foster large-scale research in logo-related fields, the LogoDet-3K dataset is available at https://github.com/Wangjing1551/LogoDet-3K-Dataset.

Simulating turbulent bubbly flows by resolving both liquid and bubble phases is computationally prohibitive for many natural scenarios. A prime example is breaking waves, where bubbles significantly affect wave impact loads, acoustic emissions, and ocean-atmosphere exchange, yet detailed simulations remain infeasible except in the simplest cases. As an alternative, we propose resolving only large scales while modeling small-scale bubbles using sub-resolution closures. This study introduces a Large Eddy Simulation (LES) Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) scheme for bubbly flows. The continuous liquid phase is captured using a semi-implicit, isothermally compressible SPH framework, coupled with a discrete Lagrangian bubble model. Interactions between bubbles and liquid are managed through volume and momentum exchanges, incorporating turbulent closures, bubble breakup and entrainment, and free-surface interaction models. By treating bubbles as individual particles, their lifecycles can be tracked, enabling integral-form closure models for sub-resolution fluctuations, deformation, breakup, and free-surface interactions that account for finite event timescales. We examined two flow types: bubble plumes and breaking waves, finding close quantitative agreement with existing experimental and numerical data. Specifically, for plunging breaking waves, the framework accurately predicts the Hinze scale, bubble size distribution, and the growth rate of entrained bubbles. This represents the first coupling of an SPH framework with a discrete bubble model, offering potential for cost-effective simulations of wave-structure interactions and more precise predictions of wave impact loads.

We utilize $1/2$-spin tautological relations to derive a specific combinatorial identity. We demonstrate that this identity is equivalent to Faber's formula concerning the proportionalities of kappa-classes on $\mathcal{M}_g$ for $g\geq 2$. Subsequently, we establish several instances of this combinatorial identity, thereby offering a novel proof of Faber's formula for those specific cases.

Future observing runs utilizing advanced detectors are expected to generate many detections of gravitational waves from neutron star binary inspirals. The combination of rare, loud signals and a large number of moderate-strength events offers the potential for rigorous constraints on neutron star matter properties, projecting a statistical uncertainty in radius measurements of $50-200$m based on approximately ${\cal{O}}(2000)$ sources. Leveraging this anticipated precision, we re-examine all underlying analysis assumptions, pinpoint sources of systematic errors, evaluate their influence on radius determination, and discuss their relative significance along with strategies for mitigation.

This research investigates the design of two-wave experiments subject to spillover effects, specifically when the goal is precise inference regarding treatment impacts. The study focuses on units linked via a single network, accounting for local interdependencies, and addresses a broad category of estimands that includes both average treatment and average spillover effects. We propose a statistical framework for two-wave networked experiments where the researcher optimizes participant selection and treatment allocation to minimize estimator variance, leveraging a first-wave pilot study to estimate said variance. We establish guarantees for treatment effect inference and regret bounds concerning the variance achieved by the proposed design mechanism. Our findings demonstrate a trade-off in selecting the pilot study size and formally define the relationship between the pilot's scale and the main experiment. Furthermore, simulations utilizing both simulated and real-world networks highlight the method's benefits.

This study investigates the existence and stability of nonlinear discrete vortex solitons within a square lattice where the conventional discrete Laplacian is substituted with a fractional variant. This modification introduces a novel effective site-energy term and inter-site coupling, with a range governed by the fractional exponent $\alpha$; notably, this coupling becomes effectively long-range as $\alpha$ approaches small values. At long distances, the coupling decays faster than exponentially, following the form $\sim \exp(- |{\bf n}|)/\sqrt{|\bf{n}|}$. Generally, we find that the stability domain for these discrete vortex solitons expands toward lower power levels as the $\alpha$ coefficient decreases, regardless of their topological charge or pattern distribution.

Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying the relationship between a subject and an object within a sentence, whereas knowledge graph link prediction (KGLP) seeks to determine a set of objects, O, based on a given subject and relation from a knowledge graph. These tasks are deeply interconnected: when a RE model identifies a relation for a subject-object pair in a sentence, that relation can be fed into a KGLP model alongside the subject to predict the object set O, implying the original object o should be included in O. Building on this connection, we introduce a multi-task learning framework that enhances RE performance by jointly training on both RE and KGLP tasks. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach by applying it to various existing RE models, empirically showing that it consistently improves their performance.

Action recognition, a fundamental challenge in computer vision, involves categorizing videos using a predefined set of action labels. Achieving high accuracy on this task requires capturing both semantic content and motion dynamics across video frames. While most state-of-the-art approaches combine deep neural networks with RGB frames for semantics and pre-computed optical flow for motion cues, it has been argued that these models fail to fully leverage motion information; instead, optical flow primarily aids in recognizing people and objects. This limitation highlights the need to investigate alternative cues or models capable of extracting motion more effectively. To address this, we propose exploring PredNet, a recurrent neural network that propagates predictive coding errors across layers and time steps. We investigate whether PredNet can better capture video motion by estimating representations from pre-trained networks over time, relying solely on video frames without requiring pre-processed optical flow inputs. Finally, we evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed model on the UCF101 and HMDB51 datasets.

We present a two-type first passage percolation competition model on infinite connected graphs where Type 1 propagates from a unique starting site at rate 1 through vacant edges, while all other locations begin empty. Upon occupation by Type 1, a site transitions to Type 2 at rate $\rho>0$. Type 2 then expands at rate $\lambda>0$ into both vacant sites and those currently held by Type 1, whereas Type 1 is restricted to spreading only through vacant sites. Type 1 is considered to survive if its occupied set remains non-empty throughout the process. Specifically, for regular $d$-ary trees with $d\geq 3$, we demonstrate that Type 1 can survive even when slower than Type 2, provided $\rho$ is sufficiently small. This finding contrasts with the behavior on the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$, where Type 1 goes extinct almost surely whenever $\lambda>1$, regardless of the value of $\rho>0$.

Smart and Connected Communities (SCC) represent an emerging branch of the Internet of Things (IoT) with significant potential to enhance human life by improving community preservation, revitalization, livability, and sustainability. However, the limited resources—such as memory, energy, and buffer space—of nodes and devices within SCC often hinder their ability to cooperate efficiently or maximize performance. To address this, a robust solution is required to discourage selfish behavior and incentivize collaboration. This article proposes a novel mechanism called Socially Omitting Selfishness (SOS) to eliminate selfishness through a socially oriented election process. This process selects leaders based on weight and cooperation levels using the VCG model, thereby encouraging nodes to participate actively and act as highly cooperative community members. Additionally, an extended Dempster-Shafer model is integrated into the SOS scheme to deter selfishness, utilizing various monitoring and gateway nodes for efficient implementation. A mathematical model was developed to evaluate these aspects, and simulations were conducted in the NS2 environment to assess the SOS scheme's performance. The results demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms contemporary approaches in terms of average delivery delay, packet delivery ratio, throughput, and average energy consumption.

Events like the MiniZinc Challenges and SAT competitions have significantly aided in evaluating different solving strategies and pushing the boundaries of their respective fields. Conventional competition frameworks typically rank solvers based on their average performance across diverse benchmark instances. Although this approach offers a reasonable assessment of relative capabilities, it fails to capture a solver's complete potential, particularly when the goal is to deploy a portfolio of solvers rather than relying on a single one for new problems. This paper introduces a portfolio-based analysis method that provides complementary insights into solver performance within competitive settings. The method is applied to data from the MiniZinc Challenges, revealing new perspectives through a portfolio-centric lens.

This study offers a thorough investigation of star-forming (SF) regions within the nearby large spiral galaxy M31. Utilizing GALEX far-ultraviolet (FUV) and near-ultraviolet (NUV) imaging, we identify young massive stars and map recent star formation across the galaxy. By combining FUV and NUV flux data with ground-based observations to estimate interstellar dust reddening, we calculate the ages and masses of these SF regions. The GALEX data, characterized by its deep sensitivity and full-galaxy coverage, reveals the complete landscape of recent star formation in M31 and its environmental variations. Since FUV and NUV measurements are sensitive to populations younger than a few hundred million years, we identified 894 SF regions exceeding 1600 pc² above an average FUV flux limit of approximately 26 ABmag arcsecond⁻² across the entire 26 kpc disk. This allows us to derive M31's star-formation history over this timescale. The star-formation rate (SFR) from the youngest UV sources (age < 10 Myr) aligns with values derived from Hα emission, as anticipated. We also examine how results vary with assumed metallicity. When integrating SFR from infrared measurements of heated dust with UV-measured SFR from unobscured populations over the recent few million years, we observe a slight decline in SFR in recent epochs. This suggests a possible peak between 10 and 100 Myrs, with an average SFR of approximately 0.6 or 0.7 M☉ yr⁻¹ over the last 400 Myrs, depending on whether the metallicity is Z=0.02 or Z=0.05, respectively.

Brain activity analysis remains a critical domain within neuroscience. Schizophrenia (Sz) is a debilitating neurological condition that significantly impacts the cognitive functions, behaviors, and emotions of individuals globally. Electroencephalography (EEG) has been validated as a highly effective biomarker for detecting Sz. Given that EEG data constitutes a non-linear time-series signal, leveraging its unique non-linear characteristics is essential for thorough investigation. This study introduces a deep learning approach to enhance Sz detection via EEG by proposing a novel hybrid model called SzHNN (Schizophrenia Hybrid Neural Network). This architecture integrates Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for extracting local features with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for classification tasks. The performance of the SzHNN was benchmarked against standalone CNN and LSTM models, as well as traditional machine learning approaches. Evaluations were conducted across two datasets: Dataset 1 comprising 19 subjects and Dataset 2 with 16 subjects. Extensive experiments were performed using various parameter configurations, frequency bands, and scalp electrode placements. Results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid model achieves the highest classification accuracy of 99.9%, outperforming existing methods. Notably, the model effectively mitigates variations across frequency bands and maintains a robust accuracy of 91% even when utilizing only five electrodes. Furthermore, the model's applicability was assessed within the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) framework, highlighting its potential for smart healthcare and remote monitoring systems.

This research examines a general cavity-QED framework involving artificial two-level dipoles interacting with the electric field of a single-mode LC resonator. From this configuration, we develop a minimal quantum mechanical model for cavity QED that incorporates both direct dipole-dipole and dipole-field interactions. The model remains valid across arbitrary coupling strengths, enabling an extension of the standard Dicke model into the non-perturbative regime of QED, where the dipole-field interaction corresponds to an effective fine-structure constant on the order of unity. Within this regime, we characterize three distinct categories of vacuum states—normal, superradiant, and subradiant—detailing their unique properties and the transitions connecting them. These results harmonize numerous previously conflicting predictions in the field and provide a unified theoretical basis for describing ultrastrong coupling phenomena across various cavity-QED systems.

Transfer learning, often referred to as knowledge transferability, is extensively utilized to adapt pre-trained models from a source domain to downstream tasks within a target domain. Consequently, investigating the factors influencing this transferability is crucial. This paper presents the first analysis demonstrating the intrinsic link between knowledge transferability and adversarial transferability—the phenomenon where adversarial examples crafted to attack one model can successfully compromise others. Our theoretical findings reveal that adversarial transferability both implies and is implied by knowledge transferability. Building on these insights, we introduce two practical metrics based on adversarial transferability to characterize this relationship, acting as bidirectional indicators between the two concepts. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and scenarios confirm a positive correlation between them. These results provide valuable guidance for future research aimed at enhancing knowledge transfer learning and analyzing adversarial transferability.

Large industrial systems integrating various services and applications have increasingly become targets for cybercriminals, presenting significant challenges regarding security, monitoring, and auditing. Analyzing security logs is a critical process for identifying anomalies, detecting intrusions, and facilitating incident response. However, the continuous rise in link speeds, user numbers, and threat complexity has generated massive volumes of log data that are difficult for Central Processing Units (CPUs) to process efficiently. To address this, this paper introduces a massively parallel Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) library called GLoP (GLoP), which is also applicable to Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) via a prefix matching method, leveraging the capabilities of standard hardware. GLoP employs two distinct algorithms utilizing different GPU memory configurations and is benchmarked against CPU-based implementations. The library supports processing nodes equipped with single or multiple GPUs, as well as GPU cloud farms. Experimental results demonstrate a throughput of 20 Gbps, confirming that modern GPUs can significantly accelerate large-scale log processing operations, thereby saving valuable time both before and after an intrusion occurs.

We introduce the inaugural neural machine translation system designed for translating between the endangered Erzya language and Russian, alongside the dataset we gathered for its training and evaluation. The system achieves BLEU scores of 17 and 19 for translation into Erzya and Russian, respectively, with over 50% of the outputs deemed acceptable by native speakers. Although we adapted the model to handle translation between Erzya and ten other languages, performance remains low due to the absence of additional parallel data. We are making the translation models, the collected text corpus, a novel language identification model, and a multilingual sentence encoder tailored for Erzya publicly available at https://github.com/slone-nlp/myv-nmt.

We employ constrained variational minimization techniques to investigate the existence of periodic solutions with a specified energy level for a specific class of second-order Hamiltonian systems featuring a $C^2$ potential function that may possess an unbounded potential well. Our findings serve as a complement to the established theorems by Benci-Gluck-Ziller and Hayashi.

Zero-shot Learning (ZSL), focused on predicting categories absent from the training data, has become a subject of intense research. The core of ZSL implementation lies in utilizing prior knowledge to establish semantic relationships among classes, facilitating the transfer of learned features from seen to unseen categories. However, existing methods often rely on limited priors with incomplete semantic information. This paper investigates richer and more competitive prior knowledge to model inter-class relationships in ZSL using ontology-based representation and semantic embedding. Additionally, to mitigate the data imbalance between seen and unseen classes, we propose a generative ZSL framework incorporating Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Our primary contributions are: (i) an ontology-enhanced ZSL framework applicable across diverse domains, including image classification (IMGC) and knowledge graph completion (KGC); and (ii) a comprehensive evaluation on multiple zero-shot datasets demonstrating that our method frequently surpasses state-of-the-art models. Specifically, on four representative IMGC baselines, ontology-based class semantics outperform previous priors, such as word embeddings, by an average of 12.4 accuracy points in standard ZSL across two datasets (see Figure 4).

We conducted numerical simulations of molecular clouds (MCs) with characteristics resembling those in the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone (CMZ). Utilizing the moving mesh code Arepo, our simulations incorporated a simplified, time-dependent chemical treatment alongside non-isothermal conditions for both gas and dust. The simulations were initialized with a density of n_0 = 10^3 cm^{-3} and a mass of 1.3x10^5 M_sun. We varied the virial parameter, defined as the ratio of kinetic to potential energy ($\alpha = E_{kin} / |E_{pot}|$), by adjusting velocity dispersion to values of 0.5, 2.0, and 8.0 to assess the influence of kinetic energy on our findings. To replicate the harsh CMZ environment, we enhanced the interstellar radiation field (ISRF) and cosmic-ray flux (CRF) by a factor of 1000 relative to the solar neighborhood. Synthetic images in various diagnostic lines were generated using the radiative transfer code RADMC-3D, specifically targeting [CII] at 158 $\mu$m, [OI] at 145 and 63 $\mu$m, and 12CO and 13CO (J=1$\to$0) at 2600 and 2720 $\mu$m, respectively. Our results indicate that high $\alpha$ values lead to turbulence dispersing significant amounts of gas, lowering mean density and permitting deeper ISRF penetration into the cloud's core; this drastically alters chemical composition by dissociating substantial portions of molecular gas. Conversely, low $\alpha$ values result in a compact cloud structure that preserves more molecular gas. We demonstrate that atomic tracers effectively mirror the physical properties of both H$_2$ and total gas in all scenarios, offering a valuable alternative to molecular lines for studying the ISM within the CMZ.

This paper outlines the potential for constructing a hadron collider encircling the Moon's equator. A proposed Circular Collider on the Moon (CCM), with a circumference of approximately 11,000 km, could achieve a proton-proton center-of-mass collision energy of 14 PeV—roughly a thousand times that of the Large Hadron Collider at CERN—under the optimistic assumption of a 20 T dipole magnetic field. The discussion covers various project facets, including site selection, construction logistics, lunar material availability, power supply, and the requirements for machine parameters, vacuum conditions, and an injection scheme, alongside identifying areas needing further study to assess concrete feasibility. Given the growing interest from multiple organizations in establishing a permanent lunar presence, a CCM could serve as the next-to-next-to-next-generation discovery engine for high-energy particle physics, acting as a natural successor to next-generation terrestrial proposals like the Future Circular Collider at CERN or the Super Proton-Proton Collider in China, as well as marine concepts such as a Collider in the Sea. Furthermore, a CCM would represent a crucial step toward realizing a Planck-scale collider within our Solar System.

For decades, it has been established that computer-based systems require modularization and decomposition to be comprehensible. We propose a universal, expressive, and intuitively appealing composition operator for Petri nets, integrated with a refinement concept and an algebraic framework for representing nets and their compositions. Case studies demonstrate how large-scale systems can be constructed from small net snippets. Future research should include additional field studies to better grasp the real-world implications of these proposed ideas.

Flagellar motility is essential for both natural and assisted reproduction. The rhythmic beating and wave propagation of the flagellum propel sperm through fluids, allowing transitions between penetrative progressive motion, activated side-to-side yaw, and hyperactivated movement linked to detachment from epithelial surfaces. Although these changes respond to fluid properties, biochemical activation, and physiological ligands, a simple mechanistic explanation for flagellar beat generation that accounts for motility modulation remains absent. This paper introduces the Axonemal Regulation of Curvature, Hysteretic (ARCH) model, a curvature control model where active moment switches based on local curvature, integrated into a geometrically nonlinear elastic flagellar model exhibiting planar beats alongside nonlocal viscous fluid dynamics. The system is fully parameterized by four dimensionless groups. Computational simulations exploring parameter variations reveal beat patterns qualitatively matching penetrative (straight progressive), activated (highly yawing), and hyperactivated (non-progressive) modes. Analysis of flagellar limit cycles and swimming velocity identifies a cusp catastrophe between progressive and non-progressive states, along with hysteresis in responses to critical curvature changes. A quantitative comparison with experimental data on human sperm showing typical penetrative, activated, and hyperactivated beats demonstrates a strong fit to the time-average absolute curvature profile, supporting the model's ability to provide a framework for quantitatively interpreting imaging data.

This paper examines a finite volume approach applied to a nonlocal variant of the Shigesada-Kawazaki-Teramoto (SKT) cross-diffusion system. We establish the existence of solutions for the scheme, derive their qualitative characteristics, and demonstrate convergence. These proofs are grounded in a discrete entropy-dissipation inequality, discrete compactness techniques, and a new adaptation of the duality method at the discrete level. Furthermore, through numerical experiments, we explore the impact of nonlocality on the scheme's convergence as an approximation of the local system and on the emergence of diffusive instabilities.

Optimal prediction in Spoken Question Answering (SQA) depends on a detailed comprehension of both spoken queries and documents. This paper introduces new training frameworks for SQA, comprising a self-supervised phase and a contrastive representation learning phase. During the self-supervised phase, we implement three auxiliary tasks—utterance restoration, utterance insertion, and question discrimination—to jointly train the model to capture consistency and coherence within speech documents without requiring extra data or annotations. Subsequently, we employ multiple augmentation strategies, such as span deletion and substitution, to learn noise-invariant utterance representations through a contrastive objective. Additionally, we introduce Temporal-Alignment attention to semantically align speech and textual cues within a shared space, thereby enhancing SQA performance. These approaches effectively guide the generation model to produce more accurate answers. Experimental findings demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across three SQA benchmarks.

As experimental efforts to detect WIMP dark matter consistently return null results, alternative models have emerged to satisfy tightening observational limits, including sub-GeV dark matter interacting via a massive vector portal (dark photon) linked to a new dark $U(1)$ gauge symmetry. Previous research has highlighted that within this framework, dark matter annihilation into dark photon pairs can dominate the freeze-out process even when kinematically forbidden for stationary dark matter, a scenario termed the "forbidden dark matter" (FDM) regime. However, earlier studies of the FDM regime assumed the "dark Higgs" responsible for breaking the dark $U(1)$ and giving mass to the dark photon was decoupled from dark matter and thus irrelevant to freeze-out. This paper investigates the impact of the dark Higgs on sub-GeV dark matter phenomenology within the FDM regime by analyzing a minimal model featuring non-trivial couplings between a single complex scalar dark matter candidate and the dark Higgs field. We demonstrate that across a broad parameter space, the dark Higgs can shift the predicted relic abundance by many orders of magnitude, with significant effects persisting even for small coupling constants. Furthermore, incorporating constraints from direct detection and CMB measurements, we find that parameter regions yielding the correct relic abundance face only mild current restrictions but are likely to be probed by near-future direct detection experiments.

This study introduces a novel analytical propagation delay model tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Recognizing that inverter delay depends intricately on multiple process variables and load capacitance, the authors developed fitting functions for each parameter using Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox. When compared to SPICE simulations utilizing the BSIM4 transistor model, this analytical approach demonstrates high accuracy, maintaining an average error below 2% across a broad spectrum of process conditions and output loads. Consequently, the proposed model is highly efficient for application across various technology nodes and for statistical gate delay characterization.

This paper introduces Random Shadows and Highlights (RSH), a novel data augmentation technique designed to enhance robustness against lighting variations. By generating random shadows and highlights on images, our approach challenges the neural network during training, fostering immunity to input corruptions encountered in real-world scenarios. As a parameter-free method, RSH can be seamlessly integrated into most vision-based learning tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSH not only significantly improves model resilience to lighting perturbations but also markedly reduces overfitting. Consequently, RSH should be regarded as essential for all vision-related learning systems. The code is available at: https://github.com/OsamaMazhar/Random-Shadows-Highlights.

We introduce an anomaly-detection approach designed to handle systematic anomalies—potentially statistically indistinguishable from legitimate inputs—that infiltrate control systems at their input and/or output points. This technique accommodates anomaly-free inputs drawn from a broad spectrum of random sequences, thereby enabling diverse applications. To demonstrate the method's functionality, result interpretation, and decision-making processes, we examine several real-world time series, transforming originally non-stationary data into stationary forms during analysis. Additionally, we present a controlled experiment utilizing anomaly-free inputs modeled by an ARMA time series under various contamination scenarios.

Contemporary minimax challenges, including generative adversarial networks and adversarial training, frequently operate within a nonconvex-nonconcave framework, making the development of efficient solution methods a priority. Recently, two extragradient (EG) variants have been investigated for this purpose. The first, EG+, is a two-time-scale EG method designed for smooth structured nonconvex-nonconcave settings, achieving a slow $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ convergence rate regarding the squared gradient norm, where $k$ represents the iteration count. The second, extra anchored gradient (EAG), incorporates an anchoring technique and is analyzed under smooth convex-concave conditions, delivering a rapid $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ rate on the squared gradient norm. Building on EG+ and EAG, this paper introduces the fast extragradient (FEG) method—a two-time-scale EG with anchoring—that attains a fast $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ rate for smooth structured nonconvex-nonconcave problems where the saddle-gradient operator satisfies the negative comonotonicity condition. Additionally, a backtracking line-search variant of FEG, termed FEG-A, is developed to handle scenarios where problem parameters are unavailable, and stochastic analysis for FEG is also presented.

The spatial configurations of the lowest $0_1^+$, $0_2^+$, $2_1^+$, and $2_2^+$ states in the $^{12}$C nucleus are investigated using the $3\alpha$ model and the Buck, Friedrich, and Wheatley $\alpha\alpha$ potential, which incorporates Pauli-forbidden states in $S$ and $D$ waves. These forbidden states within the three-body system are addressed via the exact orthogonalization method. Analysis reveals that the ground state and excited $2_1^+$ bound state energies are primarily driven by partial waves with $(\lambda, \ell) = (2,2)$ and $(\lambda, \ell) = (4,4)$, respectively. Consistent with prior findings, these bound states emerge from critical eigenstates of the three-body Pauli projector within the $0^+$ and $2^+$ functional spaces. These specific eigenstates facilitate quantum phase transitions from a weakly bound, "gas-like" phase to a deeply bound "quantum liquid" phase. Conversely, for the Hoyle resonance ($0_2^+$) and its analog ($2_2^+$), the dominant contributions arise from $(\lambda, \ell) = (0,0)$ and $(\lambda, \ell) = (2,2)$ configurations, respectively. Probability density estimates for the $^{12}$C ground state ($0_1^+$) and $2_1^+$ excited bound state exhibit a predominantly triangular structure, with $\alpha$ particles separated by approximately 2.5 fm. In stark contrast, the Hoyle resonance and its analog display a distinct structure resembling $^8$Be + $\alpha$. Within the Hoyle state, the final $\alpha$ particle orbits the doublet at distances ranging from 3.0 to 5.0 fm. Similarly, in the $2_2^+$ analog, two $\alpha$ particles are separated by roughly 15 fm, while the third $\alpha$ particle can move significantly further from the doublet, reaching distances up to 30.0 fm.

By applying a generalized Madelung transformation, we establish the hydrodynamic form of the Dirac equation for fermions in arbitrary curved spacetimes interacting with an electromagnetic field. This yields Dirac-Euler equations comprising a continuity relation and a first integral of the Bernoulli equation. Through a comparison with the Klein-Gordon equation, we derive the balance equation for fermionic particles. Furthermore, leveraging the correspondence between fermions and bosons, we formulate the hydrodynamic representation of the Weyl equation, which represents the chiral variant of the Dirac equation.

Recent years have seen significant interest in quantum nonreciprocal devices due to their ability to facilitate unidirectional quantum routing and noise isolation. This study demonstrates that spin-orbit interactions (SOI) affecting propagating phonons within a rotating acoustic ring cavity can shift resonance frequencies, thereby enabling nonreciprocal phonon blockade. By adjusting system parameters, researchers can induce nonreciprocal single- and two-phonon blockade, as well as phonon-induced tunneling, depending on the direction from which the cavity is driven. To achieve this phonon blockade, the sublevels of the lower orbit branch of the ground state of silicon-vacancy (SiV) color centers embedded in a diamond membrane are utilized to generate self-interactions among the phonons. Ultimately, this approach offers a pathway to develop acoustic nonreciprocal components, such as directional acoustic switches and quantum noise isolators, which could advance acoustic information network processing.

This study aims to design a PID controller for a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy model by utilizing the particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm. While conventional gain tuning methods, such as the Ziegler-Nichols (ZN) technique, often result in significant overshoot, modern heuristic approaches like PSO are adopted to improve upon these traditional methods. Given the considerations of computational efficiency, this paper relies exclusively on PSO. The findings demonstrate the benefits of employing a PSO-based optimization strategy for PID tuning.

This study presents the inaugural collider search for dark matter originating from a strongly coupled hidden sector, utilizing a dataset of 138 fb$^{-1}$ acquired by the CMS detector at the CERN LHC operating at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The proposed hidden sector interacts with the Standard Model through a heavy, leptophobic Z' mediator generated as a resonance in proton-proton collisions. This mediator decays into two "semivisible" jets, which consist of both visible components and invisible dark matter. Consequently, the resulting signature features moderate missing energy aligned with one of the jets—a characteristic often overlooked in conventional dark matter analyses. No structures consistent with the signal were observed in the dijet transverse mass spectra. Under the assumption that the Z' couples universally to SM quarks with a strength of 0.25, an inclusive search relevant to any model displaying this kinematic profile excludes mediator masses between 1.5 and 4.0 TeV at a 95% confidence level, contingent on other signal parameters. To improve sensitivity for this specific class of hidden sector models, a boosted decision tree (BDT) was trained using jet substructure variables to differentiate semivisible jets from Standard Model background jets. When the BDT identifies each jet in the dijet system as semivisible, the excluded mediator mass range extends to 5.1 TeV across broader signal parameter spaces. These findings represent the first-time exclusion of a wide spectrum of strongly coupled hidden sector models.

In 2003, G. Lapenta introduced a novel class of soliton-like solutions to the Grad-Shafranov Equations (GSE). By identifying a specific pair of transformations for the free fields $p$ (hydrodynamical fluid pressure) and $B_z$ (the z-component of the magnetic induction field), he successfully mapped the Helmholtz Equation to the Non-Linear Schrödinger Equation (NLSE) with cubic non-linearity. The following year, G.N. Throumoulopoulos et al. challenged Lapenta's work, arguing that his proposed field transformations were mathematically incoherent and offering an alternative perspective. In response later that same year, Lapenta provided numerical simulations within a Magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) plasma framework that confirmed the existence of solitonic structures. This present work aims to establish a critical condition for a complex poloidal flux function $\psi$ within a planar $(x,y)$ framework, yielding a class of pseudo-general NLSEs that validate the field transformation functionals proposed by both G. Lapenta and G.N. Throumoulopoulos et al.

We introduce a nonparametric specification test based on series for regression functions involving spatially dependent data, where the spatial dimension represents a broad economic or social context. The framework accommodates diverse dependence structures, including parametric, semiparametric, and combinations thereof, with dimensions that may increase, thereby encompassing a wide array of scenarios such as spatial error models of varying complexity. Under a novel condition ensuring smooth spatial dependence, the test statistic converges asymptotically to a standard normal distribution. To demonstrate this result, we derive a central limit theorem for quadratic forms in linear processes within an increasing dimension framework. A simulation study evaluates the test's finite sample performance, validates and demonstrates a bootstrap procedure, and real-world data applications illustrate the test's utility.

The practical applicability of registration is primarily governed by three factors: accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. In real-time contexts, robustness and efficiency take precedence. To enhance these capabilities, we formulate multi-view registration as a clustering problem. By uniformly sampling centroids from the initially aligned point sets, we achieve a highly efficient and effective clustering process. Each point is then assigned to a specific cluster, with corresponding updates made to the cluster centroids. Following this, the geometric shape formed by all centroids is utilized to sequentially estimate rigid transformations for each point set. To ensure both accuracy and stability, we iteratively alternate between clustering and transformation estimation across all point sets. Evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets, alongside comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, confirm that our approach effectively delivers the required efficiency and robustness for registering multi-view point sets.
