To achieve optimal performance, UEs would need to be spaced approximately 30° apart in azimuth and 15° in elevation, a condition that is challenging to satisfy in practical scenarios.

MBA (mixed boolean and arithmetic) expressions are difficult to simplify, a characteristic exploited by malware to obfuscate code and impede analyst diagnosis. Although high-performance MBA simplification techniques exist, they are limited to "linear" MBA expressions, enabling efficient logic or term-rewriting solutions. These constraints, however, are inadequate for the general MBA expressions typically found in malware. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of a "semi-linear" MBA expression, a new category extending beyond linear forms, and present SSLEM, a novel MBA simplifier grounded in the simplification of semi-linear expressions and program synthesis.

Driven by the pseudogap-Fermi liquid transition in doped Mott insulators, we investigate excitations within a $t$-$J$ model featuring random, all-to-all hopping and exchange. We frame the stability of quasiparticles—specifically spin-1/2 fermions, spin-1 magnons, and emergent Jordan-Wigner spinless fermions—as a localization problem within the many-body Hilbert space, analyzed using the FEAST eigensolver algorithm. At low doping levels, magnons and JW fermions remain well-defined, whereas spin-1/2 fermions are unstable. However, once doping exceeds a critical threshold near $p_c = 1/3$, the stability of these species reverses. In the vicinity of this critical doping, all quasiparticles become ill-defined, indicating that the critical point corresponds to a localization transition in the many-body Hilbert space.

We establish a local-global theory for blocks within profinite groups. For a field $k$ of characteristic $p$ and a profinite group $G$, the completed group algebra $k[[G]]$ decomposes into a product $\prod_{i\in I}B_i$ of closed indecomposable algebras, known as the blocks of $G$. To every block $B$, we associate a pro-$p$ subgroup of $G$, termed the defect group, which is unique up to conjugacy. We provide multiple characterizations of this defect group, drawing parallels with those for finite group blocks. Our principal result is a Brauer correspondence linking the blocks of $G$ possessing a specific defect group $D$ to the blocks of the normalizer $N_G(D)$ that share the same defect group $D$.

Observations of solar flare ribbons reveal significant fine structure characterized by breaking wave-like perturbations and spirals, the origin of which remains unclear but may be linked to tearing instability within the flare current sheet. This study investigates that connection by constructing an analytical three-dimensional magnetic field model representing an erupting flux rope situated above a flare current sheet. By incorporating small-scale flux ropes—representative of those generated during tearing instability in the current layer—and applying the squashing factor to the solar surface to map the presumed flare ribbons and their fine details, our analysis indicates a direct correlation between ribbon fine structure and current sheet tearing, primarily driven by oblique tearing modes. Depending on the size, position, and twist of these small-scale flux ropes, the model produces breaking wave-like and spiral features within the ribbon's hooks and straight segments that closely resemble observed phenomena. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the chirality (handedness) of these spirals or waves must match that of the main ribbon's hooks. Consequently, we conclude that tearing in the flare current layer offers a plausible explanation for the spirals and wave-like patterns observed in flare ribbons.

LHCb's superior secondary vertex reconstruction and resolution have been leveraged to create inclusive tagging algorithms for c and b-jets. Using the complete Run 1 dataset from LHCb at 7 and 8 TeV, the study validates these algorithms' performance. By analyzing muon+jet final states, researchers measured the charge asymmetries for W+c and W+b jets, as well as production ratios comparing W+c,b jets to W+ jets and W+ jets to Z+ jets. Additionally, the forward top production cross-section was determined using the muon+b-jet final state. All obtained results align with standard model predictions.

Consider the linear program $\max\;c^{\top}x:Ax\leq b$ with an $m\times n$ integral matrix $A$. In 1986, Cook, Gerards, Schrijver, and Tardos demonstrated that if an optimal solution $x^{*}$ is given and an optimal integral solution $z^{*}$ exists, then one can select $z^{*}$ such that $\left\Vert x^{*}-z^{*}\right\Vert _{\infty}<n\Delta$, where $\Delta$ represents the maximum magnitude of any subdeterminant of $A$. An open question has since persisted regarding the improvement of this bound, particularly when $b$ is also integral. This manuscript establishes that for $n\geq2$, the term $n\Delta$ can be reduced to $\frac{n}{2}\cdot\Delta$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under specific conditions, the factor $n$ can be eliminated completely.

In device-independent quantum information, the correlations between local measurement results observed by spatially separated parties in a Bell test are fundamental. Although it has long been established that the set of correlations permitted by quantum theory lies strictly between the Bell-local and no-signaling sets, numerous questions regarding the geometry of this quantum set remain unresolved. In this work, we re-examine the conditions under which the boundary of the quantum set coincides with the no-signaling set within the simplest Bell scenario. Specifically, we demonstrate that self-testing is achievable in nontrivial classes of these shared boundaries, extending beyond the previously known examples of Hardy-type correlations, and we offer numerical evidence supporting the robustness of these findings. As a secondary result, we show that if qubit strategies producing an extremal nonlocal correlation are local-unitarily equivalent, a self-testing statement based on that correlation holds. Notably, all self-testing correlations identified on the no-signaling boundary are provably non-exposed. We also provide an analogous characterization for the set $\mathcal{M}$ of quantum correlations derived from finite-dimensional maximally entangled states. In deriving this latter result, we establish that all correlations in $\mathcal{M}$ within the simplest Bell scenario can be expressed as convex combinations of those attainable via a Bell pair and projective measurements. Consequently, we determine the maximal Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Bell inequality violation achievable by any maximally entangled two-qudit state and derive a no-go theorem concerning the self-testing of such states.

Handwriting recognition is advancing rapidly, creating fresh possibilities for stylus-driven interfaces. Specifically, note-taking apps can evolve into smarter user experiences by integrating features such as autocomplete and built-in search. This study conducted a gesture elicitation session with 21 participants, who were asked to envision interactions with a hypothetical intelligent note-taking application. Our findings reveal consensus on the proposed gestures; while familiar actions like double-taps and long presses remain common, several innovative interactions—such as dragging selected content to hotspots or utilizing annotations—were also widely suggested. Furthermore, we examine the mental models participants employed to justify their gestures and identify the types of feedback necessary to encourage a shift toward more stylus-centric workflows.

This review examines measurements of the extragalactic background light (EBL) intensity spanning from radio waves to gamma-rays across more than 20 decades of wavelength. The cosmic microwave background (CMB) stands as the most precisely measured spectrum, achieving accuracy exceeding 99%. In contrast, measurements of the cosmic optical background (COB), centered at 1 micron, are significantly affected by zodiacal light caused by interplanetary dust within the inner Solar System. Consequently, the most reliable COB data currently derive from an indirect method analyzing the gamma-ray spectra of luminous blazars, where absorption features arise from pair production with COB photons. The cosmic infrared background (CIB), which peaks near 100 microns, represents an energetically significant component with intensity matching the optical background; this discovery enabled extensive far-infrared and sub-millimeter observations that revealed dusty, starbursting galaxies. The role of these galaxies in cosmic evolution remains a vibrant topic in modern astrophysics. Conversely, the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) background remains largely unexplored and poses measurement challenges due to high Galactic background noise and absorption by the intergalactic medium at EUV and soft X-ray energies. Additionally, we summarize current knowledge regarding spatial anisotropies and angular power spectra of intensity fluctuations. We advocate for a precise direct measurement of the COB between 0.1 and 5 microns using a small-aperture telescope positioned either beyond 5 AU from the Sun or outside the ecliptic plane. Future applications of such measurements include refining our understanding of TeV-era backgrounds and investigating spectral distortions in both the CMB and CIB.

We report radio observations of the millisecond pulsar PSR J0621+1002 conducted with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST). This pulsar exhibits periodic pulse intensity modulations in both its first and third pulse components. The fluctuation spectrum of the first component displays a single peak at $3.0\pm0.1$ pulse periods, whereas the third component reveals two diffuse peaks located at $3.0\pm0.1$ and $200\pm1$ pulse periods. Single pulse timing analysis was performed, allowing the pulses to be categorized into two distinct classes based on post-fit timing residuals. While we investigated the potential timing precision gains by utilizing only pulses from a single class or specifically bright pulses, no improvement in timing precision was achieved.

Although numerous resources exist for podcasters on how to craft engaging spoken content, there is a notable lack of data-driven research linking linguistic style to listener engagement. This study examines the relationship between engagement and various factors—including vocabulary diversity, distinctiveness, emotional tone, and syntax—by analyzing creators' written descriptions and audio transcripts. We developed models using diverse textual representations to demonstrate that these features are highly predictive of engagement. Our findings evaluate common beliefs regarding stylistic elements in successful podcasts, confirming certain aspects while offering novel insights into others.

I examine the higher-order terms in the Seeley expansion of the heat kernel, which vanish as inverse powers of the UV cutoff $\Lambda$ for smooth metrics. I demonstrate that these terms generate an anomalous contribution to the string effective action following the cancellation of uncertainties, $\Lambda^{-2}\times \Lambda^2$. For the Polyakov string, these anomalies exactly match the one-loop results derived by KPZ-DDK for Liouville theory using conformal field theory methods. However, for the Nambu-Goto string, I observe a deviation from this result, indicating that the two string formulations may yield different outcomes.

Systems biology employs extensive networks of biochemical reactions to simulate cellular functions, spanning from molecular to cellular scales. The dynamics of dissipative reaction networks featuring widely separated time scales can be characterized as a series of successive equilibrations involving different subsets of system variables. Specifically, polynomial systems with separation reach equilibrium when at least two monomials of opposite signs share the same order of magnitude and overshadow the remaining terms. These equilibrations and the resulting truncated dynamics—derived by removing the dominated terms—are naturally expressed within tropical analysis, providing a framework for model reduction.

We demonstrate that selecting control targets based on a quadratic function of phase dispersion allows the duration of broadband universal control pulses to be reduced by half. These pulses execute a broadband universal rotation around an axis in the Bloch sphere representation of two-level systems, defined by the aforementioned phase dispersion function. Furthermore, we introduce an effective optimal control technique designed to prevent convergence into local extrema traps.

Array operations offer a highly efficient method for performing common filtering and basic aggregation tasks, which are fundamental to the initial stages of particle physics analysis, including selection, vector manipulation, and histogram generation. The upcoming High Luminosity run of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), set to begin in 2026, will demand that physicists process datasets exceeding a petabyte in size and repeatedly analyze hundreds of terabytes that cannot reside in memory. Declarative programming addresses this by decoupling the physicist's analytical intent from the underlying mechanics of data discovery, distributed processing, and efficient execution required to produce results promptly. This paper introduces a prototype library that enables various subsystems to collaborate through an array-programming declarative interface, featuring a ServiceX data-delivery component and an awkward array subsystem working together to generate requested data using ATLAS xAOD datasets.

This paper investigates the viability of active learning in operational contexts, specifically addressing the conflict between standard active learning heuristics—which prioritize pixels based on uncertainty—and user confidence in labeling, which depends on pixel context homogeneity and scene familiarity. We introduce a filtering mechanism utilizing a classifier trained to predict user labeling confidence, thereby reducing queries where the user cannot assign a class. The study thoroughly examines the model's ability to learn user confidence and analyzes how resolution impacts this learning process. Experiments conducted on two QuickBird images of varying resolutions (with and without pansharpening), involving groups of users, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed filtering scheme. This approach outperforms traditional active learning by maximizing the proportion of useful queries.

This study details the magnetic architectures of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 as revealed by powder neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, alternating-bond spin-3/2 chains of Ru1 and Ru2 emerge. Below 15 K, the Ru1 moments become ordered while the Ru2 moments remain disordered (paramagnetic), suggesting a partially disordered (PD) state despite the high similarity between the two Ru sites. Conversely, in Nd3RuO7, Ru1 and Ru2 ions constitute independent uniform chains where both moment types order below 17.5 K. The PD state observed in Tb3RuO7 is likely driven by magnetic frustration within the exchange interactions. Specifically, the internal magnetic field produced by ordered Tb moments differs between Ru1 and Ru2 sites; we hypothesize that this nonuniform internal field amplifies the disparity in properties between the Ru1 and Ru2 moments.

The autoplotly package enables the automatic creation of interactive visualizations for a wide range of statistical results supported by the ggfortify package, offering both plotly and ggplot2 styling. These generated plots remain interactive and can be effortlessly extended using the syntax of both ggplot2 and plotly.

We develop a spinorial framework for six-dimensional differential geometry to investigate low-rank tensor fields, focusing particularly on the Weyl tensor. By leveraging the full SO(6) symmetry, we conduct an analysis analogous to the four-dimensional case, revealing insights that are difficult to discern through traditional tensorial methods. Within this spinor formalism, we classify the Weyl tensor by recasting it as a mapping between 3-vectors. This classification demonstrates a deep connection to the integrability of maximally isotropic subspaces, thereby providing a natural setting to extend the Goldberg-Sachs theorem. Furthermore, by working in complexified spaces, we demonstrate that results applicable to any signature can be derived by selecting the appropriate real slice.

Machine learning has become a cornerstone of data analysis in High Energy Physics (HEP), offering substantial gains in sensitivity over conventional methods by detecting nuanced patterns within high-dimensional feature spaces. However, these subtle patterns are often poorly captured by the simulations used to train models, which can lead to heightened sensitivity to systematic uncertainties. Rather than adhering to the traditional approach of building analysis strategies that remain invariant to such uncertainties, this study investigates classifiers explicitly designed to account for uncertainties and their associated nuisance parameters. We demonstrate that incorporating this dependence can actually boost sensitivity to parameters of interest. Through experiments on both a synthetic Gaussian dataset and a realistic HEP dataset modeling Higgs boson decays into tau leptons, we show that this uncertainty-aware methodology outperforms alternative machine learning strategies in terms of sensitivity.

Natural variations play a crucial role in the progression of infectious diseases, particularly coronavirus. Therefore, it is essential to account for the impact of irregular disturbances in epidemic modeling. This study first introduces a mathematical SIR model for coronavirus, incorporating L\'evy noise to perturb the contact rate, a method necessary for effective disease protection and control. We analyze the dynamics of the deterministic model and establish the existence and uniqueness of global positive solutions for the stochastic version. Furthermore, we investigate conditions governing the extinction and persistence of the infection. The basic reproduction number is derived to determine whether the disease will vanish or persist. Numerical results indicate that when noise levels are high or low, the COVID-19 infection disappears if the reproduction number is below one, whereas the epidemic can be controlled if the reproduction number exceeds one. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to illustrate these phenomena.

We offer high-precision forecasts for Z boson-pair production in electron-positron collisions, incorporating the complete set of one-loop scattering amplitudes, which includes electroweak (EW) corrections alongside soft and hard QED radiation. Our detailed numerical analysis spans from full EW corrections to pure QED corrections, with a specific emphasis on how initial beam polarization influences the production rate. Additionally, we present findings on left-right asymmetry and angular distributions. Initial beam polarizations significantly impact radiative corrections; utilizing completely polarized beams of $e^-_L$ and $e^+_R$ yields an improvement of approximately threefold. We observe that radiative corrections substantially alter the production rate, often resulting in a total relative correction of several tens of percent. Consequently, achieving percent-level accuracy in the process $e^- e^+ \to ZZ$ necessitates the inclusion of full EW corrections.

This research examines the one-phase and two-phase Muskat problems across all dimensions, characterized as quasilinear parabolic equations governing a free boundary. We establish that sufficiently small initial data within the scaling-invariant homogeneous Besov space $\dot B^1_{\infty, 1}$ guarantee unique global solutions. The demonstration relies on a novel structural property of the Dirichlet-Neumann operator, enabling a robust fixed-point approach. Consequently, the initial data requirement remains strictly within $\dot B^1_{\infty, 1}$, and the solution map exhibits Lipschitz continuity under this same topology. Notably, for the general Muskat problem, the previously established scaling-invariant result relied on the Wiener algebra combined with an $L^2$ assumption, a space that is strictly narrower than $\dot B^1_{\infty, 1}$.

Investigating the Cosmic Dawn—the epoch when the first stars and galaxies emerged—represents one of the final frontiers in modern astronomy and cosmology. The redshifted 21-cm emission from neutral hydrogen serves as a distinctive tool to unlock this era for both astrophysical and cosmological research. The tentative detection of the 21-cm global signal by the EDGES team at $z \sim 17$ highlights the necessity for interferometric observations to distinguish among various models attempting to explain this surprising finding. The NenuFAR Cosmic-Dawn Key-Science Program seeks to achieve this detection within the redshift range $z \sim 15 - 31$ using the NenuFAR radio telescope, a novel SKA precursor situated at the Station de Radioastronomie de Nan\c{c}ay that began operations in 2019. Thanks to its compact design, the telescope exhibits exceptional sensitivity to the large-scale 21-cm signal; reaching the sensitivity required for extreme models demands only 100 hours of observation, whereas standard models require 1000 hours. Observations have commenced, with nearly 500 hours already accumulated on the North Celestial Pole field. This contribution presents the project overview, our initial results, and specific advancements in calibration and radio frequency interference (RFI) mitigation tailored to this new instrument.

Many existing blockchains suffer from insufficient trust guarantees, which restricts their applications and user participation. Current methods to enhance trust by leveraging stronger blockchains, such as through checkpointing, necessitate that the weaker chains surrender their sovereignty. This paper introduces a suite of protocols enabling multiple blockchains to interact and form a unified ledger with significantly improved trust. We demonstrate that even if several participating chains lose their security guarantees, the resulting combined ledger remains secure; the proposed TrustBoost protocols achieve the optimal threshold for tolerating insecure chains. Moreover, these protocols function solely through smart contracts, requiring no modifications to the underlying consensus mechanisms of the involved blockchains—a concept termed "consensus on top of consensus." Designed to be lightweight, the protocols can be applied to specific transactions, such as those of high value. We validate their practicality by implementing and deploying TrustBoost as cross-chain smart contracts within the Cosmos ecosystem using roughly 3,000 lines of open-source Rust code. Our evaluation on a local testnet involving 10 Cosmos chains indicates that TrustBoost incurs a gas cost of approximately $2 and a latency of 2 minutes per request, aligning with the costs observed on high-security chains like Bitcoin or Ethereum.

This study establishes necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for abstract constrained mathematical programming problems within locally convex spaces, subject to novel qualification conditions. The methodology leverages the geometric characteristics of specific mappings, notably their structure as differences of convex functions, alongside techniques involving generalized differentiation, including subdifferentials and coderivatives. These tools prove effective even when operating outside the constraints of Asplund spaces. The paper further develops applications to infinite, stochastic, and semi-definite programming in distinct sections.

Computer simulations of the primitive model featuring explicit microions have been used to calculate structural correlations within a binary mixture of charged and uncharged spheres. For aqueous suspensions characterized by a high dielectric constant, the traditional DLVO theory of linear screening, when enhanced with hard-core interactions, quantitatively matches the structural correlations derived from the full primitive model. Conversely, in systems with lower dielectric contrast, the intensifying Coulomb coupling between macro- and microions leads to significant discrepancies. We observe a fluid-fluid phase separation into distinct regions enriched with either charged or uncharged particles—a phenomenon that DLVO theory fails to predict. These findings can be validated through scattering or real-space experiments involving mixtures of charged and uncharged colloids or nanoparticles.

This study examines a queueing system where the server represents Euclidean space and customers are modeled as random closed sets (RACS) within that same space. These RACS arrive via a Poisson process, each possessing a random service duration; specifically, if hail falls on a Euclidean plane, the service time corresponds to the hailstone's height, while the RACS represents its footprint. The server operates at a speed of 1. Service follows a strict exclusion rule: intersecting RACS cannot be served concurrently, and the discipline is First-In-First-Out (FIFO). In this scenario, only RACS touching the ground melt at speed 1, while others wait. A specific RACS must remain queued until all preceding RACS that intersect it have completely melted before it begins to melt. We derive the evolution equations for this queue and demonstrate its stability under a sufficiently low arrival intensity, assuming the typical diameter of the RACS and their typical service times possess finite exponential moments. Additionally, we analyze the percolation characteristics of the stationary configuration of the RACS within the queue.

The conventional practice of manually designing priors, such as sparsity, for addressing inverse problems is gradually giving way to richer learned priors, exemplified by deep generative networks. This study investigates the theoretical underpinnings of this learning-driven methodology. For specific generative network structures, we demonstrate a straightforward non-convex algorithmic framework that (a) offers linear convergence guarantees for both linear and nonlinear inverse problems and (b) outperforms standard methods like back-propagation in empirical settings. Our assertions are validated through experiments on diverse inverse problems. Furthermore, we introduce an extension capable of managing model mismatch, where the generative prior does not perfectly align with the data. Collectively, these contributions lay the groundwork for the principled application of generative models in inverse problems, enhancing our algorithmic comprehension of the process.

We introduce a comprehensive induction method capable of verifying a subset of quantified and quantifier-free properties for programs that handle arrays of parametric size N. Unlike traditional approaches that induct over individual loops, our technique performs induction directly on the entire program—including those with multiple loops—by leveraging the program parameter N. Notably, this method eliminates the need to generate or utilize loop-specific invariants. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we developed a prototype tool named Vajra. We further compare Vajra's performance against several state-of-the-art tools using a collection of benchmarks involving array manipulation.

It is a well-established result by Hahn and Mazurkiewicz that every Peano continuum is the continuous image of the unit interval. We demonstrate that the process of selecting a continuous mapping with a Peano continuum as its range can be performed in a Borel measurable manner. Likewise, we identify a Borel measurable method that assigns a continuous surjection from the Cantor set onto any given nonempty compact metric space, utilizing the Burgess selection theorem. Finally, we establish a Borel measurable procedure for assigning an arc connecting two chosen points within a Peano continuum.

Recent breakthroughs in transformation optics (TO) and metasurfaces have enabled the creation of groundbreaking devices, including invisibility cloaks. Nevertheless, inherent limitations in these approaches restrict their utility in real-world applications. Specifically, traditional TO methods often require bulky coating layers that are as thick as or thicker than the concealed object itself. This paper introduces an ultrathin carpet cloak derived from coordinate transformation, capable of hiding objects of arbitrary shape and size using an anisotropic material known as an infinitely anisotropic medium (IAM). Unlike prior metasurface-based carpet cloaks, the proposed IAM offers concealment from all viewing and incident angles while maintaining extreme thinness relative to the object's dimensions. Furthermore, this material bypasses the complexities typically associated with conventional transformation optics, facilitating easier implementation in practical settings. To validate the cloak's performance, multiple full-wave simulations were conducted. Additionally, the IAM was realized as a proof of concept using effective medium theory, yielding results that align closely with theoretical predictions. This innovative material represents a significant advancement toward true invisibility cloaks and holds substantial promise for enhancing the practical deployment of other TO-based devices.

Our findings demonstrate that the detachment of a flat punch from a viscoelastic substrate exhibits a straightforward behavior, bounded by Kendall's elastic solutions (at both relaxed and instantaneous moduli) and the cohesive strength limit. We observe minimal dependence of the pull-off force on specific loading details, such as preload indentation depth or loading rate, making this scenario significantly simpler than that of a spherical punch. The pull-off force reaches its maximum at the highest unloading speeds, where energy dissipation is negligible; this contrasts with de Gennes' theories on viscoelastic semi-infinite crack propagation, which link increased work of adhesion to dissipation. Furthermore, additional qualitative differences with dissipation-based models are required to account for finite size effects.

Despite the rapid proliferation of blockchain implementations, there remains a significant lack of systematic research comparing their performance characteristics. Such analysis is vital for assessing the fundamental trade-offs inherent in new consensus protocols and their deployments. Typically, these performance constraints are examined using ad-hoc benchmarking tools that focus narrowly on consensus algorithms. However, evaluating design choices effectively demands macro-benchmarks capable of delivering uniform, comprehensive system-level assessments rather than metrics for isolated components. To bridge this gap, we developed Gromit, a generic framework for blockchain analysis. Gromit models each tested system as a transaction fabric where clients submit transactions to validators. Utilizing Gromit, we conducted the most extensive blockchain study to date, examining seven representative systems with diverse consensus models. By applying a synthetic workload, we identified peak performance in terms of transaction throughput and scalability, revealing that throughput fails to scale with the number of validators. Furthermore, we investigated system resilience against network delays, finding that permissioned blockchains are highly sensitive to network conditions.

Research has demonstrated that learning-based image compression can rival the performance of leading transform-based codecs, inspiring the creation of new standards like JPEG-AI. These emerging standards specifically prioritize compression systems designed for both human and machine interpretation. This paper focuses on learning-based schemes where compressed-domain representations enable direct visual processing and computer vision tasks, a feature explicitly included in the JPEG-AI standard's scope. Our work utilizes the JPEG-AI framework to perform material and texture recognition using latent representations at various bit-rates. For comparison, we evaluate results using fully decoded pixel-domain images and original uncompressed images. The findings indicate that while decoding images can degrade classification accuracy for models trained on original data, retraining with decoded images significantly narrows this performance gap on the tested texture dataset. Furthermore, compressed-domain classification achieves competitive Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy using a more compact, reduced-complexity model.
We derive a formula that calculates the number of isomorphic classes of element systems possessing characters over finite commutative group $G$.

To better align with the realities of relativistic heavy ion collisions than the standard thermal equilibrium assumption used for calculating baryon number susceptibilities, this paper models the collision products as isotropic systems featuring a temperature gradient. Furthermore, quarks are treated as quasi-particles possessing thermal masses. Utilizing the Boltzmann transport equation, we derived results for the experimental observables $S\sigma$ and $\kappa\sigma^2$. Our findings reveal a discrepancy in values alongside a dependence on centrality, suggesting a potential link between baryon number susceptibilities and the temperature gradient within the QGP.

Electrospraying is a potent method for producing charged micro- and nanodroplets, a field that has garnered significant attention over the last century, culminating in a Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Despite this success, its application within microfluidic systems remains restricted, primarily because the behavior of the dispersing fluid when submerged in an immiscible host liquid is not yet fully understood. Immersed electrosprays generally exhibit properties nearly identical to those in air, except when surfactants are introduced into the host liquid to stabilize emulsions in lab-on-chip devices. This study reviews the characteristics of immersed electrosprays in surfactant-free baths and systematically investigates the system's response to increasing surfactant concentrations. The identified regimes are analyzed and compared against both classical and recent experimental, theoretical, and numerical research. A complex phenomenology emerges when surface tension is permitted to vary; specifically, the reduced surface tension regimes yield lower levels of electrification, a feature that could be advantageous for biological or biomedical applications where free charge poses a risk to encapsulated entities.

Learning curves, originally a concept from the social sciences, have been adapted within machine learning to evaluate an algorithm's performance relative to specific resources, such as the count of training examples or iterations. These curves are crucial in various machine learning scenarios, particularly for data acquisition, early stopping during training, and model selection. By modeling these curves, practitioners can determine early on whether an algorithm and its hyperparameter configuration are viable, often accelerating the model selection process. Numerous methods have been developed to leverage learning curves for decision-making; some address binary questions about whether an algorithm meets a performance threshold within a given budget, while more advanced approaches predict the full trajectory of the learning curve. This paper introduces a framework that categorizes these approaches based on three criteria: the decision context addressed, the fundamental learning curve question answered, and the resource types utilized. We review existing literature and classify relevant papers according to this framework.

This paper details recent advancements in the front-end and back-end systems of the four 20-meter radio telescopes comprising the Japanese Very-Long-Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) project, known as VLBI Exploration of Radio Astrometry (VERA). We provide an overview of dual-circular polarization receiving systems and ultrawideband recording units (capable of 16 Gbit s$^{-1}$) installed on each telescope, operating at 22 and 43 GHz frequencies. The expanded bandwidth enhances sensitivity for continuum emission studies, while dual-polarization support facilitates investigations into magnetic fields within relativistic jets from supermassive black holes in active galactic nuclei, as well as in star-forming regions and around evolved stars. To demonstrate the current capabilities of VERA's polarimetry, we present linear polarization intensity maps of extragalactic sources at both 22 and 43 GHz derived from the latest test observations. Finally, we outline future scientific objectives and potential technical developments following the successful implementation of VLBI polarimetry with VERA.

To combat online abuse and misinformation, social media platforms have implemented diverse moderation policies and established corresponding community guidelines. This paper aims to examine these guidelines, practices, and related research to uncover research gaps, variations in moderation techniques, and challenges that both platforms and the broader research community must address. Specifically, we analyze and synthesize the content moderation guidelines of the fourteen most popular social media platforms within the US jurisdiction. Drawing from this analysis and over one hundred interdisciplinary studies on moderation strategies, we propose three distinct taxonomies. Our findings highlight the distinctions between moderation approaches used by mainstream platforms versus fringe ones. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of Section 230, the necessity of balancing transparency and opacity in moderation, the shift from a one-size-fits-all model to a more inclusive framework, and the critical need for collaborative human-AI systems.

This study examines how the average scalar curvature influences the conjugate radius, the mean area of geodesic spheres, the average volume of metric balls, and the total volume of a closed Riemannian manifold $N$ (or more broadly, a manifold with finite volume where the negative Ricci curvature integral on the unit tangent bundle $SN$ is finite). Specifically, we demonstrate that if the average scalar curvature exceeds the lower bound of the normalized Ricci curvature, the Bishop-Gromov estimate regarding the average volume of metric balls of any radius can be sharpened. Furthermore, we establish that a specific geometric integral exhibits a monotone decreasing behavior when the average scalar curvature is bounded from below. This finding yields a comparison theorem for the average total mean curvature of geodesic spheres with radii extending up to the injectivity radius of $N$.

Although state-of-the-art Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have excelled in social event detection within closed-set scenarios, they struggle in open-set environments due to the substantial data requirements for training and the inherent difficulty neural networks face with previously unseen data. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Quality-aware Self-improving Graph Neural Network (QSGNN), a framework designed to transfer knowledge from known to unknown events by utilizing high-quality known samples and robust knowledge transfer mechanisms. To maximize the utility of labeled data, we develop a novel supervised pairwise loss function augmented with an orthogonal inter-class relation constraint for training the backbone GNN encoder. The learned representations of known events act as strong reference points for unknown ones, significantly enhancing knowledge acquisition and transfer. When applying the model to unknown data, we employ reference similarity distribution vectors to generate pseudo pairwise labels, select samples, and assess their quality, ensuring reliability and effectiveness. Adhering to active learning principles, our approach selects diverse sample pairs using these pseudo labels to fine-tune the GNN encoder. Additionally, we propose a quality-guided optimization strategy that weights pseudo label contributions based on consistency. Comprehensive evaluations on two large-scale real-world social event datasets demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes effectively to unknown events.

Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a progressive neurological condition impacting over 5.8 million individuals, predominantly the elderly. Given the intricate nature of its symptoms and its resemblance to other neurological disorders, accurate early diagnosis typically necessitates the involvement of neurologists or PD specialists, a resource often unavailable to older adults. Consequently, this study integrates smart mobile devices with artificial intelligence to address this gap. We present a framework for a PD early detection system that evaluates both motor and non-motor symptoms. This model enables users to identify PD promptly in non-clinical environments and determine the severity of their specific symptoms. Furthermore, the anticipated outcomes aim to support PD rehabilitation and facilitate the detection of additional neurological conditions.

A primary challenge in our field involves characterizing the initial state of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) and restricting its parameters through sensitive experimental observables. Recent research indicates that the Pearson Correlation Coefficient between the $n$-th order flow vector ${\bm V}_n$ and the event-wise mean transverse momentum $[p_{\mathrm{T}}]$, denoted as $\rho_{n}({\bm V}_n,[p_{\mathrm{T}}])$, offers insights into source multiplicity and size, nuclear deformation, volume fluctuations, and initial momentum anisotropy in heavy-ion collisions. This proceeding details new, high-precision measurements of the ${\bm V}_n-[p_{\mathrm{T}}]$ correlation for harmonics $n=2$, 3, and 4 in $^{\mathrm{129}}\mathrm{Xe}+^{\mathrm{129}}\mathrm{Xe}$ and $^{\mathrm{208}}\mathrm{Pb}+^{\mathrm{208}}\mathrm{Pb}$ collisions utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The observed $\rho_{n}$ values exhibit a complex, non-monotonic relationship with centrality, $p_{\mathrm{T}}$, and $\eta$, indicating that various components of the initial state influence distinct regions of phase space. Furthermore, the ratio of $\rho_{2}$ between these two systems in the ultra-central region implies that $^{\mathrm{129}}\mathrm{Xe}$ possesses significant quadrupole deformation alongside notable triaxiality. Currently, no existing model successfully reproduces many of the trends observed in the data.

Beginning with the relativistic Boltzmann equation defined by a particle distribution function, we derived a virial relation for spherical structures within an expanding background under general relativity. This generalized relation was subsequently applied to a static, spherically symmetric case to highlight differences from the Newtonian formulation, and a corresponding relativistic Mass-Temperature relation for this scenario was established, offering applicability to astrophysical compact objects. Furthermore, applying our general virial relation to non-static structures in an expanding universe reveals an additional term typically overlooked in studies of structures influenced by dark energy.

The resource theory of quantum coherence was initially established by Baumgratz, Cramer, and Plenio [PRL 113, 140401 (2014)] and subsequently advanced by Winter and Yang [PRL 116, 120404 (2016)]. This study addresses the one-shot scenario of extracting pure coherence from a single resource state. Specifically, we calculate the distillable coherence achieving a target fidelity under incoherent operations (IO) by extending the Winter-Yang protocol. These findings are contrasted with distillable coherence under maximal incoherent operations (MIO) and dephasing-covariant incoherent operations (DIO), which were previously formulated as a semidefinite program by Regula et al. [PRL 121, 010401 (2018)]. Our results are expressed using smoothed min-relative entropy distance from the set of incoherent states, alongside a variant of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy distance, respectively. Additionally, one-shot distillable coherence is linked to one-shot randomness extraction. Furthermore, the derived one-shot formulas for IO, MIO, and DIO allow us to recover the optimal distillable rate in the many-copy asymptotic limit, yielding the relative entropy of coherence. These outcomes can be compared with earlier work by some of the current authors [Zhao et al., PRL 120, 070403 (2018)] regarding one-shot coherence formation under IO, MIO, DIO, and SIO. This comparison reveals that distillable coherence amounts are essentially equivalent for IO, DIO, and MIO, despite significant differences among these operation classes. We also connect distillable coherence under strictly incoherent operations (SIO) to a constrained hypothesis testing problem and explicitly demonstrate the presence of bound coherence under SIO in the asymptotic regime.

The fractional quantum Hall (FQH) effect at the filling factor $\nu=5/2$, first observed in GaAs heterostructures over three decades ago, remains a subject of intense study. Multiple theoretical models proposing distinct topological orders have been suggested to explain this state, with some predicting the existence of non-Abelian anyons—novel quasiparticles exhibiting unique properties. If confirmed, these anyons could serve as essential components for topological quantum computing. Despite their potential, the precise nature of the $\nu=5/2$ state continues to be debated. This chapter surveys the theoretical foundations, numerical findings, and experimental data associated with this intriguing FQH regime. Additionally, we examine recent advancements and their potential interpretations, while also outlining prospective avenues for future research aimed at clarifying the identity of the $5/2$ state.

Although self-supervision can enhance performance on downstream tasks, there remains no systematic method for choosing objectives that produce the most adaptable models. This study addresses this issue using daily time-series data from wearable sensors designed to detect the onset of influenza-like illness (ILI). First, we demonstrate that employing self-supervised learning to forecast next-day time-series values enables the creation of rich representations suitable for accurate ILI prediction. Second, we conduct an empirical evaluation of three distinct self-supervised objectives to determine their adaptability to ILI prediction. Our findings indicate that predicting the next day's resting heart rate or sleep duration in bed yields superior representations for ILI prediction. These results expand upon prior research highlighting the practical utility of self-supervised learning derived from activity data for improving health forecasts.

Recently, Voltage Source Converter-based High Voltage Direct Current links (VSC-HVDC) integrated into alternating current (AC) grids have garnered significant interest due to their potential to enhance the flexibility of modern power systems. Among various strategies, AC-line-emulation control has emerged as a straightforward yet effective alternative. This approach regulates power flow proportionally to the angular difference between the two AC terminals, enabling the system to automatically adapt power distribution during contingencies in parallel AC lines. While primarily designed for steady-state operation, this controller also influences dynamic system behavior, an aspect that has received insufficient analysis. Consequently, this paper investigates the impact of AC-line-emulation controllers on power system transient stability. Using PSS/E, nonlinear time-domain simulations were performed on a small test system featuring an embedded point-to-point VSC-HVDC link. The study utilized the critical clearing time (CCT) of a test fault to evaluate the overall system's transient stability margins. Finally, the paper offers design recommendations for AC-line-emulation controllers to ensure that transient stability is not compromised.

Image segmentation serves as the foundational stage for all image analysis tasks. Over several decades, numerous segmentation algorithms have been introduced in the literature with varying degrees of success. Recently, fuzzy energy-based active contour models have garnered significant research interest, leading to the development of diverse methodologies. An effective segmentation algorithm must demonstrate robust performance across a wide range of images, even when they contain noise, blur, low contrast, or region inhomogeneity. Nevertheless, most existing fuzzy energy-based active contour models have typically been assessed on a limited dataset. This article aims to review current fuzzy active contour models theoretically and experimentally evaluate them on an extensive collection of images under various conditions. Analyzing these models across a broad spectrum of images offers objective insights into their respective strengths and weaknesses. Finally, the paper addresses several critical issues and outlines future research directions in this specific field.

Software logs frequently capture critical runtime data to aid in troubleshooting, prompting numerous studies to leverage this information for building machine learning models that identify system anomalies. However, our empirical investigation reveals that current log-based anomaly detection methods are heavily compromised by parsing errors stemming from 1) out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words and 2) semantic misinterpretations, which can lead to the loss of vital detection information. To overcome these shortcomings, we introduce NeuralLog, an innovative approach that bypasses the need for log parsing entirely. Instead, NeuralLog derives the semantic meaning of raw log messages and encodes them as semantic vectors, which are then fed into a Transformer-based classifier capable of capturing contextual nuances within log sequences. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method effectively grasps the semantic content of logs and delivers precise anomaly detection. Notably, NeuralLog surpasses existing techniques, achieving F1-scores exceeding 0.95 across four public datasets.

Logo retrieval presents a significant challenge due to the subjective nature of defining similarity and the scarcity of known similar examples, unlike standard image retrieval tasks. To address this, we introduce a straightforward yet effective segment-based augmentation method designed to generate artificially similar logos for training deep neural networks. This novel approach differs from traditional image-level techniques by identifying specific segments within a logo and applying transformations such as rotation, scaling, and color modifications to them. Furthermore, we investigate whether the recently proposed Smooth-AP ranking-based loss function is superior for learning similarity in logo retrieval. Experiments conducted on the large-scale METU Trademark Dataset demonstrate that (i) our segment-based augmentation outperforms both baseline models and conventional image-level augmentation strategies, and (ii) Smooth-AP yields better results than traditional loss functions for this specific task.

Measuring the in-plane birefringence ($\Delta{n}$) of ultrathin films is difficult because material properties in this regime deviate significantly from those in bulk states. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) offers a high-resolution method to detect refractive index changes in such films. This study presents a simulation of SPR within a Kretschmann configuration designed to measure $\Delta{n}$ in organic thin films with nematic-like ordering on a 2D gold surface. Simulations revealed that the plasmonic field distribution on the gold surface is anisotropic, implying that its coupling with the ordered organic film will also be non-isotropic. Consequently, SPR measurements taken parallel and perpendicular to the optic axis (OA) of the in-plane nematic ordering yielded a non-zero difference in resonance angles ($\Delta\theta$). A calibration surface correlating $\Delta\theta$ with both film thickness and $\Delta{n}$ was established for shape-anisotropic, tilted molecules exhibiting nematic-like ordering. This calibration was applied to determine the $\Delta{n}$ of single-layer Langmuir-Blodgett films of cadmium stearate (CdSA) and 4'-octyl-4-biphenylcarbonitrile (8CB) deposited on SPR chips. While film thickness was determined via X-ray reflectivity, $\Delta\theta$ was measured using a custom-built SPR instrument. The results indicated $\Delta{n}$ values of 0.012 for the ultrathin CdSA film and 0.022 for the 8CB film.

We introduce a weighted quadrature scheme for hierarchical B-splines designed to enable the rapid construction of system matrices in adaptive isogeometric Galerkin methods utilizing graded hierarchical meshes. By leveraging a local tensor-product framework, we generalize the development of weighted rules from standard tensor-product bases to the hierarchical spline context. The resulting algorithm exhibits a computational cost linear with respect to the number of degrees of freedom and demonstrates improved performance as the spline degree increases. To validate the method's efficacy and verify theoretical predictions, we present a series of numerical experiments in both 2D and 3D.

This work details the design, fabrication, and low-power evaluation of a terahertz-driven field emission electron gun. The two-cell standing-wave structure is engineered to operate with a 110 GHz gyrotron, generating 360 keV electrons using 500 kW of input power. Various gun configurations were manufactured via high-precision diamond turning followed by copper electroforming. The field emission source consists of a copper tip with a 50 $\mu$m radius positioned halfway into the first cell. Cavity resonance frequencies were adjusted through mechanical azimuthal compression. Additionally, this study includes electromagnetic and particle simulations of the design, as well as cold test measurements of the fabricated components.

Analyzing how communities within developer social networks (DSNs) surrounding open-source software (OSS) projects evolve offers significant insights into the socio-technical dynamics of OSS development. While prior research indicates that community evolution can be characterized by specific patterns—such as splitting, shrinking, merging, expanding, emerging, and becoming extinct—current pattern-based methods are constrained in their ability to support quantitative analysis. Furthermore, treating these patterns as mutually exclusive may be problematic when describing community evolution. This study proposes that multiple patterns can occur concurrently between any pair of communities, albeit to varying degrees. To address this, we developed four entropy-based indices to quantify the extent of splitting, shrinking, merging, and expanding, respectively, providing a comprehensive and quantitative assessment of community evolution in DSNs. These indices possess desirable properties for quantification, including monotonicity and bounded maximum and minimum values that align with meaningful scenarios. Additionally, they can be integrated to describe complex patterns like emergence and extinction. Experiments conducted on real-world OSS projects validate the proposed indices, demonstrating their ability to effectively capture community evolution. The results align with existing approaches in detecting evolution patterns in DSNs with an accuracy of 94.1%. Moreover, the indices prove useful for predicting OSS team productivity, achieving an accuracy of 0.718. In conclusion, this approach represents one of the first methods to quantify the degree of community evolution across different patterns, showing great promise for future research and applications concerning DSNs and OSS development.

Accurate astrometry and a well-characterized point spread function (PSF) are fundamental for numerous astrophysical investigations, particularly time-delay cosmography, which utilizes strongly lensed quasars to measure the Hubble constant and other cosmological parameters. Uncertainties in the positions of multiply-imaged sources directly impact the precision of inferred distances and, consequently, the Hubble constant. Likewise, understanding the PSF wings is essential for separating the light of background sources from that of the foreground deflector. We analyzed adaptive optics (AO) images of the strong lens system J0659+1629, captured with the W. M. Keck Observatory's laser guide star AO system. Our findings demonstrate that utilizing a reconstructed PSF enables i) astrometric precision better than 1 milliarcsecond (mas), which meets the requirements for time-delay cosmography, and ii) the complete subtraction of point-like images, leaving residuals consistent with the noise floor. The developed methodology extends beyond strong lensing and is broadly applicable to various scientific scenarios involving multiple nearby point sources.

We investigate nonlocal conservation laws featuring a discontinuous flux function with $\mathsf{L}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ regularity in the spatial dimension. We establish the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions within the space $\mathsf{C}\big([0,T];\mathsf{L}^{1}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R})\big)$ and derive associated maximum principles. This well-posedness is attained through a specific reformulation as a fixed-point problem, which requires analyzing the existence, uniqueness, and stability of a particular class of discontinuous ordinary differential equations. At the ODE level, we contrast the solution concept introduced here with the standard Carath\'eodory and Filippov solutions.

We contend that a type IIB Euclidean supergravity configuration described by $\mathbb{R}\times S^1\times \mathbb{T}^8$ and featuring imaginary self-dual $F_1$ flux along $\mathbb{R}\times S^1$ fits within the sequence of $AdS_d\times S^d\times \mathbb{T}^{10-2d}$ vacua characterized by (imaginary) self-dual $F_d$ flux for $d\leq 5$. These vacua arise as near-horizon limits of D$(d-2)$/D$(8-d)$ branes and maintain supersymmetry when $d$ is odd. For the case $d=1$, we hypothesize that the signature of conformal symmetry in the dual matrix model is a zero free energy. This matrix dual, recently proposed in arXiv:2101.01732, extends the IKKT model by incorporating matrix interactions derived from strings connecting D$(-1)$ and D$7$ branes. We demonstrate that the associated supergravity solution possesses a vanishing on-shell action. Furthermore, specific $F_5$ fluxes must be activated as a result of a T-dual implementation of the Hanany-Witten effect.

We integrated Gaia EDR3 astrometry with precise photometry, employing a probabilistic mixture model to determine the systemic proper motions of 52 Milky Way dwarf spheroidal (dSph) satellite galaxies. For the 46 dSphs with known line-of-sight velocities from the literature, we calculated orbits within both a Milky Way potential and a combined Milky Way + Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) potential, identifying Car II, Car III, Hor I, Hyi I, Phx II, and Ret II as probable LMC satellites. We found that 40% of our sample exhibits a greater than 25% shift in pericenter and/or apocenter when using the MW + LMC potential. For these specific orbits, we performed Monte Carlo sampling to account for observational uncertainties in each dSph as well as uncertainties in the MW and LMC potentials. By comparing the average density of each dSph to the MW density at its pericenter, we predict that Ant II, Boo III, Cra II, Gru II, and Tuc III are undergoing tidal disruption. Additionally, dSphs with high ellipticity (CVn I, Her, Tuc V, UMa I, UMa II, UMi, and Wil 1) display a tendency for their orbital direction to align with their major axis, even those with large pericenters. Comparing the radial orbital phases of dSphs to subhalos in Milky Way-like N-body simulations reveals no excess of satellites near pericenter. Looking ahead, we project that with future Gaia data releases, the precision of dSph orbits will be constrained more by uncertainties in distance and/or the MW potential than by proper motion precision. Finally, we release our membership catalogs to facilitate community follow-up observations.

Roadside units (RSUs), equipped with robust computing power and positioned near vehicles, are extensively utilized to handle delay-sensitive and computation-heavy tasks generated by vehicles. Nevertheless, the high mobility of vehicles often causes them to exit the RSU coverage area before retrieving the results of their offloaded tasks. To address this, this paper introduces a mobile edge computing framework for vehicular networks, enabling vehicles to offload tasks to either nearby vehicles via V2V links or proximate RSUs through vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) links. Furthermore, to prevent scenarios where vehicles fail to receive processed results due to lost connectivity, tasks are migrated using V2V or infrastructure-to-infrastructure (I2I) links. Accounting for mutual interference between offloading and migration activities on the same link, we formulate a game-theoretic model for vehicle offloading decisions aimed at minimizing computational overhead. We demonstrate that this game guarantees convergence to a Nash equilibrium by leveraging the finite improvement property. Subsequently, we propose a Task Migration (TM) algorithm incorporating three task-processing strategies and two migration mechanisms. Building on this, we develop the Computation Overhead Minimization Offloading (COMO) algorithm. Extensive simulations confirm that both the TM and COMO algorithms effectively reduce computational overhead and enhance the success rate of task processing.

This study examines electromagnetic fields possessing angular momentum density within locally non-rotating reference frames across Schwarzschild, Kerr, and Kerr-Newman spacetimes. We analyze the characteristics of these fields through the perspectives of two observer families: locally non-rotating observers and those with zero Poynting flux. Utilizing the 3+1 decomposition formalism, we derive the velocity fields of the zero-Poynting observers relative to the locally non-rotating frames. Methodologically, and based on a classification of electromagnetic fields by their invariants, it is advantageous to distinguish the zero-Poynting observers into two categories corresponding to pure and non-pure fields; furthermore, in regions where the field rotates at the speed of light (light surfaces), these observers must be subdivided into two subfamilies. We illustrate several astrophysically and theoretically significant examples, including pure rotating dipolar-like magnetic fields and the electromagnetic field associated with the Kerr-Newman solution. For the Kerr-Newman case, we demonstrate that zero-Poynting observers also detect a vanishing super-Poynting vector, aligning with recent literature. Finally, we provide the 4-velocity fields for zero-Poynting observers in arbitrary spacetimes for all non-null electromagnetic fields.

Multi-task indoor scene understanding is regarded as a compelling approach because the synergy between various tasks often enhances overall performance. This paper addresses the novel challenge of jointly parsing semantics, affordances, and attributes. Successfully solving this problem demands a model capable of capturing long-range dependencies, learning from weakly aligned data, and effectively balancing sub-tasks during training. To achieve this, we introduce an attention-based architecture called Cerberus along with a specialized training framework. Our approach effectively overcomes these challenges and attains state-of-the-art results across all three tasks. Furthermore, in-depth analysis reveals concept affinities that align with human cognition, prompting an exploration of weakly supervised learning possibilities. Remarkably, Cerberus delivers robust performance using merely 0.1% to 1% of annotated data. Visualizations attribute this success to shared attention maps across tasks. The code and models are available at https://github.com/OPEN-AIR-SUN/Cerberus.

We extend the determinant formulation of KP $\tau$ functions to encompass 2D Toda $\tau$ functions. Specifically, we identify that generating functions for weighted Hurwitz numbers constitute a parametric family of 2D Toda $\tau$ functions, for which we derive a corresponding determinant representation. This allows us to establish a finite-dimensional system of equations for the weighted Hurwitz numbers $H^d_{G}(\sigma,\omega)$, where the dimension matches $|\sigma|=|\omega|=n$. Leveraging this system, we compute weighted Hurwitz numbers for dimensions $0$, $1$, and $2$, and provide a recursion formula for determining those in higher dimensions. For any specified weighted generating function $G(z)$, the weighted Hurwitz number reduces to the standard Hurwitz number when $d=0$, enabling a matrix representation for these numbers. Furthermore, we observe that generating functions for weighted paths in the Cayley graph of the symmetric group also form a parametric family of 2D Toda $\tau$ functions, yielding a determinant representation for these weighted paths.

Observations of the most luminous quasars at high redshifts ($z > 6$) indicate that supermassive black holes (SMBHs) at these early epochs are significantly more massive relative to their host galaxies than local relations suggest, pointing to rapid early growth. We present an assembly model for SMBHs residing in rare, massive $\sim10^{12}~M_{\odot}$ halos at $z \sim 6-7$, incorporating a kinetic feedback prescription for super-Eddington accretion derived from radiation hydrodynamic simulations of accretion-flow evolution. High inflow rates into these halos during their formation allow for the creation of SMBHs exceeding $10^9~M_{\odot}$ by $z \sim 6$, even starting from stellar-mass seeds at $z \sim 30$ and despite outflows that diminish the feeding rate, particularly in early stages. This mechanism naturally produces a black hole-to-galaxy mass ratio greater than $0.01$ before the SMBH mass surpasses $10^9~M_{\odot}$ at $z \sim 6$. Furthermore, these rapidly growing SMBH progenitors are sufficiently bright to be detected by the James Webb Space Telescope across a broad redshift range ($7 < z < 15$), irrespective of their initial seeding mechanisms.

This paper introduces a novel concept concerning galaxy formation through the accretion of baryonic matter (BM) and dark matter (DM) onto an existing density over-density. While BM is captured by such structures, DM particles typically pass through static over-densities without being retained. We propose a straightforward model for DM capture: if the over-density's mass increases during a particle's transit, slow-moving DM particles become trapped, thereby increasing the over-density's mass further, whereas faster particles decelerate by transferring energy to the galaxy. We calculate the minimum initial velocity required for a particle to pass through the galactic center without capture and derive a nonlinear equation governing the rate of galactic mass growth. Applying catastrophe theory, our analysis suggests that if the baryonic mass increase surpasses a specific threshold, it can trigger an intense capture of dark matter. We hypothesize that this mechanism may relate to matter accretion or galactic mergers. Furthermore, the intergalactic DM density must exceed a certain threshold for this process to occur; under these conditions, the DM mass growth rate can significantly outpace that of baryonic matter. However, once the DM density falls below this threshold—for instance, due to cosmic expansion—the capture rate drops sharply.

Although lattice-based cryptosystems are thought to withstand quantum attacks, they often suffer from implementation inefficiencies. This drawback is addressed by ring- and module-based approaches like Ring-LWE and Module-LWE, which leverage algebraic structures to reduce keysizes and accelerate computations. While various rings can define these schemes, cyclotomic rings are the industry standard due to their cyclic properties that simplify multiplication. However, it remains uncertain whether this structure can be exploited by adversaries. This paper demonstrates that the decomposition group of a cyclotomic ring with any conductor can be used to substantially lower the dimension of the ideal (or module) lattice needed to solve a specific Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) instance. Furthermore, we identify a large set of rational primes such that if the prime ideal factors of an ideal lie over primes of this type, they generate "easy" SVP instances. Crucially, this research on ideal SVP does not compromise Ring-LWE, as its security relies on a one-way reduction from the worst-case ideal SVP to the average-case Ring-LWE.

This paper investigates the effective signal-to-noise ratio performance of different enumerative amplitude shaping methods. We demonstrate that their comparative performance can be understood through either the temporal autocorrelation function or the energy dispersion index.

Over the past thirty years, Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) and its Matrix Product States (MPS) variants have been the preferred methods for analyzing one-dimensional quantum systems. However, their utility in two-dimensional contexts is restricted by the limited entanglement within the wave-function ansatz; as system size grows, maintaining accuracy necessitates exponentially more resources, confining DMRG to narrow geometries. This study presents a novel ansatz that integrates disentanglers with DMRG to encode an entropic area law. Crucially, this approach retains the $O(D^3)$ computational efficiency of standard DMRG. Benchmark tests on the two-dimensional transverse Ising and Heisenberg models demonstrate that accuracy is preserved even as the system size increases. Consequently, this new ansatz offers a promising and highly useful framework for future investigations into two-dimensional quantum systems.

This paper introduces continuous-time linear logic (CLL), a probabilistic linear-time temporal logic designed to reason about the probability distribution executions of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs). We define the syntax of CLL over the space of probability distributions, incorporating multiphase timed until formulas and a semantics that supports time reset to analyze relative temporal properties. A corresponding model-checking algorithm for CLL formulas is derived, whose correctness relies on Schanuel's conjecture—a prominent open problem in transcendental number theory. Additionally, we present a running example of CTMCs to demonstrate our approach.

The literature contains various non-Fourier heat conduction models, expressed as partial differential equations, which are crucial for addressing numerous practical issues. These models demand robust and efficient solution techniques. This paper examines analytical solutions for two specific non-Fourier frameworks—the Maxwell-Cattaneo-Vernotte and Guyer-Krumhansl equations—chosen for their solid thermodynamic foundations and widespread utility. While many scenarios assume spatially homogeneous initial conditions, real-world applications often involve more complex states. Consequently, this study investigates the implications of nonhomogeneous initial conditions, highlighting the physical constraints necessary to ensure solution admissibility. Finally, we present a method for calculating initial time derivatives that aligns with thermodynamic principles, thereby preventing logical inconsistencies.

This note demonstrates that the space of all metrics with positive Ricci curvature on a spin manifold of dimension 4k-1 (where k ≥ 2) contains infinitely many path components, assuming the manifold supports a specific type of metric.

Research into machine curiosity has been a significant area of study. Investigations into human and animal curiosity, specifically focusing on specific curiosity, have revealed several advantageous properties for machine learning that remain underexplored in artificial intelligence. This work introduces three of these immediate properties—directedness, stopping upon satisfaction, and voluntary exposure—and demonstrates their joint implementation in a proof-of-concept reinforcement learning agent. We further illustrate how these traits manifest in the agent's behavior within a simple, non-episodic grid-world environment featuring curiosity-inducing locations and targets. As anticipated, the agent displays short-term directed behavior while updating long-term preferences to adaptively pursue curiosity-driven situations. Consequently, this research offers a novel perspective on the operation of specific curiosity and its potential integration into goal-seeking, decision-making agents in complex settings.

This paper provides a complete characterization of nuclear Volterra composition operators $T^\phi_g$ and $S^\phi_g$ mapping from $\mathcal H^\infty_\nu$ to $\mathcal H^\infty_\mu$, expressed via their symbols $g$ and $\phi$ along with the weights $\nu$ and $\mu$, specifically when these weights are normal in the sense of Shields and Williams. Additionally, we characterize nuclear Volterra composition operators acting between little weighted type spaces and Bloch spaces of order $\beta$.

Tyler (2020) suggested that the dissipation of ocean potential energy could be a new mechanism driving high-power states in Enceladus. I demonstrate that this process actually arises from viscoelastic dissipation within the crust. Using standard methods for calculating static deformations of solid layers due to equilibrium tides, it is possible to compute crustal dissipation for reasonable estimates of Enceladus's ocean thickness.

This paper investigates the matching problem for regular tree languages, specifically determining whether there exists a substitution $\sigma$ such that $\sigma(L) \subseteq R$, where $L$ and $R$ are regular tree languages defined over the union of a finite ranked alphabet $\Sigma$ and a variable alphabet $\mathcal{X}$. The substitution $\sigma$ maps each variable $x \in \mathcal{X}$ to a set of trees in $T(\Sigma \cup H) \setminus H$, with $H$ representing a set of "holes" used to define a specific "sorted" tree concatenation. This problem was previously examined by Conway in 1971 for finite words, where he proved that if $L$ and $R$ are regular, the existence of a non-empty substitution $\sigma$ satisfying $\sigma(L) \subseteq R$ is decidable. Furthermore, Conway demonstrated that there are only finitely many maximal solutions, which are regular and effectively computable. We extend these findings to regular languages of both finite and infinite trees, applying language substitution in an "inside-out" manner as defined by Engelfriet and Schmidt (1977/78). Specifically, we establish that for regular tree languages $L \subseteq T(\Sigma \cup \mathcal{X})$ and $R \subseteq T(\Sigma)$ over finite or infinite trees, the problem of finding a non-empty substitution $\sigma$ such that $\sigma_{\mathrm{io}}(L) \subseteq R$ is decidable. Additionally, there exist only finitely many maximal regular substitutions that are effectively computable. However, the analogous question for the "outside-in" extension $\sigma_{\mathrm{oi}}$ remains unresolved, even when restricted to finite trees.

Bike Sharing Systems (BSSs) have been implemented in numerous major cities globally to address traffic congestion and carbon emissions. While existing methods have explored using either bike trailers through crowdsourcing or carrier vehicles to reposition bicycles to appropriate stations at the right times, none of these approaches simultaneously utilize both resources. This paper proposes a strategy that leverages both bike trailers and carrier vehicles to minimize demand loss associated with crowdsourced bike trailers and reduce the fuel costs of carrier vehicles. Experimental results across multiple datasets from bike-sharing companies demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline methods.

This study examines first passage percolation on specific isotropic random graphs within $\mathbb{R}^d$. We assume that passage times $T(x,y)$ exhibit exponential concentration on a scale $\sigma_r$ whenever the distance $|y-x|$ scales with $r$, where $\sigma_r$ grows proportionally to $r^\chi$ for some $0<\chi<1$. Heuristically, this implies that the transverse deviation of geodesics should not exceed $\Delta_r = (r\sigma_r)^{1/2}$. We demonstrate that uniform exponential concentration and wandering bounds are indeed valid: with probability exponentially close to one in $t$, no points $x,y$ within a natural cylinder of length $r$ and radius $K\Delta_r$ satisfy either (i) a deviation of the passage time from its expectation of at least $t\sigma_r$, or (ii) a geodesic wandering more than $\sqrt{t}\Delta_r$ from the cylinder's axis. Furthermore, we prove that for the time constant $\mu = \lim_n ET(0,ne_1)/n$, the nonrandom error term $|\mu|x| - ET(0,x)|$ is bounded by a constant multiple of $\sigma(|x|)$.

Drawing inspiration from A. Mihail's 2015 work on the canonical projection between the shift space of an IIFS and its attractor, this paper defines an operator H for every generalized iterated function system F of order m. This operator maps C^m to C, where C denotes the space of continuous functions on the shift space associated with the system's metric space. We establish sufficient conditions regarding the constituent functions of F that ensure H is continuous, a contraction, a phi-contraction, a Meir-Keeler contraction, or contractive. Furthermore, we identify conditions guaranteeing that H possesses a unique fixed point. We demonstrate that, under these conditions, the image of this fixed point corresponds to the attractor of F, and the fixed point itself serves as the canonical projection for F. Consequently, this work offers a partial resolution to the open problem posed in the final paragraph of Mihail's cited paper.

This review provides a historical overview of spinor fields spanning the last century, noting their increasing exploration across diverse contexts in recent decades. Furthermore, the volume of scholarly work on this subject has surged in the past ten years compared to previous periods. Drawing on the author's own research, the paper revisits classifications of spinor fields on both bulk and compactified seven-manifolds. It also examines specific findings within these areas, including the generation of branes via singular spinors in the bulk, invariants associated with five-dimensional black holes, and the spectral decomposition of quantum fields on compactified dimensions at low energies.

This work investigates the perturbative structure of threshold-enhanced logarithms appearing in the coefficient functions of deep inelastic scattering (DIS) and semi-inclusive $e^+e^-$ annihilation (SIA), establishing a framework to resum these terms to all orders in perturbation theory. These threshold logarithms manifest as distributions $((1-z)^{-1} \log^i(1-z))_+$ arising from soft plus virtual (SV) effects and as $\log^i(1-z)$ from next-to-soft-virtual (NSV) contributions.
