This approach is particularly relevant to our field of ocean system modeling, where oracles are seldom present, yet the symmetries of the underlying physical systems are well understood. Due to the specific demands of this domain, the input datasets are substantial. This paper details ongoing research into automatically generating metamorphic test scenarios via machine learning. We have expanded upon our prior method [1] to detect metamorphic relations with lower computational overhead. Initially, these relations are modeled as identity maps. We define a cost function that seeks to minimize the identification of relations orthogonal to those already discovered while penalizing the identity map itself. A machine learning algorithm then identifies all feasible metamorphic relations by minimizing this cost function. Furthermore, we propose utilizing dimensionality reduction to pinpoint input attributes exhibiting high variance across the identified relations. By applying mutations to these selected attributes, we can discover distinct metamorphic relations with reduced computational complexity. For experimental validation, we applied this method to two different implementations of an ocean-modeling application to demonstrate how metamorphic relations can be used to test both versions.

Weakly-supervised Table Question Answering (TableQA) models have reached state-of-the-art results by leveraging pre-trained BERT transformers to jointly encode questions and tables, generating structured queries. However, real-world deployments often involve table corpora with topic and vocabulary distributions that differ significantly from BERT's pre-training data. To address this, we simulate practical topic shifts by introducing novel benchmark suites, WikiSQL-TS and WikiTQ-TS, which feature train-dev-test splits across five distinct topics derived from the WikiSQL and WikiTableQuestions datasets. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that, despite training on vast open-domain text, model performance deteriorates substantially when evaluated on unseen topics. In response, we propose T3QA (Topic Transferable Table Question Answering), a pragmatic adaptation framework consisting of: (1) injecting topic-specific vocabulary into BERT, (2) a novel natural language question generation pipeline using text-to-text transformers (like T5 or GPT-2) to create topic-specific training data, and (3) a logical form reranker. We show that T3QA establishes a solid baseline for our topic shift benchmarks. We believe these topic-split benchmarks will foster more robust TableQA solutions better equipped for practical deployment.

We introduce a novel approach to address the integrability problem for evolutionary differential-difference equations of any order. This method allows us to derive necessary integrability conditions, assess the integrability of specific equations, and further the classification of integrable equations. Within this paper, we establish and expand a symbolic representation for difference polynomial rings, difference operators, and formal series. To formulate these necessary conditions, we propose a new quasi-local extension of the difference ring, which facilitates progress in classifying integrable evolutionary differential-difference equations of arbitrary order. Specifically, we resolve the classification challenge for equations of order $(-3,3)$ within the significant subclass of quasi-linear equations, yielding a list of 17 equations that meet the necessary integrability criteria. For each equation in this list, we provide an infinite family of integrable higher-order relatives. Additionally, some of the derived equations are entirely new.

When selecting messages, individuals often anticipate how recipients will interpret them. In settings like politics, people frequently process information in ways that align with their pre-existing, motivated beliefs. This paper examines how senders adjust their behavior in response to receivers' motivated beliefs through two experiments. The first experiment, involving online social media users, found that incentivizing senders to appear truthful actually led them to send less truthful messages; specifically, they increased the spread of false information that matched receivers' political motivations, even after controlling for current beliefs. Notably, senders did not foresee these negative consequences of their incentives. The second experiment isolated the role of information processing by having senders choose messages generated by a computer for their earnings. In this scenario, senders predicted that receivers would distort information based on political alignment, sought data on receivers' political views, and strategically selected less truthful computer-generated messages contingent on those political preferences.

Determining dental age remains one of the most dependable techniques for ascertaining an individual's age. Forensic physicians and pathologists utilize dental panoramic radiography (DPR) to estimate the chronological age of subjects lacking valid legal documentation or medical records. However, existing methods require significant labor, time, and the expertise of qualified professionals. The advent of deep learning in medical image analysis has enhanced the accuracy of truth value predictions, although it has historically impacted processing speeds. This study introduces an automated framework to estimate forensic ages for individuals between 8 and 68 years old using a dataset of 1,332 DPR images. Initial experiments evaluated transfer learning models—specifically InceptionV3, DenseNet201, EfficientNetB4, MobileNetV2, VGG16, and ResNet50V2—leading to the selection and modification of InceptionV3 to create a novel neural network. By reducing the number of parameters in this architecture, the model achieved faster and more precise age estimation. The resulting performance metrics included a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.13, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 4.77, and a correlation coefficient (R²) of 87%. Consequently, this new model is proposed as a reliable and practical auxiliary tool for applications in forensic science and dentistry.

This study examines a novel linear-quadratic mean-field stochastic Stackelberg differential game involving one leader and two followers, where the leader possesses the option to terminate her strategy at a stochastic time. The primary objective is to determine the Stackelberg equilibrium for both the leader and the followers within this framework. Utilizing the backward induction approach, the state equation is decomposed into two distinct stages. Furthermore, by applying the maximum principle alongside the verification theorem, we derive the Stackelberg solution for the proposed model.

Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) is a mature biometric technology widely deployed in critical security sectors like banking and access control. However, prior research indicates that ASV is vulnerable to adversarial attacks; these attacks generate inputs that appear normal to human observers but cause the system to make erroneous predictions. Because adversarial attacks on ASV have only recently emerged, effective defenses remain scarce. Prioritizing ASV security, this work introduces a "voting for the right answer" strategy to mitigate risky decisions in the system's blind spots through random sampling and voting. Experimental findings demonstrate that this approach enhances robustness against limited-knowledge attackers by shifting adversarial samples out of blind spots and against perfect-knowledge attackers by introducing randomness and increasing their required computational budgets.

As technology advances, threats to sensitive data privacy, such as location information, are intensifying. While adding noise to achieve geo-indistinguishability is a standard approach for mitigating these risks, we contend that this method alone does not address all privacy concerns. Specifically, the current state-of-the-art Laplace mechanism (LAP) fails to protect isolated locations. Instead, we propose a mechanism derived from the Blahut-Arimoto (BA) algorithm in rate-distortion theory. Beyond ensuring geo-indistinguishability, BA introduces an elastic metric that effectively resolves isolation issues. We evaluate BA's utility regarding statistical precision in inferring the original distribution, utilizing the Iterative Bayesian Update (IBU)—a statistical instance of the expectation-maximization method—to identify the most probable distribution for any given obfuscation. Our findings indicate that BA offers superior statistical utility compared to LAP under high privacy constraints, performing comparably as privacy requirements loosen. Notably, we demonstrate a duality between BA and IBU, two methods originally developed for distinct purposes. Leveraging this duality and BA's privacy properties, we introduce PRIVIC, an iterative framework for service providers to collect location data from users in a privacy-friendly, incremental manner. PRIVIC not only extends geo-indistinguishability guarantees and maintains better statistical utility than LAP but also achieves an optimal balance between information leakage and service quality. We validate the soundness and functionality of our approach through both analytical proofs and experimental results.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) constitute a prevalent class of neural architectures, yet they suffer from two primary limitations. Firstly, they are frequently regarded as opaque black-box models, making it challenging to discern their learned representations or the rationale behind specific predictions. Secondly, despite possessing the theoretical capacity for long-term memory, they often underperform on sequences demanding such retention. This work introduces a modified class of RNNs that employs a stochastic state transition mechanism between cell activations, termed "state-regularization." This approach enables RNNs to transition among a finite set of learnable states. We evaluate state-regularized RNNs across three domains: (1) regular languages for automata extraction; (2) non-regular languages requiring external memory, such as balanced parentheses and palindromes; and (3) real-world sequence tasks including sentiment analysis, visual object recognition, and text categorization. Our findings demonstrate that state-regularization (a) facilitates the extraction of finite state automata reflecting the RNN's dynamic state transitions; (b) encourages RNNs to function more like automata with external memory rather than finite state machines, potentially fostering structural memory; and (c) enhances interpretability and explainability by utilizing a probabilistic finite state transition mechanism over time steps.

Existing covariate-shift adaptation techniques rely on unlabeled data solely to calculate importance weights or domain-invariant features, leaving the final model training to labeled data exclusively. This work addresses a specific instance of covariate shift that enables learning from unlabeled data by integrating adaptation with semi-supervised learning. Drawing on causal principles, we posit that this necessitates learning from both the causes ($X_C$) and effects ($X_E$) of a target variable ($Y$), resulting in a framework we term a semi-generative model, $P(Y,X_E|X_C,\theta)$. Our method demonstrates robustness against domain shifts in causal feature distributions and utilizes unlabeled data by establishing a direct mapping from causes to effects. Empirical evaluations on synthetic datasets reveal substantial classification performance gains compared to purely supervised and importance-weighting baselines.

Quasiprobability distributions provide a valuable framework for developing the phase space representation of quantum mechanics. We compute these distributions for Kink and Sine-Gordon solitons. Their utility lies in enabling the calculation of physical quantities such as charge distributions, current densities, and the upper bound on the quantum speed limit. Using the derived quasiprobability distributions, we determine the charge distributions and current densities for both soliton types.

Nearly quasi-Einstein and pseudo quasi-Einstein manifolds, serving as generalizations of Einstein manifolds, hold significant interest and utility in the study of general relativity. This paper investigates extended quasi-Einstein manifolds, which are derived from pseudo quasi-Einstein manifolds. Following an existence theorem for these manifolds, we outline several specific geometric characteristics. Additionally, we examine extended quasi-Einstein manifolds in the context of generalized Ricci solitons or Riemann solitons. Finally, we provide nontrivial examples to demonstrate these structures.

We examine the standard deviation $\delta v(\tsamp)$ of the variance $v[\xbf]$ computed for time series $\xbf$ over a finite sampling interval $\tsamp$, with a specific focus on non-ergodic systems where independent configurations $c$ become trapped within meta-basins of a generalized phase space. Consequently, the sequence in which averages are performed over configurations $c$ and over time series $k$ for a given configuration is crucial. Three distinct variances for $v[\xbf_{ck}]$ are identified: the total variance $\dvtot = \dvint + \dvext$, comprising the typical internal variance $\dvint$ within meta-basins and the external variance $\dvext$, which characterizes the dispersion between different basins. We also explore simplifications applicable to physical systems where the stochastic variable $x(t)$ arises from a density field averaged across a large system volume $V$. These relationships are demonstrated through shear-stress fluctuations in quenched elastic networks, low-temperature glasses composed of polydisperse particles, and free-standing polymer films. Finally, the distinct statistics of $\svint$ and $\svext$ are revealed by their differing dependencies on system size.

A Query Performance Predictor (QPP) estimates how effective an Information Retrieval (IR) system will be for a specific query. A defining feature of QPP evaluation is that the ground truth for retrieval effectiveness can be measured using various metrics, meaning the ground truth is not absolute; this contrasts with other retrieval tasks like ad-hoc retrieval. Driven by this observation, this paper investigates how variations in the ground truth for QPP evaluation influence experimental outcomes. This analysis covers not only the absolute values of reported metrics (such as Pearson's $r$ and Kendall's $\tau$) but also the shifts in the ranking of different QPP systems based on their metric scores. The experiments demonstrate that QPP outcomes can fluctuate significantly, affecting both the absolute metric values and the relative ranks of the systems. Based on this analysis, the paper identifies optimal pairings of QPP evaluation metrics and experimental settings that are most likely to minimize variations in observed results.

As robotics transition from controlled laboratory environments to real-world applications, motion planning must increasingly address model uncertainty and associated risks. This is particularly critical for motions involving intermittent contact, where failing to establish or sustain contact can lead to catastrophic outcomes. In this work, we model uncertainties in both terrain geometry and friction properties, integrating a risk-sensitive objective with chance constraints to balance robustness against uncertainty with high-probability constraint satisfaction. We validate our approach using two benchmark scenarios: a push-block system and a single-legged hopper. Our results indicate that while chance constraints alone yield trajectories comparable to those generated via strict complementarity constraints, combining them with a robust objective allows for a controlled trade-off between handling uncertainty and ensuring strict constraint adherence. Consequently, this research marks a significant advancement in reasoning about contact uncertainty within motion planning frameworks.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) is commonly utilized to address data scalability challenges, yet most existing approaches focus on classifying independent discrete labels. In contrast, many applications, such as medical diagnosis, involve labels that are both discrete and ordered. To handle UDA for ordinal classification, it is essential to incorporate a non-trivial ordinal distribution prior within the latent space. Consequently, this work defines a partially ordered set (poset) to constrain latent vectors. Rather than employing the standard i.i.d. Gaussian latent prior, we adopt a recursively conditional Gaussian (RCG) set to model ordered constraints, which facilitates a tractable joint distribution prior. Additionally, the density of content vectors violating poset constraints can be regulated using a straightforward "three-sigma rule." We explicitly disentangle cross-domain images into a shared ordinal content space governed by an ordinal prior and two separate source/target spaces unrelated to ordinals, restricting self-training exclusively to the shared space for ordinal-aware domain alignment. Comprehensive experiments on UDA tasks involving medical diagnoses and facial age estimation confirm the method's effectiveness.

The well-established trace reconstruction problem involves deducing an unknown binary string $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ from independent "traces," which are copies of $x$ corrupted by a $\delta$-deletion channel that removes each bit with probability $\delta$ and reassembles the remaining ones. This paper focuses on the extreme data-limited scenario where only one trace is available for reconstruction. Since exact recovery is impossible in this setting, the goal shifts to determining the maximum achievable accuracy for approximating the source string. We provide a comprehensive analysis of this question, presenting algorithms and lower bounds across high, intermediate, and low deletion rates for both worst-case scenarios (where $x$ is arbitrary) and average-case scenarios (where $x$ is uniformly random). In many instances, the lower bounds we derive are matched by computationally efficient algorithms we propose. Specifically, our findings for the high deletion rate regime indicate:
*   In the worst-case setting, having a single trace is highly beneficial; an efficient algorithm can achieve significantly better reconstruction accuracy with even a very short trace than it could without any traces.
*   Conversely, in the average-case setting, a single trace is provably not very useful; no algorithm, regardless of computational efficiency, can attain substantially higher accuracy with a trace of length $o(n)$ bits compared to having no traces at all.

The standard trace reconstruction problem aims to \emph{exactly} recover an unknown source string $\mathsf{x} \in \{0,1\}^n$ from independent traces, where each trace is a copy of $\mathsf{x}$ corrupted by a $\delta$-deletion channel that independently removes each bit with probability $\delta$ and then concatenates the remaining bits. In contrast, this work investigates the \emph{approximate} trace reconstruction problem, where the objective is to achieve a high-accuracy estimate of $\mathsf{x}$ instead of an exact one. We present an efficient algorithm and a near-matching lower bound for approximately reconstructing a random source string $\mathsf{x} \in \{0,1\}^n$ using a small number of traces. Our primary algorithmic contribution is a polynomial-time method with the following guarantee: for any deletion rate $0 < \delta < 1$ (potentially dependent on $n$), for almost all source strings $\mathsf{x} \in \{0,1\}^n$, and for any number of traces $M \leq \Theta(1/\delta)$ drawn from $\mathrm{Del}_\delta(\mathsf{x})$, the algorithm produces a hypothesis string $\widehat{\mathsf{x}}$ with an edit distance to $\mathsf{x}$ of at most $n \cdot (\delta M)^{\Omega(M)}$. Furthermore, we establish a near-matching information-theoretic lower bound demonstrating that for a random $n$-bit string $\mathsf{x}$, given $M \leq \Theta(1/\delta)$ traces from $\mathrm{Del}_\delta(\mathsf{x})$, the minimum achievable expected edit distance by any algorithm, regardless of computational complexity, is $n \cdot (\delta M)^{O(M)}$.

A frequently cited challenge in federated learning is data heterogeneity, where client data follows distinct distributions. While various optimization methods have been proposed to tackle this issue, literature typically evaluates them by initiating training from random initialization. In contrast, many practical scenarios allow the server to utilize proxy data for pre-training a model before federated training begins. This study empirically investigates the impact of pre-trained initialization across four standard benchmark datasets. As expected, pre-training reduces the time needed to achieve target error rates and yields models up to 40% more accurate than random initialization. Surprisingly, data heterogeneity appears far less impactful when starting from a pre-trained model; instead, adaptive server-side optimizers like \textsc{FedAdam} consistently achieve superior accuracy. We recommend that future evaluations of federated optimization methods assess performance under both random and pre-trained initializations. Furthermore, this research highlights several avenues for further investigation into the role of heterogeneity in federated optimization.

The theoretical reasons behind deep learning's effectiveness across diverse tasks remain enigmatic. This paper addresses this by constructing a geometric representation of deep learning systems through analogies with two established frameworks: quantum computation geometry and the geometry of diffeomorphic template matching. Within this framework, we delineate the geometric underpinnings of various architectures, including convolutional, residual, recursive, and recurrent neural networks, as well as the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, we analyze the correlation between these geometric structures and the algorithmic performance of different networks, suggesting that this geometric perspective can inform the design of future deep learning systems and their algorithms.

We demonstrate the equivalence of two classical mechanics approaches for a massive spinning particle within special relativity. The first is the spherical top model developed by Hanson and Regge, reformulated using a Hamiltonian framework with enhanced handling of covariant spin constraints. The second is the massive twistor model, adapted to include the Regge trajectory that links mass to total spin angular momentum. By calculating the Dirac brackets of the physical phase space—which encompasses three rotational and three translational degrees of freedom—we establish this equivalence. Lorentz and little group covariance strictly define the physical phase space structure; notably, while the Regge trajectory influences the equations of motion, it does not alter the phase space itself. Following quantization, the twistor model yields a spectrum that aligns precisely with the massive spinor-helicity description introduced by Arkani-Hamed, Huang, and Huang for scattering amplitudes across all masses and spins.

Staircase patterns in response functions occur when physically measurable quantities change discretely in response to the continuous adjustment of a control parameter. A classic instance of this phenomenon is the quantization of Hall conductivity in two-dimensional electron gases subjected to strong magnetic fields. In this study, we demonstrate that similar staircase behavior emerges in the magnetization of spin-1 atomic ensembles governed by various spin-squeezing Hamiltonians. We examine three specific cases—two mesoscopic and one macroscopic—in which the magnetization vector exhibits discrete jumps as the applied magnetic field or atom density is varied continuously, thereby generating a magnetization staircase. These scenarios correspond to Hamiltonians that have already been realized experimentally within the frameworks of spin and spin-nematic squeezing. Consequently, our findings offer immediate opportunities for experimental verification using spin-1 ferromagnetic $^{87}$Rb and anti-ferromagnetic $^{23}$Na condensates.

Although modern image inpainting systems have advanced significantly, they frequently fail when handling large missing regions, intricate geometric patterns, and high-resolution imagery. We attribute this limitation primarily to insufficient receptive fields within both the inpainting network and the loss function. To address this, we introduce Large Mask Inpainting (LaMa). This approach integrates three key elements: i) a novel network architecture utilizing fast Fourier convolutions (FFCs) to achieve an image-wide receptive field; ii) a perceptual loss function with an extensive receptive field; and iii) the use of large training masks, which fully leverages the capabilities of the first two components. Our method surpasses state-of-the-art results across various datasets and delivers superior performance in difficult cases, such as reconstructing periodic structures. Furthermore, the model demonstrates remarkable generalization to resolutions exceeding those encountered during training, all while maintaining lower computational and parameter costs compared to competitive baselines. The source code can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/saic-mdal/lama}.

Recently, the HAL QCD Collaboration utilized lattice QCD simulations to determine the interaction potentials for $N-\Omega$ and $\Omega-\Omega$ systems. Building on these findings, bound states for $N\Omega$ ($^5S_2$) and $\Omega\Omega$ ($^1S_0$) were predicted, with binding energies estimated at a few MeV. Furthermore, HBT correlation functions for $N-\Omega$ pairs have been measured by both the STAR and ALICE Collaborations. These data offer crucial dynamical insights into the existence of $\Omega$-dibaryons within the interaction framework. Beyond interaction dynamics, a viable experimental environment capable of producing and sustaining these bound states is essential. Specifically, two conditions must be met to constrain the production probability: a requisite short-range attractive interaction to form the state, and an experimental setup, such as heavy-ion collisions, that supplies sufficient strangeness and nucleon multiplicity. This Letter employs $\Omega-\Omega$ and $\Omega$-nucleon potentials derived from lattice QCD to calculate the corresponding $\Omega\Omega$ ($^1S_0$) and $N\Omega$ ($^5S_2$) wave functions. Subsequently, the production rates of $\Omega$-dibaryons are estimated using a dynamical coalescence mechanism for relativistic heavy-ion collisions at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV and 2.76 TeV.

Determining how galaxies form, assemble, and stop forming stars remains a primary focus of modern galaxy evolution research, with these processes leaving distinct marks on the galaxy stellar mass function (SMF). Utilizing the COSMOS survey, we present constraints on the SMF's shape and evolution, the fraction of quiescent galaxies, and the cosmic stellar mass density spanning 90% of the Universe's history, from redshift $z=7.5$ down to $0.2$. Leveraging the deeper and more uniform near-infrared data from the COSMOS2020 catalog, we exploit the survey's 1.27 deg$^{2}$ effective area to enhance statistical robustness, better assess cosmic variance—especially for rare, massive galaxies—and extend analysis to higher redshifts with improved mass completeness compared to prior work. We categorize the total stellar mass function into star-forming and quiescent populations using $NUVrJ$ color-color selection. By fitting these measurements with Schechter functions, we infer the intrinsic SMF, the evolution of its parameters, and the cosmic stellar mass density out to $z=7.5$. Our results reveal a smooth, monotonic evolution in the galaxy SMF since $z=7.5$, consistent with earlier findings. The number density of star-forming systems shows remarkably consistent growth across four decades in stellar mass from $z=7.5$ to $2$, after which high-mass systems predominantly become quiescent, illustrating the phenomenon of downsizing. However, an excess of massive systems with unusually red colors at $z\sim2.5-5.5$, including some newly identified objects, increases observed number densities to a level where the SMF cannot be reconciled with a Schechter function. Since systematics such as cosmic variance and/or AGN contamination are unlikely to fully account for this excess, we hypothesize that contributions may arise from dust-obscured objects akin to those detected in far-infrared surveys.

Let $k = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d}, \zeta_3)$, where $d > 1$ is a cube-free positive integer, $k_0 = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ denote the cyclotomic field containing a primitive cube root of unity $\zeta_3$, and let $G = \operatorname{Gal}(k/k_0)$. The prime factorizations of $d$ considered in our primary result [2, Thm. 1.1] lead to novel observations regarding the chain $\Theta = (\theta_i)_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}$ of lattice minima within the underlying pure cubic subfield $L = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ of $k$. The objectives of this study are to establish criteria for identifying generators of primitive ambiguous principal ideals $(\alpha) \in \mathcal{P}_{k}^G/\mathcal{P}_{k_0}$ within the lattice minima $\Theta$ of $L$, and to elucidate the exceptional behavior of the chain $\Theta$ for specific radicands $d$, which influences the determination of the principal factorization types of both $L$ and $k$ via Voronoi's algorithm.

Governments, healthcare systems, and private entities worldwide have deployed digital tracking to manage the spread of COVID-19. While this approach helps contain the pandemic, it raises serious privacy concerns regarding "Contact Tracing Apps" facilitated by Cellphone Service Providers (CSPs), which enable real-time spatial and temporal user monitoring. Consequently, it is plausible that CSPs are gathering data in ways that violate privacy regulations such as GDPR, CCPA, and others. To investigate this, we performed a detailed analysis comparing privacy laws with the actual practices of CSPs. Our findings indicate that three regulations (GDPR, COPPA, and CCPA) classify mobile location data as private, yet two of the five CSPs examined (T-Mobile US and Boost Mobile) failed to comply with COPPA. These violations pose a significant threat, particularly concerning children's data, underscoring the urgent need for robust security and privacy audits. We conclude by offering actionable recommendations to mitigate these risks and ensure privacy-preserving monitoring of the pandemic via contact tracing applications.

This study examines the advantages of exploring the vicinity of a current solution when addressing a problem. By identifying specific problem and neighbourhood characteristics, the paper presents two new proofs demonstrating that neighbourhood search outperforms blind search. First, it proves that a single step within a neighbourhood has a higher probability of finding an improving solution compared to blind search. Second, it establishes that a sequence of local improvements via neighbourhood search is likely to yield greater overall gains than a sequence of blind search steps. To assess the practical implications of these properties, various problem sets and neighbourhoods were generated, each satisfying these conditions to varying extents. Experimental results indicate that the benefits of neighbourhood search can differ significantly. Finally, the analysis of random instances of a classical combinatorial optimization problem confirms that the theoretical findings align with practical outcomes.

We utilize a recent, straightforward method that accelerates the computation of localized collisions within holography to investigate more realistic heavy ion collision models through gauge/gravity duality. The initial conditions incorporate the irregular nuclear structure of actual heavy ions and align the projectile's aspect ratio with the Lorentz contraction observed in RHIC collisions. At the moment of hydrodynamization in the central quark-gluon plasma region, we observe that the majority of the vorticity three-vector's magnitude is deposited distant from the hydrodynamized plasma, leaving only relativistic corrections to thermal vorticity in that region as significant. Finally, we compare the post-collision transverse flow derived in this study against prior results lacking granular initial conditions, calculating the proper energy density and fluid velocity within a hydrodynamized subregion of the plasma.

Probabilistic (Bayesian) modeling has seen widespread adoption across nearly all quantitative disciplines and industrial sectors. This expansion is fueled by improved estimation algorithms, versatile software, enhanced computing capabilities, and a heightened recognition of the advantages offered by probabilistic learning. Despite these advancements, a rigorous Bayesian modeling workflow remains incomplete, with numerous challenges yet to be addressed. To support future research and the implementation of principled Bayesian workflows, we address two core questions: (a) "What constitutes a Bayesian model?" and (b) "What criteria define a good Bayesian model?" In response to the first, we introduce the PAD model taxonomy, which categorizes Bayesian models into four types based on the assumed joint distribution of all variables (P), the posterior approximator (A), and the training data (D). Regarding the second question, we propose ten dimensions for holistic model evaluation: (1) causal consistency, (2) parameter recoverability, (3) predictive performance, (4) fairness, (5) structural faithfulness, (6) parsimony, (7) interpretability, (8) convergence, (9) estimation speed, and (10) robustness. Additionally, we present two example utility decision trees that illustrate the hierarchies and trade-offs among these utilities, tailored to the specific inferential objectives guiding model construction and assessment.

The mechanical behavior of alloys is significantly influenced by their grain structure, necessitating a thorough grasp of how grain boundaries (GBs) evolve during manufacturing to engineer these structures effectively. To address this, we introduce a computationally efficient framework that captures the simultaneous development of bulk plasticity and GBs. In this approach, GBs are modeled as diffused geometrically necessary dislocations, with their evolution representing GB plasticity. Consequently, the coupled evolution of GBs and bulk plasticity is unified through the evolution equation for the plastic deformation gradient, a core component of classical crystal plasticity theories. To minimize degrees of freedom, we propose a method that consolidates the governing equations for individual slip rates into a single set of equations for the plastic deformation gradient. Additionally, we detail a technique for implementing a synthetic potential to induce the migration of flat GBs.

The model's validity is supported by three numerical examples. First, a scaling test confirms the framework's computational efficiency. Second, we analyze the evolution of a tricrystal created by embedding a circular grain within a bicrystal, showing qualitative alignment between our model's predictions and molecular dynamics simulations by Trautt and Mishin (2014). Finally, we illustrate the impact of applied loading on texture evolution by simulating a synthetic polycrystal under imposed displacements.

We introduce a variant of the quantum relational Hoare logic from Unruh (POPL 2019) that incorporates "expectations" into pre- and postconditions. Specifically, when reasoning about pairs of programs, this logic enables quantitative analysis of the degree to which pre- and postconditions regarding the relationship between program inputs and outputs are satisfied.

This study introduces an efficient Proper Orthogonal Decomposition-based Reduced-Order Model (POD-ROM) for nonstationary Stokes equations, integrating the classical projection method with POD techniques. The proposed scheme offers two primary benefits: first, it significantly reduces computational costs by decoupling the reduced-order velocity and pressure variables through the classical projection method, while POD further enhances efficiency. Second, it avoids the need to verify the classical LBB/inf-sup condition for mixed POD spaces by employing a pressure-stabilized Petrov-Galerkin (PSPG)-type projection method. In this approach, the inherent pressure stabilization term permits the use of non-inf-sup-stable elements without requiring additional stabilization. We first establish the convergence of the PSPG-type finite element projection scheme and subsequently analyze the stability and convergence of the proposed projection POD-ROM. Finally, numerical experiments confirm our theoretical findings.

This study highlights the potential of deep learning for modeling the clustering of particles aerodynamically coupled to turbulent fluids. By employing a Lagrangian particle module in the ATHENA++ hydrodynamics code, we simulate particle dynamics under Epstein drag within a periodic domain of isotropic, forced hydrodynamic turbulence. This configuration serves as an idealized representation of collisional growth for dust particles ranging from microns to millimeters in size during the early stages of planet formation. We utilize the resulting simulation data to train a U-Net deep learning model capable of predicting gridded three-dimensional representations of particle density and velocity fields based on corresponding fluid field inputs. The trained model qualitatively reproduces the filamentary structures of clustered particles even in highly non-linear regimes. To evaluate model fidelity, we compute metrics for density structure (radial distribution function) and velocity fields (relative velocity and relative radial velocity between particles). Despite being trained solely on spatial fields, the model predicts these statistical quantities with errors typically under 10%. Our findings indicate that, with appropriately expanded training datasets, deep learning can accelerate calculations of particle clustering and collision outcomes in protoplanetary disks and in related two-fluid turbulence problems across other disciplines.

This paper extends the classical Denjoy--Wolff Theorem, which explores the connection between the orbits of interior and boundary points under iterates of holomorphic self-maps of the unit disc, to a broader framework involving sequences $(F_n)$ of holomorphic maps between arbitrary simply connected domains. We demonstrate that while certain classical findings can be generalized—often with significant reliance on the specific geometry of the domains—a far wider array of dynamical behaviors becomes possible, with some results being novel even within the traditional context. Our methodology is particularly applicable to non-autonomous dynamical systems, where $(F_n)$ represents forward compositions of holomorphic maps, as well as to the analysis of wandering domains in holomorphic dynamics. To illustrate these diverse behaviors, we construct specific examples. The proofs employ techniques from geometric function theory, measure theory, and ergodic theory, utilizing a "weak independence" variant of the second Borel--Cantelli lemma and the ergodic theory concept of "shrinking targets."

Hot Jupiters circling rapidly spinning stars along inclined paths exhibit tidally driven nodal precession that can be measured across multi-year observation periods. WASP-33 b and KELT-9 b stand out as especially compelling subjects due to their extreme temperatures and orbits around relatively massive stars. By examining both archival and newly acquired data spanning 11 and 5 years for these systems, we aim to refine their tidal precession models. Our analysis confirms nodal precession in the WASP-33 system and reports the first definitive detection of such precession in KELT-9 b. We calculate the gravitational quadrupole moments for WASP-33 and KELT-9 as $(6.3^{+1.2}_{-0.8})\times10^{-5}$ and $(3.26^{+0.93}_{-0.80})\times10^{-4}$, respectively. Furthermore, we estimate their precession periods at $1460^{+170}_{-130}$ years and $890^{+200}_{-140}$ years, projecting that transits will end around the years $2090^{+17}_{-10}$ and $2074^{+12}_{-10}$ CE. Our investigation into tidal and orbital evolution suggests that high-eccentricity tidal migration could have formed both systems, and neither planet is expected to be engulfed by its host before the main sequence phase concludes.

Defect corrections to the polarization and dielectric functions of Bloch electrons within quantum wells are initially computed. Subsequently, the first two moment equations derived from Boltzmann transport theory are formulated and utilized to examine how defects influence the magneto-transport of these electrons. Concurrently, the momentum-relaxation time and mobility tensor for Bloch electrons are determined analytically using the screened, defect-corrected polarization function. Building upon quantum-statistical theory, the dynamics of defect capture and charging are further analyzed by implementing a parameterized physics model for defects to derive defect wave functions. This approach enables the self-consistent calculation of capture and relaxation rates, along with the density of captured Bloch electrons, as functions of temperature, doping density, and various defect types. Through the application of the energy-balance equation, the number of occupied energy levels and the chemical potential of defects are established, facilitating the determination of the defect capture transition rate. Leveraging these findings, the defect energy-relaxation, capture, and escape rates, alongside the Bloch-electron chemical potential, are derived self-consistently. Simultaneously, the Bloch-electron energy- and momentum-relaxation rates, as well as the current suppression factor, are quantitatively investigated. Ultimately, by synthesizing these analyses, the temperature dependence of Hall and longitudinal mobilities for Bloch electrons in both single- and multi-quantum wells is demonstrated, providing a framework for quantifying burst noise in transistors and blinking noise in photo-detectors.

Machine learning models powering intelligent systems typically rely on resource-intensive and expensive procedures, including extensive data gathering, labeling, network training, and model fine-tuning. Transfer learning, which involves sharing and reusing these sophisticated models across intelligent systems operating in distinct environments, can enhance user service adoption and accelerate the deployment of intelligent solutions in domains like smart cities and smart buildings. In this context, knowledge exchange and communication between AI-driven environments rely on intricate networks of systems, digital assets, and interdependencies that deviate from the centralized structures of traditional information systems. Instead, they necessitate an adaptive, decentralized architecture bolstered by capabilities such as data provenance, workflow transparency, and participant validation. This research introduces a decentralized and adaptive software framework leveraging blockchain and knowledge graph technologies to enable transparent and trustworthy knowledge exchange and interoperability among IoT-enabled environments.

Globally, prostate cancer ranks as the second most common cancer and the sixth leading cause of cancer-related mortality among men. A primary challenge for specialists is accurately localizing Regions of Interest (ROI) that contain tumor tissue. While manual segmentation by experts is currently the standard, it suffers from low detection rates (approximately 27-44%) or instances of overdiagnosis. Consequently, numerous studies have aimed to automate the segmentation and feature extraction of ROIs from magnetic resonance images (MRI) to support diagnostic and therapeutic processes. However, automation remains difficult due to ambiguous prostate boundaries, inherent tissue heterogeneity, and diverse prostate shapes. This study trained and evaluated six deep learning models using an MRI dataset from the Centre Hospitalaire de Dijon and Universitat Politecnica de Catalunya. The models assessed included U-Net, Attention U-Net, Dense-UNet, Attention Dense-UNet, R2U-Net, and Attention R2U-Net, utilizing categorical cross-entropy as the loss function. Performance was measured via three standard segmentation metrics: Dice score, Jaccard index, and mean squared error. The R2U-Net emerged as the top performer for segmenting all zones, achieving a Dice score of 0.869, a Jaccard index of 0.782, and a mean squared error of 0.00013.

To explain the EDGES anomaly, a model involving millicharged dark matter subcomponents that cool baryons through Coulomb interactions has been proposed, yet it faces significant conflicts with cosmological and stellar emission constraints. This study investigates a scenario where these millicharged particles exist as composite blobs. At high temperatures, the relevant degrees of freedom are tiny elementary charges that combine at lower temperatures to form blobs with larger charges; these blobs are responsible for cooling baryons enough to match the EDGES observation. In this framework, cosmological and stellar limits—which pertain to high-temperature processes—constrain only the feebly interacting elementary charges, not the blobs themselves. This distinction preserves a substantial portion of the parameter space for millicharged blobs capable of resolving the EDGES anomaly and additionally creates new possibilities for direct detection experiments at low momentum transfers.

3D object detection is vital for autonomous driving and various robotics tasks, yet existing detectors typically depend on vast quantities of labeled data, which are costly and time-intensive to acquire. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised approach that utilizes extensive unlabeled point cloud videos by training 3D detectors through temporal graph neural networks. Our core hypothesis is that temporal smoothing enhances detection accuracy on unlabeled data, enabling the generation of pseudo-labels to retrain the model. We implement this temporal reasoning using a graph neural network, where edges denote relationships between candidate detections across different time steps. Following semi-supervised training, our method attains state-of-the-art performance on the demanding nuScenes and H3D benchmarks, surpassing baselines trained with equivalent labeled data. The project and source code are available at https://www.jianrenw.com/SOD-TGNN/.

Simulators play a pivotal role in contemporary robotics research, enabling the study of perception and decision-making strategies in a virtual environment before real-world deployment, thereby reducing both time and expenses. Although substantial advancements have been made in sim-to-real algorithms, their evaluation remains fragmented, lacking a unified set of tests and metrics. This paper addresses that deficiency by introducing a comprehensive framework and benchmark suite designed to assess algorithms focused on transferring simulation-learned models and policies to physical systems. Through extensive experiments across various established simulated environments, we characterize these methods and provide insights into their performance. Our findings offer valuable guidance for practitioners, facilitating informed decisions regarding the characteristics and behaviors of sim-to-real approaches. Additionally, we have open-sourced the benchmark, training datasets, and pre-trained models, available at https://github.com/NVlabs/sim-parameter-estimation.

This study re-examines the viability of a strong first-order electroweak phase transition (SFOEWPT), essential for electroweak baryogenesis, alongside recent $m_W$ precision data within Type-I and Type-II Two-Higgs-Doublet Models (2HDMs). The presence of new scalars at the O(100) GeV scale in 2HDMs aligns with the requirements for SFOEWPT and accounts for the observed shift in $m_W$. Current constraints indicate that both Type-I and Type-II 2HDMs can simultaneously accommodate SFOEWPT, Z-pole observables, Higgs precision measurements, and the CDF-II $m_W$ results; notably, all these precision tests are sensitive to the heavy Higgs mass splitting in 2HDMs. The permitted parameter spaces are defined as $\Delta m_{A/C} \in (-400, 400) \text{ GeV}$ and $\tan\beta \in (1, 50)$ for Type-I, and $\Delta m_{A/C} \in (-200, 300) \text{ GeV}$ and $\tan\beta \in (1, 12)$ for Type-II. Additionally, future measurements of Higgs and $Z$ boson properties at lepton colliders could further investigate or potentially exclude this scenario.

Although transliteration is prevalent on social media, current neural models struggle to process such text effectively for various NLP tasks. To address this, we integrate data augmentation with a Teacher-Student training framework within a cross-lingual transfer setting, specifically designed to fine-tune leading pre-trained multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R. We tested our approach on transliterated Hindi and Malayalam, presenting new benchmark datasets for real-world applications: one focused on sentiment analysis in transliterated Malayalam, and another on classifying crisis tweets in transliterated Hindi and Malayalam related to the 2013 North India and 2018 Kerala floods. Our method achieved an average F1 score improvement of +5.6% for mBERT and +4.7% for XLM-R compared to their robust baselines.

The nuclear modification of hadron production in deep inelastic lepton-nucleus scattering offers a method to investigate parton propagation within cold nuclear matter. Utilizing an analytic parameterization of the quenching weight derived from the BDMPS formalism, which incorporates target nuclear geometry effects, we performed leading-order calculations for hadron multiplicity ratios. These calculations were compared with HERMES data on charged pion production to examine quark hadronization occurring outside the nucleus. This analysis reveals a relationship between the quark transport coefficient and measurable kinematic variables in deep inelastic scattering. Four models for the quark transport coefficient were proposed; however, the constant, power-law, and double power-law models were excluded because experimental evidence shows that transverse momentum broadening increases with photon virtuality $Q^2$. Consequently, the quark transport coefficient was determined as a function of the Bjorken variable $x$ and the scale $Q^2$. The resulting trend of the quark transport coefficient regarding $x$ and $Q^2$ shows qualitative partial agreement with HERMES experimental data on transverse momentum broadening. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to a better understanding of the jet quenching phenomenon observed in relativistic heavy ion collisions.

This research examines algebraic cycles within complex Gushel-Mukai (GM) varieties. We establish the generalised Hodge conjecture, the (motivated) Mumford-Tate conjecture, and the generalised Tate conjecture across all GM varieties. Furthermore, we calculate every integral Chow group for these varieties, with the sole exception of the two infinite-dimensional scenarios: 1-cycles on GM fourfolds and 2-cycles on GM sixfolds. Finally, we demonstrate that if two GM varieties are generalised partners or generalised duals, their rational Chow motives in the middle degree are isomorphic.

We introduce a methodology for assessing gender representation within online product funnels, serving as a component of our broader equity framework to gain deeper insights through funnel analysis. By applying coarsened exact matching techniques from causal inference, we demonstrate that our custom-designed funnel survival ratio metric effectively identifies inherent representation disparities. Grasping the magnitude of these differences across various member groups, alongside the factors driving them, is essential for cultivating more equitable outcomes.

The volume of data, including features and variables, accessible to machine learning algorithms continues to grow. This trend can cause classifiers to overfit within high-dimensional spaces, result in models that lack interpretability, and severely restrict applications due to the substantial CPU and memory requirements for processing large datasets. Variable and feature selection address these challenges by identifying a subset of features that most effectively captures the available information. This paper outlines the general methodology and emphasizes specific approaches.

This paper introduces a control and stabilization strategy for a rotary inverted pendulum utilizing a general controller framework. Rooted in classical control theory, the proposed approach highlights the critical role of an integrator in rejecting disturbances. System dynamics are derived using the Euler-Lagrange method and approximated under small-angle conditions, with the goal of maintaining the pendulum's balance. Experimental outcomes confirm that the control scheme effectively stabilizes the non-linear system. Furthermore, the boundedness and convergence of the system under the proposed controller, given specific initial conditions, are verified.

By November 2020, COVID-19 cases were surging rapidly across numerous nations. While strict lockdowns in Europe initially curbed the virus in late spring, a second wave emerged throughout the autumn. This study reconstructs the time-dependent effective reproduction number, ${\cal R}(t)$, for each country by solving the classic SIR model equations. Countries are then clustered based on their estimated ${\cal R}(t)$ trajectories using a specific time series dissimilarity measure. The findings indicate that simple dynamical mechanisms drive how nations react to shifting case counts. Building on this, we extend the SIR model to incorporate a social response that explains the daily new case count, $X(t)$. As a first-order approximation, we model the social response as $d_t{\cal R}=-
u (X-X^*)$, where $X^*$ represents a response threshold. The response rate $
u$ varies based on whether $X$ is below or above $X^*$, relying on parameters $
u_1,\;
u_2,\,
u_3,$ and time $t$. When incidence is low ($X<X^*$), $
u=
u_1$ reflects the impact of relaxed interventions. When incidence is high ($X>X^*$), $
u=
u_2\exp{(-
u_3t)}$ captures intervention effects, with $
u_3$ representing intervention fatigue—the diminishing efficacy of measures over time. This model successfully replicates typical epidemic wave patterns seen globally. By estimating parameters $
u_1,\,
u_2,\,
u_3$ and initial conditions like ${\cal R}_0$ for various countries, we can identify key dynamics in their social responses. A primary conclusion is that the intense second wave in Europe during the fall of 2020 was not primarily caused by summer relaxation of interventions, but rather by the development of general intervention fatigue during the autumn.

We examine a specific class of singular weighted anisotropic $p$-Laplace equations. We establish sufficient conditions on the weight function, which may vanish or become unbounded near the origin, guaranteeing the existence of at least one weak solution in the purely singular scenario and at least two distinct weak solutions in the perturbed singular scenario.

This work introduces a framework designed to extract and analyze decision-making data from deep neural network (DNN) classifiers used in jet substructure tagging. The core methodology involves augmenting inputs with expert variables, termed "eXpert AUGmented" (XAUG) variables, followed by applying layerwise relevance propagation (LRP) to networks configured both with and without these augmentations. XAUG variables are integrated into intermediate layers following network-specific operations like convolution or recurrence and utilized within the final layers. Comparative results demonstrate that XAUG variables enhance discrimination capabilities when paired with low-level features, fully capture classifier behavior in certain scenarios, and aid in interpreting network decisions. By combining LRP with XAUG variables, researchers can identify relevant information, rank features, and derive a reduced feature set that retains partial network performance. In the presented studies, incorporating XAUG variables into low-level DNNs improved classifier efficiency by up to 30-40%. Furthermore, the study offers an approach to quantify numerical uncertainties associated with training these DNNs.
It has been demonstrated that the Finiteness Problem is undecidable for any sufficiently broad class of modular lattices.

Earlier sparse principal component analysis (PCA) methods assumed that the $p \times k$ eigen-basis matrix itself was approximately sparse. In contrast, our proposed method assumes that this matrix achieves approximate sparsity following a $k \times k$ rotation. The algorithm's simplest form begins by initializing with the leading $k$ principal components, which are then subjected to an orthogonal $k \times k$ rotation to induce sparsity, followed by the application of soft-thresholding. This strategy diverges from previous approaches by employing orthogonal rotation to approximate a sparse basis, allowing sparse components to represent mixtures of leading eigenvectors rather than being restricted to single leading eigenvectors. Consequently, we introduce a novel rotated basis for sparse PCA. Furthermore, this method eliminates the need for "deflation" and the multiple tuning parameters typically associated with it. Our versatile framework extends naturally to two-way data analysis for simultaneous dimensionality reduction of both rows and columns. Empirical evidence indicates that for equivalent sparsity levels, our method offers greater stability and explains more variance than alternatives. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of this modern sparse PCA approach through three applications: image sparse coding, transcriptome sequencing analysis, and large-scale social network clustering.

Automatic segmentation of lesions in thoracic CT scans facilitates the rapid quantitative assessment of lung involvement in COVID-19. However, acquiring extensive voxel-level annotations to train segmentation networks is prohibitively costly. To address this, we introduce a weakly-supervised segmentation approach utilizing dense regression activation maps (dRAMs). While most weakly-supervised methods rely on class activation maps (CAMs) for object localization, these are often imprecise because they are trained for classification rather than segmentation. In contrast, our method generates high-resolution activation maps by leveraging dense features from a segmentation network trained to predict per-lobe lesion percentages, thereby incorporating knowledge about the necessary lesion volume. Furthermore, we propose an attention neural network module designed to refine dRAMs, which is jointly optimized with the primary regression task. Evaluated on 90 subjects, our algorithm achieved a Dice coefficient of 70.2%, significantly surpassing the CAM-based baseline of 48.6%.

Optical transient surveys have uncovered numerous tidal disruption events (TDEs) caused by massive black holes at galactic centers. However, despite thorough searches, X-ray follow-ups have yielded little to no detections in most cases. We report the discovery of delayed X-ray brightening approximately 140 days after the optical outburst in the TDE OGLE16aaa, accompanied by multiple flux dips during its decay. These characteristics are atypical for standard TDEs and may indicate the presence of a supermassive black hole binary or patchy obscuration. In both scenarios, X-rays are generated promptly post-disruption but are initially blocked, potentially by a radiation-dominated ejecta responsible for the primary optical and ultraviolet emission. Our results suggest that reprocessing plays a critical role in the early evolution of TDEs, and X-ray observations hold great promise for identifying supermassive black hole binaries.

Linear spectral unmixing is a fundamental method in hyperspectral image analysis. Recently, deep learning techniques have demonstrated significant potential in this field, with unsupervised autoencoder-based approaches emerging as a notable trend. These autoencoders excel by automatically learning low-dimensional representations (abundances) and reconstructing data using their corresponding bases (endmembers). This article investigates the effective integration of spatial and spectral information within autoencoder-based unmixing frameworks, discussing key insights derived from this exploration. Building on these findings, we introduce SSCU-Net, a spatial-spectral collaborative unmixing network. SSCU-Net employs an end-to-end, two-stream deep architecture that jointly trains a spatial and a spectral autoencoder to enhance unmixing performance. Furthermore, we propose a novel spatial autoencoder that incorporates a superpixel segmentation method driven by abundance information, which significantly boosts the utilization of spatial cues and improves unmixing accuracy. Extensive ablation studies were conducted to evaluate the performance improvements offered by SSCU-Net. Experimental results on both synthetic and real hyperspectral datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness and competitiveness against several state-of-the-art unmixing techniques.

Keyword spotting (KWS) has become an essential component of numerous intelligent devices, as audio remains one of the most effective methods for human-device interaction. While researchers have primarily focused on enhancing the accuracy and performance of KWS systems, leading to significant advancements through deep learning, the expanding integration of KWS into IoT devices has made energy efficiency a critical requirement alongside performance. We argue that KWS solutions optimizing both hardware and neural network (NN) architecture for power consumption offer distinct advantages over existing literature, which predominantly addresses only architectural aspects. In this study, we developed an optimized KWS convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for end-to-end energy efficiency when deployed on the MAX78000, an ultra-low-power CNN accelerator. By combining hardware and model optimization, we achieved 96.3% accuracy across 12 classes with an inference energy consumption of only 251 µJ. We benchmark these results against other small-footprint, neural network-based KWS solutions found in the literature. Furthermore, to clarify the effectiveness of our chosen hardware, we also report the energy consumption of our model when executed on a power-optimized ARM Cortex-M4F.

The Fontaine-Mazur Conjecture stands as a central pillar in contemporary arithmetic geometry. Since its initial formulation in 1993, multiple versions have been proposed, with researchers exploring diverse approaches to address it. In a seminal 1992 paper, Boston introduced purely group-theoretic techniques—distinct from representation-theoretic methods—to establish certain special cases of the conjecture. These approaches were subsequently advanced by Maire and his collaborators, yielding novel insights into the conjecture's underlying objects. This survey article examines existing results in this specific direction and highlights intriguing related questions that the authors are currently investigating.

Accurately characterizing uncertainty in human motion prediction is just as critical as achieving high predictive accuracy. We introduce CovarianceNet, a novel method designed to precisely estimate the uncertainty linked to the predicted distribution of future trajectories. Built upon a Conditional Generative Model with Gaussian latent variables, our approach predicts the parameters of a bi-variate Gaussian distribution. By integrating CovarianceNet with a motion prediction model, we create a hybrid system that outputs a uni-modal distribution. Our results demonstrate that several state-of-the-art methods tend to be overconfident in their uncertainty estimates when evaluated against our proposed metric and validated on the ETH dataset \cite{pellegrini2009you}. In contrast, CovarianceNet successfully predicts uncertainty, rendering it highly suitable for applications relying on predicted distributions, such as planning and decision-making.

We introduce high-quality bi-concave 2D focusing diamond x-ray lenses with an apex radius of $R=100~\mu$m, manufactured through laser ablation and further refined by mechanical polishing. We analyze the residual figure errors for both individual polished and unpolished lenses, as well as stacks of ten, using x-ray speckle tracking, and benchmark these findings against commercial beryllium lenses ($R=50~\mu$m) with equivalent focusing power and aperture. Additionally, we provide measured 2D out-of-focus beam profiles and wire scans to determine focal plane beam sizes for two stacks of ten diamond lenses (polished and unpolished) alongside a stack of eleven beryllium lenses. These data are supplemented by small angle x-ray scattering (SAXS) measurements comparing polished and unpolished diamond lenses to a beryllium counterpart. Our results indicate that polished diamond lenses exhibit figure errors comparable to commercial beryllium lenses and achieve similar focal plane beam sizes; however, the SAXS signal from the polished diamond lenses is significantly reduced.

Recent advancements in deep neural network architectures have significantly enhanced the performance of document image information extraction tasks, which include text localization, transcription, and named entity recognition. Traditionally, however, these tasks are handled by separate methods. This study introduces an end-to-end model that integrates a one-stage object detection network with distinct branches for recognizing text and named entities, enabling the simultaneous learning of shared features based on the training error of each task. Consequently, the model achieves page-level handwritten text detection, transcription, and named entity recognition through a single forward pass. We comprehensively evaluate this approach across various datasets, comparing its benefits and constraints against sequential methods. The findings demonstrate that the model effectively leverages shared features to concurrently address these interdependent tasks.

We present a novel Domain Expert Mixture (DEMix) layer designed to condition language models (LMs) on the specific domain of the input text. Comprising a set of specialized feedforward networks, each dedicated to a particular domain, the DEMix layer renders the LM modular, allowing experts to be added, removed, or combined after the initial training phase. Comprehensive experiments conducted on autoregressive transformer LMs (ranging up to 1.3B parameters) indicate that DEMix layers lower test-time perplexity, enhance training efficiency, and facilitate rapid adaptation with minimal overhead. By employing a parameter-free weighted ensemble to mix experts during inference, we demonstrate improved generalization across heterogeneous or previously unseen domains. Furthermore, our findings show that experts can be incrementally added to incorporate new domains without causing catastrophic forgetting of older ones, and they can be selectively removed to block access to undesired domains, all without requiring additional training. Collectively, these results highlight the advantages of explicitly conditioning on textual domains within language modeling.

Achieving trustworthy machine learning in healthcare requires solving the domain generalization challenge in medical image classification. Our analysis reveals that current domain generalization methods, which rely on ground-truth abnormality segmentations to regulate feature attributions, underperform compared to the standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) baseline when tested on out-of-distribution (OOD) data. By examining critical image regions, we discovered that background areas outside the segmented abnormalities contain valuable signals. Consequently, we introduced a novel task-specific mask encompassing all relevant regions. Applying this improved segmentation significantly boosts the OOD performance of existing approaches. Furthermore, to surpass ERM in generalization capabilities, it is essential to combine the use of these task-specific masks with an increase in training data volume.

This paper examines Euclidean preferences within the plane under $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_{\infty}$ norms. For scenarios involving four candidates, we demonstrate that the maximum number of pairwise distinct preferences for Euclidean profiles under $\ell_1$ or $\ell_{\infty}$ norms is 19. Regardless of the total number of candidates, we establish that at most four distinct candidates can occupy the last rank in a two-dimensional Euclidean profile under these norms; this extends the well-known one-dimensional result where no more than two candidates can be ranked last. We further generalize this finding to $2^d$ (for $\ell_1$) and $2d$ (for $\ell_{\infty}$) across $d$-dimensional Euclidean preferences. Additionally, we show that the maximal size of a two-dimensional Euclidean profile on $m$ candidates under the $\ell_1$ norm scales as $\Theta(m^4)$, matching the order of magnitude observed under the $\ell_2$ norm. Finally, we offer a streamlined proof that two-dimensional Euclidean profiles under $\ell_2$ for four candidates can be described by three voter-maximal two-dimensional profiles, providing a simpler alternative to the approach by Kamiya et al. in *Advances in Applied Mathematics*.

Physical mechanisms that strip or redistribute angular momentum from protoplanetary disks are believed to drive mass accretion onto stars and influence planet formation, yet the specific processes responsible remain uncertain despite widespread observational evidence of accretion. In this study, we provide evidence of rapid inflow at the disk surface of a Class I source, indicated by redshifted molecular absorption in its spectrum. High-resolution mid-infrared spectroscopy of GV Tau N reveals a complex absorption spectrum featuring individual lines of water, ammonia, HCN, and C2H2. Based on the characteristics of this molecular absorption, we infer a substantial accretion rate ranging from ~1e-8 to ~1e-7 Msun/yr, which aligns with the rates seen in active T Tauri stars, suggesting we are directly observing disk accretion. These findings may offer observational support for supersonic "surface accretion flows" predicted by magnetohydrodynamic simulations of magnetized disks. Furthermore, this work marks the first detection of ammonia within the planet-forming region of a protoplanetary disk. Since ammonia's abundance is comparable to HCN, it cannot account for a major missing nitrogen reservoir; if the primary nitrogen reservoir in inner disks is indeed N2, as anticipated, its high volatility would hinder incorporation into forming planets, potentially explaining the low nitrogen content found in bulk Earth.

Image datasets frequently suffer from class imbalance, presenting a significant hurdle for deep learning models. This paper introduces a solution to rebalance imbalanced image data by integrating two simultaneous approaches: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and capsule networks. Within our framework, the generative and discriminative networks engage in a unique competitive dynamic where the generator produces samples for specific classes drawn from a multivariate probability distribution. The discriminator is engineered not only to distinguish between real and synthetic samples but also to classify the inputs. Since standard GANs often struggle with imbalanced data by generating similar samples that lead to overfitting due to reliance on fully observed data, our method mitigates this by jointly incorporating all available class information during adversarial training. This strategy enhances learning from imbalanced datasets by embedding the majority class distribution structure into the generation of new minority samples. Additionally, the generator utilizes a feature matching loss function to accelerate training convergence. This approach effectively prevents outlier generation without distorting the majority class space. Evaluation results confirm the efficacy of our proposed method; specifically, the combined capsule-GAN demonstrates superior performance in recognizing highly overlapping classes using significantly fewer parameters compared to conventional convolutional-GANs.

The lecture comprises the following sections: Systems and States; Brownian Motion; Segmental Relaxation and the Glass Transition; Dynamics of a Free Chain; and Entanglement and Reptation. The appendices address Linear response theory (covering relaxation, dissipation, and fluctuation); Debye's theory of dielectric relaxation; and Zimm's theory of chain dynamics in solution.

This study presents a direct search for charged lepton-flavour violation within top-quark decays, utilizing $79.8\ \text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS experiment at the LHC with a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13\ \text{TeV}$. The analysis examines top-quark pair production events where one top quark decays into an up-type quark and a pair of opposite-sign, different-flavour charged leptons, while the other undergoes a semileptonically decay consistent with the Standard Model. Consequently, the signal signature involves three charged leptons, a light jet, and a $b$-jet. A multivariate discriminant is employed, with its distribution serving as input to determine the signal strength. Assuming no signal is present, an upper limit on the branching ratio of ${\cal B}(t \to \ell \ell' q) < 1.86 \times 10^{-5}$ is established at the 95\% confidence level.

Recent studies indicate that mixed-initiative conversational search, which leverages user-computer interactions to refine queries, offers significant benefits. However, integrating user-provided conversational information presents challenges, as irrelevant words used for grammatical correctness in multi-turn dialogues can confuse the system. To address this, we present an end-to-end document retrieval pipeline that utilizes two newly collected datasets for conversational keyword extraction. We evaluate two neural models, BERT and sequence-to-sequence, based on extraction accuracy and alignment with human annotations. Additionally, we analyze the impact of these keywords on overall neural information retrieval performance, demonstrating that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art models. The two datasets are now publicly released to encourage further research in this domain.

While social networks have successfully connected people online, they have also become vulnerable to influence operations designed to manipulate society. The use of software-controlled accounts, such as social bots, has emerged as a highly effective tool for these operations, prompting the development and widespread adoption of detection tools. However, existing literature lacks a unified approach, with case studies employing diverse and unique measurement methods. To address this fragmentation, we propose a standardized framework for analyzing the interference of social bots on Twitter. This methodology evaluates non-authentic actors against regular users from multiple angles to generate objective metrics for assessing their actual impact. We validated this framework using a dataset of Twitter activity from the weeks leading up to the 2019 Spanish general election. Our analysis demonstrates that the framework enables quantitative evaluation of unauthentic groups, revealing that while social bots altered the natural dynamics of the network during this period, they did not exert a significant overall influence. Furthermore, we posit this methodology as a practical instrument for qualitatively interpreting experimental results; specifically, within the context of the aforementioned election, our findings suggest that semi-automated accounts may pose a greater threat than fully automated ones.

This thesis seeks to bridge two research schools by integrating syntactic inductive biases into deep learning architectures. We introduce two distinct families of these biases: one tailored for constituency structure and another for dependency structure. The constituency bias prompts deep learning models to allocate separate units (or neurons) for handling long-term and short-term information. This division enables the construction of latent hierarchical representations from sequential data, where higher-level abstractions are formed from and decomposable into lower-level components. For instance, even without access to ground-truth structures, our model learns to process logical expressions by synthesizing representations of variables and operators into complete expression representations based on syntactic rules. Conversely, the dependency bias encourages models to uncover latent relationships between entities within an input sequence. In natural language, these relations are typically represented as directed dependency graphs, wherein each word has exactly one parent node and zero or more children nodes. When applied to a Transformer-like architecture, this constraint allows the model to induce directed graphs that closely align with human expert annotations and achieves superior performance across various tasks compared to standard Transformers. We posit that these findings offer a promising alternative direction for the future evolution of deep learning models.

Natural language processing relies heavily on representation learning. Although recent Transformer models like BERT excel at generating textual representations through token- and sentence-level objectives, they fail to incorporate inter-document relatedness, thereby restricting their effectiveness at the document level. However, for scientific document applications such as classification and recommendation, these embeddings currently yield strong task performance. To address this, we introduce SPECTER, a novel approach for creating document-level embeddings of scientific texts by pretraining a Transformer model on the robust signal provided by citation graphs. Distinct from existing pretrained models, SPECTER can be readily applied to downstream tasks without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Furthermore, to stimulate further research into document-level modeling, we present SciDocs, a new evaluation benchmark comprising seven tasks spanning citation prediction, document classification, and recommendation. Our results demonstrate that SPECTER surpasses various competitive baselines across this benchmark.

The Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP) framework remains a leading Dark Matter (DM) hypothesis, though it faces stringent constraints, particularly from direct detection experiments. Adhering to the WIMP hypothesis, we examine a Dirac fermion DM candidate interacting with the Standard Model (SM) through a spin-1 $Z'$ boson.
