By applying group labels to both EEG and speech signals and constructing transition signals that blend corresponding EEG and speech inputs in specific proportions, the model creates effective bridges between signals lacking shared features, thereby enabling one-to-one cross-domain translation. This method successfully translates both word-length and sentence-length neural activity sequences into speech. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods in handling both auditory word and sentence stimuli.

How can a smooth cosmic distance ladder arise from observations made from a single point within a lumpy universe? Distances to Type Ia supernovae in the Hubble flow are anchored by local distance measurements to nearby sources. We detail how this framework functions in a perturbed universe, where inhomogeneities are modeled as small deviations from a flat Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetime. Our analysis reveals a significant modification (approximately 11%) to the background FLRW area distance caused by inhomogeneities in the observer's immediate vicinity. This correction originates from the electric component of the Weyl tensor, signifying tidal distortions in the local spacetime around the observer. We provide a detailed examination of how this effect influences the calibration of the absolute magnitude of Type Ia supernovae in the Hubble flow. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this mechanism could simultaneously resolve the tensions regarding the Type Ia supernova absolute magnitude and the Hubble constant, eliminating the necessity for invoking early or late dark energy.

This study introduces a pipeline utilizing persistent homology to characterize and constrain cosmological initial conditions. The focus is on the cosmic web of large-scale structure, specifically targeting non-Gaussianities (NG) in primordial density perturbations. We calculate persistence diagrams and associated statistics from simulations of dark matter halos featuring both Gaussian and non-Gaussian initial conditions. To align with experimental observations and address computational constraints, the pipeline analyzes persistence within sub-boxes of full simulations and employs subsampling to achieve uniform halo number densities. Using simulations with high non-Gaussianity ($f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}=250$) as templates, we identify data containing mild non-Gaussianity ($f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}=10$). Across multiple $40~(\textrm{Gpc/h})^{3}$ cubic volumes, our optimal single statistic detects the $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}=10$ signal at a $97.5\%$ confidence level in approximately $85\%$ of the volumes. Throughout this process, the interpretability of topological features as inputs for statistical inference enables connections to prior first-principles calculations and facilitates new predictions.

The emergence of on-body wearable sensing has made human activity recognition a promising field of study. By embedding sensors into comfortable e-textiles, researchers can now monitor human movement outside laboratory settings over extended durations. Despite this capability, a persistent challenge involves handling motion artifacts caused by the relative movement between clothing and the body. Contrary to expectations, recent empirical evidence indicates that sensors attached to fabric can outperform rigidly mounted sensors in activity recognition accuracy, especially within short time windows. This study introduces a probabilistic model that attributes this enhanced accuracy and responsiveness to the greater statistical distance observed in movements captured via fabric sensing. Both simulated and real-world human motion capture experiments validate the model's predictions, confirming that this counterintuitive phenomenon is accurately represented.

Gaining insight into defect-phonon interactions is vital for advancing our understanding of quantum platforms. This study employs first-principles calculations to model a defect consisting of two spin-1/2 particles interacting with phonon modes within a one-dimensional lattice. Utilizing a bottom-up methodology, we start with a dipolar magnetic interaction to derive the spectral density function and a time-local master equation that characterizes the open dynamics of the defect. We present both theoretical and numerical analyses of the non-Markovian characteristics arising from pure dephasing in the Bell basis. Furthermore, we evaluate two non-Markovianity measures based on canonical rates and coherence to better understand the influence of the spectral density function and temperature, while also outlining potential experimental implementations.

For every positive integer r, the r-associated Stirling number of the second kind counts the ways to partition the set {1, 2, 3, ..., n} into k non-empty, disjoint subsets where each subset has a minimum size of r. This paper introduces degenerate versions of both the r-associated Stirling numbers of the second and first kinds. These new numbers serve as degenerate counterparts to their standard r-associated forms and coincide with the classical degenerate Stirling numbers when r equals 1. The primary objective of this study is to establish recurrence relations for both of these degenerate number types.

The Web community has established a collection of standards and technologies designed to represent, query, and manipulate a globally distributed data structure called the Web of Data. Advocates of this initiative envision a future where much of the world's data is interconnected and freely available to the public. While this vision mirrors the Web of Documents in its openness, the primary focus shifts from making documents and media accessible to making data itself openly available. This shift has fueled the Open Data movement, which parallels the Open Source movement; however, whereas Open Source centers on software, Open Data concentrates on the legal and licensing frameworks governing publicly exposed data. Collectively, these technological and legal tools are establishing the foundation for global-scale data management on the Web. Currently, in its nascent stage, the Web of Data hosts diverse datasets ranging from encyclopedic facts and biological information (such as drugs and proteins) to metadata on music, books, and scholarly articles, as well as social network representations and geospatial data. The scale and variety of this data demonstrate the adaptability of the underlying standards and the overall viability of the project. This article aims to review the technological foundations of the Web of Data and identify the challenges that must be addressed for it to become the de facto medium for data representation, distribution, and processing.

We examine a class of one-dimensional vector Non-linear Schrödinger Equations (NLSE) featuring an external complex potential, balanced loss-gain (BLG) mechanisms, and linear coupling (LC) between the components of the Schrödinger field. This study investigates the solvability of the general system across various configurations of time-modulated LC and BLG terms, space-time-dependent nonlinear interaction strengths, and complex potentials. By applying a non-unitary transformation and reformulating the differential equation in a new coordinate system, we map the NLSE to solvable equations. Several physically motivated examples of exactly solvable systems are provided for different combinations of LC, BLG, external complex potentials, and nonlinear interactions. Exact localized nonlinear modes with spatially constant phases can be derived for any real potential where the corresponding linear Schrödinger equation is solvable. Furthermore, a method rooted in supersymmetric quantum mechanics is developed to construct exact localized nonlinear modes for specific classes of complex potentials; notably, the real superpotential from any exactly solved linear Schrödinger equation can be utilized to determine a complex potential yielding exact localized nonlinear modes for the NLSE. Additionally, solutions characterized by singular phases are derived for a limited set of complex potentials.

This study introduces a novel SLAM framework that integrates an event-based camera with Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar to facilitate drone navigation. Both sensors are handled by a bio-inspired Spiking Neural Network (SNN) employing continual Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP), a mechanism mirroring biological learning. Unlike conventional learning-based SLAM systems, which typically demand a representative dataset and an offline training stage, this approach eliminates the need for offline training. Instead, the SNN adaptively learns features from incoming data in real-time through STDP. Simultaneously, the SNN's outputs serve as feature descriptors for loop closure detection and map refinement. Through extensive experiments benchmarking the system against leading RGB-based methods, we demonstrate the robustness of our DVS-Radar SLAM solution under significant lighting fluctuations.

This work details the characteristics of both fermion and boson fields within the framework of second quantization, provided that this quantization arises from describing the field's internal space using "basis vectors." These vectors are constructed as superpositions of either odd (for fermions) or even (for bosons) products of Clifford algebra operators $\gamma^a$. When these "basis vectors" are tensor-producted with the basis of ordinary space to form creation operators, the resulting anticommutativity of fermions or commutativity of bosons emerges naturally, thereby elucidating the postulates of second quantization for both field types. Furthermore, the creation operators for boson fields exhibit all the properties of the gauge fields associated with their corresponding fermion fields, offering a novel perspective on the relationship between fermion and boson fields.

This work investigates the cohomological structure of the moduli space of $\mathrm{SL}_n$-Higgs bundles, which may be singular, defined over a genus $g$ curve for arbitrary degrees relative to an effective divisor with degree greater than $2g-2$. We establish a support theorem for the $\mathrm{SL}_n$-Hitchin fibration that generalizes de Cataldo's result from the nonsingular setting and present a formulation of the Hausel-Thaddeus topological mirror symmetry conjecture adapted for intersection cohomology. These findings yield a broad extension of the Harder-Narasimhan theorem regarding semistable vector bundles across all degrees. Our primary method relies on a recently developed Ng\^{o}-type support inequality, which remains valid for potentially singular ambient spaces and intersection cohomology complexes.

We present a novel approach to partitioning a graph's edge set, which serves as a substitute for Szemerédi's Regularity lemma in specific graph embedding contexts, alongside an accompanying algorithmic framework.

The analysis involves eighty collections of layer groups, with each collection comprising four specific types: ordinary single and double layers, as well as gray single and double layers. The structural characteristics of these groups, specifically their factorization into cyclic subgroups and their grading based on sequences of halving subgroups, facilitate efficient symbolic computation using the POLSym code. This process focuses on determining real and complex irreducible representations, as well as allowed half-integer (co-)representations. The workflow begins with classifying irreducible domains by combining group actions within the Brillouin zone and torus topology. Furthermore, band (co-)representations derived from the irreducible (co-)representations of Wyckoff position stabilizers (site symmetry groups) are decomposed into their irreducible components. Relevant theoretical data concerning layer group symmetry, which is particularly significant for layered materials, is compiled into tables and published on the project's website.

The visibility counting problem involves preprocessing a set $S$ of $n$ disjoint line segments in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ to enable rapid computation of the number of segments visible from any query point $p$. While existing approaches rely on approximation algorithms balancing space and query time, we introduce a new randomized algorithm that computes the exact solution. For any $0 < \alpha < 1$, the algorithm achieves space, preprocessing time, and query time complexities of $O_{\epsilon}(n^{4-4\alpha})$, $O_{\epsilon}(n^{4-2\alpha})$, and $O_{\epsilon}(n^{2\alpha})$, respectively. In this notation, $O_{\epsilon}(f(n))$ denotes $O(f(n)n^{\epsilon})$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is an arbitrary constant.

Measurements were conducted on the emission angles and transverse momentum distributions of projectile fragments resulting from the fragmentation of $^{56}$Fe ions at 471 A MeV on CH$_{2}$, C, and Al targets. Results indicate that for a given target, both the mean and width of the angular distribution diminish as the projectile fragment's charge increases. Conversely, for a specific fragment, the average angle rises while the distribution width narrows as the target's charge number increases. The transverse momentum distribution aligns with a single Gaussian model, showing that the average transverse momentum per nucleon drops as the fragment charge grows. Furthermore, the cumulated squared transverse momentum distribution fits well to a single Rayleigh distribution. Finally, the temperature parameter of the emission source, derived from this Rayleigh distribution, declines as the size of the projectile fragment increases.

Canonical models of star formation in magnetized settings forecast the development of hourglass-shaped magnetic fields during the prestellar collapse. However, recent observations of protostellar cores indicate that magnetic fields in inner regions are highly distorted and complex, shaped by rotational forces and outflows. We performed resistive, nonideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of a protostellar core and utilized the radiative transfer code POLARIS to generate synthetic polarization segment maps. Comparing our mock-polarization maps, which feature a toroidal-dominated magnetic field in the outflow region, with observed polarization vectors from SiO lines in Orion Source I yields reasonable agreement when the magnetic axis is inclined at $\theta = 15^{\circ}$ relative to the plane-of-sky and assuming SiO line polarization aligns parallel to the local magnetic field. Although the observed data stems from SiO lines while our synthetic maps represent polarized dust emission, this comparison remains valuable as it helps clarify the ambiguity regarding whether line polarization is parallel or perpendicular to the local magnetic field direction.

Order picking stands as the most labor-intensive and expensive operation in warehouses, heavily influencing overall facility performance due to the significant workforce required. Consequently, numerous methods have been developed to optimize this process using various economic metrics. However, the majority of these strategies focus on a solitary economic goal while neglecting ergonomic factors. Furthermore, the impact of item placement is often underestimated, leading to insufficient attention on the interdependence between storage assignment and order picking. This study aims to optimize both storage assignment and order picking within a mezzanine warehouse by considering their mutual influence. We introduce a customized Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) for storage assignment and an Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) algorithm for order picking. Both methods simultaneously integrate multiple economic and ergonomic constraints. Additionally, these algorithms leverage knowledge of the interdependence between the two problems to enhance overall warehouse efficiency. Evaluation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithms yield superior storage assignments and picking routes compared to conventional techniques, as measured by Coverage, Generational Distance, Euclidean Distance, Pareto Front Size, and Inverted Generational Distance. Moreover, the assessment of the interaction between the two algorithms indicates improved performance when they are combined.

In Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), post-hoc interpretability methods are designed to help users understand the predictions of trained decision models. Incorporating prior knowledge into these methods seeks to enhance explanation clarity and enable personalized insights tailored to individual users. This paper introduces a cost function that explicitly embeds prior knowledge into interpretability objectives, presenting a general framework for optimizing post-hoc interpretability. We demonstrate that user knowledge can be integrated into any method by adding a compatibility term to the cost function. Applying this formalization to counterfactual explanations, we propose a new method called Knowledge Integration in Counterfactual Explanation (KICE). Finally, an experimental study across multiple benchmark datasets characterizes the counterfactual instances produced by KICE in comparison to existing reference methods.

This paper introduces a new class of test statistics designed to detect mean change points in high-dimensional independent data. Our method synthesizes the U-statistic approach from \cite{hdcp} with the $L_q$-norm based test from \cite{he2018}, inheriting desirable traits such as the absence of tuning parameters and asymptotic independence for even $q$ values. By combining test statistics across various $q$ values, we achieve an adaptive power property, ensuring effectiveness against both sparse and dense alternatives. Regarding estimation, we derive the convergence rate of the test statistic's maximizer (standardized by sample size) for a single mean change-point with $q=2$, and suggest integrating our tests with a Wild Binary Segmentation (WBS) algorithm to identify the number and locations of multiple change-points. Empirical evaluations using both simulated and real datasets highlight the superior performance of our adaptive test and associated estimation procedure.

We define a product of pairs within the double complex spaces $C^n_m(V, \mathcal{W}, \mathcal{F})$ concerning the gradig-restricted vertex algebra cohomology of codimension one foliations on complex curves. Furthermore, we introduce a vertex algebra analogue of the classical product-type cohomological class, utilizing the orthogonality conditions of elements in these double complex spaces relative to the defined product.

We provide a comprehensive operator-based description of a lossy photon-subtraction protocol using characteristic functions of quantum states. By inputting a single-mode squeezed vacuum into a tunable beam splitter and detecting photons in one output port, a wide range of multiphoton-subtracted squeezed vacuum states (MSSVSs) can be produced in the remaining channel, with losses accounted for at both the input and output stages. While this approach was previously examined in Ref. [Phys. Rev. A 100, 022341 (2019)], our work distinguishes itself by detailing the optical fields throughout every stage of the process. Furthermore, we derive analytical formulas and conduct numerical simulations to evaluate the success probability, quadrature squeezing, photon-number distribution, and Wigner function of the resulting MSSVSs, yielding several insightful findings regarding the impact of losses.

This study examines the causal-observational languages proposed by Barbero and Sandu (2018), which offer a unified approach to interventionist counterfactuals and functional dependencies. Specifically, we systematically evaluate the expressive capabilities of these languages within causal team semantics and develop complete natural deduction systems for each. Additionally, we propose a generalized semantics capable of modeling uncertainty regarding causal laws, and we analyze both the expressive power and proof theory of the causal-observational languages under this expanded framework.

This research examines a single, freely floating, inextensible, elastic filament subjected to a linear shear flow defined by $\mathbf{U}_{0}(x,y) = \dot{\gamma} y \hat{x}$. The model assumes that elastic energy arises solely from bending, the strain rate $\dot{\gamma} = S \sin(\omega t)$ varies periodically with time $t$, and filament-flow interaction is modeled via local isotropic drag. Depending on the filament's configuration, five distinct dynamical phases are identified: straight, buckled, periodic (including periods of two, three, four, etc.), chaotic, and a regime characterized by chaotic transients. Within the chaotic phase, the iterative map for the angle between the filament's end-to-end vector and the tangent at one end exhibits period-three solutions, confirming chaos via the period-three theorem. Additionally, the flow demonstrates efficient mixing properties during this chaotic phase.

This work examines momentum operators defined on intrinsically curved manifolds. Since these operators correspond to Killing vector fields with geodesic integral curves, the analysis demonstrates that the manifold must either be flat or possess compact topology with constant positive sectional curvature in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Explicit forms for the momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are derived specifically for the 3-sphere ($S^3$). It is confirmed that the structure constants of the underlying Lie algebra scale proportionally with $2\hbar/R$, where $R$ denotes the curvature radius of $S^3$. Consequently, freely moving particles in $S^3$ exhibit a countable spectrum of energy and momentum. Furthermore, the maximum resolution for momentum is established as the de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda_R=\pi R$, which coincides with the manifold's diameter. Finally, covariant position operators are formulated using geodesic normal coordinates, and the resulting commutation relations between position and momentum are derived.

This paper establishes Rubio de Francia extrapolation theorems for quasi-monotone functions within Lebesgue and grand Lebesgue spaces using $QB_{\beta,p}$ weights. Additionally, extrapolation results in Lebesgue spaces under the $QB_{\beta,\infty}$ weight class are examined. As a practical application, we determine the boundedness conditions for the Hardy averaging operator acting on quasi-monotone functions in grand Lebesgue spaces.

The ALICE detector at the LHC measured the production of prompt D$^{0}$, D$^{+}$, and D$^{*+}$ mesons at midrapidity (|y|< 0.5) during Pb-Pb collisions at a nucleon-nucleon centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. These D mesons were identified through their hadronic decays, with yields determined for both central (0-10%) and semicentral (30-50%) collision events. The measurements extended up to transverse momenta ($p_{\rm T}$) of 36 or 50 GeV/$c$, varying by meson type and centrality. Notably, this study marked the first time in LHC Pb-Pb collisions that D$^0$ yields were measured down to $p_{\rm T}$ = 0, enabling a model-independent calculation of the $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yield per unit rapidity (d$N$/d$y$). The nuclear modification factor ($R_{\rm AA}$) for prompt D mesons showed a maximum suppression of 5 and 2.5 times at $p_{\rm T}$ = 6-8 GeV/$c$ for the 0-10% and 30-50% centrality classes, respectively. These $R_{\rm AA}$ results were compared against those of charged pions, charged hadrons, J/$\psi$ mesons, and various theoretical models. By analyzing the consistency between the measured $R_{\rm AA}$, elliptic ($v_2$), and triangular ($v_3$) flow with model predictions, researchers constrained the charm spatial diffusion coefficient $D_s$. Additionally, comparing $R_{\rm AA}$ and $v_2$ across different implementations of the same models offered significant insights into the roles of radiative energy loss and charm quark recombination within hadronization processes.

We develop electric and magnetic Newton-Hooke and Carroll Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity theories by leveraging the isomorphism between Newton-Hooke$_\pm$ and (A-)dS Carroll algebras within $(1+1)$-dimensional spacetime. Our approach begins with the non-relativistic and Carroll formulations of Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, as presented in [15], without imposing geometric constraints.

Analyzing and interpreting diverse flow patterns within urban settings has become crucial, as they enable the development of novel strategies to combat climate change by enhancing our understanding of pollutant dynamics in cities. This research employs higher-order dynamic mode decomposition (HODMD) to examine a high-fidelity dataset of turbulent flows across various simplified urban configurations. The simulated geometry comprises two buildings separated by a specific distance, with three distinct cases investigated, each corresponding to a regime identified in existing literature. We identify the characteristics of the well-known arch vortex that forms on the leeward side of the first structure and elucidate potential mechanisms for its generation and destruction based on the resulting temporal modes. These specific vortex-generating and vortex-breaking modes undergo further analysis through proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate that the arch vortex significantly influences pollutant dispersion in urban areas, where its formation leads to increased concentrations; consequently, the identified mechanisms are of paramount importance for urban sustainability.

We introduce a direct approach for computing the decay width of a hadron into two photons, bypassing the conventional reliance on extrapolating off-shell form factors. This novel technique offers a straightforward means to investigate finite-volume effects. As a demonstration, we apply the method to the $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$ decay. By utilizing three $N_f=2$ twisted-mass gauge ensembles with varying lattice spacings, we determine the final decay width to be $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV, with the systematic uncertainty incorporating fine-tuning adjustments for the charm quark mass. Furthermore, this methodology is applicable to other processes featuring leptonic or radiative particles in the final state.

Recent advancements in text-video retrieval have been driven by utilizing large-scale pretraining on visual and audio data to build robust video encoders. Conversely, despite the inherent symmetry, the development of algorithms that harness large-scale language pretraining has been largely neglected. This study pioneers the exploration of such algorithms by introducing TeachText, a novel generalized distillation technique that aggregates complementary signals from multiple text encoders to strengthen the supervisory input for retrieval models. Additionally, we adapt this approach to video-side modalities, demonstrating that test-time performance remains uncompromised even when reducing the number of utilized modalities. Our method significantly outperforms existing approaches on various video retrieval benchmarks without incurring any computational cost during inference. Finally, we highlight the method's utility in filtering noise from retrieval datasets. The code and data are available at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/research/teachtext/.

This study presents the design specifications of a compact, continuous nuclear demagnetization refrigerator (CNDR) featuring two PrNi$_5$ nuclear stages capable of maintaining temperatures below 1 mK, alongside experimental results for a novel thermal contact technique employing Zn soldering instead of Cd for the PrNi$_5$ stage. By analyzing the residual electrical resistance of a test sample, the thermal contact resistivity between the PrNi$_5$ rod and the silver wire thermal link was determined to be $1.8\pm0.1 \times 10^{-4} T^{-1}~\rm{Km^2W^{-1}}$. Utilizing this figure in conjunction with both 2D numerical and 1D analytical thermal simulations, the maximum temperature gradient across the nuclear stage was found to be negligible ($\leq$ 2 %) at 1 mK, given a 10 nW heat leak corresponding to the system's anticipated cooling capacity.

**Context.** Our prior research proposed that magnetic reconnection, driven by significantly higher-than-previously-understood magnetic flux cancellation at the photosphere, is responsible for diverse dynamic events such as various jets and solar atmospheric heating. **Aims.** While earlier theories focused on energy release within a two-dimensional current sheet, this study advances the framework by modeling an axisymmetric current sheet in three dimensions, avoiding complex variable theory. **Methods.** We conduct an analytical examination of reconnection by treating the current sheet as a three-dimensional entity, specifically applying the model to the interaction of two equal but oppositely signed flux fragments moving toward each other within an overlying horizontal magnetic field. **Results.** Energy release unfolds in two distinct stages. In Phase 1, a separator forms, driving reconnection as it ascends to a peak altitude before descending back to the photosphere, a process that heats the plasma and propels a jet. In Phase 2, the fluxes cancel at the photosphere, accelerating a blend of cool and hot plasma upward.

Time series datasets frequently suffer from contamination by outliers or various anomalies. Detecting these irregularities serves either as a primary objective in anomaly detection or as a strategy to enhance the performance of other time series tasks, such as forecasting. Current deep-learning methods for both anomaly detection and forecasting typically assume that anomalies constitute a negligible fraction of the training data, effectively treating unlabeled data as originating from the nominal distribution. We introduce a straightforward yet powerful technique to augment existing time series models, enabling them to explicitly handle anomalies present in the training set. By integrating a latent anomaly indicator variable into the training data—whose distribution is inferred alongside the underlying model via Monte Carlo EM—our approach simultaneously identifies anomalous points and boosts model performance on normal data. We validate the method's efficacy by applying it to a simple feed-forward forecasting model. Furthermore, we examine the impact of anomalies within the training set on the development of forecasting models, which are often repurposed for anomaly detection, demonstrating that our method significantly improves this training process.

Whitby serves as the server component of an Intelligent Tutoring System designed to teach System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA), a methodology for ensuring safety in systems that can be modeled. The system's reasoning engine is based on Situation Calculus, a many-sorted logic encompassing situation, action, and object categories. This logic underpins Whitby's two core functions: Ontology Authoring and Contingent Scaffolding. Consequently, numerous fluents and actions are aggregated from these sub-applications and the system itself, yet they are all accessible via a unified situation query interface that operates independently of specific fluents or actions. Within Whitby, each STPA project is represented as a single situation term; this term is queried to retrieve relevant ontological fluents and to identify appropriate pedagogical interventions. Originally developed in Prolog with a module system, Whitby was later refactored into Logtalk to achieve a cleaner architecture, enhanced code reuse, and greater extensibility. This refactoring involved decoupling the Situation Calculus reasoner, the Ontology Authoring framework, and the Contingent Scaffolding framework into reusable third-party libraries. This separation was accomplished by inverting dependencies using Logtalk protocols and categories, which act as reusable interfaces providing cohesive sets of predicate declarations and definitions. This paper evaluates the architectures of Whitby's two iterations, assessing them against the original motivations for refactoring: establishing a clean architecture that facilitates code reuse and extensibility.

This study investigates alterations in charged particle distributions relative to high transverse momentum ($p_\mathrm{T}$) jets traversing a quark-gluon plasma, utilizing data from the CMS detector. The analysis focuses on back-to-back dijets in lead-lead and proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} =$ 5.02 TeV, examining charged particle correlations across bins of relative pseudorapidity and angular distance from the jet axes. Comparisons between lead-lead and proton-proton collision data reveal that modifications to the charged-particle relative distance and momentum distributions near the jet axis depend on the dijet momentum balance, defined as $x_j$ (the ratio of subleading to leading jet $p_\mathrm{T}$). For events where $x_j \approx 1$, such modifications are detected for both the leading and subleading jets. Conversely, while subleading jets exhibit significant modifications in events with large dijet momentum imbalance, the leading jets in these same events display only minimal modifications.

In evidence synthesis, effect measure modifiers are usually characterized as variables that generate individual-level treatment effect heterogeneity via treatment-covariate interactions within an outcome model specified at that level. Consequently, effect modification is defined relative to a conditional measure. Nevertheless, health technology assessment demands marginal effect estimates for population-level decisions. For non-collapsible effect measures, purely prognostic variables—which do not predict individual treatment responses—can alter marginal treatment effects at the population level. This distinction carries significant implications for evidence synthesis practices. First, unadjusted indirect comparisons of marginal effects may yield bias if individual-level treatment effect heterogeneity is absent. Second, covariate adjustment might be required to address cross-study imbalances in purely prognostic variables. Common meta-analytic summary statistics, such as odds ratios and hazard ratios, are non-collapsible. In contrast, collapsible measures would enhance the transportability of marginal effects between studies by: (1) eliminating the reliance on model-based covariate adjustment when individual-level treatment effect homogeneity exists; and (2) streamlining the selection of baseline characteristics for covariate adjustment in the presence of heterogeneity.

Coherence remains one of the most frequently utilized attributes in seismic interpretation. This paper introduces an enhancement to the recently developed Generalized Tensor-based Coherence (GTC) by imparting directional selectivity. This selectivity is realized through the application of a directional Gaussian preprocessing kernel and a 3D rotational matrix to its covariance matrix. By weighting traces or voxels within the analysis cube according to their relative proximity to a reference point, the method significantly improves attribute clarity. Moreover, the incorporation of directional weighting grants interpreters increased flexibility in exploring and comprehending seismic data. Results from the Netherlands North Sea F3 block demonstrate that this approach substantially boosts coherence clarity and reveals structures that remain undetectable using traditional C3 or GTC coherence methods.

Crowd counting is a critical task with significant potential in public safety, drawing growing interest in recent years. Current research primarily focuses on improving counting accuracy and estimating crowd density. While deep learning has significantly advanced this domain, accurately counting crowds against cluttered backgrounds remains a formidable challenge. To address this, we introduce the ScaleAware Crowd Counting Network (SACCN), which integrates regional and semantic attention mechanisms. SACCN leverages regional self-attention in shallow layers and semantic self-attention in deep layers to effectively differentiate crowds from backgrounds. Additionally, we propose an Asymmetric Multi-scale Module (AMM) to handle scale diversity, while employing regional attention-based dense and skip connections to mitigate variations in crowd scales. Extensive experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that SACCN achieves superior performance, outperforming most state-of-the-art methods. The code and pretrained models will be made available shortly.

In recent years, numerous techniques for assessing machine learning fairness have emerged. Yet, despite an increase in publications and implementations, there remains a significant gap in literature connecting fair machine learning with social sciences like philosophy, sociology, and law. This field guide aims to bridge that divide by synthesizing and expanding on insights from both formal sciences (machine learning and statistics) and social sciences regarding fairness. Beyond providing the mathematical and algorithmic foundations of key statistical and causal fairness methods, we elucidate the philosophical and legal principles underpinning them. Additionally, we examine criticisms of current fair machine learning approaches from sociological and philosophical perspectives. Ultimately, we hope this guide enables practitioners to better comprehend how their algorithms align with core humanistic values, such as fairness, and fosters the development of methods and metrics that more effectively serve oppressed and marginalized communities.

This study utilizes Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to approximate steady-state, particle-resolved fluid flow around a fixed particle of interest within a dispersed multiphase system containing randomly distributed stationary particles. Given the problem's rotational symmetry about the mean velocity (streamwise) direction, the research employs an SE(3)-equivariant CNN architecture, which ensures equivariance under both translation and three-dimensional rotations. The primary focus is on evaluating the generalization capabilities and advantages of this SE(3)-equivariant network. By applying a symmetry-aware, data-driven approach, the study generates accurate synthetic flow fields for Reynolds numbers ranging from 86.22 to 172.96 and particle volume fractions between 0.11 and 0.45.

We establish a straightforward uniform continuity bound for the sandwiched R\'enyi conditional entropy, valid for $\alpha \in [1/2, 1) \cup (1, \infty]$, that does not rely on the dimension of the conditioning system.

Particle acceleration within a quasilinear plasma wake offers high acceleration gradients while preventing the self-trapping of background electrons. Nevertheless, the plasma's reaction to the injected witness bunch causes fluctuations in focusing fields along the bunch's length, potentially increasing emittance. To assess how this emittance growth affects overall beam quality, we created a single figure of merit tailored to a potential high-energy application of the AWAKE experiment at CERN. Our findings indicate that this figure of merit inherently imposes constraints on the tunability and stability of the initial witness bunch parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distinct physics of the quasilinear wake results in broad tolerances for the witness bunch radius at injection, as the plasma wakefields naturally self-match to the witness bunch.

Monte Carlo simulations performed away from half-filling encounter a sign problem that can be mitigated by deforming the integration contour. While this transformation introduces a Jacobian determinant into the Boltzmann weight that can be handled via neural networks, the determinant cost for standard architectures scales cubically with volume, hindering large-scale applications. We introduce a novel architecture utilizing complex-valued affine coupling layers to reduce this scaling to linear. The effectiveness of this approach is validated across various system sizes, including the largest case, which remains intractable for other Monte Carlo methods due to its intense sign problem.

This study demonstrates the existence of universal rogue wave patterns within integrable systems. These patterns consist of fundamental rogue waves organized into geometric shapes like triangles, pentagons, and heptagons, potentially featuring a lower-order rogue wave at their center. Such patterns emerge when specific internal parameters in the bilinear representations of rogue waves become large. Analytically, these structures are derived from the root configurations of the Yablonskii-Vorob'ev polynomial hierarchy via linear transformations. Consequently, the resulting space-time patterns correspond directly to the roots of Yablonskii-Vorob'ev polynomials subjected to operations such as dilation, rotation, stretching, shearing, and translation. As illustrations, these universal patterns are explicitly calculated and visualized for the generalized derivative nonlinear Schrödinger equation, the Boussinesq equation, and the Manakov system. Furthermore, the paper examines the parallels and distinctions between these newly identified patterns and those previously reported in the context of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

We examine a one-parameter family of states within two-dimensional holographic conformal field theories, constructed through the Euclidean path integral of an effective theory defined on hyperbolic slices in the dual bulk geometry. This effective theory arises from a CFT deformed by $T\overline{T}$, a process that "folds" the boundary CFT toward a bulk time-reflection symmetric slice. We propose that these novel Euclidean path integral states in the CFT correspond to continuous tensor network (CTN) states. Furthermore, we argue that these CTN states adhere to a Ryu-Takayanagi-like upper bound on the entanglement entropy of boundary intervals, with the coefficient matching $\frac{1}{4G_N}$; specifically, the CTN associated with the bulk time-reflection symmetric slice saturates this bound. Finally, we contend that the original CFT state can be expressed as a superposition of these CTN states, where the associated wavefunction is the bulk Hartle-Hawking wavefunction.

This study introduces a new electric field-ionization setup designed for high-resolution laser spectroscopy on bunched, fast atomic beams arranged in a collinear configuration. By combining this technique with multi-step resonant excitation to Rydberg states via pulsed lasers, the method achieves greater sensitivity for isotope separation and atomic parameter measurement compared to non-resonant laser ionization. The system was evaluated at ISOLDE-CERN's Collinear Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy experiment to measure transitions in indium atoms from the 5s$^2$5d~$^2$D$_{5/2}$ and 5s$^2$5d~$^2$D$_{3/2}$ states to 5s$^2$($n$)p~$^2$P and 5s$^2$($n$)f~$^2$F Rydberg states, reaching a principal quantum number of $n$ = 72. These measured Rydberg energies allowed for a revised calculation of the indium ionization potential at 46670.1055(21) cm$^{-1}$. Additionally, hyperfine structure constants for the nuclear magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole, along with level isotope shifts for the specified indium states, were determined for $^{113,115}$In. When compared to relativistic coupled-cluster theory calculations, the results showed strong agreement regarding the ionization potential and isotope shifts; however, discrepancies in the hyperfine structure constants suggest that electron correlations play a more significant role in these excited states. To further enhance detection sensitivity for exotic isotopes, a systematic investigation of the field-ionization arrangement was conducted, leading to a simulated and presented improved design that offers better background suppression regardless of the distance between field ionization and ion detection.

Utilizing machine learning to enhance optimization is a developing area with the potential to overcome the computational limits of traditional iterative solvers in applications demanding near-real-time performance. Most current methods aim to reduce iteration counts by learning data-driven optimizers. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel strategy: replacing iterative solvers entirely with a trainable parametric set function that delivers optimal parameters for an optimization problem in a single forward pass. We refer to this approach as Learning to Optimize the Optimization Process (LOOP). Our results demonstrate the viability of learning these parametric functions to address various classic optimization tasks, such as linear and nonlinear regression, principal component analysis, transport-based coresets, and quadratic programming within supply management contexts. Furthermore, we present two distinct methodologies for training these functions, one incorporating a solver and one excluding it. Extensive numerical experiments confirm that these trained solvers achieve speeds orders of magnitude greater than traditional iterative solvers while delivering near-optimal solutions.

This research examines $n\times n$ Hankel determinants formed from moments of a Hermite weight featuring a Fisher-Hartwig singularity on the real line, specifically analyzing cases where the singularity lies in the bulk and exhibits both root-type and jump-type characteristics. We derive large $n$ asymptotic behavior for these determinants, noting a critical transition that occurs as the jump magnitude scales with $n$. These mathematical objects appear in the context of thinning generalized Gaussian unitary ensembles and in generating special function solutions to the Painlevé IV equation.

We introduce a link-by-link rule-based approach to generate the complete ensemble of spanning trees for any recursively generated, finitely articulated graph, including the DGM net. These recursive structures enable the exact analytical solution of numerous large-scale properties within the spanning tree ensemble. We demonstrate how strategically applying the defined growth rules can isolate specific subsets of spanning trees that exhibit desired characteristics, such as small-world behavior, extended diameter, or specific degree distributions, thereby addressing various optimization challenges. Furthermore, this analysis of spanning trees increases the utility of recursive graphs as advanced models for complex networks found in everyday life.

The NA62 experiment at CERN, utilizing the full dataset acquired between 2016 and 2018, conducted searches for lepton number violating decays of $K^+\to\pi^-e^+e^+$ and $K^+\to\pi^-\pi^0e^+e^+$. At a 90% confidence level, the resulting upper limits on the branching fractions are $5.3\times 10^{-11}$ and $8.5\times 10^{-10}$, respectively. The limit for the first decay mode represents a fourfold improvement over the prior best measurement, whereas the second result establishes the initial constraint on the $K^+\to\pi^-\pi^0e^+e^+$ decay rate.

Circularly polarized (CP) gamma-ray sources offer significant versatility across nuclear, high-energy, and astrophysics. While laser-plasma particle accelerators promise gamma-ray fluxes far exceeding conventional methods, the circular polarization of emitted photons has historically been overlooked. This study demonstrates that high-quality CP gamma-ray beams can be produced by combining laser plasma wakefield acceleration with plasma mirror techniques. Using a weakly nonlinear Compton scattering process at moderate laser intensities, the helicity of the driving laser is transferred to the emitted gamma photons, achieving an average polarization degree of approximately 37% (21%) with a peak brilliance exceeding $10^{21}$ photons/(s $\cdot$ mm$^2 \cdot$ mrad$^2 \cdot$ 0.1% BW) at energies around 1 MeV (100 MeV). Furthermore, the proposed approach is both practical and robust against variations in laser and plasma parameters.

Natural language processing (NLP) profoundly influences society through tools like machine translation and search engines. However, despite its achievements, NLP remains predominantly accessible only for high-resource languages such as English and Chinese, leaving many others underserved due to a lack of data and benchmarks. This study addresses this gap by focusing on developing resources for Indonesian languages. Although Indonesia boasts the second-highest linguistic diversity globally, most of its languages are classified as endangered, with some already extinct. We introduce the first-ever parallel resource for ten low-resource Indonesian languages, comprising datasets, a multi-task benchmark, lexicons, and a parallel Indonesian-English corpus. We present comprehensive analyses and outline the challenges encountered during resource creation. Ultimately, we aim to inspire further NLP research on Indonesian and other underrepresented languages.

Recent gravitational wave detections enable the investigation of gravity within strong and dynamic field regimes. This study examines Einstein-dilation Gauss-Bonnet gravity, a theory inspired by string theory, utilizing two newly identified neutron star black hole binaries (GW200105 and GW200115) alongside GW190814, which aligns with both binary black hole and neutron star black hole binary interpretations. By employing the leading post-Newtonian correction and conducting Bayesian Markov-chain Monte Carlo analyses, we establish a 90% credible upper limit for the theory's coupling constant of $\sqrt{\alpha_{GB}} \lesssim 1.33\,\rm km$, a result validated through an independent Fisher analysis. This constraint surpasses previous limits derived from selected binary black hole events in the GWTC-1 and GWTC-2 catalogs. Furthermore, a combined analysis stacking GW200105, GW200115, GW190814, and selected binary black hole events yields a tighter bound of $\sqrt{\alpha_{GB}} \lesssim 1.18\,\rm km$. To assess the impact of higher post-Newtonian terms, we calculated waveform phase corrections up to the second post-Newtonian order by translating results from scalar-tensor theories to Einstein-dilation Gauss-Bonnet gravity. Our findings indicate that incorporating these higher-order terms strengthens the bounds by 14.5% for GW200105 and 6.9% for GW200115.

A meander system comprises two arc systems that define non-crossing pairings of the set $[2n] = \{1, \ldots, 2n\}$ within the upper and lower half-planes. This paper examines random meander systems, specifically demonstrating that for simply-generated meander systems, the cycle count in a system of size $n$ increases linearly with $n$, and the length of the longest cycle in a uniformly random meander system grows at a rate of at least $c \log n$ where $c > 0$. Additionally, numerical data suggests that for simply-generated meander systems of size $n$, (i) the number of cycles with length $k \ll n$ follows an asymptotic behavior of $\sim n k^{-\beta}$ with $\beta \approx 2$, and (ii) the longest cycle's length scales as $\sim n^\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is approximately $4/5$. These findings are contrasted with other meander families, namely rainbow meanders and comb-like meanders, which exhibit markedly distinct growth patterns.

This study presents an experimental investigation into manipulating colloidal particles within a drop resting on a hydrogel using diffusiophoresis, a mechanism where solute gradients induce directed particle motion. By establishing a concentration difference between the drop and the hydrogel, we achieve controlled particle movement in a stable suspension, overcoming typical stability challenges. Our findings demonstrate that diffusiophoresis can drive particles either toward or away from the liquid-air interface, contingent upon the solute gradient's direction and the particles' surface charge. We experimentally measured particle adsorption and validated these results using a one-dimensional numerical model. Furthermore, we confirm that diffusiophoretic effects are significant at the scale of a drop on a hydrogel, indicating a straightforward approach for depositing particles onto hydrogels.

The orbital dynamics of the event horizons in binary black hole systems are examined. Although recent numerical studies indicate that apparent horizons can complete numerous orbits during coalescence, this work focuses on the event horizon. We analyze the number of orbital periods event horizons sustain prior to merging, finding that they coalesce much earlier than apparent horizons, unable to complete even a single half-orbit while the latter persist for many cycles.

This study examines the connection between $y$-friable (or $y$-smooth) integers and the Dickman function. Previously, under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), an asymptotic formula for the count of such integers up to $x$, denoted $\Psi(x,y)$, was established only for $y \ge (\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ by Hildebrand and Saias. In this work, we provide an unconditional asymptotic formula for $\Psi(x,y)$ within the broader range $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula takes the form $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ multiplied by correction factors that account for contributions from zeta zeros and prime powers. Using this result, we address two inquiries posed by Hildebrand and Pomerance.

First, regarding Hildebrand's conjecture that $\Psi(x,y)$ is not asymptotically equivalent to $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ when $y < (\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, we confirm unconditionally that his assertion was correct.

Second, concerning Pomerance's question of whether $\Psi(x,y) \ge x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ holds for $x/2 \ge y \ge 2$, we demonstrate that if RH is false, the inequality fails infinitely often. If RH holds, the inequality is valid for $x/2 \ge y \ge 2$ with $x$ sufficiently large, except possibly near the critical region $y \approx (\log x)^2$. In this vicinity, the issue reduces to the behavior of the limit inferior of $\frac{\psi(y)-y}{\log y \sqrt{y}}$, where $\psi$ is the Chebyshev function, with a threshold constant $L \approx -0.666217$. While this limit is expected to be $0$, even under RH we cannot exclude the possibility that it is $-\infty$.

Additionally, our formula reveals that under RH, $\Psi(x,y)$ undergoes an unexpected phase transition when $y \approx (\log x)^{3/2}$. Furthermore, we refine several existing inequalities regarding $\Psi(x,y)$.

Star formation has long been recognized as an inefficient process, where only a small fraction, $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$, of a gas cloud's mass converts into stars within one free-fall time. Developing a robust theory of star formation necessitates measuring both the average value of $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$ and its variation across different molecular clouds. Since $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$ is calculated relative to the free-fall time, these measurements depend on precise determinations of cloud volume densities. However, previous attempts to derive volume densities from two-dimensional projected data have typically assumed molecular clouds are simple, uniform spheres, ignoring their likely filamentary structures and non-uniform density distributions. This uncertainty in true volume density is a primary source of error in observational estimates of $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$. In this study, we utilize simulations of turbulent, magnetized, radiative, self-gravitating star-forming clouds to investigate whether more accurate volume density estimates can be obtained to mitigate this error. By generating mock observations from these simulations, we demonstrate that current methods relying on the spherical assumption likely underestimate volume densities by ~0.26 dex and introduce ~0.51 dex in errors. These inaccuracies correspond to a ~0.13 dex overestimation and a ~0.25 dex scatter in $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$, levels comparable to the scatter seen in observed cloud samples. We develop a predictive model that leverages information available in two-dimensional measurements—most notably the Gini coefficient of the surface density distribution—to estimate volume density with ~0.3 dex less scatter. Testing this method on recent observations of the Ophiuchus cloud reveals that it successfully reduces the scatter in $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$.

The rapid expansion of data traffic, particularly in wireless domains, is causing a substantial increase in energy usage within the last-mile telecommunications infrastructure. This rising energy demand not only heightens operators' operational expenditures (OPEX) but also significantly expands their carbon footprints. Consequently, improving the energy efficiency of broadband access networks has become essential to support social, environmental, and economic sustainability. This article offers an overview of designing and optimizing energy-efficient broadband access networks, examines the energy-saving design of passive optical networks, explores enabling technologies for next-generation broadband wireless access, and highlights emerging innovations aimed at enhancing the energy efficiency of the network's last-mile access.

To realize magnonic devices, it is essential to determine spin-wave dispersions. Although recent advancements have shown that combining time-resolved pump-probe imaging with Fourier transforms can map dispersions in the lower-wavenumber regime, these measurements remain time-consuming when high sampling rates are required. In this study, we demonstrate the rapid acquisition of spin-wave dispersions by employing compressed sensing techniques. Furthermore, we quantitatively assessed the consistency of our findings. These results are applicable to a wide range of pump-probe measurements, including those utilizing electro-optical effects.

This study introduces a novel integrated ball (pseudo)metric that bridges the gap between a selected starting (pseudo)metric $d$ and the $L_p$ distance within general function spaces. By choosing $d$ to be either the Hausdorff or Fréchet distances, the authors establish integrated, shape-sensitive variants of these supremum-based metrics. These new measures facilitate more detailed functional analyses that are inaccessible through direct application of their non-integrated counterparts. Furthermore, convergent discrete approximations ensure that these computations are practically feasible.

An edge-coloring of a graph $G$ using consecutive integers $c_{1},\ldots,c_{t}$ is defined as an \emph{interval $t$-coloring} when every color appears, and the colors assigned to edges incident to any vertex are unique and constitute a contiguous sequence of integers. A graph $G$ is considered interval colorable if it admits an interval $t$-coloring for some positive integer $t$, and the collection of all such graphs is represented by $\mathfrak{N}$. In 2004, Giaro and Kubale demonstrated that for any $G,H\in \mathfrak{N}$, their Cartesian product also resides in $\mathfrak{N}$. That same year, they posed a corresponding open question regarding graph composition. Subsequently, in 2009, the first author established that if $G,H\in \mathfrak{N}$ and $H$ is regular, then $G[H]\in \mathfrak{N}$. This paper proves that $G[H]\in \mathfrak{N}$ provided $G\in \mathfrak{N}$ and $H$ possesses a specific type of interval coloring. Furthermore, we demonstrate that all regular graphs, complete bipartite graphs, and trees exhibit this special interval coloring. Consequently, it follows that if $G\in \mathfrak{N}$ and $T$ is a tree, then $G[T]\in \mathfrak{N}$.

Shifting toward carbon-neutral electricity represents a pivotal strategy for combating climate change by tackling emission reductions in the two primary sectors responsible for greenhouse gases: power generation and transportation. However, moving to a carbon-neutral grid challenges traditional approaches to grid planning and operation. These difficulties stem largely from the vast scope of decision-making required and the uncertainties surrounding energy supply and demand. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers the potential to dramatically accelerate this transition, as numerous power grid decision processes can be modeled as complex but classic machine learning tasks. To maximize AI's influence on the decarbonization of energy systems, algorithms originally designed for other fields must be adapted across three key domains: technology, markets, and policy.

High-energy physics (HEP) experiments investigating new physics typically depend on material interactions. A rapidly growing field involves the precise design and calculation of materials for these applications. This Snowmass contribution briefly establishes the scientific imperative for applying quantum mechanical calculations to HEP materials and outlines the specific questions such methods can resolve. Based on this, I evaluate the computational requirements for *ab initio* calculations within HEP, detailing the workflows and resources employed by current state-of-the-art techniques. Finally, I highlight promising future avenues, including the integration of machine learning, strongly-correlated quantum mechanics, and the transition toward performing materials calculations on quantum computers.

Prior research by Balasubramanyam and the second author established the first moment of the pair correlation function for Hecke angles within small subintervals of $[0,1]$, obtained by averaging over extensive families of Hecke newforms of weight $k$ associated with $\Gamma_0(N)$. This paper aims to investigate the second moment of said pair correlation function. Additionally, we provide estimates for lower-order error terms in the calculation of the second moment and demonstrate that the variance approaches zero under appropriate growth conditions for these families of Hecke newforms.

This paper utilizes fixed-point techniques to establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for nonlinear implicit fractional differential equations within Banach spaces. Additionally, employing Picard and weakly Picard operator theory alongside the Pompeiu–Hausdorff functional, we demonstrate solution uniqueness and analyze the dependence of the solution on initial conditions and the functions comprising the right-hand side.

As multimedia content has increased, audio recording environments have become more diverse, suggesting that an audio processing system could benefit from a front-end module capable of identifying the acoustic domain. This paper introduces the concept of acoustic domain identification (ADI) specifically for speaker diarization. We begin by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the various domains within the third DIHARD challenge, highlighting the distinguishing factors between them. Our primary contribution is the development of a straightforward and efficient solution for ADI using speaker embeddings. We then integrate this ADI module into the speaker diarization framework for the DIHARD III challenge. Results show substantial performance gains over the baseline when agglomerative hierarchical clustering thresholds are optimized for each specific domain. Specifically, we achieved relative improvements of over 5% and 8% in Detection Error Rate (DER) for the core and full conditions, respectively, on Track 1 of the DIHARD III evaluation set.

Achieving semantic segmentation in nighttime environments is a critical yet underexplored challenge for applications such as autonomous driving. To address this, we introduce NightLab, a new framework that utilizes multiple deep learning models equipped with night-specific features to attain State-of-The-Art (SoTA) results across various benchmarks. NightLab operates at two granularities: image-level and regional. Each level integrates light adaptation and segmentation modules. When processing a night scene, the image-level model generates an initial segmentation, while a concurrent hardness detection module pinpoints difficult areas and their context for deeper analysis. The regional-level model then refines these challenging zones to deliver significantly enhanced segmentation. All components are trained end-to-end using proposed night-aware losses, eliminating the need for handcrafted heuristics. Extensive testing on the NightCity and BDD100K datasets demonstrates that NightLab outperforms concurrent methods, achieving SoTA performance.

Structured fundamental circuit elements have enabled the creation of superconducting metamaterials, sparking recent interest in unconventional quantum phenomena within circuit quantum electrodynamics (circuit-QED). We introduce a strategy to construct a one-dimensional Josephson metamaterial functioning as a chiral waveguide through programmed spatiotemporal modulation of its effective impedance. The driving modulation currents take the form of traveling waves with phase velocities significantly slower than those of microwave photons. Consequently, Brillouin scattering generates non-trivial spectral regimes allowing for unidirectional photon propagation. By analyzing the coupling between superconducting qubits and this metamaterial waveguide under both Markovian and non-Markovian conditions, we demonstrate that the qubits can dissipate photons in a single direction. Furthermore, we illustrate that this approach can be scaled into a cascaded quantum network with multiple nodes, facilitating chiral photon transport between distant qubits. Ultimately, this research suggests that SQUID metamaterials could be leveraged to achieve unidirectional photon transport in circuit-QED systems.

Analytic solutions for thermal waves in solid cylindrical media are derived from a nonlinear hyperbolic system comprising energy conservation and heat flux relaxation equations. This approach generalizes the Fourier-Cattaneo phenomenological law by allowing both the heat propagation coefficient and relaxation time to follow a general power-law dependence on temperature. Consequently, these laws preclude the formation of second-order parabolic or telegraph-type equations. Instead, the original nonlinear hyperbolic system is analyzed using a self-similar Ansatz for both heat flux and temperature distribution. The results include both continuous and shock-wave solutions, with numerous materials exhibiting temperature-dependent heat conduction coefficients cited to validate the physical relevance of these findings.

Effective communication is an essential competency for healthcare professionals, as it enhances patient outcomes and satisfaction while reducing the risk of malpractice litigation. Traditional medical training relies on role-playing and Standardized Patients (SPs)—actors—to develop these skills; however, SPs present challenges regarding standardization and resource intensity. Virtual Patients (VPs), which are interactive computer-based systems, offer a promising alternative by simulating realistic clinical scenarios and engaging learners in authentic conversations. Over the past decade, utilizing VPs for medical communication training has become a vibrant research domain, leading to a substantial increase in relevant publications. This study aims to survey recent literature to evaluate the current state of the art, with a specific emphasis on the instructional and technical design of VP simulations. Following the classification and analysis of selected VPs, we identified key areas needing further exploration and formulated practical recommendations for developers. These guidelines highlight critical design elements necessary for creating innovative and effective VP simulations or enhancing existing ones.

We provide a comprehensive collection of analytic helicity amplitudes for top quark pair production through gluon fusion at the two-loop level within QCD. Notably, this work incorporates corrections from massive fermion loops for the first time, which introduce integrals over elliptic curves. We detail the previously missing master integrals required for the amplitude calculation and derive an analytic expression for the finite remainders using iterated integrals, rationalized kinematics, and finite field sampling. Additionally, we investigate the numerical computation of these iterated integrals.

This paper investigates Daugavet- and $\Delta$-points within Banach spaces. A norm-one element $x$ qualifies as a Daugavet-point (or a $\Delta$-point) if, within every slice of the unit ball (or specifically within every slice containing $x$), one can locate an element arbitrarily close to a distance of 2 from $x$. Our focus lies in identifying criteria and properties that guarantee a norm-one element is neither a Daugavet- nor a $\Delta$-point. We demonstrate that asymptotically uniformly smooth spaces, as well as reflexive asymptotically uniformly convex spaces, do not contain $\Delta$-points. Furthermore, we establish that this absence also applies to the James tree space and its predual. Finally, we prove the existence of a superreflexive Banach space possessing a Daugavet- or $\Delta$-point, contingent upon the existence of such a space satisfying a weaker condition.

This article introduces a novel machine learning model that relies on imitation derived from linguistic descriptions of complex phenomena. The approach involves two primary steps: first, capturing the behavior of human players by constructing a computational perception network from game execution traces, and second, representing this behavior using fuzzy logic through linguistic variables and if-then rules. Utilizing this acquired knowledge, a dataset is automatically generated to train a decision tree-based learning model, which subsequently enables the automatic control of a bot's movements. The outcome is an artificial agent that replicates human player behavior. We have successfully implemented, tested, and evaluated this technology. The results are promising and demonstrate that this method offers a viable alternative for designing and implementing intelligent agent behaviors in video game development.

This study details the photon emission from Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) arising from avalanche pulses generated under dark conditions, aiming to clarify systematics relevant to future large-area SiPM-based physics experiments. A novel apparatus for spectral and imaging analysis was constructed at TRIUMF to measure light output from two SiPMs selected as photo-sensor candidates for the nEXO neutrinoless double-beta decay experiment: an FBK VUV-HD3 (VUV-HD Low Field Low After Pulse) and an HPK VUV4 Multi-Pixel Photon Counter (MPPC). Spectral measurements across the 450–1020 nm range were conducted at varying over-voltages. For the FBK VUV-HD3 at an over-voltage of $12.1\pm1.0$ V, the secondary photon yield was determined to be $(4.04\pm0.02)\times 10^{-6}$ $\gamma/e^{-}$. Its emission spectrum exhibits an interference pattern indicative of thin-film effects, while emission microscopy images (EMMIs) reveal a sparse distribution of randomly located, highly intense hotspots. Conversely, the HPK VUV4 MPPC, measured at $10.7\pm1.0$ V, yielded a secondary photon yield of $(8.71\pm0.04)\times 10^{-6}$ $\gamma/e^{-}$. Unlike the FBK device, the HPK spectrum lacks an interference pattern, likely due to a thinner surface coating, and its EMMIs display a greater number of hotspots, with a notable cluster in one corner of the device.

Existing video captioning methods focus on objectively describing content, often lacking the subjective flair and engaging expression needed for broader practical use. While video titling aims to address this gap, the field currently suffers from an absence of a suitable benchmark. To resolve this, we introduce CREATE, the first large-scale Chinese benchmark for short video retrieval and title generation, designed to advance research and applications in these areas. CREATE comprises a high-quality labeled dataset of 210K videos, supplemented by two massive pre-training sets containing 3M and 10M videos respectively. The benchmark spans 51 categories, over 50,000 tags, 537,000 manually annotated titles and captions, and more than 10 million short videos. Leveraging CREATE, we present ALWIG, a novel model that integrates video retrieval and titling tasks to achieve multi-modal alignment with generation, utilizing video tags and a GPT pre-trained foundation. By establishing this resource, CREATE paves the way for future advancements in video titling and retrieval within the domain of Chinese short videos.

Contrary to the naive expectation derived from the second law of thermodynamics, fluctuation theorems establish that observing negative entropy production is possible with non-zero probability. For particle trajectories within a fluid, Stokes' theorem allows for a geometric description of entropy production. Expanding on this framework, we develop a topological fluctuation theorem that relies exclusively on the winding number around vortex cores and remains unaffected by other force characteristics. This probability is robust against local deformations of the path, echoing topologically protected modes found in both classical and quantum systems. We show that in these highly fluctuating environments, entropy production becomes quantized and is governed by a topological invariant. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of the theorem even when the probability distributions of generated heat are non-Gaussian.

We examine a cosmological framework where dark matter consists of primordial black holes with masses around $\sim10^{-12}M_\odot$, organized into dense weakly relativistic clusters ranging from $18$ to $560M_\odot$. It is demonstrated that through multiple black hole collisions, approximately $10\%$ of the cluster's initial mass can be converted into gravitational waves between the recombination era and redshifts $z\geq 10$. At recombination, the matter density was roughly $10\%$ higher, resulting in an accelerated expansion rate of the universe. This increase shortens the sound horizon scale, a mechanism required to resolve the "$H_0$ tension."

In 2015, the PHENIX collaboration measured inclusive neutron single-spin asymmetries at very forward rapidities ($\eta>6.8$) in transversely polarized proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 200 GeV. While a prior publication from this dataset focused on nuclear effects, this analysis extracts the explicit transverse-momentum dependence of these asymmetries for proton-proton collisions using a bootstrapping-unfolding method applied to transverse momenta. Determining this dependence aims to enhance the understanding of the mechanisms generating such asymmetries.

When light propagates through a medium with a refractive index that varies rapidly over time, its frequency shifts. Recent studies on transparent conductive oxides have documented substantial frequency shifts, which were previously attributed to temporal changes in the propagation phase within the bulk material—a phenomenon known as temporal refraction. In this work, we demonstrate that frequency shifts in an indium tin oxide (ITO) epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) layer stem from both this bulk response and a significant contribution arising from temporal variations in spatial boundary conditions. For specific angles of incidence, this boundary effect can produce a dominant shift opposing the bulk effect, enabling the tailoring of the overall frequency shift via the angle of incidence and effectively decoupling amplitude and phase modulation.

Recently, there has been growing interest in applying deep learning to diverse seismic interpretation tasks. Unlike shallow machine learning models, deep learning architectures are significantly more complex, often containing hundreds of millions of parameters. This complexity necessitates substantial computational resources for training and, more critically, vast quantities of labeled training data. This study demonstrates how automatically generated weak labels can effectively address this challenge, enabling the training of powerful deep learning models for identifying seismic structures within large seismic volumes. Specifically, we generated thousands of weak labels to train a deconvolutional network for detecting faults, salt domes, and chaotic regions in the Netherlands F3 block. Additionally, we show that adjusting the loss function to incorporate weak labels helps minimize false positives in the labeling output. The primary advantage of this approach is that it facilitates the effective training and deployment of deep learning models for various seismic interpretation tasks without the need for any manual labeling. Our results on the Netherlands F3 block are excellent, demonstrating that our model outperforms other baseline methods.

Creating trenches on the surfaces of ultrathin ferroelectric (FE) films and superlattices offers a method to regulate the orientation and direction of ferroelectric domain walls (DWs). By leveraging the alignment between DWs and surface trenches (STs), systems previously known for conducting electricity can be transformed into functional nanocircuits using standard lithography. Despite this promising application, the microscopic mechanism driving this alignment has been unclear. Using ultrathin PbTiO$_3$ films as a model, we investigated this mechanism through extensive density functional theory simulations involving up to 5,136 atoms. While multiple factors likely contribute, we demonstrate that parallel DW-ST alignment is effectively explained by an arrangement of electric dipole moments that restores polar continuity within the film. These moments maintain the polar texture of the original film, thereby minimizing depolarizing fields induced by the trenches. Given the mechanism's broad applicability, we propose that STs can engineer diverse exotic polar textures in various FE nanostructures, a possibility supported by the emergence of ST-induced polar cycloidal modulations in our findings. Additionally, our simulations corroborate experimental observations of negative strains induced by STs, which are believed to influence the alignment process.

Humans possess robust class-agnostic object segmentation capabilities, enabling them to precisely delineate boundaries of unfamiliar objects. This insight motivates the proposal of BoxCaseg, a box-supervised approach for weakly-supervised instance segmentation. The BoxCaseg model employs a multi-task learning framework, jointly trained on box-supervised images and salient images. In this setup, fine-annotated salient images offer precise, class-agnostic localization guidance to enhance the box-supervised images. The object masks generated by the pretrained BoxCaseg model are then refined using a novel merged-and-dropped strategy to serve as proxy ground truth for training a Mask R-CNN under weakly-supervised conditions. Using only 7,991 salient images, the resulting weakly-supervised Mask R-CNN achieves performance comparable to fully-supervised Mask R-CNN on PASCAL VOC and significantly surpasses prior state-of-the-art box-supervised instance segmentation methods on COCO. The source code, pretrained models, and datasets are accessible at \url{https://github.com/hustvl/BoxCaseg}.

This study introduces a vehicular edge federated learning (VEFL) framework in which an edge server utilizes the onboard CPUs and local datasets of highly mobile connected vehicles (CVs) to train a global model.
