We illustrate this with $^6$Li+n, $^7$Li+n, and $^8$Li+n systems, demonstrating consistency with other \textit{ab initio} approaches, such as quantum Monte Carlo, where comparisons are possible. By comparing our ANCs and SFs against experimental values, we aim to extend this research to heavier nuclei and derive effective inter-cluster interactions for analyzing current and future experimental results.

We employ neural networks to model the characteristic function of numerous many-body Gaussian states within quantum phase space. Through a pullback mechanism, we represent transformations induced by unitary operators as linear layers capable of cascading to simulate intricate multi-particle dynamics. These layered networks facilitate the analysis of non-classical light propagation in random interferometers and enable the computation of boson pattern probabilities via automatic differentiation. Furthermore, we show that multi-particle events in Gaussian boson sampling can be optimized through the appropriate design and training of neural network weights. These findings hold significant potential for developing novel sources and sophisticated circuits for quantum technologies.

We demonstrate that for the Whitehead double of a prime algebraically tame knot, the meridional rank and the bridge number are identical. Algebraically tame knots represent a wide generalization that includes both torus knots and iterated cable knots.

This paper details the two-loop massless QCD corrections for di-Higgs and di-pseudo-Higgs boson production via quark annihilation, specifically within the large top quark mass limit. Utilizing dimensional regularisation, we apply the Larin prescription to handle the non-anticommuting $\gamma_5$. Our analysis reveals no additional contact renormalisation stemming from the short-distance behavior of two local operators, a result consistent with the operator product expansion. Furthermore, we observe a discrepancy in the highest transcendentality weight terms between these finite remainders and those associated with a pair of half-BPS primary operators in maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. These newly calculated finite remainders are essential for determining next-to-next-to-leading order observables involving di-Higgs or di-pseudo-Higgs systems. Finally, we have incorporated these results into a numerical code to facilitate further phenomenological investigations.

Humans possess a unique capacity to make decisions by logically anticipating future events, such as the actions and mental states of other agents. For instance, navigating a busy intersection requires reasoning about vehicle physics, the intentions of other drivers, and their beliefs regarding your own plans. Whether you signal a turn or move into a passing lane, other drivers may react by yielding or slowing down to allow you space. Effective drivers must therefore formulate safe responses to various potential future behaviors of others before acting, a process known as contingency planning. This involves explicitly designing conditional actions based on the uncertain outcomes of future events. In this study, we introduce a general-purpose contingency planner trained end-to-end using high-dimensional scene data and low-dimensional behavioral inputs. By employing a conditional autoregressive flow model, we generate a compact space for contingency planning and demonstrate how the model can effectively learn these contingencies from behavioral observations. Furthermore, we established a closed-loop control benchmark featuring realistic multi-agent scenarios within the CARLA driving simulator, where our method is compared against several noncontingent approaches, including state-of-the-art deep learning-based planners. Our results show that these noncontingent methods fundamentally fail on this benchmark, whereas our deep contingency planning approach achieves significantly superior performance. The code required to run the benchmark and reproduce our findings is available at https://sites.google.com/view/contingency-planning.

This study generalizes the convex body chasing problem to an adversarial framework where a player must track a sequence of convex bodies generated by an opposing agent. The objective for the player is to minimize the cumulative movement cost, whereas the opponent seeks to maximize it. Since both parties possess knowledge of a finite set of feasible convex bodies, we establish performance guarantees via max-min optimality instead of a competitive ratio. Based on the continuity of the optimal value function under specific conditions, we developed an algorithm that numerically constructs policies with assured performance. Furthermore, these theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations.

While state-of-the-art deep neural networks (DNNs) demonstrate exceptional performance in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), recent findings indicate their vulnerability to adversarial attacks, which involve introducing subtle perturbations to input images. Despite extensive research on this topic, systematic investigations into the robustness of UDA models remain absent. Consequently, this study examines the resilience of unsupervised domain adaptation against adversarial threats for the first time. We evaluate various adversarial attack and defense configurations within the domain adaptation framework and introduce a cross-domain attack strategy utilizing pseudo labels. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of different datasets, models, and specific attack and defense methodologies. Our results unequivocally demonstrate the limited robustness of current UDA models, and we aim to encourage the research community to prioritize enhancing these models' resistance to adversarial attacks.

Teleoperation remains prevalent for numerous robotic tasks due to the high costs and time demands of automation. Robot Learning from Demonstrations (RLfD) offers a solution by significantly reducing programming expenses and duration; however, traditional RLfD methods often fail to apply directly to complex scenarios like minimally invasive robotic suturing because they rely on laborious manual feature engineering from visual data. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have emerged as effective tools for modeling the intricate relationships between high-dimensional observations and low-level actions or states. Nevertheless, deploying DNNs necessitates a suitable training dataset. This paper introduces a dataset focused on two-arm da Vinci Research Kit needle insertion through soft tissues. The collection comprises (1) 60 successful trials with randomized exit points captured by six high-resolution calibrated cameras, (2) corresponding robot telemetry and calibration parameters, and (3) synchronized commanded control inputs, all specifically curated for Deep-RLfD applications. We implemented various deep RLfD architectures, ranging from simple feed-forward CNNs to diverse Recurrent Convolutional Networks (RCNs). Our findings demonstrate that while baseline feed-forward CNNs successfully learn the link between visual inputs and subsequent robot control actions, RCNs further enhance prediction accuracy. Both the dataset and our baseline RLfD implementations are publicly available for benchmarking at https://github.com/imanlab/d-lfd.

Segerman's 15+4 puzzle represents a hinged variant of the traditional 15-puzzle, featuring tiles that rotate during movement. In 1974, Wilson categorized the solution groups for sliding block puzzles. We extend Wilson's findings to puzzles akin to the 15+4, where tile rotation is permitted, demonstrating that these solution sets form subgroups within generalized symmetric groups. With the exception of two unique cases, the solution group for such puzzles is invariably either the full generalized symmetric group or one of two specific subgroups with an index of two.

This work continues the investigation into the optimal convergence rate of the explicit Euler time discretization for convection-diffusion equations, previously published in *Appl. Math. Lett.* \textbf{131} (2022) 108048, specifically addressing high-dimensional linear and nonlinear scenarios with Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions. The study introduces several novel corrected difference schemes utilizing explicit Euler methods for temporal derivatives and central differences for spatial derivatives. Detailed a priori estimates are provided for the corrected scheme under constant convection coefficients using the maximum principle, proving an optimal fourth-order convergence rate when the step ratios in each direction equal $1/6$. Compared to classical schemes, these corrected methods significantly improve the {\rm \textbf{CFL}} condition and enhance numerical accuracy. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional linear and nonlinear problems, including the Fisher, Chafee-Infante, and Burgers' equations under various boundary conditions, confirm the advantageous properties of the proposed corrected difference schemes.

We utilized electronic Raman scattering to investigate the optical signature of charge density waves (CDWs) within the multiband conductor TTF[Ni(dmit)2]2. Below 60 K, a distinct hump emerges at low energies, corresponding to the CDW amplitude mode with an energy of approximately 9 meV. Symmetry-resolved Raman measurements reveal that this amplitude mode exhibits anisotropy, indicating that the CDW arises from band nesting along the Ni(dmit)2 chains.

We introduce an algorithm designed to identify the outer boundaries of Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) events by analyzing differences in Heliospheric Imager STEREO SECCHI HI-1 images from either the A or B spacecraft, along with its Python implementation.
These lecture notes cover 2d conformal field theory from Fudan University.

As computing moves beyond GPUs and ASICs toward massively parallelized architectures, deep neural network inference accelerators have become increasingly vital. The multiply-and-accumulate operation, central to feedforward inference, utilizes crossbar columns to generate individual neuron responses, making memristor crossbar arrays highly efficient for parallelizing inference and image processing. This paper introduces `CrossStack`, a 3-D active memristor crossbar array employing stacked Al/TiO2/TiO2-x/Al device pairs with shared central electrodes. Through a CMOS-memristor hybrid cell design, CrossStack functions as a reconfigurable inference engine in two user-selectable modes: expansion mode and deep-net mode. Expansion mode doubles network resolution by increasing input capacity within the same chip area while cutting IR drop by 22%. Conversely, deep-net mode boosts inference speed for 10-bit convolutions by 29% by dedicating one TiO2/TiO2-x layer to read operations and the other to write operations. Both modes were experimentally validated on a $10\times10\times2$ array.

Style transfer represents a pivotal challenge in machine learning, underpinning many successful applications. This study introduces a new framework for style transfer that leverages infinite task learning and vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Specifically, we apply this concept to emotion transfer, aiming to convert facial images into various target emotional expressions. Our method offers a rigorous mechanism for exercising explicit control within a continuous style space. Evaluations on standard facial emotion datasets demonstrate the technique's effectiveness, yielding low reconstruction costs and superior emotion classification accuracy.

This study investigates the relationship between galaxy cluster orbits and the prominence of their central galaxies. We categorized a dataset of approximately 100 clusters and groups into four distinct samples based on the magnitude gap ($\Delta m_{12}$) between their two brightest members. By stacking systems within each sample, we constructed four representative stacked clusters to derive mass and velocity anisotropy profiles using the MAMPOSSt method. Following the determination of the mass profile, we calculated the non-parametric velocity anisotropy profile by inverting the Jeans equation. Our results indicate that in clusters with the largest $\Delta m_{12}$, galaxy orbits are predominantly radial, except near the center where they are isotropic (or tangential if the central galaxy is included). Conversely, the other three samples with smaller $\Delta m_{12}$ exhibit isotropic or only mildly radial orbits. These findings align with numerical simulations, which suggest that radial galaxy orbits drive the increase in $\Delta m_{12}$ observed in groups.

We examined inflation within the Higgs-$R^2$ framework, adopting a single-field approximation known as the minimal two-field mode to constrain the Higgs' non-minimal coupling $\xi$. Our analysis of non-gaussianity during inflation revealed that $\xi$ alone cannot generate significant non-gaussianity. Furthermore, we segmented the preheating phase into quadratic and quartic regimes; while gauge boson production dominates the quadratic regime, it fails to fully deplete the inflaton's energy. Consequently, we proposed a dark matter candidate with a substantial coupling to drain the remaining energy. We determined that for $\xi < 4.2$, oscillations persist from the quadratic into the quartic regime, yielding a reheating temperature of approximately $10^{10}$ GeV that varies with the residual inflaton energy density. Conversely, when $\xi > 4.2$, oscillations occur solely within the quadratic regime. Given the assumption that the Pauli exclusion principle applies during this phase, restricting the instant decay of gauge bosons into fermions, we anticipate a lower reheating temperature of roughly $10^9$ GeV.

Understanding heat conduction beyond Fourier's law represents a significant and enduring challenge. While low-temperature studies on ultra-pure crystals have historically revealed non-Fourier effects, recent findings indicate that heterogeneous materials with macroscopic dimensions can also exhibit thermal behaviors that the Fourier equation fails to capture. This phenomenon, termed over-diffusive propagation, appears in diverse samples such as metal foams, rocks, and composites, distinct from low-temperature observations. Although the recorded temperature profiles resemble those predicted by Fourier's law, standard evaluation methods yield unreliable thermal parameters. This report details our experiments on various rock types, utilizing multiple samples of differing thicknesses for each. We demonstrate that size-dependent thermal behavior manifests in both Fourier and non-Fourier regimes. Furthermore, utilizing the current experimental data, we establish an empirical relationship between Fourier and non-Fourier parameters, which could facilitate the development of more robust and reliable evaluation procedures in future studies.

The Covering Salesman Problem (CSP) extends the Traveling Salesman Problem by requiring that all vertices be covered by the tour, rather than visited directly. The goal is to identify a minimum-length Hamiltonian cycle over a subset of vertices that ensures complete coverage of an undirected graph. This study applies valid inequalities from the generalized traveling salesman problem to the CSP, alongside newly developed inequalities that address unique characteristics of the problem. A branch-and-cut framework is employed, integrating exact and heuristic separation routines to handle both integer and fractional CSP solutions. Computational results demonstrate that the proposed framework surpasses existing literature methods in terms of optimality gaps. Furthermore, the research successfully proved optimal solutions for several instances that had previously remained unsolved.

"Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations" (VPPMs), including redirected walking and haptics, extend the boundaries of Virtual Reality (VR) interaction beyond normal physical constraints. By exploiting the limits of human perception, these techniques subtly alter user movements to enhance VR interactivity, sometimes noticeably and sometimes invisibly. This paper investigates the dangers associated with the malicious deployment of VPPMs. We begin by defining, conceptualizing, and demonstrating VPPMs. Subsequently, through speculative design workshops, we identify and characterize potential threats, offering mitigation strategies and preventative measures. Finally, we present two prototype applications illustrating how existing VPPMs can be easily subverted to inflict physical harm. Ultimately, this work seeks to highlight that current practices in applying and publishing VPPMs may inadvertently enable the exploitation of perceptual vulnerabilities for malicious purposes.

Superconducting circuits employing coupler architectures have garnered significant interest owing to their superior scalability and tunability. While low-error single-qubit gates have been successfully realized, achieving high-fidelity two-qubit gates within this architecture remains a formidable challenge. This study rigorously investigates the origins of gate errors, focusing specifically on the physical mechanisms underlying ZZ parasitic couplings through a systematic effective Hamiltonian framework. Leveraging this approach, we offer clear and direct insights into ZZ parasitic couplings that were previously explored via numerical simulations and experiments. Our analytical findings establish precise quantitative criteria for eliminating these parasitic couplings and identify four novel, experimentally accessible parameter regimes anticipated to yield higher-fidelity two-qubit gates. Extending beyond numerical modeling, we derive a concise analytical expression for two-qubit gate error, clarifying the trade-off between qubit energy relaxation and ZZ parasitic couplings, which enables straightforward error estimation. Ultimately, this research paves the way for implementing high-fidelity two-qubit gates in superconducting coupler architectures.

We derive the equations of motion for an $N$-body system within Einstein-Cartan gravity at the first post-Newtonian order by utilizing the Weyssenhoff fluid as the spin model. Our methodology involves taking the point-particle limit of the continuous gravitational source description. The resulting equations offer insight into the validity of the effacing principle at the 1PN level within the Einstein-Cartan framework, and we also examine analogies with general relativistic dynamics concerning macroscopic angular momentum.

Previous research within Chiral Effective Field Theory ($\chi$EFT) examined the renormalization of iterated one-pion exchange (OPE) for antinucleon-nucleon ($\overline{N}\!N$) scattering in specific partial waves (Phys. Rev. C 105, 054005 (2022)). This study extends that analysis to additional higher partial waves with total angular momenta $J\leq 3$. In this framework, contact interactions are modeled as a complex spherical well in coordinate space, where adjusting the well's radius corresponds to varying the cutoff. We investigate the dependence of phase shifts, inelasticities, and mixing angles on this cutoff and demonstrate that contact interactions are requisite at leading order for channels where the singular attractive tensor potentials of OPE arise. Our findings are benchmarked against energy-dependent partial-wave analyses of $\overline{N}\!N$ scattering data, and we also discuss parallels and distinctions between our results and existing $\chi$EFT applications to the nucleon-nucleon system.

We evaluate various methods for incorporating German and Korean into BigScience's 1.3-billion-parameter pretrained multilingual model, which initially supports 13 languages. This study examines the elements influencing the model's language adaptability and analyzes the trade-offs between computational expenses and anticipated performance.

This study examines the long-time asymptotic behavior of the Cauchy problem for the defocusing modified Korteweg-de Vries (mKdV) equation, utilizing step-like initial conditions defined as $q_{0}(x)=C_{L}$ for $x<0$ and $q_{0}(x)=C_{R}$ for $x>0$, with $C_{L}>C_{R}>0$. First, we construct the direct scattering theory to formulate the corresponding Riemann-Hilbert (RH) problem for these step-like data. Subsequently, by defining a $g$-function across various space-time domains and applying steepest descent analysis, we deform the original matrix-valued RH problem into explicitly solvable models. Ultimately, we derive the distinct long-time asymptotic behaviors of the solution within four specific regions of the half-plane: $\mathcal{R}_{\xi,I}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{\xi,IV}$, representing far-left field regions, and $\mathcal{R}_{\xi,II}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{\xi,III}$, representing rarefaction wave regions.

This paper targets multi-illumination color constancy, a task where most current methods, which are tailored for single light sources, fall short. Additionally, there is a scarcity of datasets designed for learning under multiple illuminations. To address these gaps, we introduce a physics-driven seed-based approach for multi-illumination color constancy. By leveraging GANs, we frame illumination estimation as an image-to-image domain translation challenge. We also propose a new data augmentation technique specifically for multi-illumination scenarios. Experimental results on both single and multi-illumination datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques.

The voice laboratory enables the objective and noninvasive analysis of human vocal characteristics. This study examined key parameters—including pitch, formants, jitter, shimmer, and harmonic-to-noise ratio—in a cohort of young individuals. These statistical data points were derived from speakers originating from Argentina.

Real-time kinodynamic trajectory planning is essential but difficult for autonomous vehicles operating in dynamic settings. This letter introduces an efficient trajectory planning system designed for complex dynamic scenarios, utilizing iterative and incremental optimization of path and speed. By leveraging the decoupled nature of the planning problem, a Gaussian process-based path planner first creates a continuous path parameterized by arc length within the Frenet frame, accounting for static obstacle avoidance and curvature limits. We provide a theoretical proof demonstrating that this approach effectively generalizes the well-known jerk-optimal solution. To handle dynamic environments, we employ an efficient s-t graph search method to determine a speed profile along the generated path. Ultimately, the path and speed are refined through incremental and iterative optimization to guarantee kinodynamic feasibility. Simulations involving both static obstacles and dynamic agents confirm the method's effectiveness and robustness. Experimental data indicates the system operates at 20 Hz, and the source code is available as an open-source package.

This work introduces a sheaf-theoretic compositional framework designed for modeling complex event-driven systems. It demonstrates that such systems function as machines with defined inputs and outputs, capable of being composed with various other machine types under a single, unified sheaf-theoretic formalism. Using robotic systems as a primary example of complex architectures, the study rigorously applies this framework to describe actuators, sensors, and algorithms.

Analyzing extensive graph datasets is crucial for numerous contemporary applications, including social networks. Because of the high computational complexity involved, distributed processing is commonly utilized, necessitating the division of graph data across nodes. The partitioning strategy chosen significantly influences task execution time; however, no universal strategy exists that performs optimally across all graph types and algorithms. Strategy effectiveness varies based on specific data and algorithm characteristics, and manually determining the best approach is often impractical due to the inherent complexity. This work introduces a machine learning-based method to identify the most suitable partitioning strategy for a specific graph and algorithm combination. The approach enumerates potential strategies, predicts execution times for each, and selects the one with the lowest estimated duration. The underlying model is trained using features derived from graph data and algorithm pseudo-code. Additionally, we propose a technique to expand real execution logs into a large synthetic dataset. Evaluation results indicate that the selected strategies achieve an average execution time 1.46 times faster than the mean of all strategies and approximately 0.95 times the performance of the single best strategy.

The serverless computing model has increasingly integrated into the industry, providing a cost-effective solution for application development and deployment. However, this shift introduces new challenges for developers, particularly in tuning memory settings to balance cost efficiency with performance. While researchers have focused on minimizing costs and meeting Service Level Objective (SLO) constraints for individual Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) functions, there remains a gap in addressing these issues for applications composed of multiple FaaS functions forming complex workflows. To bridge this gap, we developed a tool named SLAM. SLAM leverages distributed tracing to identify relationships among FaaS functions within a serverless application and models each one to estimate execution times under various memory configurations. Based on these estimations, SLAM identifies the optimal memory setup for the entire application, adhering to specified SLOs and user-defined goals such as minimizing cost or execution time. We validated SLAM's effectiveness on AWS Lambda across four applications. Our findings indicate that the recommended memory configurations ensure that over 95% of requests complete within the predefined SLOs.

The rapid growth of Electric Vehicles (EVs) presents a significant challenge in evaluating the impact of their charging and discharging cycles on power distribution grids. This study tackles this assessment issue using a framework based on nonlinear differential equations. Specifically, we focus on a recently proposed nonlinear Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) model that describes the spatial voltage phasor profile along a distribution feeder. The assessment is formulated as a two-point boundary value problem involving this nonlinear ODE. We derive an asymptotic characterization of the problem's solutions using the standard regular perturbation method. This approach offers a mathematically rigorous and quantitative means to evaluate how EV charging and discharging influence the spatial voltage profile within distribution networks. The validity of this asymptotic characterization is demonstrated through simulations of both simple and practical power grid configurations.

We utilize the propagator method to contrast the coupled channels procedure with the semiclassical approach for modeling two-body emission, specifically $\alpha$-decay, from deformed nuclei. By expressing scattering amplitudes as a product of a propagator matrix—which accounts for the deformed field—and the ratio of internal wave function components to irregular Coulomb waves, we recover the standard form when the system is spherical. We present a rigorous three-dimensional semiclassical formulation tailored for deformed potentials, yielding exact results that are compared against the simpler Angular Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (AWKB) and Linearized WKB (LWKB) methods, including the Fr\"oman WKB (FWKB) approximation. Our findings indicate that the LWKB approach aligns more closely with the exact coupled-channels formalism than AWKB does. Furthermore, an analysis of $\alpha$-emission from the ground states of even-even nuclei highlights the significant impact of nuclear deformation on channel decay widths.

Session types specify communication protocols between concurrent processes, enabling type-safe inter-process interaction. While prior research established a clear subtyping framework where processes hold differing views of the protocol, these approaches were restricted to linear session types, assuming each communication channel has exactly one provider and one client. This paper extends subtyping to shared session types, permitting channels to serve multiple clients rather than a single one. We show that this generalization allows for the static representation of protocol requirements across multiple interaction phases between a client and a shared service provider—a capability absent in earlier proposals. Furthermore, these interaction phases are explicitly encoded within the client's type.

The VALUE (Video-And-Language Understanding Evaluation) benchmark was recently launched to assess and examine multi-modal representation learning across three specific tasks: Retrieval, Question Answering, and Captioning. Its primary goal is to develop a task-agnostic model capable of performing simultaneously across these diverse tasks. This technical report outlines the winning strategies employed for the VALUE challenge: 1) single model optimization, 2) transfer learning utilizing visual concepts, and 3) task-aware ensemble methods. The first and third strategies aim to manage the heterogeneous nature of each task, while the second leverages rich, fine-grained visual data. We offer a thorough analysis supported by extensive experimental results. Consequently, our approach secured the top rank in both the VALUE and QA phases of the competition.

Current state-of-the-art probabilistic model checkers verify explicit-state Markov models specified in high-level languages like PRISM. These low-level models often contain significant structural patterns, such as repeating substructures, which established techniques like probabilistic bisimulation minimization can exploit; however, these methods operate directly on the explicit-state representation rather than the high-level program. Conversely, approaches that reduce structured state spaces by analyzing the program itself have received limited attention. This paper introduces a novel, simple, and fully automatic technique for reducing the underlying Markov model at the program level. Our method computes the summarized behavior of adjacent locations in the program's control-flow graph, resulting in a program with fewer "control states." This reduction directly modifies the program's operational semantics, facilitating more efficient model checking. A fundamental insight is that any program variable (or combination of variables) with a finite domain can effectively serve as the program counter that dictates flow structure. Distinct from most other reduction methods, our approach is property-directed and inherently supports unspecified model parameters. Experimental results indicate that this straightforward technique achieves state-space reductions of up to 80% on practically relevant benchmarks.

The NA62 experiment at CERN utilized a dataset from 2016–2018 to investigate the forbidden $K^+\to\mu^-\nu e^+e^+$ decay, which violates Standard Model lepton number or lepton flavour conservation. This search established an upper limit of $8.1\times 10^{-11}$ for the branching fraction at 90% confidence level, representing a 250-fold improvement over prior results.

This paper examines autoregressive models applied to multivariate count time series, specifically addressing the selection of appropriate distributions for vectors of count random variables. The review concentrates on three primary methodologies: (a) integer autoregressive processes, (b) parameter-driven models, and (c) observation-driven models. The objective of this work is to underscore recent methodological advancements and suggest promising avenues for future research.

Although existing static verification methods like separation logic can verify many programs, they rely on complete and detailed specifications, imposing a heavy burden on developers. To address this, gradual verification was introduced to soundly integrate static and dynamic checking for complete, partial, or missing specifications, including those involving recursive, mutable heap data structures. However, current extensions fail to reduce dynamic checking as specifications become more precise; instead, they verify all properties dynamically. Moreover, the absence of a full implementation has hindered practical performance and applicability studies. We introduce Gradual C0, the first practical gradual verifier for recursive heap structures targeting C0, a safe educational subset of C. To enhance efficiency and minimize dynamic checks, Gradual C0 employs symbolic execution rather than the backwards reasoning based on weakest liberal preconditions found in previous approaches. Our method resolves challenges related to symbolic execution with imprecise specifications, heap ownership, and branching in both code and formulas. We also present the first empirical evaluation of a gradual verifier, demonstrating that Gradual C0 reduces runtime overhead by 50–90% on average compared to fully dynamic methods, with predictable and avoidable worst-case scenarios. This work establishes a foundation for scaling gradual verification.

We calculate the expected sensitivity regarding optical depth to reionization measurements for a ground-based experiment at Teide Observatory. This involves simulating polarized partial sky maps for the GroundBIRD experiment at 145 and 220 GHz. Using our pixel-based likelihood method, we fit these simulated maps to derive the optical depth to reionization. Assuming a three-year observing campaign with sky coverages of 0.537 at 145 GHz and 0.462 at 220 GHz, we estimate the polarization map noise levels to be 110 $\mu\mathrm{K~arcmin}$ and 780 $\mu\mathrm{K~arcmin}$, respectively. Our analysis yields an optical depth sensitivity of $\sigma_\tau$=0.030 using the simulated GroundBIRD maps, which improves to $\sigma_\tau$=0.012 when combined with simulated QUIJOTE maps at 11, 13, 17, 19, 30, and 40 GHz.

Stuart-Landau limit-cycle oscillators serve as a fundamental model for investigating both coherent and incoherent limit cycles. This study extends the conventional Stuart-Landau dimer framework by incorporating inertia-like terms and noise, analyzing the resulting dynamics and stochastic thermodynamics. In the noise-free (zero-temperature) scenario, the system exhibits a novel bistable phase characterized by the coexistence of coherent and incoherent limit cycles. At finite temperatures, we establish a stochastic thermodynamic framework, drawing analogies from the motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field, to define physically significant heat and work. While the bistable phase disappears in the stochastic regime, thermodynamic quantities such as work display bistability during temporally metastable states. We demonstrate that the inertial Stuart-Landau dimer functions as a machine that reliably generates maximum work when oscillators synchronize coherently, whereas it produces minimal work unpredictably when they remain incoherent. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical role of coherent synchronization within the working substance for the effective operation of thermal machines.

We utilize exceptionally deep optical imaging from HST/ACS in the F475W ($g_{F475W}$) and F606W ($V_{F606W}$) filters to investigate the globular cluster (GC) population within the intermediate mass lenticular galaxy PGC 087327, located in the Hydra I cluster. By analyzing both photometric (magnitudes and colors) and morphometric (compactness, elongation, etc.) characteristics of sources across a $\sim19\times19$ kpc region centered on PGC 087327 and comparing them with four adjacent fields in the same HST/ACS mosaic, we identified a list of GC candidates and examined their properties using a background decontamination technique. Compared to the four reference fields, PGC 087327 exhibits a significant excess of GCs, with $N_{GC}=82\pm9$. Given the galaxy's estimated magnitude, this corresponds to a specific frequency of $S_N=1.8\pm0.7$. Despite the limited wavelength range provided by the $g_{F475W}$ and $V_{F606W}$ passbands, the color distribution reveals a distinct bimodality, featuring a blue peak at $\langle g_{F475W}{-}V_{F606W} \rangle =0.47\pm0.05$ mag and a red peak at $\langle g_{F475W}{-}V_{F606W}\rangle =0.62\pm0.03$ mag. We also note the expected steeper radial decline for red GCs compared to blue ones. Leveraging the exceptional depth of the data, we characterize the GC luminosity function (GCLF) well beyond its theoretical turn-over point. Our measurements yield $g^{TOM}_{F475W} = 26.54\pm0.10$ mag and $V^{TOM}_{F606W} = 26.08 \pm 0.09$ mag, which, after calibration, result in a distance of $D_{GCLF} = 56.7 \pm 4.3(statistical) \pm 5.2(systematic)$ Mpc.

We introduce a formula to assess the purity of thermal equilibrium states in numerical simulations without requiring prior knowledge of the exact quantum state. Canonical typicality ensures the existence of many microscopically distinct representations of these states, which we term thermal mixed quantum (TMQ) states. When constructing a TMQ state as a mixture of $N_\mathrm{samp}$ independent pure states, the weight of each state corresponds to its norm, and the partition function is defined as the average of these norms. To measure the efficiency of this mixture, we define a quantum statistical metric known as the "normalized fluctuation of partition function (NFPF)." A lower NFPF indicates a TMQ state that more closely resembles an equally weighted mixture of pure states, implying higher efficiency and a reduced requirement for $N_\mathrm{samp}$. The maximum NFPF occurs in the Gibbs state (purity-0), necessitating an exponentially large $N_\mathrm{samp}$, whereas the minimum NFPF is found in the thermal pure quantum state (purity-1) with $N_\mathrm{samp}=1$. Purity is expressed solely through the NFPF and approximates $N_\mathrm{samp}^{-1}$. These analytical findings are validated numerically using two random sampling methods based on matrix-product-state wave functions.

Membranes are ubiquitous in all cellular and tissue structures, requiring mathematical models to describe them compactly with approximately 1 nm resolution. These membranes serve as isolators for cells because ions struggle to penetrate the dielectric barrier they form. In this work, we propose a dielectric mathematical membrane condition to supersede previous models that omitted dielectric characteristics. Our formulation incorporates a dielectric lipid bilayer interspersed with channels that facilitate selective ion conduction.

The Girardeau mapping connects pointlike interactions among 1D bosons with those among fermions, establishing a strong-weak duality where the respective coupling constants are inversely related. We introduce a regularization scheme for these interactions that maintains this duality, distinguishing it from earlier regularizations, and provide a rigorous proof of this property. This framework enables the perturbative application of the duality, which we demonstrate within the Lieb-Liniger model at strong coupling.

Effective prevention of major outbreaks relies heavily on infectious disease surveillance. Syndromic surveillance specifically seeks to create algorithms capable of identifying outbreaks at their earliest stages by analyzing data sources that reflect disease occurrences. Current research predominantly targets known, specific diseases, emphasizing the definition of their unique patterns. Conversely, little attention has been paid to non-specific syndromic surveillance, which utilizes all available data to detect any outbreak, including those caused by previously unknown pathogens. This study revisits existing methods for non-specific surveillance and introduces a suite of straightforward statistical modeling techniques to serve as benchmarks for more complex machine learning models. Experimental comparisons using both established synthetic datasets and real-world data with injected synthetic outbreaks demonstrate that these simple benchmarks yield highly competitive results and frequently surpass more elaborate algorithms.

We have created a high-performance analytical model of Galactic Chemical Evolution that incorporates delay time distributions and the sequestration of stellar yields within a thermally evolving interstellar medium. For the first time, this model explores the extensive parameter space linked to the r-process enrichment of the Milky Way by its potential sources: Neutron Star Mergers and Collapsar events. Because their distinct formation mechanisms result in different time dependencies, this characteristic has often been cited to support the dominance of collapsars as the primary r-process source. However, our findings demonstrate that even when allowing for significant variability in the galaxy's thermal, structural, and chemical properties, substantial portions of the parameter space are strongly inconsistent with observational data. Specifically, while we identify viable models where neutron star mergers generate the majority of r-process material, all scenarios in which collapsars provide the dominant yields are excluded by the data. Given the absence of any other known source, we conclude that Neutron Star Mergers must be the primary contributors to the current r-process budget of the Milky Way.

This study introduces a data-driven framework for model reduction based on noisy datasets. It begins by defining data reduction, demonstrating that applying a Petrov-Galerkin projection to systems satisfying a large-dimensional quadratic matrix inequality (QMI) yields reduced-order models that can themselves be characterized by a lower-dimensional QMI. Subsequently, a data-driven generalized balanced truncation method is developed through a two-step process: first, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for systems explaining the data to share common generalized Gramians; second, utilizing these Gramians to construct projection matrices that define a class of reduced-order models via generalized balanced truncation within a lower-dimensional QMI framework. The paper also outlines alternative procedures for calculating a priori and a posteriori upper bounds relative to the true underlying system. Finally, the proposed methodologies are validated using a cart with a double-pendulum system as a case study.

With the advancement of autonomous systems, safety becomes a critical issue, particularly in unstructured settings. To address this, the study introduces a safety layer for mechanical systems designed to identify and counteract unstable dynamics triggered by external disturbances. This layer operates independently alongside existing nominal controllers, such as those for pose or wrench tracking, by restricting power output when the system's trajectory risks instability. The method relies on calculating the Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LLE) of the error dynamics, a metric that quantifies the rate of divergence or convergence within the system. By actively monitoring this value, potentially hazardous divergent behaviors can be detected immediately. Subsequently, the LLE is integrated with Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) to enforce power limit constraints on a jerk-controlled system. The effectiveness of this architecture is demonstrated through experimental validation on an Omnidirectional Micro Aerial Vehicle (OMAV) across both free flight and interaction scenarios.

We introduce AUQ-ADMM, an adaptive uncertainty-weighted consensus ADMM framework designed to address large-scale convex optimization problems in a distributed setting. Our primary contribution is a new adaptive weighting mechanism that empirically accelerates the convergence of the consensus ADMM approach, particularly when dealing with numerous subproblems. These weights are derived from the uncertainty linked to each subproblem's solution and are efficiently calculated via low-rank approximations. We demonstrate that AUQ-ADMM converges provably and validate its performance across various machine learning tasks, including elastic net regression, multinomial logistic regression, and support vector machines. Additionally, we offer an implementation utilizing the PyTorch library.

Developing precise numerical software is challenging due to inherent uncertainties, such as the finite precision of computational implementations. We introduce a programming model where users define programs in a real-valued language that explicitly incorporates various uncertainty types. This is followed by a compilation algorithm that produces a standard implementation guaranteed to achieve the specified precision relative to real numbers. Our verification process generates conditions that handle different uncertainties uniformly, translating reasoning about floating-point roundoff errors into reasoning about real numbers. These conditions serve as a standardized format for verifying both the precision and correctness of numerical code. However, because these conditions are often non-linear, exact reasoning remains difficult. We demonstrate that current state-of-the-art SMT solvers struggle to scale when solving them. To address this, we propose a novel procedure that integrates exact SMT solving over reals with approximate, sound affine and interval arithmetic. This hybrid approach overcomes the scalability limits of SMT solvers while delivering superior precision compared to standalone affine or interval arithmetic methods. Finally, our initial implementation validates the approach's utility and effectiveness across several examples, including those involving non-linear computations.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are highly promising for edge devices because their event-driven operations consume significantly less power than Analog Neural Networks (ANNs). While training SNNs directly is challenging, numerous methods have been developed to convert trained ANNs into SNNs. However, this conversion introduces a trade-off between accuracy and latency in SNNs, resulting in substantial delays when processing large datasets like ImageNet. To address this issue, we introduce a technique called TCL, which mitigates the accuracy-latency trade-off. This approach achieves an accuracy of 73.87% with VGG-16 and 70.37% with ResNet-34 on ImageNet, all while maintaining a moderate latency of 250 cycles.

Statistical mechanics has historically struggled to describe self-gravitating Newtonian systems composed of vast numbers of particles, a paradox given that many astronomical bodies and their simulations exhibit universal equilibrium structures without an obvious physical foundation. Ten years ago, we demonstrated that maximizing the number of microstates for a fixed energy per unit mass—subject to constraints of constant total energy and mass—yields the maximum entropy state known as DARKexp, defined by the distribution $n(E) \propto \exp(-\beta(E-\Phi_0))-1$. This differential energy distribution and its resulting density profiles closely mirror dark-matter halos, featuring central cusps where $\rho \sim r^{-1}$ and outer regions where $\rho \sim r^{-4}$. In this work, we introduce a non-equilibrium functional, $S_D$, which is maximized by DARKexp and rises monotonically as idealized collisionless systems following the Extended Spherical Infall Model evolve toward equilibrium. Furthermore, systems that experience greater mixing converge more closely to the DARKexp state.

This study delivers spatially resolved stellar kinematics for 797 galaxies at redshift $z=0.6-1$ identified within the LEGA-C survey, employing axisymmetric Jeans models to determine their dynamical masses and levels of rotational support. The survey, selected based on $K_s$-band flux regardless of color or morphology, provides an initial evaluation of the stellar dynamical architecture of the general $L^*$ galaxy population at significant lookback times. Utilizing Hubble Space Telescope light profiles as tracers, our methodology accounts for observational distortions, such as seeing convolution and slit geometry, while incorporating robust priors on inclination, anisotropy, and non-luminous mass. The provided data tables feature total mass estimates across spherical apertures (1, 5, and 10 kpc; 1$\times$ and 2$\times$\re), alongside rotational velocities, velocity dispersions, and anisotropy metrics. Our findings indicate that nearly all star-forming galaxies and approximately 50% of quiescent galaxies are rotation-dominated, exhibiting deprojected $V/\sigma$ ratios between 1 and 2. Highlighting complexities in galaxy evolution, we observe that the most massive star-forming galaxies display the highest degrees of rotational support, whereas the most massive quiescent galaxies show the lowest. These results establish a new benchmark for analyzing galaxy evolution via stellar dynamical structures at large lookback times. Combined with stellar population insights from LEGA-C spectra, the presented dynamical masses and $V/\sigma$ measurements open fresh pathways for investigating galaxy evolution in the early universe.

Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) have recently emerged as a leading topic in computer vision, with image generation applications like Imagen, Latent Diffusion Models, and Stable Diffusion demonstrating remarkable capabilities that have sparked significant community interest. Beyond generation, recent research highlights their utility in various vision tasks, including image deblurring, super-resolution, and anomaly detection. Building on this success, we introduce MedSegDiff, the first DPM-based model designed for general medical image segmentation. To improve step-wise regional attention within DPMs for segmentation, we propose dynamic conditional encoding, which creates state-adaptive conditions for every sampling step. Additionally, we introduce the Feature Frequency Parser (FF-Parser) to mitigate the adverse effects of high-frequency noise during this process. We evaluate MedSegDiff across three segmentation tasks involving different image modalities: optic cup segmentation in fundus images, brain tumor segmentation in MRI scans, and thyroid nodule segmentation in ultrasound images. Experimental results demonstrate that MedSegDiff significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the model's effectiveness and strong generalization capabilities.

We provide an overview of recent research characterizing effective actions that describe the electromagnetic response of various topological materials derived from their microscopic structures. Specifically, we examine weakly tilted Weyl semimetals at zero temperature with a nonzero chemical potential, treating this scenario as a particular subset of terms within the fermionic sector of the Standard Model Extension (SME).

This study re-examines the pervasive challenge of ensuring state machine replication in blockchains that rely on iterative consensus mechanisms, such as Tendermint. Guaranteeing fairness for user transactions is essential for achieving state machine replication in consensus-based blockchains. Extensive research has explored the relationship between state machine replication and consensus across diverse system models and problem specifications over recent years. We organize this existing body of work by introducing new, rigorous abstractions for both state machine replication and repeated consensus within a system model designed for realistic blockchains. This model accommodates blocks containing multiple transactions from various users, where transaction validity and ordering are dictated by an external, application-specific function capable of representing different fairness approaches found in literature. Utilizing these abstractions, we develop a reduction from state machine replication to repeated consensus, enabling user fairness to be secured by treating the consensus module as a black box. Consequently, this methodology facilitates the implementation of fairness as a modular add-on atop preexisting consensus modules in blockchains utilizing repeated consensus.

This study introduces a new integrated model that combines phase-field methods with dislocation density-based plasticity and damage mechanics. The governing equations for dislocation density are derived from the evolution of both mobile and immobile dislocations, incorporating mechanisms such as multiplication, annihilation, mobile-to-immobile transfer via interactions, and interface blocking. Notably, the model resolves the "swallow-gap" issue frequently observed in coupled dislocation and phase-field simulations around coarsened second phases. Furthermore, it successfully captures the phenomenon of dislocations cutting into the second phase during tertiary creep—a behavior rarely accounted for in prior phase-field simulations of single crystal superalloys—thanks to the inclusion of damage coupling. The model dynamics account for long-range stresses from external loads, coherent interface misfit, plastic activity, and damage, as well as short-range stresses arising from antiphase boundaries, dislocation line tension, and forest dislocation trapping. High-temperature $\langle 001 \rangle$ creep simulations were performed on single crystal superalloys at 200 MPa and 350 MPa using this coupled approach and benchmarked against experimental data. The findings demonstrate that the simulated phase microstructures, dislocation arrangements, and creep characteristics align well with experimental results across both microscopic and macroscopic scales throughout the entire creep process.
This paper presents the integer parts of the reciprocals of the tails of the alternating Riemann zeta function for $s=1,2,3,4$, derived through several new inequalities and elementary methods.

Recent high-resolution observations from VLA and CARMA have revealed proto-stars in binary systems with unprecedented clarity, specifically detecting masses between $0.1$ and $0.25 \, M_{\odot}$ for systems like CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1. These observed masses significantly exceed the approximately $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$ values typically predicted by numerical simulations of binary formation. Driven by this discrepancy, this study investigates how the formation mass of a binary system depends on the total mass of its parent core. To do so, we conducted numerical simulations of the gravitational collapse of uniform, rotating cores, introducing azimuthally symmetric mass seeds to promote the creation of a dense filament capable of direct fragmentation into a binary. Our initial findings indicated that binary formation is suppressed as the parent core mass ($M_0$) increases. Consequently, we raised the ratio of kinetic to gravitational energy ($\beta$) initially imparted to the rotating core to facilitate the desired direct fragmentation. We subsequently confirmed that the mass of the resulting binary fragment rises with the parent core's mass, as anticipated, and quantified the relationship between the initial core mass $M_0$ and the resulting binary mass $M_f$. Furthermore, we present a schematic diagram plotting $M_0$ against $\beta$ for the target binary configurations, maintaining a constant ratio of thermal to gravitational energy ($\alpha$). Finally, we provide fundamental physical data regarding the proto-stellar fragments forming the binary, including the formation mass $M_f$ and their corresponding thermal ($\alpha_f$) and kinetic ($\beta_f$) energy ratios.

We investigate the spectrum and consistency of semiclassical rotating strings within de Sitter space. Although a direct extension of flat-space linear Regge trajectories would violate the Higuchi bound—a unitarity constraint on higher-spin particle masses in curved spacetime—curvature effects alter these trajectories to satisfy the bound. Notably, the accelerated expansion imposes a maximum spin limit on each Regge trajectory; while this ensures consistency with the Higuchi bound, it potentially hinders a string-theoretic ultraviolet (UV) completion relying on an infinite tower of higher-spin states. Extending this insight, we show that if UV completion is realized via the leading Regge trajectory of higher-spin states up to the 4D Planck scale, the vacuum energy $V$ driving cosmic inflation must be constrained by the string scale $M_s$ according to $V\lesssim M_s^4$. Applying this to early-universe inflation yields an upper limit on the tensor-to-scalar ratio, $r\lesssim 0.01\times(M_s/10^{16} \text{GeV})^{4}$, a value testable by upcoming CMB observations. Additionally, we explore the alternative scenario where UV completion arises from multiple Regge trajectories.

"Can a model predict what I would look like at age 80 or 5 based solely on a single unlabeled photo of me and a large dataset of diverse, unpaired face images across ages? The answer is likely no. Most current face aging methods rely on learning transformations between specific age groups, necessitating paired training data and labeled query images. This paper approaches the problem through generative modeling, eliminating the need for paired samples. Furthermore, given an unlabeled input, the proposed generative model can directly synthesize images with specific target ages. We introduce a Conditional Adversarial Autoencoder (CAAE) that learns a face manifold, enabling smooth simultaneous progression and regression along this manifold. In CAAE, a convolutional encoder maps the face to a latent vector, which is then projected onto the age-conditioned face manifold via a deconvolutional generator. This architecture preserves individual facial features (personality) within the latent vector while using the age condition to control the direction of aging. Two adversarial networks constrain the encoder and generator to ensure the output faces are highly photorealistic. Experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art methods and ground truth demonstrate the framework's appealing performance and flexibility."

A recent study by Carballo-Rubio [1] employs semi-classical gravity to derive a generalized Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equation, introducing a novel coupling constant $l_p$. This framework yields two distinct modified TOV forms dependent on the sign of $p'$; the negative branch converges to the standard General Relativity (GR) TOV equation as $l_p \to 0$, whereas the positive branch does not. While Carballo-Rubio successfully obtained exact solutions for the positive branch using a constant-$\lambda$ method, this work examines whether the negative branch exhibits unique characteristics of ultra-compact objects beyond those found in GR-TOV. We analyzed ultra-compact objects composed of isotropic ideal fluids using a physically motivated equation of state, $\rho = p/w + \rho_0$, for $w=1$ and $w=1/3$. Our findings indicate that the permissible range of $l_p$ is highly constrained, requiring it not to equal the integration starting radius $r_c$ (the star's center) and to be significantly larger than the Planck length ($L_\text{Pl}$). Consequently, mass-radius curves for various $l_p$ values in both $w$ cases remain indistinguishable from standard GR-TOV predictions. Thus, the negative branch of $p'(r)$ fails to introduce significant deviations from standard GR results, even when $l_p$ is not vanishingly small. This outcome aligns with Ref. [3], suggesting that ultra-compact objects derived from the negative branch of semi-classical gravity with a linear equation of state cannot produce the gravitational echoes required by demanding tests.

Multiple background sources can influence the analysis of data and detector performance at the CLIC project, with halo muons generated along the beam delivery system (BDS) being a particularly significant factor. To mitigate this muon background, magnetized muon sweepers have been employed as shielding; their application was previously outlined in a CLIC study [1]. A realistic model of the muon sweeper was constructed using OPERA, and the resulting design parameters were utilized to estimate the reduction in muon background via BDSIM Monte Carlo simulations [2, 3].

Mobile health applications are transforming the healthcare landscape by enhancing communication, operational efficiency, and service quality. In low- and middle-income nations, these apps uniquely serve as data sources regarding patient and provider outcomes and behaviors, offering a viable avenue for delivering both individualized and broad policy interventions. We introduce a framework to analyze user engagement with mobile health tools, specifically targeting healthcare workers and the digital applications designed to assist them in resource-constrained environments. Activity logs generated by these apps can be converted into daily time series that reflect each user's behavior. By applying probabilistic and survival analysis, we develop multiple personalized metrics of meaningful engagement, enabling the customization of content and digital interventions to meet the specific needs of each health worker. Particular focus is placed on identifying churn, which signifies total disengagement. We demonstrate the utility of these methods using data from Safe Delivery App users in India and Ethiopia, a capacity-building platform for skilled birth attendants. This research marks a significant advancement toward comprehensively characterizing user engagement in mobile health applications, a development poised to substantially empower health workers and, in the long term, save lives.

We introduce the Barbasch-Evens-Magyar varieties, demonstrating their isomorphism to the smooth varieties from [D.~Barbasch-S.~Evens '94] that map generically finitely to symmetric orbit closures, thus providing singularity resolutions in specific instances. Our approach mirrors [P.~Magyar '98]'s method for constructing Bott-Samelson varieties [H.~C.~Hansen '73, M.~Demazure '74]. From this perspective, we derive a graphical representation in type $A$, a stratification into closed subvarieties of identical nature, and identify the torus-fixed points. Furthermore, we illustrate how these manifolds naturally acquire a symplectic structure with a Hamiltonian torus action, and we formulate the moment polytope using that of a Bott-Samelson variety.

Inspired by the recent discovery of the doubly-charmed tetraquark state $T_{cc}^+$ by LHCb, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the $S$-wave interactions between charmed mesons ($D,\,D^{*}$) in the $H$-doublet and those ($D_{1},\,D_{2}^{*}$) in the $T$-doublet using the one-boson-exchange model. Our calculations explicitly incorporate both $S$-$D$ wave mixing and coupled channel effects. Based on our quantitative results, we propose that the $S$-wave $D^{*} D_{1}$ states with quantum numbers $I(J^{P})=0(0^{-},\,1^{-})$ and the $S$-wave $D^{*}D_{2}^{*}$ state with $I(J^{P})=0(1^{-})$ are the most likely candidates for doubly-charmed molecular tetraquarks. Additionally, we identify the $S$-wave $DD_{1}$ state with $I(J^{P})=0(1^{-})$, the $S$-wave $DD_{2}^{*}$ state with $I(J^{P})=0(2^{-})$, and the $S$-wave $D^{*}D_{2}^{*}$ state with $I(J^{P})=0(2^{-})$ as potential candidates. As experimental data accumulates during Run III and following the High-Luminosity-LHC upgrade, these predicted states are expected to become observable at LHCb in the near future.

Micro- and nanogels are extensively utilized to stabilize emulsions while simultaneously enabling responsiveness to external stimuli. A key factor enhancing emulsion stability is the softness of the nanogels. This study investigates how the softest nanogels synthesizable via the precipitation polymerization of N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM)—specifically ultra-low crosslinked (ULC) nanogels—stabilize oil-in-water emulsions. We demonstrate that ULC nanogels effectively stabilize emulsions even at low mass concentrations. These emulsions exhibit resistance to droplet flocculation, stability against coalescence, and the ability to be easily disrupted by temperature increases. The resistance to flocculation observed in ULC-stabilized emulsions parallels that of emulsions stabilized by linear pNIPAM. Conversely, the stability against coalescence and temperature responsiveness closely mirror those of emulsions stabilized by regularly crosslinked pNIPAM nanogels. This unique combination of properties arises because ULC nanogels can be conceptualized as colloids situated between flexible macromolecules and rigid particles. As polymers, they efficiently stretch to cover the interface uniformly; as regularly crosslinked particles, they protect emulsion droplets from coalescence via a steric barrier and respond rapidly to external stimuli to break the emulsion. This polymer-particle duality of ULC nanogels offers opportunities to enhance emulsion properties for diverse applications, such as in heterogeneous catalysis and food science.

The Radio Arc comprises a structured system of non-thermal filaments (NTFs) situated in the Milky Way's Galactic Center. Recent findings indicate that the magnetic fields within the Radio Arc's NTFs alternate between orientations parallel to the filaments and those rotated relative to them, a pattern that sharply contrasts with the mostly parallel fields seen in other GC NTFs. To investigate the cause of this anomaly, we examined spectro-polarimetric data from the Australian Telescope Compact Array, utilizing a dataset spanning 4 to 11 GHz with a 2 MHz spectral resolution. By applying depolarization models to the spectral polarization measurements, we characterized Faraday rotation along the line of sight and evaluated whether local structures near the Radio Arc could account for the unusual magnetic alignment. Our analysis identifies external Faraday effects as the primary driver of the observed magnetic field rotation in the Radio Arc, though internal Faraday effects also appear probable in regions where fields remain parallel. The heightened likelihood of internal effects in parallel regions may stem from nearby Galactic Center structures, potentially including the adjacent Radio Shell. Further research is required to ascertain if this alternating magnetic pattern exists in other multi-stranded NTFs or if it is a distinctive feature arising from the complex interstellar environment surrounding the Radio Arc.

This study partitions the globe into a hexagonal grid and extracts daily fire count time series from each cell to estimate and analyze global Fire Season Severity (FSS), defined as the total accumulated fire detections per season. The primary objective is to assess the accuracy of time series forecasting methods for predicting short-term (monthly) and medium-term (seasonal) FSS using solely historical active fire data. This methodology is straightforward, rapid, and relies on globally accessible data, facilitating large-scale predictions. Our findings encompass both descriptive and predictive analyses of worldwide seasonal fire activity. We confirmed that fire seasons are shorter than seven months in 99% of cells, with 57% of these cells showing a decreasing season length. Additionally, 61% of cells exhibited a declining trend in active fire counts during the season; however, regions such as Northeast Brazil and the West Coast of the USA demonstrated an increasing trend. Furthermore, the forecasting error was found to be lower than the mean FSS in 95% of cells, indicating significant predictability in FSS.

This study examines and characterizes the performance of key operations on GPUs and Many Integrated Core (MIC) architectures. Driven by the need to analyze low-dimensional spatial datasets from high-resolution sensors, such as whole-slide tissue microscopy images, we identified specific data access and computation patterns within object segmentation and feature computation tasks. We systematically implemented and evaluated these core operations across modern CPUs, GPUs, and MICs for a microscopy image analysis application. Our findings indicate that (1) both data access patterns and parallelization strategies critically influence performance; while MICs match or occasionally surpass GPUs in handling regular data access, (2) GPUs are substantially more efficient than MICs for operations involving irregular data access, due to the latter's poor performance with random access. Furthermore, (3) employing a performance-aware task scheduling strategy for coordinated execution between MICs and CPUs yields approximately a 1.29x improvement over a first-come-first-served approach. The application achieved 84% efficiency when running on 192 nodes, comprising 3,072 CPU cores and 192 MICs.

In 2021, Marco Besier and the first author proposed the concept of rationalizability for square roots to streamline arguments involving Feynman integrals. This study extends that definition to field extensions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the rationalizability of a collection of quadratic field extensions is equivalent to the rationalizability of their compositum, offering a novel approach to proving the rationalizability of sets of square roots of polynomials.

Object goal navigation focuses on guiding an agent toward a specific target using visual observations, making the design of effective scene representations crucial for determining navigation actions. This paper presents the Visual Transformer Network (VTNet), a framework designed to learn informative visual representations for navigation. VTNet is a robust architecture that leverages two fundamental properties: it captures the relationships between all object instances within a scene and prioritizes the spatial locations of objects and image regions to facilitate the learning of directional navigation signals. Additionally, we propose a pre-training strategy that links these visual representations with navigation signals to enhance policy learning. Essentially, VTNet integrates object and region features with location cues into spatial-aware descriptors, which are then combined via attention mechanisms to generate comprehensive representations for navigation. These representations enable agents to identify correlations between visual inputs and appropriate actions; for instance, if the activation map highlights the right side, the agent prioritizes turning right over turning left. Experiments conducted in the AI2-Thor environment demonstrate that VTNet significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods when tested in unseen environments.

Advancements in high-throughput sequencing and targeted therapies have catalyzed the rise of personalized medicine, where treatment recommendations—whether issued by physicians or automated algorithms—are dictated by a patient's molecular profile or specific drug-response biomarkers. As the proliferation of such algorithms increases, a critical question emerges regarding how to measure their clinical impact, particularly given that personalized strategies inherently involve multiple treatment variants. To address this, we establish a causal framework capable of handling multiple treatment versions to define and estimate the relevant effects for precision medicine using observational data that emulates clinical trials. This approach allows us to assess whether treatment assignment algorithms outperform various control groups, including gold-standard treatments, observed historical treatments, or random assignments of targeted therapies. First, causal estimates of these precision medicine effects are tested on simulated data, revealing lower bias and variance compared to naive methods that simply compare expected outcomes between treatment arms. These simulations also highlight distinct sources of bias contingent on specific clinical contexts, such as response heterogeneity or the assignment of observed treatments. Additionally, an RShiny interactive application is offered to enable users to explore custom-defined scenarios. Finally, the method is applied to patient-derived xenograft (PDX) data, where patient tumors are implanted into multiple immunodeficient mice and treated with various drugs, thereby providing access to all corresponding drug sensitivities for each patient. This unique pre-clinical dataset, which emulates counterfactual outcomes, serves to validate the reliability of the causal estimates generated by the proposed method.

We have established a persistent current lasting approximately 40 seconds within a toroidal Bose-Einstein condensate confined by an all-optical trap. A repulsive optical barrier introduces a tunable weak link in the condensate's circuit, influencing the loop current. The superflow ceases abruptly once the barrier strength causes the local flow velocity to surpass a critical threshold. The observed critical velocity aligns with energy dissipation resulting from vortex-antivortex pair generation. This setup marks the first experimental realization of a closed-loop atom circuit at an elementary level.

This work offers a combinatorial investigation into the super plactic monoid of type A, a structure linked to the representations of the general linear Lie superalgebra. We define a counterpart to Schützenberger's jeu de taquin specifically for super tableaux constructed over a signed alphabet. We demonstrate that this mechanism, which converts super skew tableaux into super Young tableaux, respects the super plactic congruence and is confluent. Furthermore, we derive properties connecting the super jeu de taquin to insertion algorithms on super tableaux. Additionally, we present the super evacuation procedure as an involution acting on super tableaux and prove its compatibility with the super plactic congruence. Finally, we characterize the super jeu de taquin using Fomin's growth diagrams to provide a combinatorial formulation of the super Littlewood--Richardson rule.

Applying Weinberg's asymptotic safety criteria to scattering amplitudes rather than the couplings of the effective action offers a way to uniquely determine ultraviolet running and circumvent certain issues within the asymptotic safety framework. This concept is demonstrated through the analysis of 4-graviton amplitudes in string theory and their associated symmetries.

This research investigates the embedding property within the category of sorted profinite groups. We define the sorted embedding property (SEP), a concept parallel to the embedding property found in standard profinite groups, and demonstrate that every sorted profinite group possesses a universal SEP-cover. Our methodology provides an alternative demonstration for the existence of a universal embedding cover for profinite groups and applies to any full subcategory of sorted profinite groups that remains closed under finite quotients, fiber products, and inverse limits. Furthermore, we introduce a weaker concept, the finitely sorted embedding property (FSEP), which is proven to be equivalent to SEP. The primary benefit of FSEP lies in its ability to be axiomatized within the first-order language of sorted complete systems. Leveraging this, we establish that any sorted profinite group with SEP admits a sorted complete system whose theory is $\omega$-stable, provided the set of sorts is countable. As a consequence, we derive the uniqueness of the universal SEP-cover for such groups, thereby extending the known uniqueness of embedding covers in profinite groups.

We establish the groundwork for a pointfree theory of Pervin spaces. A Pervin space comprises a set endowed with a bounded sublattice of its powerset, a structure known to characterize quasi-uniform spaces that are both transitive and totally bounded. Our pointfree counterpart, termed a Frith frame, consists of a frame paired with a generating bounded sublattice. This paper introduces and analyzes the category of Frith frames, demonstrating that the standard dual adjunction between topological spaces and frames generalizes to a dual adjunction between Pervin spaces and Frith frames. Contrary to the case with Pervin spaces, an equivalence does not exist between the categories of Frith frames and transitive, totally bounded quasi-uniform frames; however, we prove that the former constitutes a full coreflective subcategory of the latter. Furthermore, we investigate the concept of completeness for Frith frames as derived from quasi-uniform frames, offering a characterization of complete Frith frames and outlining the completion process for any arbitrary Frith frame.

The LHCb experiment analyzed 0.37 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data at sqrt{s} = 7 TeV collected in 2011 to search for the decays Bs -> mu+ mu- and B0 -> mu+ mu-. At the 95% confidence level, the resulting upper limits on the branching fractions are BR (Bs -> mu+ mu-) < 1.6 x 10^-8 and BR(B0 -> mu+ mu-) < 3.6 x 10^-9. Combining these findings with limits from the 2010 dataset yields improved constraints of BR (Bs -> mu+ mu-) < 1.4 x 10^-8 and BR(B0 -> mu+ mu-) < 3.2 x 10^-9 at 95% confidence level.

This study examines how acquiring a residence permit influences foreign workers' integration into the labor market and their residential ties. To address common selection bias, we leverage a unique migration lottery in Liechtenstein—a microstate between Austria and Switzerland—that randomly granted access to previously restricted permits. Applying an instrumental variable method, our findings indicate that individuals whose migration decisions complied with the lottery outcome saw their probability of employment in Liechtenstein rise by an average of 24 percentage points between 2008 and 2018. Correspondingly, their activity rates and employment duration increased by roughly 20 percentage points and 1.15 years, respectively. These robust and statistically significant outcomes are primarily attributable to individuals who were not already working in Liechtenstein before the lottery, rather than to existing cross-border commuters. Furthermore, both labor market and residential impacts proved persistent several years post-lottery, showing no signs of diminishing. These results imply that issuing residence permits to foreign workers effectively boosts labor supply, extending benefits well beyond the scope of cross-border commuting from neighboring regions.

This work investigates the trajectories of test particles and light rays orbiting neutral hairy black holes within a framework of gravity minimally coupled to a self-interacting real scalar field. We demonstrate that both time-like and null-like geodesics exhibit anomalous behavior within a specific parameter range corresponding to the dense hair region, defined by the inequality $\sqrt{\Omega(x_{h})}\leq r\leq 2MG_{N}/c^{2}$.

We investigated electron spin dynamics in high-mobility, dense two-dimensional electron gases within multilayer GaAs/AlGaAs quantum wells using time-resolved Kerr rotation and resonant spin amplification. By manipulating wave functions and quantum confinement, we achieved remarkably long spin coherence times (T2* > 13 ns) in structures doped past the metal-insulator transition. The primary constraints on spin coherence were identified as the Dyakonov-Perel relaxation mechanism and g-factor inhomogeneity. In the metallic regime, electron-electron collisions became the dominant factor in spin relaxation, surpassing microscopic scattering effects.
