Analysis of the data revealed that spin relaxation anisotropy causes the Dyakonov-Perel mechanism to be highly effective for in-plane spins but suppressed for spins aligned with the growth direction, thereby enhancing T2*. These findings—including long-lived spin coherence persisting near room temperature, spin polarization decay rates with and without magnetic fields, spin-orbit fields, and various electron relaxation and scattering times—underscore the potential of n-doped multilayer systems for spin-based devices.

We calculate the integral Chow rings for the stacks ${\mathcal H}_{g,n}^w$, which parameterize hyperelliptic curves possessing $n$ marked Weierstrass points. Our proof establishes that the integral Chow ring of each such stack is an algebra generated by any of the $\Psi$-classes, with all relations residing in degree one.

In recent years, mainstream machine learning conferences have experienced a surge in both participant numbers and diversity of viewpoints, leading community members to frequently encounter claims regarding acceptance randomness and institutional bias. This study critically examines the review process by conducting a comprehensive analysis of ICLR submissions from 2017 to 2020. We measure the extent of randomness in review scores and acceptance outcomes, and investigate the correlation between these scores and paper impact. Our results indicate significant institutional bias in accept/reject decisions, persisting even after accounting for paper quality. Additionally, we identify a gender disparity where female authors receive lower scores, face reduced acceptance rates, and garner fewer citations per paper compared to male authors. The paper concludes with recommendations aimed at future conference organizers.

Although "flat optics" is rapidly expanding across various photonic domains, its application within quantum optics remains in early stages. Notably, polarization entanglement—a cornerstone of quantum photonics owing to the ease of polarization qubit encoding and manipulation—has yet to be achieved on flat substrates. Conversely, flat nonlinear optical sources offer significant flexibility in shaping polarization characteristics due to relaxed phase-matching conditions. Leveraging this versatility, we demonstrate the generation of photon pairs with adjustable polarization entanglement through spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in a 400 nm GaP film. By adjusting the pump polarization, we can transition the polarization state of the generated pairs from fully entangled to nearly disentangled, a feat unattainable with conventional bulk SPDC sources. This combination of polarization entanglement and a broadband frequency spectrum yields an exceptionally narrow (12 fs) Hong-Ou-Mandel interference dip, paving the way for future advancements in hyperentanglement.

We characterize two types of regular invariant measures defined on the boundary path space of a second countable topological graph. This characterization enables a complete description of all extremal tracial weights on the associated C$^{*}$-algebra that lack gauge-invariance. Leveraging this description, we establish that for a free second countable topological graph, every tracial weight on its C$^{*}$-algebra is gauge-invariant. Consequently, this result implies that all tracial weights are gauge-invariant whenever the graph C$^{*}$-algebra is both simple and separable.

Leveraging the inherent flexibility and compositionality of human language, people naturally aim to direct embodied agents toward complex activities like navigation and object handling. This study addresses the critical final step for embodied agents: executing object manipulation tasks based on human verbal guidance, such as instructing an agent to "move the red mug next to the box while keeping it upright." To achieve this, we present the Automatic Manipulation Solver (AMSolver) system and establish the Vision-and-Language Manipulation benchmark (VLMbench) built upon it, which encompasses a wide array of language instructions for categorized robotic manipulation tasks. Specifically, we design modular, rule-based task templates to automatically synthesize robot demonstrations paired with linguistic commands, featuring diverse object geometries and appearances, varied action types, and specific motion constraints. Additionally, we introduce the 6D-CLIPort model, which utilizes keypoints to process multi-view visual inputs and language data, ultimately outputting a sequence of six degrees of freedom (DoF) actions. We anticipate that this new simulator and benchmark will advance future research into language-guided robotic manipulation.

The stability of solar sunspots and their internal energy transport rely heavily on their subsurface architecture. While two models—the monolithic and cluster models—have been suggested, observational data has yet to definitively favor one over the other. To investigate this structure, we examined umbral flashes in merging sunspots captured via IRIS Mg II 2796 Å slit-jaw images. These flashes are interpreted as visible signs of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) shock waves generated by convection cells beneath the photosphere. By tracing the movement of individual flashes, we identified the locations of oscillation centers, which correspond to these sub-photospheric convection cells. Our analysis revealed that these centers are predominantly situated within dark nuclei at the umbral core, avoiding brighter areas like light bridges or umbral dots. Furthermore, these centers tend to shift away from the merging interface where intense convection is anticipated. Additionally, the inferred depths of the convection cells showed no significant regional variation. These findings imply that the umbra's subsurface environment facilitates convection more readily than the convergent interface, thereby lending support to the cluster model. However, further research utilizing umbral velocity oscillations in the lower atmosphere is necessary to obtain more definitive results.

In wall-bounded shear flows approaching laminar conditions at low Reynolds numbers, turbulence manifests as oblique, localized structures. These arise from uniform turbulence through a spatiotemporal intermittent mechanism where quasi-laminar gaps randomly form and vanish. At slightly lower Reynolds numbers, periodic and nearly stationary laminar-turbulent patterns become dominant. The study analyzes the statistics of these quasi-laminar regions, focusing on spatial and temporal scale distributions and their dependence on the Reynolds number. A distinct but smooth transition is observed between uniform turbulence and flow with intermittent gaps, whereas the shift from gaps to stable patterns is more gradual. Numerical simulations in oblique domains of varying sizes examine wavelength selection, while lifetime measurements in a minimal domain confirm a preferred wavelength. Wavelet transforms applied to turbulent-laminar patterns quantify the areas and durations where specific wavelengths dominate in large domains, enabling the assessment of pattern stability relative to wavelength and Reynolds number. The findings indicate that the preferred wavelength maximizes energy and dissipation along laminar-turbulent interfaces within the large-scale flow. This optimal behavior is driven primarily by the advective characteristics of the large-scale flow, with turbulent fluctuations playing a secondary role in wavelength selection.

A primary challenge in modeling actuarial claim sizes is the absence of a standard distribution that effectively captures both the central body and the tail of the data, especially since covariates can influence small and large claims differently. To address this, we propose a deep composite regression model where the splicing point is defined by a quantile of the conditional claim size distribution instead of a fixed constant. To enable M-estimation for this framework, we define and characterize strictly consistent scoring functions for a triplet comprising a quantile and the corresponding lower and upper expected shortfalls. Subsequently, we apply this elicitation result to fit deep neural network regression models. Finally, using real accident insurance data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and show its advantages over traditional methods.

For over forty years, the anomalous surplus of low-kT photons emitted during multi-hadron production has defied resolution within the physics community. We contend that this longstanding issue stems from comparing experimental data against a flawed framework, typically referred to as the bremsstrahlung model. This model is widely regarded as an extrapolation of the Low theorem from 2->2+gamma scattering to radiative multi-particle processes (2->n+gamma) involving charged hadrons in either the initial or final state. We demonstrate that such an extension violates S-matrix unitarity, thereby contradicting the optical theorem.

Determining the conditions under which a consistent, low-dimensional convex surrogate loss can be designed for a given prediction task is a vital and ongoing focus in machine learning research. This task can be framed either as optimizing a target loss, such as in classification or structured prediction, or as estimating a conditional statistic of the data, such as in risk measure evaluation. While these two scenarios usually require distinct methods for constructing and analyzing surrogate losses, we unify them using concepts from property elicitation to establish a general lower bound on prediction dimension. For discrete predictions, this bound refines existing results by demonstrating that prior calibration-based limits can be largely derived through property elicitation. Furthermore, regarding continuous estimation, our lower bound provides a solution to an open problem concerning the estimation of risk and uncertainty measures.

Data augmentations play a crucial role in training high-performance 3D object detectors for point clouds. Despite recent initiatives to develop novel augmentations, it is surprisingly common for state-of-the-art 3D detectors to rely on only a few basic techniques. Unlike in 2D image processing, 3D augmentations must accommodate diverse input representations and be tailored to specific models, creating substantial computational overhead. To address this, we employ a search-based method and introduce LidarAugment, a practical and effective strategy for 3D object detection. Rather than tuning all augmentation policies within an exponentially large search space as previous methods did, we factorize and align the search space for each augmentation. This approach reduces the number of hyperparameters from over 20 to just two, drastically lowering search complexity. We demonstrate that LidarAugment can be adapted to various model architectures and input representations using a simple 2D grid search, consistently enhancing both convolution-based models (UPillars, StarNet, RSN) and transformer-based models (SWFormer). Additionally, LidarAugment helps mitigate overfitting and enables the scaling of 3D detectors to larger capacities. Specifically, when combined with the latest 3D detectors, LidarAugment achieves a new state-of-the-art mAPH L2 score of 74.8 on the Waymo Open Dataset.

The consistency between the Hubble horizon at matter-radiation equality ($k^{-1}_{\rm{eq}}$) and the sound horizon at last scattering ($r_s(z_*)$) offers a valuable test for the $\Lambda$CDM model and its variations. It is established that a decrease in $r_s$ can be offset by an increase in $H_0$, a relationship that also applies to the standard ruler $k_{\rm{eq}}$. While introducing additional radiation in the early universe lowers $k_{\rm{eq}}$, early dark energy (EDE) tends to raise it. We conducted analyses based on both $k_{\rm{eq}}$ and $r_s$ within the EDE and Wess-Zumino Dark Radiation (WZDR) frameworks. Our results show a discrepancy of $\Delta H_0 = 0.4$ between $r_s$- and $k_{\rm{eq}}$-derived datasets for WZDR, compared to $\Delta H_0 = 1.2$ for EDE, indicating that the dark radiation scenario aligns more closely with the two standard rulers. In a forecast analysis, we fitted both models using a mock $k_{\rm{eq}}$ prior derived from the best-fit $\Lambda$CDM parameters of \emph{Planck}. Relative to the baseline $\Lambda$CDM $H_0$, we obtained $\Delta H_0 = 1.1$ for WZDR and $\Delta H_0 = -2.4$ for EDE.

Assuming neutrinos are not Majorana fermions and that right-handed Dirac neutrinos do not exist, we propose a model where the second and third lepton generations are composite, whereas the first generation remains fundamental. These composite states consist of fundamental leptons and two new fundamental hidden scalar particles. The framework includes two additional hidden forces alongside Standard Model interactions. Initially, the gauge symmetry $SU(2)_L\otimes U(1)_{Y}\otimes U(1)_h\otimes SU(2)_h$ governing electroweak and hidden forces breaks down to $U(1)_{Y}\otimes U(1)_h$ via spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB). Within this model, neutrino masses arise from the binding dynamics of a hidden force, and neutrino oscillations are also accounted for through a dynamical framework involving these hidden forces.

The ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has measured the production of neutral pions and $\eta$ mesons at mid-rapidity within a transverse momentum range of 1 to 20 GeV/$c$ during central and semi-central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 2.76 TeV. Utilizing both photon conversion techniques and the PHOS and EMCal detectors, these findings extend the previous $\pi^{0}$ $p_{T}$ coverage from 12 to 20 GeV/$c$ and deliver the inaugural measurement of $\eta$ meson production in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC. The $\eta/\pi^{0}$ ratio remains consistent across the two centralities, stabilizing at a plateau of 0.457 $\pm$ 0.013$^{stat}$ $\pm$ 0.018$^{syst}$ at high $p_{T}$. In Pb-Pb collisions, both $\pi^{0}$ and $\eta$ meson yields exhibit a suppression of comparable magnitude relative to scaled pp collision data. The analysis interprets these results using NLO pQCD predictions and hydrodynamic models, noting a more pronounced suppression at this energy compared to lower center-of-mass energies in the 6 < $p_{T}$ < 10 GeV/$c$ interval. Furthermore, while hadronization models adequately describe the $\pi^{0}$ data for $p_{T}$ < 3 GeV/$c$, some discrepancies are observed for the $\eta$ mesons in the same region.

Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence and short video technology have established emotion recognition as a critical area within human-computer interaction. Currently, the majority of existing methods rely on single modalities, yet this approach is often ineffective in real-world scenarios where individuals frequently mask their true feelings, resulting in poor recognition accuracy. Additionally, distinguishing between similar emotional states remains a significant challenge. To address these limitations, we introduce ICANet, a novel framework for multimodal short video emotion recognition that integrates audio, video, and optical flow data. By leveraging these three distinct modalities, ICANet compensates for the shortcomings of unimodal systems and significantly enhances recognition performance. On the IEMOCAP benchmark, ICANet achieves an accuracy of 80.77%, surpassing state-of-the-art methods by 15.89%.

Adversarial Bit-Flip Attacks (BFA) on neural network weights can cause severe accuracy drops by altering just a few bits. However, existing BFA methods rely on test data, a limitation that hinders their use in scenarios involving sensitive or proprietary information. This paper introduces the Blind Data Adversarial Bit-flip Attack (BDFA), a new approach that performs BFAs without requiring access to any training or test datasets. BDFA achieves this by optimizing a synthetic dataset engineered to replicate the batch normalization statistics across various network layers and align with the target label. Experimental findings demonstrate that BDFA can drastically reduce ResNet50's accuracy from 75.96% to 13.94% by flipping only four bits.

This study examines a high-order, rapid numerical approach for solving the time-fractional Black-Scholes equation. To address the common weak initial singularities inherent in the solution, we develop a finite difference scheme utilizing variable time steps. In this framework, the fractional derivative is estimated using the nonuniform Alikhanov formula combined with the sum-of-exponentials (SOE) technique, while the spatial dimension employs an average approximation achieving fourth-order accuracy. Through the energy method, we rigorously establish the scheme's stability and convergence, confirming second-order accuracy in time and fourth-order accuracy in space. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to validate these theoretical findings.

We offer an analysis of eight corpus-based metrics for quantifying morphological complexity in natural languages, which differ in their annotation requirements. Through visual comparisons, correlation studies, and examination of typological variables, we explore the similarities and distinctions among these measures. Our primary objective is to determine if these metrics assess a single underlying dimension of complexity or multiple distinct ones. Principal component analysis reveals that the first component accounts for 92.62% of the variation across the eight measures, demonstrating a strong linear dependence among them.

We introduce the concept of a leftmost separator with a size no greater than $k$. A leftmost separator of size $k$ is defined as a minimal separator $S$ between two vertex sets, $X$ and $Y$, which cannot be shifted further toward $X$ without the separator size exceeding $k$. A primary motivation for this concept is enhancing the time complexity of treewidth approximation. While existing linear-time FPT algorithms for this problem exhibit single-exponential dependence on the treewidth parameter $k$, the coefficient within the exponent is currently large. Our objective is to reduce this coefficient to create a more practical solution, accepting a trade-off from a linear-time approach to one with $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ complexity. Previous algorithms with this complexity relied on dependencies such as $2^{24k}k!$, $2^{8.766k}k^2$ (refined to $2^{7.671k}k^2$), and worse. In this paper, we propose a treewidth approximation algorithm running in $\mathcal{O}(2^{6.755k}\ n \log n)$ time. Additionally, we enumerate leftmost separators and establish a tight upper bound for their count. We demonstrate that the number of leftmost separators of size at most $k$ does not exceed the $(k-1)$-th Catalan number, $C_{k-1}$. Finally, we provide an algorithm that outputs all such leftmost separators in $\mathcal{O}(\frac{4^k}{\sqrt{k}}n)$ time.

Current gait recognition research is primarily limited to 2D representations, such as silhouettes or skeletons, within constrained environments. However, since humans navigate unconstrained 3D spaces, projecting the body onto a 2D plane inevitably discards vital information regarding viewpoint, shape, and dynamics. Consequently, this paper investigates dense 3D representations for gait recognition in the wild, addressing a practical but overlooked challenge. We introduce SMPLGait, a novel framework that leverages the 3D Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) model. This framework comprises two specialized branches: one extracts appearance features from silhouettes, while the other learns 3D shape and viewpoint knowledge from the SMPL model. Addressing the scarcity of appropriate datasets, we created Gait3D, the first large-scale dataset based on 3D representations for gait recognition. Gait3D includes 4,000 subjects and over 25,000 sequences captured from 39 cameras in an unconstrained indoor setting. Crucially, it provides recovered 3D SMPL models for each frame, offering dense data on body shape, viewpoint, and dynamics. Extensive experiments on Gait3D demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, highlighting the superiority of our framework and the promise of 3D representations for wild gait recognition. The code and dataset are accessible at https://gait3d.github.io.

Volatility forecasting is a critical component of financial econometrics. While prior research in this domain predominantly relies on various GARCH-type models, selecting a specific GARCH model that performs well across general scenarios remains challenging. Furthermore, traditional methods often exhibit instability when addressing high-volatility periods or working with limited sample sizes. In contrast, the recently introduced Normalizing and Variance Stabilizing (NoVaS) approach offers a more robust and accurate prediction technique. This model-free method leverages an inverse transformation grounded in the ARCH framework. Drawing inspiration from the historical evolution from ARCH to GARCH models, we propose a novel NoVaS-type method that incorporates the GARCH model structure. Through extensive data analysis, we demonstrate that our model achieves superior time-aggregated prediction performance compared to the current state-of-the-art NoVaS method, particularly when forecasting short and volatile datasets. The success of our new approach not only validates this improvement but also opens new avenues for exploring alternative NoVaS structures to enhance existing models or address specific forecasting challenges.

This paper introduces a discrete Hamilton--Jacobi theory tailored for Hamiltonian dynamics on discrete contact manifolds. Initially, we establish a new geometric Hamilton--Jacobi framework for continuous contact Hamiltonian dynamics. Subsequently, utilizing the discrete contact Lagrangian formulation and applying the discrete Legendre transformation, we derive the corresponding equations for discrete Hamiltonian dynamics. Building upon the discrete contact Hamilton equations, we construct a discrete Hamilton--Jacobi equation for contact Hamiltonian dynamics and demonstrate its relationship with the continuous theory developed herein. Furthermore, we outline the geometric foundations of these discrete equations on contact manifolds using discrete contact flows. Finally, a numerical example is provided to validate the proposed theory.

Multimodal data offer complementary insights into natural phenomena by synthesizing information from diverse domains characterized by distinct statistical properties. A fundamental requirement for multimodal learning is the ability to capture both intra-modality and cross-modality information. Geometry-aware data analysis achieves this by implicitly representing data across modalities through their underlying geometric structures, a necessity since many applications explicitly define data on intrinsic geometric manifolds. While generalizing deep learning to non-Euclidean domains has become an active research area, most existing methods focus on unimodal data. This paper introduces the Multimodal Multi-scaled Graph Wavelet Convolutional Network (M-GWCN), an end-to-end framework that simultaneously derives intra-modality representations via multiscale graph wavelet transforms to enhance localization within each modality's graph domain, and cross-modality representations by learning permutations that capture correlations between modalities. Unlike many prior approaches, M-GWCN does not require homogeneous modalities with equal data counts or prior knowledge of correspondences. Experiments on three standard unimodal graph datasets and five multimodal implicit datasets demonstrate the method's superiority and effectiveness compared to spectral graph convolutional neural networks and other state-of-the-art multimodal techniques.

Research in speech communication has long struggled to develop comprehensive generative models of intonation that connect linguistic and paralinguistic functions to prosodic forms. While traditional models have been superseded by the superior performance of deep learning (DL) techniques in training general-purpose end-to-end mappings with millions of tunable parameters, this shift toward black-box machine learning has created a counter-problem: the urgent need to uncover knowledge, explain, visualize, and interpret these systems. Our work bridges the gap between a comprehensive generative model of intonation and state-of-the-art DL methods. Building on the Superposition of Functional Contours (SFC) paradigm, we introduce the Variational Prosody Model (VPM), which employs a network of variational contour generators to model context-sensitive variations in elementary prosodic contours. We demonstrate that the VPM provides insight into the intrinsic variability of these prosodic prototypes by learning a meaningful latent space representation. Furthermore, the VPM successfully captures prosodic phenomena involving multi-dimensional context-based variability. Because it relies on the principle of superposition, the VPM does not require specially crafted corpora for analysis, thereby enabling the use of big data in prosody research. In speech synthesis applications, the model can produce dynamic and natural prosodic contours that avoid averaging artifacts.

The classical Clarke subdifferential is insufficient for comprehending automatic differentiation within nonsmooth settings. Instead, we may occasionally depend on enlarged generalized gradients known as "conservative fields," which are defined via the natural path-wise chain rule; a key application lies in analyzing the convergence of gradient-based deep learning methods. In the semi-algebraic context, we demonstrate that every conservative field corresponds precisely to the sum of Clarke subdifferentials and normals to the manifolds of the underlying Whitney stratifications.

This study suggests that measuring the polarization characteristics of the $\chi_{cJ}\to \phi\phi$ decays (for $J=0,1,2$) serves as a robust test of hadronic loop contributions. Our findings indicate that the derived helicity amplitude ratios are highly stable, yielding values of $|F_{1,1}^{(0)}/F_{0,0}^{(0)}| \approx 0.359$, $|F_{1,0}^{(1)}/F_{0,1}^{(1)}| =1$, $|F_{1,1}^{(1)}/F_{0,1}^{(1)}| =0$, $|F^{(2)}_{1,0}|/|F^{(2)}_{0,0}|=|F^{(2)}_{0,1}|/|F^{(2)}_{0,0}| \approx 1.285$, $|F^{(2)}_{1,-1}|/|F^{(2)}_{0,0}|=|F^{(2)}_{-1,1}|/|F^{(2)}_{0,0}| \approx 5.110$, and $|F^{(2)}_{-1,-1}|/|F^{(2)}_{0,0}|=|F^{(2)}_{1,1}|/|F^{(2)}_{0,0}| \approx 0.465$. Utilizing these predicted ratios, we have generated Monte-Carlo simulations for the moments $\langle t_{ij} \rangle$, which are intrinsically linked to the extraction of helicity amplitudes. We recommend that future experiments at facilities such as BESIII and Belle II conduct polarization analyses of the $\chi_{cJ}\to \phi\phi$ process, as this is crucial for elucidating the fundamental decay mechanisms governing $\chi_{cJ}$ transitions.

This study reports findings from a search for the Higgs boson decaying into a Z boson and a photon (H$\to$Z$\gamma$), where the Z boson subsequently decays into an electron-positron or muon-antimuon pair (Z$\to\ell^+\ell^-$, with $\ell$ = e or $\mu$). The analysis utilizes proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC, comprising an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. To improve signal sensitivity, events are sorted into mutually exclusive categories that leverage variations in event topology and kinematics across different Higgs production mechanisms. A simultaneous fit to the invariant mass distributions of $\ell^+\ell^-\gamma$ across all categories yields a signal strength $\mu$, representing the ratio of the product of the production cross section and branching fraction [$\sigma($pp$\to$H$)\mathcal{B}($H$\to$Z$\gamma)$] to the Standard Model expectation. For a Higgs boson mass of 125.38 GeV, the extracted value is $\mu$=2.4$\pm$0.9. The observed excess of events exhibits a statistical significance of 2.7 standard deviations. This corresponds to a measured cross-section times branching fraction of $\sigma($pp$\to$H$)\mathcal{B}($H$\to$Z$\gamma)$ = 0.21$\pm$0.08 pb. At the 95% confidence level, the observed upper limit on $\mu$ is 4.1, with an expected limit of 1.8. Additionally, the ratio of branching fractions $\mathcal{B}($H$\to$Z$\gamma)/\mathcal{B}($H$\to\gamma\gamma)$ is determined to be 1.5$^{+0.7}_{-0.6}$, which aligns with the Standard Model prediction of 0.69 $\pm$ 0.04 at a 1.5 standard deviation level.

This paper addresses a general time-inconsistent optimal control problem for a non-homogeneous linear system where the state dynamics follow a stochastic differential equation with deterministic coefficients, driven by noise from both a Brownian motion and an independent Poisson point process. The objective functional incorporates running and terminal costs that explicitly depend on general discounting coefficients, encompassing both non-exponential and hyperbolic discounting scenarios. Additionally, the inclusion of quadratic terms involving the conditional expectation of the state process and a state-dependent term within the objective functional renders the problem time-inconsistent. Rather than seeking optimal controls, we construct open-loop Nash equilibrium controls utilizing a stochastic maximum principle variant. This methodology employs a stochastic system comprising a flow of forward-backward stochastic differential equations alongside an equilibrium condition. Finally, the study applies these findings to several concrete examples.

Video deblurring models leverage consecutive frames to mitigate blur caused by camera shake and object movement. Conventional approaches typically depend on homography or optical flow to align neighboring blurry frames for the purpose of utilizing sharp patches from adjacent frames. However, these explicit methods often struggle with fast motions involving significant pixel displacements. To address this, we introduce a novel implicit approach that learns spatial correspondences directly within the feature space. To establish distant pixel relationships, our model constructs a correlation volume pyramid encompassing all pixel pairs between neighboring frames. Furthermore, we develop a correlative aggregation module designed to maximize pixel-pair correlations with neighbors based on this volume pyramid, thereby enhancing reference frame features. These aggregated features are then processed by a reconstruction module to generate the restored frame. We employ a generative adversarial framework to progressively optimize the model. Our method is evaluated on the widely used DVD dataset and a newly assembled High-Frame-Rate (1000 fps) Video Deblurring Dataset (HFR-DVD). Both quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on both datasets, validating the advantages of modeling all-range spatial correspondence for video deblurring.

Conventional media coding schemes typically convert images and videos into semantic-unknown binary streams, which hinders direct support for intelligent tasks at the bitstream level. The Semantically Structured Image Coding (SSIC) framework was the first to enable image intelligent task analysis without full decoding by utilizing a Semantically Structured Bitstream (SSB); however, SSIC focused solely on static object information within images. This paper expands the concept of semantically structured coding to video and introduces an advanced Semantically Structured Video Coding (SSVC) framework tailored for heterogeneous intelligent applications. Given that video signals feature rich dynamic motion and redundancy from frame similarities, we redefine the SSB in SSVC to encompass both static object attributes and dynamic motion cues. Specifically, we employ optical flow to encode continuous motion and leverage a predictive coding architecture to minimize cross-frame redundancy, subsequently reorganizing the optical flow and residual data into an SSB. This approach allows the proposed SSVC to more adaptively support video-based downstream intelligent applications. Extensive experiments confirm that the SSVC framework can directly facilitate multiple intelligent tasks using only partially decoded bitstreams, thereby avoiding full decompression and significantly reducing bitrate and bandwidth consumption for intelligent analytics. We validate this capability across tasks such as object detection, pose estimation, action recognition, and video object segmentation.

When confined, thin sheets either wrinkle smoothly or concentrate stress into small, sharp areas. These patterns have been the subject of decades of research across fields ranging from engineering and geology to biology and art. However, a comprehensive framework explaining how various intermediate confinement levels drive spontaneous stress focusing remains elusive. To investigate this, we combine experiments with molecular dynamics simulations, flattening circular sheets centrally and pulling them quasi-statically through a ring. In this setup, wrinkles form in the free outer region before being superseded by a truncated cone that emerges during an abrupt shift to stress focusing. We model the force behind this event using an analogy to the pressure buckling of an encased ring. Subsequent cones sequentially pattern the sheet until axisymmetry is restored in most geometries. The size of these cones depends on the geometry, a relationship explained by a 1D model treating concentrated strain as an effective elastic foundation. This study advances the characterization of general confinement in thin sheets and expands the understanding of the d-cone, a fundamental component of stress focusing, within realistic contexts.

Theoretical simulations of Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (EELS) experiments are employed to study the relaxation time of collective electronic states within a two-dimensional arrangement of quantum dots. By numerically calculating the energy loss probability for an electron beam moving parallel to the distribution, the damping time of ferroelectric-like states can be estimated. This collective response is modeled by introducing mean-field interactions among the dots, with the framework further expanded to include long-range correlation effects via the Bragg-Williams approximation. Subsequently, the dielectric function, energy loss function, and relaxation time of these ferroelectric-like states are analyzed in relation to the distribution's temperature and the intrinsic damping constant of individual quantum dots. The consistency and reliability of these observed trends suggest that this analytical approach can assist experimentalists in designing tailored quantum dot distributions for specific applications.

This study performs next-to-leading-order QCD corrections for the $Z \to \eta_Q+g+g$ decay ($Q=c,b$) originating from the color-singlet $Q\bar{Q}[^1S_0^{[1]}]$ state, aiming to evaluate its effect on inclusive $\eta_Q$ decays from the $Z$ boson. Our results indicate that these QCD corrections substantially boost the leading-order predictions for the $gg$ channel, particularly for $\eta_c$, thereby significantly raising the total decay width $\Gamma_{Z \to \eta_Q+X}$ previously estimated by the dominant $Z \to \eta_{Q}[^1S_0^{[1]}]+Q+\bar{Q}$ process. Furthermore, accounting for these large corrections reveals that the $gg$ contribution plays a vital role in shaping the CS-predicted energy distributions of $\eta_Q$. In summary, within color-singlet analyses of $Z \to \eta_Q+X$, the $Z \to \eta_Q[^1S_0^{[1]}]+g+g$ channel offers phenomenologically essential contributions alongside the $Z \to \eta_{Q}[^1S_0^{[1]}]+Q+\bar{Q}$ channel.

Azimuthally differential femtoscopy measurements offer critical insights into the system's evolution dynamics and nature by probing both the source's spatio-temporal properties and the collective velocity fields at freeze-out. Specifically, HBT radius modulations relative to the second harmonic event plane primarily reflect the source's spatial geometry, whereas third harmonic results are predominantly governed by velocity fields. Consequently, radius variations tied to the third harmonic event plane definitively indicate collective expansion and anisotropy within flow fields. Event Shape Engineering (ESE) serves as a method to isolate events with specific geometrical shapes. By combining azimuthally differential HBT with ESE, researchers can conduct a comprehensive analysis of the interplay between initial geometry, anisotropic flow, and source deformation. This work presents azimuthally differential pion femtoscopy relative to second and third harmonic event planes across varying pion transverse momenta and collision centralities in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 2.76$ TeV. These findings are compared against existing models, with additional analysis on the effects of selecting events characterized by high elliptic or triangular flow.

We examine two stationary time series characterized by heavy-tailed marginal distributions to determine if a causal link exists, where a shift in one induces a shift in the other. Standard causality detection techniques often fail when causal effects are visible only within extreme values. This study introduces a method to identify causal relationships specifically among extremes by defining the "causal tail coefficient." Under certain assumptions, this metric accurately identifies asymmetric causality between series extremes, even in the presence of nonlinear dependencies and common ancestors. Additionally, the approach aids in detecting time delays between the series. We outline its asymptotic properties, demonstrate its performance through simulations, and apply it to real-world space-weather and hydro-meteorological datasets.

Meneghetti et al. recently identified an abundance of small-scale gravitational lenses within galaxy clusters. This study investigates the consequences of this finding for self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) relative to standard cold dark matter (CDM). By developing controlled N-body simulations that align with observational data, we find that early-type galaxies within cluster substructures can deepen the gravitational potential and mitigate tidal mass loss. Both SIDM and CDM scenarios necessitate a relatively high concentration of baryons in these substructures to match lensing measurements, resulting in similar tangential caustics. However, SIDM substructures may undergo gravothermal collapse, creating a steeper density profile than their CDM equivalents and increasing the radial galaxy-galaxy strong lensing cross-section, though this effect remains difficult to detect. Ultimately, our findings suggest that SIDM offers a unified framework for explaining both the small-scale lenses observed in galaxy clusters and the stellar dynamics found in dwarf galaxies.

Exploring the advantages of magnetic fields in Inertial Confinement Fusion (ICF) has led to novel experimental setups, such as the Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion (MagLIF) concept tested at Sandia National Laboratories' Z-machine and its laser-driven counterpart at OMEGA. Deploying these platforms at Megajoule-scale facilities like the Laser MegaJoule (LMJ) or the National Ignition Facility (NIF) is essential for achieving self-sustained nuclear fusion and enabling higher levels of magnetization through increased compression. This paper details a comprehensive design for a cylindrical target experimental platform utilizing magnetized implosions at the LMJ. In this setup, a seed magnetic field is produced along the cylinder's axis via laser-driven coil targets, offering reduced debris and improved diagnostic access compared to traditional pulsed power generators. We provide an extensive simulation study of the initial B-field generated by these coils, alongside two-dimensional extended magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations demonstrating that an initial 5T field can be compressed to 25kT during implosion. Under these conditions, electron magnetization significantly alters plasma conditions at stagnation; specifically, electron temperature in the hot spot rises from 1keV to 5keV, while density drops from 40g/cc to 7g/cc. We discuss diagnostic strategies using X-ray imaging, spectroscopy, and particle diagnostics, proposing the simultaneous use of Argon and Krypton dopants in the fuel to serve as spectroscopic tracers. Our analysis shows that this approach provides effective spatial resolution in the plasma, allowing for unambiguous observation of magnetic field effects. Finally, we outline a roadmap for future experiments of this nature at the LMJ.

Offline reinforcement learning facilitates policy learning from a static dataset without requiring additional environment interactions. However, this constraint renders policy training susceptible to out-of-distribution state-action pairs and the omission of beneficial actions. To address these challenges and cultivate more effective agents, we introduce a framework capable of learning flexible yet well-regularized fully-implicit policies. Additionally, we propose a straightforward adaptation of traditional policy-matching techniques to enforce regularization based on the dual formulations of Jensen-Shannon divergence and integral probability metrics. We provide theoretical proofs validating the correctness of our policy-matching method, as well as the correctness and favorable finite-sample properties of our proposed modification. Our framework is instantiated effectively through a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) structure, complemented by techniques that explicitly smooth the state-action mapping to ensure robust generalization beyond the static dataset. Comprehensive experiments and ablation studies conducted on the D4RL benchmark confirm the validity of our framework and the efficacy of our algorithmic designs.

This study introduces three distinct sliding mode control strategies for a magnetic levitation system. Initially, a proportional-integral sliding mode controller (PI-SMC) is formulated utilizing an innovative switching surface and a proportional plus power rate reaching law. This PI-SMC exhibits superior robustness against mismatched uncertainties compared to feedback linearization controllers and outperforms recent sliding mode schemes regarding convergence speed and settling time. Subsequently, to mitigate the chattering observed in the PI-SMC, a state feedback-based discrete-time sliding mode algorithm is proposed, though this comes with a partial reduction in disturbance rejection capabilities. To enhance robustness while retaining the chattering reduction advantages of the discrete-time approach, mismatched uncertainties—such as sensor noise and track input disturbances—are integrated into a robust discrete-time sliding mode design employing multirate output feedback (MROF). This method achieves the performance benefits of full-state feedback without the complexity of dynamic controllers or additional discrete-time observers. Consequently, the MROF-based discrete-time sliding mode strategy ensures excellent dynamic and steady-state performance with heightened robustness against mismatched uncertainties. The stability of the closed-loop system under these proposed controllers is validated through Lyapunov stability theory, with simulation results and analytical comparisons confirming the effectiveness and robustness of the control schemes.

This volume presents revised versions of the papers chosen for the inaugural volume of the Online Handbook of Argumentation for AI (OHAAI). While formal theories of argument and their interactions have previously been developed and examined, these foundations have recently evolved into the study of computational argument models. As a subfield of artificial intelligence, argumentation is particularly pertinent to researchers focusing on symbolic knowledge representation and defeasible reasoning. The aim of this handbook is to offer an open-access, curated anthology for the argumentation research community. Designed as a research hub, OHAAI tracks the most recent and emerging PhD-led work on both the theoretical and practical applications of argumentation across all AI-related domains.

In 1994, John Cobb posed the question: for integers satisfying $N > m > k > 0$, does a Cantor set exist within $\mathbb R^N$ such that its projections onto every $m$-plane are precisely $k$-dimensional? While Antoine (1924) addressed the case $(N,m,k)=(2,1,1)$ and Borsuk (1947) handled $(N,m,m)$, subsequent examples were developed by Cobb (1994) for $(3,2,1)$, by Frolkina (2010, 2019) for $(N,m,m-1)$ and $(N,N-1,N-2)$, and by Barov, Dijkstra, and van der Meer (2012) for $(N,N-1,k)$. This paper demonstrates that such sets are exceptional. Considering $\mathcal C(\mathbb R^N)$ as the collection of all Cantor subsets of $\mathbb R^N$ under the Hausdorff metric—a known Baire space—we establish that there exists a dense $G_\delta$ subset $\mathcal P \subset \mathcal C(\mathbb R^N)$ where every $X \in \mathcal P$ projects onto a Cantor set for any non-zero linear subspace $L \subset \mathbb R^N$. This finding offers a partial resolution to another query raised by J. Cobb in his 1994 work.

Scientific outcomes in high-energy physics and numerous other domains frequently depend on intricate software stacks. To ensure result reproducibility and enable thorough scrutiny, it is standard practice to utilize open-source tools and properly cite software packages along with their specific versions. However, given the escalating complexity of scientific software on one hand and the short IT lifecycle of just a few years on the other, establishing and validating a minimal, functional analysis environment often becomes prohibitively costly, even when source code is available. We contend that a significant gap exists between merely possessing access to versioned source code and the capability to construct a data analysis runtime environment. To maintain various iterations of these runtime environments, we engineered a snapshotting file system specifically optimized for software distribution. We share our insights on preserving the analysis environment for high-energy physics, including the software ecosystem employed to discover the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider.

Creating lifelike 3D faces is essential for computer graphics and vision tasks. Existing research primarily relies on linear statistical models of facial surfaces, yet these approaches fail to accurately capture facial textures and normals, both of which are vital for photorealistic synthesis. Although recent studies have shown that Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can produce high-quality facial textures, they typically exclude geometry and normals or require separate processes to generate 3D shape data. This paper introduces the first method capable of jointly generating high-quality textures, shapes, and normals for photorealistic creation. We propose a novel GAN designed to generate multi-modal data by leveraging their correlations, and we demonstrate the ability to condition generation on facial expressions to produce faces with diverse poses. Due to size constraints, the qualitative results in this paper are compressed; full-resolution images and a video are available in the supplementary materials. The code and models can be accessed at the project page: https://github.com/barisgecer/TBGAN.

This study numerically investigates the capillarity-driven thinning of entangled polymer solutions using the Doi-Edwards-Marrucci-Grizzuti (DEMG) and Rolie-Poly (RP) models. While both frameworks account for polymer reptation, finite chain retraction rates, and single-molecule extensibility, they differ slightly in their treatment of convective constraint release. Simulations assume cylindrical filaments with realistic entanglement densities and neglect fluid inertia. The outcomes identify three sequential stages: an initial tube-reorientation phase, a short intermediate elasto-capillary phase, and a final finite-extensibility phase approaching the pinch-off singularity. These findings highlight two critical aspects of transient extensional rheology in entangled polymers that match prior experimental observations but are inadequately captured by the commonly used FENE-P model. First, the relaxation time derived from capillary breakup extensional rheometry is significantly lower than that from steady-shear rheometry; their ratio follows a universal function of entanglement state and concentration, aligning well with experimental data across various entangled solutions. Second, at high concentrations, thinning dynamics at intermediate strain rates are dominated by tube reorientation, resulting in a distinct rate-thinning behavior in apparent extensional viscosity. Finally, the thinning dynamics of aqueous polyethylene oxide solutions (1 MDa) across dilute and entangled regimes are evaluated. As concentration rises, thinning profiles diverge from established exponential trends once the entanglement threshold is crossed, shifting toward a power-law character.

In recent years, EEG-based emotion recognition has garnered significant interest within human-machine interaction and cognitive science domains. However, the challenge of identifying emotions with scarce labeled data has emerged as a critical bottleneck in both research and practical applications. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a Self-supervised Group Meiosis Contrastive learning framework (SGMC), designed around EEG signals elicited by consistent stimuli in humans. Central to the SGMC is a new genetics-inspired data augmentation technique called "Meiosis," which leverages stimulus alignment among grouped EEG samples to generate augmented groups through pairing, cross-exchanging, and separating processes. Additionally, the model utilizes a group projector to derive group-level feature representations from EEG samples triggered by identical emotional video stimuli. Contrastive learning is then applied to maximize the similarity between group-level representations of augmented groups sharing the same stimuli. Experimental results on the publicly available DEAP dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, achieving 94.72% and 95.68% accuracy in the valence and arousal dimensions, respectively, while also showing competitive results on the SEED dataset with 94.04% accuracy. Notably, the SGMC maintains strong performance even with limited labels. Feature visualization analyses suggest that the model effectively learns video-level emotion-related features to enhance recognition, and a hyperparameter analysis further evaluates the impact of group size. Furthermore, control experiments and ablation studies were conducted to validate the architectural rationale, with the source code made available online.

Implementing a Docker-based replicability framework presents the community with a significant opportunity: accurately measuring the runtime of information retrieval systems. Since the speed at which query results are delivered to users is critical to their satisfaction, the growing complexity of neural IR re-ranking models has made query latency a primary concern. These models introduce a complex trade-off between performance and effectiveness, influenced by various factors such as the selection of encoding models, network architecture, and hardware acceleration. Notably, top-performing models, which currently rely on the BERT transformer architecture, operate orders of magnitude slower than simpler designs. Our goal is to expand the neural IR community's focus to encompass performance metrics, thereby ensuring the practical viability of these innovations. This position paper supports our argument with a case study analyzing the performance of diverse neural re-ranking models. Furthermore, we propose enhancing the OSIRRC Docker-based replicability infrastructure by introducing two benchmark scenarios specifically focused on performance.

Training humanoid robots to generate efficient locomotion from scratch remains a significant challenge, as evidenced by the "Learning to run" competition at NIPS 2017. That event tasked participants with training a bipedal model to achieve maximum speed on a simulated track using a tabula rasa reinforcement learning (RL) approach; while all submissions succeeded in producing relatively fast running behaviors, none achieved optimality. This paper introduces a method that leverages video data of human runners (such as footage from YouTube) to refine the reward function for the learning agent, thereby accelerating training and yielding superior results. Specifically, we utilize the positions of key body parts at fixed time intervals to construct a potential function for potential-based reward shaping (PBRS). Because PBRS preserves the optimal policy, this technique enables the RL agent to bypass sub-optimal movements inherent in the human video data. We first establish a high-performing baseline by combining selected techniques from the top ten NIPS competition entries with additional optimizations. Subsequently, we demonstrate that integrating video-based reward shaping further enhances performance, resulting in an RL agent that runs twice as fast as the baseline within just 12 hours of training. Additionally, we show that our approach effectively overcomes the sub-optimal behaviors present in the videos, with the learned policy significantly outperforming the running agent derived directly from the video data.

A group $G$ is considered highly transitive if it acts transitively on $k$-tuples of distinct elements for every integer $k \geq 1$. Numerous groups exhibiting rich geometric or dynamical properties possess such actions. We demonstrate that if a group $G$ admits a highly transitive action without containing the subgroup of finitary alternating permutations, then any confined subgroup $H$ of $G$ also acts highly transitively, potentially after removing a finite set of points. This finding offers a method to exclude the possibility of highly transitive actions and to categorize them for specific groups. We provide specific examples of these applications within groups arising from dynamical systems. Notably, we achieve the first non-trivial classification of highly transitive actions for a finitely generated group.

This paper introduces a framework for designing and implementing offset equivariant networks, which are neural networks that maintain uniform increments in their outputs corresponding to uniform increments in their inputs. When operating in an appropriate color space, these networks achieve equivariance regarding photometric transformations that reflect changes in lighting conditions. We evaluated the framework across three distinct tasks: image recognition, illuminant estimation, and image inpainting. Our experiments demonstrate that the performance of offset equivariant networks is comparable to state-of-the-art methods on standard data. However, unlike conventional networks, these equivariant networks exhibit consistent robustness when the color of the illuminant varies.

This study derives Killing-Yano one-forms (the duals of Killing vector fields) for a class of spherically symmetric space-times defined by four functions, using a unified and comprehensive approach. For established space-times—including Minkowski, Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordström, Robertson-Walker, and various de Sitter metrics—these forms emerge naturally as specific instances. Beyond the two standard forms, four additional de Sitter space-time forms are identified, featuring ten independent Killing vector fields that allow for the explicit specification of four distinct time evolution regimes based on symmetry constraints. Furthermore, a family of space-times is introduced where the metric functions follow a general form and admit six or seven independent Killing vector fields.

We report findings on the azimuthal correlation between net-charge and high-$p_T$ trigger particles. The shape of the net-charge correlation closely resembles that of the total-charge. On the near-side, both the net-charge and total-charge $p_T$ spectra exhibit similar profiles and are harder than the inclusive spectra. Conversely, on the away-side, the correlated spectra are only slightly harder than the inclusives; furthermore, the net-charge/total-charge ratio rises with increasing $p_T$ and aligns with the inclusive ratio.

We introduce a multistage approach for Bayesian inference across all levels of a Bayesian hierarchical model (BHM), leveraging natural data partitions to boost efficiency by enabling parallel computations tailored to specific software for each partition. The full hierarchical model is approximated by multiplying independent normal distributions representing the data component. In the subsequent stage, the Bayesian maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator is derived by maximizing this approximated posterior density with respect to the parameters. When model parameters can be expressed as normally distributed random effects, this optimization aligns with fitting a multivariate normal linear mixed model. The method accommodates both shared fixed parameters across partitions and distinct parameters unique to each. For distinct parameters, a third stage re-estimates them based on the second stage's results, ensuring that information from the entire dataset properly informs their posterior distributions. The approach is illustrated using two ecological datasets with random effects GLMs and Integrated Population Models (IPMs). Comparisons with single-stage models fitted to the full dataset reveal that multistage point estimates and posterior standard deviations closely match those from simultaneous fitting. Consequently, this method is a viable option for fitting hierarchical Bayesian models when single-step computation is computationally infeasible.

Growing attention is being paid to the evaluation, implementation, and measurement of trust within human-robot interaction (HRI), which traditionally focuses on shaping user trust through the lens of a direct dyadic relationship between the user and the robot. However, we argue this perspective overlooks a critical dimension: a robot's trustworthiness is often dependent on the user's existing relationship with and perception of the entity deploying the robot. To address this, we introduce a new HRI triad model comprising the User, Robot, and Deployer, which provides fresh insights for more comprehensively assessing and measuring trust.

This study applies a fast-forward scheme for adiabatic quantum dynamics to finite regular spin clusters of various geometries, clarifying the characteristics of the required driving interactions. The method relies on quasi-adiabatic dynamics, achieved by incorporating regularization terms into the reference Hamiltonian and subsequently rescaling time using a large factor. Utilizing regularization terms that include both pair-wise and three-body interactions, we applied the proposed formula (Phys. Rev. A 96, 052106(2017)) to N=3 systems comprising regular triangles and open linear chains, as well as to N=4 systems featuring triangular pyramids, squares, primary star graphs, and open linear chains. The symmetry induced by the geometry significantly reduces the rank of the coefficient matrix within the linear algebraic equations used to determine the regularization terms. By selecting a transverse Ising Hamiltonian as the reference, we determined that: (1) for N=3 spin clusters, the driving interaction comprises solely geometry-dependent pair-wise interactions, rendering three-body interactions unnecessary; (2) for N=4 spin clusters, geometry-dependent pair-wise interactions form the primary component of the driving force, while a universal three-body interaction independent of geometry is required but serves a secondary function. Overall, this scheme successfully predicts the practical driving interactions needed to accelerate adiabatic quantum dynamics in structured regular spin clusters.

DNA sequencing is increasingly common in both healthcare and direct-to-consumer contexts. To facilitate research, genomic data is frequently de-identified and shared via public repositories like OpenSNP or through researcher-only access-controlled databases. However, recent findings indicate that genomic data can be successfully linked to high-resolution 3D facial images, raising concerns that ubiquitous public face images could be connected to shared genetic datasets, thereby re-identifying individuals. Although these studies demonstrate the theoretical feasibility of such attacks, they assume the attackers possess highly curated data, a condition unlikely to hold in practice, which casts doubt on the attack's practical viability. Consequently, this work systematically examines the re-identification risk from two angles: first, by evaluating the success rate of linkage attacks using real facial images, and second, by exploring methods to enhance individual control over this risk. Our results suggest that the actual re-identification risk for most people is likely far lower than previously estimated. Furthermore, we show that adding a small amount of carefully designed noise to images allows for a controlled balance between re-identification success and image quality, significantly reducing risk even with noise that remains imperceptible to the human eye.

A core inquiry in inflationary cosmology concerns defining the structural characteristics of various models within the field-theoretic framework. Existing proposals often attempt to directly assess the formal structure of the theory using complexity metrics of the potentials. In contrast, an intrinsic alternative emphasizes analyzing the behavior of observables produced by different models to identify distinguishing features. This methodology is particularly valuable for nontrivial multifield theories, where a natural complexity measure may be unclear and analytical calculations of observables are frequently infeasible. In such scenarios, observables can be computed numerically to examine their behavior. A notable instance occurs when observables exhibit scaling behavior, allowing theories to be defined by their scaling amplitudes and exponents. Typically, models possess complex parameter spaces, resulting in exponents that vary as functions of these parameters. In these instances, we employ an iterative procedure to verify if these exponent functions themselves induce a scaling behavior. We demonstrate that modular inflation models can be described by families of straightforward scaling laws, and that the resulting scaling exponents further display a scaling law with respect to varying energy scales.

Recent advancements have demonstrated the efficacy of gradient-based methods for causal discovery using interventional data, even when the specific intervened variables are unidentified. Nevertheless, prior approaches typically assume a known mapping between samples and interventions, an assumption that is frequently impractical. We consider a setting involving a large dataset drawn from multiple intervention distributions alongside a single observational distribution, where the origin of each sample and the nature of the intervention remain entirely latent. To address this, we introduce a method utilizing neural networks and variational inference, which frames the problem as learning a common causal graph across an infinite mixture of intervention structural causal models governed by a Dirichlet process prior. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world data indicate that our proposed approach, including its semi-supervised variant, successfully uncovers causal relationships under these difficult conditions.

To determine the resonance-nucleon cross section within the nucleus, the photonuclear reaction cross section in the resonance region is computed. This derived resonance-nucleon cross section is then employed to assess the resonance-nucleus optical potential, which can alter the photonuclear reaction cross section generated by reaction-induced resonances. Finally, the calculated photonuclear reaction cross section is compared against experimental data to investigate how nuclear effects influence the resonance-nucleon cross section.

As generative neural networks gain traction in LHC simulations, a critical challenge emerges: how to regulate these networks and quantify uncertainties in their generated events. We demonstrate that Bayesian normalizing flows, or invertible networks, effectively capture uncertainties inherent to the training process and convert them into event weights. Fundamentally, the relationship between density and uncertainty estimates reveals that these networks learn functions akin to parameter fitting, rather than relying on binned event counts.

Accurately tracking the 6D pose of objects within video sequences is crucial for robotic manipulation. However, most existing approaches rely on having access to the target object's CAD model, either at the category level for offline training or as a template for online matching. This paper introduces BundleTrack, a general framework designed for tracking the 6D poses of novel objects without requiring any 3D models, whether at the instance or category level. By combining deep learning advancements in segmentation and robust feature extraction with memory-augmented pose graph optimization for spatiotemporal consistency, BundleTrack achieves long-term, low-drift tracking even under challenging conditions such as severe occlusions and significant object motion. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks show that this method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art category-level 6D tracking and dynamic SLAM techniques. Furthermore, it achieves performance comparable to methods relying on instance-level CAD models while requiring less information. An efficient CUDA implementation delivers real-time processing at 10Hz for the entire framework. The code is available at: https://github.com/wenbowen123/BundleTrack

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) remain a prominent research area because of their superior generation quality. However, it has been noted that many state-of-the-art GANs produce samples that resemble the training set more closely than a holdout testing set from the same distribution, suggesting that these models implicitly memorize certain training examples. This memorization is problematic for applications requiring generated data to be sufficiently distinct from known samples. Despite this, it remains uncertain whether memorization can be mitigated without degrading generation quality. This paper introduces "memorization rejection," a training strategy that filters out generated samples that are near-duplicates of training data during the training process. The proposed method is straightforward, general-purpose, and applicable to any GAN architecture. Experiments across various datasets and GAN models demonstrate that memorization rejection effectively curbs the memorization of training samples while often preserving generation quality. The code to replicate these results is available at $\texttt{https://github.com/jybai/MRGAN}$.

Luminous X-ray outbursts in accreting X-ray pulsars (XRPs) provide an opportunity to analyze the neutron star's emission in detail, revealing insights into the active accretion mechanisms. By utilizing a multi-instrument monitoring campaign involving NuSTAR, Swift/XRT, AstroSat, and NICER, we tracked the spectral and timing evolution of the Be/X-ray Binary 2S 1553-542 during a rare outburst. Our study reports the first detection of a luminosity-dependent cyclotron line energy in this source. Furthermore, variability observed in the pulse profiles and pulsed fractions aligns with the interpretation that the system shifts from a sub-critical to a super-critical accretion regime, crossing a critical luminosity threshold of approximately $4\times10^{37}$ erg/s.

The structural and thermodynamic properties of restricted primitive model electrolytes are investigated using three newly developed linear variants of the modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation. Analytical formulas for the osmotic coefficient and the electrical component of the mean activity coefficient are derived, with the resulting values compared against established mean spherical approximation, symmetric and modified Poisson-Boltzmann theories, as well as existing Monte Carlo simulation data. These linear theories demonstrate remarkable accuracy relative to simulations and align consistently with both the mean spherical approximation and modified Poisson-Boltzmann results. Furthermore, the predicted structural features, including radial distribution functions and mean electrostatic potential, show strong agreement with formal theoretical outcomes. Finally, an analytical identity is established between the excess internal energy and the electrical part of the mean activity coefficient for both the mean spherical approximation and the linear modified Poisson-Boltzmann theories.

Generating product descriptions presents a significant and largely unexplored challenge. Most existing approaches take a set of product attributes as input and generate a description from scratch in a single pass. However, this dominant paradigm may fall short when addressing dynamic user requirements to constrain descriptions, such as adding or removing content for specific attributes based on prior versions. To tackle this issue, we investigate a novel "draft-command-edit" framework for controllable text editing in e-commerce. Specifically, we enable systems to accept user commands (insertions or deletions) and generate descriptions by flexibly modifying previous versions rather than starting anew. This approach of editing existing drafts is more practical and efficient than generating content from scratch. Additionally, we introduce a data augmentation strategy to overcome data scarcity in this task, employing both model-based and rule-based techniques to simulate human edits. Alongside this new task, we release a human-annotated dataset named E-cEdits and propose a new evaluation metric called "Attribute Edit." Experimental results demonstrate that our data augmentation method significantly outperforms baseline approaches in both automatic and human evaluations.

This paper introduces a novel study focused on generating arbitrary, unseen viewpoints for infrared imagery within a non-linear feature subspace. Unlike existing methods that rely on synthetic data and frequently produce blurry or distorted results, our approach leverages semantic information from natural images to encapsulate features, ensuring that predicted unseen views maintain high-quality 3D representations. We further investigate the non-linear feature subspace, demonstrating that our network operates in a Riemannian subspace rather than a Euclidean one. Instead of learning geometric transformations to map pixel positions in new images, our model learns the underlying manifold. To validate this, we employ t-SNE visualizations for a detailed network analysis and utilize a low-shot learning classification task to evaluate the generated images.

Within public transport modeling and simulation, we tackle the discrepancy between observed and simulated transit trips. We highlight a critical flaw in current travel demand modeling: the generated trips are overly optimistic and fail to capture actual passenger behavior. To address this, we introduce "mini activities"—small tasks travelers perform during journeys—that account for the divergence between simulated and real-world data. Our approach involves mining smart card data to identify these mini activities and developing a method to embed them into generated trips. This integration technique learns from two data sources: historical trip records and trip planner suggestions. Given an input travel demand, we construct a Markov chain across the trip collection and utilize the Monte Carlo Markov Chain algorithm to incorporate mini activities, ensuring that selected characteristics align with target distributions. We evaluated this method using passenger trip data from Nancy, France, across various scenarios. Our experimental results demonstrate a significant reduction in the mismatch between simulated and observed trips.

Nearly three decades ago, Zhang and Shasha (1989) introduced a groundbreaking paper detailing an efficient dynamic programming approach to calculate tree edit distance—the minimum count of node insertions, deletions, and replacements required to convert one tree into another. Since its introduction, this metric has seen extensive application in fields such as biology and intelligent tutoring systems. Nevertheless, the original work by Zhang and Shasha can be difficult for newcomers to navigate and lacks instructions on efficiently deriving the optimal edit script. This contribution serves as a comprehensive tutorial on the Zhang and Shasha algorithm. Additionally, we demonstrate the metric properties of tree edit distance and present efficient methods for inferring the least costly edit script, along with a summary of all such optimal scripts between two trees.

We present a straightforward, local mechanism for nodes within an undirected graph to organize into non-adjacent clusters that satisfy two conditions: (1) a diameter bounded by a polylogarithmic factor, and (2) an inclusion of at least half of the total vertices. This approach immediately enables efficient deterministic distributed algorithms for computing strong-diameter network decompositions and other essential tools. Consequently, our method offers a direct and significantly streamlined approach to deriving these fundamental structures.

We introduce an equivariant formulation of Seiberg-Witten-Floer cohomology applicable to finite group actions on rational homology $3$-spheres. This construction relies on an equivariant adaptation of the Seiberg-Witten-Floer stable homotopy type developed by Manolescu. Leveraging these equivariant cohomology groups, we define a collection of $d$-invariants, denoted $d_{G,c}(Y,\mathfrak{s})$, parameterized by the group cohomology of $G$. These invariants adhere to a Froyshov-type inequality within the context of equivariant cobordisms. Furthermore, we explore diverse applications of these $d$-invariants, including concordance invariants for knots derived from branched covers, obstructions to extending group actions to bounding $4$-manifolds, solutions to Nielsen realization problems for $4$-manifolds with boundary, and barriers to equivariant embeddings of $3$-manifolds into $4$-manifolds.

The rotational states of dwarf planet-satellite systems in the transneptunian region are governed by their formation history and tidal interactions, serving as key indicators of their evolutionary paths. Earlier studies reported conflicting rotation periods for the dwarf planet Eris, ranging from hours to a period nearly synchronous with its satellite, Dysnomia's 15.8-day orbit. This letter introduces new light curve observations of Eris collected using ~1-2m ground-based telescopes, as well as data from the TESS and Gaia space missions. While TESS data failed to define a precise period, they limited light curve variations to a maximum amplitude of $\Delta m \leq 0.03$ mag for periods $P \leq 24$ h. In contrast, both the combined ground-based dataset and Gaia measurements clearly indicate a light curve period matching Dysnomia's orbital period of 15.8 days, with an amplitude of $\Delta m \approx 0.03$ mag, confirming that Eris is tidally locked. Under the assumption of a collisional origin for Dysnomia, simple tidal evolution models suggest that Dysnomia must be relatively massive (mass ratio $q = 0.01$--$0.03$) and large (radius $R_s \geq 300$ km) to have slowed Eris into synchronization. Furthermore, these simulations imply that, given typical tidal parameters for transneptunian objects, Dysnomia's density should be 1.8--2.4 $g cm^{-3}$. This exceptionally high density for an object of its size places significant constraints on the conditions of its formation.

If dark matter possesses a finite size, dark matter self-scattering inevitably generates the interaction responsible for structure formation. To model how a binding force creates dark protons with finite dimensions, we initially apply the Eikonal approximation to simplify the complex scattering between these particles to the $t=0$ limit. Subsequently, the Chou-Yang model is employed to minimize input parameters to a single value, adhering to principles of simplicity and analyticity. We clearly present a novel definition of velocity dependence and its implications for small cosmological structures within the framework of Chou-Yang dark protons. Although the parameter space remains partially uncovered, numerical results indicate that the amplitude coefficient modifies the self-scattering cross-section, enabling the recovery of previously excluded regions without invoking a binding force. Finally, we demonstrate that achieving the correct relic density via thermal freeze-out production favors super heavy dark protons.

Consistent hashing serves as a foundational mechanism for data routing and load balancing across distributed databases, cloud infrastructure, and peer-to-peer networks. However, current schemes fail to simultaneously satisfy all critical requirements: full consistency, scalability, minimal memory usage, rapid updates, and low query complexity. To address this, we introduce DxHash, a scalable consistent hashing algorithm utilizing pseudo-random sequences. For distributed storage scenarios, we propose two specific optimizations: first, Weighted DxHash enables workload adjustment across arbitrary nodes; second, the Asymmetric Replica Strategy (ARS) integrates replica management with scale-up processes to enhance system availability and lower remapping rates. Evaluation results demonstrate that DxHash outperforms state-of-the-art solutions across all five requirements. Notably, even under a 50% failure ratio, DxHash sustains a query throughput of 16.5 million per second. Furthermore, both proposed optimizations successfully deliver their intended improvements.

This study examines three key characteristics of the early evolutionary stages of low-mass stars under Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld (EiBI) gravity, a credible extension of General Relativity. The investigation focuses on the Hayashi tracks (the effective temperature-luminosity relationship), the minimum mass needed to enter the main sequence, and the maximum mass permitted for a fully convective main-sequence star. Our findings reveal that these properties depend not only on the theory's parameter but also on the star's central density, a characteristic previously observed in Palatini $f(R)$ gravity. Leveraging this insight, we analyze how these quantities evolve with the sign of the EiBI parameter, observing a divergence in the Hayashi tracks for positive versus negative branches, alongside an increase (or decrease) in the aforementioned masses for positive (or negative) parameters. Finally, we apply these results to assess the potential for detecting signatures of new physics in low-mass stars within this theoretical framework.

In recent years, Electric Vehicle (EV) adoption has surged, largely propelled by the growing flexibility and accessibility of charging infrastructure.
