The prior best-known hitting set size was $d^{O(\log w)}(nw)^{O(\log \log w)}$, with $d$ representing the individual degree. We achieve an improved hitting set size of $(ndw)^{O(\log \log w)}$.

This study focuses on model-order reduction for parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs). Specifically, we address the challenge of identifying an effective approximation subspace within the solution manifold of a PPDE when only incomplete data is accessible. Our approach relies on two information sources: first, a "rough" prior knowledge represented as a manifold that encompasses the target solution manifold; and second, partial linear measurements of the PPDE solutions, where "partial" indicates that the observation operator is non-invertible. We present and examine various tools to generate high-quality approximation subspaces by leveraging these two data sources. Initially, we determine the optimal worst-case performance attainable in this framework and suggest straightforward methods to approximate the corresponding optimal subspace. Subsequently, within a simplified context, we offer a theoretical analysis linking the achievable reduction performance to the selection of the observation operator and the extent of prior knowledge regarding the solution manifold.

We derive precise analytic formulas for the real eigenvalue and eigenvector distributions of real symmetric third-order tensors following a Gaussian distribution, specifically for $N \leq 8$. This is accomplished by explicitly calculating the partition function of a zero-dimensional boson-fermion system featuring four-interactions. These distributions are formulated using combinations of polynomial, exponential, and error functions, resulting from feasible yet complex bosonic integrals that emerge after performing fermionic integrations. By extrapolating these expressions alongside a prior result, we propose an approximate formula for the large-$N$ limit. When compared with Monte Carlo simulations, the exact expressions align precisely, while the large-$N$ approximation demonstrates strong agreement. Investigating the feasibility of the integration methods remains a subject for future research, aiming to establish a general analytic formula applicable to arbitrary $N$.

We present AutoRF, a novel framework for learning neural 3D object representations under the constraint that each training object is visible from only a single viewpoint. This stands in sharp contrast to most existing methods, which typically rely on multiple views of the same object, incorporate explicit priors during training, or demand pixel-perfect annotations. To tackle this difficult scenario, we develop a normalized, object-centric representation where the embedding disentangles shape, appearance, and pose. Each encoding offers compact, highly generalizable information about the target object, which is then decoded in a single step to synthesize a new target view. Furthermore, we enhance reconstruction quality by optimizing the shape and appearance codes at test time to fit the representation tightly to the input image. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach generalizes effectively to unseen objects, even across diverse and challenging real-world street scene datasets such as nuScenes, KITTI, and Mapillary Metropolis.

The Maxwell radiation field constitutes a fundamental physical property of galaxies. This study constructs an analytical model to simulate this field within an axisymmetric galaxy, relying on an explicit representation for source-free, axisymmetric Maxwell fields whose general applicability was previously demonstrated. The model is calibrated by fitting the aggregate spherical radiation emitted by constituent "stars." Due to the vast ratio of distance to wavelength, the implementation requires numerical precision exceeding quadruple precision. Validation is achieved through a test utilizing a spherically symmetric solution. Results for a set of "stars" representative of a disk galaxy show that the field reaches its maximum intensity near the disk axis, where the axial component of the electric field ${\bf E}$ dominates the radial component. This model will facilitate future investigations into whether interaction energy predicted by alternative gravitational theories could contribute to dark matter.

**Keywords:** Disk galaxy; Maxwell equations; axial symmetry; exact solutions; numerical model; dark matter.

This study examines Bertrand's probabilistic paradox using discrete geometry and traditional discrete probability methods. We model the unit circle in the plane by approximating it with a grid of $1/n \times 1/n$ squares and tallying the pairs of squares separated by a distance exceeding $\sqrt{3}$. As $n$ approaches infinity, the fraction of such pairs converges to $$ \frac{1+\sqrt{3}}{8}-\frac{\pi(2-\sqrt{3})}{96}=0.33273\dots\;. $$

This study applies average Hamiltonian theory to investigate selective excitation in spin-1/2 systems subjected to a train of small flip-angle $\theta$-pulses ($\theta\ll 1$) applied either periodically, corresponding to the DANTE sequence, or aperiodically. First, an average Hamiltonian framework for the DANTE sequence is constructed, proving its validity both at and far from the DANTE resonance frequencies, which occur at integer multiples of the inverse interpulse delay. In aperiodic schemes featuring pseudorandom interpulse delays, selective excitation of a single resonance is achievable by modulating the phases of the $\theta$-pulses in coordination with the time delays. This approach defines the pseudorandom-DANTE (p-DANTE) sequence, and the study identifies conditions under which its average Hamiltonian description parallels that of the standard DANTE sequence. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that averaging across multiple p-DANTE sequences targeting the same resonance suppresses excitations at off-resonance frequencies, thereby enhancing the effective selectivity of p-DANTE. The paper concludes with experimental realizations of p-DANTE sequences and a comparison of these results with theoretical predictions.

Following the emergence of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19), the majority of affected individuals have presented with high fever, dry cough, and sore throat, progressing to severe pneumonia. Consequently, analyzing lung imaging has become a critical tool for the early diagnosis of the disease. While real-time reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR) remains the gold standard for detecting the virus, this study emphasizes an automated method for diagnosing and prognosing COVID-19 using non-contrast chest computed tomography (CT) scans to facilitate timely patient triage. The prognostic component involves quantifying and assessing disease severity to assist hospitals in managing vital resources, including medical personnel, ventilators, and intensive care unit (ICU) capacity. This approach leverages deep learning to automatically calculate disease severity by measuring the area of multiple rounded ground-glass opacities (GGO) and consolidations located in the lung periphery (CP), aggregating these metrics into a severity score. This score can be correlated with prescribed medications during triage to evaluate treatment efficacy. The proposed method demonstrates promising outcomes, with the classification model achieving 93% accuracy on hold-out data.

Weather data collection relies on weather stations, which are globally distributed networks deployed by various organizations to gather information on atmospheric phenomena. These instruments transmit collected data to central processing points; however, current transmission methodologies rely on protocols ill-suited for this specific application. Consequently, existing stations are constrained by their data formats and protocols, failing to leverage available real-time data. This study investigates the technology and network capabilities of weather instruments to address these limitations. We propose OpenWeather, a protocol designed to enable more efficient and reliable data transmission. By evaluating environmental factors such as location and bandwidth availability, we developed a protocol tailored to the requirements of automatic weather stations. Furthermore, a peer-to-peer architecture is presented with a functional implementation of the OpenWeather protocol. Finally, the protocol was tested in a real-world scenario, yielding insights necessary for adapting it to common automatic weather stations.

This note demonstrates that the common assertion regarding Benford's Law—that the range of every Benford distribution covers at least several orders of magnitude—is incorrect. The proof provided is constructive, accompanied by specific examples.

This paper introduces a systematic methodology for analyzing Dirac operators $A_{\eta, \tau, \lambda}$ subjected to singular electrostatic, Lorentz scalar, and anomalous magnetic interactions with strengths $\eta, \tau, \lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, localized at points in $\mathbb{R}$, curves in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The framework relies on boundary triples and their corresponding Weyl functions. We begin with the one-dimensional case to motivate the multidimensional extension. Subsequently, for two and three dimensions, we establish quasi, generalized, and ordinary boundary triples along with their Weyl functions, offering a comprehensive characterization of the associated Sobolev spaces, trace theorems, and the mapping properties of integral operators crucial for the analysis of $A_{\eta, \tau, \lambda}$. We advance the study toward rougher interaction supports $\Sigma$, specifically general compact Lipschitz hypersurfaces. We derive conditions on the interaction strengths ensuring the self-adjointness of $A_{\eta, \tau, \lambda}$, obtain a Krein-type resolvent formula, and characterize both the essential and discrete spectra. These conditions cover purely Lorentz scalar interactions, non-critical anomalous magnetic interactions, and the confinement case, the latter being significant for mathematically describing graphene. Furthermore, utilizing a specific ordinary boundary triple, we demonstrate that $A_{\eta, \tau, \lambda}$ remains self-adjoint for arbitrary combinations of interaction strengths (including critical ones) provided $\Sigma$ is $C^{\infty}$-smooth, and we determine its spectral properties. Notably, in the critical case, we observe a loss of Sobolev regularity within the operator domain and a potential additional point in the essential spectrum.

This paper refines the triangle inequality for complex numbers by applying the Hermite-Hadamard inequality for convex functions. It subsequently presents applications of this refined result, specifically deriving operator inequalities, including those concerning the numerical radius and operator means.

Global models are optimized for maximum generalizability, making user invariance a priority as these models serve vast numbers of users; consequently, they often fail to generate personalized outputs tailored to individual data. In contrast to prevalent personalization methods relying on few-shot learning, we introduce UserIdentifier, a new framework for training a single shared model applicable to all users. This approach achieves personalization by appending fixed, non-trainable user identifiers to the input data. Empirical results on various sentiment analysis datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses the state-of-the-art prefix-tuning approach by up to 13%. Furthermore, unlike previous efforts, our technique requires no additional model parameters and eliminates the need for extra rounds of few-shot fine-tuning.

This paper introduces a thermodynamically consistent model for mass transfer across permeable moving interfaces, developed via the energy variation method. The study addresses a restricted diffusion scenario where interfacial flux is determined by conductance and the concentration gradient across the boundary. The proposed diffusive interface phase-field framework offers distinct benefits compared to sharp interface methods: it eliminates the need for explicit interface tracking and allows for the integration of interfacial conditions with variable diffusion coefficients. Rigorous asymptotic analysis demonstrates that the diffusive model converges to the established sharp interface model as interface thickness vanishes. To solve the system efficiently, a decoupled, energy-stable numerical scheme is formulated. Numerical simulations initially validate the theoretical consistency regarding the sharp interface limit, followed by convergence and energy decay tests to verify the scheme's stability and efficiency. Finally, several examples showcase the efficacy of the phase-field approach, including an investigation of two-phase mass transfer involving deformable drops suspended in a moving fluid.

This paper investigates linear-quadratic control issues concerning stochastic Volterra integral equations featuring singular and non-convolution-type coefficients. Unlike traditional approaches, the weighting matrices within the cost functional are not required to be non-negative definite. By adopting a novel perspective, we establish a framework for causal feedback strategies, where the existence and uniqueness of an optimal causal feedback strategy are determined through the associated Riccati–Volterra equation.

This paper generalizes the classical Weyl's lemma to $RCD(K,N)$ metric measure spaces. As applications, we establish the local regularity of solutions to Poisson equations and derive a Liouville-type theorem for $L^1$ very weak harmonic functions on these spaces. Additionally, we obtain a gradient estimate for solutions to a class of elliptic equations featuring discontinuous coefficients as a secondary result.

We demonstrate that the arc graph of $S_g^1$ is a coarse Lipschitz retract of the free splitting complex of $F_{2g}$. Furthermore, we establish that both the arc and curve graphs of $S_g^1$ are coarse Lipschitz retracts of the cyclic splitting graph of $F_{2g}$ as well as the maximally cyclic splitting graph of $F_{2g}$.

Although significant advances have been made in generating images from semantic labelmaps, existing approaches depend on fully annotated inputs with clear instance boundaries and pixel-level class labels. This requirement for extensive annotation limits their practical use in real-world scenarios, particularly when faced with uncertainties caused by weather, occlusion, or noise. Conversely, there is a strong need for algorithms capable of synthesizing images from sparse labelmaps or sketches, enabling content creators and artists to rapidly construct scenes by defining only a few object locations. This paper tackles the challenge of completing complex scenes from sparse labelmaps, where input details cover only about 30% of object instances. We introduce `Halluci-Net`, a two-stage deep learning framework that learns object co-occurrence relationships within scenes and leverages them to generate dense, complete labelmaps. These enhanced labelmaps serve as inputs for advanced image synthesis models such as pix2pixHD to produce the final images. Evaluated on the Cityscapes dataset, our method surpasses two baseline approaches in terms of Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), semantic segmentation accuracy, and object co-occurrence similarity. Additionally, we present qualitative results on a subset of the ADE20K dataset featuring bedroom imagery.

This study examines kinematic dynamos in incompressible, isotropic turbulent flows characterized by a high magnetic Prandtl number. We introduce a methodology that treats any magnetic field configuration as a superposition of localized perturbations, referred to as "blobs." A relationship is established between the stochastic characteristics of an individual blob and a stochastically homogeneous magnetic field distribution advected by the identical stochastic flow. This connection enables the analysis of blob evolution during late stages, specifically when the blob's size surpasses the viscous scale. Results demonstrate that in three-dimensional flows, the average magnetic field within a blob grows exponentially within the turbulence's inertial range, contrasting with the late-Batchelor stage where it declines. Our approach elucidates the dynamo generation mechanism in the inertial range for both localized blobs and homogeneous contributions, clarifying why dynamos fail in two-dimensional scenarios but thrive in three dimensions. Finally, we outline a strategy for observing this mechanism through numerical simulations.

Humans are capable of executing novel tasks by retrieving prior skills and adapting them to new contexts without any supervision. This paper seeks to enhance the cross-task generalization capabilities of large-scale multi-task language models, such as T0 and FLAN, within an unsupervised framework. We introduce ReCross, a retrieval-augmentation approach that utilizes a few unlabeled examples as queries to fetch a targeted subset of upstream data, thereby updating the model to improve its generalization performance. ReCross represents a simple yet potent retrieval strategy that integrates efficient dense retrieval with effective pairwise reranking. Empirical results and analysis demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses both non-retrieval approaches and other baseline techniques.

This research focuses on investigating, characterizing, and applying the recently introduced concept of variational convexity, alongside its strong variant, as defined by Rockafellar. Initially, we demonstrate that the variational properties of an extended-real-valued function correspond equivalently to the standard (local) convexity and strong convexity of its Moreau envelope. Subsequently, we establish new characterizations for both variational convexity and variational strong convexity of general functions by utilizing their second-order subdifferentials (generalized Hessians), which serve as coderivatives of subgradient mappings. Furthermore, we examine the connections between these concepts and local minimizers as well as tilt-stable local minimizers. Finally, these findings are employed to characterize related notions of variational and strong variational sufficiency within composite optimization, with specific applications to nonlinear programming.

We identify relationships among various characteristics of topological dynamical systems, including: every point serves as a generic point for an ergodic measure; the mapping that assigns points to the measures they generate is continuous; the system decomposes into uniquely (or strictly) ergodic subsystems; the mapping that assigns ergodic measures to their topological supports is continuous; and the Cesaro means of every continuous function converge uniformly.

We report simultaneous observations of J=1-0 emission from CO, 13CO, and C18O in 11 nearby (cz < 1000 km/s) luminous infrared galaxies. 12CO and 13CO were detected in the centers of all targets except for 13CO in NGC 3031. Additionally, C18O, CS J=2-1, and HCO+ J=1-0 emissions were observed in the nuclear regions of M82 and M51. These represent the first systematic extragalactic detections of 12CO and its isotopes utilizing the PMO 14m telescope. Mapping was performed on M82 using half-beam spacing over a 4' x 2.5' area, and major axis mapping was conducted for NGC 3627, NGC 3628, NGC 4631, and M51. The radial distributions of 12CO and 13CO in NGC 3627, NGC 3628, and M51 are well described by exponential profiles. In all mapped sources, the 12CO/13CO intensity ratio (R) decreases monotonically with galactocentric radius. Average R values are 9.9 +/- 3.0 in the centers and 5.6 +/- 1.9 in the disks, significantly lower than the anomalous R (~24) observed in M82's center. Ratios of 13CO/C18O, 13CO/HCO+, and 13CO/CS (from this study or literature) exhibit minimal variation with radius, contrasting sharply with the significant changes in R. This supports the idea that the observed gradient in R results from variations in physical conditions across the disks. Molecular hydrogen column densities derived from C18O indicate that the Galactic standard X-factor overestimates molecular gas mass in M82 by a factor of approximately 2.5. These findings suggest that the X-factor in active star-forming regions (nuclear areas) is lower than in normal star-forming disks, and the gradient in R can serve as a tracer for X-factor variations.

This study investigates how diffuse stellar light and globular clusters (GCs) can map the matter distribution within their host halos through an observational approach. Utilizing 117 simulated dark matter (DM) haloes from the $(34.4~\rm cMpc)^3$ periodic volume of the E-MOSAICS project, we compare stellar surface brightness and GC projected number density maps against the surface densities of total mass and DM. Our findings indicate that the primary structures detected in stellar light and GCs align closely with those of the DM and total mass. The proposed method remains robust against satellite presence, and its precision increases with fainter GC samples. We establish tight correlations between the profiles of stellar surface brightness and GC number density and those of the DM, suggesting that DM profiles can be accurately reconstructed from stars and GCs with a precision of $\sigma\leq0.5~$dex. Furthermore, we quantify the projected morphology of DM, stars, and GCs, revealing that stars and GCs exhibit greater flattening than DM. Additionally, the semi-major axes of the star and GC distributions are typically misaligned by approximately $10~$degrees relative to the DM. We demonstrate that deep imaging of diffuse stellar light and GCs can constrain the shape, profile, and orientation of host halos. These results are applicable to haloes with central galaxies having $M_{\star}\geq10^{10}~M_{\odot}$, and the methodology will be suitable for future data from the Euclid, Roman, and Rubin observatories.

We examine the distribution of rest-frame U-V and V-J colors for star-forming galaxies within the redshift range of 0.5 < z < 2.5. By employing stellar population synthesis, stochastic star formation histories, and a straightforward dust attenuation model that incorporates galaxy shape and inclination, we develop a theoretical framework for galaxy color distributions. Remarkably, this model, which relies on just two free parameters, successfully replicates observed galaxy colors across varying redshifts and stellar masses. Our findings indicate that the broad variation in dust attenuation values seen in star-forming galaxies at specific redshifts and masses is almost exclusively driven by inclination effects; were all galaxies viewed edge-on, their dust attenuation levels would be nearly identical. These conclusions hold significant implications for interpreting dust attenuation data, handling UV and IR luminosities, and aligning numerical simulations with observational results.

This study examines the properties of the cumulative residual entropy generating function and subsequently introduces the dynamic cumulative residual entropy generating function (DCREGF). It is demonstrated that the DCREGF uniquely determines a distribution. We explore various characterization results by analyzing the relationship between the DCREGF, the hazard rate, and the mean residual life function. Furthermore, a new class of life distributions based on a decreasing DCREGF is proposed, and a statistical test for this property is developed with an evaluation of its performance.

Superfluidity (or superconductivity) enables the transport of mass (or charge) over macroscopic distances with negligible dissipation. In magnetically ordered media characterized by an easy-plane topology of the order parameter space, spin superfluidity can occur even without a strict conservation law for spin. This article examines three fundamental aspects of spin superfluidity theory: the topology of the order parameter space, the Landau criterion for superfluidity, and the decay of superfluid currents through phase slip events where magnetic vortices intersect current streamlines. Additionally, the paper reviews experimental efforts aimed at detecting spin superfluidity.

The proposed DUNE experiment offers exceptional sensitivity to the electron's vector and axial couplings to the $Z$-boson through precise measurements of neutrino–electron scattering. We examine DUNE-PRISM, a movable near detector positioned perpendicular to the beam line, and determine that it will significantly enhance our capacity to constrain the electron's weak couplings. By converting these scattering measurements into a determination of the weak mixing angle at low energy scales, we estimate that seven years of data collection would allow the DUNE near detector to measure $\sin^2\theta_W$ with approximately 2% precision. Additionally, we explore the benefits of integrating neutrino–electron scattering data with neutrino trident production observations at DUNE-PRISM.

A subset $A$ of a semigroup $S$ is defined as a $chain$ ($antichain$) if for any distinct elements $x, y \in S$, the product $xy$ lies in the set $\{x, y\}$ (respectively, does not lie in $\{x, y\}$). A semigroup $S$ is termed ($anti$)$chain$-$finite$ when it contains no infinite (anti)chains. We demonstrate that every antichain-finite semigroup $S$ is periodic, and for any idempotent $e$ in $S$, the set $\sqrt[\infty]{e}=\{x\in S:\exists n\in\mathbb N\;\;(x^n=e)\}$ is finite. This characteristic of antichain-finite semigroups allows us to establish that a semigroup is finite if and only if it is both chain-finite and antichain-finite. Furthermore, we provide an example of an antichain-finite semilattice that cannot be expressed as a union of finitely many chains.

This study examines a non-linear system representing the dynamics of a linearly elastic body submerged in an incompressible viscous fluid. We establish the local existence of strong solutions and demonstrate global existence and uniqueness for small initial data. The primary contribution is characterizing the long-term behavior of the elastic displacement. Our findings indicate convergence to either a rest state or a rigid motion, or to a time-periodic pressure wave, the latter of which can only arise under specific geometric conditions.

Federated learning (FL) has gained significant attention for facilitating privacy-preserving machine learning on distributed user data without transferring it off-device. However, despite data remaining local, privacy remains compromised because the substantial computational processing of user training data is exposed via shared local models, which are vulnerable to attacks like model inversion. To address this, Secure Aggregation (SA) was introduced to ensure the server learns only the global aggregated model update, obscuring individual updates. Although SA prevents the direct leakage of individual model updates beyond the aggregate, it lacks formal guarantees regarding the privacy protection offered, as dataset information may still infer through the computed aggregated model. This work presents the first formal analysis of privacy guarantees in FL with SA, utilizing Mutual Information (MI) as a metric to derive upper bounds on potential information leakage about each user's dataset via the aggregated update. Our theoretical findings indicate that under the FedSGD aggregation algorithm, privacy leakage decreases linearly as the number of participating users increases. To validate these bounds, we employed an MI Neural Estimator to empirically assess privacy leakage across various FL configurations on MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets. Experimental results confirm our theoretical predictions for FedSGD, demonstrating that privacy leakage diminishes with larger user counts and local batch sizes, while increasing with the number of training rounds.

Zhao and a co-author (2013) developed a functor mapping o(k)-Mod to o(k+2)-Mod. This study applies that functor sequentially to derive a universal first-order differential operator realization for any highest-weight representation of o(2n+3) across (n+1)² variables and for o(2n+2) across n(n+1) variables. For dominant integral highest weights, we explicitly identify the associated finite-dimensional irreducible modules. These findings facilitate the analysis of tensor decompositions for such modules by resolving specific first-order linear partial differential equations, yielding physically relevant Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and exact solutions to the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation within the conformal field theory WZW model. Additionally, we establish a formula for counting the dimension of an irreducible o(k+2)-module as an alternating sum of dimensions of irreducible o(k)-modules. Specifically for Steinberg modules, this approach generates novel combinatorial identities of classical nature.

Reservoir computing represents a neuromorphic architecture promising viable solutions to the escalating energy demands of machine learning. Currently, most neuromorphic computing relies on software, allowing neural network characteristics and performance to be reconfigured for various computational tasks. This adaptability is absent in "physical" reservoir computing schemes, which utilize the nonlinear and history-dependent memory responses of physical systems for data processing. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate a "task-adaptive" method for physical reservoir computing capable of reconfiguring essential reservoir properties—such as nonlinearity, memory capacity, and complexity—to optimize performance across diverse tasks. As a proof of concept, we utilize the temperature- and magnetic-field-controlled spin-wave response of Cu$_2$OSeO$_3$, a material hosting skyrmion, conical, and helical magnetic phases, thereby enabling on-demand access to varied physical reservoir responses. We quantify the performance of these phase-tunable reservoirs, characterize their properties, and analyze the correlations between them. This task-adaptive strategy addresses significant previous limitations in physical reservoirs, creating new opportunities to leverage thermodynamically stable and metastable phase control across a wide spectrum of physical reservoir systems.

Neural networks, capable of identifying intricate patterns, have the potential to revolutionize materials science data analysis. This paper presents ARISE, a Bayesian deep learning approach for identifying crystal structures. ARISE represents a significant advancement by demonstrating robustness against structural noise and the ability to classify over 100 crystal structures, a capacity that is scalable. Despite being trained exclusively on ideal structures, ARISE accurately characterizes heavily perturbed single- and polycrystalline systems derived from both synthetic and experimental sources. The probabilistic framework of the Bayesian deep learning model facilitates principled uncertainty estimates, which correlate with the crystalline order of metallic nanoparticles observed in electron tomography. Furthermore, applying unsupervised learning to the model's internal representations uncovers grain boundaries and previously hidden structural regions with easily interpretable geometric properties. This work overcomes previous limitations in analyzing noisy atomic structural data from both computational and experimental contexts.

This research introduces the 'm-ar-K-FastICA' method, which combines the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') with Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') for feature extraction. While the kernel trick allows dimensionality reduction techniques to model greater non-linearity, there remains a scarcity of reproducible, open-source kernels, particularly for reliably projecting features from entropic data. By integrating the freely available, Python-compatible m-ar-K function with scikit-learn and FastICA, this approach achieves more robust feature extraction in highly random datasets, minimizing the necessity for pre-whitening. The method was evaluated across five open-access datasets with varying information entropy levels, sourced from scikit-learn and the UCI Machine Learning repository. Experimental outcomes indicate that the proposed feature extraction enhances classification performance. Furthermore, when compared against the 'FastICA' gold standard, the novel m-ar-K-FastICA approach demonstrates superior reliability and computational efficiency, regardless of the data's inherent uncertainty.

We address multiple puzzles concerning the electromagnetic response of 3+1 dimensional topological superconductors. Specifically, through analytical derivation, we demonstrate that an interface between a topological and a normal superconductor does not display a quantum Hall effect provided time-reversal symmetry remains intact. This contrasts with the analogous interface between a topological insulator and a normal insulator. The distinction lies in the fact that, for topological insulators, the electromagnetic vector potential couples to a vector current within a theory featuring a Dirac mass, whereas in superconductors, a pair of Weyl fermions are gapped via Majorana masses, causing the electromagnetic vector potential to couple instead to their axial currents.

This work reports a $^{125}$Te nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) investigation of Cu$_3$TeO$_6$, a three-dimensional spin web lattice known for hosting topological magnons. The temperature-dependent $^{125}$Te NMR spectra and Knight shift $\mathcal{K}$ exhibit a significant change at $T_\text{S}\sim 40$ K, which is notably below the N\'eel ordering temperature of $T_\text{N}\sim 61$ K; this indicates a first-order structural phase transition occurring within the magnetically ordered state. Most strikingly, the temperature evolution of the spin-lattice relaxation rate $T_1^{-1}$ reveals spin-gap-like magnetic excitations that emerge sharply at $T^*\sim 75$ K, well above $T_\text{N}$. This spin-gap behavior can be attributed to weakly dispersive optical magnon branches associated with high-energy spin excitations, which arise from the unique corner-sharing Cu hexagon spin-1/2 network characterized by a low coordination number.

We present an approximation algorithm for Quantum Max-Cut that rounds an SDP relaxation into an entangled quantum state, using the SDP to determine the parameters of a variational quantum circuit. This entangled state is modeled as a product state acted upon by the quantum circuit. The method achieves an approximation ratio of 0.582 on triangle-free graphs, surpassing the previous best results of 0.531 and 0.533 by Anshu, Gosset, Morenz, and Parekh, and Thompson, respectively. Furthermore, we examine the EPR Hamiltonian, positing it as a natural intermediate problem that isolates essential quantum features of local Hamiltonian problems. For the EPR Hamiltonian, we provide an approximation algorithm with a ratio of $1 / \sqrt{2}$ applicable to all graphs.

We investigate the collective dynamics of swarmalators, entities that combine synchronization and swarming, restricted to motion along a one-dimensional ring. Although this simplified framework captures fundamental aspects of movement in two or three dimensions, its primary advantage lies in its solvability, allowing for the exact determination of most collective states and their bifurcations. Furthermore, the model accurately reflects the behavior of real-world swarmalators that inhabit quasi-1D rings, such as border-tactic sperm and vinegar eels.

The paper introduces methods for constructing novel, broad language families composed exclusively of semilinear languages and for proving that specific families contain only such languages. It is demonstrated that for any semilinear full trio L, the minimal full AFL encompassing L and closed under intersection with languages from NCM (non-deterministic finite automata with reversal-bounded counters) is itself semilinear. Should these closure properties be effective, this result immediately ensures the decidability of membership, emptiness, and infiniteness for these generalized families. Utilizing these broader techniques, the authors define new grammar systems that extend established families of semilinear full trios, thereby guaranteeing that these extensions describe solely semilinear languages and inheriting positive decidability properties. Additionally, several characterizations of these newly defined families are provided.

This paper investigates the dynamics of both charged and uncharged test particles around a rotating black hole with nonlinear charge. Depending on the specific value of the nonlinear parameter, the spacetime asymptotics may resemble de Sitter or anti-de Sitter geometries, resulting in the possibility of one, two, or three horizons, with the additional horizon in the de Sitter scenario being cosmological. The study analyzes angular and radial motions, contrasting them with the linear electromagnetic counterpart, the Kerr-Newman black hole. Significant differences emerge: the nonlinear electromagnetic (NLE) field intensifies equatorial asymmetry and prevents charged particles from reaching one of the poles. Furthermore, a second circular orbit forms near the external horizon, and the NLE field increases curvature, thereby generating bounded orbits that lie closer to the horizon compared to the Kerr-Newman case.

The emergence of network science has recently enabled novel quantitative methods within literary analysis. This study applies these techniques to the Kyiv bylyny cycle, a collection of East Slavic epic tales rooted in modern Ukraine. By juxtaposing these narratives with other significant European epics, we uncover both unique and universal characteristics of the social networks embedded within the bylyny. Our analysis examines community structures and ranks the prominence of key characters. This methodological approach not only strengthens existing hypotheses found in humanities literature—such as those concerning Prince Volodymyr's role—but also facilitates the generation of new ones. We demonstrate that the Kyiv bylina cycle aligns closely with narrative networks from other nations, particularly heroic traditions. Beyond offering fresh narratological perspectives, we anticipate that this research will assist future scholars and the general public in better understanding Ukraine's epic heritage and recognizing its heroes.

Dynamical scaling represents an asymptotic characteristic common to the dynamics of first-order phase transitions in physical systems and is closely linked to self-similarity. Leveraging the integral representation for the marginal probabilities of a fractional non-homogeneous Poisson process, as proposed by Leonenko et al. (2017) and extending the standard fractional Poisson process, we establish dynamical scaling under relatively mild conditions. This finding also encompasses the specific instance of the standard fractional Poisson process.

To establish a sustainable human presence on the Moon by the late 2020s, humans and robots must work together, including scenarios where a human remotely controls an autonomous rover that has suffered an instrument failure. To assist operators in troubleshooting, we propose a virtual reality digital twin situated in a simulated environment. In this setup, the operator can interact with a virtual replica of the rover and robotic arm using identical controls and kinematic models. The system supports both egocentric views (first-person perspective via stereoscopic passthrough) and exocentric views (third-person perspective, allowing the operator to virtually walk around the rover and environment as if physically present). Additionally, we outline metrics for assessing the fidelity between our digital and physical robots, present an experimental concept grounded in real mission scenarios, and discuss future work comparing this platform to conventional troubleshooting approaches.

This paper investigates cybersecurity defense by integrating a new cyber security simulator with causal decision-making models grounded in optimization. We focus specifically on dynamic causal Bayesian optimization (DCBO), proposing its application as a "blue" agent that utilizes a simulated network view and a causal model of "red" agent propagation to execute optimal interventions on host nodes. The goal is to minimize the costs associated with intrusions. By presenting a comprehensive cyber-simulation system that generates observational data for DCBO, we provide numerical results that establish a foundation for future research in this domain.

Computing-in-memory (CiM) technology has emerged as a promising solution for achieving high energy efficiency in deep neural network (DNN) computations. However, many emerging devices face uncertainty challenges, causing discrepancies between the intended weight values and the data actually stored. This mismatch results in a decline in accuracy when trained models are deployed on real hardware. In this study, we provide a comprehensive analysis of how such uncertainty-induced variations affect DNN models. To mitigate the impact of device uncertainties, we introduce UAE, an uncertainty-aware Neural Architecture Search framework designed to identify DNN models that maintain both accuracy and robustness against these uncertainties.

We address large-scale mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) using distributed asynchronous saddle point computation, a method driven by the ability of MILPs to model multi-agent autonomy challenges such as task allocation and collision-avoidant trajectory planning in multi-robot systems. Our approach relaxes the MILP into a nonlinear program approximation, where precision improves as the ratio of agents to coupled constraints grows. We then construct an equivalent Lagrangian saddle point problem and apply regularization in both primal and dual spaces to yield a regularized Lagrangian that is strongly-convex and strongly-concave. A parallelized algorithm is subsequently developed to compute the saddle points of this regularized function by partitioning the problem into blocks comprising scalar or sub-vector components of the primal and dual variables. This algorithm is demonstrated to handle asynchrony in both computations and communications regarding these variables. We provide theoretical suboptimality bounds and convergence rates for reaching a saddle point, noting that the bound accounts for regularization error and the gap between the relaxed form and the original MILP. Simulation results validate these theoretical findings, confirming that the combined effects of relaxation and regularization have only a minimal impact on solution quality.

In particle technology, adhesive powders are known to exhibit diverse bulk behaviors stemming from unique particle interactions. This study employs Discrete Element simulations to examine how contact cohesion influences the steady state of dense powders within a slowly sheared split-bottom Couette cell, which generates a stable shear band. The magnitude of cohesive forces is measured using the {\em granular Bond number} ($Bo$), defined as the ratio of the maximum attractive force to the average force resulting from external compression. Our results indicate that shear banding remains largely unaffected by cohesion when $Bo < 1$; however, for $Bo \ge 1$, cohesive forces become significant, causing both the width and central position of the band to expand as $Bo$ exceeds 1. Within the shear band, the mean normal contact force remains independent of cohesion, relying solely on confining stress. Conversely, analyzing the eigen-directions of the local strain rate tensor reveals a dependence on cohesion. Forces along compressive and tensile directions are symmetric around the mean force (being larger and smaller, respectively), whereas the force along the third, neutral direction tracks the mean force. This anisotropy in the force network, along with heterogeneity across all directions (compressive, tensile, and neutral), intensifies as cohesion increases.

Medical centers are increasingly utilizing deep learning (DL) models to assist radiologists in diagnosing lung conditions via chest X-rays, typically by training these models on extensive datasets of publicly labeled images. However, the generalizability of these pre-trained models in clinical environments is often limited due to distributional discrepancies between public and private radiographic data. In chest imaging, this heterogeneity stems from variations in X-ray equipment and configurations. Within the machine learning field, this issue caused by diverse data generation sources is termed "domain shift," representing a mode shift in the generative model. This study presents a method for detecting and mitigating domain shift to address this challenge. Experimental findings demonstrate the proposed approach's efficacy in deploying pre-trained DL models for abnormality detection in chest radiographs within a clinical setting.

Let $Q$ be a bounded operator on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. A pair of bounded operators $(T_1, T_2)$ on $\mathcal{H}$ is defined as $Q$-commuting if it satisfies at least one of the conditions: $T_1T_2=QT_2T_1$, $T_1T_2=T_2QT_1$, or $T_1T_2=T_2T_1Q$. We provide an explicit construction of isometric dilations for pairs of $Q$-commuting contractions when $Q$ is unitary, thereby extending Ando's [2] isometric dilation result for commuting pairs of contractions. Specifically, when $Q=qI_{\mathcal{H}}$ with $q$ being a complex number of modulus $1$, this yields an explicit construction of isometric dilations for pairs of $q$-commuting contractions, a well-established class. While an extended definition of $q$-commutativity exists for general operator tuples, isometric dilation is not generally guaranteed for $n$-tuples of $q$-commuting contractions where $n \geq 3$. By generalizing the class of commuting contractions studied by Brehmer [8], we identify a specific class of $n$-tuples of $q$-commuting contractions and derive explicit isometric dilations for them.

A concise (subjective) overview of the current state of the Many-Worlds Interpretation (MWI) of quantum mechanics is offered. It is contended that the MWI is the sole interpretation capable of eliminating action at a distance and randomness from quantum theory. The limitations of the MWI concerning probability questions that are legitimately addressable are outlined. The ontological framework of the MWI, viewing it as a theory of the universal wave function decomposed into a superposition of world wave functions with significant components defined in three-dimensional space, is described from the perspective of our specific branch. Additionally, certain speculations regarding misconceptions that seemingly hinder the MWI from achieving consensus are noted.

The critical exponent $\gamma \succeq 1.1$ defines the mechanical susceptibility of real fluids as temperature nears the critical value. This behavior implies that the local geometry of the critical point on the thermodynamic equation of state surface possesses zero Gaussian curvature, thereby establishing a new requirement for deriving potential equations of state from empirical data. Currently, all established empirical equations of state fail to meet this criterion, as they exhibit a negative definite Gaussian curvature at the critical point rather than zero.

Breaking Hermiticity in topological systems leads to fascinating phenomena, including exceptional topology and the non-Hermitian skin effect. This study investigates a non-Hermitian topological crystalline insulator based on a Kekulé-modulated honeycomb lattice featuring balanced gain and loss. We observe that, unlike Hermitian topological crystalline insulators where edge state gaplessness critically depends on edge geometry, the non-Hermitian system's edge state gaplessness remains robust against edge geometries under moderate gain and loss. We examine two specific configurations: $PT$-symmetric and $PT$-asymmetric. In the $PT$-symmetric case, the Dirac point of topological edge states in Hermitian molecular-zigzag-terminated ribbons splits into a pair of exceptional points, while the edge gap in Hermitian armchair-terminated ribbons vanishes to form a Dirac point under moderate gain and loss. Conversely, for the $PT$-asymmetric configuration, the band gaps of both edge and bulk states in Hermitian armchair-terminated ribbons close simultaneously.

Although deep learning has made significant strides in visual recognition using large-scale balanced datasets, it struggles with real-world long-tailed data. While previous approaches often use class re-balancing to mitigate imbalance, they risk overfitting on tail classes. Recent decoupling methods address overfitting via multi-stage training but fail to capture tail class information during the feature learning phase. This paper demonstrates that soft labels offer a robust solution for integrating label correlations into multi-stage training schemes for long-tailed recognition. By leveraging the intrinsic relationships between classes encoded in soft labels, knowledge can be effectively transferred from head to tail classes.

Specifically, we introduce a conceptually simple yet highly effective multi-stage training framework called Self Supervised to Distillation (SSD). This framework consists of two components: first, a self-distillation mechanism for long-tailed recognition that automatically uncovers label relationships; and second, a novel distillation label generation module guided by self-supervision. These distilled labels combine information from both label and data domains to effectively model long-tailed distributions. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks—ImageNet-LT, CIFAR100-LT, and iNaturalist 2018—show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the strong LWS baseline by 2.7% to 4.5% across various datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/SSD-LT.

We have analyzed how embedded pitch adapters influence signal formation in n-substrate silicon microstrip sensors using both simulation results and beam test data. Simulations indicate that the pitch adapter's metal layer alters the internal electric field, causing delayed signal formation on adjacent strips and inducing a pick-up effect on the adapter itself. This can lead to reduced detection efficiency for particles traversing the pitch adapter area, an outcome that has been confirmed by beam test observations.

Recent experimental and theoretical interest has focused on the nonlinear Hall effect observed in time-reversal symmetry-protected systems and on the surfaces of three-dimensional topological insulators under in-plane magnetic fields, particularly within two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides and Weyl semimetals. This second-order phenomenon is believed to stem from a Berry curvature dipole, necessitating a low-symmetry setting. In this work, we introduce a mechanism to generate such a nonlinear Hall effect in Kane-Mele two-dimensional topological insulators through the breaking of spatial and time-reversal symmetries induced by Zeeman and Rashba couplings. Furthermore, by modulating energy gaps via external electromagnetic fields, we show that the nonlinear Hall effect exhibits distinct signatures indicative of topological phase transitions within these two-dimensional systems.

This paper presents a characterization of periodic Gibbs measures for the Potts-SOS model on a Cayley tree of order $k\geq 1$, specifically describing these measures relative to any finite-index normal subgroup within the group representation of the tree.

Investigating the co-evolution of globular cluster systems (GCS) within galaxies demands a modeling approach that addresses both large-scale dynamics (0.01–10 kpc) governing orbital paths and small-scale dynamics (sub-pc to AU) controlling internal cluster evolution. This study introduces a new methodology that integrates semi-analytic GCS models with fully self-consistent Monte Carlo simulations to concurrently evolve large GCSs. By utilizing the MASinGa population synthesis code and the MOCCA-Survey Database I, we generate synthetic globular cluster populations designed to replicate the observed characteristics of GCs in the Milky Way and Andromeda. This approach allows us to reconstruct the spatial and mass distributions of these clusters, while also constraining the mass of GC material dispersed into the galactic halo or concentrated in the center. Central accumulation can fuel the formation of nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and potentially host stellar or intermediate-mass black holes. However, our simulations yield final masses several orders of magnitude lower than observed values. This discrepancy indicates that the infalling globular cluster scenario alone cannot account for the build-up of NSCs and central black holes in galaxies like the Milky Way and Andromeda. Instead, this growth likely results from the interplay between infalling cluster interactions/mergers and gas, which can drive both in-situ star formation within the NSC and the accretion of the central black hole.

This study addresses an economic optimization problem designed to allocate flows of natural gas and hydrogen mixtures within an extensive pipeline transportation network. The physical transport of the gas blend is modeled through steady-state relationships linking pressure drop to flow rate, where these dynamics vary by location based on the local mass concentration of the components. The optimization objective captures the system's economic value by factoring in the energy delivered to withdrawn flows, the costs associated with injecting natural gas and hydrogen, and the value of avoided carbon emissions. The solution adheres to physical flow equations, nodal balance constraints, mixing laws, and engineering inequality limits. Specific constraints include upper and lower bounds for desired energy delivery rates and minimum hydrogen concentrations, respectively; the analysis further investigates the sensitivity of pressure and flow solutions to these parameters across two test networks. Results indicate that higher hydrogen concentrations necessitate increased compression energy to deliver equivalent energy content, and the proposed formulation offers a viable approach for valuing the resulting carbon emission mitigation.

This study builds upon previous research linking finite model theory logics with propositional and algebraic proof systems. We demonstrate that if non-isomorphic graphs within a specific class are distinguishable by Choiceless Polynomial Time with counting (CPT), they are likewise distinguishable by the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus (EPC), with refutation sizes in EPC roughly matching the resource usage of the corresponding CPT sentences. This finding enables the transfer of lower bounds from EPC to CPT, offering a novel strategy to better comprehend the limitations of CPT. Specifically, a super-polynomial EPC lower bound for a polynomial-time instance of the graph isomorphism problem would separate CPT from PTIME, resolving a significant open question in finite model theory. Additionally, leveraging our result, we present a model-theoretic proof establishing the separation between bounded-degree polynomial calculus and bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus.

The Universe is currently expanding at an accelerating rate, driven by the mysterious phenomenon of dark energy. One way to probe its nature is by measuring the Universe's dimensions across various redshifts, a task achievable through the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) feature found within the galaxy 2-Point Correlation Function (2PCF). To determine the distance scale, researchers typically dilate and contract a 2PCF template based on a fiducial cosmology using a scaling factor $\alpha$. Traditionally, identifying the optimal $\alpha$ involves calculating the likelihood across a grid of approximately 100 values, a computationally intensive process. This study introduces a substantially more efficient alternative. By Taylor-expanding the 2PCF as a polynomial in $\alpha$ around $\alpha = 1$—a valid approach given that the fiducial cosmology is well-understood and $\alpha$ remains within a few percent of unity—the resulting likelihood can be analytically solved for the best-fit $\alpha$. This new method is 48 to 85 times faster than direct numerical minimization approaches and approximately 12,000 times faster than the standard iterative technique. Consequently, this advancement will greatly facilitate upcoming large-scale structure redshift surveys, including those conducted by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI).

This study examines the achievable information rates (AIRs) for coded modulation schemes employing QAM constellations, evaluating both bit-wise and symbol-wise decoders. These correspond to two scenarios: one utilizing a binary code with higher-order modulation via the bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) paradigm, and the other employing a nonbinary code over a field matched to the constellation size. Specifically, we focus on hard decision decoding, a preferred approach for fiber-optic communication systems where minimizing decoding complexity is critical. While Liga \emph{et al.} previously analyzed AIRs for similar decoders, their so-called \emph{hard decision decoder} actually utilized \emph{soft information} derived from transition probabilities of a discrete-input discrete-output channel post-hard detection, resulting in a complexity comparable to that of a soft decision decoder. In contrast, this paper analyzes the AIRs for the standard hard decision decoder used in practice, which relies on the Hamming distance metric. Our results demonstrate that when using standard hard decision decoding, bit-wise decoders achieve significantly higher AIRs than symbol-wise decoders. Consequently, contrary to the findings of Liga \emph{et al.}, binary decoders combined with the BICM paradigm are recommended for spectrally-efficient fiber-optic systems. Furthermore, we designed both binary and nonbinary staircase codes and confirmed that, consistent with the AIR analysis, binary codes deliver superior performance.

In 3-3-1 models, the requirement for anomaly cancellation mandates that the count of fermion triplets matches the number of fermion anti-triplets. This condition necessitates that two quark families transform under the anti-triplet representation of $SU(3)_L$. Consequently, these models exhibit family discrimination, which primarily leads to Flavor Changing Neutral Current phenomena. This study examines the effects of such family discrimination within meson oscillation processes involving $K^0 -\bar K^0$, $B^0 - \bar B^0$, and $D^0 - \bar D^0$.

A cover of an associative ring $R$ (which need not be commutative or unital) consists of a family of proper subrings whose union is the entire set $R$. When such a cover exists, the covering number $\sigma(R)$ denotes the cardinality of a minimal cover. A ring $R$ is defined as $\sigma$-elementary if $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for every nonzero two-sided ideal $I$. This paper presents the first instances of $\sigma$-elementary rings $R$ possessing a nontrivial Jacobson radical $J$ such that the quotient $R/J$ is noncommutative, and it establishes the covering numbers for these rings.

In recent years, the volume of video content uploaded to platforms like Facebook and YouTube has surged, consequently raising the risk of children encountering adult and violent material online. To mitigate this, this work proposes an automated system for detecting violence in videos, including the identification of specific violence categories. Such a system, capable of analyzing both Hollywood films and web videos, holds significant value for parental controls, movie rating systems, video surveillance, and genre classification. The proposed method leverages both audio and visual features: audio cues are derived from MFCCs, while visual cues incorporate Blood, Motion, and SentiBank features. Binary SVM classifiers are trained on each feature set to identify violence. Final classification scores for each violence category are obtained through late fusion, utilizing a weighted sum of individual classifier outputs. Grid search is employed to determine the optimal weights for each class. The system is trained, tested, and validated using publicly available datasets, primarily the Violent Scene Detection (VSD) dataset. Performance is assessed across two tasks: Multi-Class and Binary Classification. The results indicate that the system outperforms baseline MediaEval-2014 results in Binary Classification.

Coronal Bright Points (CBPs) are prevalent, small-scale hot loops found in the quiet Sun and coronal holes, observable in EUV and X-ray wavelengths. Although essential for understanding coronal heating, fundamental questions about their heating mechanisms, the underlying chromosphere, and the impact of flux emergence remain unanswered. Utilizing the Bifrost code, we conducted a 2D simulation where a coronal-hole magnetic nullpoint evolves under realistic granulation. By generating synthetic images from SDO/AIA, Solar Orbiter EUI-HRI, and IRIS, we compared our results with observations. The experiment demonstrates that CBPs form self-consistently through stochastic granular motions alone, facilitated by intermittent, oscillatory magnetic reconnection in the corona. This process creates temperature loops in the corona and transition region that are detectable in EUV/UV data. Throughout the CBP's lifetime, magnetic flux cancellation and convergence occur at the surface of its underlying opposite polarities. The chromosphere beneath the CBP exhibits unique characteristics regarding density and spicule activity. Ultimately, the CBP undergoes an eruptive phase: granular-scale magnetic flux emergence disrupts the structure's topology, triggering events such as UV bursts, surges, and EUV coronal jets. Beyond explaining observed CBP traits, these findings open avenues for future research integrating simulations with coordinated multi-layer observations.

High-resolution 2.5-dimensional MHD simulations investigate magnetic reconnection dynamics within the solar current sheet (CS). Upon the onset of reconnection, numerous magnetic islands form intermittently and rapidly migrate upward and downward along the CS. When these downflowing islands collide with the semi-closed flux of flare loops, they trigger a secondary reconnection event with a rate comparable to that of the primary CS reconnection. Although the total magnetic energy release remains dominated by the main CS reconnection, this secondary process releases significant energy, destroying the primary islands and creating secondary islands of varying scales at the loop top. The flux distribution of these secondary islands adheres to a power law ranging from $f\left(\psi\right)\sim\psi^{-1}$ for small scales to $\psi^{-2}$ for large scales; this distribution appears independent of the background plasma $\beta$ and thermal conduction. Conversely, increasing $\beta$ or including thermal conduction reduces the spatial scale and intensity of termination shocks driven by main reconnection outflows or islands. We propose that the annihilation of magnetic islands at the flare loop top—a phenomenon absent from standard flare models—plays a non-negligible role in releasing magnetic energy to heat flare plasma and accelerate particles.

We examine baryon-number-violating decays of nucleons and dinucleons into leptonic final states within a left-right symmetric (LRS) framework featuring large extra dimensions. Specifically, we analyze (a) nucleon decays into three leptons with $\Delta B=-1$ and $\Delta L=-3$, and (b) dinucleon decays into two leptons with $\Delta B=-2$ and $\Delta L=-2$. In this LRS model, the $B-L$ symmetry is gauged and spontaneously broken by a Higgs vacuum expectation value, $v_R$, which sets the scale for $B-L$ violating processes. We demonstrate that, given the lower bound on $v_R$ derived from experimental limits on $n$-$\bar n$ oscillations, additional constraints from searches for other nucleon decay modes ensure sufficient suppression of these trilepton and dilepton decay channels, thereby remaining consistent with current experimental bounds.

We gathered data on molecular gas content and infrared-derived star formation rates (SFRs) for 112 circumnuclear star-forming regions to re-examine the disk-averaged Schmidt surface density law in starbursts. These findings were then merged with gas and SFR surface density data from 153 nearby non-starburst disk galaxies (de los Reyes & Kennicutt 2019) to analyze the combined star formation law as proposed by Kennicutt (1998; K98). Our results confirm that the combined Schmidt law fits a single power law with a slope of $n = 1.5 \pm 0.05$ (including fitting uncertainties), which is slightly steeper than the $n = 1.4 \pm 0.15$ value reported by K98. However, fitting separate power laws to starburst and non-starburst galaxies yields significantly different slopes ($n = 1.34 \pm 0.07$ and $n = 0.98 \pm 0.07$, respectively) and a marked zero-point offset of approximately 0.6 dex, placing the starburst relation at higher SFR surface densities. This offset persists even when applying a common conversion factor for CO intensity to molecular hydrogen surface density and remains confirmed when interstellar dust surface densities serve as gas proxies. Systematic bias tests on the starburst data reveal no spurious sources for this substantial offset. We tentatively conclude that the conventional global Schmidt law in galaxies is likely bimodal or multi-modal. Potential drivers for this include variations in the small-scale structure of the molecular interstellar medium or the stellar initial mass function. Despite this, a single power law with $n \sim 1.5$ continues to serve as a viable approximation or "recipe" for analytical and numerical models of galaxy formation and evolution.

M dwarf stars are ideal candidates for finding nearby habitable exoplanets due to their abundance, low mass, and low luminosity. This study examines how radial velocity (RV) jitter caused by starspots impacts the detection and characterization of planets orbiting these stars. We generated surface spot configurations featuring both random coverage and active regions, calculated synthetic spectra from these maps, and derived RV measurements via cross-correlation. By combining an orbiting planet's RV signal with the induced jitter, we analyzed the data to infer planetary parameters. Our investigation assessed planet detectability across varying levels of stellar activity and the accuracy of recovered planetary parameters. Specifically regarding orbital period recovery, we observed that even with a 2% spot filling factor, some measurements placed planets outside the "conservative Habitable Zone," despite their original orbital radius being within it; higher filling factors produced greater and more frequent deviations. Consequently, our findings indicate that extreme caution is necessary when characterizing planets around active (or potentially active) stars using the radial velocity method.

Accurately predicting biological traits from genomic information is essential for advancing precision medicine and sustainable agriculture. Although neural networks have been highly successful in domains such as computer vision, astrophysics, and targeted marketing due to their high accuracy and robustness with large datasets, they have yet to gain a foothold in biological and medical research. This lag is largely attributed to the unique nature of biological data, which is often characterized by small sample sizes, sparsity, and extreme heterogeneity. In this study, we evaluate the robustness, generalization capabilities, and predictive performance of popular convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and natural language processing (NLP) models across diverse genomic datasets. Our findings indicate that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) generally surpass CNNs in prediction accuracy, resistance to overfitting, and cross-dataset transferability. While a universally robust, ready-to-use neural network model remains elusive, we have identified specific model attributes that transfer effectively across datasets, offering a potential baseline for translational researchers.

Singular factors arising from the QCD factorisation of scattering amplitudes in soft and collinear regimes are crucial for both structuring and calculating high-order perturbative terms in hard-scattering cross sections. This presentation begins by examining the factorisation of scattering amplitudes in the collinear limit to introduce process-independent collinear functions. Defined at the fully-differential level, these functions can be integrated over an observable-specific phase space to determine logarithmically enhanced contributions. Specifically for transverse-momentum dependent observables, we demonstrate how to define these collinear functions without invoking the rapidity divergences typically found in literature. Finally, we report explicit calculations of these collinear functions up to next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD perturbation theory.

Rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) has emerged as a potent multiple access scheme, non-orthogonal transmission framework, and interference management technique for 6G. Motivated by the substantial spectral efficiency improvements RSMA offers over traditional methods in multi-user, multi-antenna environments, this paper applies RSMA to reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted multiple-input single-output (MISO) broadcast channels. To further boost spectral efficiency, we employ a generalized RIS structure known as fully connected RIS. By jointly optimizing the fully connected RIS's scattering matrix and the transmit beamformers to maximize the sum-rate, we demonstrate that the proposed fully connected RIS-aided RSMA scheme achieves significantly higher spectral efficiency than both conventional single-connected RIS approaches and systems without RIS. This method serves as a new benchmark for linearly precoded multi-user, multi-antenna networks.

Dense aqueous suspensions of granular cornstarch, which are highly sheared, exhibit complex nonlinear rheological behavior. In prior research, we identified the emergence of interfacial instabilities when shear-thinning cornstarch suspensions were displaced by a Newtonian fluid and proposed strategies to optimize displacement efficiency [Palak et al., Colloids Surf. A Physicochem. Eng. Asp., 629 (2021) 127405]. This study investigates the miscible displacement of a shear-thickening, dense cornstarch suspension by water within a quasi-two-dimensional radial Hele-Shaw cell. We systematically analyzed the growth kinetics of both the inner interface (between water and the suspension) and the outer interface (between the suspension and air). Beyond the instability growth at the inner interface, we observed a transient withdrawal of the suspension and the development of fingering instabilities at the outer interface. We show that these "reverse fingering" instabilities are highly sensitive to the water injection rate, the Hele-Shaw cell gap, and the concentration of the displaced cornstarch, significantly influencing overall displacement efficiency. We attribute the formation and evolution of these reverse fingers to the accumulation of normal stresses in the cornstarch suspension caused by high shear rates.

This study introduces a cosmological model-independent, non-local approach to constrain the Hubble Constant ($H_0$). Drawing inspiration from the `shifted' Hubble diagram of HII galaxies (HIIGx), which exhibits quasi-model-independent and $H_0$-free characteristics as defined by Wei et al. (2016), we jointly analyze this data with the parametric Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) Hubble diagram, such as the joint-lightcurves-analysis (JLA) sample. Our Bayesian Inference yields $H_0 = 71 \pm 20\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}\ Mpc^{-1}}$. Despite the substantial uncertainty, we observe that $H_0$ is strongly degenerate only with the B-band absolute magnitude ($M_B$) of SN Ia and remains nearly independent of other nuisance parameters. Consequently, precision can be simultaneously enhanced by imposing a tight, cosmological and $H_0$-independent constraint on $M_B$. Furthermore, this methodology can be extended to achieve even more strictly non-local results for $H_0$ by incorporating Hubble diagrams at higher redshifts.

This work introduces a novel set of field equations incorporating a space-time varying Newton's constant, $G(x)$, and a cosmological constant, $\Lambda(x)$, alongside matter. We demonstrate that these equations constitute the most comprehensive and physically viable set of evolution equations that remain mathematically consistent, provided they involve no more than second-order derivatives of the dynamical variables. In this revised formulation of Einstein's equations, kinetic terms specific to $\Lambda$ emerge, whereas the modified conservation equation includes derivative terms of $G$. Applying this framework to the early universe within the Asymptotic Safety paradigm, assuming a perfect fluid with a radiation equation of state, we derive cosmological solutions for all spatial curvature types. These solutions exhibit diverse cosmic evolution patterns, including detailed analyses of bouncing scenarios, recollapsing phases, and non-singular expanding universes featuring a temporary acceleration period.

We demonstrate that specific diagrams of $\infty$-logoses are reconstructed within the internal languages of their oplax limits through lex, accessible modalities. This capability allows plain homotopy type theory to reason not only about individual $\infty$-logoses but also about entire diagrams of them. Furthermore, this approach yields a higher-dimensional analogue of Sterling's synthetic Tait computability, effectively creating a type theory for higher-dimensional logical relations. To establish our primary result, we define a precise correspondence between the lex, accessible localizations of an $\infty$-logos and the lex, accessible modalities found in its internal language. In doing so, we also partially develop the Kripke-Joyal semantics of homotopy type theory within $\infty$-logoses.

Molecular dynamics simulations were employed to analyze the mechanical behavior of dense, soft, athermal sphere packings subjected to finite-rate shear. The study examines how fluctuations in shear stress and interparticle contact numbers vary with volume fraction and shear rate, quantifying these effects by defining susceptibility as the ratio of global to local fluctuations. The resulting susceptibilities exhibit ridges within the volume fraction-shear rate plane, resembling the Widom lines typically associated with critical points in equilibrium phase transitions.

Federated learning (FL) enables the private training of vast datasets through its decentralized architecture. Although Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is widely adopted in FL for its strong empirical results, sensitive user information remains vulnerable to inference via shared weight updates. This work employs Gaussian mechanisms to ensure local differential privacy (LDP) within FL models utilizing SGD. We establish appropriate metrics to analyze the trade-offs among user privacy, global utility, and transmission rates in LDP-enhanced FL. Unlike prior studies, we define query sensitivity as a variable and implement a more precise privacy accounting technique. Our proposed utility bounds accommodate heterogeneous parameters across all users, characterizing the specific reductions in utility and increases in transmission rate required for stricter privacy regimes. Moreover, for any given target privacy level, our findings guarantee substantially higher utility and lower transmission rates compared to existing privacy accounting methods.

With the growing reliance on personal data for training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in areas like medical imaging and diagnosis, differentially private DNN training has become increasingly vital, spawning extensive research aimed at optimizing privacy-utility trade-offs. Yet, interpretability remains largely overlooked, particularly regarding how differential privacy influences the quality of model interpretations. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the impacts of DP-based training on DNNs, with a specific focus on medical imaging applications using the APTOS dataset.

This study introduces a haptic interface utilizing modular linear actuators to overcome the constraints of traditional devices that rely on rotary joints. Constructed from parallel linear actuators, the proposed system offers superior backdrivability and reduced inertia. When evaluated against conventional mechanisms regarding force capacity, reflected inertia, and structural stiffness, the new interface demonstrates high stiffness, extensive range of motion, and substantial force output—attributes that are typically mutually exclusive in traditional haptic designs. The device sustains a continuous force of up to 83 N, which is triple the capacity of most existing haptic devices. In comparable conditions, the theoretical minimum haptic force density and stiffness of the proposed mechanism are 1.3 to 1.9 times and 37 times greater, respectively, than those of conventional systems. Furthermore, the system is scalable because its structural stiffness relies solely on the timing belt stiffness, whereas conventional interfaces exhibit stiffness inversely proportional to the cube of their structural lengths. The modular actuator architecture allows for adjustable degrees of freedom (DOFs) tailored to various applications. Finally, the interface was validated through interaction experiments within a virtual environment featuring rigid walls.

While Intelligent Reflective Surfaces (IRSs) offer a cost-efficient solution with high spectral efficiency potential for future wireless networks, deriving optimal IRS beamformers remains a complex task subject to various practical constraints. Under the assumption of fully-passive, sensing-free IRS operation, we propose a novel data-driven Zeroth-order Stochastic Gradient Ascent (ZoSGA) algorithm designed to optimize sum-rate in IRS-aided downlink systems. ZoSGA eliminates the need for channel model or network structure details, facilitating the joint learning of optimal long-term IRS beamformers alongside standard short-term precoding using only conventional effective channel state information. Backed by state-of-the-art convergence analysis, extensive simulations demonstrate that ZoSGA matches top-tier empirical performance, consistently surpassing standard fully model-based baselines across diverse scenarios.

To enhance post-editing assistance efficiency, we introduce a new concept termed "extended word alignment." Building on this, we propose a novel task known as "refined word-level QE," which generates refined tags and precise word-level correspondences. Unlike traditional word-level QE, this approach directly identifies specific editing operations, thereby boosting efficiency. For extracting extended word alignment, we utilize a supervised method leveraging mBERT.
