To address the refined word-level QE task, we first train a sequence-tagging regression model using mBERT and XLM-R to predict original QE tags, subsequently refining these tags with the extended word alignment. Furthermore, we extract source-gap correspondences to derive gap tags. Experiments conducted on two language pairs demonstrate the viability of our method and offer insights for future enhancements.

The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), a multi-purpose neutrino experiment, will utilize 20 kt of liquid scintillator (LS) to achieve its primary physics goal of determining the neutrino mass ordering, which necessitates an energy resolution of 3% at 1 MeV. This requirement imposes stringent constraints on the LS's light yield and transparency. To address this, four purification steps were developed, and mid-scale purification plants were constructed at Daya Bay. To evaluate the performance of the purified LS and optimize its composition, the material was injected into the antineutrino detector 1 (EH1-AD1) within the experimental hall 1 of the Daya Bay neutrino experiment. In 2017, a dedicated LS replacement system was installed in EH1 to facilitate the removal of the original gadolinium-loaded LS and its replacement with new material. By first displacing the Gd-LS with purified water and then substituting the water with purified LS, the system successfully met its design objectives. Subsequently, this system was used to incrementally increase the concentrations of fluorescence and wavelength shifter components. Data collected across various LS compositions enabled JUNO to finalize the LS cocktail formulation. This paper details the design, construction, and operational procedures of the replacement system.

We re-examine the Rellich inequality by separating the effects of radial and spherical derivatives. This approach facilitates a comparison between the norms of the standard Laplacian and those of the radial Laplacian and Laplace-Beltrami operators. Specifically, within the context of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, the three-dimensional scenario presents the most significant challenges; in this area, we enhance a finding by Evans and Lewis by determining the optimal constant. Our methodology relies on specific identities recently developed by Wadade and the second and third authors, combined with the application of spherical harmonics.

We employ exact diagonalization to investigate the square-lattice extended Hubbard model, characterized by on-site ($U$) and nearest-neighbor ($V$) interactions. Our findings indicate that non-equilibrium quench dynamics can effectively delineate equilibrium phase transition boundaries, a conclusion corroborated by calculations involving the fidelity metric, dynamical structure factor, and correlation functions. At half filling within the strong-coupling regime, the phase diagram features a spin density wave and $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave superconductivity for large positive $U$, charge density waves (accompanied by extended $s^*$-wave superconductivity) for large positive or negative $V$, and $s$-wave superconductivity for large negative $U$ with negligible $V$. Additionally, energy levels across various particle sectors assist in identifying the phase separation region. Upon carrier doping, charge fluctuations intensify the competition among different orders, complicating the identification of the leading instability on finite-size clusters. However, we observe that more exotic $p$-wave superconducting pairing is significantly enhanced under heavy overdoping (37.5%–50% holes), particularly in interaction regimes relevant to cuprate superconductors.

This study applies the sample average approximation (SAA) method to risk-neutral optimization problems constrained by semilinear elliptic partial differential equations with random inputs. By first constructing a compact set encompassing the SAA critical points, we establish nonasymptotic sample size requirements using the covering number technique. Consequently, we derive upper limits on the necessary number of samples to achieve accurate critical points for the risk-neutral PDE-constrained optimization problem via SAA. Accuracy is measured through expectation and exponential tail bounds, with numerical examples provided to illustrate these findings.

The evolution of molecular interstellar clouds represents a complex, multi-scale phenomenon. While the power-law density exponent characterizes the steepness of density profiles, its application has traditionally been restricted to spherically symmetric systems. By integrating the Level-Set Method, we introduce a new formalism capable of generating robust maps of the generalized density exponent $k_{\rho}$ across all locations within complex density distributions. Applying this approach to a high-fidelity, high-dynamic-range map of the Perseus molecular cloud—derived from Herschel and Planck satellite data—we observe that the density exponent varies significantly, ranging from approximately -3.5 to -0.5. Regions undergoing later stages of gravitational collapse correspond to steeper density profiles. Furthermore, gas situated near dense structures within a region exhibits extremely steep profiles ($k_{\rho} \approx -3$) due to depletion. This analysis of the density exponent uncovers diverse density structures, painting a coherent picture where gravitational collapse drives a continuous steepening of the density profile. We anticipate that this method will be effective for investigating other power-law-like density structures, such as granular materials and the Large-Scale Structure of the Universe.

The film industry faces the challenge of ensuring movies appear consistent across a wide range of display sizes, from massive cinema screens to compact mobile devices. However, visual induction—a perceptual effect where a scene's appearance is influenced by its surroundings—varies depending on the dimensions of the display, threatening to alter the filmmaker's intended artistic vision. This research demonstrates that a neural field model grounded in the efficient representation principle can accurately predict these induction effects. Furthermore, by regularizing the model's energy functional, the authors achieved an invertible version that retains the ability to represent induction. Based on this, a novel method is proposed to pre-process images in a manner specific to screen size, ensuring that visual induction remains constant regardless of the viewing device. The efficacy of this approach is validated through psychophysical experiments using synthetic images and qualitative analysis of natural images.

This study provides an overview of the current state of requirements engineering within the gaming sector. It reviews recent literature on the subject, analyzes the gaming industry's relationship with the broader market, and highlights potential future research directions in this field.

The Kondo effect generally results from spin-flip scattering between the localized magnetic moments of impurities and the delocalized electrons within a metallic host, generating various fascinating phenomena. In this study, we utilize scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) to investigate the Kondo effect and subatomic characteristics of a single uranium (U) adatom on graphene/6H-SiC(0001). A dip in the spectral density near the Fermi energy, identified as the "fingerprint" of the Kondo resonance in STS, is observed. Furthermore, dI/dV maps reveal two distinct subatomic features with varying symmetries: a three-lobe structure and a doughnut-like structure. The Kondo resonance is confined to a lateral distance of approximately 5 Å from the U atom center, a range significantly smaller than that seen in cobalt atoms on different surfaces, suggesting that the 5f states are more localized than 3d orbitals. Comparisons with density functional theory calculations indicate that these two symmetry-distinct subatomic features arise from the selective hybridization between U 6d and 5f orbitals and the $p_z$ orbitals of two inequivalent carbon atoms in the multilayer graphene.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) generates substantial amounts of top-quark pairs alongside final state particles, a result of the high center-of-mass energy in proton-proton collisions. A specific configuration involves a prompt photon emitted from the top quark, accompanied by the decay products of that quark. Analyzing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of data gathered at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV with the ATLAS detector, this study presents fiducial cross-section measurements for both single-lepton and dilepton channels. To enhance sensitivity, the analysis employs object-level and event-level neural networks.

Extensive literature covers various methods for monitoring batch processes, which generate unique data structures characterized by sequential measurements of multiple variables across each run. Conventional approaches often fail to account for the time-series nature of this data because standard time-series inference relies on variability within a single time domain rather than the replication inherent in batch data. Consequently, adapting this theory is necessary to simultaneously address batch-to-batch variability and the serial correlation within individual batches. To tackle this, the paper introduces a novel approach utilizing control charts based on the classical ARMA model for both monitoring and diagnosing batch process dynamics. Model coefficients are estimated for each historical batch using ordinary least squares, and modified Hotelling and t-Student distributions are derived to accommodate these estimates. A suite of control charts based on these distributions is proposed for monitoring new batches, which also aids in fault diagnosis by identifying disturbance sources. Validation through both simulated and real data demonstrates the approach's effectiveness for both monitoring and diagnostic purposes.

This short note examines the topological entropy of linear switched systems. By employing the Levi-Malcev decomposition of Lie algebras, we link fundamental aspects of topological entropy with the stability of these systems. We demonstrate that for such systems, the topological entropy associated with the evolution operator of a semi-simple subalgebra is invariably bounded above by the negative of the largest real part of the eigenvalue linked to the evolution operator of a maximal solvable ideal.

Designing integrated circuits for radiation-heavy environments like the High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) presents significant challenges, primarily due to radiation-induced Single Event Effects (SEE). In deep sub-micron technologies, triple modular redundancy serves as a mitigation strategy; by triplicating sensitive data, this approach recovers most corruption caused by interacting particles. This paper focuses on Single Event Upsets (SEU), estimating both the SEU cross-section and the efficacy of triplication through an ASIC prototype tested with a proton beam. Measurements of the SEU cross-section revealed a systematic disparity between $1\rightarrow{0}$ and $0\rightarrow{1}$ bit flip rates, and the study further evaluates the efficiency of this mitigation technique.

We outline the intersection of measure-theoretic probability and causal inference by building causal models on probability spaces using the potential outcomes framework. Our findings indicate that measure theory offers a rigorous and educational language for causality, and examining the underlying probability spaces clarifies core concepts in causal inference. Through the analysis of straightforward, illustrative examples, we reveal insights regarding causal effects, interactions, matching procedures, and randomization. Furthermore, we present a simple method for visualizing causal models on probability spaces, which aids in generating examples and cultivating causal intuition. Finally, we establish an axiomatic framework for causality and take initial steps toward a formal theory of general causal models.

Although transformer-based language models excel at numerous natural language understanding tasks, their response to implicit meaning remains largely unexamined. This study investigates this gap by analyzing the complement coercion phenomenon, exemplified by sentences like "The student finished the book about sailing," where the action of "reading" is implied. We compared the models' surprisal estimates across different critical regions in sentences containing versus those lacking implicit meaning. Results indicated that effects related to recovering implicit meaning occurred in a critical region distinct from where the sentences minimally diverge. Subsequent experiments were conducted to isolate potential confounding factors, yielding new perspectives that provide a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of the phenomenon.

Reductus is an online service for data reduction that converts experimental measurements from laboratory coordinates into physically significant quantities, calculating accurate uncertainties based on instrument properties and settings. Although this process relies on established transformations, the system's flexible application of algorithms and transforms accommodates diverse experimental designs, surpassing the limitations of rigid data reduction schemes. Users can effortlessly build custom data pipelines using a visual dataflow interface that draws from a networked, open repository. Powered by a Python backend with intelligent caching for intermediate results, the system ensures a highly responsive experience. This reference implementation enables real-time reduction of measurements for the three neutron reflectometry instruments at the NIST Center for Neutron Research (NCNR), eliminating the need for visiting scientists to install proprietary software on their personal devices.

This study employs the GALFORM semi-analytical model alongside the Planck-Millennium simulation to explore the origins of stellar mass in galaxies and their spheroids, specifically comparing the roles of mergers, disc instabilities, and the starbursts they induce. Our findings indicate that the fraction of stellar mass formed ex situ ($f_\mathrm{ex}$) rises sharply for galaxies with $M_* > 10^{11}$ M$_\odot$, peaking at $80\%$ for $M_* = 10^{11.3}$ M$_\odot$. In low-mass galaxies, we observe higher ex situ contributions at $z=0$ ($7$-$12\%$) compared to other models, with these values declining at higher redshifts. Globally, the ex situ fraction of all stellar mass drops significantly from $40\%$ at $z=0$ to $3\%$ at $z=10$. Major mergers account for approximately half of the ex situ mass, while minor mergers and smooth satellite accretion each contribute about $25\%$, remaining relatively constant across stellar masses and redshifts. Mergers are the primary builders of high-mass ($M_\mathrm{*,sph}>10^{11}$ M$_\odot$) and low-mass ($M_\mathrm{*,sph}<10^{8.5}$ M$_\odot$) spheroids, whereas disc instabilities and their associated starbursts dominate intermediate-mass spheroids ($10^{8.5}<M_\mathrm{*,sph}<10^{11}$ M$_\odot$) at $z=0$. While the mass regime for pseudobulge dominance aligns with observations, the GALFORM model predicts a peak pseudobulge fraction that is likely too high. At $z=0$, the total contributions from disc instabilities and starbursts are roughly balanced; disc instabilities dominate in lower-mass spheroids (peaking at $M_\mathrm{*,sph}=10^{9.5}$ M$_\odot$), while starbursts dominate in higher-mass ones (peaking at $M_\mathrm{*,sph}=10^{10.5}$ M$_\odot$).

As machine learning (ML) models increasingly drive critical decisions, interpretability has emerged as a vital area of research. Tabular data remains a cornerstone for diverse fields like healthcare and finance. However, many current interpretability techniques for tabular data merely report feature-importance scores—whether locally or globally—without offering insights or visualizations into feature interactions. To overcome this gap, we introduce Feature Vectors, a novel global interpretability method tailored for tabular datasets. Beyond calculating feature importance, Feature Vectors uncovers inherent semantic relationships among features through an intuitive visualization approach. Systematic experiments across multiple real-world datasets confirm the method's empirical effectiveness, and we have released a user-friendly Python package to facilitate its use.

Hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithms represent a leading approach for leveraging near-term quantum hardware, effectively bridging classical machine learning with vast quantum solution spaces. Despite their promise, research indicates that the exponential growth of these spaces with increasing qubit counts can hinder training in deep circuits due to a phenomenon called barren plateaus. This study identifies random entanglement as the primary driver of barren plateaus and analyzes them through the lens of many-body entanglement dynamics, specifically examining how they emerge based on system size, circuit depth, and connectivity. Leveraging this understanding, we introduce and validate several mitigation strategies, such as partitioning cost and non-cost registers, employing meta-learning for low-entanglement initializations, enabling selective inter-register interactions, applying entanglement regularization, incorporating Langevin noise, and rotating into preferred cost function eigenbases. Our findings suggest that limiting entanglement—whether through automated or engineered means—is essential for achieving high-accuracy training. Furthermore, we argue that since learning is an iterative organizational process while barren plateaus stem from randomization, they are not inevitable obstacles. Ultimately, this work provides both a theoretical framework and a practical toolkit, first defining barren plateaus via random entanglement and then utilizing this insight to strategically address them.

We provide an exact calculation of effective Hamiltonians for a basic model derived from Yukawa theory, where bare fermions are infinitely heavy and bare bosons remain stationary relative to the emitting or absorbing fermions. This approach accommodates arbitrarily large coupling constants. By applying the differential equation of the Renormalization Group Procedure for Effective Particles (RGPEP), we compute these Hamiltonians. Within the model, physical fermions are defined as eigenstates of these effective Hamiltonians and appear as effective fermions dressed by coherent states of effective bosons. This computation demonstrates the method's applicability to perturbative calculations of effective Hamiltonians in realistic theories, revealing how the Tamm-Dancoff approximation and perturbative expansion enhance in accuracy throughout the RGPEP evolution.

We examine how a low-mass, coplanar circumbinary disc responds to secular tidal forces from an eccentric central binary in a Keplerian orbit. The disc develops a forced eccentricity, with its magnitude determined by the specific characteristics of both the binary and the disc. Maximum eccentricities arise when a global apsidal resonance exists within the disc. This occurs because the binary's driving frequency, which is zero (matching its apsidal frequency), aligns with a free eccentric mode in the disc that also has a zero apsidal frequency. Such resonances can involve different free modes distinguished by their number of radial nodes. When the disc is not in resonance, its eccentricity distribution resembles that of a resonant disc with the closest matching aspect ratio. However, for higher aspect ratios, the forced eccentricity in a 2D disc mimics the fundamental free mode, whereas in a 3D disc it resembles higher-order free modes unless the disc is sufficiently cool. Near resonance conditions, significant phase shifts occur between the locked-in phases of the disc and binary eccentricities. Ultimately, forced eccentricity may be a critical factor in the evolutionary dynamics of both circumbinary discs and their central binaries.

Topological material phases are typically defined by topological invariants computed using various methods tailored to specific dimensions and symmetry classes. For topological systems modeled by Dirac equations, we propose a unified framework based on a "wrapping number" to derive these invariants across any dimension and symmetry category. By utilizing a unit vector that characterizes the momentum dependence within the Dirac model, the wrapping number quantifies the mapping degree from the Brillouin zone torus to a "Dirac sphere" constructed from that unit vector. This approach is inherently gauge-invariant, stemming from the fundamental properties of the Dirac model, and it unifies established topological invariants—including the Chern number, winding number, and Pfaffian—into a single conceptual framework.

In the context of heterotic supergravity, we compactify ten-dimensional spacetime to retain a four-dimensional Minkowski background. We investigate nonsupersymmetric, non-Ricci-flat solutions to the equations of motion that incorporate quadratic curvature terms. By postulating that the extra dimensions take the form of products of 2-manifolds, three distinct solution types emerge: $S^2\times T^2 \times H^2/\Gamma$, $S^2\times H^2/\Gamma \times H^2/\Gamma$, and $S^2\times S^2 \times H^2/\Gamma$, where $H^2/\Gamma$ represents a compact hyperbolic manifold. These metrics admit explicit formulations and hold potential for phenomenological applications.

Determining cell fate selection continues to be a primary challenge within developmental biology. We introduce a category of straightforward, biologically inspired mathematical models for cell differentiation that inherently produce oscillations, thereby proposing alternatives to the conventional Waddington epigenetic landscape framework. These models outline two general dynamical scenarios characterizing the differentiation process: the first involves the gradual adjustment of a single control parameter to both initiate and terminate oscillatory behavior, while the second involves two parameters, with one governing entry into and the other governing exit from the oscillatory regime. We examine the standard repressilator and four of its variants, demonstrating the distinct dynamical behaviors linked to each scenario. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the associated bifurcations and contend that gene regulatory networks exhibiting these repressilator-like features are strong candidates for describing cell fate selection via an oscillatory mechanism.

While semiconductor valence holes are recognized as having both heavy and light effective masses, the impact of this mass variation on Coulomb scattering has historically been deemed too complex to address and consequently overlooked. This neglect stems from the fact that the heavy/light designation is quantized along the hole's momentum, which shifts during a Coulomb interaction, allowing a heavy hole to transition into a light one based on the scattering angle. Due to this dynamic mass change, many-body calculations have traditionally relied on a single "average" hole mass rather than accounting for the full spectrum. To investigate the significant errors introduced by this simplification, it is essential to accurately model Coulomb scatterings involving valence holes. This work derives these interactions from the fundamental threefold valence-electron spatial level, progressing through spin-orbit splitting, the Kohn-Luttinger effective Hamiltonian, its spherical approximation, and the specific phase factors arising when converting between valence electron and hole operators, thereby addressing the unique physical characteristics of valence holes that distinguish them from simple positive charges.

The issue of electromagnetic radiation emitted by an accelerating charged particle has been one of the most contentious topics in physics since the early 20th century, remaining a prominent unsolved problem in modern physics. Although various equations of motion for a point charge—including those accounting for emitted radiation—have been proposed over time, all exhibit certain limitations. This work introduces an equation grounded in the principle of energy conservation specifically for ultra-relativistic motion. Analysis of several examples demonstrates that the energy loss by the charge aligns with the Liénard formula. Furthermore, when compared to the Landau-Lifshitz equation, the proposed formula shows strong agreement within the range where the Landau-Lifshitz equation is applicable.

Following the Event Horizon Telescope's groundbreaking direct image of a black hole, which aligns with the shadow predicted by the Kerr solution of general relativity, it remains crucial to consider alternative rotating black hole models derived from modified gravity theories. These alternatives provide a vital testing ground for such theories via astrophysical observations. Consequently, this study examines asymptotically de Sitter rotating black holes, where treating the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ as vacuum energy induces a deformation near the event horizon, yielding a new Kerr–de Sitter solution with a more complex geometric structure. We derive an analytical expression for the shadow of these new black holes and visualize them across various parameters for an observer located at coordinates $(r_0, \theta_0)$ within the domain $(r_0,\; r_c)$, allowing us to estimate $\Lambda$ from shadow-based observables. Our results show that the shadow observables of the new Kerr–de Sitter black holes differ significantly from those of the standard Kerr–de Sitter black holes across a substantial portion of the parameter space. Notably, we identify a finite region in the ($\Lambda$, $a$) parameter space where the observational signatures of the two black hole types become indistinguishable.

Adjusting hyperparameters in differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DPSGD) presents a significant challenge. Unlike standard SGD, private datasets in DPSGD cannot be repeatedly utilized for hyperparameter tuning methods such as grid search. Consequently, there is a critical requirement for algorithms capable of efficiently identifying near-optimal hyperparameters that maximize privacy-utility tradeoffs within a defined search space. This study formulates the issue as a general optimization framework to achieve desirable privacy-utility balances and systematically evaluates three cost-effective algorithms within this context: evolutionary, Bayesian, and reinforcement learning. Experimental results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that these three approaches significantly surpass the commonly used grid search baseline. Since this paper introduces a novel framework for DPSGD hyperparameter tuning, we examine current limitations and suggest avenues for future research. Given the potential impact of our work on private deep learning pipelines, we have released our code openly at https://github.com/AmanPriyanshu/DP-HyperparamTuning.

Gathering information represents one of the most intricate challenges in decision-making and planning, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional states that defy representation by parametric distributions. However, even in such complex scenarios, only a small subset of the state typically influences state transitions and observation generation. We leverage this insight to compute an information-theoretic expected reward, specifically mutual information (MI), over a significantly lower-dimensional state subset, thereby enhancing efficiency without compromising accuracy. While prior research applied similar techniques exclusively to Gaussian distributions, this work extends the approach to general distributions. Furthermore, we apply this dimensionality reduction to scenarios where new states are augmented to existing ones, maintaining accuracy. We subsequently develop a Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC)-based estimator for MI that circumvents the need to reconstruct future belief surfaces. Finally, we demonstrate the application of this method to informative planning optimization and evaluate it through an active SLAM simulation, highlighting improvements in both accuracy and computational timing.

By adapting the $\gamma$-basis to the vector space $\mathcal{G}(n,r)$, which consists of symbols associated with bit sequences containing $r$ ones and $n-r$ zeros, we derive a frame that spans the vector space $\mathcal{T}(n,r)$. This space is generated by the Tutte polynomials of matroids with rank $r$ and cardinality $n$. Each Tutte polynomial can be expressed as a linear combination of the frame's elements, utilizing non-negative integer coefficients. We provide explicit formulas defining these frame elements, which collectively yield an expansion of the Tutte polynomial where the coefficients result from summing numerical invariants across all flats sharing a specific rank and size.

Although deep learning has advanced significantly in image semantic segmentation, it often relies on extensive annotated data, prompting a shift toward Few-Shot Learning (FSL) scenarios that require minimal labels for generalizing to new classes. This shift is particularly critical in medical imaging, where acquiring dense pixel-level annotations is costly. This paper introduces Regularized Prototypical Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (R-PNODE), a technique that utilizes the inherent characteristics of Neural-ODEs, bolstered by cluster and consistency losses, to achieve Few-Shot Segmentation (FSS) of organs. By restricting support and query features from the same class to be proximate within the representation space, R-PNODE enhances performance compared to current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based FSS approaches. Furthermore, while many existing Deep CNN methods are highly susceptible to adversarial attacks, R-PNODE demonstrates greater robustness against a broad spectrum of such threats. The study evaluates the method across three public multi-organ segmentation datasets in both in-domain and cross-domain FSS contexts, alongside tests involving seven standard adversarial attack types. Results indicate that R-PNODE significantly outperforms baseline FSS methods and exhibits superior resilience against diverse attacks with varying intensities and designs.

We investigate strongly coupled ABJM theory on a 3-sphere incorporating massive quenched flavors via the AdS/CFT correspondence. The holographic dual involves type IIA supergravity supplemented by probe D6-branes. A relevant deformation representing the flavor mass induces an RG flow terminating in pure ABJM theory in the infrared. At non-zero mass, the theory on the 3-sphere undergoes a quantum phase transition at a critical sphere radius. This transition reflects a change in the topology of the D6-brane embeddings, which is dual to the meson-melting transition. We calculate the free energy on the 3-sphere holographically and employ it to build various candidate F-functions. Recently suggested within Einstein-scalar gravity, these F-functions are designed to monotonically interpolate between the free energies of the UV and IR CFTs. Our results show that although the F-functions for flavored ABJM theory yield correct UV and IR limits, they fail to be monotonic. We hypothesize that this non-monotonicity arises from the presence of the phase transition.

Social media generates a vast array of posts and comments covering every conceivable subject. While many of these entries express societal opinions, their unfalsifiable characteristics render them incompatible with traditional fact-checking processes. This study aims to extract such posts into a concise set of narratives that encapsulate the core claims surrounding a specific topic. Analyzing and visualizing these narratives can promote more educated discourse on social platforms. As an initial step toward systematically uncovering these underlying narratives, we introduce PAPYER, a fine-grained dataset of online hygiene-related comments in public restrooms, featuring numerous unfalsifiable assertions. We demonstrate a human-in-the-loop pipeline that integrates both machine and human components to identify dominant narratives, proving that this approach surpasses recent large transformer models and state-of-the-art unsupervised topic models.

This paper introduces a formula for constructing Zero-Determinant (ZD) strategies in general finite games involving $n$ players with varying numbers of strategies. By utilizing the semi-tensor product (STP) of matrices, the profile evolutionary equation for repeated finite games is derived. Leveraging this equation and adapting the technique originally proposed by Press and Dyson \cite{pre12}, ZD strategies are formulated for general finite games. A direct design formula for ZD strategies for any player is established, bypassing the original ZD design procedure. Furthermore, necessary and sufficient conditions are derived to guarantee the efficacy of these strategies. Consequently, it is demonstrated that player $i$ can unilaterally establish $|S_i|-1$ dominant linear relations regarding the expected payoffs of all players. Finally, a fictitious opponent player is introduced for networked evolutionary games (NEGs). Applying ZD strategies within this framework reveals that an individual in a network can employ these strategies to dominate the entire remaining network.

Emergency vehicles (EMVs) are vital for addressing time-sensitive incidents like medical crises and fires in urban environments. Current methods aimed at reducing EMV travel times typically utilize route optimization and traffic signal pre-emption, yet they fail to account for the interdependence between these two subproblems, often leading to suboptimal routing. Furthermore, these existing approaches neglect the minimization of disruption to general traffic flow. To resolve these limitations, this paper presents EMVLight, a decentralized reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed for simultaneous dynamic routing and traffic signal control. EMVLight adapts Dijkstra's algorithm to efficiently recalculate optimal paths for EMVs in real-time as they navigate the network. Consequently, the decentralized RL agents develop cooperative, network-wide traffic signal phase strategies that reduce both EMV travel time and the average travel time of non-emergency vehicles. Extensive experiments using both synthetic and real-world maps validate these advantages. Our findings indicate that EMVLight surpasses both traditional transportation engineering techniques and existing RL-based traffic signal control methods.

A celebrated theorem by R. E. Curto and N. Salinas establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for the unitary equivalence of commuting tuples of bounded linear operators on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Drawing inspiration from this result, we derive an alternative yet equivalent criterion for the unitary equivalence of such operators. As an application, we characterize the structure of intertwining operators and demonstrate that the decomposition of Cowen-Douglas operators is unique up to unitary equivalence.

We investigate the existence and finiteness of absolutely continuous, ergodic, stationary probability measures—specifically physical measures whose basins of attraction encompass the entire space almost everywhere—for random compositions of independent and identically distributed measurable maps defined on a Polish space. By utilizing the associated Markov operators, we categorize and rank these random maps into a hierarchy, illustrating distinctions between these classes through numerous examples such as additive noise, multiplicative noise, and iterated function systems. Furthermore, we outline practical sufficient conditions for a random map to fall within these categories. Notably, we demonstrate that any continuous random map on a compact Riemannian manifold possessing absolutely continuous transition probabilities yields a finite number of physical measures whose basins of attraction cover the manifold almost everywhere with respect to the Lebesgue measure.

High-multiplicity signatures observed at particle colliders may originate from both Standard Model processes and physics beyond it. However, these signatures often present challenges due to the expansive dimensionality of the associated kinematic space. In cases involving final states with a single particle type, this high dimensionality creates a combinatorial problem that obscures fundamental kinematic details. This study investigates the application of a neural network incorporating a Lorentz Layer to capture high-dimensional correlations. Using squark decays within R-Parity-violating Supersymmetry as a benchmark, we compare this method against classical approaches and demonstrate that it yields substantial performance improvements over traditional techniques.

High-resolution (HR) medical imaging offers detailed anatomical structures essential for precise and early diagnosis. However, in MRI, constraints such as hardware limitations, scan duration, and patient compliance often restrict the acquisition of isotropic 3D HR images, leading to extended scan times, limited spatial coverage, and reduced signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Recent research indicates that deep convolutional neural networks can recover isotropic HR MR images from low-resolution (LR) inputs using single image super-resolution (SISR) techniques. Nevertheless, most current SISR methods rely on a scale-specific mapping between LR and HR images, limiting them to fixed up-sampling rates. To handle varying rates, researchers traditionally construct multiple distinct networks, a process that is both time-consuming and resource-heavy. This paper introduces ArSSR, an Arbitrary Scale Super-Resolution framework designed for 3D HR MR image recovery. The ArSSR model defines the reconstruction of HR images at various up-scaling rates as learning a continuous implicit voxel function from observed LR data. By utilizing a set of paired HR-LR training examples, the SR task is transformed into approximating this implicit voxel function through deep neural networks. The architecture comprises an encoder and a decoder: the convolutional encoder extracts feature maps from LR inputs, while the fully-connected decoder approximates the implicit voxel function. Because the learned function is continuous, a single trained ArSSR model can reconstruct HR images at any arbitrary up-sampling rate from any LR input after training. Experiments across three datasets demonstrate that the ArSSR model achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D HR MR image reconstruction while utilizing only a single model to support arbitrary up-sampling scales.

Research in learned image compression has reached state-of-the-art performance using auto-encoder architectures based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In these models, an image is transformed into a quantized latent representation via CNNs and then reconstructed through a second set of CNNs, with the entire input image processed at once. Conversely, traditional leading compression methods for images and videos typically employ a block-by-block strategy. Recently, block-based learned compression approaches have emerged, utilizing auto-encoders on larger image segments alongside separate neural networks for intra/spatial prediction and deblocking/post-processing. This paper investigates an alternative block-based learned compression method that eliminates the need for explicit neural networks dedicated to intra prediction and deblocking. Instead, it employs a single auto-encoder with block-level masked convolutions operating on small 8x8 blocks. By applying these masked convolutions, both the encoder and decoder utilize reconstructed neighboring left and upper blocks during processing. This approach exploits the mutual information between adjacent blocks for compression and reconstruction, thereby removing the requirement for dedicated prediction and deblocking networks. As the system operates in a closed loop, it utilizes a specialized optimization technique known as asymptotic closed-loop design alongside standard stochastic gradient descent training. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves competitive image compression performance.

For a Coxeter system $(W,S)$, we define the boolean complex of involutions as a counterpart to the boolean complex of $W$ investigated by Ragnarsson and Tenner. Utilizing discrete Morse theory, we establish the homotopy type of this complex for a broad range of $(W,S)$, specifically covering all finite Coxeter groups, revealing that it corresponds to a wedge of spheres with dimension $|S| - 1$. Furthermore, we derive straightforward recurrence relations to calculate the number of spheres comprising this wedge.

Principal curves extend the concept of principal lines, which correspond to the first principal components in Principal Component Analysis. These curves can be defined stochastically as self-consistent curves derived from conditional expectations, or through variational calculus as saddle points of the expected squared difference between a random variable and its projection onto the curve, with the curve itself serving as the argument of the energy functional. Furthermore, Duchamp and St\"utzle (1993, 1996) demonstrated that planar principal curves can be calculated by solving a system of ordinary differential equations. This paper aims to extend that characterization to $\mathbb R^d$ for dimensions $d \ge 3$. After deriving the corresponding dynamical system, we present several examples of principal curves associated with uniform distributions over specific domains in $\mathbb R^3$.

Communication operates through two distinct viewpoints: the speaker's intent and the listener's interpretation. When these perspectives fail to align, it can result in negative consequences, including misunderstandings, reduced productivity, and open conflict. This study introduces a computational framework designed to analyze and compare these two dimensions within online public discourse. By merging logged data from Facebook comments with a survey of more than 16,000 individuals regarding their writing intentions or their perceptions of others' comments, we move beyond previous research that relied solely on third-party labels for metrics like sentiment or subjectivity. Our method directly captures the authors' actual intent. Specifically, we examine the distinction between stating facts and expressing opinions, as these are frequently conflated. Our results demonstrate that intent and perception diverge significantly. Individuals are more prone to perceive comments as opinions than to intend them, and the linguistic markers signaling intent often differ from those signaling perception. Furthermore, this gap between intent and perception affects conversation health; when a fact is misperceived as an opinion, the discussion is more likely to devolve into uncivil behavior compared to when the comment is correctly perceived. Collectively, these insights can guide the design of discussion platforms to foster more constructive interactions.

This study examines how the generalized uncertainty principle, arising from quantum gravity frameworks like string theory and doubly special relativity, influences cosmology. By employing generalized Poisson brackets, we derive modified Friedmann and Raychaudhuri equations and propose a dynamical dark energy model to account for the universe's late-time acceleration. Following an analysis of the interaction between dark matter and dark energy, which stems from the minimal length concept, we calculate the effective cosmological parameters and equation of state for both components. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the resulting model is mathematically equivalent to Phantom and Tachyon fields.

This study extends the analysis of quantum Markov states (QMS) by defining and explicitly calculating their mean entropies under specific conditions. This work represents a significant advancement in addressing a critical open problem in quantum probability: the computation of mean entropies for quantum Markov fields. Furthermore, it establishes new avenues for extending various notable findings regarding one-dimensional quantum Markov states and chains to multi-dimensional contexts.

Resolving delegation graphs for transitive votes is already a challenging task for many programmers. When extending the existing paradigm, where each voter is limited to a single transitive delegation, to a system allowing votes to be distributed across multiple delegations, the complexity of solving the delegation graph increases significantly. This article introduces a solution for a specific example graph and provides a non-formal proof demonstrating the algorithm's validity.

The notion of monochromatic connectivity was first proposed by Caro and Yuster. In an edge-colored graph, a path is termed a \emph{monochromatic path} when every edge along it shares the same color. An edge-coloring of $G$ is designated as a \emph{monochromatic connection coloring} (or $MC$-coloring) if a monochromatic path exists between any pair of vertices within $G$. The \emph{monochromatic connection number}, represented by $mc(G)$, refers to the maximum number of colors achievable in such an $MC$-coloring of a graph $G$. This paper investigates the monochromatic connection number across lexicographical, strong, Cartesian, and direct products, deriving various upper and lower bounds for these graph products.

Precise electromagnetic modeling of a subject's head is critical for source localization and brain stimulation. These applications depend significantly on model quality; although tissue geometry can be derived from MRI or CT scans, determining physical properties like electrical conductivity remains challenging using non-invasive methods. This paper introduces a tool designed to evaluate uncertainties in model parameters, calculate a parametric EEG forward solution, and determine current distributions for transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS).

This paper investigates ModMax nonlinear electrodynamics, a new theoretical framework that maintains duality rotations and conformal invariance, mirroring the properties of Maxwell's equations. When coupled with General Relativity, this model facilitates the examination of various gravitational effects, including charged black holes and gravitational waves. Our primary focus is on the model's dynamics and Hamiltonian analysis. We specifically examine the propagation of field discontinuities to derive their associated dispersion relations. Utilizing Plebański's first-order formalism and the Dirac method for constrained systems, we construct the effective Hamiltonian, categorize all constraints, and determine the degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the effective Hamiltonian is strictly bounded from below and explore the existence of non-trivial minima.

Semantic versioning is a prevalent method for signaling the nature of changes in package releases, yet developers often fail to adhere to it, causing breakage in dependent applications. To mitigate this issue, we propose leveraging machine learning (ML) to accurately forecast the new release type—major, minor, or patch—thereby ensuring correct semantic versioning. Our approach involves extracting various release-level features, including code complexity, change types, and development activities, and applying four distinct ML classifiers: XGBoost, Random Forest, Decision Tree, and Logistic Regression. An empirical study evaluated these classifiers using data from 31 JavaScript packages comprising approximately 6,260 releases, where 41 features were derived from historical source code and repository data. Results indicated that XGBoost outperformed the other models, achieving median ROC AUC scores of 0.78, 0.69, and 0.74 for major, minor, and patch releases, respectively. Furthermore, features related to change types emerged as the most effective predictors for determining the semantic versioning type. Finally, cross-package validation assessed the generalizability of the model, yielding median ROC AUC values of 0.76, 0.69, and 0.75 for major, minor, and patch releases, respectively.

This paper investigates the performance of an energy-efficient wireless communication system supported by a finite-element intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). Operating without instantaneous channel state information (CSI) at the transmitter, we evaluate system performance through the outage probability (OP) of energy efficiency (EE). We analyze two distinct channel models—Rician and Rayleigh—based on the presence or absence of line-of-sight (LOS) paths. For any arbitrary number of IRS elements ($N$), we derive approximate closed-form expressions for the EE OP utilizing Laguerre series and moment matching techniques. These analytical findings are corroborated by Monte-Carlo simulations. Additionally, we quantify the convergence rate of the derived expressions toward central limit theorem (CLT) approximations using the \textit{Berry-Esseen} inequality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the EE OP is a strictly pseudo-convex function of transmit power, ensuring a unique global minimum. To determine the optimal transmit power, we formulate the EE OP as a constrained optimization problem. To our knowledge, this work represents the first study of the EE OP as a performance metric in IRS-assisted wireless communication systems.

Let $N$ be a geodesically convex subset within a convex co-compact hyperbolic manifold $M$ possessing an incompressible boundary. We assume that every component of $\partial N$ is either a component of $\partial_\infty M$ or a smooth, locally convex surface inside $M$. We demonstrate that $N$ is uniquely fixed by boundary data comprising the conformal structures on the components at infinity, and either the induced metric or the third fundamental form on the locally convex surface components. We also characterize the admissible boundary data. This result extends both the hyperbolic Weyl problem and the Ahlfors-Bers Theorem. Applying this framework to quasifuchsian manifolds, we establish existence results for analogous problems regarding convex domains $\Omega \subset \mathbb{H}^3$ that intersect $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ along a quasicircle or quasidisk. The associated boundary data includes the induced metric or third fundamental form within $\mathbb{H}^3$, along with additional "gluing" information connecting distinct boundary components, situated either in $\mathbb{H}^3$ or at $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$.

This study presents a mathematical framework for tracking viral transmission within a fixed, isolated population. The model employs three color-coded states: red for currently infected and contagious individuals, green for those infected but no longer contagious, and blue for uninfected persons. This approach effectively functions as a digital representation of the classic SIR model developed by Kermack and McKendrick in 1927. In this RGB framework, the cumulative number of infections evolves through three distinct stages: an initial low level, a rapid growth phase characterized by a transition ramp, and a final plateau. Correspondingly, the growth rate starts at zero, climbs to a maximum peak aligned with the steepest part of the transition ramp, and subsequently declines back to zero. Key temporal characteristics, such as the ramp's slope, duration, and height, as well as the width and magnitude of the infection rate, are governed by a single parameter: the ratio of the contagious period of a red molecule to the average time between molecular collisions. Additionally, specific temporal milestones—including the onset of the transition ramp, the moment of maximum growth slope, and the peak of the infection rate—are influenced by both the population size and the contagious lifetime ratio. The paper derives and summarizes explicit formulas for these metrics. Furthermore, Appendix E details the impact of vaccinations.

This research examines the spectral problem linked to the equation describing small transverse vibrations of a finite-length viscoelastic tube transporting an ideal fluid. The study incorporates general boundary conditions that combine elastic and viscous damping effects acting on both the displacements and slopes at the tube's ends, encompassing standard cases such as clamped, free, hinged, and guided conditions as specific instances. Explicit asymptotic expressions for the eigenvalues are derived for generalized boundary conditions, with further specialization applied to the clamped scenario and the situation where damping influences slopes but not displacements. Specifically, the analysis investigates how eigenvalues depend on problem parameters, revealing that all eigenvalues reside within specific sectorial regions of the complex plane.

We examine deformations of cluster mutation sequences within finite type cluster algebras that break the Laurent property yet maintain the presymplectic structure dictated by the exchange matrix. The most basic instance is the Lyness 5-cycle, derived from the type $A_2$ cluster algebra, which deforms into the Lyness family of integrable symplectic maps on the plane. For types $A_3$ and $A_4$, we identify specific conditions under which these deformations yield two-parameter families of Liouville integrable maps in two and four dimensions, respectively. Furthermore, we apply Laurentification to these maps by elevating them to a higher-dimensional space of tau functions possessing a cluster algebra structure, thereby restoring the Laurent property. Additionally, we demonstrate that more general deformed mutations linked to affine Dynkin quivers correspond to four-dimensional symplectic maps resulting from reductions of the discrete sine-Gordon equation.

In topological dynamics, a distinct difference often emerges between systems driven by semigroups or monoids and those driven by groups. This brief note highlights that contrast by examining the relationship between almost periodicity and minimality.

We present a principled framework for unsupervised deep neural network structure learning. By interpreting depth and inter-layer connectivity as a hierarchical encoding of conditional independencies within the input distribution, the network's depth is naturally determined. This approach reformulates neural network structure learning as a Bayesian network structure learning problem. Rather than directly optimizing the discriminative architecture, the method learns a generative graph, derives its stochastic inverse, and subsequently constructs the discriminative graph. We demonstrate that conditional dependencies among latent variables in the generative graph are preserved in the resulting class-conditional discriminative graph. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that the deepest layers (convolutional and dense) of standard networks can be substituted with significantly more compact learned structures without sacrificing accuracy, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, our algorithm incurs minimal computational overhead and operates efficiently on standard desktop CPUs.

Traditional methods for predicting thermal preferences in buildings face challenges because they struggle to account for every environmental and personal variable. Incorporating new model features can significantly enhance a machine learning model's capacity to classify individual thermal preferences. Specifically, the spatial context of a building offers critical data regarding windows, walls, HVAC sources, air diffusers, and other elements that generate micro-environments affecting comfort. However, due to spatial heterogeneity, it is impractical to deploy sensors with the necessary resolution to capture all conditions. This research aims to extend an existing vector-based spatial model, Build2Vec, to predict the spatial-temporal indoor environmental preferences of occupants. Build2Vec leverages spatial data from Building Information Models (BIM) alongside real-world indoor localization. The framework integrates longitudinal, intensive subjective thermal comfort feedback obtained through smart watch-based ecological momentary assessments (EMA). This aggregated data is structured into a graph network representing objects and their relations, serving as input for a classification model to forecast occupant thermal preference. Test results demonstrate that this approach yields a 14-28% accuracy improvement over baseline models relying on conventional prediction inputs.

This study calculates the energy density of an electromagnetic wave propagating through both types of hyperbolic metamaterials (HMMs). By modeling a dispersive, absorbing HMM as an effective uniaxial crystal, we demonstrate that the response of type I and type II HMMs along directions perpendicular to and parallel with the optical axis resembles that of Lorentz and Drude media, respectively. Numerical examples are provided to illustrate the general characteristics of the direction-dependent energy storage capacity in both HMM configurations.

Lee and Kwon [12] defined an ordered semigroup S as completely regular if a ∈ a²Sa² for every a ∈ S. We characterize every completely regular ordered semigroup as a union of t-simple subsemigroups and every Clifford ordered semigroup as a complete semilattice of t-simple subsemigroups. Additionally, Green's Theorem has been established for completely regular ordered semigroups. In an ordered semigroup S, an element e is termed an ordered idempotent if e ≤ e². Various characterizations of regular, completely regular, and Clifford ordered semigroups are derived through their ordered idempotents, thereby establishing a foundational framework for both completely regular and Clifford ordered semigroups.

Legged robots struggle to replicate the agile behaviors seen in nature, such as sprinting and rapid turning. We introduce an end-to-end learned controller that sets a new agility benchmark for the MIT Mini Cheetah, maintaining speeds of up to 3.9 m/s. This system executes fast running and turning on varied natural surfaces, including grass, ice, and gravel, while demonstrating robust recovery from disturbances. The controller consists of a neural network trained in simulation using reinforcement learning and successfully deployed in the physical world. Two critical elements enable this success: (i) an adaptive curriculum for velocity commands and (ii) an online system identification strategy for sim-to-real transfer, adapted from previous research. Video demonstrations of the robot's capabilities can be viewed at: https://agility.csail.mit.edu/

We address a generalization of the three-spectral inverse problem: given the complete spectrum of the Dirichlet-Dirichlet Sturm-Liouville problem on the interval $[0,a]$, along with partial spectra of the Dirichlet-Neumann and Dirichlet-Dirichlet problems on $[0,a/2]$, and partial spectra of the Dirichlet-Neumann and Dirichlet-Dirichlet problems on $[a/2,a]$, we determine the potential of the corresponding Sturm-Liouville equation.

Drawing inspiration from arthropod exoskeletons, we developed a lightweight, semi-rigid framework featuring flexible joints capable of passively dissipating impact energy. By integrating the protective shell directly with the robot's core, this design preserves payload capacity. Constructed from affordable parts and consumer-grade 3D printers, the system is straightforward to assemble and modify. Our results demonstrate a sub-250g autonomous quadcopter equipped with visual navigation and sufficient processing power for deep neural networks, which can withstand multiple collisions, offers a five-fold improvement in passive energy absorption, and supports automated battery swapping. This robust platform is ideal for high-risk tasks, such as navigating cluttered environments or reinforcement learning training, ensuring safety for both the hardware and the surroundings.

This work begins an investigation into the Ramsey numbers of trails. For any integer $k \geq 2$, the Ramsey number corresponding to trails with $k$ vertices is defined as the minimum $n$ such that every graph $H$ on $n$ vertices ensures that either $H$ or its complement $\overline{H}$ contains a trail of length $k$. We establish that this Ramsey number is bounded above by $k$ and below by $2\sqrt{k}+\Theta(1)$, thereby refining the previous trivial upper bound of $\lfloor 3k/2\rfloor -1$.

This paper identifies the key characteristics that enable intelligent models to differentiate between legitimate websites and phishing sites. Phishing sites mimic the user interface and URLs of trustworthy sites to deceive users into sharing private information, which attackers may later exploit. Detecting these malicious sites using intelligent systems is crucial for safeguarding users, businesses, and online services operating over HTTP. To achieve this, models must identify and utilize the most relevant features as inputs for prediction. In this study, we introduce a novel network-based feature selection method using correlation-based networks, which are trained and tested on a standard phishing dataset. By partitioning the dataset according to instance labels, we construct three distinct networks and identify critical features by locating the network hubs. Our analysis presents these findings, marking the first application of a network-based approach to feature selection—a method proven to be both rapid and precise.

This paper addresses the challenge of designing an adaptive state observer for nonlinear systems characterized by unknown time-varying parameters and delayed measurements. While state observation has been extensively studied by numerous researchers, including Sanx et al. (2019), this work builds upon and extends results from Bobtsov et al. (2021b, 2021a, 2022a, 2022b). The solution assumes that the state matrix can be decomposed into known and unknown components, and the output vector is subject to a known constant delay. An adaptive observer is proposed to simultaneously reconstruct the unknown state and the time-varying parameters.

Coupling scalar fields to dark matter through conformal or disformal transformations creates a broad class of scalar-tensor theories with rich cosmological implications. Although this has been extensively explored for scalars, the vector counterpart remains largely unexplored. Consequently, we construct models featuring vector fields coupled to dark matter via these transformations and explicitly derive the general covariant interaction term independently of the specific gravity theory, ensuring applicability to general vector-tensor frameworks. To provide concrete examples, we adopt the standard Proca theory with an exponential potential for the vector-tensor sector and employ dynamical system techniques to analyze cosmological background dynamics under specific coupling functions. Despite this minimalist theoretical approach, the inclusion of these novel interactions significantly expands the parameter space compared to the uncoupled scenario, generating new solution branches for the vector equation of motion. As a result, distinct trajectories emerge in phase space based on the conformal and disformal coupling parameters. This analysis reveals new vector-dark matter scaling solutions and stable attractor points capable of driving late-time cosmic acceleration. Furthermore, numerical simulations are conducted to quantitatively assess the influence of these couplings on background evolution, showing that these effects are primarily governed by the magnitude and, in certain instances, the sign of the coupling parameters.

Light-shift-induced heading errors and detection dead zones represent two critical challenges in optically pumped scalar magnetometry. We present a single-beam atomic orientation magnetometry scheme that addresses both issues simultaneously by employing a Herriott cavity with path-bending and polarization reversal capabilities. Specifically, inserting a reflection mirror within the cavity bends the optical trajectories midway, splitting them into two distinct orthogonal zones to eliminate the detection dead zone. Additionally, half-wave plates are placed at the center of each optical region to invert the light's polarization upon every pass, thereby spatially averaging out light shift effects. This approach effectively removes unobserved heading errors caused by alternating current light shifts. The proposed methods are robust and easily adaptable for use in various other atomic devices.

We introduce RackLay, a deep neural network designed to predict the bird's-eye view layout of every shelf in a warehouse rack from a single monocular color image, a task we define as multi-layer layout prediction. Unlike existing methods that only estimate a single layout for the dominant ground plane, RackLay simultaneously generates both top-view and front-view layouts for each shelf within an object-populated rack. The architecture and its variants are highly adaptable, delivering accurate results across diverse scenes with varying numbers of visible shelves, different levels of shelf occupancy, and varied background clutter. Addressing the scarcity of real-world warehouse data and the challenges of data acquisition, we also provide WareSynth, a flexible synthetic dataset generation pipeline that allows users to customize the dataset for specific applications. Extensive ablation studies across architectural variants and comparisons with strong baseline models confirm RackLay's effectiveness for this novel multi-layered estimation problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fusing top-view and front-view data enables 3D reasoning tasks, such as metric-free space estimation for the rack.

Many psychophysical tasks aim to reveal how mammals make decisions in a changing environment. This study analyzes the properties of ideal and near-ideal observers within such a task, investigating how performance varies with task parameters and design to infer underlying decision-making processes. Specifically, we examine a dynamic clicks task where subjects listen to two streams of Poisson clicks with varying rates and are rewarded for identifying the side with the higher rate, which switches unpredictably. Our results indicate that a specific subset of task parameters creates regions in parameter space where optimal observers maintain constant accuracy, whereas near-optimal observers do not. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for various parameter ranges, an approximate normative model requires precise tuning to achieve near-optimal performance, offering a method to differentiate between normative models and their approximations. Additionally, we find that fitting these models using negative log-likelihood versus 0/1-loss functions yields non-equivalent results; specifically, the 0/1-loss introduces a bias in parameter recovery that grows with sensory noise. These insights provide strategies for distinguishing between difficult-to-separate models and highlight common pitfalls in experimental design, model fitting, and data interpretation.

This paper investigates a quasi-linear elliptic equation defined over the entire Euclidean space, where the nonlinearity exhibits either exponential or critical growth consistent with Trudinger-Moser type inequalities. Under specific conditions regarding the potential and nonlinearity, the study establishes the existence of a nontrivial positive weak solution for the equation. Furthermore, it demonstrates that a perturbed version of the equation admits two distinct positive weak solutions. These findings are derived by integrating the Trudinger-Moser inequality with the Mountain-pass theorem and Ekeland's variational principle.

This paper continues the investigation of graph classes where treewidth is large solely because of a large clique, focusing specifically on those with bounded tree-independence number. In a previous study by Dallard, Milani\v{c}, and \v{S}torgel (2022), it was demonstrated that the Maximum Weight Independent Packing problem—a generalization of both Independent Set and Induced Matching—admits a polynomial-time solution when the graph is accompanied by a tree decomposition with bounded independence number. We extend this line of research by identifying additional algorithmic problems solvable in polynomial time under the same assumption. These include, for every even positive integer $d$, the task of packing subgraphs at a distance of at least $d$ (which generalizes the Maximum Weight Independent Packing problem) and the search for a large induced sparse subgraph that satisfies any fixed property expressible in counting monadic second-order logic. Furthermore, as part of our methodology, we extend certain classical results concerning powers of chordal graphs to apply to general graphs within the framework of tree-independence numbers.

This paper provides an overview of searches for heavy resonances decaying into leptons or quarks. The findings utilize data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments, gathered during proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13~\textrm{TeV}$, and notably incorporate the complete dataset from LHC Run 2 for the first time.

Curvilinear structures are common objects of interest in microscopy imaging. Among these, crystallographic defects such as dislocations are extensively studied via transmission electron microscopy (TEM), where acquiring their three-dimensional structural data is crucial for understanding material properties. While 3D information is often gathered through tomography, this approach is labor-intensive as it necessitates capturing numerous images at various tilt angles under consistent conditions. Although alternative stereoscopy techniques reduce the required image count to just two, they still depend on human input and shape priors for precise 3D estimation. We introduce a fully automated pipeline capable of detecting and matching curvilinear structures in stereo pairs using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), without relying on any assumptions regarding 3D shapes. This study primarily focuses on reconstructing the 3D geometry of dislocations from stereo pairs of TEM images.

This work investigates $ZZ$ boson pair production at the LHC, examining the incorporation of electroweak (EW) corrections into theoretical predictions at fixed order and within multijet-merged parton-shower simulations. Specifically, we provide exact next-to-leading order (NLO) EW calculations for the processes $pp\to e^+e^-\mu^+\mu^-$ and, for the first time, for $pp\to e^+e^-\mu^+\mu^-j$, contrasting these with both EW virtual corrections and next-to-leading logarithmic (NLL) Sudakov approximations. We subsequently combine the exact NLO EW results with resummed Sudakov logarithms to derive an enhanced $\text{NLO EW} + \text{NLL } \text{EW}_\text{sud}^\text{exp}$ prediction. Additionally, we address the implementation of these EW corrections in MEPS@NLO event simulations using the Sherpa generator. Finally, we offer detailed phenomenological forecasts for inclusive $ZZ$ and $ZZj$ production, accounting for the most significant EW corrections via both the EW virtual approximation and exponentiated EW Sudakov logarithms.

A central tenet of the geometric approach to system theory involves analyzing the structural properties of linear dynamical systems via invariant subspaces. Typically, calculating these subspaces necessitates an explicit model of the system's dynamics. This paper addresses that constraint by deriving data-driven expressions for essential tools in geometric control. Specifically, we demonstrate that for linear systems with unknown parameters, both controlled and conditioned invariant subspaces can be identified directly from experimental data. Furthermore, we apply these methods to (i) determine a feedback gain that restricts the system state to a target subspace, (ii) calculate the invariant zeros of the unknown system, and (iii) construct stealthy attacks that evade detection.

Bernstein's characterization of Gaussian distributions is generalized to vectors through the lens of stability. This stability facilitates a soft doubling argument, which demonstrates that Gaussian vectors are optimal for specific communication channels characterized by additive Gaussian noise, such as two-receiver broadcast channels. A key innovation is that this approach does not depend on the existence of distributions that attain channel capacity.

Navigating virtual 3D environments, such as CAD or GIS models, using touch interfaces is inherently challenging because users must execute 3D operations on a 2D surface. Traditionally, this ill-posed problem is addressed through fixed, handcrafted interaction protocols that require users to memorize. We propose instead to automatically learn a new protocol that maps 2D inputs to 3D actions via reinforcement learning (RL). However, RL typically demands vast amounts of interaction data, which is scarce when human participants are involved. To mitigate this, we employ two collaborative agents: the first learns to mimic human 2D finger trajectories, while the second functions as the interaction protocol, interpreting those trajectories and translating them into 3D operations. To ensure the learned 2D trajectories remain similar to actual human gestures, we constrain the learning process by first performing state representation learning before applying RL. This step involves projecting gestures into a latent space derived from a variational autoencoder (VAE).

A primary difficulty in mining social media streams lies in identifying events actively discussed by groups within specific local or global areas, which are crucial for early warnings regarding accidents, protests, elections, or breaking news. However, neither the event lists nor the predetermined resolutions for time and space are known in advance. This study introduces an online spatio-temporal event detection system leveraging social media that operates across varying time and spatial resolutions. First, to tackle the issue of unknown spatial resolution, a quad-tree method partitions geographical space into multi-scale regions according to social media data density. Subsequently, a statistical unsupervised approach utilizing Poisson distribution and smoothing techniques highlights areas with anomalous post density. Event duration is then accurately estimated by merging occurrences within the same region across consecutive time intervals. A post-processing phase filters out spam, fake, or incorrect events. Finally, simple semantics derived from social media entities are integrated to evaluate the integrity and accuracy of detected events. The proposed method is assessed using Twitter and Flickr datasets from Melbourne, London, Paris, and New York. To validate effectiveness, results are compared against two baseline algorithms relying on fixed geographical splits and clustering. Performance is measured via manual calculation of recall and precision, alongside a newly proposed "strength index" that automatically gauges the accuracy of reported events.

Seam carving is a computational technique that resizes images based on their content rather than geometric constraints, allowing for both shrinking and expanding. While primarily used to eliminate redundant areas—regions where pixel intensities are similar—it can also manipulate images by adding or removing objects. Consequently, detecting these modifications is crucial for image security. Despite the difficulty even human observers face in spotting seam-carved images, there is a strong need for robust computational tools to identify such alterations. This paper introduces an end-to-end method for automatically detecting seam carving, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Experiments on various public and private datasets, utilizing different tampering setups, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

Using stochastic analysis on Riemannian manifolds, we establish two methods to find an explicit constant $c(D)$ for an $n$-dimensional compact manifold $D$ with boundary, ensuring that the inequality $\frac{\lambda}{n}\,\|\phi\|_{\infty} \leq \|{\rm Hess}\ \phi\|_{\infty}\leq c(D)\lambda \,\|\phi\|_{\infty}$ holds for any Dirichlet eigenfunction $\phi$ of $-\Delta$ associated with eigenvalue $\lambda$. Our findings yield the sharp Hessian estimate $\|{\rm Hess}\ \phi\|_{\infty}\lesssim \lambda^{\frac{n+3}{4}}$. Additionally, the second part of the paper derives corresponding Hessian estimates for Neumann eigenfunctions.

This paper details progress toward resolving a significant open issue in QCD thermodynamics: calculating the pressure to order $g^6$ within a weak-coupling expansion, which corresponds to four loops. Specifically, we define a category of contributing Feynman sum-integrals that contain lower-loop factors, outline the methodology for their tensor decomposition, and successfully relate them to scalar master sum-integrals that have previously been computed in existing literature.

Throughout the past 12 billion years, galaxies have adhered to a single, universal fundamental plane linking their star-formation rates (SFRs), stellar masses ($M_\star$), and chemical abundances. Departures from these scaling relations would signal a fundamental shift in galaxy evolution mechanisms. While observations previously suggested this relation might break down in the early universe, reliable measurements of chemical abundances were limited to redshifts $z \le 3.3$. Thanks to JWST, we can now analyze SFR, $M_\star$, and gas-phase metallicity in galaxies from the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang ($z \approx 7-10$). Our findings reveal that galaxies at this epoch follow universal SFR-$M_\star$ main-sequence and mass-metallicity trends, yet their chemical abundances are three times lower than predicted by the fundamental plane of later galaxies. Compared to current simulations, these results imply a faster onset of galaxy assembly and star formation than previously thought, suggesting that early galaxies remained tightly coupled with the intergalactic medium, continuously accreting pristine gas that diluted their metal content.

This study addresses Time-Domain Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) within dispersive and dissipative poroelastic media. The forward modeling involves solving an initial boundary value problem (IBVP) of poroelastic equations incorporating a memory term, while the FWI is defined as minimizing a least-square misfit function subject to this IBVP constraint. We derive the adjoint problem associated with this minimization, the solution of which determines the steepest descent direction during iterative optimization. Notably, the adjoint problem shares a numerical structure with the forward problem, allowing it to be solved using the same numerical solver. Furthermore, given the significance of energy evolution tracking in FWI for dissipative and dispersive equations, this paper also includes an energy analysis of the forward system.

This study addresses the challenge of achieving consistent depth prediction in complex environments across diverse lighting conditions.
