Current indoor datasets derived from RGB-D sensors or virtual rendering suffer from two major drawbacks: sparse depth maps (as seen in NYU Depth V2) and unrealistic illumination (found in SUN CG and SceneNet RGB-D). To overcome these issues, we introduce the Vari dataset, a new collection of indoor scenes created by sourcing internet 3D models, manually adjusting their lighting, and rendering photorealistic RGB images along with corresponding depth and BRDF maps. Our approach employs a novel convolutional block, DCA, which utilizes depthwise separable dilated convolutions on encoded features to capture global context while minimizing parameters. Furthermore, we apply cross-attention mechanisms to these dilated features to maintain depth prediction consistency under varying light settings. Experiments on the Vari dataset and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate significant performance gains. Additionally, we validate our DCA block through ablation studies, fine-tuning on NYU Depth V2, and testing on real-world data. The code, pre-trained weights, and the Vari dataset are publicly available.

We experimentally examine how externally applied strain influences the injection of 180$^\circ$ domain walls (DWs) from a nucleation pad into magnetic nanowires, a process critical for DW-based sensors. In this study, substrate bending generates strain that creates uniaxial anisotropy via magnetoelastic coupling. To evaluate these strain effects, we analyzed samples of $Co_{40}Fe_{40}B_{20}$, $Ni$, and $Ni_{82}Fe_{18}$, which exhibit in-plane magnetization and varying degrees of magnetoelastic coupling. Using a magneto-optical Kerr microscope with differential contrast imaging, we measured the magnetic field necessary for DW injection. Our results indicate that while strain increases the field required for injection, the switching mechanism is heavily dependent on the strain direction relative to the wire axis. We observe that low magnetic anisotropy aids in creating a domain wall at the pad-wire junction, whereas a strain-induced magnetic easy axis significantly raises the coercive field of the nucleation pad. Furthermore, we find that mechanical strain effects can be mitigated by introducing a magnetic uniaxial anisotropy perpendicular to the strain-induced easy axis; in $Co_{40}Fe_{40}B_{20}$, this anisotropy was successfully induced through field annealing. Micromagnetic simulations support these findings, demonstrating that effective anisotropy explains the observed behaviors, including switching mechanisms in the nucleation pad and DW pinning at the wire entrance. Given that DW injection is vital for sensor performance, these observations suggest that strain imposes a fundamental lower limit on the sensor's operational field window.

For a finitely presented group $G$, we investigate the criteria allowing automorphisms of quotients $G/N$ to extend to automorphisms of $G$. Our findings indicate that when $N$ is central in $G$, this lifting problem simplifies to solving a specific matrix equation. Leveraging these methods, we demonstrate that $Inn(G)$ is not a characteristic subgroup of $Aut(G)$ for metacyclic groups of order $p^n$ where $p \neq 2$.

High-cadence, high-quality monitoring of active galactic nuclei (AGN) reveals continuum variations that lag behind the shortest observed UV continuum, with these delays increasing as wavelength grows—a phenomenon known as "lag spectra." While these have traditionally been attributed to the central X-ray corona irradiating and heating the accretion disk, an alternative hypothesis links them to line and continuum emission from gas in the broad line region (BLR). This paper demonstrates the clear spectral signature of time-dependent diffuse gas emission within the lag spectra of six AGN. Additionally, it presents a novel lag-luminosity relationship derived from nine objects, representing a scaled-down version of the established lag(H-beta)-L(5100Å) relation. The shape and normalization of these lag spectra are fully consistent with diffuse emission from radiation-pressure-supported clouds in a BLR having a covering factor of approximately 0.2. Although contributions from an irradiated disk cannot be entirely ruled out, the data indicate that such an explanation is unnecessary.

We demonstrate that orthorhombic $t_{2g}^2$ perovskite LaVO$_3$ presents a rare instance where an orbital-ordering Kugel-Khomskii phase transition occurs, driven by factors other than Coulomb-enhanced crystal-field splitting. Consequently, the magnetic transition in this system occurs near or even above the super-exchange-driven orbital-ordering transition, contrasting with the typical scenario where magnetism emerges at significantly lower temperatures than orbital ordering. Our findings corroborate experimental observations of orbital ordering and G-type spin correlations existing just above the monoclinic-to-orthorhombic structural transition. By comparing these results with YVO$_3$ and $t_{2g}^1$ titanates to investigate the impacts of crystal-field splitting and electron filling, we show that in all such materials, the crystal-field strength is sufficient to inhibit the Kugel-Khomskii phase transition.

High-resolution precision spectroscopy offers numerous robust methods for investigating exoplanetary atmospheres. This study utilizes multiple VLT/ESPRESSO transit observations of the hot-Jupiter WASP-19b to re-examine atmospheric features previously identified in low-resolution studies but subject to dispute. By modeling the Rossiter-McLaughlin (RM) effect through spectral synthesis, we determined the system's stellar, orbital, and physical parameters. Narrow-band spectroscopy failed to detect neutral species of H\,I, Fe\,I, Mg\,I, Ca\,I, Na\,I, and K\,I, thereby establishing upper limits on their line contrasts. Cross-correlation analyses with atmospheric models yielded no detection of Fe\,I, setting a $3\sigma$ upper limit on its mass fraction of $\log\,(X_{\textrm{Fe}}/X_\odot) \approx -1.83\,\pm\,0.11$ via injection and retrieval. We demonstrate that H$_2$O remains undetectable at known abundances due to the absence of strong absorption bands and a relatively low signal-to-noise ratio. A barely significant peak ($3.02\,\pm\,0.15\,\sigma$) was observed in the cross-correlation map for TiO, aligning with previously reported sub-solar abundances; however, this serves only as a tentative hint rather than confirmation. Conversely, we confirm enhanced scattering toward blue wavelengths through chromatic RM measurements, indicating a hazy atmosphere. Furthermore, a reanalysis of low-resolution transmission spectra concludes that unocculted starspots alone cannot account for previously detected features. Our reanalysis of FORS2 spectra reveals a $\sim$100$\times$ sub-solar TiO abundance, precisely constrained to $\log\,X_{\textrm{TiO}} \approx -7.52 \pm 0.38$, which is consistent with the TiO hint from ESPRESSO. Finally, we propose plausible pathways to reconcile these findings with other seemingly contradictory results.

FIRST (Fibered Imager foR a Single Telescope) is a post-adaptive optics system designed for high-contrast imaging and spectroscopy at spatial scales finer than the diffraction limit. It attains high sensitivity and precision through a distinctive integration of sparse aperture masking, spatial filtering via single-mode fibers, and visible-light cross-dispersion. An array of microlenses subdivides the telescope pupil into sub-pupils, channeling light into single-mode fibers whose outputs are reconfigured in a non-redundant manner to measure complex visibility across the 600–900 nm spectrum for every baseline. The initial version of FIRST is currently installed on the Subaru SCExAO adaptive optics bench. This study details ongoing upgrades and testing aimed at enhancing stability and sensitivity to expand the dynamic range. The FIRSTv2 interferometric architecture utilizes a photonic chip beam combiner; we present laboratory results characterizing two distinct types of 5-input beam combiners with improved throughput. Each pair of sub-pupil interferometric recombinations is encoded onto a single output. To sample the resulting fringes, we employed temporal phase modulation by pistoning the segmented mirrors of a Micro-ElectroMechanical System (MEMS). By combining high angular and spectral resolution in the visible spectrum, FIRST provides unique capabilities for detecting and spectrally characterizing close companions, particularly on 30-meter class telescopes.

Existing value-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approaches utilize centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) to optimize individual Q-values and guide agent behaviors. Nevertheless, relying solely on expected, risk-neutral Q-values proves inadequate even within the CTDE framework due to reward stochasticity and environmental uncertainty, leading to failures when training coordinating agents in complex settings. To overcome these limitations, we introduce RMIX, a cooperative MARL framework that incorporates Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) over the learned distributions of individual Q-values. Our method first learns individual return distributions to analytically compute CVaR for decentralized execution. To address the temporal dynamics of stochastic outcomes, we develop a dynamic risk level predictor for adaptive risk tuning. During centralized training, we optimize CVaR policies by using CVaR values to estimate targets in the temporal difference error, while employing these values as auxiliary local rewards to update local distributions via Quantile Regression loss. Empirical results on demanding StarCraft II tasks demonstrate that RMIX significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior coordination and enhanced sample efficiency.

Drawing inspiration from the coupled-layer architecture of the X-Cube model, we present the X-Cube Floquet code, a dynamical quantum error-correcting scheme where the count of encoded logical qubits scales with system size. Defined on a three-dimensional lattice formed by intersecting two-dimensional layers along the $xy$, $yz$, and $xz$ axes, this code utilizes a periodic sequence of two-qubit measurements to link these layers. During each Floquet cycle, the codespace transitions between the state of X-Cube fracton order and layers of entangled, two-dimensional toric codes. We analyze the dynamics of the encoded logical qubits and contend that this novel code possesses a non-zero error threshold. Furthermore, we offer a new Hamiltonian formulation of the X-Cube model and, more broadly, investigate the phase diagram associated with the measurement sequences defining the X-Cube Floquet code.

Deep neural networks have significantly advanced single image super-resolution (SISR). However, traditional approaches remain limited to recovering a single high-resolution (HR) output based solely on visual input, which is often insufficient for predicting detailed, photo-realistic results at large upscaling factors (e.g., x8, x16). To address this, we introduce a novel perspective that frames SISR as a semantic image detail enhancement task, aiming to produce HR images that are both semantically plausible and faithful to the ground truth. By leveraging multi-modal fusion learning, we propose the Text-Guided Super-Resolution (TGSR) framework, which effectively integrates information from both text and image modalities. Unlike existing methods, TGSR employs a coarse-to-fine process to generate HR details that align precisely with textual descriptions. Extensive experiments and ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of TGSR in utilizing text references to restore realistic images.

The fundamental performance ceiling of sensors that translate physical perturbations into resonance frequency shifts is determined by the frequency stability of nanomechanical resonators (NMR). Although the impact of thermomechanical noise on this stability has recently been clarified, thermal fluctuation noise has received less focus, despite representing the ultimate limit for temperature sensing. This study presents a model for NMR frequency stability that accounts for both additive phase noise (encompassing thermomechanical and detection noises) and thermal fluctuation noise. We subsequently demonstrate, through experimentation, that optimized NMR devices can achieve frequency stability constrained solely by thermal fluctuation noise. Our findings indicate that existing models for NMR frequency stability are potentially incomplete and open pathways for NMR radiation detectors to attain the previously unreachable fundamental detectivity limits of thermal-based radiation sensing.

Future high-precision data from cosmic microwave background (CMB) lensing and tomographic galaxy surveys will enable robust cross-correlation analyses. This paper investigates the weighted skew-spectrum, a near-optimal estimator for the angular bispectrum amplitude, to efficiently extract non-Gaussian information regarding galaxy bias and cosmological parameters from bispectra correlating galaxies with CMB lensing. Our findings indicate that when combining Planck satellite data with the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the constraints on bias and cosmological parameters derived from the skew-spectrum differ from those of the full bispectrum by no more than 17%. We demonstrate agreement between our theoretical skew-spectra and those derived from N-body simulations, noting that accurate results require including gravitational non-linearities beyond perturbation theory and the post-Born effect for CMB lensing. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm to apply the skew-spectrum estimator to data; as a preliminary application, we use skew-spectra to constrain bias parameters and shot noise amplitudes via Markov chain Monte Carlo likelihood analysis, suggesting that percent-level precision for the linear bias parameter $b_1$ is achievable.

The BRST quantization of gauge fields necessitates the inclusion of auxiliary sources alongside the fields themselves, along with a bilinear anti-bracket constructed from these elements. This anti-bracket serves as a generalization of the Poisson bracket found in classical mechanics, and consequently, canonical transformations are extended into anti-canonical transformations. In this study, we extend the classical mechanical analogy further by demonstrating the derivation of anti-canonical transformations through generating functions. Additionally, we provide an example pertinent to the Hamiltonian formalism of QCD renormalization.

While the topological transitions within a grain boundary network during growth are understood for materials with uniform boundary energies, this knowledge does not extend to more realistic scenarios where variable energies permit a wider range of viable configurations. Consequently, simulating grain growth in such materials necessitates a method to enumerate every possible topological transition and identify the most energetically favorable outcome. This study develops and applies such a procedure to a microstructure modeled via a volumetric finite element mesh. Specifically, all potential transitions for a standard five-grain junction are cataloged, revealing that certain exceptional transitions remain energetically comparable to conventional ones even under uniform energy conditions. The simulation of grain growth for a representative microstructure employs a general discrete formulation for calculating boundary velocities. The approach is realized as a C++ library built upon SCOREC, an open-source, massively parallelizable framework for finite element simulations featuring adaptive meshing.

Let $T^m_f$ denote the Toeplitz quantization of a real $C^{\infty}$ function on the sphere $\mathbb{CP}(1)$, which results in a Hermitian matrix with spectrum $\lambda^m = (\lambda_0^m, \ldots, \lambda_m^m)$. According to Schur's theorem, the diagonal entries of any Hermitian matrix sharing the same spectrum as $T^m_f$ are contained within a finite-dimensional convex set whose extreme points correspond to permutations of the spectrum, specifically $\{(\lambda_{\sigma(0)}^m, \ldots, \lambda_{\sigma(m)}^m)\}$ for any permutation $\sigma$ of $(m+1)$ elements. This paper demonstrates that these convex sets converge to a significantly larger convex set in $L^2([0,1])$, characterized by extreme points of the form $f^* \circ \phi$, where $f^*$ represents the decreasing rearrangement of $f$ and $\phi$ varies over all measure-preserving transformations of the unit interval $[0,1]$.

This study examines the Klein-Gordon equation in $3+1$ dimensions featuring an external potential $V$ and a quadratic nonlinearity. We assume $V$ is regular and decaying, and that the massive Schrödinger operator $H=-\Delta+V+m^2$ possesses a positive eigenvalue $\lambda^2 < m^2$ with a corresponding eigenfunction $\phi$. This condition defines an internal mode, which generates time-periodic, spatially localized solutions for the linear system. The paper investigates the persistence of these solutions under the full nonlinear dynamics and characterizes the behavior of all solutions near zero. Under the assumption of a natural Fermi-Golden rule, our primary finding demonstrates that solutions to the nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation can be split into a discrete part, $a(t)\phi$, where $a(t)$ decays temporally, and a continuous part, $v$, exhibiting specific weak dispersive characteristics. We derive precise asymptotic data for these components, including sharp decay rates of $|a(t)| \approx t^{-1/2}$ and $\|v(t)\|_{L^\infty_x} \approx t^{-1}$ (with constants independent of the smallness of the initial data), as well as the growth of a natural weighted norm for the profile of $v$. Notably, this result generalizes the seminal Soffer-Weinstein work on cubic Klein-Gordon equations and confirms that radiation damping also occurs in the quadratic setting.

We introduce the KW-Sun database, which archives solar flares observed by the Konus-Wind instrument throughout its over 27-year operational period, spanning from November 1994 to June 2022. This regularly updated repository documents more than 1,000 events captured in triggered mode and can be accessed online at http://www.ioffe.ru/LEA/kwsun/. For every flare, the database offers time-resolved energy spectra ranging from approximately 20 keV to 15 MeV in FITS format, alongside count rate light curves for three wide energy bands (G1: ~20-80 keV, G2: ~80-300 keV, and G3: ~300-1200 keV) in high time resolution (as fine as 16 ms) available in ASCII and IDL SAV formats. This paper details the instrument's capabilities for solar observations, outlines the structure of the KW-Sun data, and describes its intended applications. The resulting homogeneous dataset, characterized by high temporal resolution and broad energy coverage across more than two complete solar cycles, serves as a valuable resource for both statistical and case studies, as well as providing essential context for solar flare research.

This study examines a specific class of stochastic reaction-diffusion equations, with primary findings focused on solution local well-posedness, regularity, and positivity. Key innovations include the incorporation of transport noise, $L^p(L^q)$-theory, non-smooth initial conditions, and higher-order solution regularity. The analysis relies heavily on maximal regularity estimates and precise blow-up criteria. These findings represent a significant advancement toward resolving open questions regarding the global well-posedness of such systems, with future work intended to apply these results to specific concrete examples.

This paper investigates how effectively finite quotients of the fundamental group can distinguish an $n$-dimensional compact flat manifold whose holonomy group is cyclic and of square-free order. Specifically, we present a formula calculating the cardinality of the profinite genus for the fundamental group of such an $n$-dimensional compact flat manifold with a cyclic holonomy group of square-free order.

Conventional nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) constructs a feature representation across the entire data space, effectively treating all features as equally important. However, practical applications often require only a subspace for accurate representation, as redundant features may be useless or detrimental. For instance, if a camera suffers sensor damage, the corresponding pixels provide no value for content identification, rendering the subspace of remaining pixels the only relevant area. This study introduces a novel NMF approach that employs adaptive weights to pinpoint critical features within the original space, ensuring that feature generation occurs solely within a selected subspace. Two strategies are presented to accomplish this: the fuzzier weighted technique and the entropy regularized weighted technique, both yielding simple iterative solutions. Empirical evaluations on various real-world datasets indicate that the proposed methods produce more precise feature representations than current alternatives. The implementation code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/WNMF1/FWNMF-ERWNMF.

Post-training quantization relies on calibration data to determine quantization ranges for network parameters and activations. However, this data is often drawn from the training set, which may be unavailable due to privacy constraints. This study investigates whether out-of-domain data can effectively calibrate trained networks without access to the original dataset. Specifically, we extend research beyond natural images to include vastly different domains such as X-ray, satellite, and ultrasound imagery. Our findings indicate that cross-domain calibration yields surprisingly stable performance for quantized models across 10 tasks in diverse image domains using 13 different calibration datasets. Furthermore, we observe that the performance of quantized models correlates with the similarity of Gram matrices between the source and calibration domains, offering a criterion for selecting optimal calibration sets. We believe this research paves the way for leveraging cross-domain knowledge to enhance network quantization and compression.

Let $D_\alpha P(z)=nP(z)+(\alpha-z)P^{\prime}(z)$ represent the polar derivative of a polynomial $P(z)$ of degree $n$ relative to a complex point $\alpha$. This paper offers a standalone proof, not relying on Laguerre's theorem, for an inequality involving the polar derivative of a polynomial with restricted zeros. This inequality was recently proposed by K. K. Dewan, Naresh Singh, and Abdullah Mir in their work "Extensions of some polynomial inequalities to the polar derivative" published in \emph{J. Math. Anal. Appl.}, \textbf{352} (2009) 807-815.

The conventional method of manually designing priors (like sparsity) to address inverse problems is gradually giving way to richer, learned priors, such as those generated by generative adversarial networks (GANs). This paper investigates the theoretical algorithmic dimensions of this learning-driven paradigm. For specific generative network architectures, we demonstrate a straightforward non-convex algorithm that (a) offers theoretical linear convergence for particular inverse problems and (b) outperforms standard techniques like back-propagation in practice. Additionally, we introduce an extension capable of managing model mismatch, where the generative prior does not perfectly align with the data. Collectively, these contributions form foundational elements for a more comprehensive algorithmic understanding of how generative models function within inverse problems.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are indeed the appropriate choice; however, their traditional reliance on fixed kernel sizes renders them too rigid, hindering feature learning and consequently reducing classification accuracy. Utilizing convolutional layers with varying kernel sizes can address this limitation by capturing more discriminative and relevant information. To this end, the proposed solution integrates the core concepts of 3D and 2D Inception networks with an Attention mechanism to enhance the performance of HSIC CNNs within a hybrid framework. This results in the \textit{attention-fused hybrid network} (AfNet), which consists of three parallel, attention-fused sub-networks. Each block employs different kernel sizes and repeatedly leverages high-level features to refine the final ground-truth maps. Essentially, AfNet selectively filters out the features most critical for classification. Experimental evaluations on HSI datasets demonstrate that AfNet achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art models, attaining an overall accuracy of 97% on Indian Pines, 100% on Botswana, and 99% on Pavia University, Pavia Center, and Salinas datasets.

Current state-of-the-art open-source network visualization platforms such as Gephi, KeyLines, and Cytoscape are ill-suited for analyzing street networks comprising thousands of roads because they lack support for polyline edges, navigable maps, GPU-accelerated rendering, interactivity, and multivariate data visualization. This paper introduces Dash Sylvereye, a new Python library designed to generate interactive visualizations of street networks on tiled web maps, thereby addressing this limitation. By leveraging WebGL for GPU acceleration, Dash Sylvereye enables the rendering of extensive street graphs on standard computers. Additionally, it offers streamlined functions for importing street topologies from OpenStreetMap using the OSMnx library. Integrated with the Dash framework, Dash Sylvereye facilitates the creation of web dashboards for temporal and multivariate street data by synchronizing visualization elements with other Dash plotting and UI components. We evaluate the library's performance on commodity hardware regarding animation CPU time and frames per second. Furthermore, to demonstrate its capabilities, we present a web dashboard application utilizing Dash Sylvereye to analyze SUMO vehicle traffic simulations.

This note examines the Wigner function representation to establish a holography-like correspondence between the phase space ('bulk') description of a general quantum system and its spacetime ('boundary') equivalent. Under specific conditions, the former may simplify to the classical dynamics of a local metric-like variable, whereas the latter manifests as bosonized collective field hydrodynamics. This generic pseudo-holographic duality does not depend on any specific system symmetry nor does it necessitate a link to an underlying 'string theory', distinguishing it from various 'ad hoc' applied holography scenarios.

This study investigates inflation within the framework of $f(R,T)$ gravity, specifically adopting the functional form $f(R,T) = R + \lambda T$, where $R$ denotes the Ricci scalar, $T$ represents the trace of the Energy-Momentum tensor, and $\lambda$ is a model parameter. We estimated the cosmological observables—the scalar spectral index $n_s$ and the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$—using a Double-Well potential. Our results indicate that when $\lambda = 115$, both $n_s$ and $r$ align well with PLANCK 2018 data. Furthermore, by assuming a Planckian vacuum expectation value within the Double-Well potential, we determined that the model remains consistent with PLANCK 2018 observations for an admissible range of the model parameter defined as $101 < \lambda < 130$.

Contemporary e-commerce platforms integrate diverse data types, including numerical ratings, textual reviews, and images, all of which can enhance recommendation systems. While textual reviews explicitly reveal user preferences, previous studies have primarily leveraged this information to refine user profiles and item features for rating prediction. However, the potential of review data for implicit-feedback tasks, such as top-N recommendation, remains largely underexplored. Addressing this gap, this study examines the efficacy of textual reviews in e-commerce top-N recommendation scenarios. We adapted several state-of-the-art review-based rating prediction models for top-N tasks and evaluated their performance and efficiency against existing implicit-feedback methods. Our findings indicate that models relying solely on review data fail to outperform standard implicit-feedback matrix factorization. Conversely, incorporating review information as a regularizer or auxiliary signal significantly boosts the performance of matrix factorization approaches. Nevertheless, the optimal architecture for integrating textual reviews into e-commerce top-N recommendation has not yet been established.

We examine the pointwise multiplier property of the half-space characteristic function within weighted mixed-norm anisotropic vector-valued function spaces of Bessel potential and Triebel-Lizorkin types.

This study utilizes data from the first six Parker Solar Probe encounters and applies the Partial Variance of Increments ($PVI$) technique to investigate the statistical characteristics of coherent structures within the inner heliosphere, specifically examining the link between magnetic field intermittency and observable phenomena like plasma heating and turbulence dissipation. Our findings indicate that proton heating occurs locally and is strongly correlated with magnetic structures where $PVI \geq 1$. On average, these events account for approximately 19% of the dataset, although this proportion fluctuates based on plasma conditions. We demonstrate that the waiting time distribution ($WT$) for these events remains consistent across all six encounters, exhibiting a power-law scaling at lower $WT$ values; this suggests that coherent structures are not uniformly distributed in the solar wind but instead cluster tightly. While the most intense magnetic discontinuities ($PVI \geq 6$), typically linked to reconnection exhausts, serve as sites for local magnetic energy dissipation and sharp proton temperature increases, their scarcity limits their overall contribution to energy dissipation. When accounting for clustering effects, we find that smaller-scale, more frequent structures with $1 \lesssim PVI \lesssim 6$ play the predominant role in magnetic energy dissipation. Furthermore, the number density of these events correlates strongly with global solar wind temperature, with denser intervals corresponding to higher proton temperatures ($T_{p}$).

The numerical sign problem has long been a significant barrier to first-principles calculations across numerous critical areas of physics. We demonstrate that the recently introduced tempered Lefschetz thimble method (TLTM), along with its worldvolume extension (WV-TLTM), offers a promising solution due to its reliability and adaptability.

Self-supervised learning has become a dominant approach for training high-quality vision transformers, making it crucial to optimize their performance on devices with limited memory and compute resources. However, the field has not yet investigated how to distill knowledge from one self-supervised Vision Transformer (ViT) to another. Furthermore, current self-supervised knowledge distillation (SSKD) techniques, which are primarily designed for ConvNet architectures, prove suboptimal when applied to ViTs. This paper introduces ViT-SSKD, a study focused on distilling self-supervised vision transformers. We demonstrate that directly transferring information from the teacher's critical attention mechanism to the student significantly reduces the performance gap between them. Experiments on ImageNet-Subset and ImageNet-1K reveal that our proposed method, AttnDistill, surpasses existing SSKD approaches and achieves state-of-the-art k-NN accuracy compared to self-supervised learning methods trained from scratch (specifically using the ViT-S model). Additionally, we are the first to utilize the tiny ViT-T model in self-supervised learning contexts. Notably, AttnDistill is algorithm-agnostic regarding self-supervised learning strategies, allowing it to be adapted to various ViT-based SSL methods for future performance enhancements. The project code is available at: https://github.com/wangkai930418/attndistill

The sequential updating (SU) decomposition is a recognized method for attributing profit and loss (P&L), such as within a bond portfolio, by segmenting the time horizon into $n$ subintervals and altering a single risk factor—like FX, IR, CS, or calendar time—during each segment. This study demonstrates that the SU decomposition converges as $n$ increases, provided the P&L attribution can be represented as a smooth function of the risk factors. We examine the average SU decomposition, which remains independent of the sequence or labeling of risk factors, and establish sufficient conditions to substantially lower computational complexity when calculating this average.

The Nevanlinna-Pick interpolation method has evolved from a concept in classical complex analysis into a valuable instrument for addressing diverse challenges in control theory and electrical engineering. Over time, numerous generalizations of the original framework have been explored, covering various function spaces, nonstationary scenarios, multivariable contexts, and interpolation involving matrix and operator data. This paper examines a specific variant of Nevanlinna-Pick interpolation concerning positive real odd functions evaluated at real matrix points. Although Cohen and Lewkowicz investigated this issue using convex invertible cones and the Lyapunov order, a complete solution remained elusive. We provide a resolution for a particular instance termed "suboptimal," which relies on links to the classical formulation. Our approach necessitates a representation of linear matrix maps attributed to R.D. Hill, alongside an examination of the conditions under which positive linear matrix maps are completely positive—a topic we previously addressed and will briefly revisit here.

This work establishes average-case lower bounds for explicit Boolean functions against bounded-depth threshold circuits featuring a superlinear count of wires. Specifically, for every integer $d > 1$, we identify a constant $\varepsilon_d > 0$ such that the Parity function on $n$ bits exhibits a correlation of at most $n^{-\varepsilon_d}$ with depth-$d$ threshold circuits containing up to $n^{1+\varepsilon_d}$ wires. Similarly, the Generalized Andreev function on $n$ bits shows a correlation of no more than $\exp(-n^{\varepsilon_d})$ against depth-$d$ threshold circuits with at most $n^{1+\varepsilon_d}$ wires. Prior to this, only worst-case lower bounds existed for this configuration (Impagliazzo, Paturi, and Saks, SICOMP 1997).

Leveraging these findings, we advance several related inquiries. We present satisfiability algorithms that surpass brute-force search for depth-$d$ threshold circuits with superlinear wire counts, marking the first such algorithms for depths exceeding 2. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Parity on $n$ bits cannot be computed by polynomial-size $\textsf{AC}^0$ circuits equipped with $n^{o(1)}$ general threshold gates. This improves upon previous results, which could not handle more than $\log(n)$ gates in this setting, and consequently implies subexponential-time learning algorithms for $\textsf{AC}^0$ with $n^{o(1)}$ threshold gates under the uniform distribution. Additionally, we provide nearly optimal bounds regarding the gate count in depth-$d$ threshold circuits computing Parity on average and establish average-case lower bounds for threshold formulas of arbitrary depth.

Our methodology relies on adaptive random restrictions, anti-concentration techniques, the structural theory of linear threshold functions, and bounded-read Chernoff bounds.

Many scientific domains, ranging from genomics to neuroimaging, necessitate the analysis of population-level metrics that change over time. These intricate datasets, characterized by both temporal and spatial dynamics, present significant analytical challenges. This paper introduces a novel framework for averaging such data to synthesize a representative template trajectory from multiple individual paths. We demonstrate that this task requires accounting for three distinct types of invariance: temporal shifts, spatial variations, and changes in total population size (or mass/amplitude). Drawing upon Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), Optimal Transport (OT) theory, and its unbalanced extension (UOT), we propose a criterion capable of resolving all three issues. Our approach utilizes a smooth formulation of DTW (Soft-DTW) to capture temporal discrepancies and UOT to manage spatial and magnitude variations. The resulting loss function enables the definition of spatio-temporal barycenters as Fréchet means. By applying Fenchel duality, we establish an efficient, parallelizable method for computing these barycenters through a new variant of entropy-regularized debiased UOT. Experiments involving handwritten characters and brain imaging data validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed loss for handling spatio-temporal data.

Throughout the 20th century, Eta Carinae (\ec) exhibited a distinct spectrum that has recently shifted toward resembling a typical Luminous Blue Variable (LBV). Two primary hypotheses attempt to explain this evolution: (1) a dissipating occulter situated before a stable star, or (2) a declining mass loss rate from the star itself. The first hypothesis accounts for the central star's apparent brightness increasing secularly despite constant luminosity, the Homunculus nebula's stable apparent brightness, and the direct light spectrum becoming increasingly similar to the reflected LBV-like spectrum. Conversely, the second scenario fails to explain these observations and predicts an increase in wind terminal speed, which contradicts empirical data. This study presents new evidence indicating that P Cygni absorption lines are strengthening over time, a trend inconsistent with a decreasing wind-density model. CMFGEN modeling of the primary star's wind with a minor occulter aligns well with observations. While some might argue that introducing a dissipating coronagraphic occulter makes the object even more enigmatic, it actually resolves numerous apparent contradictions among various observations. Furthermore, by attributing long-term changes to circumstellar effects and periodic variations to binarity, this work reveals that the star has been more stable since the 1900s than previously believed, challenging the earlier paradigm of it being an unpredictable entity.

Achieving chiral Majorana modes remains a difficult endeavor. Our objective is to understand the phase diagrams and parameter control of real-world devices employed in the search for chiral Majoranas. Moving beyond established minimal models, we have developed a numerical simulation framework based on a self-consistent Schrödinger-Poisson method to investigate, for instance, an s-wave superconductor coupled with a MnBi₂Te₄ thin film. Our findings indicate that both the superconducting proximity effect and the tunability of the chemical potential for topological surface states are heavily impacted by gate-induced electrostatic potentials. This introduces significant experimental challenges, resulting in a topological region that is markedly narrower than those predicted by previous minimal models. However, we demonstrate that chiral Majorana modes persist across a broad range of experimentally feasible parameters with practical tunability.

This study reports on a direct imaging survey targeting brown dwarf companions around the Sun's nearest stars, conducted in the mid-infrared at 10 microns ($\lambda_{c}$=8.7$\mu$m, $\Delta\lambda$=1.1$\mu$m) using the CanariCam instrument on the 10.4 m Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC). We observed the 25 closest stellar systems within 5 parsecs of the Sun that have declinations $\delta > -25^{\circ}$, noting that at least half of these systems host planets detected via radial velocity. The survey achieved a mean detection limit of 11.3$\pm$0.2 mag (1.5 mJy) in the Si-2 8.7$\mu$m band across angular separations ranging from 1 to 10 arcseconds. These capabilities would have permitted the discovery of substellar companions with projected orbital distances between $\sim$2 and 50 au, effective temperatures as low as 600 K, and masses exceeding 30 $M_{Jup}$, assuming an average age of 5 Gyr; for objects younger than 1 Gyr, the sensitivity extended down to the deuterium-burning mass limit. The absence of such detections allowed us to establish upper limits on the occurrence rate of these companions at depths and orbital separations previously unexplored by deep imaging initiatives. Specifically for the M dwarfs, which constitute the primary component of our sample, we determined at a 90% confidence level that fewer than 20% of these low-mass stars possess L and T-type brown dwarf companions with $m \gtrsim 30 M_{Jup}$ and $T_{eff} \gtrsim$ 600 K at projected orbital separations of $\sim$3.5--35 au.

The spherical harmonic transform serves as a vital instrument for analyzing spherical datasets, including cosmic microwave background observations. This study introduces an innovative scheme for spherical harmonic transforms capable of running on both CPUs and GPUs, offering particular efficiency when processing extensive collections of sky maps. A comparison with the standard Libsharp-HEALPix software reveals that our CPU implementation achieves a 2-10 fold speedup, while utilizing a cutting-edge GPU yields performance gains of up to 30 times. The corresponding open-source software package is hosted on GitHub.

This study examines the expansion behavior of one-dimensional strongly interacting bosons released from a harmonic trap using first-principles calculations. We employ the multiconfigurational time-dependent Hartree method for bosons (MCTDHB) to solve the many-body Schrödinger equation with high precision; this approach utilizes basis sets that are explicitly time-dependent and optimized via the variational principle. Our investigation focuses on regimes of very strong interaction where the system is not in the Tonks-Girardeau (TG) limit, meaning integrability is lost. The dynamics are analyzed through metrics of expansion radius and velocity. Results indicate that across a broad spectrum of strong interaction strengths, the expansion follows a trimodal pattern, contrasting with the unimodal behavior observed in non-interacting systems. Specifically, we identify three distinct time scales: the inner-core, outer-core, and the entire cloud. Additionally, we analyze higher-body densities and correlations, noting an antibunching effect. The two- and three-body densities exhibit a correlation hole along the diagonal due to intense interactions, a feature resembling the Pauli exclusion principle, which expands as the bosonic cloud disperses. Furthermore, we explore the expansion dynamics of 1D dipolar bosons. While very strong contact interactions drive the system toward a fermionization limit, strong interactions in dipolar bosons result in a crystal phase. Similar to the contact case, dipolar boson expansion is trimodal; however, the expansion velocity is significantly higher and diverges, unlike the convergent velocity seen with contact interactions. This divergent behavior is attributed to the unbounded energy associated with long-range interactions.

This study introduces a technique for constructing explicit tensor-train (TT) representations. We demonstrate that a broad spectrum of tensors can be explicitly modeled using sparse TT-cores, often achieving optimal TT-ranks. Numerical experiments indicate that our approach surpasses current methods in various practical scenarios, including game theory applications. Furthermore, theoretical analysis of computational complexity reveals that for specific tasks, such as calculating permanents, our method achieves operation counts nearly matching the known optimal asymptotics, which are typically derived through entirely different methodologies.

Machine Translation (MT) is typically perceived as a de novo process that produces target language equivalents from source text in a single pass. In contrast, this study explores a broader framework where an existing target sequence is refined into a valid translation of the source, thereby re-establishing source-target alignment. To address this bilingual synchronization challenge, we evaluate various architectures, including both autoregressive and non-autoregressive models, alongside different training strategies and practical scenarios such as simulated interactive MT, Translation Memory (TM) utilization, and TM cleaning. Our findings indicate that a single generic edit-based system, after fine-tuning, can match or surpass specialized systems trained specifically for these tasks.

The CMS experiment has conducted the inaugural search for the rare decay of the W boson into three charged pions, analyzing proton-proton collision data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 77.3 fb$^{-1}$. No significant excess over the predicted background was detected. Consequently, an upper limit of 1.01 $\times$ 10$^{-6}$ on the W boson's branching fraction to three charged pions was established at the 95% confidence level, offering a compelling motivation for theoretical studies of this decay mode.

In numerous real-world contagion scenarios, the number of contacts required for an individual to adopt a spreading entity varies across the population. Consequently, we investigate a contagion model featuring heterogeneous adoption thresholds. By deriving mean-field equations for the proportion of adopted nodes, we construct phase diagrams based on transmission probability and the fraction of nodes necessitating multiple contacts for adoption. Our analysis reveals a double phase transition characterized by an initial continuous transition followed by a discontinuous jump in the adoption fraction, driven by the heterogeneity of these thresholds. Furthermore, we identify hysteresis loops in the adoption fraction, attributed to the presence of adopted nodes within the densely connected core of the network.

This report stems from a project financed by JISC between 2010 and 2011 under its 'Managing Research Data' initiative, which aimed to investigate the management of Big Science data and formulate relevant recommendations. Big Science data is distinct due to its massive scale and unique sharing and utilization patterns compared to other fields. Using Gravitational Wave data from the LSC as a case study, this project analyzed these differences and generated advice intended for JISC, the funding council (STFC), and the LSC community.

Section 1 defines 'big science' and outlines its data culture, emphasizing how it necessarily or contingently diverges from other disciplines. Section 2 examines the advantages of a formal data-preservation strategy and the arguments for open data and robust preservation. Consequently, the report recommends that funders adopt light-touch guidelines for data preservation planning; since current practices in this area already align with excellent standards elsewhere, the primary suggestion is to formalize this planning to enhance auditability and openness to constructive feedback.

Section 3 provides a brief overview of the LIGO data management plan and aggregates available information on estimating digital preservation costs. Throughout the document, the OAIS reference model for an open archive serves as the guiding framework.

We demonstrate that an atom freely falling into a Kerr black hole within a Boulware-like vacuum emits radiation characterized by a Planck spectrum at the Hawking temperature. When considering a cloud of such atoms with random initial times, the resulting radiation is thermal. This emission arises from the acceleration of vacuum field modes relative to the falling atom, and its characteristics stem from the dominant influence of conformal quantum mechanics (CQM) near the event horizon. Although we illustrate this phenomenon using a scalar field, the underlying acceleration radiation exhibits a universal conformal behavior applicable to all fields in the background of generic black holes.

This series of papers investigates the chromospheric and coronal characteristics of solar active regions, beginning with a description of a comprehensive image dataset from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), curated for large-scale analysis. Aligned with and constructed to match the "Active Region Patches" identified by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) pipeline, the resulting "AIA Active Region Patches" (AARPs) offer an unbiased, multi-wavelength collection of FITS files. These files are spatially downsampled only through HARP-centered patch extractions, retaining full spatial resolution, and are temporally downsampled while still capturing both short-term kinematics and long-term trends. The AARPs database facilitates physics-informed parametrization and analysis via Nonparametric Discriminant Analysis in the series' second paper and is validated using Differential Emission Measure techniques. Spanning from mid-2010 to December 2018, the dataset occupies approximately 9TB and is accessible via the Solar Data Analysis Center.

We investigate particle pair production within a strong external electric field in a large N Non-supersymmetric Yang Mills theory via holographic duality. Through numerical analysis of inter-quark and effective potentials, and by examining rectangular Wilson loops, we analytically determine the critical electric field threshold that triggers catastrophic pair creation. Additionally, we compute the pair production rate under an external electric field using perturbative methods applied to circular Wilson loops. Our findings indicate that the vacuum of this Non-supersymmetric gauge theory becomes unstable across a specific range of Non-supersymmetric parameters.

We investigate the stability of tree-level positivity bounds on Standard Model effective field theory (SMEFT) operators when subjected to quantum corrections, specifically within the context of four-Higgs interactions. Our findings include: (i) even in minimal extensions of the Standard Model, such as those involving a single new scalar singlet or a neutral triplet, certain positivity bounds are strictly broken; (ii) for the first time, we calculate the renormalization mixing of dimension-eight operators, demonstrating that this process can push them outside their positivity region; (iii) however, the running of dimension-eight interactions induced solely by dimension-six terms adheres to these bounds. Consequently, our results imply that any observed deviations from positivity in SMEFT data do not automatically signal a violation of unitarity or causality, nor do they necessarily indicate new light degrees of freedom. Conversely, these findings impose stringent constraints on the structure of specific anomalous dimensions.

Electrohydrodynamics plays a pivotal role in various nanofluidic and biotechnological fields. At these miniature scales, the interplay between fluid dynamics and ion movement becomes more intricate due to the significant impact of thermal fluctuations. This study introduces a mesoscale approach utilizing the Dissipative Particle Dynamics (DPD) framework. By augmenting the standard DPD model with two scalar variables representing the count of positive and negative ions per particle, we establish a comprehensive framework. This framework utilizes the free-energy definition of DPD particles to derive fluctuation-dissipation relations and formulas for ionic fluxes, thereby connecting system dynamics with equilibrium characteristics. The model's validity is confirmed through simulations of planar electroosmotic flow under conditions of both overlapping and non-overlapping electric double layers. Furthermore, employing a Van der Waals equation of state allows for the inclusion of ionic finite size effects, which substantially alter concentration and velocity profiles compared to ideal solution scenarios.

The classical Cahn-Hilliard equation represents a gradient dynamics framework used to model phase separation in binary mixtures. Within the spinodal region, an initially uniform state spontaneously undergoes large-scale instability, evolving into drop, hole, or labyrinthine concentration patterns characterized by a specific structural length, followed by a continuous coarsening phase. In this study, we examine coupled Cahn-Hilliard dynamics involving two concentration fields, demonstrating that nonvariational (also termed active or nonreciprocal) coupling can trigger a small-scale Turing instability. At the primary bifurcation point associated with this instability, a branch of periodically patterned steady states arises. Additionally, localized states are identified, comprising patterned regions coexisting with a homogeneous background. The branches of these steady states, both parity-symmetric and asymmetric, organize into a slanted homoclinic snaking structure, a feature characteristic of systems governed by conservation laws.

The Euclid satellite, scheduled for ESA launch in 2022, will serve as a pivotal tool for cosmology over the coming decades. It integrates two instruments: the Visible (VIS) camera and the Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP). This study evaluates the impact of correlated readout noise within NISP detectors on final in-flight flux measurements. Specifically, analyzing the Multiple Accumulated (MACC) readout mode—which averages Up-The-Ramp (UTR) exposure frames in groups—we developed an analytical formula for the noise covariance matrix between groups when correlated noise is present. Additionally, we characterized the properties of correlated readout noise in NISP engineering-grade detectors through long dark integration periods. Assuming a $(1/f)^{\,\alpha}$-like noise model, we fitted the parameters to the data, yielding typical values of $\sigma = 19.7^{+1.1}_{-0.8}$ e$^{-} \rm{Hz}^{-0.5}$, $f_{\rm{knee}} = (5.2^{+1.8}_{-1.3}) \times 10^{-3} \, \rm{Hz}$, and $\alpha = 1.24 ^{+0.26}_{-0.21}$. Furthermore, through realistic simulations and a maximum likelihood flux estimator, we determined the bias between input and recovered flux. Our results show that applying the derived analytical expression for the correlated noise covariance matrix reduces this bias by up to a factor of four compared to the white noise approximation. Finally, we conclude that the bias in final in-flight NISP flux measurements remains negligible even under the white noise approximation, which serves as the baseline for Euclid's on-board data processing.

We introduce and analyze an optimal control framework for malaria dynamics, modeled through a system of fractional differential equations utilizing left and right Caputo fractional derivatives. We derive the necessary optimality conditions for this controlled dynamical system and employ the forward-backward sweep method combined with a generalized Euler scheme to numerically solve the resulting optimality system.

This study investigates how generating a "chain of thought"—a sequence of intermediate reasoning steps—enhances the capacity of large language models to handle complex reasoning tasks. Specifically, we demonstrate that such reasoning capabilities arise naturally in sufficiently large models through a straightforward technique known as chain of thought prompting, which involves providing a few examples of reasoning chains as prompts. Experiments conducted across three large language models reveal that this prompting method boosts performance on various arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning challenges, with empirical results that are notably significant. For example, when a 540-billion parameter language model is prompted with merely eight chain of thought exemplars, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the GSM8K math word problem benchmark, outperforming even finetuned GPT-3 equipped with a verifier.

We introduce novel algorithms for identifying and fixing errors in matrix products, matrix inverses, or other matrix operations over any field. These methods rely solely on the original inputs and the flawed output, requiring no extra encoding or auxiliary data. When the error count is low, the algorithms achieve softly linear runtime relative to the number of non-zero entries, while leveraging fast matrix multiplication to maintain efficiency even when errors are numerous. Our approach extends upon recent findings by Gasieniec et al. (2017) regarding matrix product correction, alongside established techniques in verification, sparse low-rank linear algebra, and sparse polynomial interpolation.

Estimating sparse hierarchical components from resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) data reveals patterns of brain functional connectivity, enhancing our grasp of the brain's organization and facilitating the development of disease biomarkers. Nevertheless, inter-scanner variability and other confounders hinder the robust and reproducible estimation of interpretable brain networks and their corresponding biomarkers. Furthermore, because the brain exhibits a hierarchical structure, single-scale decomposition methods fail to capture this complexity. This paper proposes leveraging recent advances in adversarial learning to derive interpretable hierarchical patterns in human brains using rsfMRI, ensuring robustness against "adversarial effects" like inter-scanner differences. By formulating the estimation task as a minimization problem solved through alternating updates, the study demonstrates, via extensive simulations and real-world data, that its components achieve superior reproducibility compared to established methods.

In developing recommendation systems, the goal is to present users with a curated set of relevant items. Internally, ranking models evaluate candidate pairs to determine the superior option, yet converting these pairwise judgments into a final list requires care. Since learned ranking models are inherently imperfect, relying solely on their predictions offers no assurance of reliability. We propose a method that, starting from a pre-trained ranking model, generates an item set with a rigorous guarantee of containing predominantly high-quality items. Our approach provides strict finite-sample control over the false discovery rate (FDR), independent of the underlying data distribution. Furthermore, our calibration framework allows for the principled and straightforward incorporation of multiple objectives within recommender systems. For instance, we demonstrate how to maximize recommendation diversity while maintaining a user-defined FDR threshold, eliminating the need to manually balance diversity and accuracy losses. Throughout, we address the challenge of learning to rank potential recommendations, validating our techniques on the Yahoo! Learning to Rank and MSMarco datasets.

The space of polynomial differential equations of a specific degree possessing a center singularity consists of numerous irreducible components. We demonstrate that the set of pull-back differential equations constitutes one such irreducible component. The approach employed in this work draws inspiration from the methods developed by Ilyashenko and Movasati. Central to our analysis are the Picard-Lefschetz theory applied to a two-variable polynomial with complex coefficients, the associated Dynkin diagram of that polynomial, and the concept of iterated integrals.

This paper introduces a serial chain hinge support, a rigid yet flexible structure designed to enhance the mechanical performance and robustness of soft-fingered grippers. Gravity often compromises the integrity of soft fingers during horizontal approaches, leading to reduced maximum payload capacity due to excessive finger deflection. To verify this, we conducted experiments measuring the payload and deflection of the SofIA gripper during both horizontal and vertical approaches. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this reinforcement preserves the gripper's original compliant behavior and kinematic model functionality. We also highlight the proprioceptive and exteroceptive capabilities, utilizing an RGB-D camera and flex sensors, to address two opposing manipulation tasks: grasping both small and large objects. Finally, we validated the enhanced SofIA gripper through applications in agriculture and daily activities.

Collaborative filtering (CF) is fundamental to recommender systems, where most approaches employ encoders to map users and items into a shared latent space, typically optimizing via the Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) loss. While current research predominantly focuses on enhancing encoder architectures (such as graph neural networks) to improve representation quality, there has been limited investigation into the intrinsic properties of these representations. Understanding these properties is crucial for elucidating the mechanisms of existing CF methods and creating new learning objectives. This paper evaluates representation quality within CF through the lenses of alignment and uniformity on a hypersphere. We first establish a theoretical link between the BPR loss and these two properties, followed by an empirical analysis of the learning dynamics of standard CF methods using quantified metrics for alignment and uniformity. Our findings indicate that improved alignment and uniformity both correlate with superior recommendation performance. Leveraging these insights, we propose a new learning objective called DirectAU, which directly optimizes these two properties. Extensive experiments across three public datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework, even when paired with a simple matrix factorization model, achieves significant performance gains over state-of-the-art CF methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/THUwangcy/DirectAU.

Autonomous robots can significantly benefit from human-supplied semantic descriptions of uncertain environments and states; however, creating integrated strategies that enable robots to model, communicate, and act upon this "soft data" remains difficult. To address these challenges, the Human Assisted Robotic Planning and Sensing (HARPS) framework is introduced, facilitating active semantic sensing and planning within human-robot teams. This framework formally unites the advantages of online sampling-based POMDP policies, multimodal semantic interaction, and Bayesian data fusion. By allowing humans to opportunistically define model structures and expand the scope of semantic soft data through sketching and labeling arbitrary landmarks, the system enhances performance in uncertain settings. The environment model is dynamically updated during search, enabling robotic agents to actively request new and pertinent semantic information from humans, which refines beliefs about unknown environments and states for superior online planning. Simulations of a UAV-based target search in a large-scale, partially structured environment demonstrate marked improvements in both time and belief state estimates required for interception compared to conventional planning relying solely on robotic sensing. Furthermore, human subject studies conducted in the same environment (n = 36) reveal an average twofold increase in dynamic target capture rates compared to scenarios involving only a lone robot, underscoring the robustness of active probabilistic reasoning and semantic sensing across various user characteristics and interaction modalities.

We demonstrate that the generating function for all amplitudes involving N twisted and M untwisted states—the Reggeon vertex for magnetized branes on R²—can be calculated once the correlator of N non-excited twisted states and the corresponding Green function are established. We also provide an explicit formula expressing this generating function as a functional of these objects.

We clarify the mechanism by which the interaction between diffusive mobility and number conservation stabilizes nearly phase-ordered active XY spins on a substrate. Across a broad spectrum of model parameters, stable uniform phases emerge with orientational order that is logarithmically stronger or weaker than in equilibrium; these phases exhibit either miniscule (hyperuniform) or giant number fluctuations, respectively, constituting a novel universality class. Conversely, under other parameter regimes, no stable uniformly ordered phase exists. This theoretical framework illuminates diverse systems, including active superfluids on substrates, oscillator synchronization, active carpets of cilia and bacterial flagella, and sandblasting.

Robotic rehabilitation has garnered considerable interest, particularly regarding diverse actuator and power transmission systems. Cable-driven rehabilitation robots (CDRRs), a relatively recent innovation, have seen rapid evolution in their control strategies. These robots boast advantageous characteristics, including low inertia, lightweight construction, high payload-to-weight ratios, extensive workspaces, and configurability. This paper categorizes and reviews CDRRs into three primary groups based on their applications for upper limb, lower limb, and waist rehabilitation. Within each category, we identify specific target movements and analyze promising CDRR designs concerning actuator types, controllers, and human-robot interactions, with a special focus on systems demonstrating verified clinical performance in real rehabilitation environments. A significant portion of this review compares control strategies and techniques across five main categories: impedance-based, PID-based, admittance-based, assist-as-needed (AAN), and adaptive controllers. By carefully contrasting the strengths and weaknesses of these methods, we aim to guide the design of future CDRRs.

This study provides a complete solution to the classical harmonic oscillator problem in the hyperbolic space $H_2^2$ (defined by $z_0^2+z_1^2-z_2^2-z_3^2=R^2$) using the Hamilton-Jacobi formalism. We demonstrate that, similar to other constant curvature spaces, the harmonic oscillator on $H_2^2$ is exactly solvable and constitutes a maximally superintegrable system. Furthermore, we prove that all bounded classical trajectories are closed and periodic. Specifically, orbits for bounded motion appear as ellipses or circles, whereas those for unbounded motion take the form of ultraellipses or equidistant curves.

On-chip creation and control of entangled multiphoton states are fundamental to quantum computing and communication. While lattice topologies have been developed to shield photonic states from disorder, entanglement across disparate topological configurations remained uninvestigated. We demonstrate biphoton entanglement between spatial modes with distinct topological properties within a silicon waveguide bipartite array. These findings underscore topology as a new degree of freedom for entanglement and pave the way for exploring information teleportation between trivial and topological modes.

The increasing popularity of location-based services (LBS) has driven demand for features such as finding nearby stores, proximity marketing, and on-road assistance. However, protecting sensitive user data—including identity, queries, and precise location—is paramount in these systems. In INFOCOM-BigSecurity 2019, Ma et al. introduced a privacy-preserving LBS protocol leveraging Somewhat Homomorphic Encryption (SHE). Their approach utilizes edge nodes to perform computations on encrypted location data, allowing the Location-based Server (LBS) to identify the $k$-nearest points of interest without ever accessing the user's raw coordinates, thereby safeguarding user privacy. This paper demonstrates a critical vulnerability in the protocol proposed by Ma et al.: their secure comparison mechanism suffers from a correctness flaw that prevents accurate comparisons. Consequently, standard attempts to rectify this error would inadvertently compromise security, enabling the LBS to recover the actual locations of users in every query.

For a compact, oriented, triangulated 3-manifold, we identify a non-trivial condition governing specific labelings of tetrahedra by elements of an arbitrary abelian group, termed angle structures. The smoothness of the manifold plays a crucial role in this framework. Inspired by the concept of volume in hyperbolic manifolds—which corresponds to the case where the abelian group is the multiplicative group of complex numbers—this construction offers a more general approach that relies exclusively on the abelian group structure.

Leveraging recent measurements of the cosmic star formation rate (SFR) density at redshifts $z\gtrsim 4$, we establish astroparticle limits for three dark matter models beyond standard cold dark matter (CDM): warm dark matter (WDM), fuzzy dark matter ($\psi$DM), and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM). Our methodology utilizes UV luminosity functions observed by the Hubble Space Telescope up to $z\lesssim 10$ and extending to UV magnitudes $M_{\rm UV}\lesssim -17$. By extrapolating these data to fainter, previously uncharted magnitude ranges and applying abundance matching with halo mass functions specific to each dark matter scenario, we derive a correlation between UV magnitude and halo mass. Subsequently, we calculate the cosmic SFR density by integrating the extrapolated UV luminosity functions down to a faint limit, $M_{\rm UV}^{\rm lim}$, which is defined through the abundance matching relation using two free parameters: the minimum halo mass $M_{\rm H}^{\rm GF}$ required for galaxy formation, and the dark matter-specific parameter $X$ (particle mass for WDM and $\psi$DM, or kinetic temperature at decoupling $T_X$ for SIDM). Employing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Bayesian inference, we compare our derived SFR density with current observational data at $z\gtrsim 4$ to constrain the WDM particle mass to $m_X\approx 1.2^{+0.3\,(11.3)}_{-0.4\,(-0.5)}$ keV, the $\psi$DM particle mass to $m_X\approx 3.7^{+1.8\,(+12.9.3)}_{-0.4\,(-0.5)}\times 10^{-22}$ eV, and the SIDM temperature to $T_X\approx 0.21^{+0.04\,(+1.8)}_{-0.06\,(-0.07)}$ keV at $68\%$ ($95\%$) confidence levels. Finally, we project how these constraints could be tightened by future refined SFR density estimates, contingent upon the confirmation of early JWST data on the UV luminosity function at $z\gtrsim 10$ down to ultra-faint magnitudes.

A \emph{power} refers to a word structured as $\underbrace{uu...u}_{k \; \text{times}}$, where $u$ represents a word and $k$ is a positive integer; this concept is also termed a {\em $k$-power}, with $k$ serving as its {\em exponent}. We demonstrate that for any $k \ge 2$, the maximum count of distinct non-empty $k$-power factors within a word of length $n$ falls between $\frac{n}{k-1}-\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ and $\frac{n-1}{k-1}$. Furthermore, we establish that the maximum number of distinct non-empty power factors with an exponent of at least 2 in a word of length $n$ does not exceed $n-1$. Both of these upper bounds extend the recent finding by Brlek and Li (2022), which set an upper limit of $n-1$ for the number of distinct square factors in a word of length $n$.

This paper investigates the efficacy of the simulated bifurcation (SB) algorithm for signal detection within multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, a critical area in contemporary wireless communications. Our findings demonstrate that the SB algorithm yields substantial performance gains compared to the conventional linear minimum-mean square error decoder regarding bit error rate versus signal-to-noise ratio, and also outperforms the coherent Ising machine approach for MIMO detection.

This study introduces a framework for building decay amplitudes within an orbital ($L$) and spin ($S$) coupling scheme applicable to particles of any spin. In $1\to 2$ decays involving solely massive particles, the angular dependence is entirely captured by the angular momentum component, while the daughter spins are coupled in the mother particle's rest frame, yielding only a constant contribution. For sequential decays, the total amplitude is formed by combining two $1\to 2$ amplitudes calculated in their respective mother particles' rest frames, which are then transformed into a common reference frame—typically the laboratory frame—using specific Lorentz transformations. This approach facilitates the coherent summation of amplitudes for various possible decay chains. When massless particles appear in the final states, polarizations are defined using the helicity basis, and the amplitudes are adjusted accordingly.

Identifying all possible name combinations becomes challenging and costly when entity names contain other names within them. We introduce a novel approach to detect both the outermost and inner nested entities. Our method trains a neural model using an objective function that treats the tag sequence of nested entities as the second-best path within their parent entity's span. Furthermore, we implement a decoding strategy for inference that iteratively extracts entities from the outermost to the innermost in an outside-to-inside manner. Unlike widely used Conditional Random Field models for flat named entity recognition, our approach requires no additional hyperparameters. Experimental results show that our method outperforms or matches existing nested entity handling techniques, achieving F1-scores of 85.82%, 84.34%, and 77.36% on the ACE-2004, ACE-2005, and GENIA datasets, respectively.

We demonstrate the formulation of celestial twistor amplitudes for Yang-Mills (YM) and gravity theories. This approach relies on a refined holographic correspondence linking the half-Fourier transform in split signature to the light transform within the boundary Lorentzian conformal field theory (CFT). Consequently, the derived celestial twistor amplitudes correspond to light-transformed correlators defined on the celestial torus. By employing an ambidextrous basis of twistor and dual twistor variables, we obtain explicit expressions for three- and four-point amplitudes in both YM and gravity. Notably, the four-point amplitudes assume a particularly compact form using elementary functions, revealing a striking structural similarity between the YM and gravity results. We also establish celestial twistor BCFW recursion relations and illustrate their application in constructing the four-point YM amplitude, identifying features that facilitate the computation of higher-multiplicity light-transformed correlators. Our calculations leverage the distinct properties of the split signature boundary structure; to properly motivate and emphasize these features, we initially develop our methodology in Lorentzian signature, which further enables us to prove a correspondence between Fourier and shadow transforms.

This research investigates the existence of solutions to the equation $(-\Delta)^{\frac{n}{2}}u = Qe^{nu}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, subject to the condition $V := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}e^{nu}dx < \infty$, where $Q$ takes the values $(n-1)!$ or $-(n-1)!$. Generalizing the findings of Wei-Ye and Hyder-Martinazzi to any odd dimension $n\geq 3$, we demonstrate that, to a significant degree, the asymptotic behavior of $u$ and the constant $V$ can be specified concurrently. Notably, when $Q=-(n-1)!$, the value of $V$ may be selected as any positive number. This result stands in contrast to the case where $n=3$ and $Q=2$, in which Jin-Maalaoui-Martinazzi-Xiong proved that $V\le |S^3|$ is necessary, as well as the case where $n=4$ and $Q=6$, where C-S. Lin established the bound $V\le |S^4|$.

Text-to-SQL semantic parsing is a crucial NLP task that enhances user-database interaction and serves as a core component of numerous human-computer systems. While recent advancements in this field have been propelled by large-scale datasets, most of these resources focus primarily on English. This study introduces MultiSpider, the largest multilingual text-to-SQL dataset encompassing seven languages: English, German, French, Spanish, Japanese, Chinese, and Vietnamese. Based on MultiSpider, we examine the lexical and structural challenges inherent to text-to-SQL, attributing them to specific language characteristics and dialectal expressions, and evaluate their severity across different languages. Experiments conducted under three scenarios (zero-shot, monolingual, and multilingual) demonstrate a 6.1% absolute decrease in accuracy for non-English languages. Furthermore, both qualitative and quantitative analyses were performed to elucidate the reasons behind the performance decline in each language. In addition to the dataset, we propose a straightforward schema augmentation framework called SAVE (Schema-Augmentation-with-Verification), which improves overall performance by approximately 1.8% and narrows the inter-lingual performance gap by 29.5%.

This study investigates the dynamics of a Brownian particle in one dimension subject to spatially periodic noise, employing both analytical methods and computer simulations. Without a deterministic force, the Langevin equation admits an exact formal integration. We analyze the short- and long-time behavior of the mean displacement (MD) and mean-squared displacement (MD), specifically observing a very slow $t^{-1/2}$ scaling for the mean displacement over time. When an additional external periodic force is applied near the critical tilt, we calculate the stationary current derived from the Fokker-Planck equation and detect an essential singularity when the noise strength's minimum reaches zero. Furthermore, to clarify how random periodic driving influences diffusion, we incorporate a phase factor into the spatial noise relative to the external force, determining the specific phase shift that maximizes the random force's impact on the long-time drift velocity and diffusion coefficient.

This study focuses on determining the existence of solutions for the initial value problem (IVP) and boundary value problem (BVP) associated with a coupled system of $\Psi$-Hilfer hybrid fractional differential equations (FDEs). The analysis relies on two fixed point theorems involving three operators defined within a Banach algebra. To demonstrate the practical applicability and effectiveness of the obtained results, specific examples are provided.

Research into the stability of liquid crystal elastomers offers a significant and productive field of study. At a fixed temperature, stretching a nematic body in its homogeneous state triggers instability, resulting in alternating shear stripes even under minimal stress. Additionally, these materials exhibit classic mechanical behaviors inherited from their polymeric networks, including necking, void nucleation, cavitation, and inflation instability. This study addresses two key questions: first, how instabilities in nematic bodies differ from those in purely elastic solids; and second, how these phenomena shift when material constants fluctuate. To address these inquiries, we conduct a systematic investigation of instabilities in nematic liquid crystal elastomers, analyzing the role of the nematic component alongside fluctuating model parameters governed by probability distributions. This integrated analysis aims to facilitate more accurate predictions of mechanical damage in nematic solid materials.
