This paper demonstrates that any real $H$-selfadjoint matrix admits a $\gamma$-FOCS Jordan form, which is simultaneously both flipped orthogonal and $\gamma$-conjugate symmetric.

Building on prior research regarding gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglows with hot thermal electrons at the base of a shock-accelerated tail, we calculate broadband emission spanning from radio waves to TeV gamma-rays using an electron distribution derived from first-principles simulations. This study marks the first presentation of how thermal electron distributions influence synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) emission. We demonstrate that thermal electrons introduce distinct temporal and spectral structures throughout the observable afterglow, creating a profile substantially distinct from models relying on pure power-law electron distributions. Specifically, for our standard parameters, early-time TeV emission is amplified by over an order of magnitude, accompanied by a time-varying spectral index absent in pure power-law scenarios. Additionally, we find that the presence of thermal electrons alters the "closure relations" in X-rays into a unique, time-dependent form; notably, the trajectory traced by the X-ray afterglow qualitatively matches observed data from traditional decay phases.

Determining the bulk compositions of transiting exoplanets located within the M dwarf radius valley, known as keystone planets, provides a critical method for discerning whether this gap results from atmospheric erosion or intrinsic formation processes. This study confirms a new keystone planet, TOI-1695 b, orbiting an early M dwarf ($M_s = 0.513 \pm 0.012\ M_\odot$), with an orbital period of 3.13 days and a radius of $1.90^{+0.16}_{-0.14}\ R_\oplus$. Positioned between theoretical models of thermally-driven mass loss and gas-depleted formation, TOI-1695 b serves as a vital test case for understanding the origin of the radius valley around early M dwarfs. The planetary nature of TOI-1695 b was validated using five sectors of TESS data alongside follow-up observations, including 49 precise radial velocity measurements obtained with the HARPS-N spectrograph. We determined a planetary mass of $6.36 \pm 1.00\ M_\oplus$, indicating that the planet cannot be composed solely of iron and magnesium silicates, suggesting instead a water-rich interior. This non-terrestrial composition contradicts the hypothesis that the system was sculpted by thermally-driven mass loss. Furthermore, a statistical analysis of the seven known keystone planets suggests that a thermally-driven mass loss scenario is improbable for this group. These results align with the growing consensus that the M dwarf radius valley stems from planetary formation mechanisms—where planets are born rocky, volatile-rich, or with gas envelopes—rather than from atmospheric stripping processes.

A multitype continuous-state branching process (MCSBP), denoted by ${\rm Z}=({\rm Z}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$, is defined as a Markov process taking values in $[0,\infty)^{d}$ and obeying the branching property. Its distribution is uniquely determined by its branching mechanism, which consists of $d$ Laplace exponents associated with $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued spectrally positive L\'evy processes, where each exponent features $d-1$ increasing components. We provide a formula for the probability that an MCSBP converges to 0 as time approaches infinity, expressed through its branching mechanism. Furthermore, we establish that extinction occurs at a finite time if and only if a specific condition regarding the branching mechanism is satisfied; this condition generalizes Grey's well-known criterion for the one-dimensional case ($d=1$). Our proofs rely on fluctuation theory elements for spectrally positive additive L\'evy fields, as recently developed in \cite{cma1}, and an extension of the Lamperti representation to higher dimensions, as demonstrated in \cite{cpgub}.

The growing potential of capsule robots in medical endoscopy has made precise dynamic control increasingly critical. Given the miniature scale of these devices, friction between the capsule and its surroundings is a vital component of the dynamic model, yet it is often challenging to predict beforehand. This study presents a tethered capsule robot system actuated by a robotic manipulator, featuring a powerful magnetic Halbach array mounted on the end-effector to regulate the capsule's state. To enhance control precision, the interaction friction is estimated using demonstrated motion trajectories. Experimental results utilizing this learned friction model show a 5.6% reduction in tracking error.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the standard for classification in numerous medical imaging domains. Concurrently, recent developments in interpretable machine learning have demonstrated significant promise in elucidating classifier decisions. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is among these emerging techniques, designed to offer visual insights into network outputs. This study presents the inaugural application of 3D CNNs combined with LRP for analyzing neonatal T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. By employing LRP, we convert the trained classifier's predictions into heatmaps that highlight the relevance of each voxel to the final decision. The resulting heatmaps uncover anatomically reasonable features that effectively differentiate preterm neonates from those born at term.

Dependency parse trees facilitate the identification of opinion words in aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA); however, static trees generated by standard parsers often yield sub-optimal results because they fail to capture the specific interactions between aspects and opinions. This study proposes learning an aspect-centric tree structure to minimize the syntactic distance between aspects and their corresponding opinion words. By adaptively correlating these elements within the learned structure, the model achieves closer proximity than traditional dependency trees, thereby improving polarity detection in ABSA. Experimental results across five datasets demonstrate that the proposed model significantly outperforms recent strong baselines. Additionally, comprehensive analysis on the SemEval Restaurant14 dataset reveals that the average distance between aspects and opinion words is reduced by at least 19%.

Recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) with function approximation have introduced numerous algorithms. Despite distinct algorithmic frameworks, these methods often share implementation nuances that are independent of the core logic yet frequently overlooked. This conflation of algorithmic novelty with implementation craftsmanship complicates the rigorous analysis of performance variations. This study examines a sequence of off-policy, inference-based actor-critic methods—specifically MPO, AWR, and SAC—to disentangle their theoretical innovations from their practical design choices. By deriving a unified control-as-inference objective, we classify each algorithm based on whether it employs Expectation-Maximization (EM) or direct Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence minimization, treating remaining specifications as implementation details. Extensive ablation studies reveal significant performance degradation when implementation choices do not align with the underlying algorithmic strategy. These findings highlight which code details are co-adapted with specific algorithms versus those that are transferable; for instance, tanh Gaussian policies and network sizes are highly specific to algorithmic types, whereas layer normalization and ELU activations are essential for MPO but also yield notable improvements when applied to SAC. We aim to inspire future research to better understand the origins of performance gains across algorithms, enabling researchers to leverage both algorithmic and implementational breakthroughs from one another.
We provide algorithms to build the N\'eron Desingularization and the straightforward case of the General N\'eron Desingularization found in \cite{KK}.

This study examines specific characteristics of degenerate Feller processes that terminate upon leaving a relatively compact region. The primary finding establishes broad criteria guaranteeing the existence of a quasi-stationary distribution for such processes, which may not be unique. Additionally, we address conditions that ensure both uniqueness and exponential convergence. Finally, these theoretical results are applied to nonelliptic and hypoelliptic stochastic differential equations.

Hybrid neural network models integrate the adaptive fitting capabilities of neural networks with differential equation models to capture real-world physical dynamics, making them highly effective for time-series analysis. While existing research predominantly addresses linear hybrid models, investigations into nonlinear scenarios remain scarce. This study introduces a hybrid nonlinear epidemic neural network to evaluate its efficacy in predicting the precise infection trajectory of an epidemic model. To ensure model trainability, we develop a new loss function that merges the bifurcation theory of nonlinear differential models with mean-squared error. Additionally, we establish unique existence conditions for ordinary differential equations required to estimate the correct infection function. Through numerical experiments utilizing the Runge-Kutta method, we validate the robustness of our proposed approach. Finally, we apply the model to actual COVID-19 data to accurately uncover the evolution of its infectivity patterns.

This paper outlines our approach for SemEval-2022 Task 3, PreTENS (Presupposed Taxonomies Evaluating Neural Network Semantics), which aims to determine the acceptability of sentences based on the taxonomic relationships between noun pairs. For Sub-task 1 (binary classification), we introduce a method to improve the robustness and generalizability of language models, specifically utilizing a two-stage fine-tuning process on the ELECTRA model enhanced with data augmentation. Through rigorous multi-task learning and data-enriched fine-tuning experiments, our proposed UU-Tax model demonstrates strong generalization capabilities. For Sub-task 2 (regression), we developed a classifier trained on features extracted from the Universal Sentence Encoder (USE). Beyond detailing our submitted systems, we also explore additional experiments involving pre-trained models and data augmentation. Error analysis was conducted for both sub-tasks to better understand model behavior. Our final results include a global F1-Binary score of 91.25% for Sub-task 1 and a rho score of 0.221 for Sub-task 2.

Identifying structural change is essential when analyzing time series and panel data. As the time span increases, the probability that model parameters have shifted due to significant disruptive events, such as the 2007-2008 financial crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, also rises. Consequently, detecting and dating these breaks is vital not only for accurate estimation but also for comprehending the drivers of change and their impact on relationships. This article presents a new community-contributed command, xtbreak, which offers researchers a comprehensive toolkit for analyzing multiple structural breaks in both time series and panel data. xtbreak is capable of identifying the presence of breaks, estimating their number and location, and generating confidence intervals for break dates. The command is applied to investigate shifts in the relationship between COVID-19 cases and deaths in the United States, utilizing both country-level time series data and state-level panel data.

Synonymy and translational equivalence represent the sameness of meaning both within a single language and across different languages. Serving as the core relations in wordnets and multi-wordnets, they are essential to computational lexical semantics; however, the field currently lacks a shared formal framework to define their characteristics and interconnections. This paper introduces a unified approach to these two relations, supported by experimental validation using existing resources. We argue that synonymy and translational equivalence are merely distinct forms of semantic identity. Consequently, this theory provides a robust basis for critically reassessing previous research in cross-lingual semantics and enhancing the development, verification, and improvement of lexical resources.

Utilizing novel qubits that inherently protect against noise offers a viable path to enhancing coherence in superconducting quantum circuits. Nevertheless, many such protected qubits operate at low transition frequencies, complicating their integration with standard transmon architectures. This study introduces and analyzes a method to entangle a tunable transmon with a Cooper-pair parity-protected qubit, a representative low-frequency system that encodes quantum data in opposite parity states of a superconducting island. We demonstrate that by adjusting the external flux on the transmon, non-computational states can facilitate a two-qubit entangling gate that maintains Cooper-pair parity regardless of the specific pulse sequence used. Notably, this gate functions similarly to a controlled-phase gate found in conventional transmon setups. Consequently, our findings indicate that established high-precision calibration techniques for standard gates can be adapted for use in hybrid qubit systems.

Recent empirical research has identified distinct thermodynamic phases governing collective animal motion; however, applying this thermodynamic framework to human movement remains ambiguous, largely because current tracking technologies lack sufficient resolution. In this Letter, we employed a novel ultra-wideband radio frequency identification system to capture high-resolution spatio-temporal data of movements within a classroom setting. By calculating the effective temperatures of the underlying systems, we identified two social phases—gas and liquid-vapor coexistence—corresponding to different temperature ranges. Furthermore, we introduced a straightforward statistical physics model capable of replicating these empirically observed phases.

Replicator equations reveal markedly distinct dynamics in zero-sum versus non-zero-sum games. In zero-sum scenarios, heteroclinic cycles emerge whenever population species cyclically dominate one another, as seen in Rock-Paper-Scissors; these erratic oscillations can lead to the divergence of time averages. Conversely, it is widely assumed that the most plausible replicator equations for non-zero-sum games adhere to the "Folk Theorem of Evolutionary Game Theory." This theorem posits that: (i) Nash equilibria correspond to rest points; (ii) stable rest points are Nash equilibria; (iii) strict Nash equilibria are asymptotically stable; and (iv) any interior convergent orbit approaches a Nash equilibrium. However, this paper introduces two broad classes of replicator equations derived from similar-order preserving mappings that display both stable and mean-historic behaviors. In the latter instance, time averages exhibit slow oscillations throughout the system's evolution without converging to a limit, ultimately resulting in the divergence of higher-order repeated time averages.

By characterizing Levin-Wen model excitations as Wilson lines, we calculate the energy level degeneracy for any given anyon theory and any trivalent graph embedded on an orientable compact surface. This finding enables the derivation of the finite-size and finite-temperature partition function, demonstrating that thermal phase transitions do not occur.

Despite the administration of billions of COVID-19 vaccines, significant hesitation persists, largely driven by vaccine misinformation spread across social media platforms. This paper introduces VaccineLies, a comprehensive dataset of tweets containing false information regarding both COVID-19 and Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines. The dataset organizes misinformation targets into vaccine-specific taxonomies that highlight dominant themes and concerns, offering insights into the discourse surrounding these vaccines. Structured into training, testing, and development sets, VaccineLies facilitates the creation of new supervised methods for detecting vaccine misinformation and identifying user stances on Twitter. Additionally, it serves as a foundation for future datasets focused on misinformation targeting other vaccines.

Inverse protein folding—the task of creating sequences that adopt specific three-dimensional structures—is a cornerstone challenge in bio-engineering and drug development. Historically, this field has relied on learning from sequences with experimentally determined structures; however, the limited volume of known structures restricts model learning capabilities. The advent of forward folding models like AlphaFold, which accurately predict structures from sequences, presents a new opportunity. Integrating these forward models into inverse folding workflows could significantly enhance performance by providing feedback on generated sequences via predicted structures or confidence metrics. Currently, though, the computational slowness of these forward models prevents their use in training optimization loops. This study proposes knowledge distillation of the folding model's confidence metrics (such as pTM or pLDDT) to create a compact, rapid, and end-to-end differentiable surrogate. This distilled model can then be embedded within a structure-consistency regularized inverse folding framework. Furthermore, the proposed regularization method is versatile and applicable to other design tasks, including sequence-based protein infilling. Extensive experiments demonstrate clear advantages over non-regularized baselines, yielding up to a 3% increase in sequence recovery and a 45% boost in protein diversity while maintaining structural consistency.

When wind passes over a water surface, it creates ripples that act as perturbations to the wind field, modeled as a parallel inviscid flow. For a specific wavenumber $k$, the perturbed wind streamfunction and the complex phase speed correspond to the eigenfunction and eigenvalue of the Rayleigh equation within a semi-infinite domain. Given the negligible air-water density ratio ($\rho_{\rm{a}}/\rho_{\rm{w}}\equiv\epsilon<<1$), the interaction between wind and ripples is weak, allowing the eigenvalue problem to be solved via perturbation methods. At the leading order, the eigenvalue matches the phase speed $c_0$ of surface waves. At the order of $\epsilon$, the eigenvalue acquires a finite imaginary component, indicating wave growth. Miles (1957) demonstrated that this growth rate is proportional to the squared magnitude of the leading-order eigenfunction evaluated at the critical level $z=z_c$, where wind speed equals $c_0$ and energy transfer from wind to waves occurs. In this study, we derive uniform asymptotic approximations for the leading-order eigenfunction applicable to long waves to compute the growth rate as a function of $k$. Under strong wind conditions, our findings indicate that the most rapidly growing wave occurs when aerodynamic pressure is in phase with the wave slope, a result validated through numerical confirmation.

We are developing an experiment designed to detect dark matter in the form of dark photons within the nano- to milli-eV mass spectrum. This project serves as the electromagnetic counterpart to magnetic dark radio experiments and operates as a frequency-time dual in two respects: it identifies high-Q signals within wide-band data instead of tuning a high-Q resonator, and it measures electric fields rather than magnetic ones. This paper outlines a pilot study utilizing room-temperature electronics that confirms feasibility and establishes constraints on the kinetic coupling constant $\epsilon \sim 10^{-12}$ across the 50–300 MHz range. By increasing real-time spectral coverage by a factor of 2,000 and reducing system noise, the experiment will soon be capable of probing a broad mass range with 100-fold improved sensitivity. The proposed setup consists of two phases: Phase-I will deploy a wide-band, 5-million channel real-time FFT processor covering 30–300 MHz, coupled with a back-end time-domain optimal filter to detect the predicted $Q \sim 10^6$ signal line using low-noise amplifiers. We have already conducted spot frequency calibrations with a biconical dipole antenna in a shielded environment, projecting a $5\sigma$ coupling limit of $\epsilon \sim 10^{-13}$ per month of integration. Phase-II aims to extend the search up to 20 GHz by incorporating cryogenic preamplifiers and novel antennas.

This paper aims to derive findings on Infinite Iterated Function Systems by utilizing Tarski-Kantorovitch fixed-point principles applicable to maps on partially ordered sets. To achieve this, we define two novel classes of Infinite Iterated Function Systems that are particularly compatible with these principles. Furthermore, we examine specific characteristics of the canonical projection mapping the shift space of an Infinite Iterated Function System from one of these new classes onto its attractor.

Based on the stationary vortex filament solutions derived by Castillo-Castellanos et al. (2021) for the far-wake of a rotor featuring tip-splitting blades, we establish our baseline flow. This study examines scenarios involving a single blade and a two-blade configuration with a hub vortex. In these configurations, each blade produces two tightly spaced, co-rotating tip vortices that arrange into a braided helical structure within the far-wake. Using the same vortex filament framework, we investigate the long-wave stability of these solutions by analyzing both the linear spectrum and linear impulse response. Our analysis reveals distinct instability modes. The first type involves the local pairing of adjacent helical turns, effectively modeled by the instability of a uniform helical vortex where the core size matches the average separation between the paired vortices. The second type arises from the pairing of consecutive turns within a vortex pair; this occurs exclusively in densely braided patterns and is accurately described by the instability of two interlaced helical vortices formed by straightening the baseline helix. The third type of unstable mode alters the separation distance between vortices in each pair while amplifying specific linear wavelengths; these modes also exhibit spatial spreading, albeit at a reduced rate.

Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) has become a premier method for extracting spatiotemporal coherent structures from high-dimensional datasets, largely due to its robust link to nonlinear dynamical systems through the Koopman operator. This study synthesizes two recent advancements that adapt DMD for systems involving actuation [Proctor et al., 2016] and those utilizing heavily subsampled measurements [Brunton et al., 2015]. Their integration creates a new framework for compressive system identification, with source code available at https://github.com/zhbai/cDMDc. This approach enables the derivation of low-order models from sparse input-output data and the reconstruction of full-state dynamic modes via compressed sensing, thereby enhancing the interpretability of reduced-order models. Furthermore, when complete state data exists, the framework significantly speeds up subsequent computations by initially compressing the data. We validate this unified approach on two benchmark systems, examining the impacts of sensor noise, various measurement types (such as point sensors and Gaussian random projections), compression ratios, and distinct actuation strategies (including localized and broadband inputs). The first case study applies the architecture to a test system featuring known low-rank dynamics but an artificially expanded state dimension. The second case involves a real-world engineering scenario: fluid flow over a pitching airfoil at low Reynolds numbers. This application serves as a rigorous and realistic validation of the method, demonstrating that dominant coherent structures are accurately characterized even in the presence of actuation and heavily subsampled data.

This study investigates learning methods for forward models utilizing local cell transition functions. We establish a formal definition for local forward models and introduce two fundamental learning strategies. Our analysis utilizes the game Sokoban, where incorrect moves can result in unsolvable states, making precise prediction of action outcomes essential to prevent such failures. Unlike learning the entire state transition function, local forward models enable the extraction of multiple training instances from a single state transition. Consequently, the Hash Set and Decision Tree models rapidly learn to forecast upcoming state transitions for both training and test data. Furthermore, when applied via a statistical forward planner, the most effective models demonstrated satisfactory performance even on unseen test levels. Our evaluation further examines various local neighborhood patterns and sizes to assess learner robustness regarding attribute quantity; results indicate that extracting too many attributes negatively impacts model performance.

We introduce a novel method for modeling musculoskeletal anatomy that diverges from prior techniques by avoiding the representation of individual muscle shapes as geometric primitives like polygonal meshes or NURBS. Instead, our approach utilizes volumetric segmentation, assigning each point within the volume to specific tissues such as muscle, fat, or bone. We offer an interactive tool where users manipulate muscle curves to control segmentation, with muscle shapes visualized through volumetric rendering. These curves provide both intuitive and powerful control over muscle morphology. This volumetric framework automatically resolves intersections between different tissue types (muscle-muscle, muscle-bone, and muscle-skin) during modeling and streamlines the calculation of muscle fiber fields. Furthermore, we present a new algorithm for converting the volumetric muscle data into tetrahedral or surface geometries suitable for downstream applications. Finally, we provide an interactive skeleton authoring tool that enables users to construct skeletal anatomy from a skin mesh using a library of bone components.

Extragalactic planetary nebulae (PNe) provide a reliable method for measuring distances to their host galaxies by utilizing the nearly universal shape of the planetary nebula luminosity function (PNLF). Achieving accurate distance estimates requires well-sampled PNLFs, as the count of observable PNe correlates with the galaxy's stellar mass. Consequently, researchers must either employ wide-field surveys or concentrate on the bright central regions of galaxies. This study adopts the latter strategy, conducting a census of PNe in the central areas of Fornax cluster galaxies using VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy on early-type galaxies from the Fornax3D survey. By meticulously separating nebular emission from the stellar continuum, we identified [OIII] 5007 {\AA} sources, excluded unresolved impostors and kinematic outliers, and compiled a catalogue of 1350 unique PNe across 21 early-type galaxies. This catalogue includes source positions, [OIII] 5007 {\AA} line magnitudes, and line-of-sight velocities. Leveraging these catalogued PNe, we derived independent distance estimates for each galaxy by fitting the observed PNLF while rigorously accounting for detection incompleteness. These individual measurements yield an average distance to the Fornax cluster of 19.86 $\pm$ 0.32 Mpc ($\mu_{PNLF}$ = 31.49 $\pm$ 0.04 mag). Our PNLF-based distance results align closely with prior estimates derived from surface brightness fluctuations, revealing no significant systematic offsets between the two methodologies, contrary to some earlier reports.

Medical institutions globally generate vast quantities of physiological data daily, sparking growing research interest in applying statistical methods to enhance diagnostic capabilities. However, analyzing these large datasets demands sophisticated computational power and efficient processing systems. Existing solutions often fall short in meeting performance needs or lack user-friendly, flexible programming interfaces. To overcome these limitations, we introduce \emph{LifeStream}, a high-performance stream processing engine tailored for physiological data. LifeStream effectively balances ease of use, achieved through robust temporal query language support, with superior performance, utilizing optimizations that leverage the periodic characteristics of medical data. Our evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates that LifeStream delivers end-to-end performance up to $7.5\times$ faster than leading streaming engines and $3.2\times$ faster than hand-optimized numerical libraries.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is frequently employed in statistical process control and anomaly detection. For bivariate datasets, we demonstrate that the minor projection—representing the direction of least variance in PCA-rotated data—is the most sensitive indicator of distributional shifts, with sensitivity quantified by the Hellinger distance between pre- and post-change distributions. Specifically, when a single parameter of a bivariate normal distribution changes, indicating a sparse alteration, this property holds almost invariably. Furthermore, simulations reveal that minor projections maintain high sensitivity across a broad spectrum of changes and initial configurations in higher-dimensional spaces. These findings provide a strong rationale for utilizing minor projections to identify sparse distributional changes within high-dimensional data.

Text data serves as a large-scale medium for investigating human cognition. While methods such as emotion analysis have become standard for computational social scientists, they often depend on third-party annotations with uncertain validity. As an alternative, this paper proposes applying online emotion induction techniques from experimental behavioral research to text-based emotion analysis. Participants were randomly assigned to happy, neutral, or sad conditions for data collection. The results validate the mood induction procedure. Subsequently, the study evaluated how effectively lexicon-based approaches could recover the induced emotions. All methods demonstrated statistically significant differences between the true emotional conditions. However, text-based measurements captured no more than one-third of the variance in emotion. Additionally, pretrained classifiers proved ineffective at detecting true emotions. The paper concludes by outlining limitations and proposing directions for future research.

The newly identified rapid transient GN-z11-flash is proposed to be the prompt ultraviolet flash linked to a gamma-ray burst that serendipitously occurred within the ultra-high-redshift galaxy GN-z11. By situating this flash within the framework of early gamma-ray burst ultraviolet emission, we demonstrate that its properties align with the known luminosity distribution of such events.

We develop a quantum mechanical model treating perfectly isotropic amorphous solids as fuzzy crystals, thereby establishing an analytical theory for glass vibrations at low temperatures. This framework is grounded in the principle that glass disorder mirrors classical fluid disorder, which is mathematically represented using noncommutative coordinates within the Lagrangian formulation of fluid mechanics. Our results show that the density of states in acoustic branches flattens considerably, naturally producing a boson peak in specific heat as a van Hove singularity. The model's validity extends to approximately 10% of the Debye temperature, matching the range of Debye's theory. Within this limit, theoretical predictions align excellently with experimental data for two representative glasses: a-GeO$_2$ and Ba$_{8}$Ga$_{16}$Sn$_{30}$-clathrate. Furthermore, the model reinforces the concept that the boson peak reflects liquid-like disorder, while offering a novel, mathematically streamlined framework for the unitary analysis of thermodynamic and transport properties in amorphous materials. It also serves as a robust foundation for incorporating additional complexities specific to various glass types.

This work addresses a problem in inverse scattering theory concerning whether an incident wave exists that produces no scattering for a given penetrable obstacle. We demonstrate that any penetrable obstacle with a real-analytic boundary possesses such a non-scattering incident wave. Furthermore, utilizing quadrature domains at zero frequency, we establish that obstacles featuring inward cusps also exhibit this property. Conversely, assuming the incident wave does not vanish, we prove a dichotomy for boundary points of any penetrable obstacle with this characteristic: the boundary is either regular, or the region outside the obstacle is extremely thin in the vicinity of that point. These findings are derived by applying results from the theory of free boundary problems.

Slender fibers are prevalent across biology, physics, and engineering, with notable instances such as cytoskeletal fibers and bacterial flagella. In this context, slender body theories (SBTs), which asymptotically determine resistance based on the fiber's slenderness parameter $\epsilon$, serve as valuable analytical and computational tools. However, challenges emerge when addressing twist and cross-sectional rotation: since a filament's angular velocity depends on the magnitude of the applied torque, asymptotic theories must accurately model rotational dynamics across a wide spectrum of angular velocities. This paper begins by reviewing the difficulties of applying existing SBTs—rooted in either full boundary integral or singularity representations—to rotating filaments, specifically demonstrating their failure to consistently handle rotation-translation coupling in curved geometries. We then introduce an alternative method that approximates three-dimensional dynamics using a one-dimensional line integral of Rotne-Prager-Yamakawa regularized singularities. Although this approach cannot precisely resolve the flow field in the immediate vicinity of the filament, it yields a grand mobility matrix with symmetric rotation-translation and translation-rotation coupling, rendering it effective across various angular velocities. To enhance fidelity to the three-dimensional geometry of the filament, we employ our regularized singularity model to derive a simple empirical equation linking the mean force and torque along the centerline to the cross-sectional translational and rotational velocities. The single unknown coefficient in this model is determined numerically through three-dimensional boundary integral calculations on a rotating, curved filament.

The economic instability triggered by the Great Recession necessitated unprecedented intervention by Central Banks, with unconventional policies impacting various economic sectors, including stock market volatility. To assess these impacts, we introduce a model-based classification system for Central Bank announcement dates, incorporating Markov Switching dynamics into a recent Multiplicative Error Model. This framework distinguishes whether an announcement leads to increased, decreased, or unchanged volatility. Specifically, we propose two smoothed probability-based classification methods derived from the model estimation, which yield results comparable to those of a classical k-means clustering procedure. Applying this approach to four Eurozone market volatility series successfully classified 144 European Central Bank announcements.

We introduce piXedfit, a Python package designed for pixelized spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting, which enables the analysis of spatially resolved galactic properties using either multiband imaging data alone or in conjunction with integral field spectroscopy (IFS). The software consists of six modules capable of managing all aspects of spatially resolved SED fitting. The core SED fitting module employs Bayesian inference, utilizing two distinct posterior sampling techniques: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and random densely-sampling of parameter space (RDSPS). Performance evaluations using mock SEDs from simulated IllustrisTNG galaxies demonstrate that both sampling methods effectively recover physical properties and star formation histories. Further validation was conducted on 20 galaxies from the CALIFA and MaNGA surveys, utilizing 12-band imaging data from GALEX, SDSS, 2MASS, and WISE, alongside IFS data from CALIFA or MaNGA. piXedfit successfully aligns imaging and IFS data in terms of resolution and sampling. Fitting solely photometric SEDs allows piXedfit to accurately predict spectral continua, $\text{D}_{\rm n}4000$, $H_{\alpha}$, and $H_{\beta}$, with derived star formation rates (SFR) consistent with those obtained from $H_{\alpha}$ emission. The RDSPS method yields fitting results comparable to MCMC while offering significantly faster computation. Equipped with a parallel computing module for efficient processing of large datasets, piXedfit is a versatile tool set to be made publicly available at https://github.com/aabdurrouf/piXedfit.

This study systematically examines how reducing the dimensionality of hyperspectral pixels influences pixel classification. We evaluated five reduction techniques—PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE—to compress 301-dimensional hyperspectral pixels, which were then utilized for classification tasks. By analyzing classification accuracy alongside compression ratios and reconstruction errors, we offer a new perspective on selecting optimal compression methods for pixel classification. The research utilizes three high-resolution hyperspectral image datasets covering common landscapes (urban, transitional suburban, and forest) acquired by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling laboratory at the University of Toronto. Our findings indicate that PCA, KPCA, and ICA offer superior signal reconstruction capabilities; however, their classification scores decline when compression rates exceed 90%. Conversely, AE and DAE achieve higher classification accuracy at a 95% compression rate, though their performance diminishes as the rate approaches 97%. These results highlight that both the choice of compression method and the specific compression rate are critical factors when designing a hyperspectral pixel classification pipeline.

The stringent performance demands of the European Spallation Source (ESS) have catalyzed significant advancements in neutron detector technology. To maximize the brilliance of the ESS source, optimizing detector and instrument designs has become increasingly critical. While most simulation tools currently available to the neutron scattering community focus on instrument optimization up to the sample position, they often neglect detector specifics. To address this limitation, the ESS Detector Group has expanded the capabilities of existing simulation software. An extensive framework has been created to support efficient and collaborative development of necessary simulations and analyses, utilizing the Geant4 Monte Carlo toolkit with enhanced physics features for specific scenarios, such as Bragg diffraction of thermal neutrons in crystals. Additionally, the MCPL (Monte Carlo Particle Lists) particle data exchange format, which is compatible with major community tools like McStas, Geant4, and MCNP, streamlines the integration of detector simulations with existing instrument models. Together, these resources provide a robust set of tools for customizing detector and instrument designs to meet specific application needs.

The LHCb experiment analyzed proton-proton collision data acquired at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 5.1 $fb^{-1}$, to search for $K_{\textrm{S(L)}}^0\rightarrow\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decays. No signal evidence was observed. This study establishes the first 90\% confidence level upper limits for both decay modes, yielding $B(K_{\textrm{S}}^0\rightarrow\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) < 5.1\times 10^{-12}$ and $B(K_{\textrm{L}}^0\rightarrow\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) < 2.3\times 10^{-9}$.

User interactions with search results are inherently biased by position, as items ranked lower are less likely to be examined and clicked, regardless of their true quality relative to others. While the standard method for unbiased click-based learning-to-rank (LTR) relies on counterfactual inverse-propensity-scoring (IPS), the counterfactual doubly-robust (DR) estimation technique—common in general reinforcement learning—has not previously been applied to this domain. This paper presents a novel DR estimator, the first specifically tailored for position-bias. A key challenge in addressing position-bias is that the treatment (user examination) is unobservable in click data; consequently, our estimator substitutes the actual treatment used in prior DR methods with the expected treatment per rank. Compared to the existing IPS approach, our new estimator offers more robust conditions for unbiasedness and significantly reduces variance. Experimental results demonstrate that it converges to optimal performance with several orders of magnitude fewer data points. Ultimately, this DR estimator advances the unbiased LTR field by delivering superior state-of-the-art performance alongside the most rigorous theoretical guarantees currently available.

Fine-tuning large pre-trained language models with task-specific heads has improved performance on numerous natural language understanding benchmarks, yet these models demand extensive training data, rendering them prone to learning and leveraging dataset-specific superficial patterns that fail to generalize. Prompting mitigates this data dependency by repurposing the language model head and structuring inputs to align with pre-training objectives; consequently, it was hypothesized that few-shot prompt-based models would avoid exploiting such superficial cues. This study empirically investigates whether few-shot prompting models also rely on these superficial patterns. Analysis of few-shot prompt-based models across MNLI, SNLI, HANS, and COPA datasets demonstrates that they indeed exploit superficial cues. Although these models achieve strong performance on instances containing such cues, they frequently underperform or merely marginally exceed random accuracy on instances lacking them.

This study introduces a method for analyzing and forecasting the spatio-temporal evolution of infectious diseases by employing a partial differential equation (PDE) formulation of the Susceptible, Infected, Recovered, and Deceased (SIRD) epidemiological model, wherein population compartments are represented as densities. Expanding upon previous research, we substitute global polynomial basis functions with locally supported ones, similar to those used in the finite element method, to spatially represent SIRD parameters. Temporal dynamics are handled by estimating constant parameters across time intervals aligned with the time steps of semi-discrete numerical schemes. Collectively, this approach constitutes a field inversion technique applied to SIRD parameters at each time step. When applied to ten months of 2020 data from Michigan and all of Mexico, the system successfully inferred spatio-temporally varying PDE SIRD parameters that accurately replicate pandemic progression and generated precise predictions for a three-week period extending into 2021. Notably, this method yields insights into the spatio-temporal fluctuations of infection, recovery, and death rates, as well as population mobility patterns indicated by compartmental diffusivities.

Numerical and experimental investigations into the velocity and temperature profiles near horizontal conducting plates in turbulent Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection were conducted across Rayleigh numbers ranging from $10^8$ to approximately $3\times10^{11}$ and Prandtl numbers from $0.7$ to $5.4$. The findings indicate that both velocity and temperature profiles align closely with the classical Prandtl-Blasius laminar boundary-layer profiles when re-sampled within dynamic reference frames that adjust to the instantaneous thermal and velocity boundary-layer thicknesses.

The universe is anticipated to evolve toward a de Sitter state where the horizon resides in thermal equilibrium. This article investigates the energy stored on this horizon and its associated thermodynamic fluctuations using the holographic equipartition law. Initially, it is demonstrated that a flat Friedmann--Robertson--Walker universe converges toward a de Sitter configuration, based on a cosmological model similar to the $\Lambda$CDM framework. Subsequently, applying the holographic equipartition law, the energy density within the Hubble volume is derived from the energy on the de Sitter horizon; this density is found to be constant and aligns in magnitude with the observed cosmological constant. Furthermore, thermodynamic fluctuations around stable thermal equilibrium are analyzed by employing a standard canonical ensemble formulation for the de Sitter horizon. These energy fluctuations are determined to be a universal constant equivalent to the Planck energy, independent of the Hubble parameter. Conversely, relative energy fluctuations are defined by the ratio of single-degree-of-freedom energy to the Planck energy. Currently, the order of magnitude for these relative fluctuations falls within the discrepancy range associated with the cosmological constant problem, approximately $10^{-60}$ to $10^{-123}$. These findings suggest that the energy stored on the Hubble horizon may correspond to an effective form of dark energy, while the energy maximally storable on the horizon could behave as effective vacuum-like energy within an extended holographic equipartition law.

This study demonstrates how real-time predictions of length-of-stay (LOS) can redirect outpatients from their designated facilities to less congested alternatives. We present the implementation of this diversion strategy across two primary health centers (PHCs), where patients are routed from their assigned center to the other based on predicted LOS estimates for both locations. Using a discrete-event simulation of patient flow within an Indian district, we identified significantly longer LOS at one PHC due to unequal patient distribution. The approach involves calculating the expected LOS at the moment of arrival by leveraging current system state data, generating real-time predictions by estimating wait times within the PHC's queueing subsystems. Subsequently, patients are diverted to the PHC with the more favorable predicted LOS, and simulation results confirm that this framework achieves more equitable resource utilization for outpatient care.

Neural closure models have recently emerged as an efficient method for approximating small-scale dynamics in multiscale systems using neural networks. The accuracy and stability of these models are heavily influenced by the selection of the loss function and the associated training strategy. This study systematically evaluates three distinct procedures: "derivative fitting," "trajectory fitting" utilizing a discretise-then-optimise framework, and "trajectory fitting" utilizing an optimise-then-discretise framework. Derivative fitting offers the simplest conceptual approach and the highest computational efficiency; it performs adequately on the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky test case but fails on the Burgers equation. In contrast, trajectory fitting is computationally more demanding but demonstrates greater robustness, making it the preferred method. Between the two trajectory fitting strategies, the discretise-then-optimise approach yields more accurate models. Although the optimise-then-discretise method can also generate accurate results, it requires careful selection of trajectory length to balance the training of long-term behaviors with the generation of accurate gradients. Furthermore, two existing theorems are reinterpreted to provide novel insights into the long-term accuracy of neural closure models based on their short-term performance.

An ambiguity arises when selecting field-strength renormalization factors within the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme beginning at the 3-loop order in perturbation theory. More critically, the naive choice of Hermitian factors has been demonstrated to yield divergent renormalization group functions, which are typically expected to be finite. We establish that these divergences cancel out within the renormalization group equation owing to the Ward identity linked to flavor symmetry. Furthermore, we show that any resulting divergences can be eliminated through the inherent renormalization ambiguity, making the flavor-improved $\beta$-function the preferred approach. Our findings clarify the source of divergence issues in earlier 3-loop Standard Model Yukawa $\beta$-function calculations and present the inaugural computation of flavor-improved 3-loop Standard Model $\beta$-functions in the gaugeless limit.

We address the Scale-Free Adversarial Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB) problem, where a player begins knowing only the number of arms $n$, without prior knowledge of the adversary's loss magnitudes, scale, or the total number of rounds $T$. In every round, the player observes bandit feedback regarding the loss vectors $l_1, \dots, l_T \in \mathbb{R}^n$, with the objective of bounding regret as a function of $n$ and the norms of these losses. We propose a bandit Follow The Regularized Leader (FTRL) algorithm featuring an adaptive learning rate, which yields two distinct regret bounds depending on the exploration strategy employed. Specifically, using non-adaptive exploration results in a regret of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{nL_2} + L_\infty\sqrt{nT})$, whereas adaptive exploration achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{nL_2} + L_\infty\sqrt{nL_1})$. Here, $L_\infty = \sup_t \| l_t\|_\infty$, $L_2 = \sum_{t=1}^T \|l_t\|_2^2$, and $L_1 = \sum_{t=1}^T \|l_t\|_1$, with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}$ notation omitting logarithmic factors. These represent the first MAB bounds that adapt to the $\|\cdot\|_2$ and $\|\cdot\|_1$ norms of the losses. Furthermore, the second bound establishes the first data-dependent scale-free MAB result where $T$ does not explicitly appear in the regret expression. Additionally, we introduce a novel technique for deriving a broad class of local-norm lower-bounds for Bregman Divergences. This method is pivotal in our analysis for managing regret when employing importance-weighted estimators for unbounded losses and may hold independent interest.

This report provides an overview of key topics from Session A3, which focused on the mathematical analysis of field equations at GRG18 in Sydney. Due to space limitations, certain subjects discussed during the session are either briefly addressed or omitted entirely. The summary primarily draws upon extended abstracts submitted by speakers and those who presented posters. I would like to express my gratitude to all participants for their contributions and assistance in compiling this summary.

Counting functions are developed to determine the number of sums of the form $u_1^{j/k} + u_2^{j/k} + ... + u_l^{j/k}$ (where $u_i$ are positive integers) that do not exceed a specified positive value $w$. These functions utilize convolution exponentials and exhibit a strong connection to the Riemann zeta function. The analysis concludes by deriving various estimates, with particular focus on the scenario involving sums of square roots, where $j=1$ and $k=2$.

Medical image datasets frequently rely on collaborative assessments by multiple human graders to annotate disease severity. Although intra-observer variability arising from individual differences is an inherent part of this process, its impact is frequently overlooked. This paper reframes intra-observer variability as an uncertainty issue, integrating label uncertainty as guidance to enhance the disease screening model's final decisions. The core approach involves categorizing images into simple and challenging cases based on uncertainty metrics, followed by the development of a multi-stream network to address each category distinctly. Specifically, for difficult cases, the network's ability to capture accurate disease features and mitigate uncertainty interference is strengthened. Experimental results from a fundus image-based glaucoma screening study demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses several baselines, with notable improvements in handling hard cases.

Polarisation Filter Array (PFA) cameras enable the straightforward and economical analysis of light polarization. Functioning similarly to the Bayer pattern in color cameras, these arrays share comparable benefits and limitations. A key challenge involves demosaicing raw images while accounting for local PFA variations and scene characteristics. While non-linear phenomena, such as cross-talk between adjacent pixels, are hard to model explicitly—suggesting that data-driven learning could be advantageous—the fixed nature of the PFA on the sensor hinders the acquisition of ground-truth polarization data for training. To address this, we introduce a novel CNN-based model that directly converts raw camera images into per-pixel Stokes vectors. Our contributions are twofold: first, we present a network architecture utilizing a sequence of Mosaiced Convolutions that align with the local filter arrangement; second, we develop a new method using a consumer LCD screen to collect real-world training data, ensuring invariance to monitor gamma and external lighting. Extensive comparisons against both algorithmic and learning-based demosaicing techniques demonstrate that our method achieves consistently lower errors, particularly regarding polarization angles.

This study addresses the novel challenge of distinguishing between image pairs through natural language descriptions. Unlike prior single-image captioning methods, this task requires extracting linguistic representations from two independent visual inputs. To tackle this, we propose an effective encoder-decoder captioning framework built upon a Hyper Convolutional Net. Furthermore, we introduce several novel techniques for fusing pairwise visual features and a discriminating referee to assess the pipeline's performance. Addressing the scarcity of suitable datasets, we have curated and annotated a new large-scale dataset using Amazon Mechanical Turk, comprising 14,764 images and 26,710 image pairs with free-form captions. This dataset marks the first resource dedicated to the relative difference captioning task. We evaluate our model on two existing benchmarks in the field, where it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

Precise and tailored assessments of task difficulty hold significant potential for enhancing user experiences; however, inherent user diversity complicates this process, as empirical data from one group often fails to generalize to others. This paper introduces a novel method for estimating game level difficulty on a personalized basis, adapting techniques from content recommendation systems. By applying factorization machines (FM) to a substantial dataset from a commercial puzzle game, we predict the number of attempts needed to complete future levels using attempt history from prior levels and data from other players. Beyond their performance and scalability, FMs allow the latent variable model to analyze the specific traits of players and levels that influence difficulty. We benchmark this approach against a non-personalized baseline and a personalized Random Forest model. Our findings indicate that FMs serve as a promising tool for game designers, facilitating both the optimization of player experiences and deeper insights into player behavior and game mechanics.

We will present a set of symmetries for simply-laced quantum connections, extending the quantum/Howe duality that links the KZ and Casimir connections. These symmetries emerge from quantizing the classical symmetries of simply-laced isomonodromy systems, which themselves generalize Harnad duality. The process of quantizing these classical symmetries entails constructing the quantum Hamiltonian reduction of the representation variety for any simply-laced quiver, applicable to both filtered and deformation quantization frameworks.

Detecting changes in Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery is a vital but difficult endeavor. Current approaches primarily concentrate on spatial domain feature extraction, often neglecting the frequency domain. Moreover, patch-based analysis can inadvertently introduce noise from marginal regions. To address these issues, we introduce a Dual-Domain Network. This model incorporates features from the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) domain, reshaping DCT coefficients to form a dedicated frequency domain branch. By leveraging representations from both spatial and frequency domains, the network effectively mitigates speckle noise. Additionally, we develop a multi-region convolution module that prioritizes the central area of each patch, adaptively modeling both contextual information and central features. Experiments across three SAR datasets validate the model's efficacy, and the source code is accessible at https://github.com/summitgao/SAR_CD_DDNet.
This paper primarily focuses on an early finding demonstrating that the orbifold stack is globally representable through specific $\infty$-categorical methods.

Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) involves determining whether a formula is satisfiable under specific background first-order theories. This paper concentrates on SMT(IA), which addresses satisfiability within integer arithmetic, encompassing both linear and non-linear variants. While dominant SMT approaches typically invoke CDCL-based SAT solvers in either eager or lazy modes, local search—a competitive method for combinatorial problems like SAT—has seen limited application in SMT. We introduce the first local search algorithm for SMT(IA) that operates directly on variables, thereby moving beyond traditional frameworks. Our proposed framework accounts for the differences between Boolean and integer variables, featuring novel operators and scoring functions designed specifically for integer arithmetic, along with a two-level operation selection heuristic. These components form LS-IA, a local search solver for SMT(IA). Evaluations on SMTLIB benchmarks demonstrate that LS-IA is both competitive and complementary to state-of-the-art solvers, showing particular strength on formulas containing only integer variables. Furthermore, a simple sequential portfolio combining LS-IA with Z3 surpasses current state-of-the-art results on satisfiable SMT-LIB benchmark sets.

Real-time bidding (RTB) has emerged as a dominant approach in display advertising, where every ad impression triggered by a user visit is auctioned instantly. In this process, demand-side platforms (DSPs) automatically submit bid prices, typically based on estimated impression values and optimal pricing strategies. However, existing bid strategies often neglect the significant randomness inherent in user behaviors, such as clicks, as well as cost uncertainties arising from auction competition. This study explicitly incorporates the uncertainty of estimated ad impression values and models a DSP's risk preference within a specific state and market environment using a sequential decision-making framework. Specifically, we introduce a novel adaptive, risk-aware bidding algorithm with budget constraints driven by reinforcement learning; it is the first method to simultaneously account for estimation uncertainty and the dynamic risk tendencies of a DSP. Theoretically, we reveal the intrinsic relationship between uncertainty and risk tendency based on Value at Risk (VaR). Consequently, we propose two implementations for modeling risk tendency: one based on expert knowledge that integrates three essential properties, and another utilizing a self-supervised reinforcement learning approach for adaptation. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework surpasses state-of-the-art methods in practical scenarios.

Wigner negativity and quantum correlations serve as key indicators of nonclassicality in continuous-variable quantum systems. This study explores their interplay within the framework of conditionally generating Wigner negativity. Previous research established that for Gaussian states shared between Alice and Bob, Bob can induce Wigner negativity on Alice's side through local measurements if and only if Gaussian steering exists from Alice to Bob. We extend these results to a significantly broader range of scenarios involving non-Gaussian states. Our findings demonstrate that if Alice can steer Bob's system using Wigner-positive measurements, Bob can remotely generate Wigner negativity in Alice's subsystem. While this confirms that quantum steering is a sufficient condition, we also establish that quantum correlations are generally not required for the conditional creation of Wigner negativity.

SPECT images typically suffer from low resolution and high noise levels due to the scarcity of detected counts and various physical degradation factors encountered during acquisition. This study investigates and evaluates the application of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for denoising static SPECT images. To simulate data, a cohort of 4D extended cardiac-torso (XCAT) phantoms was employed to represent 10 male and female patients with varying organ dimensions and activity uptakes. An analytical projector generated 120 projections spanning from right anterior oblique to left posterior oblique positions at two distinct noise levels. The first level corresponded to a standard clinical protocol involving a 987 MBq injection and a 16-minute acquisition (low noise), whereas the second level utilized one-eighth of that count rate (high noise). For training, high-noise and low-noise reconstructed SPECT images from 9 patients were paired, comprising 1,026 images (9 patients × 114 axial slices) each. The trained GAN model was subsequently tested on high-noise SPECT images from a single patient. Results demonstrated a substantial reduction in noise within the high-noise reconstructed images following GAN processing. This approach holds significant potential for lowering SPECT image noise, enabling a trade-off between reduced injection doses or shorter acquisition times and the maintenance of image quality comparable to original low-noise images for clinical diagnostic purposes.

This paper introduces "exit-ensemble distillation," a new knowledge distillation approach designed to enhance the classification capabilities of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) without relying on a pre-trained teacher model. By leveraging a multi-exit architecture that incorporates auxiliary classifiers (referred to as exits) within a standard CNN to facilitate early inference, our method trains the network using an ensemble of these exits as the distillation target. This strategy significantly boosts overall classification performance and establishes a novel distillation paradigm: whereas traditional distillation involves a teacher instructing a student, our approach demonstrates that students can assist one another and even aid the teacher in learning more effectively. Experimental findings indicate that this method yields substantial performance gains across various popular CNN architectures, including VGG, ResNet, ResNeXt, and WideResNet. Additionally, it accelerates learning convergence and enhances stability. The associated code will be made available on Github.

Adversarial machine learning has highlighted significant security vulnerabilities in neural networks, becoming a critical area of recent research. Traditionally, "adversarial perturbations" have been defined strictly within the input space as imperceptible modifications that induce model errors. This study extends that concept to the model weight space, specifically targeting the injection of backdoors into trained deep neural networks (DNNs), thereby revealing a security risk associated with deploying publicly available pre-trained models. In this context, a backdoor enables a model to produce a specific outcome when a trigger pattern is present in the input, while maintaining normal predictions for inputs without the trigger. From an adversarial perspective, these weight perturbations are constrained within an $\ell_{\infty}$ norm of the original weights. We propose introducing such perturbations by applying a composite loss function—balancing the original model's predictions against the desired trigger response—optimized via projected gradient descent. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that these adversarial weight perturbations are universally applicable across various computer vision and natural language processing tasks. Furthermore, our findings indicate that effective backdoor injection can be achieved with minimal average relative changes to the model's weight values across multiple applications.

We investigate a pseudoscalar dark-matter framework originating from a complex singlet extension of the Standard Model (SM), demonstrating that dark-matter--nucleon scattering is inhibited when two CP-even scalars are degenerate. Within this degenerate-scalar scenario, we examine the parameter space compatible with direct detection limits and dark matter relic density constraints. Furthermore, we propose verifying this scenario using the recoil mass technique at the International Linear Collider. Our analysis indicates that a pair of states with a mass separation of 0.2 GeV can be resolved from the single SM-like Higgs state at a $5\sigma$ significance level with an integrated luminosity of 2 ab$^{-1}$.

The Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) integrates smart vehicles, Autonomous Vehicles (AVs), and roadside units (RSUs) to facilitate wireless communication for enhanced transportation services, including reduced congestion, improved traffic efficiency, and fewer accidents. However, IoVs face significant challenges regarding security, privacy, and trust. Blockchain technology has emerged as a decentralized solution to bolster security without relying on trusted third parties. It offers advantages such as trustworthiness, immutability, and the mitigation of single points of failure and various attacks. This work reviews the state-of-the-art in Blockchain-enabled IoVs (BIoV), focusing on applications like crowdsourcing, energy trading, traffic congestion alleviation, collision avoidance, and infotainment with content caching. Additionally, we explore in-depth applications of federated learning (FL) within BIoVs. The paper investigates key challenges arising from integrating Blockchain with IoVs across domains such as edge computing, machine learning, and FL. Finally, it outlines open issues and future opportunities concerning AI-enabled BIoVs, hardware-assisted security, and quantum computing attacks.

We report a neutron scattering study of Ce1-xYxAl3 examining the effects of chemical pressure, which drives a shift from heavy-fermion characteristics in CeAl3 (TK=5 K) to a mixed-valence regime at x=0.5 (TK=150 K). This transition is precisely described on an absolute intensity scale by an enhancement of the k-f hybridization strength, Vkf, within the Anderson impurity model. Surprisingly, the primary consequence of increasing Vkf is not the broadening of low-energy features in the dynamic magnetic susceptibility, but rather the transfer of spectral weight to higher energies.

Recent advances have demonstrated that contextualized learning on extensive language corpora, exemplified by embeddings like ELMo, significantly enhances word semantics and improves state-of-the-art performance across numerous natural language tasks. This study incorporates acoustic data into contextualized lexical embeddings by introducing multimodal inputs to a pretrained bidirectional language model trained on spoken language comprising both text and audio. The resulting multimodal representations capture paralinguistic cues that can alter word meanings and convey affective information. We demonstrate that these embeddings surpass previous multimodal state-of-the-art models in emotion recognition tasks using the CMU-MOSEI dataset.

Let $H$ be a fixed undirected graph with $k$ vertices. The $H$-hitting set problem seeks to remove the minimum number of vertices from a graph $G$ such that the remaining graph contains no subgraph isomorphic to $H$. As a special case of the vertex cover problem on $k$-uniform hypergraphs, this problem admits an efficient $k$-factor approximation algorithm. This article aims to determine for which graphs $H$ this basic approximation ratio of $k$ can be improved.

The Non-Uniform $k$-Center problem extends the classic $k$-center clustering task by requiring the coverage of a point set in a metric space using balls with predefined radii. Specifically, in the $t$-NU$k$C Problem, there are exactly $t$ distinct radii, with $k_i$ balls of radius $r_i$ permitted for each $i$ from $1$ to $t$. Chakrabarty et al. introduced this problem, proving that a constant approximation is impossible when $t$ is unbounded; however, they provided a bicriteria approximation that allows a constant factor violation in both the number of balls and the radii. They further conjectured that a constant approximation is achievable if $t$ remains a fixed constant. Since that introduction, significant strides have been made toward validating this conjecture: constant approximations for $3$-NU$k$C are now established through work by Chakrabarty and Negahbani [IPCO 2021] and Jia et al. [To appear in SOSA 2022]. This work advances the field by delivering an $O(1)$-approximation for the Non-Uniform $k$-Center problem involving four distinct radius types. Achieved through a new synthesis of techniques from the $k$-center literature, our findings illustrate the strong interconnections between $k$-center generalizations with non-uniform radii and multi-coverage constraints (such as colorful $k$-center). We anticipate that these insights will deepen the understanding of the $t$-NU$k$C problem and move us closer to resolving the CGK conjecture.

Current state-of-the-art adversarial attacks on neural networks rely on costly iterative techniques and multiple random restarts from varied starting points. In contrast, iterative FGSM-based approaches that omit restarts sacrifice performance for computational speed, as they fail to sufficiently explore the image space and remain overly sensitive to step size selection. We introduce a Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) variant that employs a random step size to enhance performance without incurring the expense of random restarts. Our proposed method, Wide Iterative Stochastic crafting (WITCHcraft), outperforms classical PGD attacks on the CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets while maintaining equivalent computational costs. This straightforward PGD modification renders attack crafting more economical, a critical advantage for scenarios such as adversarial training that require real-time attack generation.

Spectral Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) rely on graph signal filters, and although recent models can learn arbitrary spectral filters, their theoretical expressive power remains underexplored. This paper addresses that gap by providing a theoretical analysis of spectral GNN expressiveness. We demonstrate that even linear spectral GNNs can generate arbitrary graph signals, provided two conditions are met: the graph Laplacian possesses no multiple eigenvalues, and the node features contain no missing frequency components. Furthermore, we link the expressive power of spectral GNNs to Graph Isomorphism (GI) testing, a metric commonly used for spatial GNNs. From an optimization standpoint, we investigate performance differences among spectral GNNs with identical expressive power, suggesting the use of an orthogonal basis where the weight function aligns with graph signal density in the spectrum. Guided by these insights, we introduce JacobiConv, which leverages the orthogonality and adaptability of the Jacobi basis to handle various weight functions. Notably, JacobiConv achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets despite lacking nonlinearity, outperforming all baseline methods.
This paper calculates the effect of mod $p$ Steenrod operations on the modular invariants of linear groups, where $p$ is an odd prime.

This study employs first-principles calculations to examine the structural, electronic, mechanical, phononic, and superconducting characteristics of the body-centered tetragonal Zr$_2$Ir compound. The analysis confirms that Zr$_2$Ir is both mechanically and dynamically stable, regardless of whether spin-orbit coupling (SOC) is included. Calculations of elastic constants, bulk and Young's moduli, Poisson's ratio, Debye temperature, and sound velocity indicate that the material is ductile. A comparison of elastic constants $C_{11}$ and $C_{33}$ reveals that the application of SOC reverses the anisotropy, shifting greater compressibility from the x-axis to the z-axis. Electronic band structure and density of states confirm the compound's metallic nature. The superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) and electron-phonon coupling constant ($\lambda$) are determined to be 7.50 K and 0.93 without SOC, and 7.62 K and 0.96 with SOC, respectively. Consequently, while Zr$_2$Ir exhibits strong electron-phonon coupling, the inclusion of SOC slightly diminishes both its critical temperature and coupling constant.

A primary challenge in data stream processing systems involves employing operator migration to manage highly fluctuating workloads cost-effectively and adapt dynamically to immediate needs. Operator migration is a sophisticated procedure that entails modifying the state and stream management of an active query, ideally ensuring zero data loss and minimal disruption to execution. This survey offers a historical and goal-oriented overview of migration solutions, introducing a conceptual model to unify terminology and categorize existing approaches. The analysis distinguishes between the mechanism of migration and the decision to migrate, highlighting the often-neglected or implicit cost-benefit analysis crucial for such operations. By describing available solutions, the text clarifies design alternatives from an algorithmic standpoint. Furthermore, an empirical study complements this overview, offering quantitative insights into how different design choices impact migration mechanisms.

For any subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, positive integer $n$, and distance $d > 0$, we define $G(S^n, d)$ as the graph with vertex set $S^n$ where vertices are adjacent precisely when their Euclidean distance equals $d$. The central inquiry of this work is whether, for given $n$ and a distance $d$ that occurs between points in the rational space $\mathbb{Q}^n$, there exists a finite graph $G$ that is a subgraph of $G(\mathbb{Q}^n, d)$ but fails to be a subgraph of $G(\mathbb{R}^{n-1}, 1)$. We affirmatively answer this question for all $n \leq 5$, and in the process, address several related problems.

Singular value decomposition (SVD) is a widely used matrix factorization method that generates optimal low-rank approximations. While it finds extensive use in fields like signal processing, data science, and machine learning, standard SVD algorithms often fail when applied to massive matrices that exceed the main memory of typical computers. These conventional approaches rely on fast random access and substantial space for intermediate computations, rendering them impractical for such large-scale data. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a scalable, fully parallelizable randomized SVD solution designed for out-of-core (external memory) processing. This implementation can factor both sparse and dense matrices of any size, operating efficiently within strictly limited memory constraints by leveraging external storage as required. Our approach employs an innovative matrix partitioning strategy that facilitates parallel and out-of-core processing, while also enabling automatic load balancing, performance tuning, and optimized memory and I/O management. Additionally, the use of persistent external storage (such as HDDs or SSDs) allows users to resume interrupted calculations without recalculating prior steps, effectively addressing a significant challenge in decomposing extremely large matrices.

Designing robotic assistance for manipulation tasks presents significant challenges. This study focuses on enhancing the accuracy and usability of semi-autonomous systems, including human-operated manipulators and exoskeletons. The core concept involves creating a system that leverages context- and user-awareness to make superior assistance decisions. Context-awareness is achieved by automatically generating candidate grasps and reach-to-grasp trajectories within new, cluttered environments. User-awareness is realized through a linear time-variant feedback controller that guides motion toward the most viable grasp. The approach is illustrated using a simple 2D scenario where participants grasp specific objects in a cluttered scene. Furthermore, this method reduces the number of controllable dimensions for the user by limiting direct control to the x- and y-axes, while the system automatically infers the end-effector's orientation and finger pose. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach improves both accuracy and execution time compared to purely manual control.

Utilizing $980\ {\rm fb}^{-1}$ of data acquired by the Belle detector at the KEKB asymmetric-energy $e^+e^-$ collider, we present the determination of masses and the inaugural measurements of intrinsic widths for the $\Sigma_c(2455)^+$ and $\Sigma_c(2520)^+$ charmed baryons. Our results yield $M(\Sigma_c(2455)^+)-M(\Lambda_c^+) = 166.17\pm 0.05^{+0.16}_{-0.07}\ {\rm MeV}/c^2$, $\Gamma(\Sigma_c(2455)^+) = 2.3 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.3\ {\rm MeV/c^2}$, $M(\Sigma_c(2520)^+)-M(\Lambda_c^+) = 230.9 \pm 0.5 ^{+0.5}_{-0.1}\ {\rm MeV}/c^2$, and $\Gamma(\Sigma_c(2520)^+) = 17.2^{+2.3\ +3.1}_{-2.1\ -0.7}\ {\rm MeV/c^2}$, with uncertainties denoting statistical and systematic errors respectively. These findings offer a means to evaluate models concerning the fundamental quark structure of $\Sigma_c$ states.

This work offers a comprehensive survey of the methods proposed so far for Open Information Extraction. We outline the primary challenges these systems encounter, trace the progression of proposed approaches, and illustrate the particular problems each aims to resolve. Furthermore, we critically examine standard evaluation practices used to measure Open IE performance and suggest potential avenues for future research.

This study addresses offline reinforcement learning with model-based control, aiming to derive a dynamics model from replayed experience and develop an agent guided by pessimistic principles. Existing model-based constraints typically employ either explicit uncertainty penalties or implicit conservative regularization that suppresses Q-values for out-of-distribution state-action pairs while elevating those within the distribution.
