Although uncertainty estimation offers loose calibration for complex dynamics, implicit regularization yields marginally superior performance. To advance the concept of regularization independent of uncertainty quantification, we introduce Distributionally Robust Offline Model-Based Policy Optimization (DROMO). This approach utilizes principles from distributionally robust optimization to penalize a wider spectrum of out-of-distribution state-action pairs compared to standard empirical Q-value minimization. Theoretically, we demonstrate that DROMO optimizes a lower bound on ground-truth policy evaluation and can be integrated with any existing policy gradient algorithm. Furthermore, we examine the theoretical characteristics of both linear and non-linear instantiations of DROMO.

The practice of defining sense inventories through lexical translations has a long-standing history in lexical semantics. We introduce a theoretical framework that explains why this seemingly plausible approach failed to yield practical results. Through formal proofs, we establish propositions regarding the connection between word translations and their senses, as well as the interplay between synonymy and polysemy. Our theoretical conclusions are empirically validated using BabelNet, and we illustrate their application in performing unsupervised word sense disambiguation for a significant portion of the lexicon.

This study introduces an optimal control strategy designed to manage both slewing and vibration in flexible spacecraft. By accounting for dynamics operating across different time scales, the optimal control problem is discretized using a multirate variational approach on both micro and macro time grids. System descriptions and requisite optimality conditions are established via the discrete Lagrange-d'Alembert principle. This discrete formulation maintains the conservation properties inherent in the continuous model while enabling high-fidelity simulations at a lower computational expense. Simulations of a single-axis rotational maneuver confirm effective vibration suppression, matching the accuracy of single-rate methods but with significantly reduced computational costs.

This paper investigates out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in neural algorithmic reasoning, focusing on learning algorithms like sorting, BFS, and DFS from input-output pairs via deep neural networks. We argue that OOD generalization in this context differs markedly from standard OOD scenarios; for instance, phenomena like "accuracy on the line" seen in image classification are absent, and data augmentation techniques often fail because their underlying assumptions are violated. Furthermore, we examine key challenges in the current leading benchmark, CLRS \citep{deepmind2021clrs}, which covers 30 algorithmic reasoning tasks, including input distribution shift, non-representative data generation, and uninformative validation metrics. To address these, we propose solutions such as a straightforward yet effective correction for input distribution shift and enhanced data generation methods. Finally, we introduce an attention-based 2WL-graph neural network (GNN) processor that complements message-passing GNNs, with the combined approach surpassing the state-of-the-art by an average margin of 3% across all algorithms. Our code is accessible at: \url{https://github.com/smahdavi4/clrs}.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) play a pivotal role in decision-making across numerous critical sectors, including medicine, society, and the judiciary. Because the stakes of these decisions are so high, understanding how these models function is essential. We present a novel approach to interpreting image segmentation models by identifying specific image regions where noise can be introduced without degrading the model's downstream performance. We demonstrate this technique by segmenting the pancreas in CT scans, offering a qualitative comparison against established explainability methods like Grad-CAM and occlusion sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that, in contrast to other approaches, our interpretability framework allows for quantitative evaluation by measuring performance on images with obscured regions.

In real-world environments, robots often encounter identical objects within dense clutter, necessitating that target-driven grasping systems understand spatial relationships—such as proximity, adjacency, and occlusions—between scene objects. To address this efficiently, we introduce a system that concurrently evaluates object relations and predicts 6-DoF grasp poses. This approach models a densely cluttered scene as a grasp graph, where nodes represent object geometries in the grasp coordinate frame and edges denote spatial relations. We then employ a Grasp Graph Neural Network (G2N2) to analyze this graph and identify the most feasible 6-DoF grasp pose for a target. Furthermore, we propose a shape completion-assisted sampling method that enhances sample quality and grasping efficiency. Comparative evaluations against multiple baselines in both simulated and real-world settings demonstrate that our method achieves a 77.78% grasping accuracy with novel objects in dense clutter, outperforming the best baseline by over 15%. Additional materials can be found at https://sites.google.com/umn.edu/graph-grasping.

Traversing a quantum critical point within a finite timeframe violates the adiabatic condition because the energy gap closes, inevitably generating excitations. While such non-adiabatic excitations are usually considered harmful and have prompted various mitigation strategies, we demonstrate that they can instead be controlled and utilized to achieve beneficial outcomes. Specifically, we examine closed cycles in fully-connected models that reach a quantum critical point, illustrating two key applications. First, we present a quantum battery that charges by approaching this critical point, where repeated cycles cause both stored and extractable work to grow exponentially. Second, we describe a method for rapidly generating spin-squeezed states rich in multipartite entanglement, providing a metrological edge. In both instances, the performance metrics rely heavily on universal critical exponents and the scaling behavior of the driving protocol near the transition. These findings underscore the complex interplay between quantum thermodynamics and metrology within the realm of critical nonequilibrium dynamics.

The physics governing the origin and makeup of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) is a cornerstone of cosmology. While existing literature confirms Gaussianity in CMB anisotropies based on full multi-frequency temperature maps, this thesis employs clustering algorithms to perform a targeted statistical analysis of CMB hotspot distributions. We detail the data processing and clustering methods used, with findings that definitively demonstrate the CMB hotspot counts-in-cells distribution deviates from a Poisson model. Instead, the data aligns significantly better with both the Negative Binomial Distribution (NBD) and the Gravitational Quasi-Equilibrium Distribution (GQED). Consequently, we infer that structural formations likely existed in the early universe during the recombination epoch, potentially offering novel perspectives on galaxy formation.

To evaluate and generate alternative taxi schedules, as well as to offer drivers and passengers valuable insights regarding upcoming trips, it is essential to predict trip durations or Estimated Times of Arrival (ETAs). To achieve high prediction accuracy, machine learning models currently represent the state of the art. However, a promising yet underutilized approach to further enhance precision involves combining multiple ETA models into an ensemble. Although this likely improves accuracy, the sophisticated architecture of such ensembles often reduces transparency. To address this limitation, explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) can be applied. This paper presents a three-fold contribution: first, we introduce a novel two-level stacked ensemble model by integrating multiple machine learning models from our prior work, surpassing previous state-of-the-art static, route-free ETA methods. Second, we utilize existing XAI techniques to interpret both the first- and second-level models within the ensemble. Third, we propose three distinct methods for merging first-level explanations with second-level ones, thereby enabling the explanation of stacked ensembles for regression tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that these ETA models successfully identify the importance of input features that drive their predictions.

A collaborative team of artist-engineers from Portland Community College, working alongside artists with intellectual and developmental disabilities, utilized open-source and creative coding frameworks to prototype an ensemble of adapted instruments and synthesizers. These tools enable real-time, in-key collaboration by using diverse sensors to transmit musical controls to software sound generators via MIDI. The design process carefully balanced the freedom of expression with the curation of possible sonic outcomes as a form of adaptation. While evaluating these adapted instruments requires different frameworks than those used for traditional instruments or mass-market products, the results of this focused, individualized design hold various potential applications.

Genetic information is now commonly employed to investigate population history, including changes in size, subdivision, and gene flow. Although numerous formal statistical techniques exist for testing hypotheses and fitting models, it often remains ambiguous which specific hypotheses or models are most appropriate. Consequently, there is a demand for less formal approaches to facilitate the exploratory analysis of genetic data. One such method utilizes *nucleotide site patterns* to offer a straightforward summary of genetic data structures. This article demonstrates how to apply these patterns in exploratory data analysis.

Recent findings from the LHCb experiment indicate that the direct CP asymmetries for the decay channels $D^0\rightarrow \pi^+\pi^-$ and $D^0\rightarrow K^+K^-$ share the same sign. This observation unexpectedly violates an enhanced $U$-spin limit sum rule with a significance of $2.1\sigma$. Utilizing this new data, we have, for the first time, extracted the imaginary component of the CKM-subleading, $U$-spin breaking $\Delta U=1$ correction to the $U$-spin limit $\Delta U=0$ amplitude. The imaginary part of the $\Delta U=0$ amplitude is derived from $\Delta a_{CP}^{\mathrm{dir}}$, although the associated strong phases remain undetermined and could potentially be measured via future time-dependent analyses. Under the assumption that non-perturbative rescattering induces $\mathcal{O}(1)$ strong phases, the ratio of $U$-spin breaking contributions to $U$-spin limit contributions in the CKM-subleading amplitudes is calculated to be $(173^{+85}_{-74})\%$. This value significantly surpasses the Standard Model (SM) prediction of approximately $30\%$ $U$-spin breaking, with a significance of $1.95\sigma$. Should this anomaly be validated by future data, it would suggest, within the SM framework, a failure of the $U$-spin expansion in the CKM-subleading amplitudes of charm decays. Alternatively, new physics models introducing an additional $\Delta U=1$ operator could resolve the issue without disrupting the $U$-spin power expansion; potential examples include extended scalar sectors or flavorful $Z'$ models.

This study examines the Quantum Natural Gradient Descent (QNGD) method, recently introduced for training variational quantum algorithms. QNGD functions as Steepest Gradient Descent (SGD) within the complex projective space, utilizing the Fubini-Study metric. We introduce an adaptive QNGD variant leveraging Armijo's rule, an efficient backtracking line search with proven convergence guarantees. The algorithm was evaluated on three distinct models using noisy simulators and various initialization strategies. Our findings indicate that Adaptive QNGD dynamically adjusts the step size and consistently surpasses the original QNGD, which demands precise knowledge of an optimal step size to remain competitive. Furthermore, the added computational overhead of the line search in Adaptive QNGD is negligible, ensuring that the performance benefits outweigh the complexity increase. Additionally, benchmarking reveals that a standard SGD algorithm operating in Euclidean space, when paired with this adaptive scheme, can achieve results comparable to QNGD with an optimal step size. These results further validate the significance of differential geometry in variational quantum computing. Indeed, we anticipate that advanced mathematics will play a pivotal role in the NISQ era by guiding the development of faster and more efficient algorithms.

Growing privacy concerns have catalyzed the development of Private Inference (PI), a framework where both the client's data and the service provider's model remain confidential. Current state-of-the-art PI protocols integrate multiple cryptographic techniques, including Homomorphic Encryption (HE), Secret Sharing (SS), Garbled Circuits (GC), and Oblivious Transfer (OT). Despite recent performance gains and the critical need for such privacy, PI remains largely theoretical and too slow for practical deployment. This paper tackles these limitations by providing a comprehensive analysis of a standard high-performance protocol to establish foundational knowledge for the systems community. The study identifies all inefficiency sources—compute, communication, and storage. A key contribution is the evaluation of inference request arrival rates rather than analyzing individual requests in isolation. Previous research, which ignored arrival rates, assumed that PI pre-computations could be handled offline with negligible overhead; however, this work demonstrates that offline costs are so substantial that they frequently manifest online due to insufficient downtime to mask pre-computation latency. Based on these insights, we propose three optimizations targeting computation (via layer-parallel HE), communication (through wireless slot allocation), and storage (using Client-Garbler). Compared to the current state-of-the-art PI protocol, these optimizations achieve a total speedup of 1.8× and enable the system to sustain inference request rates up to 2.24× higher.

The World Health Organization has officially designated the new coronavirus outbreak as a global pandemic. To address its rapid dissemination, most nations have imposed bans on both indoor and outdoor gatherings and mandated that residents remain at home. Amidst this evolving crisis, mental health has emerged as a critical societal challenge. This paper examines the analysis of social media content to identify indicators associated with depression. We employ topic modeling alongside a suite of psycholinguistic and mental well-being metrics to construct statistical models capable of characterizing and representing the subtler dimensions of depression. Additionally, we forecast the potential for depression-related signals to intensify over time. Our top-performing classifier achieves F-1 scores of up to 0.8, outperforming the established baseline by a significant margin of 0.173. Finally, we outline several directions for future research.

This research examines various forms of intuitionistic fuzzy continuities (IFCs) and intuitionistic fuzzy boundedness (IFBs) within intuitionistic fuzzy pseudo normed linear spaces, analyzing both internal and external relationships between these concepts.

Photon production at hadron colliders occurs through both direct generation and fragmentation mechanisms. Standard theoretical predictions for isolated photon and photon-plus-jet cross-sections typically apply idealized isolation criteria that exclude fragmentation effects, thereby creating a systematic discrepancy when compared to experimental data. We provide next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) predictions for the photon-plus-jet cross-section that incorporate experimental isolation conditions, accounting for both direct and fragmentation contributions. Furthermore, we compare predictions derived from two distinct parton-to-photon fragmentation functions to estimate the uncertainty associated with these poorly constrained functions.

Fundamentally, this paper proposes powerful laser technology as a viable tool for experimentally manipulating the lifetime and branching ratios of unstable particle decays. Following our previous theoretical study [arXiv:2101.00224] on the leptonic decay of the $W^{-}$-boson ($W^{-}\rightarrow \ell^{-} \bar{\nu}_{\ell}$) under circularly polarized laser influence, which demonstrated a significant reduction in the leptonic decay rate, this work extends those findings to the hadronic decay channel ($W^{-}\rightarrow q \bar{q}'$). By integrating the analytical results from both studies, we investigate how an intense laser's field strength and frequency impact three key observables in $W^{-}$-boson decay: the total decay rate, lifetime, and branching ratios. Our findings indicate that the laser substantially lowers the total decay rate, thereby extending the particle's lifetime. Crucially, the branching ratios for both leptonic and hadronic channels are modified (either increased or decreased) by the strong external electromagnetic field. Together, these complementary analyses offer a comprehensive theoretical framework that will be valuable for future experimental investigations.

Research indicates that fully supervised deep learning models often depend on "shortcut" features—inputs correlated with the target in training data but absent or irrelevant during testing or deployment. In this study, we present experiments demonstrating that recent self-supervised models trained on image and text data generate more robust image representations and decrease reliance on such visual shortcuts in a realistic medical imaging context. Furthermore, we observe that when fine-tuned on labeled data, these self-supervised models discard shortcut features more rapidly than their fully supervised counterparts. While not a definitive fix, our findings offer strong evidence that self-supervised approaches trained on multimodal data provide greater resilience against visual shortcut features.

Online social media platforms are increasingly utilizing Natural Language Processing (NLP) to identify abusive content at scale and reduce harm to users. However, these systems are often hindered by sampling and association biases inherent in their training data, leading to inferior performance on content involving marginalized groups and potentially exacerbating the harms they face. Existing research on such biases has primarily examined a limited number of disparity axes and subgroups for which annotated lexicons exist, largely overlooking biases within non-Western contexts. This paper presents a weakly supervised approach to robustly detect lexical biases across broader geocultural settings. Using a case study on a publicly available toxicity detection model, we show that our method uncovers significant cross-geographic error patterns. Furthermore, we validate that these patterns align with human assessments of offensive versus inoffensive language within those specific geographic regions. Additionally, we analyze a model trained on data with ground truth labels to better understand these biases and present preliminary experiments aimed at mitigating them.

This paper examines generic conformally flat hypersurfaces within the Euclidean $4$-space $\mathbb{R}^4$ through the lens of M\"{o}bius geometry. Initially, we categorize locally these hypersurfaces possessing a closed M\"obius form under the M\"{o}bius transformation group of $\mathbb{R}^4$. These instances arise from cones, cylinders, or rotational hypersurfaces defined over surfaces with constant Gaussian curvature in $3$-spheres, Euclidean $3$-spaces, or hyperbolic $3$-spaces, respectively. Subsequently, we analyze the global properties of such generic conformally flat hypersurfaces and derive specific integral formulas concerning them.

Introducing multilayer nanopatterned structures into modern imaging systems can significantly improve their efficiency, compactness, and utility by manipulating light according to its fundamental properties. However, achieving high transmission efficiency in multispectral imaging remains challenging because standard filter arrays waste most incident light, and most cameras fail to exploit the rich information contained in polarization and spatial degrees of freedom. Although optical metamaterials can address these electromagnetic properties, their reliance on single-layer geometries has restricted their performance and multifunctionality. This study employs advanced two-photon lithography to create multilayer scattering structures capable of performing complex optical transformations immediately prior to the focal plane array. We fabricated computationally optimized devices for multispectral and polarimetric sorting with submicron features, validated experimentally in the mid-infrared range. Additionally, simulations demonstrate a final structure that redirects light based on its angular momentum. These results confirm that precise three-dimensional nanopatterning allows for the direct modification of sensor array scattering properties to develop sophisticated imaging systems.

While deep neural networks excel at feature extraction, their excessive size makes them difficult to deploy. The vast number of parameters renders layer-wise interpretability non-trivial, often leading to their classification as "black boxes." Although simpler models offer greater explainability, discovering them is challenging. A sparse network trained from scratch to fit the data would facilitate parameter interpretation. In response, the lottery ticket hypothesis posits that dense neural networks inherently contain small, sparse sub-networks capable of achieving comparable test accuracy within the same number of training steps. This study aims to evaluate the existence of such trainable sub-networks within natural language models (NLMs). To accomplish this, we will examine advanced compression methodologies, including quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning.

We provide results establishing a connection between the Hopf cyclic cohomology of the Hopf algebra of moving frames and that of the DG Hopf algebra of moving coframes, drawing a parallel to the van Est isomorphism that links Lie algebra cohomology with continuous group cohomology.

Historically, determining the 3D structure of the solar coronal magnetic field has relied on two distinct methodologies: (1) Nonlinear force-free field (NLFFF) extrapolations, which utilize photospheric vector magnetograms as boundary conditions, and (2) stereoscopy of coronal magnetic loops observed in EUV images from multiple viewpoints. Each approach possesses specific advantages and limitations. Extrapolation techniques are vulnerable to noise and inconsistencies within boundary data, whereas stereoscopy accuracy depends on the capability to identify identical structures across different images and the angular separation between viewing perspectives. Consequently, applying these two methods to the same observational data often yields non-coincident 3D coronal magnetic field models. In a previous study (Paper I), we enhanced our NLFFF optimization code by integrating stereoscopic constraints. This method was validated using synthetic data, and in the present work, we apply the newly developed code to a combined dataset from SDO/HMI, SDO/AIA, and the two STEREO spacecraft. The extended technique, designated S-NLFFF, incorporates an additional term designed to monitor and minimize the angle between the local magnetic field direction and the orientation of 3D coronal loops reconstructed via stereoscopy. Our findings indicate that prescribing the shape of these stereoscopically reconstructed loops significantly improves the agreement between the modeled field and the loop structures. Furthermore, we observe an appreciable reduction by a factor of two in the angle between the current and the magnetic field, demonstrating the superior quality of the force-free solution achieved by the S-NLFFF method.

Both the collection of finite lists of integers and the set of binary trees with integer labels are countably infinite, a property shared by many types defined inductively. This paper formalizes the syntax of first-order inductive definitions within Coq and demonstrates their countability, subject to specific constraints. Rather than employing a meta-language proof generator, we construct an axiom-free proof directly in Coq's object logic. Specifically, we define a dependently typed Coq function that maps the syntax of an inductive definition to its countability. Leveraging this proof, we introduce a Coq tactic capable of automatically establishing the countability of specific inductive types. Additionally, we have created Coq libraries for both countability and the syntax of inductive definitions, which hold independent value.

The innate human drive for knowledge, or curiosity, is fundamental to acquiring skills. By leveraging artificial curiosity, we can enhance control techniques like Reinforcement Learning to achieve more natural exploration. A notable strategy involves utilizing Bayesian surprise—measuring the discrepancy between prior and posterior beliefs regarding model parameters—to encourage exploration. This work proposes applying Bayesian surprise within a latent space that captures the agent's understanding of system dynamics, significantly lowering computational demands. We rigorously assess the method by evaluating exploration performance in continuous tasks and game scores in video games. Our approach is computationally efficient and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across various problems. Additionally, we examine how environmental stochasticity impacts curiosity-driven agents, a common source of failure; our results indicate that this approach remains robust against stochastic transitions.

Measurements of dijet pseudorapidity distributions as a function of their mean transverse momentum ($p_\mathrm{T}^\text{ave}$) have been conducted in proton-lead (pPb) and proton-proton (pp) collisions using data from the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC, recorded at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. Significant deviations between the pPb and pp spectra were observed across all examined $p_\mathrm{T}^\text{ave}$ ranges. These ratios were evaluated against next-to-leading-order perturbative quantum chromodynamics predictions utilizing unbound nucleon and nuclear parton distribution functions (PDFs). The findings provide the initial evidence that the gluon PDF at large Bjorken $x$ within lead ions exhibits strong suppression compared to that in unbound nucleons.

Research indicates that humans frequently provide contrastive explanations, clarifying why a specific event occurred instead of a counterfactual alternative. Although contrastivity is a fundamental aspect of human reasoning, it remains largely absent from current methods for explaining natural language processing (NLP) models. We introduce Minimal Contrastive Editing (MiCE), a technique that generates contrastive explanations by applying input edits that shift model predictions to the contrasting scenario. Experimental results across three domains—binary sentiment analysis, topic classification, and multiple-choice question answering—demonstrate that MiCE produces edits that are contrastive, minimal, and fluent, aligning closely with human behavior. Furthermore, we illustrate two applications of MiCE in NLP system development: debugging erroneous model outputs and identifying dataset artifacts. These findings suggest that generating contrastive explanations represents a promising avenue for advancing model interpretability.

Identifying previously visited locations remains a critical yet unresolved challenge in autonomous navigation. Existing visual place recognition (VPR) benchmarks generally test models' ability to determine the location of query images from sequential datasets containing both spatial and temporal elements. Recently, Echo State Networks (ESNs) have demonstrated exceptional power in machine learning tasks requiring spatio-temporal modeling. These architectures are simple yet potent neural networks that, by exhibiting memory across multiple time-scales and utilizing non-linear high-dimensional representations, can uncover temporal relationships in data while preserving linearity during the learning phase. This paper introduces a series of ESNs and evaluates their suitability for VPR. We report that integrating ESNs with pre-processed convolutional neural networks resulted in a significant performance increase compared to non-recurrent networks across five of six standard benchmarks (GardensPoint, SPEDTest, ESSEX3IN1, Oxford RobotCar, and Nordland), proving that ESNs effectively capture the temporal structure intrinsic to VPR problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ESN-enhanced models can surpass leading VPR systems that also leverage sequential data dynamics. Finally, our findings indicate that ESNs enhance generalization, robustness, and accuracy, further validating their appropriateness for VPR applications.

We present both theoretical and experimental evidence that a specifically engineered microcavity, operating in the optical parametric oscillation regime, produces lighthouse-like emission, characterized by a beam focused in a single direction. Notably, the orientation of this micro-lighthouse's emission can be continuously adjusted via the linear polarization of the input laser, achieving angular beam steering across a full 360 degrees. From a theoretical standpoint, this novel phenomenon results from the interaction between the nonlinear optical properties of microcavity exciton-polaritons, the asymmetry between the subcavities comprising the microcavity, and the device's rotational symmetry.

This study reports the initial observation of the $B_s^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-$ decay alongside the most accurate measurement of the branching fraction for the $B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-$ mode. These findings derive from an analysis of $pp$ collision data with an integrated luminosity of $3.0~\textrm{fb}^{-1}$, collected by the LHCb detector at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The branching fraction for $B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-$ was determined relative to $B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 \pi^+ \pi^-$ as:
$$\frac{\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-)}{\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 \pi^+ \pi^-)} = (6.9 \pm 0.4 \pm 0.3)\%,$$
where the first uncertainty represents statistical error and the second is systematic. Additionally, the branching fraction for the $B_s^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-$ mode relative to the corresponding $B^0$ decay is:
$$\frac{\mathcal{B}(B_s^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-)}{\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-)} = (93.0 \pm 8.9 \pm 6.9)\%.$$
By utilizing the established branching fraction of ${B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 \pi^+ \pi^-}$, the absolute values were calculated as ${{\mathcal B}(B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^- )=(6.1 \pm 0.4 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-5}}$ and ${{\cal B}(B_s^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-)=}$ $(5.7 \pm 0.5 \pm 0.4 \pm 0.5) \times 10^{-5}$. In these results, the third uncertainties stem from the branching fractions of the decays ${B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 \pi^+ \pi^-}$ and $B^0 \to \overline{D}^0 K^+ K^-$, respectively.

Most existing approaches to sketch-based image retrieval focus on learning embeddings that ignore modality-specific details. However, since instances from different modalities often offer complementary insights into the underlying concept, we introduce XModalViT, a cross-attention framework for Vision Transformers that integrates rather than discards such specific information. Our method first maps paired data from photo and sketch modalities into fused representations that unify information from both sources. Subsequently, we decouple the input space of this fusion network into independent encoders for each modality by employing contrastive and relational cross-modal knowledge distillation. These encoders are then utilized for downstream tasks, including cross-modal retrieval. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the expressive power of our learned representations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on three fine-grained sketch-based image retrieval benchmarks: Shoe-V2, Chair-V2, and Sketchy. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/abhrac/xmodal-vit.

Classical shadows offer an efficient approach to characterizing various properties of quantum states through randomized measurements. This work investigates the sample complexity required to estimate Pauli operator expectation values using "shallow shadows," a variant where the randomization is achieved via a local unitary circuit with a tunable depth $t$. We demonstrate that the state-averaged shadow norm, which dictates average sample complexity, can be formulated in terms of the Heisenberg time evolution of operators under the twirling circuit—specifically, the dynamics of the weight distribution describing the number of sites where an operator acts nontrivially. For spatially contiguous operators of weight $k$, this involves a balance between operator spreading (expanding the operator's support) and operator relaxation (increasing the density of identity operators within the bulk). Based on this framework, we derive (i) an upper bound on the shadow norm showing that a depth of $t \sim \log(k)$ yields an exponential improvement in sample complexity over the $t=0$ baseline across all spatial dimensions, and (ii) quantitative findings in one dimension using a mean-field approximation, which includes a universal subleading correction to the optimal depth that aligns remarkably well with infinite matrix product state simulations. This study bridges fundamental concepts in quantum many-body dynamics with practical applications in quantum information, establishing a foundation for highly optimized protocols for learning quantum state properties.

It is a established fact that the Laplace-Stieltjes transform of a nonnegative random variable or vector uniquely defines its distribution function. This study extends that uniqueness theorem by applying the Muntz-Szasz Theorem alongside a novel identity linking Laplace-Stieltjes and Laplace-Carson transforms of distribution functions, an identity not previously documented to our knowledge. Specifically, for two nonnegative random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint distribution $H$, the function $H$ can be uniquely characterized by a specific set of countable values derived from its bivariate Laplace-Stieltjes transform. This analysis also covers the general high-dimensional scenario. Furthermore, the uniqueness theorem for standard Laplace transforms attributed to Lerch is generalized. The proposed identity further offers a method to streamline the computation of Laplace-Stieltjes transforms when the underlying distributions include singular components. Finally, illustrative examples are provided to demonstrate how the characterization results function within the context of the uniqueness theorem.

We examine the efficacy of spectral kurtosis (SK), a statistical radio frequency interference (RFI) mitigation method, using simulated realistic RFI scenarios. SK calculates the kurtosis of M power values within a single channel, offering a detection metric capable of distinguishing between anthropogenic RFI and incoherent astronomical signals. Our tests evaluate SK's capacity to identify signals across diverse modulation types, data rates, duty cycles, and carrier frequencies. We experimented with various accumulation lengths M and employed multi-scale SK, which aggregates data from neighboring time-frequency bins to address limitations inherent in single-scale SK. Our results indicate that signals exhibiting significant sidelobe emissions due to high data rates, those with a 50% effective duty cycle, and those possessing weak signal-to-noise ratios are more difficult to detect. Furthermore, multi-scale SK utilizing at least one additional channel can identify both central channel and side-band interference, achieving detection rates exceeding 90% provided the bin channel width in frequency exceeds the RFI width.

This work examines the geometric quantization of Chern--Simons theory applied to closed genus-one surfaces and semisimple complex groups. Initially, we define a complexified analogue of the Hitchin connection within the framework of Kähler quantization. This approach utilizes polarizations derived from the nonabelian Hodge hyper-Kähler geometry of moduli spaces of flat connections, offering a complement to Witten's real-polarized methodology. Subsequently, we analyze Witten's connection and demonstrate its equivalence to the complexified Hitchin connection by employing a variant of the Bargmann transform acting on polarized sections defined over these moduli spaces.

Suppose $\Gamma$ is a group of type $F_n$ and $X$ denotes the $n$-skeleton of the universal cover of a $K(\Gamma,1)$ simplicial complex, where the $n$-skeleton itself is finite. We demonstrate that if $\Gamma$ satisfies the strongly $n$-Kazhdan property, then for any collection of finite-index subgroups $\{\Lambda_i\}_i$, the associated family of quotient complexes $\{\Lambda_i\backslash X\}_i$ constitutes a family of bounded-degree $n$-dimensional spectral expanders. Leveraging this result, we generate novel examples of $2$-dimensional spectral expanders.

Multi-robot manipulation tasks consist of control entities that can be divided into dynamically independent components, a scenario typified by dual-arm manipulation. Directly solving such complex tasks using reinforcement learning is often impractical because the sample complexity and exploration demands increase with the dimensionality of the state and action spaces. Consequently, these environments are better approached as multi-agent systems where multiple agents manage distinct portions of the overall task. However, decentralizing action generation necessitates inter-agent coordination via channels restricted to task-relevant information. This paper introduces a method for coordinating multi-robot manipulation through learned latent action spaces shared across agents. We evaluate this approach on simulated multi-robot manipulation tasks, showing that it outperforms existing baselines in both sample efficiency and learning performance.

This study examines how constraints on cosmic tensor perturbations rely on prior assumptions. Typically, researchers enforce the strong prior of the single-field inflationary consistency relation, which links the tensor spectral index ($n_T$) to the tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$). Removing this constraint yields markedly different results for $n_T$, permitting both positive and negative values with similar probabilities, and boosts the upper bound on $r$ at scales of $k = 0.01 \text{ Mpc}^{-1}$ to $0.05 \text{ Mpc}^{-1}$ by more than an order of magnitude. Furthermore, even when adopting the consistency equation, a uniform prior on $r$ at one scale does not translate to a uniform prior at another, meaning that constraints vary based on the selected pivot scale. We evaluate the magnitude of this dependency and identify the optimal scale for limiting the tensor amplitude, analyzing scenarios both with and without the consistency relation.

The transverse and longitudinal magnetoelectric susceptibilities (MES) were quantitatively measured in (001) heteroepitaxial BiFeO$_{3}$-CoFe$_{2}$O$_{4}$ nanostructures. Both MES values exhibited a sharp enhancement at magnetic fields under 6 kOe and displayed asymmetric lineshapes relative to the dc magnetic field, indicating a strain-induced magnetoelectric effect. The peak transverse MES, reaching approximately 60 mV/cm Oe, was roughly five times greater than the longitudinal MES. This finding suggests that the transverse magnetostriction of the CoFe$_{2}$O$_{4}$ nanopillars exceeds bulk values, driven by preferred magnetic domain alignment along the [001] direction resulting from compressive heteroepitaxial strain.

Regression trees and random forests serve as widely used and effective non-parametric estimators in practice. While a recent study by Athey and Wager established that random forest estimates at a single point converge to a Gaussian distribution asymptotically, this paper extends that finding to the multivariate setting, demonstrating that the vector of estimates across multiple points follows a joint normal distribution. Specifically, the covariance matrix of this limiting distribution is diagonal, indicating that estimates at any two distinct points become independent in sufficiently deep trees. Furthermore, the off-diagonal elements are bounded by metrics reflecting the probability that two points fall into the same partition within the tree structure. These findings depend on specific stability conditions regarding split construction, with examples provided for splitting rules that either satisfy or violate this assumption. Finally, numerical simulations are used to evaluate the proposed covariance bound and the coverage rates of the resulting confidence intervals.

This study utilizes process algebra to elucidate communication mechanisms within quantum systems, with the primary goal of formally modeling interactions between distributed quantum entities. Our proposed communication model refines Lalire's Quantum Process Algebra (QPAlg) by incorporating significant modifications, most notably the formal specification of the Quantum Teleportation protocol. Furthermore, we have introduced programmatic formal descriptions that clarify protocol operations and adhere to rigorous specifications. Illustrative examples demonstrate the enhanced algebra's capability to formally depict the transmission and reception of both classical and quantum data, ensuring alignment with fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

The International Large Detector (ILD), designed for the future International Linear Collider (ILC), plans to employ a Time Projection Chamber (TPC) as its primary tracking instrument. To meet necessary point resolution standards, Micro-Pattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) will serve in the amplification phase. A readout module featuring a triple-layer Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) stack for gas amplification was created and evaluated at the DESY II Test Beam Facility. Following an introduction to the module and the associated test infrastructure, this report details the performance of three such modules regarding single-point and double-hit resolution. Subsequent sections present findings on particle identification via specific energy loss (dE/dx), along with simulation studies designed to quantify how high granularity influences dE/dx resolution. Additionally, the text describes an upgraded TPC field cage and the LYCORIS Large-Area Silicon-Strip Telescope, which will be utilized at the test beam facility within the Persistent Current Magnet (PCMAG). The LYCORIS telescope is intended to deliver precise particle trajectory references, thereby validating the momentum resolution of a large-scale TPC prototype.

Although online shopping offers customers limitless choices supported by comprehensive details and reviews from the safety of their homes, it cannot match the immediate satisfaction and tactile experience provided by brick-and-mortar stores. Conversely, shopping in physical locations often presents challenges due to an overwhelming array of similar options and a lack of accessible product data, such as specifications and ratings. To address this, we introduce ARShopping, a web-based prototype designed to project detailed online product information onto portable smart devices (including phones, tablets, and glasses) within the physical retail environment. Leveraging augmented reality (AR) to identify items and overlay relevant data, this system aids consumers in making informed decisions that meet their needs while reducing the time required to choose. Our approach employs a data fusion algorithm to enhance product detection accuracy and integrates AR visualizations to enable easy comparison of multiple products and features. Furthermore, the prototype was developed based on interviews with 14 participants to ensure its utility and user-friendliness.

Clinically, precise lesion or tissue annotation greatly enhances disease diagnosis. For instance, segmenting the optic disc and cup in fundus images aids in diagnosing glaucoma, while segmenting skin lesions in dermoscopic images assists in identifying melanoma. As deep learning advances, numerous methods have shown that segmentation can also support automated disease diagnosis models. However, current approaches are constrained by their ability to capture only static regional correlations within images. Drawing inspiration from the global and dynamic characteristics of Vision Transformers, this paper introduces the Segmentation-Assisted Diagnosis Transformer (SeATrans), designed to transfer segmentation knowledge into disease diagnosis networks. Specifically, we propose an asymmetric multi-scale interaction strategy to link individual low-level diagnostic features with multi-scale segmentation features. Furthermore, we implement the SeA-block strategy to enhance diagnostic features through these correlated segmentation inputs. To model the interaction between segmentation and diagnosis, the SeA-block first encodes diagnostic features using segmentation information and then maps the resulting embedding back into the diagnostic feature space via a decoder. Experimental results indicate that SeATrans outperforms various state-of-the-art segmentation-assisted diagnosis methods across multiple disease diagnosis tasks.

Oblique plane microscopy (OPM) facilitates rapid, volumetric fluorescence imaging using a single-objective setup. Although OPM is a powerful tool for investigating biological phenomena in animal models, its application for in vivo human imaging remains largely untapped due to reliance on exogenous fluorescent dyes. This study presents a scattering-contrast oblique plane microscope (sOPM) capable of label-free imaging of blood cells flowing through human capillaries. The sOPM projects an oblique light sheet onto a capillary bed in the ventral tongue to capture side- and back-scattered signals from blood cells. By synchronizing the sOPM with a standard capillaroscope, we obtain paired axial and widefield images of cells traversing a capillary loop. The widefield capillaroscope offers absorption contrast to verify red blood cell (RBC) presence, while sOPM images help distinguish whether optical absorption gaps (OAGs) between RBCs consist of cellular or acellular material. Additionally, we highlight the functional differences between fluorescence and scattering OPM variants by sequentially imaging identical polystyrene beads with each method. Finally, we validate these in vivo findings by performing in vitro imaging of isolated red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets within 3D agar phantoms. These findings establish a promising new direction for in vivo blood analysis.

Strong electron-electron interactions in graphene generate a correlated, momentum-conserving flow that mimics the Hagen-Poiseuille behavior of a classical fluid. This study examines the electronic signatures of this viscous charge transport in high-mobility graphene field-effect transistors (FETs). Utilizing two complementary measurement techniques, we monitored the differential resistance across varying channel widths and effective electron temperatures. By integrating these methods, we confirmed viscous effects within a temperature range spanning from 178 K to room temperature. Finite element simulations of the graphene channel corroborate our experimental results and offer design guidelines for optimizing device geometries to enhance viscous phenomena. Furthermore, the observation of viscous effects near room temperature enables the development of functional hydrodynamic devices, including geometric rectifiers such as Tesla valves and charge amplifiers leveraging the electronic Venturi effect.

The Dicke model undergoes a quantum phase transition between normal and superradiant states when light-matter coupling surpasses the ultrastrong regime; however, observing this transition in real systems is difficult due to constraints on coupling strength or finite two-photon $A^2$ contributions. We demonstrate that applying periodic frequency modulation to the two-level systems within a standard strong-coupling Dicke model enables the creation of an anisotropic Dicke model featuring tunable rotating and counter-rotating terms characteristic of the ultrastrong coupling regime. By calculating the ground state and excitation spectrum as functions of modulation parameters, our findings indicate that superradiant phases are accessible in cavity- or circuit-quantum electrodynamics setups operating under strong coupling conditions.

We present BROUTE, a benchmark suite designed for vehicle routing optimization algorithms. This suite defines a set of traditional algorithms used in this field, which embody key features applicable to optimization tasks across various domains, including local search move evaluation, memory allocation, dynamic programming, and list insertion or deletion. Every algorithm included is deterministic. These benchmarks are implemented across multiple programming languages and data structures. BROUTE is available as free, open-source software and can assist in early project planning by helping teams decide on the most suitable programming language.

In a study by Angella, Otal, Ugarte, and Villacampa, the authors proposed two conjectures concerning compact Hermitian manifolds. The first suggests that if a Gauduchon connection, distinct from the Chern or Strominger connections, is Kähler-like, the underlying Hermitian metric must be Kähler. The second conjecture posits that if two such Gauduchon connections are both Kähler-like, the metric must likewise be Kähler. This paper addresses partial results regarding the first conjecture and provides a complete proof for the second. During this investigation, we identified a notable "duality" phenomenon among Gauduchon connections that appears deeply connected to the problem, although we currently lack a physical explanation for its existence.

It is demonstrated that the generalized Rota-Baxter operators presented in [W.A. Martinez, E.G. Reyes & M. Ronco, Int. J. Geom. Meth. Mod. Phys. 18 (2021) 2150176] represent a specific instance of Rota-Baxter systems [T. Brzezi\'nski, J. Algebra 460 (2016), 1-25]. When these systems are expanded through the inclusion of homothetisms, they yield examples of Dyck$^m$-algebras.

Magnetic skyrmions and skyrmion bags represent nano-scale spin textures that are promising candidates for future data storage and logic systems due to their stability, tunable size, and manipulability. As composite entities possessing any integer topological degree, skyrmion bags exhibit emergent characteristics absent in single-degree skyrmions. This study introduces theoretical models and descriptions of skyrmionic division, illustrating how individual skyrmions or bags can be split into multiple smaller skyrmionic structures. Such findings may enable the development of novel skyrmion-based devices, significantly advancing spintronics and neuromorphic computing.

In recent years, investigating the existence and stability of de-Sitter solutions within string theory has become a primary focus for the research community. The de-Sitter conjecture posits that such vacua are inherently unstable in this framework. This study examines de-Sitter solutions and their temporal stability using the $O(d,d)$ symmetry method, which facilitates the derivation of the generic string theory effective action. We specifically analyze the previously unexplored scenario of a constant generalized dilaton alongside the general form of dilaton couplings. Our results indicate that de-Sitter solutions are unstable for a constant generalized dilaton, regardless of the presence of matter. Additionally, we discovered that for the theory to remain weakly coupled, the general dilaton coupling must take the form of a cosmological constant.

Inadequate Social Cost of Carbon (SCC) estimation techniques and myopic decision-making timelines have impeded carbon emitters from adequately addressing the negative externalities of climate change and prevented nations from effectively balancing economic and climate policies. To address these shortcomings, we present Retrospective Social Cost of Carbon Updating (ReSCCU), an innovative framework that adjusts policies as empirically verified data accumulates. Applied to carbon taxation, we propose Retroactive Carbon Pricing (ReCaP), a market-based approach where polluters transfer the cost of ReSCCU adjustments to insurers. Furthermore, to mitigate systemic risks and reduce government dependency, we introduce the Private ReCaP (PReCaP) prediction market, a mechanism suitable for real-world deployment through the participation of a select group of high-net-worth individuals or independent institutions.

This study employs the Standard-Model Extension as an effective field theory to explore potential Lorentz and CPT violations within gravitational wave propagation. We apply a modified dispersion relation that accounts for isotropic, anisotropic, and birefringent effects. Leveraging the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA algorithm library, we conducted a joint Bayesian analysis to infer source parameters alongside coefficients related to spacetime symmetry breaking. Analyzing a subset of 45 high-confidence events from the GWTC-3 catalog, we determined a maximum constraint of $3.19 \times 10^{-15}$~m (at 90\% CI) for the isotropic coefficient $k_{(V)00}^{(5)}$, assuming vanishing anisotropic coefficients. When all dispersion parameters are considered collectively, the resulting limits for the 16 $k_{(V)ij}^{(5)}$ coefficients reach approximately $10^{-13}$~m. To assess the reliability of our inference, we compared constraints derived from various waveform models, revealing that incomplete physical descriptions in simulated waveforms can mimic spacetime symmetry breaking-induced dispersion in certain events.

This study introduces ProCS, a method designed for the swift and precise prediction of protein backbone amide proton chemical shifts, which serve as critical indicators of the hydrogen bond geometries essential for protein structure. Parameterized using quantum mechanical (QM) calculations, ProCS successfully replicates high-level QM data from a small protein, achieving an RMSD of 0.25 ppm and a correlation coefficient of 0.94. Integrated with the PHAISTOS simulation software, ProCS enables the inference of statistical protein ensembles that align with experimentally observed amide proton chemical shifts. When applied to high-resolution X-ray structures of Protein G, ubiquitin, and the SMN Tudor Domain, these chemical shift-driven refinements yield average chemical shifts, hydrogen bond geometries, and trans-hydrogen bond ($^3hJ_{NC'}$) coupling constants that closely match experimental data. Our findings demonstrate that the structural sensitivity inherent in QM-based amide proton chemical shift predictions is crucial for achieving such agreement. Consequently, ProCS provides a potent new instrument for refining hydrogen bonding networks to high accuracy, with broad applications including the analysis of protein flexibility during ligand binding.

This study focuses on analyzing strong solutions to the Abels-Garcke-Grün (AGG) model in three dimensions. We first establish the existence of local-in-time strong solutions starting from an initial condition $(\mathbf{u}_0, \phi_0)\in \mathbf{H}^1_\sigma \times H^2(\Omega)$, where $\mu_0 \in H^1(\Omega)$ and $|\overline{\phi_0}|\leq 1$. For initial data strictly separated from pure phases, we demonstrate that the corresponding strong solutions are locally unique. Furthermore, we derive a stability estimate comparing solutions of the AGG model with those of the model H. These findings extend the author's previous analysis published in {\it Calc. Var. (2021) 60:100} to three-dimensional bounded domains.

Clinical data indicates that suppressing ribs in chest X-rays (CXRs) enhances the reliability of diagnosing pulmonary conditions. Nevertheless, prior methods for generating rib-suppressed CXRs struggle to eliminate rib artifacts while maintaining fine details. To address this, we introduce RSGAN, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework utilizing disentanglement learning. This approach leverages anatomical information from unpaired computed tomography (CT) scans to perform rib suppression. Specifically, we use a residual map to capture intensity variations between the original CXR and its rib-suppressed counterpart. By disentangling images into structure- and contrast-specific features, we transfer rib structural priors derived from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) generated by CT to predict the residual map within the CXR domain. Additionally, an adaptive loss function is employed to further suppress rib residues and retain critical details. Extensive experiments conducted on 1,673 CT volumes and four benchmark CXR datasets (over 120,000 images in total) demonstrate that: (i) RSGAN produces superior image quality compared to existing state-of-the-art rib suppression techniques; and (ii) integrating our rib-suppressed results with standard CXRs improves performance in lung disease classification and tuberculosis lesion detection.

$\upsilon$ Sgr serves as the prototype for four identified hydrogen-deficient binary (HdB) systems. These systems feature an A-type primary star lacking hydrogen, variable hydrogen emission lines, and a secondary component that is typically invisible, likely an upper main-sequence star. Their orbital periods span from tens of days up to 360 days. TESS data from all four HdBs reveal flux variations with well-defined periods between 0.5 and 0.9 days; these intervals are too brief to originate from the supergiant primary and instead suggest the rotation period of the secondary, potentially linked to surface chemical asymmetries or low-order non-radial oscillations. This observed rotation period aligns with recent analyses of the $\upsilon$ Sgr secondary. Consequently, these observations provide the first direct view of the secondary in all four systems and may aid in elucidating the mechanism by which the primary was stripped to form a low-mass hydrogen remnant.

Accurate analysis of secure bounds is critical for the practical implementation of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems. However, current analyses often overlook the impact of randomness seed uniformity during the privacy amplification phase. This paper introduces and proves a quantum leftover hash lemma tailored for non-uniform random seeds using min-entropy, establishing a precise QKD secure bound analysis based on this framework. Using the two-decoy BB84 protocol as a case study, we simulated how seed uniformity influences system security. The results demonstrate that if the average min-entropy of the random number generator falls below 0.95, the QKD system's secure bound is severely compromised.

This study examines the connections between various solar transients—including blinkers captured at 304~{\AA}, extreme ultraviolet coronal bright points (ECBPs) at 193~{\AA}, and X-ray coronal bright points (XCBPs) at 94~{\AA} via AIA—alongside magnetic features detected by HMI throughout the ten-year span of solar cycle 24. Employing an automated detection technique for transients and the YAFTA algorithm for magnetic feature extraction, we identified a total of 7,483,827 blinkers, 2,082,162 ECBPs, and 1,188,839 XCBPs. Their respective birthrates were calculated as approximately $1.1\times10^{-18}$ ${\rm m}^{-2}{\rm s}^{-1}$, $3.8\times10^{-19}$ ${\rm m}^{-2}{\rm s}^{-1}$, and $1.5\times10^{-19}$ ${\rm m}^{-2}{\rm s}^{-1}$. Our analysis reveals that roughly 80\% of blinkers occur at supergranule boundaries, with 57\% and 34\% linked to ECBPs and XCBPs, respectively. Furthermore, approximately 61{--}80\% of these transients are connected to isolated magnetic poles in the quiet Sun, and the normalized maximum intensities of the transients exhibit a power-law correlation with the photospheric magnetic flux of these poles. These findings strongly indicate a magnetic origin for the transients, and their synchronized behavior offers additional insights into the coupling across different layers of the solar atmosphere. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the occurrence of these transients is significantly anti-correlated with the sunspot cycle, a discovery that may enhance our understanding of solar dynamo processes and magnetic structures at various scales during the solar cycle.

Using the classical $L^2$-energy within the Lyapunov second method, we investigate the nonlinear stability of plane Couette and Poiseuille flows. Our findings demonstrate that streamwise perturbations maintain $L^2$-energy stability across all Reynolds numbers, directly contradicting the conclusions of Joseph [10], Joseph and Carmi [12], and Busse [4]. This result confirms that the critical nonlinear Reynolds numbers correspond to two-dimensional spanwise perturbations, as originally hypothesized by Orr [16]. When combined with recent insights from Falsaperla et al. [8] regarding tilted rolls, this conclusion offers a potential resolution to the Couette-Sommerfeld paradox.

Human activities, including online transactions, health records, and spatial movement, generate vast amounts of data organized as event sequences in continuous time. Applying deep learning to these sequences is challenging because it requires modeling dynamic factors such as increasing timestamps, inter-event intervals, event categories, and intra- and inter-sequence event interactions. These difficulties are compounded by data collection constraints, such as limited availability, incomplete sequences, and privacy limitations. This work investigates the properties of continuous-time event sequences (CTES) and develops robust, scalable neural network models to address these challenges. Specifically, we utilize marked temporal point processes (MTPP) to model the underlying generative distribution of events for solving diverse real-world problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed methods against state-of-the-art baselines and outline current research directions.

The HORIZON-T experiment observed multimodal events (MME) in very high-energy extensive air showers, which were investigated for a potential link to the strongly penetrating component detected in homogenous lead emulsion chambers by the Pamir and Chacaltaya experiments. Our findings suggest that these two observations are interconnected and likely represent the same physical phenomenon: the penetration of a strangelet through matter. In the context of the emulsion chambers, the strangelet generates long-range cascades with multiple maxima. Conversely, within the HORIZON-T detectors, the successive interactions of the strangelet in the atmosphere appear as consecutive signals, with time intervals ranging from dozens to several hundred nanoseconds.

This study introduces an infeasible interior-point algorithm for convex optimization that incorporates arc-search methodologies. The method concurrently determines the centering parameter and step size to maximize performance in each iteration. Explicit analytical formulas are derived for the arc-search process to ensure high efficiency. Furthermore, the algorithm's convergence is rigorously proven, and a polynomial bound is established. Initial numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach is both efficient and effective.

Although semantic segmentation is a well-established area in computer vision, developing video processing networks that are both rapid and precise remains difficult. Furthermore, deploying these models on embedded hardware often necessitates sacrificing accuracy to meet speed requirements, making the latency-accuracy trade-off central to designing real-time systems. In the specific context of video analysis, models can exploit computations from prior frames to offset accuracy reductions while maintaining real-time performance. This work addresses fast future video segmentation prediction by introducing convolutional layers with time-dependent channel masking. This approach updates only a selected subset of feature maps at each time step, simultaneously reducing computational load and latency while enabling the network to utilize previously calculated features. We applied this method to various efficient architectures and experimentally validated its advantages for the future prediction subtask.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC measured the production of non-prompt ${\rm D}^{0}$ mesons originating from beauty-hadron decays at midrapidity ($\left| y \right| < 0.5$) during Pb-Pb collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02~\mathrm{TeV}$. For the first time, their nuclear modification factor ($R_{\rm AA}$) was determined down to $p_{\rm T}=1~\mathrm{GeV}/c$ within the $0-10$% and $30-50$% centrality intervals. The results reveal a substantial suppression, reaching approximately a factor of three for $p_{\rm T} > 5~\mathrm{GeV}/c$ in the most central ($0-10$%) Pb-Pb collisions. These observations align with models that incorporate both collisional and radiative energy loss mechanisms for beauty quarks in the quark-gluon plasma, alongside quark recombination and fragmentation as hadronization processes. Furthermore, in the $0-10$% central collisions, the ratio of non-prompt to prompt ${\rm D}^{0}$-meson $R_{\rm AA}$ exceeds unity for $p_{\rm T} > 4~\mathrm{GeV}/c$, a trend consistent with models predicting that heavier beauty quarks lose less energy than lighter charm quarks within the quark-gluon plasma.

The development of multifunctional two-dimensional (2D) materials, particularly those combining properties like piezoelectricity with topological insulating phases or ferromagnetism, is highly significant. This study introduces a Janus monolayer of $\mathrm{SrAlGaSe_4}$, derived from the 2D $\mathrm{MA_2Z_4}$ family, which exhibits dynamic, mechanical, and thermal stability. Due to its lack of inversion symmetry, this material is piezoelectric. While the unstrained $\mathrm{SrAlGaSe_4}$ monolayer acts as a narrow-gap normal insulator (NI) under spin-orbit coupling (SOC), applying biaxial strain triggers a transition to a topological insulator (TI) phase, resulting in a piezoelectric quantum spin Hall insulator (PQSHI). Notably, this phase transition occurs at merely 1.01% tensile strain, with the nontrivial band topology persisting up to 1.16% tensile strain. Furthermore, the PQSHI state displays Rashba spin splitting in the conduction bands, attributed to the absence of horizontal mirror symmetry combined with SOC. Under uniaxial strain, the monolayer generates both in-plane and significantly weaker out-of-plane piezoelectric polarizations. At 1.06% tensile strain, the calculated piezoelectric strain coefficients ($d_{11}$ and $d_{31}$) are -1.865 pm/V and -0.068 pm/V, respectively, characterizing it as a representative TI. These findings suggest that PQSHIs can be realized across the $\mathrm{MA_2Z_4}$ family; for instance, the $\mathrm{CaAlGaSe_4}$ monolayer also achieves the coexistence of piezoelectricity and topological orders at approximately 1.04% tensile strain. Ultimately, the Janus monolayer $\mathrm{SrAlGaSe_4}$ serves as a pure 2D system for PQSHI, paving the way for future research into the interplay between piezoelectricity and topological orders for potential applications in electronics and spintronics.

This report outlines a methodology for simulating multi-body interactions within actively controlled systems. Specifically, this study examines the control mechanisms and contact dynamics of a two-dimensional bipedal robot as it kicks a spherical ball.

This paper establishes that no special timelike Frenet curve constitutes a Bertrand curve in $\mathbb{E}_2^4$, and in $\mathbb{E}_\nu^{n+1}$ for $n \ge 3$, the concept of a Bertrand curve is strictly defined only within $\mathbb{E}_1^2$ and $\mathbb{E}_1^3$. Consequently, a generalization termed the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve is introduced for $\mathbb{E}_2^4$, alongside a detailed characterization of this curve type within the same space.

We have examined the structure of the Hercules supercluster (SCL160) using data initially sourced from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-DR7). By analyzing the mass distribution across the field via numerical density weighted by $r^\prime$-luminosity, and categorizing galaxies according to their spatial location and redshift, we were able to investigate the overall kinematics of the supercluster as well as the internal kinematics of individual clusters, an aspect previously unexplored. Our findings confirm that the Hercules supercluster comprises the galaxy clusters A2147, A2151, and A2152. Specifically, A2151 contains five subclusters, A2147 has two, and A2152 has at least two; these three constitute the core of the supercluster. Additionally, we identified two further gravitationally bound clusters, thereby expanding the known membership of the supercluster. We estimated the total mass of the Hercules supercluster to be $2.1\pm0.2 \times 10^{15}$ M$_\odot$. To derive dynamical masses, we employed both the $M_{200}-\sigma$ scaling relation and the caustic technique. Comparisons with simulated data from bimodal merging clusters revealed that both the caustic method and $\sigma$-based masses are influenced by merger age, exhibiting an increase immediately following pericentric passage. This observation contradicts the fundamental principle of the caustic method, which asserts independence from the cluster's dynamical state.

Contemporary binary classification algorithms typically depend on an intermediate regression task to ensure computational feasibility. This paper introduces a geometric distinction between classification and regression that enables a more precise relationship between their respective risks. Specifically, we observe that classification risk relies solely on the regressor's direction; by leveraging this scale invariance, we enhance existing bounds that relate classification risk to the risk of the underlying regression problem. Our analysis, built upon these improved guarantees, allows for more accurate comparisons among algorithms and suggests viewing classification as distinct from regression rather than merely a derivative of it. While regression seeks convergence toward the conditional expectation function in terms of location, we argue that classification should instead focus on recovering the correct direction.

Recent years have seen computer vision in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) and autonomous driving (AD) increasingly rely on deep neural network architectures. Although performance on benchmark datasets continues to improve, research often fails to adequately address numerous real-world challenges. This paper presents an extensive literature review of computer vision applications within ITS and AD, highlighting key obstacles related to data, modeling, and intricate urban environments. Data-related issues include difficulties in collecting and labeling training data relevant to real conditions, inherent dataset biases, the massive volume of data requiring processing, and privacy concerns. Deep learning models often prove too complex for real-time execution on embedded hardware, suffer from a lack of explainability and generalizability, and are difficult to validate in actual settings. Furthermore, complex urban traffic scenarios present irregular lighting, occlusions, and surveillance cameras that may be mounted at various angles, become dirty, shake due to wind, and operate under highly heterogeneous traffic conditions involving rule violations and complex interactions in crowded areas. Representative applications affected by these issues include traffic flow estimation, congestion detection, autonomous driving perception, vehicle interaction, and edge computing for practical deployment. The paper also explores potential solutions to these challenges, with a focus on facilitating practical deployment.

Recent experiments have identified multifold fermions in materials such as AlPt and XSi (where X is Rh or Co), characterized by multifold degeneracy at band crossings and Fermi surfaces with nontrivial Chern numbers. This study significantly broadens the known class of multifold fermion materials by revealing that several established noncentrosymmetric superconductors actually function as multifold fermion metals. Crucially, the normal-state topological attributes of these materials, previously overlooked, are shown to be vital for their superconducting behavior. Using Li$_2$Pd$_3$B and Li$_2$Pt$_3$B as case studies, we discovered numerous unconventional degenerate points near the Fermi energy, including double spin-1, spin-3/2, Weyl, and double Weyl crossings, all yielding finite Chern numbers on the Fermi surfaces. Additionally, Li$_2$Pd$_3$B exhibits long Fermi arc states derived from its nontrivial band topology. Experimental results confirm that Li$_2$Pd$_3$B is a fully gapped superconductor while Li$_2$Pt$_3$B is gapless. Our analysis of pairing symmetries suggests that Li$_2$Pd$_3$B could be a DIII class topological superconductor hosting Majorana surface states, despite its negligible spin-orbit coupling. Conversely, the gapless nature of Li$_2$Pt$_3$B points to it being a nodal topological superconductor with dispersionless surface Majorana modes. Furthermore, we identified several other noncentrosymmetric superconductors—Mo$_3$Al$_2$C, PdBiSe, Y$_2$C$_3$, and La$_2$C$_3$—as multifold fermion superconductors, noting that their normal-state topological characteristics have been neglected in prior research.

Interacting quantum many-body systems driven dynamically can display behaviors that contradict equilibrium statistical mechanics laws. A prominent example is the impulsively driven antiferromagnetic Mott insulator, which is theorized to produce exotic transient phenomena such as dynamical phase transitions into thermally prohibited states and highly non-thermal magnon distributions. Yet, these far-from-equilibrium regimes, where standard time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theories break down, remain difficult to prepare and measure experimentally, particularly in solid-state materials. In this study, we employ a hybrid approach combining time-resolved second harmonic optical polarimetry and coherent magnon spectroscopy to investigate ultrafast magnetic order parameter dynamics induced by n-type photo-doping in the Mott insulator Sr$_2$IrO$_4$. We reveal an anomalous far-from-equilibrium critical regime where the divergences of magnetic correlation length and relaxation time become decoupled. This departure from conventional thermal criticality stems from the interplay between photo-doping and non-thermal magnon population effects that drive demagnetization. Our results, summarized in a non-equilibrium "phase diagram," offer a framework for engineering out-of-equilibrium properties of quantum matter, holding promise for terahertz spintronics applications.

This study introduces a cloud energy storage (CES) framework designed to facilitate renewable energy integration for building consumers (BCs). Unlike prevalent third-party energy storage (ES) sharing schemes where the energy storage operator (ESO) profits from leasing capacity, our CES approach enables the ESO to sell renewable utilization services (RUS)—representing the volume of local renewable generation redirected to meet consumer demand. We establish a quadratic pricing mechanism for RUS and model the interactions as a Stackelberg game that guarantees an equilibrium. The analysis demonstrates that the CES model surpasses individual ES (IES) models in terms of social welfare. Through case studies comparing CES with both IES and an existing VES sharing model, we show that the CES model can generate 2 to 4 times the profit for the ESO compared to VES. Additionally, the CES model ensures greater cost reductions for BCs. Finally, we illustrate that while other ES models fall short, the CES model achieves near-optimal social welfare and high energy storage efficiency.

This study examines the deployment and utility of multi-variable grid-forming hybrid angle control (HAC) for high-power converters within transmission networks. We analyze the system-level performance and robustness of this HAC approach compared to alternative grid-forming strategies, specifically power-frequency droop and matching controls. Our results indicate that, much like ac-based droop control, HAC improves small-signal frequency stability in grids with low inertia; similarly, akin to dc-based matching control, it demonstrates robustness regarding practical converter limitations. Consequently, HAC integrates these complementary benefits. Additionally, we demonstrate that adjusting specific parameters in grid-forming controls can further enhance frequency performance. Finally, as distinct contributions, we present an alternative control augmentation that bolsters robustness and offers theoretical guidance for extending HAC stability certificates to multi-converter configurations.

This paper investigates the computational complexity of determining an evolutionary stable strategy (ESS) within multi-player symmetric games. For two-player scenarios, we established that deciding whether an ESS exists is {\Sigma} 2 -complete, corresponding to the second level of the polynomial time hierarchy. We demonstrate that determining the existence of an ESS in multi-player games is intimately linked to the second level of the real polynomial time hierarchy. Specifically, we prove the problem is hard for the complexity class \exists D . \forall R and resides within \exists\forall R; the former class is a subset of the latter where existentially quantified variables are restricted to Boolean values rather than real numbers. As a specific consequence of these findings, deciding if a particular strategy constitutes an ESS is \forall R-complete. We also examine locally superior strategies (LSS), a concept closely tied to ESS. By extending our analysis, we show that determining the existence of an LSS in a multi-player game is similarly hard for \exists D \forall R and a member of \exists\forall R, with the special case that verifying whether a given strategy is an LSS is \forall R-complete.

This study presents the initial measurements of dielectron production at midrapidity ($|\eta_{c}|<0.8$) in proton-proton and proton-lead collisions at the LHC, conducted at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm{NN}}}$ = 5.02 TeV. Using the ALICE detector, the dielectron cross section was evaluated across the invariant mass range $m_{\rm{ee}}$ < 3.5 GeV/$c^{2}$ and transverse momentum range $p_{\rm{T,ee}}$ < 8.0 GeV/$c^{2}$ for both collision types.
