Furthermore, we employ standard consistency regularization to align predictions from two different input views, thereby creating a more compact target feature space. We evaluate our proposed CPR method on three standard benchmarks, achieving results that are either comparable to or surpass existing state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, we conduct extensive ablation studies to validate the key design choices within our framework.

Accurate segmentation of cardiac anatomical structures in cardiac magnetic resonance images (CMRI) is essential for the automated diagnosis and prognosis of cardiovascular conditions. To enhance the robustness and efficacy of segmentation techniques, this research integrates automatic segmentation with the evaluation of segmentation uncertainty to identify image regions prone to local failures. Three leading convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were trained to segment cardiac structures and generate two uncertainty metrics: entropy and a measure derived from Monte Carlo dropout. Subsequently, a fourth CNN was trained to utilize these uncertainty scores to pinpoint local segmentation errors that may require expert correction. The study then simulated the manual correction of these identified regions. Using publicly available CMR data from the MICCAI 2017 ACDC challenge, the investigation examined the effects of CNN architecture, loss functions, and uncertainty measures on performance. Evaluation metrics included the Dice coefficient and 3D Hausdorff distance compared against manual segmentations. The results demonstrate that combining automatic segmentation with the simulated manual correction of detected failures yields a statistically significant improvement in performance.

Acoustic-to-articulatory inversion (AAI) aims to derive articulator movements from speech signals. However, achieving speaker-independent AAI remains challenging due to data limitations, and most existing approaches rely solely on audio inputs, creating a performance bottleneck. To address these issues, we first pre-train a speech decomposition network to extract speaker and content embeddings as personalized features, adapting the model for speaker-independent scenarios. Second, we introduce a novel auxiliary feature network to estimate lip features from these personalized speech representations. Experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art audio-only methods, our approach reduces the average RMSE by 0.25 and increases the average correlation coefficient by 2.0% in speaker-dependent cases. More significantly, in the speaker-independent setting, the average RMSE decreases by 0.29 and the average correlation coefficient improves by 5.0%.

We present a purely image-driven approach designed to solve ruler-and-compass geometric constructions within the Euclidea game. This technique combines the Mask R-CNN neural network architecture with a tree-based search algorithm. In a supervised learning framework, the model successfully solved all 68 types of construction problems from the first six level packs with an average accuracy of 92%. When tested on novel problem types, it managed to solve 31 out of the 68 varieties. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance of purely image-based learning being trained to tackle geometric constructions of this complexity.

This research investigates dualities within differential equations and inequalities, specifically between comparison theorems, and derives dualities in the "swapping" of these theorems. These findings yield comparison results for mixed-type differential equations (Types I and II) and establish comparison theorems in Riemannian geometry, with applications spanning analysis, geometry, partial differential equations, and physics. Notably, we prove Hessian and Laplacian comparison theorems under diverse assumptions regarding radial Ricci or curvature, thereby generalizing and expanding upon the contributions of Han-Li-Ren-Wei and Wei. Furthermore, we extend the concepts of growth for functions and differential forms to various types of bundle-valued differential forms, analyzing their interrelations. These developments offer tools for generalizing the integrability and decomposition of generalized harmonic forms to their bundle-valued counterparts, introducing "Condition W" for such forms, and proving duality and unity theorems that generalize the work of Andreotti, Vesentini, and Wei. Subsequently, we apply the established Hessian and Laplacian comparison theorems to derive results on mean curvature, generalized sharp Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg and Hardy-type inequalities on Riemannian manifolds, embedding theorems for weighted Sobolev spaces, geometric differential-integral inequalities, monotonicity formulas, and vanishing theorems for vector bundle-valued differential forms of degree $k$. These applications include $F$-Yang-Mills fields (reducing to Yang-Mills fields when $F$ is the identity), generalized Yang-Mills-Born-Infeld fields, Liouville-type theorems for $F$-harmonic maps, and solutions to Dirichlet problems on starlike domains for vector bundle-valued 1-forms and $F$-harmonic maps.

We introduce a planning and control framework designed for physics-based manipulation under uncertainty, centered on interleaving robust open-loop execution with closed-loop control. By leveraging contraction theory, we derive robustness metrics to plan trajectories resilient to both state uncertainty and model inaccuracies. Since fully robust trajectories are often infeasible or difficult to compute in many multi-contact scenarios, we decompose a trajectory into robust and non-robust segments using a minimum cost path search on a robustness graph. Robust segments are executed open-loop, while non-robust segments utilize model-predictive control. Experiments conducted on a real robotic system for reaching tasks in clutter demonstrate that this hybrid approach yields up to 35% higher success rates compared to open-loop baselines and reduces execution time by 40% relative to model-predictive control. Furthermore, we show for the first time that our partially open-loop plans achieve success rates comparable to model-predictive control while enabling more fluent, real-time execution. Real-robot demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/rPOPCwHfV4g.

This paper introduces a compact, recursive, non-linear filter based on the Gauss-Newton (GNF) algorithm, which utilizes weighted least squares and the Newton method for local linearization. Adapted to the Levenberg-Marquardt approach, this recursive variant (RGNF) applies to both linear and nonlinear process state models alongside linear and nonlinear observation schemes. Simulation studies confirm the robustness of the RGNF and demonstrate a significant reduction in computational memory usage, addressing a key historical limitation of the GNF.

This study analyzes the evolution of song complexity from 1960 to 2010 using data from the Million Song Dataset (MSD), focusing on pitch, timbre, loudness, and rhythm. Comparisons between Billboard Hot 100 hits and random samples reveal that popular songs exhibit a narrower distribution of complexity around the mean, which aligns with the hypothesis of an inverted U-shaped relationship between complexity and hedonistic appeal. The temporal analysis highlights consistent decade-to-decade shifts, including a reduction in average loudness complexity since the 1960s and a general rise in timbre complexity, though the latter increase is not observed in popular songs. Contrary to assertions that popular music has become more homogenous over time, our findings indicate no significant increase in similarity regarding pitch or rhythm compared to fifty years ago; however, timbre similarity displays unique era-specific patterns, while loudness similarity has grown. Lastly, we demonstrate that distinct complexity profiles allow for the differentiation of musical genres.

This letter initiates an investigation into visible signals from the dark sector associated with binary neutron star mergers. We concentrate on dark photons emitted within 10 milliseconds to 1 second post-merger, demonstrating their potential to generate bright, transient gamma-ray bursts. These emissions are expected to be nearly isotropic and, across a significant portion of the relevant parameter space, exhibit thermal characteristics with an apparent temperature around 100 keV. Such properties allow us to differentiate this dark photon signal from standard short gamma-ray bursts resulting from neutron star mergers, which are characterized by non-thermal spectra and narrow beaming angles. We compute the anticipated signal intensity and find that for dark photon masses between 1 and 100 MeV, the total luminosity can readily exceed $10^{46}$ ergs over much of the unconstrained parameter space. Furthermore, this signal offers a means to explore a substantial fraction of the parameter space favored by freeze-in dark matter models involving dark photon-mediated interactions. Finally, we discuss potential enhancements in observational capabilities once future telescopes and mid-band gravitational wave detectors become operational.

This research addresses an online revenue maximization scenario where consumers arrive independently and identically distributed from an unknown distribution to purchase product bundles from sellers. While classical methods typically assume full knowledge of consumer utility functions, and recent studies have focused on unknown linear utilities, this paper investigates the online posted-price model under conditions of unknown consumer distribution and unknown, concave consumer utilities. Specifically, it tackles two inquiries: i) under what conditions the seller's online maximization problem becomes concave, and ii) how to determine the optimal pricing strategy for non-linear utilities. The first question is resolved by enforcing a third-order smoothness condition on the utilities. The second is addressed through two algorithms, both proven to achieve sub-linear regrets of $O(T^{\frac{2}{3}} (\log T)^{\frac{1}{3}})$ and $O(T^{\frac{1}{2}} (\log T)^{\frac{1}{2}})$, respectively.

This study investigates the chemistry of 294 dense cores within 12 molecular clumps using data from the ALMA Survey of 70 $\mu \rm m$ dark High-mass clumps in Early Stages (ASHES). By detecting outflows and molecular transitions with high upper energy levels ($E_{u}/k > 45$ K), we classified 97 objects as protostellar cores and 197 as prestellar core candidates. N$_{2}$D$^{+}$ emission was detected in 38% of protostellar cores compared to only 9% of prestellar cores, demonstrating that N$_{2}$D$^{+}$ is not a sole tracer of prestellar stages. Conversely, DCO$^{+}$ emission was observed in 35% of prestellar cores and 49% of protostellar cores, rates higher than those for N$_{2}$D$^{+}$, indicating that DCO$^{+}$ is more prevalent in both core types. Furthermore, the abundances of both N$_{2}$D$^{+}$ and DCO$^{+}$ decline as cores evolve from the prestellar to the protostellar phase. Emission lines from DCN, C$_{2}$D, and $^{13}$CS were rarely detected in these early evolutionary dense cores. Regarding other species, H$_{2}$CO emission was detected in 52% of dense cores, a rate three times greater than that of CH$_{3}$OH (17%). Additionally, H$_{2}$CO detection rates, abundances, line intensities, and widths all increase with the evolutionary status of the core, suggesting that H$_{2}$CO line emission is a sensitive indicator of protostellar activity.

3D gaze estimation aims to predict a person's line of sight within a three-dimensional environment. However, person-independent models often suffer from reduced precision due to individual anatomical variations, while person-specific calibrated approaches impose strict limitations on scalability. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel method called Facial Landmark Heatmap Activated Multimodal Gaze Estimation (FLAME). This technique integrates eye anatomical data via eye landmark heatmaps to achieve accurate gaze prediction without requiring any person-specific calibration. Our evaluation shows competitive performance, achieving approximately a 10% improvement on benchmark datasets such as ColumbiaGaze and EYEDIAP. Additionally, we performed an ablation study to further validate the effectiveness of our approach.

Let $T$ be an orientation-preserving circle homeomorphism with a single break point $x_b$, belonging to the class $C^{2+\varepsilon}(S^1\setminus\{x_{b}\})$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, and possessing a rotation number $\rho_T=[k_{1},k_{2},..,k_{m},1,1,...]$ where $m\geq1$. We examine the stochastic recurrence relation $\overline{z}_{n+1}(z_0,\sigma) = T(\overline{z}_{n}) + \sigma \xi_{n+1}$, initialized at $\overline{z}_{0}:=z_0\in S^1$. Here, $\{\xi_{n}\}$ represents a sequence of independent, mean-zero real-valued random variables of comparable magnitude, and $\sigma$ denotes a small positive parameter. While de la Llave and colleagues previously established a Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and its convergence rate for stochastic perturbations of one-dimensional interval maps using renormalization group techniques, this paper extends those findings to circle homeomorphisms with break points. This extension relies on the thermodynamic formalism recently developed by Dzhalilov et al. for such maps. By combining this formalism with the dynamical partition $P_n(T,x_b)$ induced by the break point, and following the approach of Vul et al., we construct a symbolic dynamics for any $z\in S^1$ and define a transfer operator. The leading eigenvalue of this operator is utilized to bound the Lyapunov function. Furthermore, for a specific subsequence $\{n_m\}$ as $m\to\infty$, the barycentric coefficient of any iterate $z_k=T^kz_0$ that does not intersect the orbit of $x_b$ remains universally bounded within the corresponding interval of $P_{n_m}(T,x_b)$. A Taylor expansion of $\overline{z}_{n}(z_0,\sigma)$ with respect to the noise terms $\{\xi_i\}$ decomposes the process into the deterministic term $T^n(z_0)$, a linearized effective noise component, and higher-order noise terms. However, this expansion is valid only within specific neighborhoods $A_k^{n_m}$ surrounding the points $T^k z_0$ that exclude the break points of $T^{q_{n_m}}$, where $q_n$ denotes the first return times of $T$. Ultimately, proving the CLT for this linearized process enables the demonstration of our extension to the results originally obtained by de la Llave et al.

Scenarios like employees sharing office spaces across a workweek can be modeled as multi-round matching problems between agents and resources. In these scenarios, agents' constraints define compatible resources and preferred rounds. By treating this as a multi-round matching problem on a bipartite compatibility graph, we demonstrate that an efficient solution exists if one is possible. To address cases where no perfect solution exists, we explore two extensions. First, we define a benefit function for each agent to maximize total benefit through multi-round matching; for a specific class of functions satisfying properties like diminishing returns—including utilitarian and Rawlsian welfare functions—we prove efficient solvability, whereas we show the problem becomes NP-hard for another benefit function. Second, we aim to provide advice to agents by suggesting which requirements to relax within a budget constraint to ensure matching, a task we identify as NP-hard. For this, we develop an integer linear programming formulation and a local search-based heuristic. We experimentally assess these algorithms using synthetic networks and real-world applications involving shared office spaces and course-to-classroom assignments.

Taylor's theorem, along with its variations, plays a significant role in various branches of mathematical analysis, such as numerical analysis, functional analysis, and partial differential equations. This article demonstrates that the most general form of Taylor's theorem can be derived simply as a direct result of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTOC). The proof highlights the profound link between Taylor expansions and fixed-point iteration, a cornerstone concept in both numerical and functional analysis. Additionally, an elegant variant of this proof illustrates the application of combinatorics and symmetry within mathematical analysis. Given that the proof underscores concepts and techniques essential to modern science and industry, it would be a valuable component of undergraduate mathematics education.

Quantum chromodynamics functions as a non-Abelian gauge theory describing strong interactions, where parity symmetry is broken by tunneling effects arising from the non-trivial $\theta$-vacuum. This $\theta$-vacuum generates local domains with odd parity, causing reactions within them to be influenced by tunneling and resulting in parity-odd quantities. This paper examines the fragmentation process by introducing parity-odd fragmentation functions. By decomposing the quark-quark correlator, we define these functions: out of a total of 16 fragmentation functions, eight conserve parity while the remaining eight violate it, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between them. We derive positivity bounds for these one-dimensional functions and provide an explicit operator definition for the parity-odd correlator. Based on this definition, we demonstrate that parity-odd fragmentation functions are local quantities and prove that they sum to zero across all hadrons $h$.

We estimate the maximum jet power for the Blandford-Znajek (BZ), Blandford-Payne (BP), and hybrid models under a coronal magnetic field. While BZ and hybrid jet powers rely on black hole spin, the BP mechanism's power is spin-independent. At high spin rates, the hybrid model yields greater jet power than either BZ or BP. Our findings indicate that the hybrid model adequately explains the jet power of nearly all gamma-ray narrow line Seyfert 1 galaxies (gamma-NLS1s), with the exception of one source exhibiting a jet power of 0.1 Eddington luminosity. We propose that for this outlier, jets are accelerated by magnetization-driven outflows where the accretion disk drags magnetic fields inward.

PyLlama is a convenient Python framework designed to calculate electromagnetic reflection and transmission characteristics for arbitrary multilayered linear media, accommodating anisotropic conditions. Utilizing a $4 \times 4$-matrix formalism, the toolkit implements both the widely used transfer matrix method and the numerically robust scattering matrix method, which remains stable in challenging scenarios such as thick, highly birefringent cholesteric structures under grazing incidence. Designed for practical utility, PyLlama enables users to effortlessly create, modify, and assemble layers or complex multilayered domains. This article details the electromagnetic principles behind these matrix methods, outlines PyLlama's architecture and key features, and validates the code against analytical solutions to demonstrate its versatility and numerical stability through modeling of cholesteric media with varying complexity. A comprehensive user manual with documentation and tutorials is available separately. The toolkit's applications span from optical component design and the modeling of polaritonic effects in polar crystals to the investigation of structurally colored materials in nature.

We introduce a methodology for designing control systems governing $n$ bodies in the real line $\Bbb R^1$ and on the unit circle $S^1$ to ensure they remain collision-free and controllable. This challenge is equivalent to constructing a control-affine system within $\Bbb R^n$ and the $n$-torus $T^n$, respectively, that navigates around specific obstacles. We establish the system's controllability by demonstrating that the vector fields defining the control-affine system, along with their first-order brackets, span the entire tangent space of the state space, followed by the application of the Rashevsky-Chow theorem.

Phase correlations offer an efficient method for retrieving astrophysical insights that remain largely independent of the power spectrum. We introduce an estimator for the line correlation function (LCF) of projected fields, defined as the correlation among harmonic-space phases at three equidistant locations along a great circle. Applying this method to data from the 2MPZ survey, we achieve an initial $6.5\sigma$ detection of phase correlations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the LCF can substantially tighten constraints on parameters governing the galaxy-halo connection, particularly for those that are typically degenerate when relying solely on two-point statistics.

In Euclidean 3-space, reflection across a line induces an almost paracomplex structure on the space of oriented lines, which remains isometric under the canonical neutral Kähler metric. Extending beyond Euclidean 3-space, the space of oriented geodesics for any real 3-dimensional space form supports both isometric and anti-isometric paracomplex structures. This study investigates the existence of isometric and anti-isometric almost paracomplex structures $j$ on a pseudo-Riemannian 4-manifold $(M,g)$ where $j$ is parallel relative to the Levi-Civita connection. The results demonstrate that if such a structure on a conformally flat manifold is parallel, the metric's scalar curvature must vanish. Furthermore, $j$ is parallel if and only if its eigenplanes are tangent to two mutually orthogonal foliations composed of totally geodesic surfaces.

When a Riemannian metric is combined with a parallel isometric almost paracomplex structure $j$, it produces a neutral metric $g'$. It is proven that $g$ is Einstein precisely when $g'$ is both conformally flat and scalar flat. Additionally, the vanishing of the Hirzebruch signature is identified as a necessary topological requirement for a closed 4-manifold to possess an Einstein metric with a parallel isometric paracomplex structure. Consequently, although the K3 manifold supports an Einstein metric with an isometric paracomplex structure, this structure cannot be parallel; the same limitation applies to specific connected sums of complex projective 2-space and its conjugate.

A puzzling yet significant finding from research conducted in the 1990s and 2000s is that the ratio of vacuum energy density fluctuations to their mean in generic spacetimes approaches unity. This was originally established by computing noise kernels, which represent the correlators of the stress-energy tensor for quantum fields. This paper revisits the topic using a quantum thermodynamic framework, specifically calculating two key quantities: heat capacity and quantum compressibility for model geometries containing quantum fields at both high and low temperatures. Heat capacity at constant volume serves as a measure of energy density fluctuations relative to the mean; when this ratio reaches or exceeds one, the applicability of the canonical distribution becomes doubtful. Similarly, compressibility at constant pressure acts as a test for the validity of the grand canonical ensemble. We derive the free energy density to obtain expressions for these thermodynamic quantities for thermal and quantum fields across various spacetimes, including 2D Casimir space, the 2D Einstein cylinder, and the 4D ($S^1 \times S^3$) Einstein universe. To explore dimensional dependence, we also derived these quantities for Einstein universes with even spatial dimensions ($S^1 \times S^2$ and $S^1 \times S^4$). This collection of spacetimes allows us to assess the thermodynamic stability of quantum matter fields and draw qualitative conclusions regarding the compatibility conditions necessary for the coexistence of quantum fields and spacetimes, a central challenge in the intersection of quantum mechanics and gravity.

This paper focuses on constructing invariant regions for a generalized m-component reaction-diffusion system featuring a tri-diagonal Toeplitz matrix for diffusion coefficients and establishing the global existence of solutions via a Lyapunov functional. The study considers nonhomogeneous boundary conditions and polynomial growth in the non-linear reaction term.

This study compares the Kurganov-Tadmor (KT) two-dimensional second-order semi-discrete central scheme, implemented via a dimension-by-dimension formulation, with a novel two-dimensional approach introduced here and tested through numerical simulations of two-phase flows in heterogeneous formations. The KT scheme relies on Rusanov's method but incorporates more accurate local wave propagation speeds calculated at each Riemann Problem across two spatial dimensions. Our findings indicate that the dimension-by-dimension KT scheme offers a simpler mathematical framework than the genuinely two-dimensional version, albeit with slightly increased numerical diffusion, especially around viscous fingers. However, the dimension-by-dimension KT approach can yield incorrect boundary behaviors in standard porous media geometries, such as a quarter of a five-spot pattern. The authors have addressed this issue with the new semi-discrete scheme proposed in this work. The paper concludes with numerical examples illustrating two-dimensional, two-phase flows in two distinct flooding scenarios: flow within a rectangular heterogeneous reservoir (slab geometry) and flow in a homogeneous five-spot reservoir.

The ALICE experiment at CERN is gearing up for a significant upgrade ahead of the third data-taking run (Run 3), which coincides with the onset of the Large Hadron Collider's high-luminosity phase. This surge in beam luminosity will drive the interaction rate so high that the data acquisition speed must surpass 3 TB/sec. To manage this increased data volume and capture every event, the readout electronics architecture must shift from a triggered to a trigger-less acquisition mode. In this updated design, a specialized electronics module known as the Common Readout Unit (CRU) serves as the central hub for aggregating detector data and distributing timing, trigger, and control (TTC) information. Within this trigger-less framework, TTC data is transmitted via two asynchronous high-speed serial links: TTC-PON and GBT. We conducted a study to assess the integrity of the timing signals forwarded by the CRU through these bridge connections. Four key performance metrics were employed to characterize the communication bridge: (a) the latency introduced by firmware logic, (b) the jitter reduction capability of the PLL on the timing signal, (c) Bit Error Rate (BER) analysis for quantitative signal quality assessment, and (d) the impact of optical transceiver settings on signal strength. Furthermore, we evaluated the bridge connection's reliability in maintaining timing phase consistency by executing multiple power-on/off, firmware upgrade, and reset assertion/de-assertion cycles (PFR cycles). The results are presented and discussed regarding the performance of the TTC-PON and GBT communication chain using the CRU prototype and its adherence to ALICE timing specifications.

This study introduces a new Synthetic Iteration Scheme (SIS) designed to solve Kramer's problem within the Lattice Boltzmann Equation (LBE) framework with high accuracy and efficiency. The process begins by solving the velocity distribution function using a standard iterative method, which is then refined through a specific modification in each iteration: (i) the flow velocity is directed by an asymptotic-preserving ordinary differential equation at the Navier-Stokes limit, and (ii) the shear stress is constrained to match the average shear stress. Evaluated against the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook model, the SIS demonstrates both efficiency and precision. The research further examines Kramer's problem for gases interacting via inverse power-law, shielded Coulomb, and Lennard-Jones potentials, under diffuse-specular and Cercignani-Lampis gas-surface boundary conditions. Results indicate that when the Tangential Momentum Accommodation Coefficient (TMAC) is one or less, the Knudsen layer function is significantly influenced by the intermolecular potential, with its magnitude and width growing as the effective viscosity index rises; furthermore, this function shows consistent behavior across different TMAC values when the potential remains constant. Conversely, for the Cercignani-Lampis condition with a TMAC exceeding one, both the viscous slip coefficient and the Knudsen layer function are impacted by the intermolecular potential, particularly near the "backward" scattering limit. Finally, utilizing Jiang and Luo's asymptotic theory regarding the singular behavior of velocity gradients near solid surfaces, the study confirms that the entire Knudsen layer function can be accurately approximated by a power series.

The reciprocal sum of the Zhang sequence does not equal the Distinct Distance Constant. This paper presents a $B_2$-sequence with a greater reciprocal sum and offers a more accurate estimation for the reciprocal sums of both the Mian-Chowla and Zhang sequences.

We introduce a method for achieving ground-state cooling of the fundamental out-of-plane (flexural) mode in a suspended graphene sheet. This approach utilizes the interaction between a driven Rydberg atom and the graphene resonator, made possible by vacuum forces. Due to the high polarizability of Rydberg states, the resulting Casimir-Polder force is orders of magnitude stronger than that produced by atoms in their ground state. By adjusting the separation distance between the atom and the graphene membrane, we demonstrate that resolved sideband cooling is achievable, reducing the occupation number of the fundamental flexural mode to its quantum limit. These results are anticipated to encourage further physical applications of graphene at ultra-low temperatures.

Let $G$ be a finite group with $H$ as a subgroup. We calculate the probability, $P_G(H)$, that a left transversal of $H$ in $G$ is simultaneously a right transversal, thereby forming a two-sided transversal. Furthermore, we introduce and denote by $\mathrm{tp}(G)$ the common transversal probability of $G$, defined as the minimum value of $P_G(H)$ across all subgroups $H$ of $G$. This paper establishes various results concerning the invariant $\mathrm{tp}(G)$, including determining its feasible values and deriving both lower and upper bounds. Additionally, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{tp}(G)$ reveals structural characteristics of $G$. The work concludes by presenting and discussing several open problems.

Randomized trials in educational technology generate detailed log data on student and teacher usage as a byproduct. While these datasets could reveal causal mechanisms, effect heterogeneity, or optimal usage strategies, they present methodological hurdles: the implementation itself is not randomized (only the treatment group is defined), and the log data possess a complex structure. This paper outlines three methods to address these challenges. First, an observational study approach uses treatment-group data to estimate how usage impacts outcomes. Second, causal mediation analysis assesses the extent to which usage drives the overall effect. Third, principal stratification estimates overall effects for student subgroups sharing the same "potential" usage levels. Applying these three methods to hint data from an evaluation of the Cognitive Tutor Algebra I curriculum yields potentially conflicting findings: both the observational study and mediation analysis indicate that hints lower posttest scores, whereas principal stratification suggests treatment effects correlate with higher hint request rates. The paper concludes by discussing these mixed results and offering broader methodological recommendations.

Effective anomaly detection and diagnosis within multivariate time-series data are crucial for contemporary industrial sectors. Nevertheless, constructing a system capable of rapidly and precisely identifying anomalous points remains a significant challenge, primarily due to the scarcity of labeled anomalies, high data volatility, and the stringent requirement for ultra-low inference latency. Although deep learning methods have recently advanced in this field, very few can simultaneously tackle all these hurdles. This paper introduces TranAD, a deep transformer-based model designed for anomaly detection and diagnosis. By employing attention-based sequence encoders, TranAD leverages broader temporal trends to execute swift inference. The model incorporates focus score-based self-conditioning to facilitate robust multi-modal feature extraction and utilizes adversarial training to enhance stability. Furthermore, Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) enables training with limited data. Comprehensive empirical evaluations across six public datasets reveal that TranAD surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both detection and diagnosis performance while achieving efficient training in terms of data and time. Specifically, TranAD improves F1 scores by as much as 17% and cuts training times by up to 99% compared to existing methods.

We provide a concise overview of a recently developed method for identifying pairs of nonlinearly coupled Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) that can be solved using algebraic operations. We present specific instances of this approach, focusing on systems of two first-order ODEs with polynomial right-hand sides, where $x_n' = P_n(x_1, x_2)$ for $n = 1, 2$, satisfied by two dependent variables $x_n = x_n(t)$. Here, $P_n(x_1, x_2)$ represents a particular polynomial. These examples are analogous to, yet distinct from, those previously documented.

We proceed with an analysis of the one-loop partition function for AdS$_3$ gravity, emphasizing the requirement of square-integrability for fluctuating fields. Building on prior findings that the Brown-Henneaux boundary conditions emerge naturally from the $L^2$ condition, we rederive the partition function as a ratio of Laplacian determinants through an appropriate decomposition of metric fluctuations, with particular attention to the asymptotic behavior of the relevant fields. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the standard computation involving ghost fields under the de Donder gauge is valid precisely when those ghost fields are square-integrable. Additionally, we calculate the spectrum of the pertinent Laplacians in thermal AdS$_3$, noting the absence of isolated eigenvalues and the presence of only an essential spectrum. This outcome corroborates the analytic continuation method proposed by David, Gaberdiel, and Gopakumar. The discovery of a purely essential spectrum aligns with independent findings by Lee and Delay regarding the essential spectrum of the TT rank-2 tensor Lichnerowicz Laplacian on asymptotically hyperbolic spaces.

Most contemporary methods for domain adaptive semantic segmentation depend on retaining access to source data during the adaptation phase, a requirement that is often impractical due to privacy or computational limitations. This work centers on source-free domain adaptation for semantic segmentation, where a pre-trained source model adjusts to a new target domain using only unlabeled target images. We introduce Augmentation Consistency-guided Self-training (AUGCO), a source-free algorithm that leverages pixel-level prediction consistency across various automatically generated views of target images, combined with model confidence, to pinpoint reliable predictions for selective self-training. AUGCO attains state-of-the-art performance across three standard semantic segmentation benchmarks, utilizing a straightforward approach that converges rapidly.

Let $h$ and $k$ be integers greater than or equal to 2. A set $A$ of positive integers is defined as an asymptotic basis of order $k$ if every sufficiently large positive integer can be expressed as the sum of $k$ elements from $A$. A set of positive integers $A$ is termed a $B_h[g]$-set if each positive integer can be represented as the sum of $h$ elements from $A$ in no more than $g$ distinct ways. This paper demonstrates the existence of $B_h[1]$ sets that also serve as asymptotic bases of order $2h$, utilizing probabilistic techniques.

We utilize the publicly accessible LEGA-C spectroscopic survey to analyze the stellar population characteristics of 140 massive and passive galaxies at $z\sim0.7$. We have created and released PyLick, a flexible Python tool designed to measure spectral indices ranging from UV to near-IR. Using PyLick, we investigate the H/K ratio as a novel diagnostic derived from pseudo-Lick CaII H and K indices, determining that a threshold of ${\rm H/K}<1.1$, when applied alongside other criteria, effectively selects or validates the purity of passive galaxy samples. By integrating both photometric and spectroscopic methods, we identify a robust sample of passively evolving galaxies. We constrain single-burst stellar ages, metallicities $\mathrm{[Z/H]}$, and $\mathrm{[\alpha/Fe]}$ using an optimized set of Lick indices, thoroughly examining the robustness of these measurements against various parameter combinations. Without imposing cosmological priors, the resulting ages exhibit a distinct trend consistent with the expected cosmological aging of the Universe. We detect no significant redshift evolution in metal abundance relative to $z=0$ values, with medians of $\mathrm{[Z/H]}=0.08\pm0.18$ and $\mathrm{[\alpha/Fe]}=0.13\pm0.11$. Furthermore, we observe positive correlations between $\log\mathrm{age}$, $\mathrm{[Z/H]}$, $\mathrm{[\alpha/Fe]}$, and stellar velocity dispersion, with slopes of ($0.48\pm0.14$), ($0.26\pm0.17$), and ($0.23\pm0.11$), respectively; the minimal scatter of $<0.2$ dex suggests relatively homogeneous and brief star formation histories. Collectively, these findings confirm and expand upon low-redshift results regarding mass-downsizing evolution. This study further supports the feasibility of selecting pure passive galaxy samples to serve as reliable cosmic chronometers for placing independent cosmological constraints.

This paper numerically investigates Turing patterns using Finsler geometry (FG) modeling applied to thermally fluctuating triangular lattices, which are frequently employed to represent cell and lipid membranes, with a specific focus on the origins of diffusion anisotropy. The FG modeling framework enables the assumption of direction-dependent diffusion described by a Laplacian. To incorporate this anisotropy into the FG model, an internal degree of freedom (IDF) is required; this IDF varies with direction and position and is regulated by external forces or stimuli. For a direction-dependent IDF, we utilize the velocity directions resulting from thermal fluctuations of the lattice vertices. Our findings indicate that anisotropic Turing patterns emerge along the direction in which the vertices fluctuate. In our simulations, explicit direction-dependent diffusion coefficients are not required as inputs; rather, the IDF aligns the direction of vertex fluctuation with the direction imposed by external stimuli. These results and methodologies offer insights into the mechanisms linking diffusion anisotropy to Turing patterns.

This paper introduces a new non-iterative algorithm designed to concurrently estimate the optimal rigid transformation for serial section images, a critical step in reconstructing volumes from biological tissue sections. To prevent the error accumulation and propagation common in existing methods, we impose a constraint requiring that the positions of the first and last section images remain fixed. This specific constrained simultaneous registration problem has previously remained unsolved. Our approach is non-iterative, enabling the rapid computation of rigid transformations for large sets of serial section images. We demonstrate that the algorithm yields an optimal solution under ideal conditions and validate its effectiveness using both synthetic and real-world data.

Physical computational systems are subject to operational limits that require a non-zero generation of entropy. Most real-world computers exhibit "periodicity," repeating the same physical operations, and "locality," where not all statistically linked variables are physically connected. This study examines the inevitable entropy production arising from these constraints within deterministic finite automata (DFA), a cornerstone of computer science theory. Initially, we formulate expressions for the minimum entropy production required to execute a DFA using a periodic, local physical mechanism. Subsequently, we connect these thermodynamic costs to the computational properties of the DFA. Specifically, we demonstrate that these costs categorize "regular languages" into two groups: those featuring an invertible local update map, which incur zero minimal cost, and those with a non-invertible local update map, which incur significant cost. Furthermore, we highlight the thermodynamic benefits of realizing a DFA through a physical process that remains independent of specific input data.

We investigate pasta structures and their impact on neutron star observables using the effective relativistic mean-field (E-RMF) model. To account for finite size effects and the potential for nonspherical configurations in the inner crust, we apply the compressible liquid drop model. Unified equations of state are developed across multiple E-RMF parameter sets to analyze diverse characteristics, including pasta mass and crustal thickness. These properties are found to be largely dependent on the symmetry energy within the subsaturation density regime. Leveraging Monte Carlo simulation data, we determine the crust's shear modulus in relation to quasiperiodic oscillations observed from soft gamma-ray repeaters and derive the frequency of the fundamental torsional oscillation mode in the inner crust. Furthermore, we calculate global neutron star attributes such as the mass-radius relation, moment of inertia, total crustal mass, crustal thickness, and the fractional crustal moment of inertia. Our findings align with both theoretical predictions and observational constraints.

It remains unclear how neuronal mechanisms generate robust behaviors like collision avoidance in diverse environments as animals navigate them. In flies, motion-sensitive neurons detect nearby objects, while directional cues are processed within the central complex. Unlike traditional stream-based signal processing, this system employs an event-based approach, triggering actions only when sensory changes are detected. Contrary to von Neumann architectures, neuromorphic hardware inspired by this biology processes information asynchronously and distributedly. Drawing inspiration from the fly brain, we have created, for the first time, a neuromorphic closed-loop system that replicates key insect behaviors such as navigating clutter and crossing gaps—capabilities highly pertinent to autonomous vehicles. Implemented in both software and on neuromorphic hardware, our agent perceives environmental changes to execute collision avoidance maneuvers. These actions emerge from a closed perception-action loop utilizing probabilistic decision-making, a mechanism believed to have driven neural circuit evolution since the Cambrian explosion. By closing this loop in neuromorphic systems, we advance the quest to understand neural computation in artificial agents and better model biological intelligence. Ultimately, these investigations aim to deepen our comprehension of neural network processing in both biological and artificial domains, laying the groundwork for future neuromorphic intelligence and unlocking the full potential of such systems.

In recent years, chatbots have emerged as a vital solution for addressing the surging demand for customer support on social media. However, existing chatbot research for this domain overlooks a critical factor influencing user experience: tone. This study introduces a novel, tone-aware chatbot designed to generate responses with appropriate emotional tones for social media interactions. We begin with formative research to investigate how various tones affect user experience, uncovering significant and diverse impacts. Leveraging these insights, we developed a deep learning-based system that incorporates tone information into its design. Trained on over 1.5 million real-world customer care conversations from Twitter, our system was evaluated and found to produce responses as appropriate as those from human agents. More notably, users perceive our chatbot to be even more empathetic than human counterparts.

This study examines the capacities of two variants of the multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) optical intensity channel (OIC), specifically the equal-cost constrained OIC (EC-OIC) and the bounded-cost constrained OIC (BC-OIC), subject to per-antenna peak and average-intensity limits. In the EC-OIC, input average intensities must match fixed constants, whereas in the BC-OIC, they must not exceed specified thresholds. Initially, we analyze a general vector Gaussian channel under moment constraints, demonstrating that its high-SNR capacity is governed by maximum differential entropy under mild conditions. Subsequently, we derive capacity expressions for the rank-one EC-OIC, rank-one BC-OIC, and EC-OIC with a rank equal to the number of transmit antennas minus one. These derivations yield three key findings: first, a rank-one EC-OIC or BC-OIC is equivalent to a single-input single-output (SISO) OIC with amplitude and multiple moment constraints; second, utilizing asymptotic results for the moment-constrained vector Gaussian channel, we characterize the high-SNR asymptotic capacities for the EC-OIC and BC-OIC with the aforementioned rank. Additionally, we address low-SNR capacity slopes for the general MIMO BC-OIC and establish properties of the optimal intensity allocation, thereby simplifying the associated nonsmooth optimization challenge.

Multi-Access Edge Computing (MEC) and Fog computing deliver low-latency services to subscribers, yet a federation between 3GPP MEC and Fog is necessary to enhance coverage for 3GPP users. Establishing this federation introduces challenges regarding third-party authentication and application mobility, which must be addressed to ensure continuous service during handovers from 3GPP MEC to Fog without requiring re-authentication. This paper proposes two solutions: 1) a proxy-based state transfer and third-party authentication (PS3A) mechanism that utilizes a transparent proxy to relay authentication and application state data, and 2) a token-based state transfer and proxy-based third-party authentication (TSP3A) approach that employs the proxy to transmit authentication details and application state tokens. By maintaining a transparent proxy with virtual counterparts, these solutions avoid modifying existing 3GPP MEC and Fog architectures. Implementation on a testbed demonstrates that PS3A and TSP3A achieve authentication within 0.345 to 2.858 seconds under proxy loads ranging from 0 to 100 Mbps. Furthermore, TSP3A ensures application mobility while consuming 40–52% less time than PS3A by utilizing state tokens. Both TSP3A and PS3A significantly reduce service interruption latency by 84.6% and 82.4%, respectively, compared to cloud-based services relying on tokens and prefetching.

Although ultra-thin LaNiO$_3$ films display a significant metal-insulator transition when their thickness drops below a few unit cells, the role of oxygen vacancies and their impact on correlated electronic structures remains underexplored. This study employs density functional theory plus U (DFT+U) to examine how surface termination and oxygen vacancy positioning influence the electronic properties and energetics of these films. Our findings indicate that oxygen vacancies form more readily in Ni layers with NiO$_2$-terminated surfaces (at 0.5 and 1.5 u.c. thicknesses) compared to LaO-terminated structures, with in-plane vacancies being energetically preferred over out-of-plane ones. When multiple vacancy sites are permitted, the Ni square-plane geometry proves most stable, as oxygen vacancies tend to cluster near a single Ni ion. Specifically, the in-plane vacancy in NiO$_2$-terminated films is favored because the resulting charge release can be effectively accommodated by the less-occupied $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital rather than the $d_{z^2}$ orbital. Notably, the structure featuring the Ni square-plane geometry and oxygen vacancies transitions into an insulating state within DFT+U calculations, exhibiting a band gap of 1.2 eV. This insulating behavior arises from substantial crystal field splitting between $d_{z^2}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals in the square-plane configuration, while strong electronic correlations induce a Mott insulating state in the remaining Ni sites.

We introduce a new 3D shape reconstruction technique that predicts an implicit 3D representation from a solitary RGB image. By training on single-view images across various object categories without viewpoint annotations, our method learns to generalize across multiple categories despite the absence of 3D supervision. To enable effective learning under these minimal constraints, we employ a novel categorical metric learning approach that leverages category labels to guide shape acquisition. Additionally, we incorporate adversarial and viewpoint regularization strategies to better disentangle the influences of viewpoint and shape. Our approach yields the first results for large-scale single-view shape prediction covering over 50 categories using a unified model without any 3D cues. Furthermore, we are pioneers in investigating and quantifying the advantages of class information in supervised single-view 3D reconstruction. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on the ShapeNet-13, ShapeNet-55, and Pascal3D+ benchmarks.

Concentrated colloidal suspensions and emulsions function as amorphous soft solids that are prevalent in both industrial technology and scientific research as model systems. Although these materials can be readily fluidized through mechanical stress, undergoing a yielding transition, a comprehensive theoretical description of this process remains elusive. This study examines yielding across three categories of repulsive soft solids by combining analytical and numerical modeling with experimental investigations into microscopic dynamics and mechanical responses under oscillatory shear. Our findings reveal that yielding at the microscopic scale represents a shift between two distinct dynamical states. We rationalize this observation by introducing a lattice model featuring dynamic coupling between adjacent sites, which yields a unified state diagram for yielding. By drawing parallels to the van der Waals phase diagram for real gases, we demonstrate that proximity to a critical point is pivotal in determining whether yielding exhibits first-order or second-order characteristics, thus harmonizing previously conflicting observations regarding the nature of this transition.

We present a family of reinforcement-driven stochastic processes defined by a sequence of random partitions $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$ of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, Rt\}$. At every time step $t$, $R$ new elements are introduced into the partitioned set. A random subset of these elements, selected via a time-varying probability distribution, merges into existing blocks, while the remaining elements initiate new blocks individually. Those joining pre-existing blocks select their target block with probability proportional to that block's size, independently of one another. We establish findings regarding the asymptotic size of a specific block and derive central limit theorems for the fluctuations around this limit, applying these results both to a fixed block and to the largest block among all. Furthermore, we demonstrate that with probability one, a single block eventually assumes and retains the position of having the greatest cardinality. Depending on the specific interpretation of this partition mechanism, our findings can be extended to Balls and Bins processes, Generalized Chinese Restaurant Processes, Generalized Urn models, and Preferential attachment random graphs.

The analysis of Darwin instability in binary systems, including planets, stars, and galaxies, is conducted using a model grounded in Regge-like laws. The study introduces new analytical expressions for both the relative separation of the binary components and their orbital rotation period.

By utilizing the dynamical horizon crossing condition $k = aH$, we transition from the physical time variable $t$ to the $k$ variable, allowing for a self-consistent solution of the first-order cosmological perturbation equations within chaotic $\alpha$-attractor potentials. This framework facilitates the analysis of $n_{s}$, $r$, $n_{t}$, and $N$ in $k$-space. Comparing our low-$k$ regime results with Planck data imposes constraints on the $\alpha$ parameter via microscopic calculations. Previous studies, leveraging the hyperbolic geometry of a Poincaré disk, established model-dependent constraints on $\alpha$ consistent with both the maximal supergravity model $\mathcal{N}=8$ and the minimal supergravity model $\mathcal{N}=1$, identifying allowed values as $\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}, 1, \frac{4}{3}, \frac{5}{3}, 2, \frac{7}{3}$. Minimal $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric cosmological models incorporating $B$-mode targets derived from these supergravity theories predicted $r$ values between $10^{-2}$ and $10^{-3}$. In our computations using both $E$-model and $T$-model potentials, we obtained $r$ values within this range for all the aforementioned constrained $\alpha$ values, consistent with the $68\%$ confidence level. Furthermore, we calculated $r$ for additional $\alpha$ values in both the low-$\alpha$ limit, employing $r=\frac{12\alpha}{N^{2}}$, and the high-$\alpha$ limit, using $r=\frac{4n}{N}$ for $n=2$ and $4$. Across all considered $\alpha$ values, our calculated results align with Planck-2018 data at the $68\%$ or near $95\%$ confidence level.

This note explores a specific double centralizer property within general linear supergroups. Over an algebraically closed field $\mathbb{K}$ with characteristic not equal to $2$, we examine the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-homogeneous one-dimensional extension $\underline V=V\oplus\mathbb{K}v$ of the super space $V=\mathbb{K}^{m\mid n}$, alongside the natural action of the supergroup $\tilde G:=\text{GL}(V)\times \textbf{G}_m$ on $\underline V$. We analyze the tensor product supermodule $(\underline{V}^{\otimes r}, \rho_r)$ of $\tilde G$ and establish a generalized Schur-Sergeev duality. This duality asserts that the Schur superalgebras $S'(m|n,r)$ associated with $\tilde G$ and a specific weak degenerate double Hecke algebra $\underline{\mathcal{H}}_r$ act as double centralizers. The weak degenerate double Hecke algebra is an infinite-dimensional algebra that admits a natural representation on the tensor product space; this concept is derived from \cite{B-Y-Y2020} with minor adjustments.

This study presents a sensor utilizing Rydberg atoms to measure the angle of arrival (AoA) for incoming radio-frequency (RF) signals. The method combines electromagnetically induced transparency within a Rydberg atomic vapor with a heterodyne Rydberg atom mixer. By measuring the phase of the incident RF wave at two distinct points within an atomic vapor cell, the mixer determines the phase difference, which correlates directly with the wave's direction of arrival. Experimental validation involved measuring phase differences for a 19.18 GHz signal at two locations in a cesium-filled vapor cell across various incident angles. Results from these measurements, when compared against both full-wave simulations and plane-wave theoretical models, confirm that sub-wavelength phase measurements based on atoms can effectively determine the AoA of an RF field.

We compute the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) state for a unitary Fermi gas of atoms interacting via a finite-ranged Jost-Kohn potential, recently demonstrated to model resonant interactions [2019 J. Phys. B: At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 52, 165004]. By utilizing the exact scattering solution of this potential, we derive the two-body T-matrix element used to formulate the BCS Hamiltonian in momentum space. We report findings on the energy- and range-dependence of the pairing gap and superfluid density, as well as the range-dependence of the chemical potential, across a broad spectrum of scattering lengths, including the unitary regime. In the zero-range limit, our calculated gap at the Fermi energy is nearly identical to that obtained from mean-field theory with a contact potential. Furthermore, the mean gap, averaged over the full width at half maximum of the gap function in both zero-range and unitary limits, is found to be $0.42 E_F$, aligning closely with recent quantum Monte Carlo simulation results [2018 Phys. Rev. A 97, 013601]. Additionally, the chemical potential in the zero-range limit agrees well with values derived for the contact potential.

This paper investigates the arrival and detection times of Dirac particles within a one-dimensional space. We examine particles originating from a source point within a spatial interval and traveling to detectors located at the interval's endpoints, which record the moment of arrival. In standard quantum mechanics, defining unambiguous "arrival" or "detection" times is difficult because time is not represented by a self-adjoint operator. Instead, we employ an absorbing boundary condition for Dirac's equation, originally proposed by Tumulka, to model the particle's interaction with the detectors. By deriving an explicit solution, we demonstrate that the initial-boundary value problem for the wave function is globally well-posed, yielding a smooth solution that depends smoothly on the initial data. Furthermore, we confirm that this absorbing boundary condition generates a non-negative probability density function for arrival/detection times, calculated from the flux of the conserved Dirac current. In contrast, free evolution without boundary conditions generally fails to produce a non-negative density, and Wigner's proposal for the arrival time distribution does not yield a normalized density in the absence of boundaries. Finally, as a consistency check, numerical verification shows that the arrival time statistics of Bohmian trajectories align with the probability distribution for detection time derived from the absorbing boundary condition.

Distributing open-source code to replicate findings in published research is gaining increasing traction. Since replicating machine learning (ML) experiments presents considerable challenges, substantial efforts have been directed toward minimizing result variance. Consistent reproducibility, much like in other scientific disciplines, reinforces the validity of the proposed hypotheses and warrants equal importance to the research's innovations. This work introduces a framework designed to ensure consistent reproduction of results while offering a streamlined approach to developing, training, and assessing deep learning models for natural language processing (NLP).

We demonstrate that free-standing, load-bearing structures can be constructed exclusively from rocks and elastic loops. Our investigation reveals that the critical maximum loop spacing is determined by the frictional characteristics of the grains and the elasticity of the confining loops. By developing a model based on simplified edge behavior, we analyze these relationships. We observe that increased friction results in larger stable contact angles for both grain-grain and grain-loop interactions, yielding a critical spacing function that scales linearly with friction to the first order. Conversely, greater bending rigidity allows the loops to more effectively contain the hydrostatic pressure of the grains, a phenomenon explained through a hydroelastic scale. These insights clarify how plant roots stabilize soil and may facilitate the creation of simple, adhesion-free structures using only granular materials and fibers.

We calculate the phase diagram for a polaron model incorporating both breathing-mode and Su-Schrieffer-Heeger couplings, revealing two distinct sharp transitions. This contrasts with pure models, which display either a single transition (in the case of Su-Schrieffer-Heeger coupling) or none (for breathing-mode coupling). These findings suggest that the physics of realistic mixed polaron systems is significantly more complex than that of simplified models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ultracold molecules confined in optical lattices can serve as a platform to investigate this specific mixed Hamiltonian, with the relative strengths of the two couplings adjustable via external electric fields. Existing experimental parameters position current setups within the regime where one of these transitions takes place. Finally, we outline a protocol for measuring polaron dispersion through stimulated Raman spectroscopy.

We report simulation outcomes regarding light-nuclei generation in relativistic heavy-ion collisions using the updated THESEUS framework, which integrates Three-fluid Hydrodynamics with UrQMD (Ultra-relativistic Quantum Molecular Dynamics) final-state interactions. These simulations cover Pb+Pb and Au+Au collisions across a collision energy range of $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=$ 6.4--19.6 GeV. Light-nuclei production is modeled thermodynamically alongside hadrons, with the sole additional parameter being the late freeze-out energy density, which simulates the afterburner phase since light nuclei are excluded from UrQMD evolution. This parameter is calibrated to best match proton transverse-momentum spectra obtained after the UrQMD afterburner with those predicted at late freeze-out. The revised THESEUS results reasonably, though not perfectly, reproduce bulk light-nuclei observables, particularly their mass and collision-energy dependencies. Various ratios ($d/p$, $t/p$, $t/d$, and $N(t)\times N(p)/N^2(d)$) are also analyzed. The directed flow of light nuclei proves more complex, likely necessitating an explicit treatment of the afterburner evolution that disrupts kinetic equilibrium. The imperfect agreement with light-nuclei data suggests potential medium effects within the produced nuclei.

Super-Earths and sub-Neptunes are generally believed to have originally accreted hydrogen/helium envelopes, comprising a few to ten percent of their total mass, from the primordial gas disk. Hydrodynamic escape, driven by core-powered mass loss and/or photo-evaporation, subsequently stripped much of this primordial material from lower-mass and inner planets to create the super-Earth population. This study demonstrates that following core-powered mass loss, certain super-Earths can retain small residual H/He envelopes. Such retention occurs because, in significantly depleted atmospheres, the density at the radiative-convective boundary drops enough to make the cooling time-scale shorter than the mass-loss time-scale. Consequently, the residual envelope can contract, halting further mass loss. Through both analytic calculations and numerical simulations, we show that the retained primordial H/He mass fraction, $f_{ret}$, increases with planet mass ($M_{c}$) and decreases with equilibrium temperature ($T_{eq}$), following the scaling $f_{ret} \propto M_{c}^{3/2} T_{eq}^{-1/2} \exp{[M_{c}^{3/4} T_{eq}^{-1}]}$. For typical super-Earths, $f_{ret}$ ranges from less than $10^{-8}$ to approximately $10^{-3}$. To a first approximation, the remaining H/He content depends primarily on the initial envelope mass, planet mass, equilibrium temperature, and envelope opacity. These residual hydrogen envelopes lower the atmosphere's mean molecular weight relative to a purely secondary atmosphere, a signature detectable by current and upcoming observatories. However, these remnant atmospheres may remain vulnerable to long-term erosion by photo-evaporation in many cases. Ultimately, any leftover hydrogen envelope likely plays a significant role in the long-term physical evolution of super-Earths, influencing their geology and geochemistry.

This study investigates the Higgs boson decaying into two new spin-zero particles, denoted as $H \to aa$, with each $a$-boson subsequently decaying into a $b$-quark and a muon pair. The analysis utilizes 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS experiment at the LHC during 2015 and 2016 at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. Results show no significant deviation from Standard Model expectations. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits are established for the branching ratio $(\sigma_H / \sigma_{SM}) \times B(H\to aa\to bb\mu\mu)$, spanning from $2\times 10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$ across an $a$-boson mass spectrum of 20 to 60 GeV. Additionally, model-independent constraints are derived for the visible production cross-section multiplied by the branching ratio to the $bb\mu\mu$ final state for new physics, $\sigma_{vis}(X) \times B(X\to bb\mu\mu)$, which vary between 0.1 fb and 0.73 fb for a dimuon mass ($m_{\mu\mu}$) ranging from 18 to 62 GeV.

This paper introduces the Abbott dimension for Hausdorff spaces, a dimension function conceptually derived from Edwin Abbott's \emph{Flatland}. We demonstrate that for separable metric spaces, the Abbott dimension is bounded above by the large inductive dimension. As a result, we establish that the Abbott dimension of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ equals $n$. Finally, we show that all hereditarily indecomposable continua possess an Abbott dimension of $1$, whereas such continua can exhibit arbitrarily high values for the large inductive, small inductive, and covering dimensions.

Economists are worried that recent disruptive events, including the 2007-2008 global financial crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, may have altered economic relationships, thereby affecting both estimation methods and policymaking. Driven by this concern, this paper introduces a new toolkit for detecting multiple structural breaks in panel data models with interactive effects. This toolkit comprises various tests to identify structural breaks, an estimator for determining break dates, and confidence intervals for those dates. The authors apply this toolkit to a comprehensive dataset of 3,557 US banks spanning 2005 to 2021, a period marked by extensive quantitative easing initiatives aimed at mitigating the impacts of both crises. The study investigates whether these programs successfully stimulated bank lending in the US economy, concluding with a definitive "no."

We examine the dynamics of expanding bubble walls interacting with massive dark photons, whose mass varies as they traverse the wall. In the case of sufficiently thin walls, we identify a transient kinematic regime where longitudinal modes exhibit a constant reflection probability, unlike transverse modes. This phenomenon has significant implications for the evolution of vacuum bubbles in the early Universe. Specifically, it generates a novel pressure source on the expanding interface, which depends non-monotonically on the bubble wall's $\gamma$-factor and peaks at intermediate values, a feature we term "Maximum Dynamic Pressure." If this pressure is sufficient to stop the acceleration of the bubble walls, the difference in vacuum energy densities converts a portion of the dark photons into relativistic dark radiation. Should this dark radiation remain relativistic until late times, it could yield an observable contribution to $\Delta N_\text{eff}$ for phase transitions with strengths ranging from $\alpha \sim 10^{-2}$ to $10^{-1}$.

We present Sweep, a radiative transfer code designed for the Arepo cosmological simulation framework. Utilizing a discrete ordinates method, Sweep solves the radiative transfer equation under steady-state and infinite speed-of-light assumptions by performing a transport sweep across the full computational grid. Given that Arepo employs an adaptive, unstructured grid, the sweep induces a complex dependency graph among grid cells. To address the resulting topological sorting challenge in a distributed environment, we utilize a task-based parallelism strategy. The primary benefit of this sweep approach is that its computational cost depends solely on grid size, remaining independent of the number or spatial distribution of sources; this efficiency is particularly advantageous for cosmological simulations involving vast numbers of sparsely distributed sources. We have validated the code through various physical tests, including HII region expansion, shadow formation behind dense objects, light scattering, and behavior under periodic boundary conditions. Furthermore, we evaluate its computational performance, emphasizing highly parallel, large-scale simulations.

Machine translation systems face significant challenges with out-of-domain text, highlighting the critical need for domain adaptation. However, prevailing adaptation techniques often involve fine-tuning or retraining substantial portions of the model for each new domain, a process that is resource-intensive. Conversely, semi-parametric models have demonstrated effective domain adaptation by retrieving relevant examples from an in-domain datastore (Khandelwal et al., 2021); nevertheless, these retrieval-augmented approaches are notably slower. This paper investigates multiple strategies to accelerate nearest neighbor machine translation. We adapt methods recently introduced by He et al. (2021) for language modeling and propose a straightforward yet efficient caching mechanism that eliminates redundant retrieval when similar contexts are encountered. Empirical results across various domains regarding translation quality and execution time validate the efficacy of these proposed solutions.

Federated Learning (FL) is poised to become a cornerstone for privacy-preserving machine learning in autonomous vehicles. This approach enables collaborative training of a single model across edge devices using their local data without centralizing it. Although FL reduces communication overhead compared to traditional distributed learning, scaling it for large models remains challenging. In vehicular contexts, FL must be tailored to handle scarce communication bandwidth, node mobility, and statistical data heterogeneity. Consequently, effectively leveraging communication resources alongside novel perception-focused methods is essential. To address these challenges, we introduce a new vehicular FL architecture featuring specialized learning and scheduling protocols. This system exploits vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) links to overcome communication bottlenecks by organizing vehicles into clusters that train models concurrently, transmitting only cluster-level aggregates to the Multi-Access Edge Computing (MEC) server. Our cluster formation strategy accommodates both single and multi-task learning while balancing communication efficiency and learning performance. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed framework significantly enhances learning accuracy across various non-independent and non-identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) and imbalanced datasets under mobility constraints, outperforming standard FL approaches.

Achieving effective visual representations that generalize without human supervision is a core challenge for applying machine learning to diverse tasks. Recently, two prominent families of self-supervised methods—contrastive learning and latent bootstrapping, represented by SimCLR and BYOL respectively—have achieved notable advancements. This study hypothesizes that integrating explicit information compression into these algorithms results in superior and more robust representations. To test this, we adapted SimCLR and BYOL to align with the Conditional Entropy Bottleneck (CEB) objective, enabling us to quantify and regulate the compression level within learned representations while assessing their downstream task performance. Additionally, we investigated the connection between compression and Lipschitz continuity, deriving a tractable lower bound for the Lipschitz constant of the learned encoders. Given that Lipschitz continuity is intrinsically linked to robustness, this finding offers a novel rationale for the enhanced robustness of compressed models. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating compression into SimCLR and BYOL significantly boosts linear evaluation accuracy and model resilience across various domain shifts. Notably, the compressed BYOL variant attained a Top-1 linear evaluation accuracy of 76.0% on ImageNet using ResNet-50, and 78.8% with ResNet-50 2x.

Since the latter half of the previous decade, there has been increasing focus on creating algorithms to automatically solve mathematical word problems (MWP). This challenging task requires integrating surface-level text pattern recognition with mathematical reasoning. Despite significant research efforts, we remain far from achieving robust representations of elementary math word problems or developing effective solutions for the general task. This paper critically reviews various models developed for solving word problems, evaluating their strengths, weaknesses, and future challenges. Over the past two years, numerous deep learning models have achieved competitive results on benchmark datasets, making a critical and conceptual analysis of the literature particularly timely at this stage. We step back to examine why, despite the surge in scholarly interest, the predominantly used experimental and dataset designs continue to act as obstacles. Drawing from a close analysis of the existing literature, we also aim to outline a roadmap for future research in mathematical word problems.

Let $(\Gamma,\mathbb{P})$ denote a relatively hyperbolic group pair that is relatively one-ended. In this setting, the Bowditch boundary of $(\Gamma,\mathbb{P})$ is locally connected. Although Bowditch previously proved this result under the constraints that all peripheral subgroups are finitely presented, possess an ending of one or two, and lack infinite torsion subgroups, we eliminate these limitations. Our proof imposes no restrictions on the cardinality of $\Gamma$ nor on the peripheral subgroups $P \in \mathbb{P}$.

The spin dynamics of orthorhombic TbFeO$_3$ perovskite at low temperatures have been investigated. Inelastic neutron scattering (INS) analysis revealed two distinct modes in the spectrum, each associated with a different sublattice. The iron subsystem undergoes antiferromagnetic ordering at a Néel temperature (T$_N$) of 632 K and displays high-energy magnon dispersion. Linear spin wave theory was employed to model the magnetic dynamics of this subsystem, resulting in a solution that indicates significant anisotropy between in-plane and out-of-plane exchange interactions; this methodology was previously applied to TmFeO$_3$. Three non-dispersive crystal electric field levels for Tb$^{3+}$ ions were identified below 40 meV, located approximately at 17, 26, and 35 meV. Furthermore, diffuse scattering studies across various temperatures clarified the evolution of the magnetic correlation length. The Tb$^{3+}$ ion subsystem was modeled numerically using the point charge model. The resulting numerical data align well with experimental observations and support the general single-ion approximation for the rare-earth subsystem in orthorhombic perovskites.

This study presents a novel challenge and accompanying datasets to advance research in systems capable of interpreting medical videos and generating visual responses to natural language queries. We posit that medical videos offer optimal answers for inquiries related to first aid, medical emergencies, and medical education. To this end, we developed the MedVidCL and MedVidQA datasets and established two tasks: Medical Video Classification (MVC) and Medical Visual Answer Localization (MVAL), both aimed at cross-modal understanding of medical language and video content. These resources have the potential to facilitate sophisticated downstream applications that benefit both the public and medical professionals. The datasets comprise 6,117 annotated videos for MVC and 3,010 annotated question-answer timestamp pairs derived from 899 videos for MVAL. All data has been validated and corrected by medical informatics experts. Furthermore, we benchmarked each task using the MedVidCL and MedVidQA datasets and introduced multimodal learning methods that establish competitive baselines for future research.

Current deep learning approaches for image deraining demonstrate strong results on synthetic rainy images, primarily because they depend on paired datasets of clear and simulated rainy images. Nevertheless, these techniques experience a marked decline in performance when applied to real rain, largely due to the substantial discrepancy between simplified synthetic rain patterns and the complexity of actual rain. This study posits that rain generation and removal are intrinsically linked processes that must be tightly integrated. To achieve this integration, we introduce a unified disentangled image translation framework that simultaneously learns real rain generation and removal. Specifically, we develop a bidirectional disentangled translation network where each direction incorporates two coupled loops for handling both real and synthetic rain. Concurrently, we enforce a disentanglement strategy by separating rainy images into clean backgrounds and rain layers during the removal phase. This approach, supported by cycle-consistency and adversarial losses, better preserves background identity and facilitates the translation of rain layers between real and synthetic domains. Conversely, a symmetrical composition strategy is employed for rain generation. Comprehensive experiments across synthetic and real-world rain datasets confirm that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This work presents the inaugural demonstration of a four-node, trusted-node-free metro network featuring dynamic discrete-variable quantum key distribution (DV-QKD) capabilities across all nodes. Utilizing a QKD-aware centralized software-defined networking (SDN) controller, the system enables dynamic deployment and rerouting of any QKD link between network nodes. We experimentally investigate the feasibility of coexisting quantum and carrier-grade classical optical channels within the C-band, using both field-deployed metropolitan networks and laboratory fibers (under 10 km), by measuring achievable quantum bit error rates (QBER), secret key rates (SKR), and classical signal bit error rates. Additionally, multi-hop coexistence analysis under various switching scenarios is provided. Results indicate that when one classical channel with 150 GHz spacing coexists with the quantum channel across multiple links, the SKR decreases by 43% due to Raman scattering noise leaking into the 100 GHz bandwidth of the Bob DV-QKD unit's internal filter. With four coexisting classical channels spaced 150 GHz apart, the quantum channel degrades more rapidly; the combined effects of Raman noise, other nonlinearities, and high aggregated launch power cause the QBER to surpass the 6% threshold, driving the SKR to zero bits per second at a launch power of 7 dB per channel. Finally, we examine the coexistence of a quantum channel with six classical channels through a field-deployed fiber test network.
