This work advances the investigation into the geometry of algebras associated with the Weyl groupoid, a field first explored in \cite{M22}. The Nullstellensatz establishes a one-to-one correspondence between radical ideals of these algebras and their zero loci, known as superalgebraic sets. These sets correspond precisely to the (Zariski) closed sets that remain invariant under the action of an appropriate groupoid, and the minimal superalgebraic set encompassing any given closed set can be defined explicitly. In this paper, we present multiple examples of such sets and offer various characterizations of Laurent supersymmetric polynomials. These characterizations help unify several existing definitions of the algebra of interest, $J(G)$, found throughout the literature.

Orientation and motion sensing are extensively utilized in consumer electronics like smartphones, tablets, and cameras to facilitate instant interaction with digital content. However, prototyping devices with these capabilities is a challenging endeavor due to the necessity of intricate hardware design, mathematical algorithms, and programming. This paper introduces FreeIMU, an open-source hardware framework designed to simplify the prototyping of orientation and motion sensing devices. The framework comprises a compact circuit board equipped with multiple sensors and a software library developed on the Arduino platform. Released under open licenses and backed by an active community, both the hardware and software are suitable for integration into research and commercial applications.

RDF2vec is a method for generating vector space embeddings from RDF knowledge graphs by representing each entity as a vector. The process begins by generating node sequences through random walks on the graph, followed by processing these sequences with the word2vec algorithm to produce the final embeddings. This paper investigates the application of external edge weights to direct these random walks, utilizing Wikipedia page transition probabilities as a proxy for human feedback regarding edge importance. We demonstrate that in certain contexts, an RDF2vec implementation guided by these transition probabilities can surpass both standard RDF2vec based on unweighted random walks and approaches relying solely on internal graph edge weights.

Selectivity estimation represents the SQL query optimizer's capacity to predict the cardinality of results produced by a query predicate. This calculation is fundamental, as it enables the optimizer to choose the most efficient execution plan. Although this challenge has been recognized since the mid-1970s, we were astonished to find no existing literature addressing selectivity estimation for inequality joins. An evaluation of four major database systems—Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and MySQL—revealed that the open-source platforms, PostgreSQL and MySQL, do not perform this estimation. While Oracle and SQL Server provide reasonably accurate estimates, their underlying algorithms remain proprietary. Consequently, this paper introduces a novel algorithm for estimating inequality join selectivity. We have implemented this algorithm in PostgreSQL and submitted it as a patch for inclusion in upcoming releases.

By utilizing the hypergeometric equation within the framework of the Schrödinger equation, we have derived a novel class of exactly-solvable potentials that are distinct from those previously introduced by Bose and Natanzon. Employing these newly identified solvable potentials enables the generation of corresponding complex PT-invariant potentials. Furthermore, this methodology is applicable to other Fuchs equations as well.

Counting integral orbits within prehomogeneous vector spaces is significant for arithmetic statistics. We outline a technique to establish subconvexity for the zeta function that counts these orbits, demonstrating its application by deriving a subconvex bound for the Shintani $\zeta$ function, which enumerates the class numbers of binary cubic forms.

Monte Carlo methods for estimating Value-at-Risk (VaR) are globally prevalent tools in financial risk management, though they often suffer from computational slowness and occasional inaccuracies. This paper presents a novel, high-speed, and precise Monte Carlo algorithm for determining both VaR and Expected Shortfall (ES) utilizing Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM). By clustering input data according to prevailing market conditions, GMMs eliminate the need for correlation matrices in risk calculations. The methodology involves sampling from each cluster based on its assigned weight and computing volatility-adjusted stock returns to generate potential asset price scenarios. Empirical analysis on a selection of US stocks demonstrates that the GMM-based VaR model offers both computational efficiency and accuracy. From a managerial standpoint, the model effectively replicates market turbulence, ensuring that VaR metrics accurately capture the market's highly non-normal behavior and non-linear correlation structures during pre-crisis, crisis, and post-crisis periods.

Analytical solutions for water waves generated by moving atmospheric pressures have been derived in both one-dimensional horizontal (1DH) and two-dimensional horizontal (2DH) axisymmetric frameworks. The 1DH model identifies three wave components: a locked wave traveling at the atmospheric pressure speed ($C_p$), and two free waves moving in opposite directions governed by linear frequency dispersion. Under supercritical conditions ($C_p > C$, where $C$ is the maximum wave celerity), the leading wave is the locked wave, sharing the same phase as the pressure, while the trailing free wave exhibits an opposite phase. Conversely, in subcritical conditions ($C > C_p$), the fastest free wave leads, and its surface elevation matches the sign of the atmospheric pressure. For extended pressure disturbances, the resulting free surface profile resembles the pressure distribution itself. In the 2DH axisymmetric case, the pressure decays radially as $O(r^{-1/2})$, yielding only two components due to symmetry: locked and free waves. Additionally, DART tsunami data from the Tonga volcanic eruption were analyzed after correcting for artifacts to isolate free surface elevation. Comparisons between these corrected data and the analytical solutions show order-of-magnitude agreement regarding the arrival times of leading and trailing waves and their amplitude ratios, though the discrepancies underscore the inherent complexity of the problem.

This study examines the renormalization group optimized perturbation theory (RGOPT) at the next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) within the framework of thermal scalar field theory. By comparing three successive orders of RGOPT, we demonstrate the method's efficient resummation capabilities and its strong apparent convergence. Specifically, the residual dependence of thermodynamical quantities on the renormalization scale is significantly reduced compared to standard perturbative expansions and other resummation techniques, such as screened perturbation theory. Consequently, our findings provide a valuable initial NNLO demonstration, paving the way for applying this approach to the more complex domain of thermal QCD at NNLO.

Building on the illuminating link between the AdS/CFT correspondence and operator algebra quantum error correction (OAQEC) established by Almheiri, Dong, and Harlow [arXiv:1411.7041], this work delves deeper into that relationship. We establish general findings regarding OAQEC and derive specific results for quantum codes with a holographic interpretation. Additionally, we define a novel metric termed "price" to characterize the support of a protected logical system, identifying constraints on both the price and distance for logical subalgebras within such codes. Our analysis demonstrates that holographic codes defined on bulk manifolds with asymptotically negative curvature display "uberholography," allowing a bulk logical algebra to be supported on a boundary region possessing a fractal structure. Furthermore, we argue that for holographic codes on bulk manifolds with asymptotically flat or positive curvature, the boundary physics must be highly nonlocal; this insight may have significant consequences for black holes and quantum gravity in AdS space at distance scales smaller than the AdS curvature radius.

We present a new integrated hybrid plasmonic-photonic device designed for the all-optical switching and reading of nanoscale ferrimagnetic bits. This racetrack memory, fabricated from synthetic ferrimagnetic materials with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, is integrated with a photonic waveguide on an indium phosphide membrane situated on a silicon platform. The device features a double V-shaped gold plasmonic nanoantenna coupled with a photonic crystal cavity, which enhances local absorbed energy density and the polar magneto-optical Kerr effect (PMOKE) beyond the diffraction limit to manipulate magnetization states. Numerical simulations using the three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain method demonstrate that the device can switch and read magnetization in targeted bits as small as ~100 nm, even amidst oppositely magnetized background regions within racetracks ranging from 30 to 120 nm in width, significantly outperforming a standard bare photonic waveguide. By addressing challenges such as nonlinear absorption in waveguides, weak PMOKE, and the size mismatch between spintronics and integrated photonics, this hybrid system bridges the gap between these two fields, accelerating the advancement of ultrafast and energy-efficient on-chip applications.

We provide evidence based on a sample of 544 galaxies from the DEEP2 Survey regarding the evolution of internal kinematics in blue galaxies with stellar masses between 8.0 and 10.7 (log M*/M_Sun) across the redshift range 0.2 < z < 1.2. Utilizing galaxy spectra and Hubble imaging from DEEP2, we measure emission-line kinematics and inclinations. Our extensive sample enables us to surpass the intrinsic scatter in galaxy properties to identify kinematic trends. Our results show that at a constant stellar mass, galaxies systematically exhibit reduced disordered motions and increased rotation velocities and potential well depths over time. Massive galaxies remain the most ordered at all observed epochs, displaying higher rotation velocities and lower disordered motions compared to less massive counterparts. We quantify disordered motions using an integrated gas velocity dispersion corrected for beam smearing (sigma_g), which differs from the pressure-supported velocity dispersion typical of early-type galaxies and bulges. Since both seeing and spectral slit widths constitute a significant fraction of galaxy sizes, sigma_g integrates velocity gradients over large scales, potentially reflecting non-ordered gas kinematics. We also compiled literature measurements of galaxy kinematics for 1.2 < z < 3.8 and found no redshift trends, likely due to these datasets being biased toward highly star-forming systems. In summary, over the past ~8 billion years since z=1.2, blue galaxies have evolved from disordered to ordered systems as they settled into the rotation-dominated disk galaxies seen in the present Universe, with the most massive galaxies being the most evolved at any given time.

We demonstrate the inaugural unconditional pseudo-determinism result for the entire search-BPP class. Specifically, we establish that every search problem within BPP can be solved pseudo-deterministically on average across infinitely many input lengths. In essence, for an infinite set of input lengths and any polynomial-time samplable distribution, our algorithm generates a unique solution (when one exists) with high probability over both the distribution and the random bits used.

This study introduces streamlined formulas for the local variance gamma model proposed by Carr and Nadtochiy, enhanced with a piecewise-linear local variance function. These new expressions enable the efficient calibration of the model to market option prices. Specifically, on a limited dataset, exact calibration is accomplished in under one millisecond. This approach yields an arbitrage-free interpolation of class $C^2$. Additionally, the paper suggests an effective regularization strategy for handling noisy quotes and highlights a specific issue concerning at-the-money options within the model. This same problem exists in the related one-step finite difference method by Andreasen and Huge, for which the authors provide two potential solutions.

Evaluating aquifer systems in freshwater-scarce regions requires estimating transit times to quantify the impacts of groundwater abstraction. These estimates, which vary by distribution shape, mean residence time, and contribution, are typically derived from tracer concentrations using inverse modeling to reflect hydrogeological conditions. This study executed a multi-tracer campaign in Southern Oman's Salalah Plain, utilizing CFCs, SF6, 39Ar, 14C, and 4He. Using data from three tracers, researchers evaluated a two-component Dispersion Model (DMmix) and a nonparametric model with six age bins via Bayesian statistics. A Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach was employed to determine maximum likelihood parameter estimates and their uncertainties, with model performance verified through Bayes factors and leave-one-out cross-validation. Both models indicate that groundwater in the Salalah Plain consists of a young fraction (under 30 years) and an old fraction (over 1,000 years), with the nonparametric model showing slightly superior performance. Except for one well, all sites demonstrated a reasonable goodness of fit. These findings underscore the value of Bayesian modeling in hydrology and the efficacy of nonparametric models for accurately representing aquifer dynamics.

In the age of digital healthcare, the vast amounts of daily textual data produced in hospitals represent a critical yet underutilized resource that can be leveraged by task-specific, fine-tuned biomedical language models to enhance patient care and administration. While prior studies indicate that fine-tuning broad-coverage models with large-scale, domain-specific resources significantly boosts performance for specialized fields, such data is frequently inaccessible for low-resource languages like Italian, thereby hindering local medical institutions from adapting models effectively. To bridge this divide, our research explores two viable methods for developing biomedical language models in non-English languages, using Italian as a case study: one approach utilizes neural machine translation of English resources to prioritize data volume, while the other relies on a high-quality, native Italian corpus that favors data precision. Our findings demonstrate that data quantity is a more stringent constraint than data quality for biomedical adaptation; however, combining high-quality data can still yield performance improvements even with relatively small corpora. The models resulting from this investigation hold the potential to unlock significant research avenues for Italian hospitals and academia. Furthermore, the insights gained offer valuable guidance for creating biomedical language models that are adaptable to other low-resource languages and diverse domain contexts.

High-rank line-of-sight (LOS) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems have gained significant interest for millimeter wave and terahertz communications, where short wavelengths facilitate spatial multiplexing and high data rates over long distances. These systems are also being evaluated for multi-path non-line-of-sight (NLOS) environments, yet standard plane wave-based channel models fail to account for the wave front curvature essential for modeling spatial multiplexing. This study introduces a novel and straightforward multi-path wireless channel parametrization in which each path is substituted with a LOS path featuring a reflected image source. This model remains fully valid for all paths involving specular planar reflections and effectively captures the spherical nature of each wave front. Crucially, the approach requires only two additional parameters compared to the standard plane wave model, and these parameters can be readily extracted through standard ray tracing. The method's accuracy is validated via detailed ray tracing simulations at 28 GHz and 140 GHz within a dense urban setting.

The newly identified system Gaia 0007-1605, which features a white dwarf paired with a close brown dwarf and a distant white dwarf tertiary, bears a striking resemblance to WD 1856+534, the first discovered white dwarf system with a transiting planet candidate. While we previously suggested that the inner binary of WD 1856+534 likely originated via common envelope evolution, triple star dynamics offer an alternative explanation. This study examines various formation pathways for Gaia 0007-1605. Our reconstruction of potential common envelope evolution indicates that, under standard energy budget assumptions, a viable solution exists. Consistent with other close white dwarf-brown dwarf binaries and unlike WD 1856+534, the current configuration of Gaia 0007-1605 does not require energy sources beyond orbital energy released during common envelope evolution. Furthermore, analytical models of triple dynamics suggest that Von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai oscillations could have induced tidal migration through extreme eccentricity excursions (e \gtrsim 0.997). We conclude that, similar to its counterpart WD 1856+534, the inner binary of Gaia 0007-1605 formed through common envelope evolution, triple dynamics, or a combination of both mechanisms.

Extracting funding details from academic papers offers substantial benefits to both research and industry sectors, including monitoring research outputs by funding bodies, profiling universities and researchers via their funding profiles, and aiding open access initiatives. However, identifying and linking funding entities faces two primary hurdles: (i) the sparse graph structure of the Knowledge Base (KB), which renders standard graph-based entity linking methods ineffective for this domain, and (ii) the absence of entities in the KB, which necessitates marking such mentions as NIL rather than relying on zero-shot techniques. We introduce an entity linking model designed to predict NIL cases and address data scarcity efficiently in terms of both time and resources. This model utilizes a transformer-based system for mention detection combined with a bi-encoder architecture for entity linking. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses current strong baselines.

L. B. Beasley recently introduced the concept of $(2,3)$-cordial labelings for directed graphs in [1] and proposed two conjectures that we refute in this paper. Specifically, he conjectured that every orientation of a path with a length of five or more is $(2,3)$-cordial, and that every tree with a maximum degree of $n=3$ admits a cordial orientation; we demonstrate that both conjectures are incorrect. Furthermore, we examine the $(2,3)$-cordiality of Petersen graph orientations, determine an upper limit on the number of edges a graph can possess while remaining $(2,3)$-cordial, and present an application of these labelings.

This study examines multiwinner elections within Euclidean space governed by the minimax Chamberlin-Courant rule. In this framework, both voters and candidates are positioned in a $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, with the objective of selecting a committee of $k$ candidates that minimizes the rank of the most preferred candidate for every voter. This challenge is equivalent to the ordinal variant of the classical $k$-center problem. We demonstrate that the problem is NP-hard for any dimension $d \geq 2$ and is provably difficult to approximate. Our primary contributions consist of three polynomial-time approximation schemes, each capable of identifying a committee with a guaranteed minimax score. Across all schemes, we establish that the resulting approximation bounds are either tight or nearly tight. While our analysis centers on the $1$-Borda rule, several of our findings extend to the broader $r$-Borda rule.

Currently, the AI community is heavily fixated on achieving "state-of-the-art" benchmarks, evidenced by 80% of NeurIPS papers prioritizing these scores, which often neglects critical environmental metrics. While computational power was once the primary constraint, the future challenge lies in creating algorithms that are both eco-friendly and energy-efficient. Having optimized itself over a million years, the human brain consumes power comparable to a standard laptop, suggesting that nature-inspired algorithms offer a viable solution. This study demonstrates that existing Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) diverge from biological systems, explaining why Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs)—which mimic the mammalian visual cortex and operate with lower performance—have gained significant traction. We also address the hardware limitations currently preventing large-scale adoption of spike-based computation for neuromorphic, energy-efficient chips. Replacing traditional GPUs with neuromorphic processors could enhance environmental sustainability and efficiency, making SNNs an ideal solution. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of existing gaps and the scarcity of comparative research, proposing new directions at the intersection of neuroscience and deep learning. Furthermore, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called "NATURE" to quantify the carbon footprint of AI models.

This study examines gravitational lensing within the weak-field approximation and the strong deflection limit for a Bronnikov-Kim wormhole, utilizing the same metric as the one proposed in Einstein-Dirac-Maxwell theory. As a black hole limit is approached, the metric converges to that of an extreme charged Reissner-Nordström black hole, while an ultrastatic limit transforms it into a spatial Schwarzschild wormhole. In both limiting cases, the coefficients for the divergent term and the constant term of the light deflection angle in the strong deflection regime can be derived exactly without expanding spacetime parameters. Notably, the identical values for these coefficients and constant terms are obtained in both the black hole and ultrastatic wormhole limits.

Given two sequences of positive real numbers, $\{s_n\}$ and $\{t_n\}$, we establish an exact formula for the Hausdorff dimension of the set $\mathbb{E}(\{s_n\},\{t_n\}):=\Big\{x\in(0,1): s_{n}<d_{n}(x)\leq s_n+t_n, \forall n\geq1\Big\}$, where $d_n(x)$ represents the $n$-th digit in the Engel expansion of $x$, provided that $\{s_n\}$ and $\{t_n\}$ satisfy certain mild conditions. This finding refines Lemma 2.6 from Shang and Wu (2021JNT) and serves as a valuable tool for determining the Hausdorff dimensions of specific sets within Engel expansions.

This paper examines recent advancements in resummating large logarithms at next-to-leading power (NLP) for scattering processes approaching the threshold limit. We start by outlining the diagrammatic and SCET frameworks employed to derive factorization theorems for physical observables within this specific kinematic regime. Subsequently, our analysis concentrates on the quark-gluon channel in both deep inelastic scattering and Drell-Yan processes. We demonstrate that applying consistency conditions to cancel leading poles in the hadronic cross-section enables the resummation of large leading logarithms (LLs) at NLP, utilizing either diagrammatic or SCET techniques. Furthermore, within this framework, we address the issue of endpoint divergences arising at NLP in SCET and connect their resolution to the principle of re-factorization.

To investigate spin accumulation, we assess both the spin galvanic and spin Hall effects using a semi-classical Boltzmann equation, informed by relativistic Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker Green's function inputs within the framework of density functional theory. Our calculations account for various contributions, with specific attention to skew-scattering (the scattering-in term), and are compared against three distinct approximations: isotropic and anisotropic relaxation time models. In heavy metals characterized by strong intrinsic spin-orbit coupling, nearly all observed effects are accurately captured by the anisotropic relaxation time approximation. Conversely, in light metals, the contributions from vertex corrections (scattering-in term) are comparable in magnitude to those predicted by the anisotropic relaxation time approximation. We specifically examine how the atomic nature of substitutional impurities and their spatial positions influence spin accumulation. Since impurities disrupt the thin film's space inversion symmetry, they induce both symmetric and antisymmetric components of spin accumulation. Generally, surface impurities yield the highest efficiency for charge-to-spin conversion regarding spin accumulation. Furthermore, our results align well with existing experimental data for platinum (Pt).

Automatic code generation involves creating code snippets from natural language inputs. While most mainstream approaches depend on extensive paired datasets containing both descriptions and code, this is often challenging in domain-specific contexts where such data is unavailable or requires significant manual effort to construct. Consequently, limited training data leads to poor model training, overfitting, and subpar real-world performance. To address this, we introduce a task augmentation strategy that integrates domain knowledge via auxiliary tasks and a Subtoken-TranX model, which extends the original TranX architecture to facilitate subtoken-level generation. We validated our approach using a real-world dataset, and our experiments show that the Subtoken-TranX model surpasses both the original TranX and standard Transformer models. Specifically, the task augmentation method boosted the exact match accuracy of Subtoken-TranX by 12.75%, meeting industrial application standards across various code categories. This approach has been successfully deployed in Alibaba's BizCook platform, marking, to our knowledge, the first domain-specific code generation system implemented in an industrial development environment.

We investigate giant clumps in high-redshift galaxies experiencing Violent Disc Instability, aiming to differentiate between long-lived migrating clumps and short-lived ones destroyed by feedback. By combining an analytic model validated with simulations against CANDELS data, we trace clump evolution during migration. The "bathtub" framework, accounting for stellar and gas gain and loss, relies on four parameters: accretion efficiency, star-formation-rate (SFR) efficiency, and outflow mass-loading factors for both gas and stars. All relevant timescales are comparable to the migration duration, spanning two to three orbital periods. Unlike galaxies, clumps exhibit an internal dependence of the accretion rate on their varying mass. The analytic solution, featuring exponential growing and decaying modes, identifies a primary evolution phase where gas mass and SFR remain constant while stellar mass increases linearly; consequently, the inverse specific SFR serves as an observable proxy for clump age. Subsequently, masses and SFR theoretically approach exponential growth with a constant specific SFR, though this phase is likely hypothetical given the clump's disappearance in the galactic center. The model aligns with simulations under moderate feedback conditions in both isolated and cosmological contexts. Observations confirm our predictions, suggesting massive clumps are indeed long-lived and migrating. A significant challenge remains in modeling feedback that avoids disruption in massive clumps while sufficiently suppressing the SFR to match the galactic stellar-to-halo mass ratio.

Zero forcing is a deterministic, iterative graph coloring method where vertices are assigned blue or white states; in each round, any blue vertex with exactly one white neighbor compels that neighbor to turn blue. This work examines probabilistic zero forcing, a variation where blue vertices possess a non-zero likelihood of converting each white neighbor to blue. We investigate the propagation times associated with this probabilistic process on hypercubes and grid graphs.

While Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT) benefits from high-resource languages (HRL) for low-resource languages (LRL), traditional approaches depend on static linguistic assumptions regarding similarity. This study investigates adapting MNMT to unseen LRLs through strategic data selection and model adaptation. Specifically, we utilize perplexity to identify HRL data most closely aligned with the target LRL based on language distance. We comprehensively evaluate this data selection strategy across common multilingual NMT scenarios, including zero-shot translation and adaptation from pre-trained models, covering both LRL-to-English and English-to-LRL directions. Additionally, we demonstrate that dynamically adapting the model's vocabulary yields superior segmentation for LRLs compared to direct adaptation. Experimental results indicate reduced training times and substantial performance improvements over LRL baselines, achieving up to +13.0 BLEU with zero LRL data and up to +17.0 BLEU when combining dynamic adaptation with related data selection in pre-trained models. Our approach surpasses existing methods, such as massively multilingual models and data augmentation, across four distinct low-resource languages.

By applying gauge transformations, we derive novel solutions for the (2+1)-dimensional Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP), Kaup-Kuperschmidt (KK), and Sawada-Kotera (SK) equations starting from non-zero seeds. For each equation, a Galilean-type transformation connects the newly obtained solutions, denoted as $u_2$, with the previously established solutions, $u_2^{\prime}$, which were generated from zero seeds. We provide several explicit formulas for the single-soliton solutions of both $u_2$ and $u_2^{\prime}$ and highlight two primary distinctions between them when parameters are identical: specifically, the peak line's height and location. These differences are clearly illustrated in three accompanying figures.

The integration of deep learning with compressed sensing facilitates rapid reconstruction of undersampled MR images and has delivered state-of-the-art results for Cartesian k-space sampling. Nevertheless, non-Cartesian trajectories, such as radial paths, require conversion to a Cartesian grid during every iteration of network training, which hampers speed and introduces delays. Furthermore, repeated nonuniform Fourier transforms within the network negate the efficiency gains of deep learning. Existing solutions generally rely on image-to-image architectures or pre-grid non-Cartesian data before training to bypass repeated gridding; however, image-to-image models fail to guarantee k-space consistency, and pre-processing introduces gridding errors that the network cannot correct. Drawing inspiration from Transformer networks designed for handling long-range dependencies in sequence tasks, we propose reordering radial spokes into sequential data based on their acquisition timing to enable the Transformer to predict missing spokes from acquired ones. Additionally, we introduce novel data augmentation techniques to expand training datasets from a limited number of subjects, allowing the model to adapt to various anatomical structures. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms current state-of-the-art deep neural networks.

This paper examines the convergence of power series under both p-adic and real norms. We investigate rational summability for these series in both norm contexts, subject to specific conditions. Furthermore, we analyze specially constructed power series to derive summation formulas and explore the adele and idele, utilizing convergent power series to establish related results.

A subset $A$ of an abelian group $G$ is termed sequenceable if its elements can be ordered as $(a_1, \ldots, a_k)$ such that the resulting partial sums $(s_0, s_1, \ldots, s_k)$—defined by $s_0 = 0$ and $s_i = \sum_{j=1}^i a_j$—are all distinct, except potentially for the case where $s_k = s_0 = 0$. Existing literature contains various conjectures and inquiries regarding the sequenceability of subsets within abelian groups, which are consolidated in reference $[4]$ into a conjecture stating that any subset of an abelian group excluding the element 0 is sequenceable. Furthermore, if a sequenceable set $A$ has a total sum not equal to 0, there exists a simple path $P$ in the Cayley graph $Cay[G:\pm A]$ satisfying $\Delta(P) = \pm A$. Motivated by this graph-theoretic perspective, this paper introduces a relaxed version of the conjecture. Under the same conditions, the goal is to identify an ordering where the partial sums generate a walk $W$ in $Cay[G:\pm A]$ with a girth exceeding $t$ (for a specified $t < k$) and $\Delta(W) = \pm A$. This condition is met when all partial sums $s_i$ and $s_j$ are distinct provided $i \neq j$ and $|i-j| \leq t$; such a set is defined as $t$-weak sequenceable. The primary result demonstrated is that any subset $A$ of $\mathbb{Z}_p \setminus \{0\}$ is $t$-weak sequenceable whenever $t < 7$, or when $A$ contains no pairs of the form $\{x, -x\}$ and $t < 8$.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a privacy-centric machine learning paradigm where training occurs across distributed devices without transferring raw data, thereby safeguarding user privacy. This is achieved by sending untrained or partially trained models directly to individual devices for local "on-device" training using proprietary data, after which the server aggregates these updates to refine a global model. While most FL approaches rely on gradient descent, the non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) nature of distributed data introduces distinct characteristics that differentiate it from centralized training methods. This paper examines the specific factors influencing FL training due to non-IID data distribution and contrasts these with standard centralized gradient descent techniques. We empirically analyze how the number of samples per device and the distribution of output labels impact FL performance. Beyond privacy benefits, we also investigate potential cost efficiencies in FL frameworks. Our findings indicate that FL offers cost advantages when training models of moderate size. Ultimately, we emphasize the necessity of carefully designing models to optimize both performance and cost within the federated learning context.

This work introduces the initial results for ExaHyPE, a pioneering exascale hyperbolic PDE engine designed for next-generation supercomputers to simulate the evolution of black holes, neutron stars, and binaries. The code implements a new first-order formulation of the Einstein field equations within the conformal and constraint damping Z4 (CCZ4) framework, coupled with ideal general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) via divergence-cleaning. It employs a novel communication-avoiding one-step ADER-DG scheme featuring an a-posteriori subcell finite volume limiter on adaptive spacetrees. Although the project is in its early stages, the code has successfully passed several tests in both special and general relativity.

Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) represent massive eruptions from the Sun that propagate into interplanetary space. Although they are primary drivers of space weather, understanding their characteristics within the inner heliosphere is limited due to a lack of observational data beyond 1 astronomical unit (au). Consequently, most in situ measurements come from single spacecraft, necessitating numerical models to supplement these sparse datasets. This study evaluates the linear force-free spheromak CME model within the EUHFORIA framework to characterize the radial evolution of interplanetary CMEs, thereby providing new context for observational research. By simulating one well-documented CME and positioning virtual spacecraft along the Sun-Earth line, we investigate its propagation. To facilitate a direct comparison between model outputs and real-world data, we analyze the signatures of the interplanetary CME from 0.2 to 1.9 au using time-series techniques standard in in situ data analysis. The results indicate that the model's depiction of radial evolution for both the mean solar wind and CME parameters aligns with theoretical expectations and observations. The CME expands due to decaying pressure from the surrounding wind, with rapid expansion occurring within 0.4 au and moderate expansion at greater distances. However, this early rapid expansion does not account for the overestimated CME size in our simulation, pointing to an inherent limitation of the spheromak geometry. The magnetic field profile reveals a relaxation of the CME during propagation, while magnetic asymmetry beyond 0.4 au is likely not significantly driven by ageing. Additionally, the simulated CME wake is notably shorter than what is observed. In summary, while EUHFORIA offers a consistent description of solar wind and CME radial evolution, enhancements are needed to more accurately reproduce the CME's radial extent.

This study addresses the local regularity of solutions to the Stokes and Navier-Stokes equations in the vicinity of the boundary. First, we construct a bounded solution whose normal derivatives exhibit singularities in any $L^p$ space for $1<p$ near the boundary. Conversely, we establish criteria for Stokes equation solutions near the boundary that ensure the gradients of these solutions remain bounded (indeed, they are even H\"{o}lder continuous). Finally, we offer examples demonstrating that the local regularity of solutions near the boundary is optimal.

Pre-trained models are currently the standard for many NLP tasks; however, despite their state-of-the-art performance, practical observations suggest that these models often require varying numbers of computational layers depending on the input sequence. Evaluating all layers can lead to overconfidence in incorrect predictions, a phenomenon known as "overthinking." This issue could be mitigated by adaptive computation time methods, originally developed to accelerate inference. While the recently introduced PonderNet offers a promising early-exit strategy by treating the exit layer index as a latent variable, its original exit criterion—based on sampling from a trained posterior distribution for exiting at the $i$-th layer—introduces substantial variance in exit indices, which significantly degrades model performance. This paper presents an enhancement to PonderNet through a novel deterministic Q-exit criterion and a refined model architecture. We applied this mechanism to ALBERT and RoBERTa, comparing our approach against other recent early-exit methods. Our results indicate that these modifications represent significant improvements over the original PonderNet and outperform PABEE across a broad spectrum of GLUE tasks. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive ablation study of the proposed architecture to gain deeper insights into Lambda layers and their impact on performance.

This work presents a rigorous derivation of the wave kinetic equation from the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation at the kinetic timescale, utilizing a specific scaling law for the limiting process. This achievement resolves a primary conjecture within wave turbulence theory, which governs nonlinear wave systems. The result serves as the wave equivalent of Lanford's theorem, which derives the Boltzmann equation from particle systems; in both scenarios, the thermodynamic limit is taken as the system size approaches infinity while interaction strength (or particle radius) vanishes according to a distinct scaling regime, such as the Boltzmann-Grad limit. Specifically, for dimensions $d \geq 3$, we examine the NLS equation within a large box of size $L$ subject to a weak nonlinearity of strength $\alpha$. By applying the scaling law $\alpha \sim L^{-1}$ as $L \to \infty$ and $\alpha \to 0$, we demonstrate that the long-term statistical behavior of the NLS system is accurately described by the wave kinetic equation. This approximation holds up to times that are $O(1)$ multiples of the kinetic timescale $T_{\text{kin}} \sim \alpha^{-2}$, with well-justified error bounds. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first such result for any nonlinear dispersive system.

The study of charged-particle dynamics within an axisymmetric magnetic-dipole configuration is employed to evaluate the accuracy of Hamiltonian guiding-center theory, specifically incorporating higher-order corrections related to polarization caused by magnetic-field inhomogeneities. For regular magnetically-confined orbits—where the guiding-center magnetic moment remains adiabatically invariant—it is demonstrated that the guiding-center approximation, which preserves both energy and azimuthal canonical angular momentum, accurately reflects the actual particle trajectory when polarization effects are considered.

We introduce a pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter (pGDM) candidate within the framework of $SO(10)$ grand unified theory (GUT). Because of its Goldstone characteristics, this pGDM avoids the stringent limits imposed by direct detection experiments, which typically restrict dark matter model parameters. In this $SO(10)$ model, the pGDM arises as a linear combination of Standard Model (SM) singlet scalars contained in the ${\bf 16_H}$ and ${\bf 126_H}$ representations. We analyze two pathways for the intermediate symmetry breaking of $SO(10)$ down to the SM: the $SU(5) \times U(1)_X$ scenario and the Pati-Salam $SU(4)_c \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ (4-2-2) scenario. The vacuum expectation value of ${\bf 126_H}$, responsible for breaking the $U(1)_X$ and 4-2-2 symmetries in these respective cases, dictates the pGDM lifetime; consequently, astrophysical lower bounds on this lifetime impose one of the most rigorous constraints on the model. For the 4-2-2 route, achieving successful SM gauge coupling unification necessitates a breaking scale of approximately $10^{11}$ GeV, which excludes most of the viable parameter space. Conversely, in the $SU(5) \times U(1)_X$ scenario, the $U(1)_X$ breaking scale can be substantially higher, permitting a broad range of parameter space. Additionally, proton decay in the $SU(5)$ case is predicted to occur at a rate corresponding to a lifetime of $4.53 \times 10^{34}$ years, a value well within the detection capabilities of the Hyper-Kamiokande experiment. Finally, we assess the model's parameter space against constraints from the Large Hadron Collider as well as indirect dark matter searches conducted by Fermi-LAT and MAGIC.

Traditional models suggest that nonperturbative resonance production during preheating, immediately following inflation, transfers only a first-order fraction of energy from the inflaton to radiation, a limit imposed by backreaction effects. We introduce a particle production mechanism capable of enhancing the depletion of inflaton energy density by up to four orders of magnitude. This enhancement arises from the rapid perturbative decay of resonantly generated daughter particles. Functioning as a "spillway," these decays drain the daughter particles, thereby diminishing their backreaction on the inflaton and sustaining effective resonant production for an extended duration. Consequently, we term this scenario "spillway preheating." Furthermore, we demonstrate that within this framework, the remaining fraction of energy density in the inflaton follows a simple inverse power-law scaling. Overall, spillway preheating represents a significantly more efficient energy dissipation mechanism, with potential applications in particle physics model construction.

The study demonstrates the surprising emergence of stability in a time-modulated magnetic guide achieved without external offset fields. A steady periodic solution was identified around which the nonlinear dynamics are linearized. To assess the orbital stability of the guidance, a formal criterion utilizing the eigenvalues of the system dynamics' monodromy matrix is applied. To overcome the challenge of deriving analytical expressions for these eigenvalues, a Lyapunov transformation of the system variables is introduced. This transformation yields an equation of state for the system parameters, enabling the estimation of an upper bound for the calculated stability domains. Specifically, a general formula for the threshold modulation frequency below which guidance becomes unstable is derived. Finally, using experimentally feasible parameters, the stable guidance of 87Rb atoms is examined.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) holds significant promise for achieving quantum advantage in optimization tasks on near-term quantum hardware. However, its practical application is constrained by stringent gate fidelity requirements, as encoding the objective function into the phase-separating operator necessitates a large number of gates that often conflict with hardware connectivity limits. Focusing on the MaxCut problem, we numerically demonstrate that an alternative phase operator can effectively replace the standard objective-encoding operator, provided it shares the same ground state. Our results indicate that deviations in ground state energy typically lead to a reduced approximation ratio when using such alternative operators. Furthermore, we find that aligning the low-energy subspace of the alternative operator more closely with the original improves performance. Building on these insights, we introduce a sparsification strategy that lowers the resource demands of QAOA. Finally, we evaluate this approach against other classical graph sparsification techniques, confirming its effectiveness.

I introduce an efficient approach for quantifying the non-linear coupling between the collective axial breathing mode and the radial rocking mode, a phenomenon driven by mutual Coulomb repulsion in linear ion crystals. This quantum sensing method relies on laser-induced coupling between a specific vibrational mode and an ion's internal spin states, enabling the estimation of non-linear coupling through either phonon probability distribution measurements or direct observation of Ramsey-type spin oscillations. I demonstrate that non-linear phonon coupling causes off-resonance interactions between the ion spin states and the axial breathing mode to result in spin-dependent phonon squeezing of the radial rocking mode; consequently, the coupling parameter can be determined by analyzing the population distribution of this motional squeezed state. Additionally, I show that off-resonance interaction between the spin and the radial rocking mode generates a spin-dependent beam splitter operation between the two vibrational modes, allowing parameter estimation via detection of ion spin populations. Finally, I establish that measurement uncertainty precision can achieve the Heisenberg limit by employing entangled states between the two collective modes.

This study examines a model that integrates Electric Vehicle (EV) driving and charging behaviors. The driving component utilizes a Traffic Assignment Problem (TAP), while charging operations are simulated using an exact load flow analysis on a basic distribution network. This approach enables a precise evaluation of the combined effects of driving and charging choices. Specifically, various charging strategies are formulated and evaluated against a cost metric derived from load flow calculations to manage the charging demand generated by driving activities. The results indicate that proposed strategies not relying on load flow analysis can achieve performance comparable to load flow-based methods while requiring significantly less computational time and data. Furthermore, numerical simulations demonstrate the impact of transportation tolls on charging outcomes.

The advancement of computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) and image scanning has led to the widespread adoption of Whole-slide Image (WSI) scanners in pathological diagnostics, making WSI analysis a cornerstone of modern digital pathology. Since 2004, the use of WSI within CAD systems has steadily increased. Given that machine vision approaches typically rely on semi- or fully automated computing, they offer significant efficiency and labor savings. Integrating WSI with CAD for segmentation, classification, and detection enables histopathologists to achieve more stable, quantitative, and objective results while reducing labor costs. This paper provides a review of machine learning-based WSI analysis methods. It begins by outlining the current state of WSI and CAD technologies, followed by a discussion of publicly available WSI datasets and evaluation metrics for segmentation, classification, and detection. Subsequently, the paper reviews recent advancements in machine learning applied to these three tasks. Finally, it examines existing methods, analyzes their applicability, and forecasts future prospects for WSI analysis in this field.

Compressing deep learning models is essential for their deployment on edge devices, where optimization algorithms can automate the selection of compression parameters to adapt to varying hardware and application requirements. This article presents Multi-Objective Hardware-Aware Quantization (MOHAQ), a method that treats hardware efficiency and inference error as dual objectives for mixed-precision quantization. To effectively evaluate candidates within a vast search space, the approach utilizes a two-step process: first, it applies post-training quantization for rapid inference-only evaluation, and second, it employs a "beacon-based search" to retrain selected solutions as beacons, thereby estimating the impact of retraining on other candidates without exhaustive retraining. Using a Simple Recurrent Unit (SRU) speech recognition model trained on the TIMIT dataset, the method was tested on SiLago and Bitfusion platforms. Experimental results demonstrate that SRU can be compressed by up to 8x via post-training quantization with negligible error increase. On the SiLago platform, the method identified configurations achieving 97% and 86% of the maximum potential speedup and energy savings, respectively, with only minor error trade-offs. On Bitfusion, the beacon-based search improved upon inference-only search by reducing error gains by up to 4.9 percentage points.

Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) seeks to derive near-optimal policies from imperfect, static datasets without further interacting with the environment. Leveraging diverse offline data holds the promise of broadening RL's applicability by rendering training safer, faster, and more efficient. This work explores strategies to enhance offline RL performance, robustness to data quality, and generalization capabilities. We propose Offline Model-based RL with Adaptive Behavioral Priors (MABE), an approach grounded in the insight that dynamics models facilitate within-domain generalization while behavioral priors enable cross-domain generalization; combining these complementary elements significantly boosts policy performance and adaptability. Evaluated on the D4RL benchmark, MABE surpasses existing model-free and model-based methods in average performance. Furthermore, in tasks demanding cross-domain generalization, MABE exceeds the results of prior techniques. Our project website can be found at https://sites.google.com/berkeley.edu/mabe.

Future wireless systems will elevate communications and networking by seamlessly merging terrestrial, aerial, satellite, maritime, and underwater infrastructures. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) represent an innovative technology capable of accelerating this universal connectivity through their unique capabilities. Driven by RIS's exceptional properties, this article comprehensively examines its role in enabling and optimizing future integrated terrestrial/non-terrestrial (INTENT) networks. Specifically, we analyze the integration of RIS into non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-based satellite networks, demonstrating performance improvements through numerical simulations. The article concludes by outlining promising avenues for future research in this domain.

Although extensive research has addressed the nonequilibrium dynamics of systems instantaneously quenched from disordered to ordered phases, such dynamics under finite-rate quenches remain less explored. This study investigates slow quench dynamics in two classical statistical mechanics models—the one-dimensional kinetic Ising model and the mean-field zero-range process—specifically as the system is annealed toward the critical point. By deriving the Kibble-Zurek scaling laws from the time evolution equations governing spin-spin correlations in the Ising model and mass distributions in the zero-range process, we evaluate a recent proposal that critical coarsening, often overlooked in standard Kibble-Zurek arguments, significantly influences dynamics near the critical point. Our findings indicate that, provided the final quench point is reached sufficiently rapidly, both the defect density in the Ising model and the scaled mass distribution in the zero-range process decay linearly toward their critical values as the quench concludes; otherwise, the decay is sublinear. Furthermore, since linear scaling also emerges when a system undergoing an instantaneous quench is permitted to coarsen for a finite duration, we conclude that critical coarsening accurately captures the scaling behavior near the critical point whenever the annealing rate is not excessively slow.

When applying deep learning to optical coherence tomography (OCT) data, it is standard practice to train classification networks on 2D images derived from volumetric scans. Due to the micrometer-scale resolution of OCT systems, successive images often exhibit high similarity in both structural features and noise patterns. Consequently, improper data partitioning can lead to significant overlap between training and testing sets, a critical issue frequently ignored in existing literature. This study demonstrates the impact of flawed dataset splitting on model evaluation across three classification tasks using three widely utilized open-access OCT datasets: Kermany's and Srinivasan's ophthalmology collections, and the AIIMS breast tissue dataset. The findings reveal that classification performance is artificially inflated by 0.07 to 0.43 in Matthews Correlation Coefficient (representing accuracy gains of 5% to 30%) for models evaluated with improperly split data, underscoring the profound influence of data handling on assessment results. Ultimately, this research aims to highlight the necessity of rigorous dataset splitting in response to the growing interest in deep learning applications for OCT analysis.

Epidemiologic and genetic research into chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and numerous other complex conditions indicates the existence of subgroup disparities, such as those based on sex. This issue is examined through an integrative analytical lens that synthesizes data from diverse perspectives, including genomics, proteomics, and clinical records. Current integrative methods fail to account for subgroup heterogeneity, and while stacking views can address heterogeneity, it does not model associations between different data types. To overcome these analytical hurdles, we introduce a statistical framework for joint association and prediction that capitalizes on the unique strengths of each data view. This approach identifies molecular signatures shared by or specific to males and females that influence COPD variation, as quantified by airway wall thickness. The proposed Heterogeneity in Integration and Prediction (HIP) method accommodates subgroup heterogeneity, supports sparse variable selection, handles both multi-class and continuous univariate or multivariate outcomes, and allows for covariate adjustment. We have implemented efficient algorithms using PyTorch. Our analysis of COPD data revealed specific proteins, genes, and pathways that are either common to or distinct between sexes; while some are already linked to COPD, others offer novel insights into the mechanisms driving sex differences in the disease.

We present partially observable concurrent Kleene algebra (POCKA), an algebraic system designed to analyze concurrent programs featuring control structures like loops and conditionals. This framework supports reasoning over programs that interact with variables and values, as demonstrated by specific examples. We establish that POCKA provides a sound and complete axiomatization for a model of partial observations and demonstrate that its semantics satisfies a critical test for sequential consistency.

Smile and Learn operates as an Ed-Tech enterprise managing a smart library featuring over 100 interactive stories, games, and applications designed for children aged two to ten and their families. By collecting thousands of data points from user interactions, the platform generates reports and personalized recommendations. Due to the extensive nature of the content, a recommender system is employed to assist navigation. This paper evaluates two specific facets of this system regarding child users: how recommendation order affects exploratory behavior and how different recommendation algorithms influence engagement. Based on data gathered from October 15 to December 1, 2018, the study analyzed click-through rates relative to item ordering and conducted an A/B/C test comparing two standard algorithms against a random baseline. The findings indicate a clear correlation between recommendation sequencing and user interest, demonstrating that popularity-based recommendations outperform other alternatives.

Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number within the interval $(0,1)$. Consider the random graph $G_n$, defined with edge probability $1/n^\alpha$, which is known to obey the 0-1 law for first-order logic. This discussion focuses on the breakdown of this law when applied to stronger logical systems, specifically $\mathbb{L}_{\infty,\omega}$ for sufficiently large $\omega$ and inductive logic.

As a prominent subclass of discrete optimization, binary optimization is crucial for mathematical optimization and finds extensive use in machine learning and computer vision. However, these problems are typically NP-hard and challenging to solve because of binary constraints, particularly when dealing with a large number of variables. Current approaches often struggle with high computational costs, significant accumulated quantization errors, or limited applicability to specific tasks. To address these issues, we introduce a fast algorithm designed to find effective approximate solutions for general binary optimization problems. Our method iteratively minimizes problems based on linear surrogates of loss functions, updating the binary variables that most significantly impact the loss value at each step. This approach supports a broad range of empirical objective functions, whether or not they impose restrictions on the counts of $1$s and $-1$s in the binary variables. Additionally, we provide a proof of theoretical convergence and derive explicit convergence rates for objective functions with Lipschitz continuous gradients, which are standard in practical applications. Extensive experiments across various binary optimization tasks and large-scale datasets confirm that our algorithm outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in both effectiveness and efficiency.

Drawing causal conclusions in network contexts requires careful attention to the intricate dependencies among actors' outcomes, particularly regarding treatment spillovers and interference effects. This work addresses causal inference within connected actor structures, offering a novel model for scenarios where the network is unobserved and actor covariates change stochastically over time. By developing a joint model for both relational and covariate generation processes, we bypass restrictive separability and deterministic network assumptions that are often invalid in real-world social settings. Our approach leverages the broad class of Exponential-family Random Network models (ERNM), of which Markov Random Fields (MRF) and Exponential-family Random Graph models (ERGM) are specific instances. We introduce Bayesian inference based on potential outcomes and suggest a streamlined modification to the exchange algorithm to facilitate sampling from ERNM posteriors. Simulation results confirm the method's validity, and a case study on adolescent smoking patterns within friendship networks illustrates the framework's practical utility.

Standard analyses of Type Ia supernova peak apparent magnitudes in a lumpy universe typically rely on the idealized Friedmann-Lema\^itre Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetime, often ignoring corrections arising from inhomogeneities. This study applies recent findings on area distance in inhomogeneous universes to investigate the monopole and Hubble residual of these supernovae. We demonstrate that at low redshifts, the FLRW model for apparent magnitude requires adjustments due to relative velocity perturbations in the observed redshift. Furthermore, we illustrate how these velocity perturbations can induce variance in the Hubble residual and affect the calibration of Type Ia supernova absolute magnitudes within the Hubble flow. Finally, we show that this effect may help resolve the tension between Hubble rate determinations derived from baryon acoustic oscillations and local measurements.

Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) serves as an effective method for acquiring skills from demonstrations. This paper tackles IRL challenges where prior knowledge indicates that optimal policies must strictly adhere to specific constraints. Standard methods that overlook these constraints typically require a large volume of demonstrations to converge. We introduce XOR-Maximum Entropy Constrained Inverse Reinforcement Learning (X-MEN), which is theoretically guaranteed to reach the optimal policy at a linear convergence rate relative to the number of iterations. X-MEN integrates XOR-sampling—a proven technique that converts the #P-complete sampling problem into queries for NP oracles—within the maximum entropy IRL framework. Furthermore, X-MEN ensures that the resulting policy never produces trajectories violating the defined constraints. Empirical evaluations in navigation tasks show that X-MEN converges more rapidly to optimal policies than baseline methods and consistently generates trajectories that satisfy complex, multi-state combinatorial constraints.

Profile-guided optimization (PGO) significantly enhances compiler performance by leveraging dynamic behavior; however, gathering profile data is costly, tedious, and necessitates frequent updates to stay current. This paper introduces a new statistical method for estimating branch probabilities that boosts the performance of programs compiled without PGO. By performing offline training on a vast collection of binaries containing branch probability data, we create a model that allows compilers to predict branch likelihoods in standard, uninstrumented code, thereby guiding optimization choices. We have incorporated this method directly into LLVM, augmenting existing human-crafted compiler heuristics. Evaluations across various benchmarks show measurable improvements compared to compilation without profile data. In practical deployment, the approach eliminates the need for profiling runs and incurs negligible overhead on compilation time.

This paper introduces a new OFDM waveform designed to achieve a low peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) and high resilience against phase noise (PN), adhering to the DFT-s-OFDM signal framework. The proposed 3MSK modulation draws inspiration from continuous-phase frequency shift keying (FSK) but operates with three baseband frequencies—0 and $\pm f_{symbol}/4$—which limits phase transitions between symbols to 0 and $\pm \pi/2$ radians. Leveraging a phase-controlled modulation approach, the system allows for varying degrees of phase continuity while maintaining low-complexity receiver processing. Signal quality is enhanced by generating an initial time-domain signal with a nearly constant envelope at a rate exceeding the symbol rate, ensuring smooth phase transitions between 3MSK symbols. Furthermore, the study explores the use of excess bandwidth by transmitting non-zero subcarriers outside the standard DFT-s-OFDM active subcarriers, a method that significantly reduces PAPR. Since information is encoded in phase transitions, a receiver architecture capable of tracking phase variations without reference signals is developed. Consequently, this modulation is well-suited for non-coherent receivers, even under severe phase noise conditions, thereby minimizing reference signal overhead. Performance evaluations were conducted on transmitter metrics including PAPR, out-of-band (OOB) emissions, and achievable output power post-power amplifier (PA). Additionally, coded radio link assessments demonstrate that 3MSK achieves bit error rate (BER) performance comparable to traditional QPSK.

The electronic states of chosen nanosystems are examined using the Exact Diagonalization Ab Initio (EDABI) method, with a detailed analysis of incipient Mott–Hubbard localization effects and their associated properties.

We investigate how the conductance of Coulomb Blockade peaks varies with temperature in a superconducting island hosting Majorana modes. At low temperatures, we identify a coherent double Fu-teleportation (FT) mechanism, wherein every independent tunneling event necessitates two coherent FTs. Additionally, we observe an anomalous universal scaling transition, shifting from a $[\max(T,eV)]^6$ to a $[\max(T,eV)]^3$ conductance dependence as the energy scale increases. In the high-temperature regime, applying the standard rate equation approach reveals that conductance scales inversely with temperature and exhibits a non-monotonic temperature profile. These distinctive features—the anomalous power-law scaling and the non-monotonic temperature behavior—differ significantly from traditional Coulomb blockade peaks, serving as definitive signatures of non-local transport within the topological superconducting island.

Although automated hyperparameter optimization (HPO) offers numerous advantages, many contemporary algorithms function as black boxes, obscuring the decision-making process that yields specific configurations. This lack of transparency erodes trust in HPO and impedes its widespread adoption. In this work, we investigate integrating HPO with interpretable machine learning (IML) techniques, such as partial dependence plots. However, we note that naively applying these methods post-hoc to HPO experimental data can lead to distorted interpretations due to the optimizer's inherent sampling bias. To address this, we introduce a modified HPO approach that efficiently balances the pursuit of a global optimum based on predictive performance with the accurate estimation of IML explanations for the underlying black-box function. By coupling Bayesian optimization with Bayesian Algorithm Execution, our method demonstrates on both synthetic benchmarks and neural network hyperparameter tuning that it yields more reliable explanations of the black-box without compromising optimization efficacy.

The temporal development of occupation numbers is investigated for fermionic or bosonic oscillators that are linearly and fully coupled to multiple heat baths of both fermionic and bosonic statistics. At large time scales, the impact of reservoir characteristics with differing statistical properties on non-stationary population probabilities is examined. Furthermore, the potential applications of equilibrium absence in such systems for establishing dynamic (nonstationary) memory storage are explored.

This study introduces a simulation-driven optimization framework designed for real-time, city-scale estimation and calibration of dynamic demand models, with a specific focus on disaggregated microsimulation within congested networks. The calibration methodology employs sequential optimization for demand estimation over short intervals, utilizing continuous streams of traffic count data from IoT sensors placed on selected roads. Building on a standard bi-level optimization structure, the upper-level problem is formulated as a bounded variable quadratic program for each time frame, ensuring computational feasibility. Within every interval, probabilistic parameters for the route choice model are derived through iterative feedback loops between the upper-level Origin-Destination (OD) optimization and parallel lower-level Dynamic Traffic Assignment (DTA) simulations. To maintain temporal continuity, the microsimulation state is carried forward to the subsequent time frame. Furthermore, convergence is expedited by applying the fixed-point method to road-segment travel times. This sequential calibration approach offers significant computational efficiency compared to existing methods by dividing calculations into short time frames and assuming that demand relies solely on current and past data, without requiring reliable prior demand information. By processing field measurements as a stream and leveraging the algorithm's efficient time complexity per frame, the method effectively addresses high-dimensional real-time and online applications. Validation using both synthetic data and a real-world case study in Tartu, Estonia, demonstrates that the approach achieves high accuracy even under strict computational constraints.

**Context.** As imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes age from exposure to light and weather, their response to incident $\gamma$-ray-initiated atmospheric showers alters. These aging effects distort reconstructed event energies and $\gamma$-ray fluxes. **Aims.** This study details the deployment of signal calibration techniques within the Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System (VERITAS) to compensate for temporal variations in optical throughput and detector performance. **Methods.** A Cherenkov telescope's total throughput is defined as the product of camera-specific elements, including photomultiplier tube (PMT) gains and quantum efficiencies, alongside mirror reflectivity and Winston cone response. This document outlines methods for tracking the evolution of camera gains and mirror reflectivity over time and integrating these corrections into reconstruction pipelines. The approach is validated using seven years of VERITAS Crab Nebula observations, a standard reference in very-high-energy astronomy. **Results.** Consistent optical throughput monitoring and associated signal calibrations are proven essential for accurately reconstructing extensive air shower images. The proposed method applies PMT signal corrections to telescope simulations, generating refined instrument response functions. This technique effectively calibrates acquired $\gamma$-ray data, restoring accurate event energies and photon fluxes, while maintaining low computational costs for generating Monte Carlo simulations.

Kagome-lattice materials have garnered significant attention for their potential to host superconductivity, quantum spin liquids, and topological electronic phases. Specifically, transition-metal Kagome lattices are notable for integrating topological characteristics, diverse magnetism, and complex orbital physics. This study presents an inelastic neutron scattering investigation into the spin dynamics of the Kagome-lattice antiferromagnetic metal Fe$_{0.89}$Co$_{0.11}$Sn. While magnetic excitations are detectable up to approximately 250 meV, distinct spin waves are observed only below roughly 90 meV. These low-energy spin waves can be described using linear spin-wave theory with a Heisenberg exchange model featuring ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor ($J_1$) and next-nearest-neighbor ($J_2$) in-plane couplings, alongside antiferromagnetic interlayer coupling ($J_c$). Above the 90 meV threshold, the spin waves merge into the itinerant Stoner continuum, transforming into heavily damped particle-hole excitations. At the K point within the Brillouin zone, we identify a potential band crossing of the spin wave, suggesting the existence of a Dirac magnon. These findings elucidate the transition of spin excitations from a planar to an axial antiferromagnetic state in Fe$_{0.89}$Co$_{0.11}$Sn, resolve the magnetic Hamiltonian for both configurations, and validate the substantial impact of itinerant magnetism on spin dynamics.

Identity verification is crucial for maintaining security in everyday life. Biometric methods, particularly those based on activity, are preferred because of their high fidelity, universality, and resilience. However, most current machine learning approaches follow a traditional workflow where models are trained once and remain static, lacking user involvement and failing to adapt to the dynamic nature of learning. This rigidity often results in high rates of false positives or false negatives, necessitating expert intervention to interpret outputs and provide high-quality observations. To leverage both human expertise and computational power, a tightly coupled incremental learning process is essential for improved performance. This study introduces RLTIR, a reinforcement learning-based interactive identity recognition system that adjusts identification models through human guidance. The approach begins with a base tree-structured identity recognition model, incorporates an expert to provide feedback on model outputs, and updates the model using strategies automatically learned within a specific reinforcement learning framework. To our knowledge, this represents the first effort to integrate human expert knowledge with model learning in identity recognition. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed reinforced interactive framework surpasses baseline methods in terms of recognition accuracy and robustness.

The concept of the limit of a sequence, defined using $\varepsilon$, is introduced through the analogy of checkmate in two moves. This idea is further extended to establish the definition of the limit of a function using $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$.

In quantum devices utilizing spin-based architectures, decoherence is primarily driven by the hyperfine interaction between electron spin qubits and their surrounding nuclear spin environment. This paper offers a concise review of recent theoretical progress in describing qubit decoherence dynamics. We subsequently investigate qubit-environment entanglement, quantified via negativity. Assuming the environment begins in a maximally mixed state, we analyze how negativity evolves with respect to the environment's size, specifically by varying the count of environmental nuclei and their collective spin. Additionally, we examine the influence of the magnetic field on the timescales associated with qubit-environment disentangling.
This report outlines the discussions, outstanding issues, key takeaways, and conclusions from the 2nd SCAV workshop.

Rich user behavior data is highly valuable for Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction in industrial recommender, search, and advertising systems. However, leveraging long-term user behaviors in real-world applications is challenging due to strict online serving latency constraints. Existing approaches typically rely on retrieval-based strategies that first select a limited subset of user behaviors for attention; however, these methods are sub-optimal, incur information loss, and struggle to balance retrieval efficiency with effectiveness.

To address this, we introduce SDIM (Sampling-based Deep Interest Modeling), a simple yet effective end-to-end sampling approach for modeling long-term user interests. SDIM generates hash signatures for candidate items and items in a user's behavior sequence using multiple hash functions, then directly aggregates behaviors sharing the same hash signature with the candidate item to infer user interest. Both theoretical analysis and experiments demonstrate that SDIM matches the performance of standard attention-based models in capturing long-term interests while offering significantly faster inference speeds.

We further detail the deployment of SDIM in our production system by decoupling the computationally intensive behavior sequence hashing from the CTR model through a dedicated module called BSE (Behavior Sequence Encoding). This design ensures the CTR server remains latency-free, enabling the modeling of extremely long behavior sequences. Offline and online experiments confirm SDIM's effectiveness, and it is currently deployed in the search system of the Meituan APP.

Reconstructing objects in three dimensions is a fundamental requirement for numerous critical computer vision tasks, including autonomous driving and mobile robotics. A standard method for solving the inverse problem of deriving 3D objects from 2D projections involves integrating prior object knowledge by creating a 3D model and aligning it with the 2D image plane. However, existing methods are often constrained by insufficient shape priors and inadequate image-derived observations, which hinder reliable alignment with the 3D model. This paper demonstrates how 3D reconstruction can be enhanced through a more advanced shape prior and the integration of multiple observation types inferred from images. We propose a deformable vehicle model that is subcategory-aware, utilizing vehicle type predictions to regularize the shape more effectively. Additionally, we introduce a multi-branch Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that predicts vehicle type and orientation, providing this data as prior information for model fitting. The CNN also extracts vehicle keypoints and wireframes, which are highly suitable for associating the model with the image and facilitating fitting. Pose estimation and reconstruction are handled by a flexible probabilistic model. Extensive experiments on two challenging real-world datasets demonstrate the advantages of the proposed shape prior. Comparative analyses with state-of-the-art vehicle pose estimation methods reveal that our approach performs as well as or better than existing techniques, validating the effectiveness of the developed shape prior and probabilistic model for vehicle reconstruction.

A primary objective in nuclear physics has long been to comprehend nuclear structures and reactions from first principles. Few- and many-body systems serve as exceptional environments for investigating these nuclear interactions. Over the last two decades, the modeling of such interactions has advanced substantially, largely due to the emergence of chiral effective field theory ($\chi$EFT), which offers a low-energy effective description of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Within the framework of $\chi$EFT, numerous studies have focused on constructing two- and three-nucleon interactions. This article aims to offer a concise overview of chiral interaction models that are local in configuration space and to present selected recent findings on nuclear systems derived using these interactions.
