In the zero-$G$ limit (z$G$KN) of the maximally analytically extended Kerr–Newman spacetime, the discrete spectrum of the Dirac operator for a point electron is determined, subject to specific constraints on the electrical coupling constant and the ring-singularity radius. This spectrum is defined by a triplet of integers corresponding to the winding numbers of dynamical system orbits on cylinders. A mapping is constructed that connects this spectrum to the established hydrogenic Dirac spectrum, accompanied by numerical examples and a list of open questions.

This study details outcomes from nine simulations of radiatively-inefficient magnetically arrested disks (MADs), exploring a range of black hole spin parameters ($a_*$) from -0.9 to 0.9. Each simulation extended to approximately $t \gtrsim 100,000\,GM/c^3$ to achieve equilibrium in disk inflow at large radii. Our findings confirm prior research that the saturated magnetic flux—and thus jet power—of MADs is highly sensitive to black hole spin. Prograde disks reach significantly higher relative magnetic flux levels and generate more potent jets than retrograde ones. Furthermore, MADs around rotating black holes naturally produce jets with generalized parabolic profiles, where jet widths scale as a power of distance from the black hole; for distances up to $100\;GM/c^2$, the power-law index ranges between $k \approx 0.27$ and $0.42$. A strong link exists between disk-jet geometry and dimensionless magnetic flux, causing prograde systems to exhibit thinner equatorial accretion flows and broader jets near the black hole compared to retrograde systems. Variability trends also differ between prograde and retrograde MADs: while accretion rate variability rises with increasing spin for $a_*>0$, it stays nearly constant for $a_*\lesssim 0$, whereas magnetic flux variability follows the inverse pattern. In the MAD state, jets extract more angular momentum from black holes than is accreted, effectively slowing the black hole's rotation. Consequently, if powerful jets from natural MAD systems persist, this angular momentum loss could significantly diminish black hole spin over cosmic epochs.

Driven by blockchain's substantial energy consumption and recent advances in low-power computing, we conduct a detailed time-energy analysis comparing blockchain performance on low-power versus high-performance nodes. Our study evaluates three low-power systems spanning the performance-power spectrum across both x86/64 and ARM architectures. We find that full-node operation on low-end devices is primarily hindered by limited memory capacity and bandwidth. Conversely, low-power systems with a balanced power-to-performance ratio deliver viable performance while drastically reducing energy usage. For instance, Jetson TX2 nodes achieve approximately 80% and 30% of the throughput of Parity and Hyperledger, respectively, while consuming 18x and 23x less energy than traditional Intel Xeon-based servers.

The quantum simulation kernel serves as a critical, lengthy gate sequence within numerous quantum applications. This paper introduces Paulihedral, a block-wise compiler framework designed to deeply optimize this subroutine by leveraging high-level program structures and optimization opportunities. Paulihedral utilizes a novel Pauli intermediate representation that preserves high-level semantics and constraints, thereby enabling large-scale optimizations that are difficult to achieve at the low gate level. Specifically, we present two technology-independent instruction scheduling passes and two technology-dependent code optimization passes that harmonize the circuit synthesis, gate cancellation, and qubit mapping stages of the compiler. Experimental findings demonstrate that Paulihedral surpasses current state-of-the-art compiler infrastructures across a broad spectrum of applications, benefiting both near-term superconducting quantum processors and future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

This work computes the cohomology of $\mathfrak{sl}_3(k)$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ with characteristic $p>3$, using simple modules and Weyl modules as coefficients, and additionally provides descriptions of the corresponding cohomology for $\mathfrak{gl}_3(k)$.

Gaze tracking is becoming a critical element in Augmented and Virtual Reality systems. However, current gaze tracking algorithms are computationally intensive, typically running at only 5 Hz on mobile processors, even though near-eye cameras can capture data in real-time at rates exceeding 30 Hz. This paper introduces a real-time eye tracking algorithm that operates at an average of 30 Hz on mobile hardware, achieving gaze accuracies between 0.1° and 0.5°. Notably, the model requires only 30,000 parameters, which is one to two orders of magnitude fewer than state-of-the-art solutions. The core innovation is an Auto ROI mode that continuously predicts Regions of Interest in near-eye imagery and processes exclusively those areas for gaze estimation. To facilitate this, we propose a novel, lightweight ROI prediction algorithm that mimics event camera behavior. We explain how software-based event emulation allows for precise ROI prediction without the need for specialized hardware. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/horizon-research/edgaze.

This study examines radial oscillations in non-rotating neutron stars using unified equations of state (EoSs) capable of supporting stars with a mass of 2 M$_\odot$. By solving the Sturm-Liouville problem, we calculate the 20 lowest radial oscillation modes and their eigenfunctions for neutron stars modeled with eight selected unified EoSs derived from Skyrme-Hartree Fock, Relativistic Mean-Field, and quarkyonic frameworks. We analyze how the eigenfrequencies differ between hadronic and quarkyonic EoSs as central densities change. Specifically, the fundamental (f-mode) frequency shows significant variation between these two EoS classes at 1.4 M$_\odot$ but drops to zero at their respective maximum masses, aligning with the stability condition $\partial M/\partial\rho_c > 0$. Additionally, our calculation of large frequency separations reveals that including the crust in the EoS substantially lowers the frequencies of higher-order modes.

This paper introduces the concepts of Rickart and Baer lattices alongside their duals. We demonstrate that significant aspects of the theory of Rickart and Baer modules can be grasped through lattice-theoretic techniques alone. To achieve this, we employ linear morphisms as defined by T. Albu and M. Iosif. Specifically, we examine a submonoid with zero, $\mathfrak{m}$, within the monoid of all linear endomorphisms of a lattice $\mathcal{L}$. This approach provides a more general framework for applying our findings to module theory. Furthermore, we establish that $\mathfrak{m}$-Rickart and $\mathfrak{m}$-Baer lattices can be characterized by annihilators in $\mathfrak{m}$ generated by idempotents, mirroring the characterization found in module theory.

This paper investigates the error and perturbation bounds for two classes of absolute value equations (AVEs), specifically $Ax - B|x| = b$ and $Ax - |Bx| = b$, by introducing a new class of absolute value functions. The study presents several practical error and perturbation bounds for these equations and applies them to derive useful bounds for the horizontal linear complementarity problem (HLCP). Additionally, two new error bounds for the linear complementarity problem (LCP) are established; these coincide with existing results. Furthermore, a novel perturbation bound for the LCP is provided without imposing constraint conditions. The paper also offers computable estimates for the aforementioned upper bounds that do not restrict the matrix type; under specific conditions, these estimates are sharper than previous findings. Finally, numerical examples derived from LCPs are included to demonstrate the viability of the proposed perturbation bounds for AVEs.

We investigate the distribution of complex eigenvalues $z_1,\ldots, z_N$ associated with random Hermitian $N\times N$ block band matrices that include a finite-rank complex deformation. Under the assumption that the band width $W$ increases faster than $\sqrt{N}$, we demonstrate that the limiting density of the imaginary parts $\Im z_1,\ldots, \Im z_N$, when approximated by a sigma-model, matches that of the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This approach utilizes the methodology outlined in arXiv:1802.03813.

Word alignment serves as a critical foundation for downstream cross-lingual understanding and generation tasks. Although recent neural models have surpassed statistical approaches in performance, they remain dependent on complex translation architectures. This study introduces MirrorAlign, a super lightweight unsupervised word alignment model that leverages bidirectional symmetric attention trained via contrastive learning, alongside an agreement loss to enforce mirror-like symmetry in attention maps. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks indicate that MirrorAlign matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance while substantially cutting training and decoding times. Further ablation studies and case analyses confirm the model's superiority. Notably, this work pioneers the unification of bilingual word embeddings and word alignments, delivering a 16.4X speedup over GIZA++ and achieving 50X parameter compression compared to Transformer-based methods. To support the research community, the code is available at: https://github.com/moore3930/MirrorAlign.

This Comment highlights that the reported measurement accuracy of approximately 10^-9 in the Letter [Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 120405 (2014)] does not reflect the accuracy achievable with a single antiparallel or parallel laser beam due to the Doppler effect. Instead, the accuracy for a single beam is significantly lower, around 10^-4, representing a five-order-of-magnitude difference. The substantial improvement in total accuracy results from the coupling of the Doppler effects associated with two laser beams.

With information extraction (IE) systems advancing in whole-document capabilities, the traditional task of \emph{template filling} has regained attention as a standard benchmark for evaluation. However, this position paper challenges its appropriateness for this role. We contend that the task necessitates definitive resolutions to complex issues regarding \emph{event individuation}—specifically, distinguishing separate events—where even human experts lack consensus. Through annotation studies and error analysis, we demonstrate concerns regarding the utility of template filling metrics, the quality of available datasets, and the capacity of models to master this task. Finally, we explore potential remedies.

Drawing from the principles of geometric quantization, we examine representations of the Heisenberg–Weyl group generated by hypercomplex characters of its center. This approach unifies three primary scenarios—quantum mechanics (associated with elliptic characters), hyperbolic mechanics, and classical mechanics (linked to parabolic characters)—under a single framework known as p-mechanics. Within this structure, we derive the respective dynamic equations and establish rules for probability addition for each case. Significantly, we successfully recover the entirety of classical mechanics without relying on any semiclassical approximation where the Planck constant approaches zero.

Keywords: Heisenberg group, Kirillov's method of orbits, geometric quantization, quantum mechanics, classical mechanics, Planck constant, dual numbers, double numbers, hypercomplex, jet spaces, hyperbolic mechanics, interference, Segal–Bargmann representation, Schrödinger representation, dynamic equation, harmonic and unharmonic oscillator, contextual probability.

Estimating the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) as a causal parameter typically involves a two-step process: first, modeling the treatment and outcome while accounting for potential confounders; second, utilizing these predictions in ATE estimators like the Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) method. Given concerns about unknown or nonlinear relationships between confounders and the treatment or outcome, there is growing interest in applying non-parametric methods, such as Machine Learning (ML) algorithms. Some existing approaches suggest using two separate Neural Networks (NNs) without parameter regularization, relying solely on Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for optimization. However, our simulations demonstrate that the AIPW estimator performs poorly without regularization. We propose a normalized version of AIPW, termed nAIPW, which offers advantages in specific contexts. Provable theory confirms that nAIPW retains the same double-robustness and orthogonality properties as standard AIPW. Furthermore, if the first-step algorithms converge sufficiently quickly under regularization, nAIPW achieves asymptotic normality. Finally, we evaluate the performance of both AIPW and nAIPW regarding bias and variance when small to moderate L1 regularization is applied to the Neural Networks.

Robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) are extensively studied for dynamic optimization in uncertain settings, and their core properties and algorithms, including value and policy iteration, naturally extend from standard MDPs. Surprisingly, however, no convex optimization framework for RMDPs has been established. This paper presents the first convex formulation for RMDPs under both sa-rectangularity and s-rectangularity assumptions. By employing entropic regularization and exponential variable transformations, we derive a formulation that maintains a linear count of variables and constraints, albeit with large coefficients. This approach enables the integration of efficient convex optimization techniques to develop new algorithms for RMDPs involving uncertain probabilities. Additionally, we provide a simplified formulation for RMDPs with polyhedral uncertainty sets. Ultimately, this work establishes a new research avenue for RMDPs and serves as a foundational step toward achieving a tractable convex representation.

Virtual knot theory exhibits several distinctive properties absent in classical knot theory, such as parity and picture-valued invariants. This paper leverages these unique aspects of virtual knot theory to develop novel representations of classical (pure) braids.

We examine a quantum fully packed loop model defined on a square lattice, characterized by a frustration-free projector Hamiltonian and ring-exchange interactions localized on plaquettes. By introducing a boundary Hamiltonian that promotes domain-wall boundary conditions, we connect ground state properties to established literature on combinatorics and the six-vertex model. We analyze how this boundary term partitions the Hilbert space into Krylov subspaces and demonstrate that the Hamiltonian is ergodic within each subspace, resulting in a series of exact eigenstates with equidistant energies at the bottom of the spectrum. Within this set, we systematically categorize both product eigenstates and those with finite entanglement. Furthermore, utilizing an exact recursion relation alongside the enumeration of half-plane fully packed loop configurations with diverse boundary conditions on one side, we conduct a numerically exact lattice calculation of the ground state bipartite entanglement entropy, which exhibits area law scaling. Finally, we establish that the spectrum remains gapless in the thermodynamic limit by employing a trial wave function derived from a twisted superposition of the ground state.

Consider the Gel'fand triple $\mathcal{S}\subset \mathcal{L}^2 \subset \mathcal{S}^*$ defined over the Bernoulli space, where elements within $\mathcal{S}^*$ are designated as Bernoulli generalized functionals. This paper establishes the integration of these functionals with respect to a spectral measure—a projection operator-valued measure—within the context of the aforementioned triple, while investigating their core characteristics. The study introduces novel concepts, derives various results, and provides illustrative examples.

Data-driven modeling is essential for numerous analyses in collider experiments, yet the inferred physical properties often depend heavily on the specifics of the fitting procedure. This study introduces a principled Bayesian framework, grounded in marginal likelihood, to unify data modeling and signal extraction within a common collider physics context. Initially, the marginal likelihood-based approach is employed to construct background processes more rigorously by systematically evaluating various candidate shapes. Subsequently, this framework is expanded to utilize marginal likelihood as an effective instrument for addressing anomaly detection challenges in particle physics. This proposal provides deeper insights into accurately determining background models and illustrates a versatile method for extending signal determination beyond traditional bump hunting.

We establish an analyticity property for the Dirichlet-Neumann operator in any dimension within an unbounded, infinite-depth domain subject to space-periodic boundary conditions. Furthermore, we derive an analytic bifurcation theorem for analytic Stokes waves—specifically, space-periodic traveling solutions to the water wave equations in deep water.

We demonstrate that within the character variety of representations from surface groups into the Lie group $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{R}) \times \mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{R})$, the maximal component's compactification, as introduced by the second author, forms a closed ball subject to the action of the mapping class group. This paper examines the dynamics of this action and characterizes the boundary points geometrically as $(\overline{A_{1} \times A_{1}},2)$-valued mixed structures.

We present a technique for achieving homogeneous atom-cavity coupling by retaining only $^{87}$Rb atoms that exhibit near-maximal coupling to the cavity's standing-wave mode. This selection process involves applying an AC Stark shift to the ground-state hyperfine microwave transition frequency via light coupled into the cavity. Subsequently, resonant microwaves induce a spin flip specifically in the strongly coupled atoms. Finally, radiation pressure forces eject all atoms remaining in the original spin state from the cavity. Improving the uniformity of this coupling could significantly advance entanglement generation, intracavity driving of atomic transitions, cavity-optomechanics, and quantum simulations. Furthermore, this methodology is readily adaptable to other atomic species possessing microwave or optical transitions.

Although pre-trained language models have achieved significant advancements in dialogue processing, they are generally trained on surface-level text, resulting in a limited ability to grasp the core semantic meaning of dialogue contexts. To address this, we explore Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) as a means of injecting explicit semantic knowledge into pre-training to better capture essential dialogue information. Specifically, we introduce a semantic-focused pre-training framework that builds upon the standard approach (Devlin et al., 2019) by incorporating three tasks designed to learn 1) fundamental semantic units, 2) semantic relationships, and 3) holistic semantic representations based on AMR graphs. Empirical results on both casual and task-oriented dialogues demonstrate the superiority of our model. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first application of deep semantic representations for dialogue pre-training.

The emergence of deep learning and extensive autonomous driving datasets has propelled monocular 3D object detection (Mono3D) to new heights of success. Nevertheless, a significant yet underexplored obstacle hinders practical cross-domain application: severe performance drops due to the absence of labeled data in target domains. This paper begins by thoroughly examining the root causes of the domain gap in Mono3D, highlighting a critical depth-shift issue stemming from geometric misalignment between domains. We introduce STMono3D, a novel self-teaching framework designed for unsupervised domain adaptation in Mono3D. To address the depth-shift, we implement a geometry-aligned multi-scale training strategy that decouples camera parameters and ensures geometric consistency across domains. Building on this, we establish a teacher-student architecture to produce adaptive pseudo-labels for the target domain. Leveraging the richer information provided by our end-to-end framework regarding these pseudo-labels, we devise a quality-aware supervision strategy that incorporates instance-level pseudo-confidence scores to enhance target-domain training efficacy. Furthermore, we propose positive focusing training and dynamic thresholding mechanisms to manage the large volume of false negatives and false positives within the pseudo-labels. STMono3D demonstrates exceptional performance across all tested datasets, even outperforming fully supervised methods on the KITTI 3D object detection benchmark. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural study to effectively explore unsupervised domain adaptation techniques for Mono3D.

This study examines two-dimensional quantum field theories underpinned by BMS symmetry extended with $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ currents, which are anticipated to holographically describe charged Flat Space Cosmologies (FSCs) within asymptotically flat three-dimensional spacetimes. We analyze the modular characteristics of these theories by constructing characters for the highest weight representations of the symmetry algebra and deriving the partition function. Utilizing the modular properties of both the partition function and the torus one-point function, we calculate the density of primary states, determine the entropy, and extract the asymptotic values of the structure constants. The resulting expression for these structure constants reveals shifts in weights and one central term, alongside an additional phase, distinguishing it from prior literature on BMS-invariant theories lacking $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ currents. Furthermore, we corroborate our field-theoretic findings regarding the structure constants through a bulk computation utilizing a scalar probe in the background of a charged FSC.

For stacked simplicial complexes, with trees as a specific subclass, we establish an explicit bijection between facet partitions (edges in the case of trees) and vertex partitions into independent sets. More broadly, we demonstrate bijections linking facet partitions where parts maintain a minimal distance of at least $s$ to vertex partitions where parts maintain a minimal distance of at least $s+1$. As a result, we derive findings regarding partitions of natural numbers characterized by minimum spacing constraints on their parts.

We propose two architectures for sentence-level Sign Language Recognition (SLR), a task involving the mapping of sign language video sequences to corresponding gloss label sequences. Both models utilize Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) as their classifier to eliminate the need for pre-segmenting sentences into individual words. The first approach employs an LRCN framework, where a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) extracts features from each frame before an LSTM processes them; this model operates without prior knowledge, feeding raw frames directly into an 18-layer LRCN with a CTC layer. The second approach utilizes a Multi-Cue Network that integrates three distinct characteristics of signs—hand shape, hand position, and hand movement—extracted via MediaPipe. Hand shape 2D landmarks generate a skeletal representation fed into a CONV-LSTM, while hand locations and positions (calculated as relative distances to the head) are processed by separate LSTMs. These three information streams are combined within the Multi-Cue network, culminating in a CTC classification layer. Evaluated on the RWTH-PHOENIX-Weather dataset, and following an extensive hyperparameter search covering feature maps, input dimensions, batch size, sequence length, LSTM memory cells, regularization, and dropout, the models achieved a Word Error Rate (WER) of 35.

By employing a navigation framework based on the datum $(F,V)$, where $F$ denotes a Finsler metric and the smooth tangent vector field $V$ satisfies $F(-V(x))>1$ globally, one can induce a Lorentz Finsler metric $\tilde{F}$. For this metric $\tilde{F}$, isoparametric functions and hypersurfaces—whether defined with or without a smooth measure—can be established. Specifically, when the vector field $V$ within the navigation datum is homothetic, we demonstrate the local relationships between isoparametric functions and hypersurfaces prior to and following the navigation transformation. Leveraging these correspondences, we present several examples of isoparametric functions and hypersurfaces within a Funk space of Lorentz Randers type.

While one-dimensional (1D) stellar models have advanced our knowledge of stellar structure and evolution, they are constrained by uncertainties regarding multi-dimensional phenomena within stellar interiors. Recent computational breakthroughs now allow these 1D models to be refined and validated using detailed three-dimensional (3D) hydrodynamics, which can simulate complex multi-dimensional processes over brief periods. Among these phenomena, turbulent entrainment driving mixing across convective boundaries remains one of the most significant yet least understood aspects. This study presents hydrodynamic simulations of the neon-burning shell in a massive star, interpreted through the lens of turbulent entrainment laws derived from geophysics. Unlike previous investigations, our simulations offer an unprecedented level of realism in replicating the stellar environment. Crucially, the strong entrainment observed reveals substantial deficiencies in how convective boundary mixing is currently implemented in 1D models. Consequently, this work urges a major overhaul of convective boundary modeling in 1D frameworks, specifically regarding entrainment mechanisms. These revisions will have profound implications for theories concerning supernovae, nucleosynthesis, and the physics of neutron stars and black holes.

This study addresses Automatic Question Generation (AQG), where the objective is to formulate a question given a passage and an answer. The resulting question must be grammatically sound, answerable based on the passage, and specifically tailored to the provided answer. However, analysis reveals that current AQG models often fail to meet one or more of these criteria, producing outputs that resemble incomplete drafts requiring refinement. To address this limitation, we introduce a method that emulates the human questioning process by generating an initial draft followed by a refinement stage. Specifically, we present Refine Network (RefNet), which employs two decoders. The second decoder utilizes a dual attention mechanism to focus on both the original passage and the initial question draft produced by the first decoder, effectively refining it to enhance correctness and completeness. We evaluated RefNet across three datasets—SQuAD, HOTPOT-QA, and DROP—demonstrating that it surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods by 7-16% on all of them. Furthermore, we show that the quality of the second decoder can be further improved on metrics like fluency and answerability by explicitly rewarding revisions that enhance these attributes during training. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrekshaNema25/RefNet-QG.

Variational hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (VHQCAs) hold promise for near-term quantum computing, yet recent concerns have arisen regarding the extensive measurement requirements needed for their convergence. To address this, we examine the role of classical optimizers within VHQCAs and propose a new method called the individual Coupled Adaptive Number of Shots (iCANS). This adaptive strategy efficiently determines the number of measurements—both per iteration and per stochastic gradient descent partial derivative. We numerically evaluated iCANS using the variational quantum eigensolver and variational quantum compiling, testing both noisy and noise-free conditions. Results demonstrate that iCANS consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art optimizers, particularly in noisy environments. Consequently, we believe this adaptive approach will be highly valuable for realistic VHQCA applications where measurement resources are constrained.

Although deep neural networks excel at visual pattern recognition, they often struggle with reasoning tasks that humans find straightforward. Humans can extrapolate strategies learned on simple tasks to tackle harder ones, frequently by dedicating more time to think. For instance, someone who masters small mazes can apply the same search methods to larger ones simply by spending more time. In computing, this is typically handled by algorithms that scale to any difficulty level at the expense of increased computation. Conversely, the reasoning capacity of feed-forward networks is capped by their depth; those trained on simple tasks cannot extend their logic to handle more complex scenarios. This paper demonstrates that recurrent networks trained on simple problems using few steps can successfully solve far more complex issues merely by performing additional steps during inference. We validate this algorithmic capability in recurrent networks across prefix sum calculations, mazes, and chess. In each domain, networks trained on basic instances extend their reasoning capabilities at test time simply by "thinking longer."

Active Learning (AL) strategies seek to reduce the amount of training data needed for model development. In pool-based AL, the process begins with a small set of randomly selected and labeled samples to initiate iterative cycles where the most informative unlabeled instances are chosen for labeling. Although recent research has primarily assessed the robustness of different query functions within AL, there has been minimal focus on optimizing the design of the initial labeled pool specifically for deep active learning. Leveraging recent advancements in self-supervised and unsupervised representation learning, this study explores whether an intelligently constructed initial pool can enhance deep AL performance. We examine the impact of such intelligent sampling, including self-supervised and unsupervised approaches, on deep active learning methods. The experimental setup, hypotheses, methodology, and implementation were vetted by peer review prior to execution. While results did not definitively demonstrate that intelligently sampled initial pools outperform random ones in the long term, a Variational Autoencoder-based sampling strategy exhibited promising trends warranting further investigation.

Although generative models that define joint distributions over parse trees and sentences are valuable for parsing and language modeling, they limit feature scope and are frequently surpassed by discriminative approaches. We introduce a framework that combines a generative model with a discriminative recognition model within an encoder-decoder architecture. By offering interpretations grounded in expectation maximization and variational inference, we demonstrate that this approach allows for both parsing and language modeling within a unified implementation. Evaluations on the English Penn Treebank reveal that our framework achieves competitive results in constituency parsing while matching the state-of-the-art performance for single-model language modeling.

Quantum software is essential for unlocking the complete capabilities of quantum computing systems, a factor that has recently heightened interest in the field. As quantum programming research matures, evidenced by numerous active studies and practical applications, software metric experts must adapt to this new paradigm to assess it rigorously and quantitatively. This paper initiates that process by introducing foundational metrics for quantum software, primarily targeting the measurement of its size and structural complexity. These metrics are defined across various abstraction levels to explicitly capture different size and structural attributes within quantum programs. Consequently, the proposed framework enables the evaluation of quantum software from multiple perspectives.

This paper examines the geometry of billiards within ellipses by utilizing the characteristics of confocal central conics. The intersections of the billiard's extended sides occur on confocal ellipses and hyperbolas, thereby establishing a Poncelet grid. When a billiard is periodic, it remains closed regardless of the initial vertex selected on the ellipse, resulting in a continuous variation known as billiard motion, which differs from both Euclidean and projective motions. Extending this motion to the associated Poncelet grid yields fresh insights and invariants.

This study examines a graphene-based valleytronic device featuring charge separation across distinct sublattices and associated nonequivalent valleys. We analyze the conditions for maximizing valley polarization and explore the parameters enabling coherent carrier control and data storage through the valley degree of freedom. Valley polarization is governed by the pulse amplitude and carrier envelope phase, as well as the curvature of electron trajectories in reciprocal space. Under strong field excitation, the optical selection rules of perturbative optics are superseded by nonadiabatic geometric effects, inducing nonperturbative valley polarization in two-dimensional Dirac materials even without an intrinsic bandgap. Microscopically, this nonreciprocal response of graphene to a chiral electric field is encoded by the quantum Berry phase, manifesting as a (pseudo)magnetoelectric monopole.

Uncovering the hidden dynamics within stochastic data presents a significant challenge due to the inherent randomness influencing data evolution, a difficulty that escalates when trajectory information is unavailable. We introduce a novel approach to model these dynamics without relying on trajectories by leveraging the weak form of the Fokker-Planck (FP) equation, which dictates the evolution of probability densities in Brownian processes. By employing Gaussian functions as test functions within this weak form, we shift derivatives onto the Gaussians, thereby approximating the equation through the expectation of data sums. Utilizing a dictionary-based representation for unknown terms, we construct and solve a linear system via regression to uncover the latent dynamics. Consequently, we designate this methodology as Weak Collocation Regression (WCR), reflecting its core components: the weak form, Gaussian kernel collocation, and regression. Numerical experiments demonstrate that WCR is both flexible and efficient, revealing dynamics in multi-dimensional settings within seconds and scaling effectively to high-dimensional data, such as 20 dimensions. Furthermore, the method accurately identifies hidden dynamics in complex scenarios involving variable-dependent diffusion and coupled drift, exhibiting robust performance with high accuracy even when noise is present.

This research presents and leverages ensembles of experimental data to compare and validate two models for simulating variable density, compressible turbulent mixing. While Reynolds Averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) and Large Eddy Simulations (LES) have been extensively validated against canonical flows in prior work, this study introduces novelty through its geometric complexity, ensemble-based validation strategy, and the uniform computational framework used for testing. Furthermore, the authors executed all experimental and computational tasks, creating a tightly coupled experimental setup with its corresponding digital twin. The study details the experimental divergent shock tube facility and its data acquisition methods, replicating them within the simulation environment. A 2D Euler model, which ignores turbulent mixing at the interface, was optimized using a Gaussian process and serves as the foundation for subsequent 2D RANS and 3D LES studies comparing against experimental mixing layer data. Results indicate that RANS aligns well with experimental data only at later flow development stages. Conversely, LES ensembles generally demonstrate good agreement with experimental data but exhibit sensitivity to initial condition characterization; resolution-dependent behavior is also noted for specific higher-order statistics. Overall, the LES model effectively captures the influences of divergent geometry, compressibility, and the combined non-linear instabilities intrinsic to the problem. The successful prediction of mixing width and its growth rate underscores the presence of three distinct regimes in instability development, each resembling previously studied instabilities.

Measurements of heat capacity and magnetic torque investigate the anisotropic temperature-field phase diagram of the frustrated spin dimer Ba3Mn2O8 within a magnetic field range of 0 to 18 Tesla. When the field is aligned along the c-axis, only a single magnetically ordered phase exists in this range, whereas an a-axis orientation reveals two distinct phases. These findings uncover a surprising non-monotonic evolution of the phase diagram as the field rotates within the [001]-[100] plane. The angle-dependent behavior of the critical field (Hc1), which signifies the closure of the spin gap, is quantitatively explained by a minimal spin Hamiltonian that includes nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor superexchange, Zeeman energy, and single-ion anisotropy. This model also predicts a non-monotonic transition between the two ordered states upon field rotation in the a-c plane; however, the experimentally observed effect is significantly larger in magnitude. This discrepancy suggests that the minimal Hamiltonian may be incomplete or that the structure of the magnetically ordered states differs slightly from previous proposals.

Many-body Green's functions encapsulate the complete properties and excitations of interacting electron systems. Although their precise evaluation on classical machines remains difficult, recent initiatives focus on developing quantum algorithms to achieve a quantum advantage for this purpose, leveraging hardware expected to emerge soon. This study presents a new near-term quantum algorithm for calculating one-particle Green's functions using their Lehmann representation. Our approach extends the quantum equation of motion method to access the system's charged excitations. We validate this proposal by successfully computing the Green's function for a two-site Fermi-Hubbard model on an IBM quantum processor.

Secure communication requires more than just robust cryptography and strong keys; it demands assurance that the keys in use are authentic and belong to the intended contact. Without this verification, users remain vulnerable to impersonation and man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks. Mega addresses this challenge through a hierarchical authentication system for contacts and keys. To simplify the management of multiple key types and pairs, the entire mechanism is streamlined into a single "identity key."

We introduce a novel, lightweight technique for novel-view synthesis capable of generalizing to any forward-facing scene. Unlike existing methods that are computationally heavy, demand per-scene optimization, or utilize memory-intensive representations, our approach begins by modeling the scene with a collection of fronto-parallel semitransparent planes, which are subsequently transformed into deformable layers through an end-to-end process. Furthermore, we implement a feed-forward refinement step that aggregates data from input views to correct the estimated representation. This method eliminates the need for fine-tuning on new scenes and accommodates an unrestricted number of views. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our approach outperforms recent models across standard metrics and human assessments, offering significant benefits in inference speed and the compactness of the resulting layered geometry; please see https://samsunglabs.github.io/MLI for more details.

This study presents an accumulation of findings regarding the fundamental algebraic properties of polynomial composites. Given their polynomial nature, results concerning monoid domains are also integrated throughout. The second section explores the connections between polynomial composites, Galois theory, and the theory of nilpotents. The third part introduces several cryptosystems, offering generalizations of established ciphers that accommodate infinite alphabets through straightforward algebraic techniques. Additionally, two specific cryptosystems are identified where the underlying structure involves Dedekind rings, with certain elements being equivalent to fractional ideals. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates the application of polynomial composites and monoid domains within the field of cryptology.

This study examines the recently introduced low-degree-of-freedom model by Moffat and Kimura [1,2], which describes how incompressible Euler fluid equations approach a finite-time singularity. The model posits an initial finite-energy state consisting of two vortex rings arranged symmetrically on inclined planes. The Hamiltonian structure of the inviscid limit is derived, revealing a noncanonical Poisson bracket [3] along with two invariants: one functioning as the Hamiltonian and the other as a Casimir invariant. The system is demonstrated to be integrable, with its solution residing at the intersection of these two invariants, analogous to how solutions for a free rigid body in mechanics lie at the intersection of kinetic energy and angular momentum surfaces. Furthermore, a direct quadrature is provided to illustrate the Leray form of finite-time singularity within the model. Consequently, assuming the Moffat and Kimura model accurately reflects Euler's ideal fluid equations, this work establishes the existence of finite-time singularities.

In a base phi system, a natural number is expressed as a sum of powers of the golden mean, $\varphi$. While multiple representations exist, the standard form introduced by George Bergman in 1957 ensures uniqueness by forbidding consecutive powers, $\varphi^n$ and $\varphi^{n+1}$. This paper proposes a novel representation that permits the simultaneous occurrence of $\varphi^0$ and $\varphi^1$ while still disallowing all other consecutive powers. We demonstrate that this new approach aligns more closely with the classical representation of natural numbers using integer powers than Bergman's standard method does.

As we integrate devices for quantum information processing, quantum communication technologies will be pivotal in the near future; however, their deployment remains difficult due to gate errors and signal loss. Quantum error correction codes serve as a key solution to these challenges, with Quantum Reed-Solomon codes proving particularly efficient for communication tasks. Despite their efficiency, the substantial physical resources they demand hinder practical application. Recent advancements in quantum multiplexing, which leverage multiple photon degrees of freedom, have demonstrated the ability to mitigate these resource requirements. This study proposes a method that utilizes quantum multiplexing to decompose multi-controlled gates with fewer $\rm{CX}$ gates. We demonstrate that this approach significantly lowers the number of $\rm{CX}$ gates required in encoding circuits for Quantum Reed-Solomon codes. Furthermore, our technique is versatile and applicable to various other quantum error correction schemes and algorithms, such as Grover's search and quantum walks.

Enhancing the accessibility and ease of use for smart devices requires developing models capable of interpreting user interfaces (UIs) to aid users in completing tasks. However, specific UI characteristics present unique hurdles, particularly in effectively utilizing multimodal features—comprising images, text, and structural metadata—and achieving robust performance without access to high-quality labeled data. To overcome these obstacles, we present UIBert, a transformer-based joint image-text model trained via innovative pre-training tasks on extensive unlabeled UI datasets to learn generalized feature representations for UIs and their constituent parts. Our core premise is that heterogeneous UI features are self-aligned, meaning image and text attributes of UI components predict one another. Leveraging this alignment across different features within a component and among various components in a UI, we propose five pre-training tasks. We validate our approach on nine real-world downstream UI tasks, where UIBert surpasses strong multimodal baselines by up to 9.26% in accuracy.

Several forthcoming Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) missions primarily rely on extensive arrays of superconductive Transition-Edge Sensor (TES) detectors paired with polarization modulators, such as continuously rotating Half-Wave Plates (HWP). While a high number of detectors is essential for maximizing raw sensitivity, historical data indicates that systematic errors are increasingly the primary obstacle to achieving the sensitivity levels needed to detect primordial $B$-modes. Consequently, polarization modulators have gained popularity as a means to suppress these systematic issues. HWPs necessitate a rotation mechanism to modulate incoming polarized light; however, minimizing heat dissipation from this mechanism is a critical constraint, especially for space-based missions like $LiteBIRD$. To address this, superconductive magnetic bearings can be utilized to levitate the rotor, enabling contactless rotation. A drawback of this approach is the generation of magnetic fields. This study examines the impact of such fields on a TES detector prototype, finding no detectable shifts in the critical temperature ($T_c$) under constant (DC) magnetic fields, but a measurable response to varying (AC) magnetic fields. We quantify the worst-case TES responsivity to AC magnetic fields at approximately $10^5$ pA/G and offer a preliminary explanation for the signal pickup mechanism.

The adaptability of timed automata has spurred extensive research into their extensions, with pushdown timed automata (PDTA)—featuring a potentially unbounded stack—being a particularly prominent variant. Although various algorithms have been developed for reachability across different PDTA models, most remain purely theoretical and lack efficient implementations. A primary obstacle is that existing approaches rely on region-based abstraction or other complex methods rather than the more implementable zone-based abstraction. This paper demonstrates that naively extending the zone-based reachability algorithm for timed automata to handle stacks is unsound for control state reachability. By providing an inductive rule-based perspective on the zone reachability algorithm for timed automata, we analyze and modify these rules to function effectively within PDTA. Consequently, we present the first terminating, sound, and complete zone-based algorithm for PDTA. Implemented in the TChecker tool, our approach is validated through experiments, offering a practical pathway for verifying pushdown timed systems.

The IVOA Provenance Data model utilizes container classes for entities, agents, and activities to characterize dataset provenance, linking executed tasks and responsibilities to specific agents. Additionally, it offers classes for defining activity types, their configuration templates, and the configurations actually applied during task execution. This text highlights lessons learned from implementing the CDS ProvHiPS service, which distributes provenance metadata for both HST HiPS data collections and the original HST archive images used to generate HiPS tiles. Built upon the ProvTAP protocol—an emerging TAP standard for disseminating provenance metadata—ProvTAP queries can quickly become highly complex. The discussion examines various graph representation strategies considered for this purpose, including ad hoc solutions, triplestores, and SQL CTEs.

This study introduces a new bulk-surface virtual element method (BSVEM) designed for numerically solving elliptic bulk-surface partial differential equations (BSPDEs) in three dimensions. The approach relies on discretizing the bulk region using polyhedral elements with any number of faces, which consequently generates a polygonal approximation of the surface. First, we provide a geometric error analysis for bulk-surface polyhedral meshes that remains independent of the specific numerical technique used. Subsequently, we demonstrate that BSVEM achieves optimal second-order spatial convergence, assuming the exact solution belongs to $H^{2+3/4}$ in the bulk and $H^2$ on the surface; the extra $\frac{3}{4}$ regularity requirement arises from the interplay between surface curvature and polyhedral elements near the boundary. Furthermore, we show that utilizing general polyhedra can streamline the computational cost of matrix assembly. Finally, a numerical experiment on the unit sphere is conducted to verify these optimal convergence properties.

\emph{Funnelling} (Fun) is a recently introduced approach for cross-lingual text classification (CLTC) that leverages a two-tier ensemble for heterogeneous transfer learning (HTL). This ensemble utilizes first-tier classifiers, each operating within a distinct, language-specific feature space, to generate calibrated posterior probability vectors for every document. A subsequent metaclassifier then determines the final classification decision based on these vectors, allowing it to leverage class-class correlations—an advantage that Fun holds over CLTC systems unable to utilize such correlations. This paper introduces \emph{Generalized Funnelling} (gFun), an extension of Fun featuring an HTL architecture where first-tier components can be any \emph{view-generating functions}. These functions are language-dependent but produce language-independent representations ("views") of monolingual documents. We detail a specific gFun instance where the metaclassifier inputs a vector of calibrated posterior probabilities (similar to Fun) alongside other embedded representations capturing diverse correlations, including word-class, word-word, and word-context relationships encoded via \emph{Word-Class Embeddings}, \emph{Multilingual Unsupervised or Supervised Embeddings}, and \emph{multilingual BERT}, respectively. Experimental results on two large, standard datasets for multilingual multilabel text classification demonstrate that this gFun instance significantly outperforms both Fun and state-of-the-art baselines. The code implementing gFun is publicly accessible.

Translating between programming languages presents a distinct challenge compared to natural language translation, primarily because programming languages adhere to far stricter structural and grammatical constraints. While prior research has employed tree-to-tree encoder-decoder models to capitalize on the inherent tree structure of code, standard neural decoders typically fail to incorporate the known grammar rules of the target language. This paper introduces a tree decoder designed to leverage grammatical knowledge, ensuring the exclusive generation of syntactically valid programs. Our findings demonstrate that this grammar-aware tree-to-tree model surpasses the current state-of-the-art tree-to-tree approach in translating between two programming languages on a previously established synthetic task.

This study employs three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations to examine the origin of multiple stellar populations (MSPs) in globular clusters (GCs) relative to their host galaxies. Our proposed mechanism posits that the second generation (2G) of stars arises from a combination of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) polluters and unprocessed gas accreted from the parent galaxy. While prior research suggests this "AGB with dilution" framework can resolve issues inherent to the classical AGB model, the specific dynamics of pristine gas accretion onto GCs within a galactic context remain unexplored. We present initial findings from a custom simulation code that tracks the formation of GCs from giant molecular clouds and their subsequent gas accretion. By modeling the genesis of 2G stars over a 370-million-year period, we show that the proportion of 2G stars is tightly coupled to the cluster's environment. Our simulations account for diverse abundance patterns, kinematics, and 2G concentrations by varying the initial conditions of both the GC progenitor and the host galaxy. Significantly, we reproduce a direct correlation between the 2G star fraction and the cluster's initial mass. We analyze the physical consequences of this scenario, compare our results with observations of the Galactic globular cluster 47 Tucanae (47 Tuc), and derive scaling relations applicable to the broader GC population to guide future observational efforts.

Sparse quantum states can be efficiently represented using straightforward classical data structures. We demonstrate the feasibility of employing classical databases to encode quantum states across several practical scenarios and advocate for additional optimizations in quantum simulation aimed at simpler, so-called 'semi-quantum' circuits.

We report lattice-QCD computations of hadronic form factors governing the semileptonic decays $D	o\pi\ell
u$, $D	o K\ell
u$, and $D_s	o K\ell
u$. These calculations employ the highly improved staggered quark (HISQ) action for both valence and sea quarks across $N_f=2+1+1$ MILC ensembles featuring lattice spacings from approximately $0.12$ fm to $0.042$ fm. Ensembles with physical-mass light quarks are present at nearly all lattice spacings. The HISQ formalism treats all quarks uniformly via a relativistic light-quark action, facilitating nonperturbative renormalization through the partial conservation of the vector current. By integrating our findings with experimental differential decay rates, we determine $|V_{cd}|^{D	o\pi}=0.2238(11)^{m Expt}(15)^{m QCD}(04)^{m EW}(02)^{m SIB}[22]^{m QED}$ and $|V_{cs}|^{D	o K}=0.9589(23)^{m Expt}(40)^{m QCD}(15)^{m EW}(05)^{m SIB}[95]^{m QED}$. The derived value for $|V_{cd}|$ represents the current most precise result, marking the first instance where the lattice-QCD uncertainty in a semileptonic extraction matches the experimental uncertainty. Leveraging recent BES III data, we provide the initial determination of $|V_{cd}|^{D_s	o K}=0.258(15)^{m Expt}(01)^{m QCD}[03]^{m QED}$ from the $D_s	o K \ell
u$ channel. Furthermore, our work yields new Standard Model predictions for the lepton flavor universality ratios $R^{D	o\pi}=0.98671(17)^{m QCD}[500]^{m QED}$, $R^{D	o K}=0.97606(16)^{m QCD}[500]^{m QED}$, and $R^{D_s	o K}=0.98099(10)^{m QCD}[500]^{m QED}$, all of which align with experimental measurements within $2\sigma$. Finally, combining our extractions of $|V_{cd}|$ and $|V_{cs}|$ with a value for $|V_{cb}|$ offers the most accurate test of second-row CKM unitarity to date, confirming agreement with unitarity at the one-standard-deviation level.

The rapid advancement of technology has catalyzed the proliferation of Demand-Driven Services (DDS) in urban environments, encompassing ridesharing, on-demand delivery, express logistics, and warehousing. Within DDS, a service loop serves as a fundamental unit, comprising service workers, providers, and their respective targets, where workers are tasked with transporting humans or parcels from providers to destinations. Consequently, planning tasks in DDS are categorized into two distinct phases: Dispatching, which involves creating service loops based on demand and supply distributions, and Routing, which determines the specific sequence of service within established loops. Developing high-quality strategies for both phases is crucial for DDS advancement but presents significant challenges. Concurrently, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has emerged as a potent solution, capable of learning parametric models with minimal problem-specific assumptions and optimizing long-term outcomes through sequential decision-making. This survey defines DDS, outlines its common applications and key decision/control issues, and comprehensively reviews existing DRL approaches for each problem. Furthermore, it introduces open simulation environments for developing and evaluating DDS applications, concluding with an analysis of current challenges and future research opportunities in applying DRL to DDS.

This study evaluates whether integrating a Reed-Solomon (RS) code or a multidimensional parity check (MDPC) code with an auxiliary channel can enhance throughput and extend transmission range in THz systems. Although various coding methods address channel quality and other approaches utilize additional channels for effective system configuration, their combined application represents a novel strategy with the potential to significantly improve data transmission quality. Our proposed solution corrects data bits at the physical layer using a low-complexity erasure code (either MDPC or RS), where original and parity data are transmitted simultaneously over two parallel THz channels: a main channel and an auxiliary channel. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this new approach can boost throughput, enable higher modulation levels, and facilitate longer-distance data transfer in THz communications.

Since the conclusion of 2009, the LHCb experiment has collected data at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), utilizing the Ring-Imaging Cherenkov (RICH) system as a critical detector component. This system enables charged particle identification across a broad momentum spectrum, ranging from 2 to 100 GeV/c. The text details the RICH system's operational and control software, along with its online monitoring capabilities, and presents particle identification performance metrics derived from LHC data. These measurements demonstrate exceptional separation between different hadronic particle types, specifically pions, kaons, and protons.

This study investigates whether language models align their syntactic representations with grammatical rules when handling complex sentences. To answer this, we introduce AlterRep, an intervention-based technique that tests specific linguistic features by generating counterfactual representations. This method modifies the encoding of a particular feature while keeping all other aspects of the original representation unchanged. By observing shifts in word prediction behavior after substituting these counterfactual inputs, we can determine the causal impact of the targeted linguistic feature on the model. We applied AlterRep to examine how BERT models of varying sizes process relative clauses (RCs). Our findings indicate that BERT variants utilize RC boundary information in ways that conform to English grammatical rules. Furthermore, this reliance on boundary information generalizes across diverse RC types, implying that BERT encodes relative clauses as an abstract linguistic category.

This paper introduces a novel spacetime symmetry termed semiconformal curvature collineation and defines its connections to established symmetry properties. Furthermore, we investigate this new symmetry within the context of both non-null and null electromagnetic fields.

The Belle Collaboration has recently refined its analysis of cross sections for the reactions $e^+ e^- \to \Upsilon(nS)\, \pi^+ \pi^-$ (where $n = 1, 2, 3$) within the center-of-mass energy range of 10.52 to 11.02 GeV. This update led to the discovery of a new structure, identified as $Y_b (10750)$, characterized by a mass $M (Y_b) = (10752.7 \pm 5.9^{+0.7}_{-1.1})$~MeV and a Breit-Wigner width $\Gamma (Y_b) = (35.5^{+17.6 +3.9}_{-11.3 -3.3})$~MeV. We characterize $Y_b (10750)$ as a compact $J^{PC} = 1^{--}$ state dominated by a tetraquark component. Due to mixing induced by gluonic exchanges—which become significant in the limit of a large number of quark colors—the mass eigenstate $Y_b (10750)$ is modeled as a superposition of diquark-antidiquark and $b \bar b$ configurations. The mixing angle between $Y_b$ and $\Upsilon(5S)$ is derived from the recently measured electronic width, $\Gamma_{ee} (Y_b) = (13.7 \pm 1.8)$~eV. This mixing offers a viable explanation for the production of $Y_b (10750)$ in high-energy collisions via its $b \bar b$ content, allowing us to calculate the Drell-Yan and prompt production cross sections for $p p \to Y_b (10750) \to \Upsilon (nS)\, \pi^+ \pi^-$ at the LHC. Additionally, we present the resonant portion of the dipion invariant mass spectrum for the decay $Y_b (10750) \to \Upsilon (1S)\, \pi^+ \pi^-$, along with the angular distribution of $\pi^+$ mesons in the dipion rest frame.

Although natural language processing (NLP) algorithms are advancing quickly, they frequently encounter difficulties with out-of-distribution data. A key strategy to bridge this domain gap is domain adaptation, which involves fine-tuning a model trained on a source domain for a new target domain. We introduce a novel framework termed "domain adaptation from scratch," which is essential for expanding NLP applications into sensitive areas while maintaining privacy. In this framework, the goal is to efficiently annotate source domain data so that the resulting model performs effectively on a sensitive target domain where data cannot be annotated. Our research evaluates various methods for this complex scenario, including data selection techniques, domain adaptation algorithms, and active learning strategies, across two NLP tasks: sentiment analysis and Named Entity Recognition. Our findings indicate that employing these approaches helps narrow the domain gap, and integrating them yields even better performance.

This work presents an original, phase-space-based analysis of the Hong-Ou-Mandel experiment. We treat time and frequency as quantum continuous variables, drawing a direct parallel to the position and momentum of massive particles or the quadratures of an electromagnetic field. Our discussion covers how this setup enables the direct measurement of the time-frequency Wigner function and the implementation of logical gates within these variables. Additionally, we examine the quantum and classical facets of the experiment, offering a general formula for intensity correlations that clearly distinguishes between classical Hong-Ou-Mandel dips and their quantum counterparts. Although the manuscript frequently focuses on systems utilizing AlGaAs waveguides to generate photon pairs via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, our findings are applicable to other analogous experimental configurations and various degrees of freedom.

The stellar initial mass function (IMF) is a critical factor in determining stellar masses and tracing galaxy star formation histories. This study specifically targets the most massive galaxies in the local universe, defined as those with $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})>11.2$. We analyzed 41 early-type galaxies (ETGs) from the MASSIVE survey using high-quality Magellan/LDSS-3 long-slit spectroscopy, covering a broad wavelength range of $0.4\mu{\rm m}-1.01\mu{\rm m}$ and achieving high signal-to-noise ratios within an aperture of $R_{\rm e}/8$. Through comprehensive stellar synthesis modeling, we derived the elemental abundances and stellar IMFs for each galaxy. Results indicate that all ETGs in our sample possess IMFs steeper than the Milky Way (Kroupa) IMF. The best-fit IMF mismatch parameter, $\alpha_{\rm IMF}=(M/L)/(M/L)_{\rm MW}$, varies between 1.12 and 3.05, with a mean value of $\langle \alpha_{\rm IMF} \rangle=1.84$, implying that, on average, the IMF is more bottom-heavy than the Salpeter distribution. When comparing stellar masses to dynamical masses, most galaxies exhibit stellar masses lower than their dynamical masses within $1\sigma$ uncertainties. Augmenting our sample with lower-mass galaxies from existing literature, we confirm positive correlations between $\log(\alpha_{\rm IMF})$ and $\log(\sigma)$, $\log(M_{\star})$, and $\log(M_{\rm dyn})$, indicating that the IMF in the centers of more massive ETGs is increasingly bottom-heavy. Furthermore, $\log(\alpha_{\rm IMF})$ shows positive correlations with both [Mg/Fe] and the total metallicity [Z/H]. We present suggestive evidence that the effective stellar surface density $\Sigma_{\rm Kroupa}$ may drive variations in $\alpha_{\rm IMF}$. Ultimately, we conclude that velocity dispersion ($\sigma$), [Mg/Fe], and [Z/H] are the primary factors governing global stellar IMF variations.

As demand for textile goods rises, the industry faces intensifying competition. Because expanding production capacity is often impractical, optimizing current systems offers a more viable solution. This study focuses on a felt manufacturing system within a Turkish textile factory, aiming to reduce production costs by optimizing machine speeds and developing efficient lot sizing plans over a specific planning horizon. To achieve this, we introduce the Lot Sizing and Machine Speed (LSMS) nonlinear model, which dynamically adjusts machine operating speeds based on demand to minimize work-in-process and finished goods inventories while determining optimal processing times and production quantities. Given that the LSMS nonlinear optimization problem is NP-hard, we developed a Two-Phase heuristic that iteratively solves a linear programming model using a commercial solver at each stage. Extensive testing with randomly generated scenarios for demand, planning horizons, and machine-hour capacities demonstrates that our Two-Phase heuristic effectively identifies local-optimal solutions within a reasonable timeframe.

Modern cyber-physical systems, such as robotics, generally consist of physical and software elements whose properties can evolve over time. Design-time assumptions often fail during execution, particularly when systems operate for extended durations spanning decades. Self-adaptation aims to identify system reconfigurations to address these runtime discrepancies, and planners are utilized to execute optimal adaptations within this dynamic setting. Nevertheless, for highly configurable systems, planning becomes computationally infeasible due to the vastness of the adaptation space. To address this, this paper proposes an approach that (a) leverages machine learning to identify Pareto-optimal configurations without exhaustive search and (b) limits the search space to these configurations, thereby rendering planning tractable. We apply this method to robot missions requiring the balancing of task timeliness and energy usage. Independent evaluations demonstrate that our approach yields high-quality adaptation plans even in uncertain and adversarial environments.

Following the initial impact in relativistic heavy ion collisions, a highly occupied, non-thermal gluonic state known as the Glasma is formed. Phenomenological success indicates that this Glasma evolves rapidly into a thermal quark-gluon plasma, with hydrodynamic behavior emerging at extremely early times ($\sim \hat{o}(1)$ fm/c). The mechanism driving this "apparent thermalization" and its role in linking initial conditions to the hydrodynamic onset remains a major theoretical and phenomenological challenge. This work briefly surveys current ideas and recent advancements in understanding how the Glasma approaches a thermalized quark-gluon plasma, with a specific focus on the kinetic theory description of the evolution of this far-from-equilibrium, highly overpopulated, yet weakly-coupled and strongly interacting state.

In Conformal Field Theories (CFTs), the inclusion of irrelevant operators alters the standard Weyl transformation of the metric and activates a metric beta-function, thereby modifying the associated Weyl anomalies. This paper investigates the connection between bulk diffeomorphisms and boundary Weyl transformations in the presence of a massive scalar field that couples to the bulk metric and sources irrelevant operators at the boundary. By accounting for the backreaction induced by this scalar field, we offer a holographic formulation of the boundary metric's beta-function and anomalies. These findings serve as a further validation of the AdS/CFT correspondence.

The shortest path problem is modeled as an $l_1$-regularized regression task, referred to as lasso. This formulation reveals a link between Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and the least angle regression (LARS) method used for lasso. Specifically, the lasso solution path, generated by decreasing the regularization parameter from infinity to zero, aligns with the shortest path trees found in the bi-directional Dijkstra algorithm. While both Dijkstra's algorithm and the LARS approach yield exact solutions, they are often computationally infeasible for very large graphs. To address this limitation, the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is introduced to solve the lasso formulation. The resulting algorithm delivers rapid and effective approximations of the shortest path, trading off exactness which is often unnecessary in many practical scenarios. Numerical experiments are included to demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed method.

Quantum computing offers a promising method for exploiting strong correlations within molecular systems, yet existing hardware currently necessitates hybrid quantum-classical algorithms with limited circuit depths, such as the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). This study highlights the critical role of Hamiltonian symmetry in the adaptive construction of VQE circuits. We observe that standard treatments often neglect symmetry, which degrades the fidelity convergence toward the exact solution and necessitates deeper circuits. Conversely, we demonstrate that symmetry projection serves as a straightforward yet powerful remedy by ensuring the quantum state remains within the correct symmetry subspace, thereby minimizing the total number of gate operations. Furthermore, our illustrative calculations underscore the importance of maintaining symmetry when calculating molecular properties.

We employ a first-passage time framework to analyze the statistical properties of trapping durations caused by the persistent movement of active particles interacting with flat surfaces. Exact calculations are performed for both active Brownian and run-and-tumble particles regarding the angular first-passage time distribution and mean first-passage time, with a subsequent comparison of the outcomes. These theoretical findings align exceptionally well with Langevin simulations. Consequently, our results provide deeper insight into the phenomenon where active particles exhibiting distinct dynamics may appear equivalent in the bulk environment but display divergent behaviors in the vicinity of boundaries or obstacles.

Why do models frequently focus on salient words, and how does this behavior develop during training? We model the training process as a two-stage progression: initially, when attention weights are uniform, the model learns to map individual input words to outputs based on frequent co-occurrence. Subsequently, it learns to attend to specific inputs because it has already established that they translate to the correct outputs. To formalize this, we introduce the property "Knowledge to Translate Individual Words" (KTIW)—the ability to know that input `i` translates to output `o`—and argue that this property drives attention learning. This assertion is supported by the observation that KTIW can be acquired from word co-occurrence statistics before the attention mechanism itself is learned, but not vice versa. Specifically, we demonstrate that if the training distribution makes KTIW difficult to acquire, attention learning fails, preventing the model from even performing the simple task of copying input words to the output. Our approximation clarifies why models attend to salient words and inspires a toy example showing how a multi-head attention model can overcome such difficult training distributions by refining learning dynamics rather than increasing expressiveness. We conclude by addressing the limitations of our approximation framework and proposing future research directions.

This research investigates a quantum switch designed to distribute maximally entangled multipartite states to multiple users. The entanglement switching mechanism involves two phases: initially, each user attempts to establish bipartite entanglement with the switch, followed by the switch executing local operations and measurements to generate multipartite entanglement among a group of users. We analyze a simplified version of this architecture where the switch possesses infinite memory and the connections between users and the switch are uniform. Additionally, we assume that successfully generated quantum states maintain perfect fidelity and that decoherence effects are negligible. This formulation is relevant to various distributed quantum applications, while the technical contributions advance queueing theory. By extensively employing Lyapunov functions, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for system stability and provide closed-form expressions for both the switch capacity and the expected number of qubits retained in memory.

We define the motive of an algebraic stack within the Nisnevich topology. For stacks that are locally quotient stacks in the Nisnevich sense, we provide a description of their motive using simplicial schemes. Additionally, we demonstrate that for quotient stacks, motivic cohomology coincides with the integer-coefficient Chow groups established by Edidin, Graham, and Totaro.

Object detection serves as a critical element in numerous vision-based applications, including advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and sophisticated video surveillance setups (AVSS). While contemporary detectors predominantly rely on deep convolutional neural networks like the YOLO series, their substantial computational demands often prevent real-time processing of high-resolution video streams, particularly under strict energy constraints. This paper introduces a hardware implementation of a recognized pedestrian detector utilizing HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients) for feature extraction and SVM (Support Vector Machine) for classification. Deployed on an AMD Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC, the proposed system achieves real-time performance on 4K Ultra High Definition (3840 x 2160 pixels) video at 60 frames per second, capable of identifying pedestrians at a single scale. These findings validate the efficacy of reprogrammable hardware for the real-time execution of embedded vision solutions.

The FatGHol library, employed in Murri2012 to calculate the rational homology of the moduli space of Riemann surfaces, exemplifies non-numeric scientific computing. It primarily generates graphs—represented as complex Python objects—and computes their isomorphisms via nested Python lists. These operations are executed repeatedly; for instance, specific spaces are triangulated by 4,583,322 and 747,664 graphs, respectively. This scenario presents a significant opportunity to demonstrate the optimization capabilities of various Python runtimes. The study aimed to evaluate the maturity of alternative Python implementations regarding CPython 2.7 compatibility and performance acceleration. This paper presents a comparative analysis of results and experiences obtained by running FatGHol across six distinct environments: CPython 2.7.5, PyPy 2.1, Cython 0.19, Numba 0.11, Nuitka 0.4.4, and Falcon.

Forecasting ocean characteristics using computational intelligence, particularly for predicting Significant Wave Height (SWH), plays a vital role in mitigating social and economic damages in coastal regions. While traditional empirical or numerical models exist, "soft computing" techniques, such as machine and deep learning, have demonstrated significant success recently. This study aims to enhance deep learning capabilities by enabling them to capture both short-term and long-term spatial-temporal dependencies for SWH forecasting. We introduce a Wavelet Graph Neural Network (WGNN) that combines the strengths of wavelet transforms with graph neural networks. The proposed method involves training multiple parallel graph neural networks on wavelet-decomposed data, where the final SWH prediction is derived from reconstructing each model's output. Experimental findings indicate that the WGNN approach surpasses other methods, including numerical models, machine learning algorithms, and various deep learning architectures.

This study examines the extent of agreement between experts and non-experts regarding difficulty levels within a crowdsourcing experiment. We tasked non-experts (Swedish second-language learners) and two distinct groups of experts (teachers of Swedish as a second/foreign language and CEFR specialists) with ranking multi-word expressions. Our findings reveal a very high correlation among the rankings provided by all three groups, indicating that comparative judgments are not significantly influenced by professional expertise in Swedish as a second language.

The type-III see-saw mechanism, which offers a compelling explanation for the tiny masses of neutrinos, also promises rich phenomenological prospects at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Various LHC searches have targeted triplet fermions; however, signals in leptonic final states are hampered by both suppressed branching fractions of Standard Model (SM) bosons and substantial SM backgrounds. Consequently, existing searches lack the sensitivity to probe triplet fermions significantly heavier than 1 TeV. To address this limitation, we conduct a search for triplet fermions in final states characterized by multiple leptons and fat-jets, offering a cleaner environment than conventional LHC searches and enabling kinematic reconstruction of the triplets. Following a systematic and comprehensive analysis across seven distinct final states, we project the necessary luminosities for achieving $3\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ discovery significance as a function of the triplet fermion mass. Our results indicate that triplet fermions with masses up to 1265 (1380) and 1480 (1600) GeV could be discovered with $5\sigma$ ($3\sigma$) significance at integrated luminosities of 500 and 3000 fb$^{-1}$, respectively.

Over the past few years, ALMA has successfully identified large-scale substructures within protoplanetary disks. By comparing these observations with planet-disk interaction models, researchers have determined that most features can be attributed to Neptune-mass or more massive planets located between 5 and 100 astronomical units from the star. However, higher resolution is required to examine regions closer to the star where terrestrial planets likely form, as well as to detect gaps carved out by planets less massive than Neptune. This study evaluates the potential of extending ALMA to double its maximum baseline length, aiming to resolve and detect substructures caused by Super Earths and Earth-mass planets at distances of 1 to 5 au.
