Through simulations of disk models using this enhanced ALMA setup in Bands 6 and 7, we demonstrate that an upgraded array could identify gaps created by Super Earths as close as 1 au and detect Earth-mass planets between 2 and 3 au from young stars in nearby star-forming regions.

Creating extensive, fully annotated training datasets is expensive, particularly for medical image segmentation tasks. While scribbles—a less rigorous annotation type—are easier to acquire in practice, training segmentation models using only limited scribble supervision remains difficult. To overcome these challenges, we introduce CycleMix, a novel framework for medical image segmentation based on scribble learning. This framework integrates mix augmentation and cycle consistency. For supervision augmentation, CycleMix employs the mixup strategy combined with a specialized random occlusion design to incrementally and decrementally adjust scribbles. For supervision regularization, it strengthens the training objective using consistency losses that penalize inconsistent segmentations, leading to significant performance gains. Experiments on two public datasets, ACDC and MSCMRseg, demonstrate that CycleMix achieves remarkable results, matching or surpassing the accuracy of fully supervised methods. The code and expert-generated scribble annotations for MSCMRseg are available at https://github.com/BWGZK/CycleMix.

Over the past few years, event cameras (also known as Dynamic Vision Sensors or DVS) have emerged as viable alternatives or supplements to conventional cameras within vision systems. These sensors are distinguished by their high dynamic range, exceptional temporal resolution, minimal latency, and robust performance under low-light conditions—attributes that are critical for advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and autonomous vehicles. This study investigates the feasibility of applying these emerging sensors to the widely recognized task of traffic sign detection. We evaluate various event data representations, including event frames, event frequency, and exponentially decaying time surfaces, utilizing the FireNet deep neural network for video frame reconstruction. Detection is performed using the YOLOv4 deep convolutional neural network. Depending on the specific representation, we achieved detection accuracies ranging from 86.9% to 88.9% mAP@0.5. By fusing these representations, we developed a detector with an improved accuracy of 89.9% mAP@0.5, compared to the 72.67% mAP@0.5 achieved using only FireNet-reconstructed frames. These findings highlight the potential of event cameras for automotive use, whether operating independently or in conjunction with standard frame-based cameras.

In decentralized cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents pool information to derive policies that optimize a team-average objective. Although agents are willing to collaborate, they often avoid directly sharing local states, rewards, and value functions due to privacy concerns. This paper presents a decentralized actor-critic algorithm utilizing TD error aggregation that safeguards privacy and operates under assumptions of time-varying communication delays and packet loss. The trade-off for these relaxed assumptions is a higher communication load per agent, quantified by the dimension of transmitted data. Notably, this burden scales quadratically with network size, making the method viable for large-scale systems. Furthermore, we offer a convergence analysis using diminishing step sizes to demonstrate that the agents successfully maximize the team-average objective.

Named Entity Disambiguation (NED) is a pivotal operation for applications processing natural language text. Consider a graph-based knowledge base (hereafter, Knowledge Graph) where nodes signify diverse real-world entities, including individuals, locations, organizations, and concepts. When utilizing data sources like social media streams and web pages, the task of Entity Linking involves connecting extracted named entities to their corresponding entries within the Knowledge Graph. This challenge is inherently complex due to several factors: most data sources lack a formal ontology, the input is unstructured, context is often limited, and ambiguity arises when multiple entities share the same name. This report examines two state-of-the-art systems utilizing distinct methodologies: graph-based Accurate Online Disambiguation of Entities (AIDA) and Mined Evidence Named Entity Disambiguation (MENED), which relies on statistical inference. Both approaches are evaluated using the dataset and queries from the Knowledge Base Population (KBP) track at the 2011 NIST Text Analytics Conference (TAC). The report starts with an overview of these respective methods, proceeds to a detailed description of the experimental configuration, and concludes with findings derived from the benchmarking exercise.

We offer a pedagogical overview of the generalized uncertainty principle (GUP), demonstrating its natural emergence when gravitational effects are incorporated into measurement processes. After reviewing key physical predictions, we concentrate on experimental constraints on the deformation parameter $\beta$ and the hypothesis of black hole remnants as a potential dark matter candidate. Additionally, we briefly mention a theoretically computed value for $\beta$ and note the extensive unexplored parameter space awaiting investigation by future experiments.

This study introduces multi-stage linear decision rules (LDRs) for dynamic planning of power generation and energy storage under uncertainty, coupled with chance-constrained optimization that offers performance guarantees. First, these optimized LDRs ensure that the resulting investment plans remain feasible regarding operational and carbon policies, even when the distribution of planning uncertainty is ambiguous. Second, the LDRs incorporate the system planner's tolerance for the stochastic variance of investment outcomes, ultimately generating a quasi-deterministic plan that is both insensitive to uncertainty like deterministic planning and robust to its realizations like stochastic planning. Finally, we certify the performance of these LDRs by bounding the sub-optimality inherent to their linear functional form; using this bound, we guarantee that the preference for LDRs over less restrictive but poorly scalable scenario-based optimization will not result in financial losses exceeding said bound. A testbed of the U.S. Southeast power system is utilized to expose the trade-offs between cost, stochasticity, and feasibility in LDR-based investments. Furthermore, we conclude that LDR sub-optimality is contingent upon the level of uncertainty and the strictness of chance constraints applied to operational, investment, and policy variables.

A central unresolved issue in the study of relativistic jets concerns their microscopic interaction with the surrounding environment. This work investigates the early evolution of both electron-proton ($e^{-}-p^{+}$) and electron-positron ($e^{\pm}$) relativistic jets that possess helical magnetic fields, specifically analyzing their engagement with ambient plasma. We conducted simulations of "global" jets featuring these helical fields to assess their impact on kinetic instabilities, including the Weibel instability, the kinetic Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (kKHI), and the Mushroom instability (MI). In these initial simulations, the aforementioned kinetic instabilities are suppressed, allowing new instability types to develop. In the $e^{-}-p^{+}$ jet model, a recollimation-like instability arises, causing significant perturbation to the jet electrons. Conversely, the $e^{\pm}$ jet model exhibits a recollimation-like instability at early stages followed by a kinetic instability, resulting in a structure comparable to simulations lacking helical magnetic fields. To comprehensively trace the evolution of global jets with helical magnetic fields, future research must employ simulations with substantially larger system scales.

This work outlines recent findings regarding the model companions of set theory, situating them within contemporary philosophical discussions on mathematics. We begin by examining how model companionship relies on the chosen signature, followed by a detailed analysis of this relationship specifically within set theory. We contend that the most natural model companions of set theory, as the signature for axiomatizing set theory changes, correspond to theories of $H_{\kappa^+}$ where $\kappa$ iterates through all infinite cardinals. Furthermore, we identify $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$ as the sole resolution to the Continuum problem capable of (and indeed belonging to) a model companion of set theory when augmented with large cardinal axioms. Lastly, we elucidate and defend this model-theoretic perspective on set-theoretic validities by invoking a notion of maximality rooted in Hilbert's axiom of completeness.

We examine $\rho$ vector meson production in $ep$ collisions at HERA featuring leading neutrons using the dipole formalism. Within a mixed-space framework, the dipole-pion interaction is modeled via the Marquet-Peschanski-Soyez saturation model, which relies on traveling wave solutions of the nonlinear Balitsky-Kovchegov equation. We quantify the absorption effects and contrast our findings with an earlier full coordinate space analysis of this process. Unlike that prior approach, our study yields absorption $K$ factors that align with previous theoretical predictions for semi-inclusive processes.

Land cover classification (LCC) and the tracking of land use changes are vital for mitigating and adapting to climate change. Current machine learning methods for LCC, which utilize Earth observation data, depend on fully annotated and segmented datasets; however, the significant effort required to create these datasets has become a bottleneck for scaling LCC applications. This study introduces Scene-to-Patch models, an alternative LCC framework based on Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) that operates using only high-level scene labels. This approach accelerates dataset development while still delivering patch-level segmentation, thereby enhancing the accessibility of LCC across various scenarios. Evaluated on the DeepGlobe-LCC dataset, our method surpasses non-MIL baselines in both scene- and patch-level predictions. Consequently, this work lays the groundwork for broadening LCC applications within climate change mitigation strategies for technology, government, and academic sectors.

This paper investigates the learning dynamics arising from strategic agents repeatedly engaging in a game featuring an unknown payoff-relevant parameter. Within this framework, players continuously update their beliefs about the parameter using Bayes's rule, based on observed strategies and realized payoffs. Simultaneously, players refine their strategies by calculating best responses to their current beliefs. We demonstrate that, with probability one, both beliefs and strategies converge to a fixed point where the belief accurately reflects the payoff distribution for the prevailing strategy, and the strategy constitutes an equilibrium relative to that belief. However, we note that the unknown parameter is not always successfully identified, as the belief estimate depends on game outcomes endogenously produced by the players' strategic choices. Furthermore, we establish sufficient and necessary conditions ensuring that learning converges to a globally stable fixed point representing a complete information Nash equilibrium. Additionally, we outline sufficient conditions guaranteeing the local stability of fixed points for both beliefs and strategies.

This study experimentally examines how miscibility and liquid wettability affect droplet impacts on thin wall films. Even when liquid properties and impact conditions are comparable, variations in the splashing threshold, crown expansion, and the length of the ascending phase are observed. These discrepancies stem from the interfacial tension within the droplet/wall-film liquid pairs, a factor governed by their miscibility and wettability. Specifically, calculations of crown surface energy reveal that the energy stored in the interface between the droplet and the wall-film is substantial; this stored energy results in reduced crown extensions and necessitates greater kinetic energy to trigger splashing. Furthermore, by defining a modified capillary time that incorporates all relevant surface and interfacial tensions, we demonstrate that interfacial tension functions as a significant recoiling force, thereby shortening the ascending phase duration. The dynamics of this ascending phase are accurately modeled across various wall-film thicknesses when accounting for changes in the mass of moving liquids. Collectively, droplet/wall-film interactions can be characterized as inertio-capillary systems where the interfacial tension between the droplet and wall film critically influences energy storage and crown kinetics throughout the impact. Additionally, this analysis underscores that viscous losses exert a major impact during the crown extension phase, dissipating nearly half of the initial energy for impacts on thin wall films, and likely affecting the capillary time scale through damping effects.

Search-based test generation relies on feedback from one or more fitness functions, which act as scoring mechanisms to evaluate solution quality. Selecting informative fitness functions is vital for achieving a tester's objectives. However, several critical goals—such as inducing exceptions in the target class, enhancing test suite diversity, and achieving Strong Mutation Coverage—lack effective fitness function formulations. We hypothesize that addressing these challenges requires treating the identification of fitness functions as a secondary optimization step. Specifically, we propose an adaptive algorithm capable of varying fitness function selection throughout the generation process to maximize goal attainment based on the current test suite population. To validate this hypothesis, we implemented two reinforcement learning algorithms within the EvoSuite framework, using them to dynamically configure fitness functions for the three aforementioned goals. Our evaluation, conducted on a set of Java case studies using the resulting EvoSuiteFIT framework, demonstrates significant improvements for two of the three goals and limited gains for the third when the number of evolutionary generations is constrained. Furthermore, EvoSuiteFIT identified faults that other techniques missed. The capacity to adaptively select fitness functions enables strategic choices that yield more effective test suites efficiently; analyzing these choices provides insights into achieving specific testing objectives. Consequently, we conclude that adaptive fitness function selection is a potent technique for pursuing testing goals when no single effective fitness function currently exists.

This study investigates a specific class of non-AdS holography, where the three-dimensional bulk gravity is described by Generalized Minimal Massive Gravity (GMMG). We focus on the spacelike warped $AdS_3$ ($WAdS_3$) black hole solution within this framework, which corresponds to a two-dimensional warped conformal field theory (WFCT) on the dual boundary. The compatibility between the bulk isometry charge algebra and the boundary vacuum symmetry charge algebra serves as evidence for the proposed duality. Additional support comes from the equality of entanglement entropy and modular Hamiltonians across both sides. Specifically, we analyze the modular Hamiltonian for a single boundary interval linked to vacuum modular flow generators and compute the gravitational charge associated with asymptotic Killing vectors that satisfy the metric boundary conditions. Assuming the validity of the entanglement entropy first law, we establish matching conditions between the dual variables, demonstrating that variations in the modular Hamiltonian correspond to variations in the gravitational charge on both sides. Consequently, our results reinforce the conclusion that the dual theory of the $WAdS_3$ black hole solution in GMMG is indeed a Warped Conformal Field Theory.

This note presents the construction of two minimal surfaces of general type characterized by a geometric genus of 3, an irregularity of 0, and a self-intersection number of the canonical divisor K² equal to either 20 or 24. In both cases, the canonical map has a degree of 20. Notably, for one of these surfaces, the canonical linear system includes a non-trivial fixed component. To the best of our knowledge, these represent the inaugural examples of minimal surfaces of general type possessing a canonical map of degree 20.

Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) serve as highly efficient instruments for detecting individual photons, with applications spanning quantum optics research, optical quantum computing, and quantum communication. Following the detection of a photon, the device enters a dead time during which it cannot register subsequent events; its sensitivity is then gradually restored. We have incorporated this characteristic into photodetection theory by deriving a specific photocounting formula. Under continuous-wave detection conditions, the photocounting statistics exhibit nonlinear dependence on the density operator, a phenomenon driven by the memory effect of prior measurement intervals. The provided examples illustrate the significant impact of both the relaxation process and the memory effect on the final photocounting statistics of SNSPDs.

This study introduces a hybrid stochastic individual-based model for proliferating cells exhibiting chemotaxis, formulated as a branching diffusion process linked to a partial differential equation governing the concentration of a chemotactic factor. It is demonstrated that as the cell population approaches infinity in the hydrodynamic limit, the model converges to the solution of a nonconservative Patlak-Keller-Segel-type system. Furthermore, a nonlinear mean-field stochastic model is defined, and it is proven that the trajectory of descendants from a single cell in the individual model converges to this mean-field process.

Lepton number and flavor violations represent crucial components of lepton physics, closely linked to neutrinoless double beta decay and muonium-to-antimuonium transitions. While the former offers profound insights into fundamental physics and is the subject of numerous experimental efforts, the latter remains a compelling phenomenon with upcoming high-intensity muon beamline experiments poised to refine its experimental limits. In models featuring a doubly charged scalar, both processes can occur alongside the radiative generation of active neutrino masses, with charged lepton flavor-violating decays serving as constraints on the model's flavor parameters. This study investigates conditions under which the muonium-to-antimuonium transition rate reaches current experimental bounds, emphasizing that future tighter limits will be vital for distinguishing models that induce neutrinoless double beta decay via doubly charged scalars. Additionally, we explore a potential extension of this framework to the left-right model, which also facilitates neutrinoless double beta decay.

This study extends Enskog theory to model the self-diffusion coefficient of patchy colloidal fluids within disordered porous media. The theoretical framework incorporates contact values for both fluid-fluid and fluid-matrix pair distribution functions, adjusted to account for the dependence on probe particle porosity ($\phi$). This adjustment is essential for accurately capturing the trapping effects exerted by the matrix on fluid particles. The proposed expressions for these modified contact values consist of three distinct components: a hard sphere contribution derived in previous work [Holovko M. F., Korvatska M. Ya., Condens. Matter Phys., 2020, 23, 23605]; a depletion term arising from cluster-cluster and cluster-matrix repulsions; and an intramolecular correlation term within the clusters. The analysis reveals that the intramolecular correlation term causes a significant reduction in the self-diffusion coefficient at low fluid densities, an effect that diminishes as matrix porosity decreases. At intermediate densities, the depletion contribution results in an elevated self-diffusion coefficient compared to a hard sphere fluid. Conversely, at sufficiently high densities, the hard sphere effect dominates, causing a sharp decline in the self-diffusion coefficient. Furthermore, the study provides a detailed investigation and discussion regarding the impacts of cluster size, cluster type, and porous media parameters.

Recent studies indicate that appropriately deploying self-supervision can significantly boost supervised learning performance. However, the potential of self-supervision remains underutilized because existing pretext tasks are optimized for unsupervised representation learning rather than supervised goals. To address this, we first outline three key properties that auxiliary tasks should possess to effectively support the supervised objective: they must encourage the model to learn rich features, the transformations applied should minimally disturb the training distribution, and the tasks should be lightweight and generic to ensure broad applicability to prior methods. Following this, we demonstrate how existing pretext tasks can be adapted to meet these criteria for supervised learning by introducing a simple auxiliary task called Localizable Rotation (LoRot). Comprehensive experiments confirm that LoRot enhances robustness and generalization when tailored for supervised learning. The code is accessible at https://github.com/wjun0830/Localizable-Rotation.

This study investigates the quenching properties of 328 isolated dwarf galaxies ($10^{8} < M_{\rm star}/M_\odot < 10^{10}$) within the \Rom{} cosmological hydrodynamic simulation. By employing mock observation techniques, we identified these quenched isolated dwarfs and directly compared their quenched fraction to that of the NASA Sloan Atlas (NSA). Consistent with other simulations, we discovered a population of quenched, isolated dwarfs below $M_{\rm star} < 10^{9} M_\odot$ that remains undetected in the NSA. Our findings indicate that massive black holes (MBHs) in \Rom{} are primarily responsible for the existence of these quenched isolated dwarfs, whereas isolated dwarfs lacking an MBH align with quiescent fractions seen in the field. Quenching takes place between $z=0.5$ and $z=1$, driven by MBH feedback which heats or removes star-forming gas. Mergers or interactions appear to play negligible roles in initiating this MBH feedback. For low stellar masses ($M_{\rm star} \lesssim 10^{9.3} M_\odot$), quenching evolves over several Gyr as the MBH gradually heats central gas. Conversely, at higher stellar masses ($M_{\rm star} \gtrsim 10^{9.3} M_\odot$), quenching happens rapidly within 1 Gyr, with the MBH evacuating gas from the central few kpc and pushing it toward the halo outskirts. These results suggest that MBH feedback can substantially suppress star formation in field dwarf galaxies. However, the apparent over-quenching of dwarfs due to MBH activity implies a need for higher resolution and/or improved modeling of MBHs in dwarf systems, with quenched fractions serving as a means to constrain current models.
We investigate the boundedness properties from $L^p(\mathbb{H}^n)$ to $L^q(\mathbb{H}^n)$ for specific convolution operators featuring singular measures on the Heisenberg group.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) from the early Universe represent a promising candidate for dark matter. The initial detection of black hole-neutron star (BH-NS) gravitational wave events by the LIGO/Virgo collaboration, specifically GW200105 and GW200115, initially sparked speculation regarding non-astrophysical origins. This study presents the first analysis of total volumetric merger rates for PBH-NS binaries formed through two-body gravitational scattering, revealing that these rates are lower than those of astrophysical BH-NS systems. Unlike binary black holes, where a substantial portion may be primordial—whether formed in dark matter halos or the early Universe—PBH-NS merger rates cannot be significantly boosted by processes preceding star formation. Consequently, our results indicate that the observed BH-NS events are of astrophysical origin, even if primordial PBH-PBH mergers contribute notably to gravitational wave observations.

Noise and uncertainty are typically detrimental to machine learning, as noise in training data often results in inaccurate and uncertain predictions. Conversely, we propose a machine learning architecture that leverages noise itself to extract critical information and enhance prediction quality. This approach computes uncertainty within one target variable to forecast a second variable. We demonstrate this formalism using PbZr$_{0.7}$Sn$_{0.3}$O$_{3}$ crystals, where uncertainty in the dielectric constant allows for the extrapolation of heat capacity, successfully predicting a phase transition that standard methods miss. In a second application involving single-particle diffraction of droplets, we combine particle counts with their associated uncertainties to estimate the ground truth diffraction amplitude, achieving superior results compared to using counts alone. This general framework facilitates the strategic use of uncertainty in machine learning, offering extensive applicability across physical sciences and other fields.

This paper investigates an excitable biophysical system capable of propagating nerve impulse waves. We examine a slow-fast FitzHugh-Rinzel neuron model in which only membrane voltage undergoes diffusive interaction, leading to the creation of spatiotemporal patterns. Our analysis concentrates on local nonlinear excitations and varied neural responses within one- and two-dimensional configurations of diffusively coupled FitzHugh-Rinzel neurons. Understanding these emerging spatiotemporal patterns is crucial for elucidating the operational mechanisms across different brain regions. We analytically determine the coefficients of amplitude equations near Hopf bifurcations and characterize multiple patterns, such as spirals with intricate geometric substructures. Additionally, we analytically establish the conditions for antispiral development near the bifurcation point. Broken target waves are observed to form spiral-like profiles, while the spatial dynamics of the excitable system display two- and multi-arm spirals under small diffusive couplings. Our findings uncover a wide range of neural excitabilities and the specific conditions facilitating spiral-wave formation. Finally, we demonstrate that coupled excitable systems with distinct firing characteristics engage in collective behaviors that may significantly contribute to irregular neural dynamics.

We introduce rotation periods for late K- and early M-dwarfs within the 4 Gyr old open cluster M67 to serve as gyrochronology calibrators and to test stellar spin-down models. Leveraging Gaia EDR3 astrometry for membership determination and Pan-STARRS (PS1) photometry to identify binaries, we compiled these rotation periods using observations from the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope's MegaPrime wide field imager. From our identified 1807 M67 members, 294 are candidate single stars with significant rotation period detections. We fitted a polynomial to the observed relationship between rotation period and effective temperature derived from color. Our findings indicate that the rotation of very cool dwarfs aligns with a simple solid-body spin-down model between 2.7 and 4 Gyr. When comparing our rotational sequence to gyrochronological predictions, the best fit is a Skumanich-like spin-down ($P_{rot} \propto t^{0.62}$) applied to the Ruprecht 147 sequence. This implies that for K7-M0 spectral types with near-solar metallicity, once spinning down resumes, a simple Skumanich-like evolution suffices to describe their rotation through M67's age. Furthermore, for stars ranging from M1 to M3, our data suggest that spin-down must have resumed before M67's age, contradicting the latest spin-down model predictions.

Network architectures and learning mechanisms are fundamental to creating complex functions within artificial neural networks (ANNs) and spiking neural networks (SNNs). SNNs represent a next-generation approach by integrating more biological characteristics than ANNs, such as dynamic spiking neurons, specialized functional architectures, and efficient learning strategies. This paper introduces a Motif-topology and Reward-learning enhanced SNN (MR-SNN) designed for efficient multi-sensory integration. The MR-SNN utilizes 13 distinct 3-node motif topologies, initially derived from independent single-sensory learning tasks and subsequently combined for multi-sensory classification. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed MR-SNN achieves superior accuracy and robustness compared to conventional SNNs lacking motif integration. Additionally, the introduced reward learning framework is biologically plausible and effectively elucidates the cognitive McGurk effect arising from conflicting visual and auditory inputs.

We introduce a unification framework for clumpy obscurers in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and examine the characteristics of the resulting X-ray spectra. Designed to match the observed column density distribution of AGNs and cloud eclipse events regarding their angular scales and occurrence rates, we have created and released XARS, a generalized Monte Carlo X-ray radiative transfer code for modeling such spectra. The specific geometry induces strong Compton scattering, allowing soft photons to escape even along Compton-thick sight lines, rendering our model spectra highly comparable to the Brightman & Nandra TORUS model. Nevertheless, achieving accurate fits to NuSTAR data requires adding an extra Compton-thick reflector near the corona. This component can be interpreted as a dust-free portion of the broad-line region, an inner rim, or a warped disk, but it cannot be a simple disk since it must simultaneously obscure the corona and reflect its radiation. We provide our model as an Xspec table and include corresponding CLUMPY infrared spectra, facilitating self-consistent multi-wavelength investigations.

The quantum kicked rotor is famously recognized for its dynamical (Anderson) localization. Recent findings indicate that a periodically kicked Tonks gas invariably localizes and settles into a finite energy steady-state, which behaves thermally with an effective temperature determined by the kick parameters. In this study, we investigate a generalization involving quasi-periodic driving with three frequencies—a setup that, in the absence of interactions, exhibits a metal-insulator Anderson transition. We demonstrate that a quasi-periodically kicked Tonks gas undergoes a dynamical many-body delocalization transition as the kick strength increases. While the localized phase remains characterized by a low effective temperature, the delocalized phase represents an infinite-temperature state where temperature rises linearly over time. Notably, at the critical point, the momentum distribution of the Tonks gas shows distinct scaling behaviors at small and large momenta, differing from the non-interacting scenario and indicating a failure of the one-parameter scaling theory of localization.

In \cite{MMP84}, curves were built through the gaps of cantori for exact area-preserving twist maps, with a conjecture that they minimize flux among those passing through the cantorus points. However, \cite{Pol} noted that if a rotational invariant circle with a different rotation number exists, these curves fail to minimize flux; conversely, if the cantorus is hyperbolic, the curves possess locally minimal flux even without the constraint of traversing the cantorus points. Building on \cite{M94}'s criterion for locally minimal flux surfaces in 3D volume-preserving flows, this paper revisits the finding and demonstrates that, generally, analogous curves through rotationally-ordered periodic orbits or their heteroclinic connections do not exhibit locally minimal flux. The discussion also raises several questions and summarizes findings for systems with higher degrees of freedom.

We propose a correspondence between interacting agegraphic dark energy models and the quintessence scalar field within a non-flat universe. We show that the agegraphic evolution of the universe can be entirely described by a single quintessence scalar field. Subsequently, we reconstruct the potential for the interacting agegraphic quintessence dark energy and the dynamics of the scalar field based on the evolution of the agegraphic dark energy.

This study introduces the first generic min-max bilevel multi-objective optimization framework, with specific applications in hyperparameter tuning and representation learning. Addressing scenarios in meta-learning, multi-task learning, and representation learning where tasks share a subset of parameters alongside unique ones, we leverage recent nonconvex min-max optimization advancements to develop the MORBiT algorithm. This gradient descent-ascent approach identifies robust shared parameters across all tasks and mitigates distributional shifts between training and testing phases. Theoretical analysis confirms that MORBiT converges to a first-order stationary point at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}K^{-2/5})$ for certain nonconvex problems, where $K$ represents total iterations and $n$ the number of tasks. In summary, we define a min-max bilevel multi-objective optimization problem, present a single-loop two-timescale algorithm with proven convergence rates, and establish theoretical bounds on the optimizer's generalization capabilities. Empirical evaluations on sinusoid regression and representation learning demonstrate that MORBiT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, corroborating our findings on convergence and generalization.

**Context:** Although star formation has been extensively studied on both large molecular cloud scales and small core or disk scales over recent decades, the link between extensive interstellar material and the densest small-scale cores remains largely unexplored.

**Methods:** Utilizing the NOEMA and IRAM 30\,m telescopes, we conducted extensive mapping (covering 640\,arcmin$^2$) of the prototypical star-forming complex Cygnus X at 3.6\,mm wavelengths, observing both line and continuum emissions.

**Results:** We outline the scope of the Cygnus Allscale Survey of Chemistry and Dynamical Environments (CASCADE). Focusing on the first observed subregion, DR20 within Cygnus X, our study encompasses sources ranging from cold, pristine gas clumps to evolved ultracompact H{\sc ii} regions. Data spanning cloud-to-core scales with a linear resolution of $<5000$\,au reveal multiple kinematic cloud components, likely representing large-scale flows feeding central cores. We analyzed the temperature structure using the HCN/HNC intensity ratio and compared it against dust-derived temperatures. Our findings indicate that deuterated DCO$^+$ emission is almost exclusively found in regions with temperatures below 20\,K. Furthermore, by examining the slopes of spatial power spectra for dense gas tracers (HCO$^+$, H$^{13}$CO$^+$, and N$_2$H$^+$), we identified comparatively flat slopes ranging from $-2.9$ to $-2.6$, which aligns with high Mach numbers and/or active star formation within DR20.
This paper establishes compactness and existence results for a Branson-Paneitz type problem defined on a bounded domain in R^n subject to Navier boundary conditions.

Recent interest in quantum scattering amplitudes for massive particles has been driven by their relevance to classical calculations in gravitational-wave physics. These amplitude techniques are now utilized for high-precision computations of observables describing the gravitational dynamics of bound massive systems, such as black holes, with a specific focus on incorporating spin effects essential for modeling rotating (Kerr) black holes. While three-point higher-spin amplitudes proposed by Arkani-Hamed, Huang, and Huang are well-established in the effective description of Kerr black-hole physics, the corresponding Compton higher-spin amplitudes remain an unsolved challenge. In this work, we leverage findings from the higher-spin literature to demonstrate that physical principles can uniquely determine Compton amplitudes up to spin 5/2 by enforcing a constraint on a three-point higher-spin current, which is a prerequisite for an underlying unitary theory. We provide the unique effective Lagrangians up to spin 5/2 and verify that they reproduce previously known amplitudes. Furthermore, we predict that no additional corrections are expected for multi-graviton amplitudes analogous to the Compton case, rendering them uniquely determined. To facilitate this analysis, we introduce a modified massive spinor-helicity formalism, which streamlines the derivation of higher-spin states, propagators, and compact amplitude expressions.

Although Covid-19 vaccines are widely accessible in the United States, vaccination rates have fallen significantly short of 100%. Furthermore, CDC data indicates that even in areas with initially high vaccine acceptance, this willingness did not consistently translate into sustained high vaccination rates over time. We constructed a model to explain such shifts, utilizing parameters consistent with data from Alabama. Simulations of this model suggest that local interactions alone would have reinforced an initial consensus favoring vaccine acceptance; however, this outcome did not occur in reality. Consequently, we incorporated the influence of mega-influencers, including mass media and state officials, into our model. Our results demonstrate that a single vaccine-hesitant mega-influencer with broad reach can drastically shift the population consensus from acceptance to hesitancy. Remarkably, this effect persists even when the influencer only reaches those already somewhat inclined to agree, and under the conservative assumption that the population weights the influencer no more heavily than a single friend or neighbor. Additionally, while a competing mega-influencer with an opposing view can reverse the average population opinion, it fails to restore the tightness of the consensus around that new view. Our code and data are available in the ODyN (Opinion Dynamic Networks) library at https://github.com/annahaensch/ODyN.

Long Range (LoRa) stands as a leading and widely adopted Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) physical layer technique for Low-Power Wide-Area Networks (LPWANs). By varying spreading factors, LoRa achieves diverse spectral and energy efficiencies, catering to a broad spectrum of Internet-of-Things (IoT) applications; however, its low bit rate remains a significant constraint. Until recently, minimal research focused on enhancing LoRa's achievable data rate, but several CSS-based PHY layer alternatives have since been introduced. This survey uniquely offers the first comprehensive analysis of waveform designs for CSS-based LoRa alternatives proposed between 2019 and 2022, evaluating fifteen such schemes. Unlike other surveys that primarily address LoRa networking, deployment in massive IoT environments, or architectural aspects, this work specifically elucidates the waveform designs of these alternatives. The studied CSS schemes are categorized into single chirp, multiple chirp, and index modulation based on their multiplexing patterns. The research examines the complete transceiver architectures and assesses performance regarding energy efficiency (EE), spectral efficiency (SE), and Bit-Error Rate (BER) in additive white Gaussian noise, as well as BER under phase and frequency offsets. Results indicate that EE, SE, and robustness against offsets are fundamentally tied to the transmit symbol frame structure. To foster reproducible research, public versions of the MATLAB codes for the analyzed CSS schemes will be made available.

Natural language understanding has seen exponential growth in recent years, yielding impressive results across various tasks. This progress has spurred researchers to investigate the knowledge encoded within these models; however, efforts to decipher their semantic capabilities have often yielded inconclusive or contradictory findings. Using a probing classifier grounded in WordNet-based concept relatedness, we extracted the underlying knowledge graphs of nine influential language models, including word embeddings, text generators, and context encoders. Our results indicate that while all models encode this knowledge, they suffer from notable inaccuracies. Additionally, we demonstrate that different architectures and training strategies result in distinct model biases. Through a systematic evaluation, we identified specific factors explaining why certain concepts pose challenges. We hope these insights will inspire the development of models that capture concepts with greater precision.

Over the last decade, Capsule Networks have achieved remarkable progress, surpassing conventional CNNs in numerous tasks thanks to their equivariant characteristics. By employing vector inputs and outputs that encode both magnitude and directional information, these networks hold immense potential for unsupervised visual representation, such as multi-class image classification. This paper introduces the Contrastive Capsule (CoCa) Model, a Siamese-style Capsule Network that leverages contrastive loss alongside a novel architecture, training, and testing framework. Evaluated on the unsupervised CIFAR-10 dataset, the model attains a top-1 accuracy of 70.50% and a top-5 accuracy of 98.10%. Thanks to its efficient design, CoCa requires 31 times fewer parameters and 71 times fewer FLOPs than current state-of-the-art models in both supervised and unsupervised settings.

Although deep neural networks (DNNs) are now standard for numerous machine learning applications, their internal decision logic and interpretability remain obscure. In contrast, conventional decision trees are both theoretically robust and easily interpretable. This work demonstrates that by converting discrete node activation values into binary representations, one can extract decision trees that elucidate the classification mechanism of every layer within a ReLU-activated multilayer perceptron (MLP). These extracted trees are subsequently integrated with established feature attribution methods to generate layer-specific interpretations of the model. Finally, the study analyzes the resulting interpretations, examines the behavior of the binary encodings, and explores their relationship to the sample groupings formed during neural network training.

Emotions, such as fear, anger, sadness, and happiness, serve as foundational elements of human behavior and significantly influence mental well-being. Subtle variations in emotional states can be analyzed through disturbances in speech or conversation, where examining acoustical features of a speech signal reveals critical indicators of an individual's mental health. Consequently, this domain has become a vital area of research within Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). Previous research demonstrated that contrasting Hurst-Exponent values, derived from the non-stationary and nonlinear characteristics of "angry" and "sad" English speech from the Toronto Emotional Speech Set (TESS), facilitate the early detection and diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease. Building on this, the current study extends the analysis by calculating Hurst-Exponents for similar emotional speech recorded in German. Results indicate that the Hurst-Exponent effectively distinguishes between "anger" and "sadness" in German speech, mirroring its performance with English. This suggests that the Hurst-Exponent can differentiate speech based on emotional state in a language-independent manner. We propose an algorithm for a language-independent application capable of the early, non-invasive detection of various severe neurocognitive disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease, Motor Neuron Disease (MND), Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), depression, and suicidal tendencies, capabilities that exceed the current limits of state-of-the-art medical science.

This paper introduces an implicit-explicit finite volume method for solving the Euler equations. The approach begins with non-dimensionalized Euler equations, decomposing the pressure into slow and fast acoustic components. A Suliciu-type relaxation model is employed, divided into an explicit component resolved via a Godunov-type scheme utilizing an approximate Riemann solver, and an implicit component that solves an elliptic equation for the fast pressure. Relaxation source terms are handled by projecting the solution onto the equilibrium manifold. The resulting scheme preserves positivity for density and internal energy and is asymptotic preserving, converging to the incompressible Euler equations. Furthermore, a second-order extension of this first-order method is presented, which retains the positivity property. Numerical experiments in both 1D and 2D demonstrate the scheme's applicability, and convergence results for the second-order extension are provided.

In computer vision, developing models capable of generalizing to unseen domains with limited annotated data is crucial. This study addresses the novel and practical challenge of Open Domain Generalization (OpenDG), which involves training on diverse source domains to achieve superior performance on an unknown target domain, even when distributions and label sets differ across all domains. This approach is broadly applicable to various source domains and holds significant value for real-world scenarios. To address this, we introduce a Domain-Augmented Meta-Learning framework designed to acquire representations that generalize across open domains. This method enhances domains at the feature level using a novel Dirichlet mixup technique and at the label level through distilled soft-labeling, thereby supplementing each domain with missing classes and relevant domain knowledge. Furthermore, we implement meta-learning across domains by creating specialized meta-learning tasks and loss functions that simultaneously preserve unique domain characteristics and facilitate cross-domain generalization. Experimental results on multiple multi-domain datasets show that our proposed Domain-Augmented Meta-Learning (DAML) framework surpasses existing methods in recognizing unseen domains.

Fluctuations and uncertainties in renewable energy generation transmit from electricity grids to natural gas networks, forcing operators to modify supply nominations to maintain operational safety. To mitigate the high costs associated with these supply adjustments, we propose control strategies that utilize linepack—the gas stored within pipelines—as a flexible resource to balance stochastic gas withdrawals. These strategies employ multi-stage linear decision rules optimized over a finite discrete horizon to direct controllable infrastructure elements, such as compressors and valves, toward feasible operating conditions. This methodology supports three primary control applications. First, it leverages linepack as a primary flexibility source to absorb power system disturbances without significantly altering nominal gas supply. Second, the policies can be refined to minimize the variability (stemming from renewable intermittency) and variance (arising from renewable uncertainty) of network state variables like pressure. Finally, the approach facilitates topology optimization to segment the network and halt the propagation of uncertainty across the system. These capabilities are validated through illustrative numerical experiments.

We present an idealized model of an intelligent forager where greater intelligence expands the spatial range for food detection. When food lies beyond this detection radius $R$, the forager moves randomly; however, it travels directly toward the nearest food when it is within range. Simultaneously, the metabolic cost per step rises with intelligence. A low-intelligence forager wanders aimlessly and risks missing nearby food, leading to starvation, whereas a highly intelligent forager suffers high metabolic costs that also threaten starvation. Consequently, we demonstrate that the forager's lifespan is maximized at an optimal, intermediate level of intelligence.

Equilibrium phase transitions between a normal state and a photon condensate state (often termed superradiant phase transitions) have been a contentious subject for forty years, characterized by alternating proposals and no-go theorems. Earlier no-go theorems established that gauge invariance prevents transitions to a photon condensate if the cavity-photon mode is assumed to be spatially uniform. Nevertheless, theoretical predictions suggest that three-level systems coupled to light can undergo a first-order transition to a photon condensate state. Additionally, recent findings indicate that truncating the matter system's Hilbert space can impact the theory's gauge invariance, although gauge-invariant approximate Hamiltonians can still be constructed within such truncated spaces. In this work, we present a general no-go theorem applicable to truncated, gauge-invariant models, which prohibits both first- and second-order superradiant phase transitions in the absence of a magnetic field, consistent with broader theoretical principles.

Thermodynamic and kinetic uncertainty principles reveal trade-offs between the fluctuations of observables and thermodynamic metrics like dissipation and dynamical activity. While these relationships are well-established for classical systems, their application to the quantum domain remains largely uncharted. This study examines such trade-offs within Markovian open quantum systems governed by quantum jump dynamics, including thermalization and measurement processes. We derive finite-time lower bounds on the relative fluctuations of dynamical observables and their first passage times for arbitrary initial states. These bounds demonstrate that observable precision is limited not only by thermodynamic factors but also by quantum coherence. Specifically, we observe that for a broad class of dissipative processes involving systems with nondegenerate energy levels, the product of relative fluctuation and either entropy production or dynamical activity is amplified by quantum coherence. These results offer new insights into how classical uncertainty relations persist in quantum contexts.

The tau lepton ($\tau$) plays a crucial role in the recent experimental hints of lepton flavor universality violation (LFUV) within B-physics, suggesting it warrants heightened theoretical scrutiny in the near future. This urgency is amplified by the significantly larger data samples expected from Belle-II, with similar prospects applying to LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS. Additionally, the ability of $\tau$ decays to yield valuable insights into its spin structure offers a distinct advantage. This capability becomes particularly significant if the current new physics signals are confirmed, as naturalness arguments would imply the presence of new CP-odd phases. Furthermore, with a mass of approximately 1.8 GeV—substantially lower than that of the B-meson—the $\tau$ presents an ideal candidate for highly detailed and precise lattice QCD studies. Such precision will be essential for rigorously testing both the Standard Model and Beyond Standard Model theories.

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) serves as the foundation for contemporary machine learning (ML) systems. Although computationally efficient, SGD's reliance on random data access creates a bottleneck in environments utilizing block-addressable secondary storage like HDDs and SSDs, a limitation prevalent in frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, as well as in-DB ML systems processing large datasets. To bridge this gap between the need for randomness and the efficiency of sequential I/O, various data shuffling techniques have been developed to optimize the trade-off between convergence speed and input/output performance. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation of current shuffling methods, demonstrating that all existing approaches offer room for improvement due to compromises in either I/O efficiency or convergence rates. Consequently, we introduce CorgiPile, a novel hierarchical shuffling strategy. Unlike previous methods, CorgiPile eliminates the need for a complete data shuffle while sustaining a convergence rate comparable to that of a full shuffle. We support this approach with non-trivial theoretical analysis regarding its convergence properties. Furthermore, we have integrated CorgiPile into PyTorch via a new CorgiPileDataSet API featuring custom parallel and distributed shuffle operators, and into PostgreSQL through three optimized physical operators. Experimental findings indicate that CorgiPile achieves convergence rates on par with full-shuffle SGD for both deep learning and generalized linear models. Specifically, for ImageNet-based deep learning tasks, CorgiPile is 1.5 times faster than PyTorch with full shuffling. Additionally, for in-DB linear models, it outperforms two leading systems, Apache MADlib and Bismarck, by 1.6 to 12.8 times on both HDD and SSD storage.

Consider two dual multi-hypergraphs, $\mathcal{A} = \{A_1, \ldots, A_m\}$ and $\mathcal{B} = \{B_1, \ldots, B_n\}$, defined over the shared ground set $O = \{o_1, \ldots, o_k\}$. These structures may contain identical or nested edges. An edge is defined as containment minimal (or simply minimal) if it does not strictly contain another edge; however, multiple equal minimal edges can occur. By the principle of duality, the following hold: (i) every pair consisting of an edge $A \in \mathcal{A}$ and an edge $B \in \mathcal{B}$ has a non-empty intersection; and (ii) if $A$ is minimal, then for every element $o \in A$, there is a corresponding $B \in \mathcal{B}$ such that their intersection is exactly $\{o\}$. We extend claim (ii) as follows: given a linear order $\succ$ on $O$, which induces a unique lexicographic order $\succ_L$ on the power set $2^O$, let $A$ be a lexicographically maximal (lexmax) edge in $\mathcal{A}$. Then, (iii) $A$ is minimal, and for each $o \in A$, there exists a minimal $B \in \mathcal{B}$ such that $A \cap B = \{o\}$ and $o \succeq o'$ for all $o' \in B$. This property is significant in game theory, as it implies the Nash-solvability of tight game forms, a result previously established by the first author in 1975 and 1989. In this work, we provide a new, concise proof of (iii). Furthermore, the edges $A$ and $B$ described in (iii) can be identified in polynomial time. This is straightforward when $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are explicitly provided, but it also holds when only $\mathcal{A}$ is given via a polynomial containment oracle that determines, in polynomial time, whether a subset $O_A \subseteq O$ contains an edge from $\mathcal{A}$.

This note highlights novel findings regarding the non-existence and localization of eigenvalues for the Dirac and Klein-Gordon operators. These results are derived by applying the well-known Birman-Schwinger principle to established resolvent estimates found in existing literature.

This thesis investigates the operational mechanisms of gossip networks supporting three prominent cryptocurrencies: Ethereum, Nano, and IOTA. Key areas of inquiry include peer discovery upon node entry, bandwidth consumption, message passing protocols, and storage optimizations for the shared ledger. This subject is frequently neglected in blockchain literature. Due to the direct financial consequences involved, vulnerabilities and inefficiencies in these systems carry greater weight than those in typical open-source projects. With the exception of Bitcoin, which has existed for nearly a decade, few other projects offer comprehensive documentation on their operational specifics, relying instead on fragmented code comments. The research presented here is derived primarily from an analysis of the reference implementations' source code.

We assess the application of Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables and the Graphene protocol to reduce block propagation latency and bandwidth requirements for specific messages. Realistic simulations demonstrate substantial performance gains. Furthermore, we deliver a full implementation of Graphene within Geth, Ethereum's primary node software, and validate it against the live Ethereum blockchain. Additionally, we conducted a crawl of the selected cryptocurrency networks to identify publicly accessible nodes, providing an Autonomous System-level analysis to estimate the feasibility and impact of attacks such as BGP hijacks. The code utilized for the Graphene implementation in Geth, simulations, and other auxiliary tasks is available on GitHub at https://github.com/sunfinite/masters-thesis.

This paper introduces a generalization of the L-tensor product, extending the well-known tensor cosine and T-products originally defined for third-order tensors using the fast Fourier transform (FFT) and discrete cosine transform (DCT). We apply these methods to tensor completion tasks, utilizing the Proximal Gradient Algorithm (PGA) to address associated optimization problems. Furthermore, numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, including specific tests leveraging GPU computation.

We introduce a novel approach for diachronic semantic shift detection that utilizes contextual embeddings to produce time-specific word representations derived from BERT. Experimental results on the domain-specific LiverpoolFC corpus indicate that our method achieves performance on par with current state-of-the-art solutions without necessitating any time-intensive domain adaptation on large datasets. Furthermore, testing on a newly developed Brexit news corpus demonstrates the method's effectiveness in identifying short-term, annual semantic shifts. Finally, the model yields promising outcomes in multilingual scenarios, successfully detecting both differences and similarities in diachronic semantic shifts across various languages.

This study examines the bias induced by spatially-varying multiplicative shear (m-bias) on tomographic cosmic shear angular power spectra. By employing a computationally efficient pseudo-Cl approach to estimate the mode-coupling matrix linked to an m-bias map, we are able to account for m-bias effects at high multipoles. Subsequently, a Fisher matrix analysis is performed to predict the resulting biases in cosmological parameters. In a Euclid-like survey scenario featuring an m-bias with a zero mean and an rms of 0.01, we observe that parameter biases can reach approximately 10% of the expected statistical error when including multipoles up to $l_{max} = 5000$. Consequently, while the impact of spatially-varying m-bias might be sub-dominant, it represents a potentially non-negligible component of the error budget for future weak lensing surveys. Furthermore, we explore how parameter biases depend on the amplitude and angular scale of spatial variations within the m-bias field, concluding that constraints on the rms of these spatial variations are necessary in addition to limits on the mean value. Our findings indicate that for a Euclid-like survey, biases typically surpass roughly 30% of the statistical error for m-bias rms values between 0.02 and 0.03, and may exceed the statistical error entirely for rms values around 0.04 to 0.05. These results establish specific requirements for the permissible amplitude of spatial variations in m-bias caused by systematics in upcoming weak lensing observations.

The Russian invasion of Ukraine has reignited interest in brain drain, defined as the departure of human capital from nations, though measuring this phenomenon in real-time during crises remains challenging. This measurement difficulty impedes our understanding of the underlying causes, mechanisms, and anticipated outcomes. To bridge this gap, I utilize and expand a comprehensive dataset tracking the locations of highly active software developers from February 2021, predating the invasion by one year. By re-examining developers based in Russia in 2021, I verify a substantial outflow by late June 2022. Specifically, 8.6% of Russian developers relocated to a new country, compared to only 2.4% of developers from non-conflict neighboring nations. Additionally, 11.3% of Russian developers concealed their locations, whereas just 1.9% did so in the comparison group. The data further reveals variations in who departs versus who stays and identifies their destinations. Those leaving Russia were markedly more active and central within the collaboration network than those remaining, indicating that the most vital developers have already departed.

Our paper (arXiv:2101.11629) includes a technical mistake that alters certain conclusions. We are grateful to Streltsov, Pedernales, and Plenio for identifying the core of this error. In this note, we detail the mistake, analyze its implications, and propose ways to address the resulting limitation in the suggested experiment.

Telluric water vapor absorption, which fluctuates significantly over time, often hinders ground-based astronomical observations, particularly complicating near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy and photometry. To detect Earth-sized exoplanets in the NIR with the necessary sensitivity, it is crucial to monitor precipitable water vapor (PWV) simultaneously, thereby reducing the impact of variable telluric lines on radial velocity data and transit light curves. To solve this, we introduce the Camera for the Automatic Monitoring of Atmospheric Lines (CAMAL), an affordable, independent six-inch telescope installed at the Fred Lawrence Whipple Observatory on Mount Hopkins specifically for PWV measurement. CAMAL employs three narrowband NIR filters to track atmospheric water vapor levels affecting concurrent observations by the MINERVA and MINERVA-Red telescopes. This paper outlines CAMAL's current design, details our data analysis techniques, and presents results from 11 nights of PWV measurements. For seven of these nights, we derived independent PWV values from high-resolution stellar spectra obtained via the Tillinghast Reflector Echelle Spectrometer (TRES), also located on Mount Hopkins, using these spectra to calibrate CAMAL's absolute PWV scale. Comparisons between CAMAL and TRES estimates demonstrate excellent agreement, with a match within 1 mm across a 10 mm PWV range. Furthermore, analysis of CAMAL's photometric precision indicates PWV measurements accurate to better than 0.5 mm under dry conditions (PWV < 4 mm). Additionally, CAMAL-derived PWVs show a strong correlation with GPS-based water vapor monitor data from Kitt Peak National Observatory, situated approximately 90 km away, exhibiting a root mean square difference of 0.8 mm.

Enhancing computational methods for news coverage can boost journalistic volume and refine reporting quality. This project specifically addresses the coverage of crime stories in Los Angeles by implementing a machine-in-the-loop system. This system handles individual crimes through two mechanisms: (1) identifying structural archetypes from traditional crime reports to understand their organization, and (2) utilizing Los Angeles Police Department data to create "lede paragraphs," the initial component of crime articles. We propose a probabilistic graphical model for learning article structures alongside a rule-based approach for generating leads. Our goal is to facilitate systems that integrate these elements to construct the foundational skeletons of crime-related news pieces. This research was completed as part of Jonathan May's Advanced Natural Language Processing Course during the Fall 2019 semester.

A geo-marketplace enables users to monetize their location information. While privacy-conscious users might demand higher compensation for precise location data and accept lower rates for vaguer information, buyers aim to minimize costs yet may incur higher expenses to achieve required accuracy. We define this dynamic relationship among privacy, utility, and price as \emph{spatial privacy pricing}. Mathematically formalized through a case study of a buyer evaluating the viability of opening a restaurant by purchasing location data to estimate potential customer traffic, the scenario is modeled as a sequential decision-making process. In this framework, the buyer first selects specific data points to acquire and ultimately decides whether to proceed with the restaurant venture. We introduce two algorithms to address this problem, supported by experimental results demonstrating their superiority over baseline methods.

This study examines the application of wavelet transforms within quantum field theory models formulated using light-front coordinates. While W.N. Polyzou's recent work [Phys. Rev. D 101(2020) 096004] treated the $x^+$ variable as 'time' and restricted the wavelet transform to spatial coordinates—resulting in an asymmetry between space and time—our approach generalizes the concept of a continuous causal path, fundamental to path integration, to sequences of causally ordered spacetime regions. We provide evaluation rules for Feynman path integrals over these sequences using the wavelet transform. Unlike the previous asymmetric treatment, both the path integrals and the wavelet transform in our framework maintain symmetry with respect to the light-front variables ($x^+, x^-$). Furthermore, the definition of a spacetime event in this generalization closely mirrors the definition of an event in probability theory.

Determining the local detection rate of interstellar objects enables estimates of the total population of similar bodies within the Milky Way's thin disk. Should artificial interstellar objects be identified, the total count could be reduced by a factor of approximately $10^{16}$ if they are targeting the Sun's habitable zone. We present a model for quantifying both natural and artificial interstellar objects based on their velocity and observed density. This model is first applied to chemically propelled rockets potentially launched by extraterrestrial civilizations and subsequently to three known interstellar objects: the origin-unknown 'Oumuamua, and the interstellar meteors CNEOS 2014-01-08 and CNEOS 2017-03-09.

Combinatorial optimization problems, prevalent in areas like logistics and manufacturing, often present NP-hard challenges that make finding exact solutions difficult for significant problem sizes. Consequently, practitioners frequently rely on a variety of generic and problem-specific local search variants to generate approximate solutions; however, selecting the most appropriate variant for a specific problem remains a complex decision, even for experts. This paper addresses this challenge by identifying three independent algorithmic components of local search and formalizing their sequential selection during optimization as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We developed a deep graph neural network to serve as a policy model for this MDP, creating a learned controller named NeuroLS. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that NeuroLS surpasses both established general-purpose local search controllers from Operations Research and recent machine learning-based approaches.

The study examines general aspects of hadron production in proton-proton collisions at LHC energies, specifically focusing on hadrons located outside identified jet cones. To refine earlier approaches, we introduce surrounding rings or belts around these jet cones, enabling detailed analysis of events with multiple jets. The underlying event is defined as hadrons collected from regions outside both the jet cones and these surrounding belts, and their specific characteristics are investigated. Using a PYTHIA-generated dataset of proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 7 \text{ TeV}$, we apply our new methodology alongside the widely used CDF method. The analysis includes angular correlations and momentum distributions, with results compared and discussed between the two approaches.

Algorithmic interpretability is essential for establishing trust, guaranteeing fairness, and maintaining accountability. Yet, no formal method currently exists to measure it. This study leverages programming language theory and cognitive load theory to construct a framework for quantifying algorithmic interpretability, mirroring the process by which humans learn algorithms. We demonstrate that the proposed framework and its resulting cognitive complexity score satisfy key properties: universality, computability, uniqueness, and monotonicity. The paper illustrates the framework using a toy example, details its structure and theoretical foundations, and highlights its advantages, particularly for managers navigating trade-offs during algorithm selection.

This study investigates the dissipative dynamics of two valley excitons located in the $K$ and $K^\prime$ valleys of a bare WSe$_2$ monolayer and a monolayer integrated into a bimodal optical cavity. In the bare system, partially entangled stationary states are only achievable when the exciton-field detunings in both valleys are precisely equal (resonant detuning); otherwise, the concurrence of the exciton qubits drops to zero. Conversely, within the bimodal cavity system, entanglement oscillates between the subsystems (exciton/light and light/exciton). Consequently, a finite stationary concurrence is consistently generated for the exciton qubits, regardless of whether the detuning is resonant or non-resonant. Notably, this concurrence can reach a maximum value of 1, indicating a maximally entangled state of the two valley excitons. Since no real system maintains strictly resonant detuning, embedding the WSe$_2$ monolayer in a bimodal optical cavity offers a solution to the limitations of the bare material, thereby unlocking new possibilities for potential qubits.

The Taishan Antineutrino Observatory (TAO) has developed a liquid scintillator (LS) designed as a ton-level neutrino detector capable of measuring the reactor antineutrino spectrum with sub-percent energy resolution using Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) as photosensors. To mitigate SiPM dark noise to acceptable levels, the LS must operate at temperatures of -50°C or lower. A specialized CCD-based apparatus was created to evaluate the transparency of liquid samples within a cryostat. Research revealed that water content in the LS causes transparency degradation at low temperatures, a issue resolved by bubbling dry nitrogen to eliminate moisture. Additionally, incorporating 0.05% ethanol as a co-solvent addressed the reduction in solubility of the fluor compounds PPO and bis-MSB at cold temperatures. Ultimately, a Gadolinium-doped liquid scintillator (GdLS) containing 0.1% Gd by weight, 2 g/L PPO, 1 mg/L bis-MSB, and 0.05% ethanol by weight in the LAB solvent demonstrated excellent transparency at -50°C alongside a strong light yield.

Data augmentation (DA) serves as a cornerstone for achieving robust sequence-to-sequence learning across various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, most existing DA methods constrain the decoder to predict based solely on perturbed input representations, thereby failing to fully exploit the supervised information contained within those perturbations. To address this, we introduce BLISS, a framework-level approach for robust sequence-to-sequence learning that leverages self-supervised input representations to complement data-level augmentation strategies. Our core methodology involves supervising the sequence-to-sequence framework using both standard supervised signals ("input $\rightarrow$ output") and self-supervised signals ("perturbed input $\rightarrow$ input"). We conducted extensive experiments across multiple tasks, including machine translation, grammatical error correction, and text summarization, to validate BLISS's effectiveness. The results demonstrate that BLISS significantly outperforms the vanilla Transformer and consistently surpasses five other contrastive baselines across all evaluated tasks. Furthermore, in-depth analyses indicate that BLISS acquires both robust representations and rich linguistic knowledge, validating our hypothesis. The source code will be made available upon publication.

Although machine learning methods have effectively modeled interatomic potentials, they have historically been slower than conventional approaches. This performance gap stems from the intricate structural fingerprints describing local atomic environments, as well as the extensive cutoff radii and neighbor lists required for their computation. Even contemporary machine-learned techniques remain at least ten times slower than traditional formalisms. This paper introduces a rapid artificial neural network (RANN) style potential implemented within the LAMMPS molecular dynamics package, which employs angular screening to lower computational complexity without sacrificing accuracy. For the smallest network architectures, this approach matches the speed and accuracy of the modified embedded atom method (MEAM); conversely, networks operating at roughly one-third the speed of MEAM still achieve chemical accuracy in reproducing training data. The numerical precision of the LAMMPS implementation is evaluated by confirming energy conservation, aligning calculated forces and pressures with energy derivatives, and ensuring stability during dynamic simulations. Furthermore, the potential style is tested using a magnesium force field, where computational efficiency across various architectures is benchmarked against traditional models and alternative ANN formalisms. Results indicate that predictive accuracy is comparable to that of slower methods.

This letter examines the variations in the quantum vacuum energy density of a massless scalar field within a Casimir cavity orbiting a Morris-Thorne wormhole, situated in an isotropic cosmological model embedded within an FLRW universe. We analyze how the global curvature and scale factor at a specific moment in cosmic history, alongside local geometric properties and inertial forces, influence the Casimir energy density. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of this quantity when the cavity plates remain stationary on opposite sides of the wormhole throat, considering both zero and finite temperatures, while accounting for the effective distance between the plates mediated by the throat.

This study reexamines one-loop oblique corrections stemming from scalar superpartners in the MSSM, specifically squarks, sleptons, and Higgs sector scalars. We explicitly derive the complete one-loop expressions for the self-energy corrections to the electroweak gauge bosons and their associated $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters, which can be directly utilized to constrain the MSSM parameter space. Our findings regarding one-loop self-energies align with those of Drees, Hagiwara, and Yamada (1992) and Pierce et al. (1997); however, the calculated $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters do not match the results obtained by Dobado, Herrero, and Penaranda (1999).

This study illustrates the effectiveness of integrating concurrent learning for parameter estimation with non-parametric Gaussian Processes for online disturbance learning. A control strategy is formulated by applying these methods sequentially within a feedback linearization framework. The concurrent learning algorithm identifies system parameters associated with structured uncertainty without the need for persistent excitation, facilitating the design of the feedback linearization law. Subsequently, a non-parametric Gaussian Process addresses unstructured uncertainty. Stability of the closed-loop nth-order system is established via the Lyapunov stability theorem. Simulation outcomes indicate that tracking error is minimized under three conditions: (i) when true model parameters are unknown, (ii) when disturbances occur after parameters have converged to their true values, and (iii) when system parameters have not yet converged to their true values while disturbances are present.

Recent progress in Generalized Ensemble simulations and microcanonical analysis has enabled the study of structural transitions in polymer models across a wide spectrum of local bending and torsion strengths. It is plausible to suggest that electrostatic forces are crucial for stabilizing and facilitating these transitions in polymers. We introduce a bead-spring polymer model featuring randomly distributed charged monomers that interact through a screened Coulomb potential. By integrating the Replica Exchange Wang-Landau (REWL) technique with energy-dependent monomer updates, we generated a hyperphase diagram mapping temperature ($T$) against charged monomer concentration ($\eta$). Within the full concentration range, the coil-globule transition is second-order, while the globular-solid transition is first-order. Nevertheless, when the concentration exceeds a threshold of $\eta=80\%$, electrostatic repulsion prevents the formation of solid and liquid globules; instead, the competition between enthalpic and entropic forces results in liquid pearl-necklace and solid helical structures. The probability distribution, $P(E,T)$, reveals that at high $\eta$, the pearl-necklace liquid phase freezes into a stable solid helix-like structure, characterized by a free energy barrier that surpasses that of the freezing globule transition observed at low $\eta$.

We introduce an algorithm capable of synthesizing new views from arbitrary perspectives and any given timestamp, utilizing only a monocular video of a dynamic environment. Leveraging recent progress in neural implicit representations, our approach employs continuous and differentiable functions to model both the evolving structure and appearance of the scene. By jointly training a time-invariant static NeRF and a time-varying dynamic NeRF, we learn to blend their outputs in an unsupervised fashion. Since inferring such an implicit function from a single video is highly ill-posed—admitting infinitely many solutions consistent with the input—we incorporate regularization losses to promote physically plausible outcomes. We demonstrate our method with extensive quantitative and qualitative results on dynamic view synthesis from casually recorded videos.

Compelling cosmological and astrophysical data indicate that dark matter constitutes approximately 27% of the universe's energy budget, yet it has eluded direct detection. While the long-standing hypothesis of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) has driven decades of experimental progress, large-scale searches have yielded no results to date. This lack of success necessitates exploring more exotic dark matter models that can be probed with novel methods and fewer resources; one such method involves utilizing nuclear isomers. Specifically, $^{180m}$Ta represents the rarest known isotope with the longest-lived metastable state, featuring partial half-life limits ranging from 10$^{14}$ to 10$^{16}$ years. We examine the collision of strongly interacting and inelastic dark matter with $^{180m}$Ta, which could trigger its de-excitation.
