The energy released during this transition serves as a signature for thermalized dark matter within a well-shielded underground facility. We present findings from a direct detection experiment searching for these dark-matter-induced decay events, which have further restricted the viable parameter space. Additionally, we propose an indirect geochemical approach to detect decay products of $^{180m}$Ta accumulated in tantalum minerals over a billion years.

A BiHom-associative algebra consists of a nonassociative algebra $A$ equipped with two commuting multiplicative linear maps, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, satisfying the condition $\alpha(a)(bc) = (ab)\beta(c)$ for all $a, b, c \in A$. This notion emerged from the investigation of algebras within group Hom-categories. In this work, we also define BiHom-Lie algebras and BiHom-bialgebras, utilizing a categorical framework. We examine these novel structures by outlining fundamental properties and constructions, including representations, twisted tensor products, and smash products.

This paper investigates search methodologies for creating parameterized quantum circuits. We introduce multiple optimization techniques—combining random search with survival of the fittest, reinforcement learning using both classical and hybrid quantum-classical controllers, and Bayesian optimization—to automatically design quantum circuits for specific tasks, such as multi-labeled classification on datasets. We present non-trivial circuit architectures that are difficult to design manually yet highly efficient regarding trainability. Furthermore, we incorporate the reuploading of initial data into quantum circuits as a strategy to discover more general designs. Numerical experiments demonstrate that certain proposed architectures achieve superior results on the Iris dataset compared to established parameterized quantum circuit designs found in existing literature. Additionally, we examine the trainability of these structures on the unseen Glass dataset, reporting significant advantages over benchmarks for Glass classification, which supports the conclusion that the suggested designs are inherently more trainable.

The differentially heated rotating annulus serves as a popular tabletop laboratory model for simulating general mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. This simple setup effectively captures the two primary drivers of cyclogenesis: rotation and the meridional temperature gradient. By adjusting the radial temperature difference within the cylindrical tank and the rotation speed, researchers can induce tilted isothermal surfaces, which in turn generate baroclinic waves. These waves were analyzed using infrared thermography across a broad spectrum of rotation rates (with constant radial temperature differences) and various initial conditions. Concurrently, five groups within the MetStröm collaboration performed numerical simulations in the same parameter space, utilizing diverse methods, solvers, initial states, and perturbations. The resulting baroclinic wave patterns from both experimental and numerical sources were assessed and compared based on their dominant wave modes, spatio-temporal variance characteristics, and drift velocities. Consequently, specific "benchmarks" have been established to function as test cases for validating atmospheric numerical models in the future.

To address new tasks efficiently within complex settings, intelligent agents must accumulate reusable knowledge. For instance, learned world models encapsulate environmental understanding applicable to novel tasks, while skills represent general behaviors that can be reused. This paper explores the integration of these two strategies into a unified reinforcement learning framework. Specifically, we employ partial amortization to facilitate rapid adaptation during test time. In our approach, actions are generated by a temporally learned policy conditioned on skills selected via online planning. We validate our design choices across a collection of demanding locomotion benchmarks, showing that our method outperforms competitive baselines in both sample efficiency for individual tasks and performance when transferring knowledge from one task to another. Videos demonstrating these results are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/latent-skill-planning/

This study tackled the challenge of learning networks characterized by communication between vertices, modeled as perturbations on the measure. The analysis focuses on a scenario where samples are drawn from a uniform ergodic Random Graph Process (RGP), offering a suitable mathematical framework for the problem. In the context of binary classification, the findings establish uniform learnability by defining worst-case theoretical limits. We introduced structural Rademacher complexity, which integrates naturally with VC theory to bound the first moment. By employing the martingale method and Marton's coupling, we derived tail bounds for uniform convergence, thereby ensuring consistency for the empirical risk minimizer. The techniques developed to achieve these high-probability bounds are of independent interest to other mixing processes, regardless of whether they possess network structure.

This study introduces a Bayesian estimation technique for passively localizing acoustic sources in shallow water environments. Our probabilistic focalization method determines the time-varying position of a source by correlating observed direction of arrival (DOA) data with DOAs predicted from a statistical model. By integrating embedded ray tracing, the approach accounts for environmental parameters and captures the nonlinear nature of the acoustic waveguide. We validate the superior performance of this method relative to matched field processing using data from the SWellEx-96 experiment.

Assessing individual risk for drug consumption and misuse is a critical issue. To address this, an online survey was conducted to gather data on Big Five personality traits (NEO-FFI-R), impulsivity (BIS-11), sensation seeking (ImpSS), and demographics, alongside usage information for 18 central nervous system psychoactive drugs. Correlation analysis revealed distinct groups of drugs with strongly linked consumption patterns, categorized into three pleiades named after their central substances: ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. An exhaustive search identified the optimal combination of input features and data mining techniques to classify users versus non-users for each specific drug and group. Various classification algorithms were tested, including decision trees, random forests, k-nearest neighbors, linear discriminant analysis, Gaussian mixture models, probability density function estimation, logistic regression, and naïve Bayes, with the most effective model selected for each case. Classification quality proved unexpectedly high, with leave-one-out cross-validation showing sensitivity and specificity exceeding 70% for nearly all tasks. Notably, sensitivity and specificity surpassed 75% for cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse (VSA).

We investigated lepton-flavor violating decays of the $	au^-$ lepton into $e^-$ or $\mu^-$ accompanied by an invisible spin-0 boson, $\alpha$. Utilizing electron-positron collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $10.58$ GeV and an integrated luminosity of $62.8$ fb$^{-1}$ from the SuperKEKB collider and Belle II detector, we analyzed the lepton-energy spectra of the standard $	au^-	o e^- ar
u_e 
u_	au$ and $	au^-	o \mu^- ar
u_\mu 
u_	au$ processes to identify any excess events. We established 95\%-confidence-level upper limits on the branching-fraction ratios ${\mathcal B}(	au^-	o e^- \alpha) / {\mathcal B}(	au^- 	o e^-  ar
u_e 
u_	au)$ and ${\mathcal B}(	au^-	o \mu^- \alpha) / {\mathcal B}(	au^- 	o \mu^-  ar
u_\mu 
u_	au)$, which span $(1.1-9.7) 	imes 10^{-3}$ and $(0.7-12.2) 	imes 10^{-3}$ respectively, for $\alpha$ masses ranging from $0$ to $1.6$ GeV/c$^2$. These findings represent the tightest constraints to date on the production of invisible bosons from $	au$ decays.

Reinforcement learning (RL) formalizes learning through interaction, yet faces significant hurdles in real-world scenarios characterized by vast state or action spaces—such as in Go, StarCraft, protein folding, and robotics—or in non-Markovian environments. This work tackles the challenge of large action spaces by sequentially decomposing actions, which drastically reduces the action space size, potentially to just two actions, albeit at the cost of a longer planning horizon. We present explicit, exact constructions and equivalence proofs for all relevant quantities across arbitrary history-based processes. For Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), this approach benefits bootstrapping algorithms, while in non-MDP contexts, it substantially tightens Extreme State Aggregation (ESA) bounds. ESA transforms any non-Markovian, non-ergodic, history-based RL problem into a fixed-sized non-Markovian state-space via a surrogate Markovian process, offering optimality guarantees comparable to Markovian models; however, the resulting aggregated state-space size grows exponentially with the original action-space size. To address this, we propose binarizing the action space, providing an upper bound on the states of the binarized ESA that is logarithmic relative to the original action-space size, representing a double-exponential improvement.

Calculating $GW$ quasiparticle bandstructures and Bethe-Salpeter Equation (BSE) absorption spectra for materials exhibiting spin-orbit coupling (SOC) has traditionally been handled by applying $GW$ corrections and SOC as independent perturbations to density-functional theory. However, achieving accuracy for systems with strong SOC often necessitates a fully relativistic framework utilizing spinor wavefunctions within the Kohn-Sham, $GW$, and BSE formalisms. Such capabilities have only recently emerged, particularly for BSE applications. This study details the implementation of this fully relativistic approach in BerkeleyGW, a highly parallelized and widely adopted plane-wave pseudopotential $GW$/BSE code. We provide reference data for quasiparticle bandstructures and optical absorption spectra of solids spanning various SOC strengths, specifically Si, Ge, GaAs, GaSb, CdSe, Au, and Bi$_2$Se$_3$. Our calculated quasiparticle band gaps align with experimental values within a few tens of meV. Notably, the fully-relativistic $GW$-BSE absorption spectrum for GaSb accurately reproduces the large spin-orbit splitting of spectral peaks. For Bi$_2$Se$_3$, we observe a significant alteration in the low-energy bandstructure relative to DFT, where the fully-relativistic $GW$ approximation successfully captures the parabolic character of the valence and conduction bands by incorporating off-diagonal self-energy matrix elements. Furthermore, we outline the detailed methodology, strategies for handling spatial symmetries with spinors, comparisons with other codes, and performance metrics relative to spinless $GW$/BSE and perturbative SOC approaches. Ultimately, this work seeks to encourage further advancement of spinor $GW$/BSE methodologies in software dedicated to excited-state research.

We reveal the characteristics of structural disorder in bottom-up zigzag graphene nanoribbons and analyze their impact on magnetism and electronic transport, utilizing scanning probe microscopies and first-principles calculations. Our findings indicate that edge-missing m-xylene units, which arise during the cyclodehydrogenation phase of on-surface synthesis, constitute the most prevalent point defects. These "bite" defects function as spin-1 paramagnetic centers, significantly disturbing the conductance spectrum near band extrema and inducing spin-polarized charge transport. Furthermore, we demonstrate that electronic conductance in graphene nanoribbons is more susceptible to "bite" defects located at zigzag edges compared to armchair ones. This study provides a thorough understanding of the low-energy electronic properties of disordered bottom-up graphene nanoribbons.

The coupling of spatially separated oscillators holds significant promise for quantum and communication applications. This study demonstrates that two antiferromagnetic oscillators situated within an electromagnetic cavity cooperatively interact with terahertz modes, resulting in the formation of hybridized magnon-polariton states. These findings are substantiated by a systematic investigation of reflection spectra from two parallel hematite ($\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$) slabs, analyzed across varying temperatures and separation distances alongside theoretical modeling. In this experiment, the crystals themselves constituted the mediating cavity, with measurements conducted over practical distances of several millimeters at room temperature. Such cavity-mediated coupling facilitates the design of intricate resonators that are governed by their geometry and by the shared characteristics of their constituent parts.

Detecting minute objects represents a primary challenge impeding progress in object detection, as generic detectors often suffer significant performance drops in these scenarios. This paper argues that both the box priors in anchor-based models and point priors in anchor-free models are ill-suited for tiny objects. Our central finding is that existing label assignment strategies in these frameworks generate numerous outlier ground truth samples with tiny sizes, causing detectors to prioritize larger objects over tiny ones. To address this, we introduce a Gaussian Receptive Field based Label Assignment (RFLA) strategy. RFLA leverages the prior knowledge that feature receptive fields follow a Gaussian distribution; rather than relying on Intersection over Union (IoU) or center sampling, it proposes a novel Receptive Field Distance (RFD) metric to directly quantify the similarity between the Gaussian receptive field and the ground truth. Furthermore, acknowledging that traditional IoU-threshold and center sampling methods are biased toward large objects, we develop a Hierarchical Label Assignment (HLA) module based on RFD to ensure balanced learning for tiny objects. Extensive evaluations across four datasets validate the efficacy of our approach, with results showing a 4.0 AP point improvement over state-of-the-art methods on the AI-TOD dataset. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chasel-Tsui/mmdet-rfla.

Diagnosing cyber-physical systems involves identifying faulty behaviors, their underlying causes, and strategies for mitigation or prevention. Consequently, diagnosis depends on integrating a model of both functional and erroneous system behaviors with runtime observations. Key challenges include the computationally expensive process of constructing models, the risk of state explosion during root cause analysis, and the need for result interpretability. This paper introduces a scalable algorithm to address these issues by employing a Bayesian network to automatically learn a structured model and refining it through a genetic algorithm. Our method diverges from existing approaches in two ways: rather than selecting features beforehand, we derive a global representation from all available data and convert it into a compact, label-specific set, while prioritizing interpretability to aid repairs. Evaluation results demonstrate that our approach achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms while offering superior interpretability and a significantly reduced model size.

We introduce a versatile Bayesian inference algorithm designed for expensive likelihoods, substituting the stochastic component of the Langevin equation with a deterministic density gradient. Particle density is assessed at current positions via a Normalizing Flow (NF), which offers differentiability and robust generalization in high-dimensional spaces. By leveraging NF preconditioning and NF-based Metropolis-Hastings updates, we achieve accelerated convergence. Empirical results across multiple examples demonstrate that this approach performs comparably to leading sampling techniques.

Unsupervised anomaly detection addresses the challenge of identifying anomalies within unlabeled datasets, a task that has gained significant traction recently due to the high cost and difficulty of labeling data. Among these methods, Isolation Forest (iForest) is widely used for assigning anomaly scores via an ensemble of specialized isolation trees, which are constructed through a rapid and efficient random partitioning process. However, the standard iForest algorithm can be optimized regarding memory usage, latency, and performance, improvements that are critical for low-resource environments and TinyML deployments on ultra-constrained microprocessors. Furthermore, current anomaly detection methods often fail to leverage weak supervision; since these systems are frequently deployed in Decision Support contexts, sporadic user feedback represents an underutilized information source. This work highlights the limitations of iForest training and introduces TiWS-iForest, a novel approach that incorporates weak supervision to reduce computational complexity while enhancing detection accuracy. The efficacy of TiWS-iForest has been validated on real-world datasets, and the corresponding code is publicly available to promote reproducibility.

This manuscript introduces a non-invasive technique for reconstructing the network topology of dynamical systems. Drawing inspiration from the determination of oscillation modes in extensive electrical grids, we suggest employing controlled probing inputs alongside response measurements. We demonstrate that this methodology is analytically feasible for a broad category of dynamical systems, validating our results through numerical simulations of Kuramoto oscillator networks. Furthermore, our approach enables the estimation of the total number of agents within the network by probing and measuring only a single agent.

This study examines the tree-level production of a charged Higgs boson in association with a charged weak $W$-boson ($H^{\pm}W^{\mp}$) through $e^{+}e^{-}$ annihilation within a circularly polarized laser field. Initially, employing analytical methods, we derived the differential cross section expression incorporating both $Z$ and $\gamma$ diagrams. Subsequently, we demonstrated that the cross section within the laser field is proportional to the form factor $F_{HWV}$ and relies on the charged Higgs boson's mass and the center-of-mass energy. Furthermore, we analyzed how the total laser-assisted cross section varies with the number of exchanged photons across two distinct form factor scenarios. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the maximum number of transferable photons is determined solely by the laser parameters.

Future large-scale ensembles of time delay lenses hold promise for offering cosmological constraints that complement other methodologies. In a flat universe model with a constant equation of state parameter $w$ and a Planck prior, LSST time delay observations of approximately 4,000 lenses are projected to constrain the local Hubble constant $h$ to within ~0.007 (~1%), the dark energy density $\Omega_{DE}$ to ~0.005, and $w$ to ~0.026 (all at 1-sigma precision). Comparable precision could be achieved by a specialized gravitational lens observatory (OMEGA), which would secure accurate time delay and mass model measurements for roughly 100 extensively analyzed lenses. We evaluate these results, alongside those for general cosmological models, against the "optimistic Stage IV" projections for weak lensing, supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, and cluster counts as defined by the Dark Energy Task Force. Time delays offer a moderate constraint on an evolving $w(z)$, with the strongest sensitivity occurring at the pivot redshift of $z \approx 0.31$. We provide our Fisher matrix calculations to facilitate straightforward comparison and combination with data from other experiments. Additionally, we demonstrate how cosmological constraining power depends on the number of lenses, uncertainties in lens models, time delay precision, redshift precision, and the ratio of four-image to two-image lenses.

We modified the Appleby-Battye-Starobinsky $F(R)$ gravity model to investigate double cosmological inflation and the generation of primordial black holes (PBHs) with masses reaching $10^{19}$ g within a single-field framework. Our findings indicate that the power spectrum of scalar curvature perturbations can be amplified beyond the Hawking evaporation limit of $10^{15}$ g. Consequently, PBHs formed from the gravitational collapse of these substantial perturbations could persist in the current universe and contribute to cold dark matter. These results are consistent with present cosmic microwave background measurements at the $3\sigma$ level, though they necessitate fine-tuning of the model parameters.

The experimentally accessible rare decay of a Higgs boson into a lepton-antilepton pair and a photon via the dominant gluon-fusion mechanism is being studied at the LHC, focusing on the impact of higher-order QCD corrections on the fiducial cross sections for electrons and muons. These corrections, calculated up to NNLO QCD, are found to be substantial. While generally uniform across kinematic variables associated with the Higgs boson itself, they exhibit distinct characteristics within the kinematics of its individual decay products.

A World Model functions as a generative framework designed to simulate environments, successfully learning spatial and temporal representations within Reinforcement Learning settings. Occasionally, these models allow agents to train exclusively within simulated "dream" worlds. This research investigates methods to enhance the generalization of agents from these dream environments to real-world scenarios, specifically addressing the Dream2Real transfer problem. We introduce a cost-effective general approach to improve a controller's ability to transition from a neural network-based dream simulation to reality. Drawing inspiration from Domain Randomization—which involves randomizing simulator parameters as extensively as possible without altering the core task—we adapt this concept for cases where a pre-built simulator is unavailable. By employing dropout during the training of the World Model, the dream environment can generate a vast array of diverse scenarios. While prior applications of dropout typically either avoid it during inference or average predictions via Monte-Carlo Dropout, our method, Dropout's Dream Land, utilizes each unique dropout mask to construct a varied collection of dream environments. Experimental results demonstrate that Dropout's Dream Land effectively bridges the gap between simulated dreams and reality. Additionally, we conducted extensive ablation studies to validate these findings.

An experimental investigation examines the development of the liquid bridge connecting two merging sessile drops with yield stress. The results indicate that the bridge's height increases proportionally to time ($h_0 \sim t$), mimicking a viscous Newtonian fluid, before halting at a long duration without reducing its liquid/gas interfacial energy. Numerical simulations determine the final arrested profile, which is governed by the fluid's yield stress ($\tau_y$) and the coalescence angle ($\alpha$). This relationship is characterized by a modified Bingham number ($\tau_y h_{drop} / \sigma$) that incorporates the drop's height-to-width aspect ratio. Furthermore, a scaling argument is proposed for the bridge's temporal evolution, utilizing the length scale derived from the arrested shape analysis alongside the similarity solution for the bridge's progression.

This paper establishes a bijection between rook placements on double staircases (originally defined by Josuat-Verg\`es in 2017) and increasing binary trees. We define two specific subsets of these placements, termed left-aligned and right-aligned rook placements. By enumerating these subsets while monitoring a particular statistic, we derive the $\gamma$-vectors associated with the Eulerian polynomials. The work concludes by discussing a related bijection that complements our primary result, as well as potential extensions of it. Our main bijection represents a specific instance of a broader bijection introduced by Tewari in 2019.

Hierarchical matrices offer a robust framework for substantially lowering the computational demands of dense kernel matrices. While interpolation-based techniques are commonly employed to construct these matrices efficiently for general kernels, this paper introduces HiDR, a rapid hierarchical data reduction procedure achieving $O(n)$ complexity. This method facilitates the memory-efficient creation of hierarchical matrices using nested bases, where $n$ denotes the number of data points. By hierarchically compressing the data, HiDR derives $O(1)$ representations for both nearfield and farfield interactions. Building on HiDR, we propose a linear complexity $\mathcal{H}^2$ matrix construction algorithm. The data-driven approach yields superior efficiency compared to other general-purpose methods and allows for flexible computation without direct access to the kernel function. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method significantly enhances memory efficiency across a broad spectrum of kernels relative to interpolation-based alternatives. Furthermore, although not specifically optimized for particular kernels, benchmark tests on the Coulomb kernel demonstrate that this general-purpose algorithm delivers competitive performance against several state-of-the-art hierarchical matrix construction techniques.

This paper extends a recent generalization of the Conley index to discrete multivalued dynamical systems lacking a continuous selector, a development driven by applications in data-driven dynamics. Building on this framework, we investigate attractor-repeller pairs and Morse decompositions, specifically establishing the Morse equation and deriving Morse inequalities.

Temporal data often exhibits patterns across varying scales, ranging from days to months, which complicates the effective visualization of time-based information. To address this, we introduce a novel method that enhances focus and context within temporal charts, facilitating the interpretation of patterns across different timeframes. This approach utilizes a central focus area defined by a time axis and a secondary axis capable of displaying either quantities or categories, alongside adjacent periphery plots that can aggregate data along temporal, value, or combined dimensions. We outline a framework for these periphery plots and illustrate their practical utility through two specific use cases.

This paper investigates the task of identifying a maximum-cardinality collection of $r$-cliques within an undirected graph where the maximum degree is fixed at $\Delta$, under the constraints that the cliques are either vertex-disjoint or edge-disjoint. While it is established that for $r=3$, the vertex-disjoint (edge-disjoint) problem admits linear-time solutions when $\Delta=3$ ($\Delta=4$) but becomes APX-hard for $\Delta \geq 4$ ($\Delta \geq 5$), we extend these findings to any fixed $r \geq 3$, offering a comprehensive complexity classification for both variants across all maximum degrees $\Delta$. Specifically, we demonstrate that the vertex-disjoint problem can be solved in linear time when $\Delta < 3r/2 - 1$, in polynomial time when $\Delta < 5r/3 - 1$, and is APX-hard when $\Delta \geq \lceil 5r/3 \rceil - 1$. Furthermore, for $r \geq 6$, these same implications apply to the edge-disjoint problem. However, when $r \leq 5$, the edge-disjoint problem is solvable in linear time if $\Delta < 3r/2 - 1$, in polynomial time if $\Delta \leq 2r - 2$, and is APX-hard if $\Delta > 2r - 2$.

Advanced LIGO-Virgo's ongoing detection of binary merger events has uncovered the statistical characteristics of binary black hole (BBH) populations. Investigating a stochastic gravitational wave background (GWB) offers a valuable method to explore the cosmological evolution of these compact mergers. This paper establishes an upper limit on a GWB generated by BBH mergers whose stellar ancestors are believed to drive reionization during the cosmic dawn. Because early reionization by these progenitors would result in a universal optical depth conflicting with {\it Planck} data, the cumulative mass density is constrained to $\rho_\star \lesssim 10^7~M_\odot~{\rm Mpc}^{-3}$. Despite this limit, the GWB amplitude from high-redshift BBH mergers is projected to reach $\Omega_{\rm gw}\simeq 1.48_{-1.27}^{+1.80}\times 10^{-9}$ at $f\simeq 25$ Hz, with a current merger rate consistent with or below observed local event rates. Such a GWB level is detectable by Advanced LIGO-Virgo at design sensitivity, suggesting a significant contribution of high-$z$ BBHs to local GW detections. Furthermore, the spectral index is anticipated to be notably flatter than the standard $\simeq 2/3$ value typically associated with lower-redshift, less massive BBHs. Additionally, if the mass function is more top-heavy than in the local universe, the GWB spectrum shifts further toward lower frequencies, enabling the extraction of mass function details for merging BBHs at high redshifts.

Optimizing problems that require significant computational resources is difficult. Bayesian optimization offers a probabilistic solution that reduces performance requirements by utilizing mathematically simpler models of the problem. Specifically, the Gaussian Process approach models the problem using a mixture of Gaussian functions. This paper details specific modifications to Gaussian Process optimization components found in existing scientific libraries. These modifications were entered into the BlackBox 2020 challenge, where they surpassed the performance of several conventional optimization libraries.

This work examines the asymptotic behavior of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions in two-dimensional vibrating systems where mass density is perturbed near closed curves. We specifically analyze the threshold scenario where the resonance frequencies of the membrane and the thin inclusion are coincident or nearly so. The perturbed eigenvalue problem is modeled as a family of self-adjoint operators acting on varying Hilbert spaces. However, the limit operator, which dictates the asymptotics of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, is non-self-adjoint and features Jordan chains of length $2$. Beyond this lack of self-adjointness, the operator also has a non-compact resolvent. Consequently, its spectrum exhibits a complex structure, including a countable set of eigenvalues with infinite multiplicity.

We demonstrate that for any polyhedron $\mathcal P$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, every point in space that fails to see any vertex of $\mathcal P$ must observe at least eight edges, and this limit is sharp. This result holds more broadly for any finite configuration of internally disjoint polygons within $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Most studies on modeling conversation history in Conversational Question Answering (CQA) typically report a single main result on standard benchmarks. Although current models achieve impressive scores on CQA leaderboards, it is unclear if they remain robust when facing shifts in settings (such as more realistic scenarios), training data sizes (e.g., scaling from large to small datasets), or domains. This work presents the first large-scale robustness study of history modeling approaches for CQA. Our findings reveal that high benchmark scores do not guarantee strong robustness, and various methods can perform vastly differently across different settings. Leveraging these insights, we developed a novel prompt-based history modeling approach that demonstrates superior robustness across diverse conditions. Inspired by methods that highlight historical answers within passages, our technique differs by inserting textual prompts directly into the passage text rather than modifying token embeddings. This approach is simple, easily adaptable to almost any model, and highly effective, making it an ideal starting point for future developers. Furthermore, we hope our study and findings will increase awareness of the necessity for robustness-focused evaluation alongside high leaderboard scores, ultimately leading to better CQA systems.

The adoption of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in gaming and serious applications is rapidly evolving into a standard practice. Although these systems offer deep immersion, they frequently cause user discomfort, including nausea, sickness, and headaches. This issue is particularly critical in health-related VR applications, where such symptoms can significantly disrupt therapeutic treatments. This study investigates the root causes of these problems and proposes design guidelines to mitigate them. Specifically, we explore a dynamic focus solution aimed at reducing discomfort during first-person navigation in immersive virtual environments. This approach utilizes a real-time heuristic model of visual attention. Furthermore, the paper presents a case study involving a first-person spatial shooter demo that implements both this solution and the suggested design guidelines.

Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a cornerstone tool in financial risk management. Accurately estimating VaR for loss return distributions at extreme levels is critical for both operational and regulatory purposes, with a specific focus on dynamically estimating extreme VaR based on recent historical data. This study introduces a two-step bias-reduced methodology named GARCH-UGH (Unbiased Gomes-de Haan). The approach involves filtering financial returns using an AR-GARCH model followed by applying a bias-reduced estimator of extreme quantiles to the standardized residuals to calculate one-step ahead dynamic extreme VaR. Empirical results demonstrate that GARCH-UGH estimates outperform the combination of standard AR-GARCH filtering and extreme value estimation, showing superior accuracy in both in-sample and out-of-sample backtests across various financial time series of historical daily returns.

The significant adaptability of direct laser writing stems from its capacity to create precise three-dimensional microstructures and its compatibility with a wide variety of materials. Nevertheless, many promising materials remain currently inaccessible, necessitating the ongoing creation of new photoresists. This study introduces a novel bio-derived resist based on N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, the monomeric unit of chitin, thereby extending the range of existing plant-based biopolymer resists to include an animal-derived bio-monomer. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that employing a combination of two photoinitiators offers advantages over using a single one. In this approach, the first photoinitator serves as an efficient two-photon absorber at the specific wavelength, whereas the second photoinitator has limited two-photon absorption capabilities but excels at monomer crosslinking. The first initiator acts as a sensitizer, absorbing light and transferring energy to the second initiator, which then generates radicals to initiate polymerization. This sensitization mechanism provides a new pathway for utilizing reactive photoinitiators with low two-photon absorption cross-sections in direct laser writing, without requiring modifications to their chemical structures.

This study investigates whether three-dimensional inviscid Euler flows, initiated from smooth conditions on a periodic domain $\mathbb{T}^3$, can develop singularities within a finite timeframe. Building on Kato's (1972) established result regarding the local existence of classical solutions in the Sobolev space $H^m(\mathbb{T}^3)$ for $m > 5/2$, we infer that any singularity formation necessitates an unbounded increase in the $H^m$ norm of the velocity field as the critical time approaches. To explore this possibility, we systematically search for "extreme" Euler flows by solving a PDE-constrained optimization problem designed to maximize the $H^3$ norm of the solution at a specific time $T > 0$, subject to appropriate normalization constraints. This optimization is executed using a state-of-the-art Riemannian conjugate gradient method, with gradients derived from an adjoint system. Numerical computations at progressively higher resolutions reveal that, consistent with Kato's theorem, if the optimization interval $[0, T]$ is sufficiently brief, the $H^3$ norm remains bounded in the resulting extreme flows, confirming the well-posedness of the Euler system over this short duration. Conversely, when the interval $[0, T]$ is extended—potentially exceeding the local existence time guaranteed by Kato's theorem—the $H^3$ norm of these extreme flows diverges as numerical resolution increases, suggesting a potential singularity on this longer timescale. The identified extreme flow for the long time window manifests as two colliding vortex rings exhibiting specific symmetries, with the region where a singularity might arise being nearly axisymmetric.

MINOS operates as an accelerator-based neutrino oscillation experiment at Fermilab, where a high-energy neutrino beam is directed to a near detector on-site and a 5 kTon far detector located 735 km away in the Soudan mine, northern Minnesota. After several years of operation yielding millions of events at the near detector and hundreds at the far detector, this presentation highlights recent findings, including a precise determination of $|\Delta m^2_{32}|$, constraints on sterile neutrino components derived from neutral current data, and a search for $
u_\mu 	o 
u_e$ appearance. The primary focus is the analysis of $
u_\mu 	o 
u_e$ conversion. Based on an exposure of $3.14	imes 10^{20}$ protons on target, electron-type events were identified in both detectors; the near detector data was used to estimate backgrounds extrapolated to the far detector. The analysis identified 35 events in the signal region against an expected background of $27\pm 5(stat)\pm 2(syst)$. These results establish a 90% C.L. upper limit of $\sin^2 2 	heta_{13} < 0.29$ assuming $\delta_{cp} = 0$ and a normal mass hierarchy. Ongoing analysis aims to further reduce backgrounds and enhance sensitivity.

Quark masses play a pivotal role in high-energy physics. This study investigates heavy meson systems by solving the Lippmann-Schwinger equation with the Martin potential to determine heavy quark masses. We further applied the Martin potential to derive a viable mass spectrum for heavy quarkonia, utilizing a minimal phenomenological model (M. Melles, Phys. Rev. D 62: 074019, 2000). The mass spectra for $b\bar{b}$ and $c\bar{c}$ systems were computed without incorporating relativistic corrections or spin-dependent effects. The resulting spectra align well with experimental data. Leveraging the conventional spectrum, we extracted the pole masses of heavy quarks and, by applying the relationship between the $\overline{MS}$ mass (modified minimal subtraction scheme) and the on-shell quark mass, determined the $\overline{MS}$ masses. These calculated $\overline{MS}$ mass values show strong consistency with existing literature.

Frequency-dependent squeezing is essential for achieving broadband quantum noise reduction in future gravitational wave detector runs. This technique requires reflecting squeezed vacuum from a Fabry-Perot filter cavity that is detuned by half its linewidth. Because the squeezed vacuum lacks classical amplitude, auxiliary control beams must co-propagate to ensure the filter cavity maintains stable length, alignment, and incident beam pointing. In our experiment at the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, we employed a control beam at a harmonic of the squeezed vacuum wavelength and observed visible detuning variations linked to the angular drift of suspended mirrors; such variations can compromise quantum noise reduction. We examined several mechanisms driving these detuning fluctuations and found that fixing the incident beam pointing and implementing automatic alignment for the filter cavity sufficiently mitigated the drift. Additionally, we identified an optimal beam position on the filter cavity mirror that minimizes detuning fluctuations. This study reports a stabilized filter cavity detuning variation of under 10 Hz, compared to the cavity's 113 Hz linewidth. Relative to previous results [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 171101 (2020)], this level of detuning stability is adequate to reduce fluctuations in the gravitational wave detector's detection range caused by detuning drift from 11% to within 2%.

The NASA Kepler and K2 missions (2009-2018) established a lasting legacy by discovering thousands of exoplanets and gathering high-precision, long-duration time-series data for hundreds of thousands of stars, including various pulsating variable types. This article highlights ongoing findings from Kepler data concerning $\delta$ Scuti pulsating variables, which are core hydrogen-burning stars with approximately twice the Sun's mass. We examine several unresolved issues regarding the variability properties of these stars and discuss how Kepler data has advanced asteroseismology—the use of stellar pulsations to deduce internal structures.

This study employs a first-principles *ab initio* approach to investigate the electronic, magnetic, and linear phonon dispersion characteristics of phosphorene monolayers. As a semiconductor with a dimension-dependent variable band gap, the monolayer's geometry and physical properties were analyzed by introducing vacancies. The calculations encompass pristine, vacancy-induced, and doped vacancy-induced monolayers, with dopant concentrations optimized to preserve dilute magnetic semiconducting behavior. Analysis of the density of states and partial density of states reveals the contributions of individual orbitals. Both vacancy and doped vacancy configurations exhibit band closing, indicating metallic behavior and dense states in these perturbed phases. To comprehensively understand the system's physical properties, calculations included both antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic orderings. Furthermore, Landau energy levels were mapped onto the Fermi surface using linear dispersion relations derived from phonon vibrational density of states. These findings regarding the linear phonon density of states are consistent with the electronic density of states.

The surge in handheld device usage has enabled location-based services to obtain precise, real-time positioning data, which has sparked significant privacy concerns. To mitigate this, the concept of geo-indistinguishability was introduced, adapting differential privacy principles for location systems. However, geo-indistinguishability treats space uniformly by adding identical noise levels across all map areas, which is a limitation. This paper introduces a novel elastic distinguishability metric that warps geometric distance to reflect varying regional densities. Consequently, the proposed mechanism dynamically adjusts noise levels while maintaining a consistent degree of privacy throughout. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this elastic metric can seamlessly integrate the concept of a "geographic fence," a common strategy for protecting frequently visited locations like homes or workplaces. We conducted an extensive evaluation by developing an elastic metric for Paris using semantic data from OpenStreetMap. Our results, compared against the Planar Laplace mechanism under standard geo-indistinguishability using real-world datasets from Gowalla and Brightkite, indicate that the elastic mechanism effectively adapts to area semantics, reducing noise outside the city center and thereby providing superior overall privacy.

We report early-time photometric and spectroscopic data for the Type Ia Supernova (SN Ia) 2021aefx. Its early u-band light curve exhibits an excess flux relative to typical SNe Ia. We propose that this early blue flux surplus results from a rapid shift in spectral velocity during the first few days after the explosion, caused by the Ca II H&K emission line migrating from the u to the B bands over a period of just a few days. This phenomenon could be the primary driver of early-excess u-band flux in all SNe Ia displaying broad absorption features and initial velocities exceeding 25,000 km/s. Consequently, this effect is likely to dominate in UV filters and in scenarios where the supernova's spectral energy distribution rapidly rises toward longer wavelengths. However, such a rapid velocity change can only generate a monotonic flux variation in the u-band; therefore, for lower-velocity explosions or those with more complex early-excess structures, an additional parameter must account for the observed diversity. Further early-time observations, especially early spectra, are necessary to quantify the significance of this effect across the SN Ia population.

This study examines the T-dualities of non-supersymmetric string models derived from twisted compactifications. We demonstrate that the T-duality groups for these models arise from imposing congruence conditions on $O\left( d_{L},d_{R},\mathbb{Z}\right) $, indicating that such models remain invariant under congruence subgroups of this group. Furthermore, we highlight that transitions between different non-supersymmetric models can be achieved by applying $O\left( d_{L},d_{R},\mathbb{Z}\right) $ transformations.

Kinetic Sunyaev-Zeldovich experiments face a well-known issue called the optical-depth degeneracy, where cosmological constraints are entangled with optical depth measurements. To address this, we present a novel statistic derived from the first moment of relative velocities within triplets. This metric allows for the determination of cosmological parameters without relying on optical depth or $\sigma_8$. By analyzing 22,000 simulations from the Quijote suite via Fisher matrix forecasts, we demonstrate that this statistic yields robust constraints on cosmological parameters, with significant precision gains for the summed neutrino mass. Compared to results from mean pairwise velocities and redshift-space halo power spectra, our method improves constraints on all cosmological model parameters by factors ranging from 2.3 to 5.7 and 6.2 to 12.9, respectively. Consequently, this new statistic offers a viable pathway to independently constrain cosmological parameters using solely future kinetic Sunyaev-Zeldovich data, bypassing the limitations of optical depth and $\sigma_8$.

Intense femtosecond laser pulses induce double ionization of rubidium dimers situated on helium nanodroplet surfaces, resulting in their fragmentation into two $\mathrm{Rb^+}$ ions. We demonstrate that analyzing the kinetic energy of these fragment ions allows for the differentiation between dimers originating from the ground state, $X$ $^1\Sigma_{\mathrm{g}}^+$, and the lowest-lying triplet state, $^3\Sigma_{\mathrm{u}}^+$. Experimental data reveals that the ratio of dimers in the triplet ($a$) to ground ($X$) states varies with average droplet size, ranging from 4:1 to 5:1. This method is broadly applicable to alkali atom dimers and trimers, as further validated with $\mathrm{Li_2}$, $\mathrm{Na_2}$, and $\mathrm{K_2}$, and holds the potential to facilitate femtosecond time-resolved investigations of their rotational and vibrational dynamics, potentially achieving atomic structural resolution.

The daily generation of vast amounts of online dialogue creates an urgent demand for advanced conversation understanding. To structure discussions, we focus on identifying the relational links that connect response utterances to their initiations. Determining who replied to whom involves analyzing the consistency of topic content and the dependency of discourse roles, a distinction made since most prior research overlooks latent factors influencing word occurrences. We introduce a model designed to learn latent topics and discourse structures within word distributions, predicting pairwise initiation-response connections by leveraging topic consistency and discourse dependency. Experimental evaluations on both English and Chinese datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving an MRR of 79 compared to 73 on Chinese customer service dialogues. Furthermore, we investigate our model's outputs to clarify how topics and discourse mechanisms reveal user interactions within conversations.

The rapid evolution of technology and widespread internet access are transforming how real-time information is shared. However, the freedom to express opinions without prior credibility verification has facilitated the spread of misinformation, posing severe risks to both individuals and society. This surge in fake news is particularly rampant in India, where debunked stories are often repackaged with altered descriptions to claim they depict entirely different events. To combat these fabricated narratives, it is crucial to investigate and deduplicate such false claims. While most existing research on automated fact-checking and fake news detection focuses exclusively on English, this limitation is problematic for India, where only 10% of the literate population speaks English; consequently, the role of regional languages in disseminating falsehoods cannot be ignored. This paper introduces FactDRIL, the first large-scale multilingual fact-checking dataset designed for regional Indian languages. We compiled an extensive dataset over seven months spanning 11 low-resource languages. The collection includes 9,058 English samples, 5,155 Hindi samples, and 8,222 samples distributed across various regional languages, including Bangla, Marathi, Malayalam, Telugu, Tamil, Oriya, Assamese, Punjabi, Urdu, Sinhala, and Burmese. Furthermore, we provide a detailed characterization of the dataset's three defining "M"s—multi-lingual, multi-media, and multi-domain—along with a comprehensive list of its unique attributes. Finally, we outline potential use cases for the dataset, which we anticipate will serve as a vital resource and a foundational step in curbing the proliferation of fake news in low-resource languages.

The emergence of superconductivity in the heavy-fermion paramagnet UTe$_2$ has garnered significant interest, especially because superconductivity is enhanced near magnetic quantum phase transitions induced by pressure and magnetic fields. A current challenge lies in characterizing the effects of combined pressure and magnetic fields applied along various directions within this strongly anisotropic system. This study investigates the electrical resistivity of UTe$_2$ under pressures up to 3~GPa and pulsed magnetic fields reaching 58~T along the hard magnetic crystallographic axes $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$. We construct three-dimensional phase diagrams demonstrating that near the critical pressure, the enhancement of superconductivity coincides with an increase in effective mass, associated with the collapse of metamagnetic and critical fields at the boundaries between the correlated paramagnetic regime and the magnetically-ordered phase. Beyond the critical pressure, field-induced transitions occur before the destruction of the magnetically-ordered phase, indicating an antiferromagnetic character. By providing new insights into the interplay between magnetism and superconductivity, this work calls for microscopic theories that describe the anisotropic properties of UTe$_2$ under pressure and magnetic fields.

Artisanal and Small-scale Gold Mining (ASGM) serves as a vital livelihood for numerous households yet generates significant social and environmental impacts, particularly within the rainforests of developing nations. Sentinel-2 satellites capture multispectral imagery capable of identifying shifts in water extent and quality, thereby revealing mining site locations. This study concentrates on identifying ASGM operations in the Peruvian Amazon. Researchers evaluated multiple semi-supervised classifiers utilizing Support Vector Machines (SVMs) to detect water body changes between 2019 and 2021 in the Madre de Dios region, a global epicenter for ASGM. Experimental results indicate that SVM-based models yield reasonable performance with minimal annotation requirements, achieving a Cohen's $\kappa$ of 0.49 on RGB images and 0.71 on 6-channel images. Additionally, the study examines the effectiveness of integrating the Lab color space for change detection.

This paper investigates the elastic and locomotive characteristics of Miura-ori paper origami. Experimental analysis of individual paper creases reveals that their non-elastic properties are fundamental to the system. The origami structure is subsequently modeled as an assembly of these creases, its ability to propel small objects is assessed, and the corresponding equation of motion is derived. Consequently, the theoretical and experimental height of the launched ball is examined as a function of the relevant governing parameters.

Knowledge-intensive natural language processing tasks gain advantages by connecting text to facts within a Knowledge Graph (KG). However, while facts are language-independent, their labels are typically available only in a limited number of languages, making it difficult to associate these facts with sentences in other languages. To solve this, we introduce Multilingual Fact Linking (MFL), a task aimed at linking sentence-expressed facts to their corresponding KG entries even when the KG fact labels lack the sentence's language. To support research in this domain, we present IndicLink, a new dataset comprising 11,293 linked WikiData facts and 6,429 sentences in English and six Indian languages. We propose ReFCoG, a Retrieval+Generation model that scales to millions of KG facts by integrating a Dual Encoder for retrieval with a Seq2Seq generation model constrained to produce only valid KG facts. ReFCoG surpasses standard Retrieval+Re-ranking models by 10.7 points in Precision@1. Despite this improvement, the model's overall score of 52.1 indicates significant room for further enhancement. The ReFCoG code and IndicLink dataset are accessible at https://github.com/SaiKeshav/mfl.

This paper provides a detailed analysis of QCD corrections to the forward-backward charge asymmetry of heavy quarks within the $\mathrm{e^+e^-\rightarrow Q\overline{Q}(g)}$ process at the Z pole. We demonstrate that applying simple cuts on jet acollinearity can decrease the magnitude of these corrections by an order of magnitude. This reduction is projected to lower systematic uncertainties to approximately $\Delta \mathrm{A_{FB}^{0,Q}} \approx 10^{-4}$, thereby enabling high-precision electroweak measurements involving heavy flavors at future high-luminosity $\mathrm{e^+e^-}$ facilities such as the FCC-ee.

We demonstrate that for any $\alpha, \beta > 0$ satisfying $\alpha + \beta > 1$, there exists an integer $N$ such that for all $n \geq N$, every binary phylogenetic tree $T$ with $n$ leaves can be uniquely represented as a perfect phylogeny by a set of $\lfloor n^\alpha \rfloor$ characters, where each character utilizes at most $\lfloor n^\beta \rfloor$ distinct states. This combinatorial result is established through a concise proof utilizing the probabilistic method.

Hemagglutinin in the influenza virus plays a critical role in attaching to host cells and constitutes a genetic region highly prone to mutation. Given the necessity of forecasting these mutations to create effective, cost-efficient vaccines, recent research has focused heavily on solving this challenge. While historical mutation data has traditionally trained predictive models, the significant imbalance between mutated and preserved proteins remains a major obstacle requiring resolution. This study proposes addressing this issue through anomaly detection (AD), a well-established machine learning domain designed to identify unseen anomalies using solely normal training data. By framing mutations as anomalous behaviors, we leverage recent advancements in this field, which are particularly suited to handling the extreme disparity between unmutated and mutated samples. Our approach seeks to generate a compact representation of unmutated samples while ensuring anomalies are distinctly separated, thereby maximizing the shared unique representation of normal data. This strategy enhances the model's ability to discern and detect mutated samples from unmutated ones during testing. We validate the method's efficacy through extensive experiments across four public datasets, including three hemagglutinin protein sets and one SARS-CoV-2 dataset, demonstrating success using various standard evaluation metrics.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of singularly perturbed phase-transition functionals defined by $ F_k(u)=\frac{1}{\epsilon_k}\int_A f_k(x,u,\epsilon_k\nabla u)\,dx $. In this framework, $u \in [0,1]$ represents a phase-field variable, and $\epsilon_k > 0$ denotes a singular-perturbation parameter approaching zero as $k \to +\infty$. The integrands $f_k$ are constructed such that for any $x$ and $k$, the function $f_k(x,\cdot ,0)$ constitutes a double well potential with minima at 0 and 1. We demonstrate that, up to subsequences, the functionals $F_k$ $\Gamma$-converge to a surface energy functional given by $ F_\infty(u)=\int_{S_u\cap A}f_\infty(x,\nu_u)\,d\mathcal H^{n-1} $. Here, $u$ belongs to the space $BV(A;\{0,1\})$, and the limiting density $f_\infty$ is determined by the double limit of appropriately scaled minimization problems. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to stochastic homogenization, establishing a $\Gamma$-convergence result for stationary random integrands.

For any constant $c > 0.55$, every sufficiently large integer $n$ can be expressed as $p + ab$, where $p$ is prime, both $a$ and $b$ are substantially smaller than $x^{1/2}$, and the product $ab$ remains below $n^c$. This finding improves upon a theorem by Heath-Brown, which previously required $c > 3/4$. The proof utilizes a novel technique described as "intersecting two sieves."

The first-order approximation of electron-photon interaction, described as a spinor-vector field coupling within the de Sitter ambient space formalism, is examined. The study presents the corresponding interaction Lagrangian and scattering matrix, noting that in this approximation, the matrix can be expressed as an expansion of the Lagrangian. Furthermore, the tree-level diagram for the electron-photon scattering amplitude is computed, followed by an analysis of the Minkowski limit.

Coupled-cluster theory including single and double excitations (CCSD) represents a viable *ab initio* approach for the electronic structure of three-dimensional metals, where second-order perturbation theory (MP2) fails to converge in the thermodynamic limit. Nevertheless, the prohibitive computational cost and slow convergence of CCSD relative to basis set expansion often result in significant basis set errors when applied to periodic systems. While a standard "composite" strategy employs MP2 to recover missing dynamical correlation energy via focal-point corrections, the unsuitability of MP2 for metallic systems casts doubt on this technique. This study outlines a method to "downfold" high-energy excitations handled by MP2 into a low-energy active space for CCSD treatment. Evaluations on the uniform electron gas reveal that the downfolding approach converges more rapidly with increasing basis set size. However, the composite method remains surprisingly accurate because it avoids the flawed MP2 treatment of double excitations near the Fermi surface. Applying these techniques to estimate CCSD correlation energy within the combined complete basis set and thermodynamic limits, we determined that CCSD recovers over 90% of the exact correlation energy at $r_s=4$. Additionally, substituting MP2 with the random-phase approximation in both composite and downfolding frameworks yields a method that is more efficient but computationally more demanding.

While Transformers are crucial for pretraining success in NLP, alternative architectures generally require attention mechanisms to achieve comparable benchmark accuracy. This study investigates pretraining methods that omit attention, specifically evaluating recently developed routing layers derived from state-space models (SSMs) alongside architectures utilizing multiplicative gating. When combined, these modeling choices significantly influence pretraining performance. Empirically, the proposed Bidirectional Gated SSM (BiGS) matches BERT's pretraining results without relying on attention and supports long-form pretraining of 4,096 tokens without approximation.

Utilizing the Keck Cosmic Web Imager integral-field unit spectrograph, we achieved two primary objectives: first, we determined global stellar population parameters for the ultra-diffuse galaxy (UDG) Dragonfly 44 (DF44) with unprecedented precision, surpassing previous capabilities for any UDG; second, we conducted the inaugural measurement of spatially-resolved stellar population parameters within a UDG. Our findings reveal that DF44 lies beneath the mass--metallicity relation defined by canonical dwarf galaxies, both within and outside the Local Group. We observed a flat radial age gradient ($m_{\rm age} \sim +0.01_{-0.08}^{+0.07}$ log Gyr kpc$^{-1}$) and a flat-to-positive metallicity gradient ($m_{\rm [Fe/H]} \sim +0.08_{-0.11}^{+0.11}$ dex kpc$^{-1}$), profiles that contradict those found in similarly pressure-supported dwarf galaxies. Additionally, we detected a flat-to-negative [Mg/Fe] gradient ($m_{\rm [Mg/Fe]} \sim -0.18_{-0.17}^{+0.17}$ dex kpc$^{-1}$), indicating that the central 1.5 kpc of DF44 exhibits stellar population characteristics akin to metal-poor globular clusters. Collectively, these results demonstrate that DF44 lacks internal properties comparable to other dwarf galaxies and refutes the hypothesis that it was expanded via a prolonged, bursty star-formation history as proposed by certain simulations. Instead, the data suggest DF44 underwent an intense phase of "inside-out" star formation followed by early and catastrophic quenching, resulting in a cessation of star formation more rapid than observed in typical dwarf galaxies.

We provide an in-depth analysis of the low-energy band structure and Fermi surface (FS) topology for $A$Co$_2$As$_2$ (where $A$ represents Ca, Sr, Ba, or Eu) via high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Our experimental findings regarding FS topology and band dispersion align well with theoretical full-potential linearized augmented-plane-wave (FP-LAPW) simulations. Notably, the FS maps of these cobalt arsenides differ markedly from those of the parent compounds found in Fe-based high-temperature superconductors. Additionally, the FS of CaCo$_2$As$_2$ remains largely unchanged across its antiferromagnetic transition temperature. Band dispersions measured along various momentum $(k_{\it x}, k_{\it y})$ directions reveal a small electron pocket at the Brillouin zone (BZ) center and a larger one at the BZ corner. Crucially, the absence of a hole FS in these materials prevents nesting between pockets at the Fermi energy ($E_{\rm F}$), contrasting with $A$Fe$_2$As$_2$-type parent compounds. Interestingly, hole bands are shifted 300–400~meV below $E_{\rm F}$, varying by the specific $A$ element. Furthermore, nearly flat bands near $E_{\rm F}$ correlate with a high density of states at the Fermi level. These insights are vital for comprehending the physical properties and potential for superconductivity in related materials.

With the growing need for software capable of handling and analyzing vast radio astronomy datasets during the SKA era, this work highlights the interactive workflow, data mining, processing, and visualization features of DUG Insight. We evaluated the system's performance and adaptability by processing nearly 68,000 full-sky radio images generated by the Engineering Development Array (EDA2) within three days. The primary objectives were to passively detect and identify known Resident Space Objects (RSOs), including satellites and orbital debris, and to explore how radio interferometry could monitor aircraft traffic. These signals are detectable through reflected terrestrial FM radio waves and out-of-band transmissions from RSOs. Such surveillance of low Earth orbit and airspace contributes to space situational awareness and aircraft tracking technologies. Based on these observations, we identified 40 instances of 19 unique RSOs within a 1,500 km range of the EDA2. This result represents a substantial improvement over a prior study of the same dataset, demonstrating DUG Insight's flexible capabilities for processing complex data at scale. Future iterations of the DUG Insight workflow will focus on achieving real-time acquisition, detecting unknown RSOs, and continuing to process data from facilities relevant to the SKA.

This paper presents the development and analysis of efficient, stable numerical methods for accurately simulating nonlinear dynamic shear ruptures on non-planar faults within 3D elastic solids, utilizing dual-parity (DP) summation by parts (SBP) finite difference (FD) schemes. Specifically, regarding nonlinear dynamic earthquake ruptures, we show that DP SBP FD operators, as detailed by K. Mattsson (2017), produce spurious catastrophic high-frequency wave modes that persist even with mesh refinement. Conversely, our newly proposed dispersion relation preserving (DRP) SBP FD operators, introduced by C. Williams and K. Duru (2021), offer superior numerical dispersion properties and effectively avoid supporting these toxic high-frequency modes. We validate the method's effectiveness through 3D numerical simulations on geometrically complex fault surfaces. Furthermore, our approach accurately replicates dynamic rupture benchmark problems established by the Southern California Earthquake Center while requiring less computational effort than standard methods based on traditional SBP FD operators.

Dynamical systems evolving continuously are pervasive across science and engineering. Machine learning (ML) offers data-driven methods to model and forecast these dynamics. However, a fundamental limitation is that ML models are usually trained on discrete data using techniques that ignore the system's inherent continuity, often failing to represent the true continuous behavior. Consequently, such models have restricted applicability in many scientific and engineering contexts. To overcome this, we propose a convergence test grounded in numerical analysis theory. This test determines whether a model has accurately learned a function approximating the system's continuous dynamics. Models failing this test do not capture essential dynamics and remain of limited value for prediction tasks, whereas those passing it support superior interpolation and extrapolation. Our findings demonstrate how integrating rigorous numerical analysis methods with standard ML training and testing protocols can effectively validate models for scientific and engineering purposes.

This study presents a dynamic change of measure methodology for deriving analytical solutions regarding the expected future prices (and consequently, expected returns) of contingent claims within a finite time frame. The proposed method develops hybrid probability measures known as "equivalent expectation measures" (EEMs); these measures reflect the physical expectation of a claim's price prior to the horizon date and function as pricing measures from the horizon date onward. The EEM framework is applicable to empirical studies examining both the cross-sectional and term structure of returns for contingent claims, including Treasury bonds, corporate bonds, and financial derivatives.

This research examines the scaling limits of nonlinear functions $G$ applied to a random grain model $X$ defined on $\mathbb{R}^d$, characterized by long-range dependence and a marginal Poisson distribution. Aligning with Kaj et al. (2007), we posit that the intensity $M$ of the underlying Poisson grain process scales with the parameter $\lambda$ as $M = \lambda^\gamma$, where $\gamma > 0$. These findings are relevant to the Boolean model and exponential $G$, utilizing a Charlier polynomial expansion alongside a generalized Mehler's formula. Furthermore, the study explores applications to solving Burgers' equation using initial data derived from aggregated random grains.

This study examines frames composed of exponential functions within $L_2[-\pi,\pi]^d$, focusing on their role in the oversampling and nonuniform sampling of bandlimited signals. We establish a multidimensional nonuniform oversampling formula applicable to bandlimited functions with broadly defined frequency domains. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of this formula regarding perturbations in the sampled data and present a computationally efficient simplification of the primary oversampling theorem. The work also explores a higher-dimensional extension of Kadec's $1/4$ Theorem. Finally, the proposed methods are applied to approximate specific biorthogonal functions associated with exponential Riesz bases in $L_2[-\pi,\pi]$, thereby recovering Levinson's well-known theorem as a corollary.

Magnetostatic fields in accelerators are typically characterized using multipoles. This work demonstrates that, within a two-dimensional framework, multipole fields indeed satisfy Maxwell's equations, and it examines the necessary electric current distributions and ferromagnetic geometries (under idealized conditions) to produce specific multipole configurations. Furthermore, the methods for identifying multipole components within an existing field are explored. Finally, the two-dimensional multipole approach is generalized to three dimensions; this extension enables the representation of fringe fields and the primary fields in devices like undulators and wigglers as a series of modes, with each mode constituting a valid solution to Maxwell's equations.

Drawing inspiration from recent advancements in self-supervised computer vision that utilize data augmentations to generate supervision, we investigate a novel, general-purpose approach to audio representation learning. We propose a method that learns robust audio representations from a solitary audio segment, without requiring relationships between distinct time segments of the audio. To realize this principle, we introduce Bootstrap Your Own Latent for Audio (BYOL-A, pronounced "viola"), a self-supervised audio learning framework adapted from BYOL for general-purpose representation. Unlike prior audio self-supervised methods that typically depend on the agreement of nearby segments or the disagreement of distant ones, BYOL-A generates contrasts within an augmented pair derived from a single audio segment. By combining normalization and augmentation techniques, BYOL-A achieves state-of-the-art performance across various downstream tasks. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation studies have elucidated the individual contributions of each component and their synergistic effects.

This study investigates the relationships between half-light radius versus black hole mass, and luminosity versus black hole mass, within active galactic nuclei (AGN) where accretion discs are heated by X-ray coronal emission. Utilizing KYNSED, a newly developed spectral model for broadband AGN energy distributions, we analyzed both non-illuminated Novikov-Thorne discs and X-ray illuminated discs, the latter employing a Novikov-Thorne radial temperature profile. We also examined scenarios where this temperature profile is adjusted by a colour-correction factor. Our model assumes that X-ray luminosity corresponds to the accretion power dissipated into the disc below a specific transition radius. Results indicate that the half-light radius of X-ray illuminated discs can be three to four times larger than that of a standard disc, even for non-spinning black holes, because absorbed X-rays serve as a secondary energy source that raises disc temperatures. While non-illuminated discs align with observations only at the 2.5sigma level, X-ray illuminated discs successfully explain both the half-light radius–black hole mass and luminosity–black hole mass relations across a broad range of physical parameters. Furthermore, the observed X-ray luminosity of gravitationally lensed quasars matches the luminosity required to heat the disc. Although X-ray disc illumination was originally proposed to account for features in AGN X-ray spectra, recent work has demonstrated its ability to explain UV/optical time-lags; this study adds that the same model resolves the quasar micro-lensing disc size problem. These findings collectively support the hypothesis of X-ray disc illumination in AGN.

A complementary label (CL) denotes an incorrect class for an instance, yet models trained on CLs can successfully identify the true class. However, the current framework restricts each example to a single CL, significantly limiting its effectiveness because annotators can often identify multiple complementary labels (MCLs) per example. This paper introduces a new setting that accommodates MCLs for each instance and presents two learning approaches. The first approach employs two wrappers that decompose MCLs into numerous single CLs, enabling the use of existing CL-based methods; however, this decomposition conceptually dilutes the information contained in the MCLs. Consequently, the second approach derives an unbiased risk estimator that treats each set of MCLs as a unified whole, offering an estimation error bound. We further refine this second approach by minimizing appropriately selected upper bounds. Experimental results indicate that while the first approach performs well, the second yields superior performance.

For a machine learning (ML) system to be effective in real-world deployment, it must not only replicate a target function on training data but also generalize to unseen scenarios to ensure accurate predictions. Since users typically cannot exhaustively list every possible input, achieving robust generalization is essential for building reliable and high-performance ML systems. Although generalization is theoretically well-defined for many hypothesis classes, the exceptional generalization capabilities of deep neural networks have posed significant challenges to theorists. In the realm of deep reinforcement learning (RL), understanding generalization becomes even more complex due to the tension between generalization and stability inherent in popular RL algorithms. This thesis aims to advance the understanding of generalization by investigating the learning dynamics of deep neural networks across both supervised and reinforcement learning contexts.

The Ethiopic/Amharic script stands as one of Africa's most ancient writing systems, serving over 120 million people across at least 23 languages in East Africa, such as Amharic and Tigrinya. This Abugida-based system comprises 282 syllables, 15 punctuation marks, and 20 numerals. Its syllabic matrix is constructed from 34 base consonants, to which up to 12 diacritics or vocalic markers are added. Because syllables sharing common consonants or vocalic markers often appear visually similar, they pose significant challenges for text recognition. This study introduces the first comprehensive public datasets—HUST-ART, HUST-AST, ABE, and Tana—specifically designed for Amharic script detection and recognition in natural scenes. We performed extensive experiments to assess how well state-of-the-art methods perform on these datasets for detecting and recognizing Amharic scene text. The results highlight the robustness of our datasets for benchmarking purposes and their potential to foster the development of more reliable Amharic script detection and recognition algorithms. Ultimately, these outcomes will benefit the people of East Africa, including diplomats from various nations and international organizations.

This study investigates the potential benefits and efficiency of integrating recurrence into the Transformer architecture by incorporating a highly straightforward recurrent module. We benchmark our approach against baselines using the same training and evaluation protocols as BERT. Our findings validate that recurrence can consistently enhance Transformer performance without necessitating low-level optimizations or increasing the parameter count. Specifically, our base model delivers an average absolute improvement of 2.1 points across ten tasks and exhibits greater stability during fine-tuning across various learning rates.

An active galactic nucleus (AGN) demands a mechanism to channel gas toward the galaxy's core, with bar-driven processes frequently proposed as a solution. While numerous studies have examined the link between bars and AGNs, their findings remain contradictory. These discrepancies may stem from variations in the spatial and temporal scales of gas inflow, black hole accretion, and AGN emission, or from sample biases arising from differing methods used to detect bars and classify AGN activity. This study revisits the bar-AGN connection using a sample from SDSS to investigate whether bars influence AGN activity. AGN status was identified via emission line diagnostics, while bar properties were previously derived using \texttt{BUDDA} for 2D bulge-bar-disk decomposition. To mitigate selection biases before comparing active and inactive galaxies, the sample underwent careful selection, and control groups were constructed using propensity score matching to align with the AGN sample based on specific object parameters. Our analysis reveals that AGNs are more prevalent in barred galaxies and exhibit higher accretion rates within barred systems, but only when distinct $M$-$\sigma$ relations are applied to estimate black hole mass ($M_\bullet$) based on central velocity dispersion ($\sigma$) for barred versus unbarred galaxies. Conversely, no correlation exists between bar strength and activity level. Collectively, these results support theoretical models positioning bars as a key mechanism in disc galaxies for supplying gas to AGNs, while also suggesting that other mechanisms are significant, especially at scales below approximately 100 pc.

Nonlinear field theories generate unstable yet long-lasting structures called oscillons, which have been investigated using both symmetric and asymmetric double-well potentials as well as other potential forms. This study explores higher-order field theories by applying a generalized symmetric double-well potential alongside a $\phi^6$ potential. Our results demonstrate the existence of $3+1$ spherically symmetric oscillons that exhibit notably extended lifetimes without requiring fine-tuning of parameters.

A primary obstacle in millimeter wave (mmWave) communications is its vulnerability to blockages, which compromises link connectivity and overall network reliability. This study examines a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted mmWave system designed to improve reliability and connectivity under random blockage conditions. To strengthen the robustness of hybrid analog-digital beamforming against such disruptions, we formulate a stochastic optimization problem aimed at minimizing the sum outage probability.
