Addressing large-scale, resource-constrained environments such as the Internet of Things, we introduce a new data-driven distributed control algorithm synthesized directly from trajectory data. Our approach, termed Data-driven Distributed and Localized Model Predictive Control (D$^3$LMPC), extends the data-driven System Level Synthesis (SLS) framework, enabling the parameterization of \emph{closed-loop} system responses directly from collected open-loop trajectories. The resulting model-predictive controller supports distributed computation and requires only local information exchange. By enforcing locality constraints on the system response, we demonstrate that the data requirements for our synthesis problem remain independent of the global system's size. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees for recursive feasibility and asymptotic stability. Finally, simulation experiments confirm the algorithm's optimality and scalability.

Probability intervals offer a compelling method for handling uncertainty, yet they differ from belief functions by lacking a native probability transformation suitable for utility-based decision-making. This paper introduces the intersection probability—a transform initially developed for belief functions within the geometric approach to uncertainty—as the most appropriate solution. We revisit its rationale and definition, evaluate it against other potential representatives for systems of probability intervals, analyze its credal interpretation as a focal pair of simplices within the probability simplex, and sketch a decision-making framework for probability intervals that mirrors the Transferable Belief Model used for belief functions.

We examine a formulation of the entanglement entropy for a quantum scalar field expressed through its spacetime two-point correlation functions. We explore how this formulation applies to investigating entanglement entropy across diverse contexts within causal set theory. These contexts encompass sprinklings of causal diamonds in multiple dimensions within flat and de Sitter spacetimes, both massless and massive theories, configurations involving multiple disjoint regions, and nonlocal quantum field theories.

We have derived the entanglement, magnetization, and magnetic susceptibility for a finite chain of the 1D antiferromagnetic Heisenberg XXX model with spin 1 and spin 3/2, incorporating Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, single-ion anisotropy, and an external magnetic field.

This paper establishes a logarithmic convexity linked to an observability estimate at a specific time instant for the one-dimensional heat equation featuring dynamic boundary conditions. As a result, we demonstrate impulse approximate controllability for the impulsive heat equation under similar dynamic boundary constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit upper limit for the cost associated with impulse control. Finally, we provide a constructive algorithm to calculate the impulsive control with the minimal $L^2$-norm, accompanied by numerical experiments that verify the theoretical findings and illustrate the algorithm's efficiency.

Observational data indicates that white dwarf (WD) mergers serve as a highly efficient process for mass accretion within the galaxy. This study demonstrates that such mergers naturally generate uniformly rotating, highly magnetized WDs, with a significant fraction falling within a narrow mass range near the Chandrasekhar limit ($M_{\rm Ch}$). These near-$M_{\rm Ch}$ merger products rapidly spin up and compress over approximately $10^2$ years, potentially triggering central ignition and a standard SN Ia via the double-detonation (DDT) mechanism, or resulting in a failed detonation and SN Iax through pure deflagration. The resulting SNe Ia and SNe Iax exhibit spectral features, light curves, polarimetric properties, and nucleosynthetic yields comparable to those predicted by the canonical near-$M_{\rm Ch}$ single degenerate (SD) channel, yet they display a $t^{-1}$ delay time distribution typical of the double-degenerate (DD) channel. Additionally, unlike events from the SD channel, these WD merger-induced explosions will not yield observable signatures of a companion star. We explore various implications of these results, ranging from SN Ia explosion mechanisms to the galactic nucleosynthesis of iron-peak elements, such as manganese.

We demonstrate Euler's theorem in number theory by constructing an argument rooted in quandles. A quandle is an algebraic structure whose axioms correspond to the three Reidemeister moves used in knot theory.

Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR) involves generating a high-resolution image from a low-resolution input by increasing pixel density. This technique has garnered significant research interest due to its applicability across diverse real-world scenarios, including satellite and aerial imaging, as well as the enhancement of compressed images and video. Although deep learning has advanced the field, most existing networks rely on traditional convolutions, primarily aiming for greater depth or width, with innovations often derived from integrating successful concepts from other domains. This study moves beyond conventional convolutions by adopting the capsule network concept. Given the outstanding performance of capsules in image classification and segmentation, we investigate their potential suitability for SISR. Furthermore, we observe that current solutions frequently share similar configurations, arguing that this homogeneity limits the exploration of diverse network architectures. Our experiments evaluate various strategies to enhance performance, ranging from novel loss functions to modifications within capsule layers. Our network demonstrated strong results with a reduced number of convolutional layers, suggesting that capsules are a promising approach for image super-resolution.

This paper evaluates the performance of both encrypted and conventional DNS protocols across thousands of U.S. home networks over a one-month period in 2020. Data was collected from 2,693 participants in the FCC's Measuring Broadband America initiative. Our findings indicate that clients need not sacrifice performance to gain privacy; specifically, DoT demonstrated faster median response times than standard DNS for certain resolvers, even amidst increased latency. Additionally, we observed substantial variability in DoH performance among different recursive resolvers. Consequently, we advise DNS clients, such as web browsers, to regularly measure latency and response times to dynamically select the optimal protocol and resolver, as no single solution consistently outperforms others for all users.

We present ALMA observations of polarized dust emission alongside CS($J=5 \rightarrow 4$) and C$^{33}$S($J=5 \rightarrow 4$) lines in the high-mass star-forming region NGC6334I(N). A distinct "hourglass" magnetic field structure was deduced from polarized dust data and confirmed directly by polarized CS emission across various velocities, with the polarization aligning parallel to the field. Integrating prior results, the field maintains a pinched morphology traceable from envelope scales (captured by ALMA) down to clump scales, indicating its dynamic significance across multiple length-scales. The CS total intensity is optically thick ($\tau_{\mathrm{CS}} = 32 \pm 12$), whereas the C$^{33}$S emission is optically thin ($\tau_{\mathrm{C^{33}S}} = 0.1 \pm 0.01$). These findings imply that anisotropies beyond large velocity gradients—specifically those in the radiation field—are necessary to account for the ALMA-detected polarized CS emission. Applying four variants of the Davis-Chandrasekhar-Fermi technique and angle dispersion function (ADF) methods, we derived average magnetic field strengths projected onto the plane of the sky: $\left< \mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{pos}} \right> = 16$ mG from dust and $\left< \mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{pos}} \right> \sim 2$ mG from CS. Since each tracer corresponds to different molecular hydrogen number densities, this approach effectively provides a tomographic perspective of the magnetic field within a single ALMA observation.

This research addresses the unsupervised discovery and segmentation of object parts, which serve as intermediate local representations to reveal intrinsic object structures and yield more interpretable recognition outcomes. While recent unsupervised techniques have significantly reduced reliance on expensive annotated data, they often still depend on auxiliary inputs like segmentation masks or saliency maps. To eliminate this dependency and enhance part segmentation quality, we introduce a novel method that disentangles object part appearance and shape through reconstruction losses without requiring additional mask information. To prevent degenerate solutions, we incorporate a bottleneck block that compresses and expands the appearance representation, thereby facilitating a more effective separation of geometry and appearance. Furthermore, by integrating a self-supervised part classification loss with an enhanced geometry concentration constraint, the approach achieves the segmentation of consistent, semantically meaningful parts. Extensive experiments across diverse object categories, including faces, birds, and PASCAL VOC instances, validate the efficacy of our proposed framework.

Design patterns represent a catalog of common programming practices derived from numerous real-world systems. However, certain object-oriented patterns become distorted or unnecessarily complex due to the absence of specific language constructs or mechanisms. This paper analyzes published design patterns to identify idiomatic workarounds for implementation constraints. Based on this analysis, we propose a set of general-purpose language constructs and mechanisms that, if integrated into statically typed, object-oriented languages, would significantly enhance pattern implementation and, by extension, improve the development of many real systems. Our proposed catalog includes distinct subtyping separate from inheritance, lexically scoped closure objects independent of classes, and multimethod dispatch. These concepts are not radically new but are synthesized from various languages and research into programming languages in a novel, orthogonal fashion. We argue that expressing design patterns using these proposed constructs simplifies their descriptions, making them more accessible to diverse language communities. Furthermore, constructs missing from a specific language can be realized through paradigmatic idioms.

Generalized text representations underpin numerous natural language understanding tasks. To effectively leverage diverse corpora, models must inherently grasp the relationships between them. However, many existing approaches overlook this interconnectivity by directly applying a single-channel model (a coarse paradigm) across all tasks, a strategy that lacks sufficient rationality and interpretability. Furthermore, some prior works attempt to learn downstream tasks by stitching skill blocks (a fine paradigm), which can lead to suboptimal results due to redundancy and noise. In this study, we first examine task correlations through three distinct lenses: data characteristics, manual design, and model-based relevance, subsequently grouping similar tasks. We then introduce a hierarchical framework utilizing a coarse-to-fine paradigm, featuring a bottom layer shared across all tasks, a middle layer segmented by task groups, and a top layer dedicated to individual tasks. This architecture enables the model to acquire fundamental language properties from the entire dataset, enhance performance on related tasks, and mitigate the adverse effects of irrelevant ones. Experiments across 13 benchmark datasets spanning five natural language understanding tasks confirm the superiority of our proposed method.

We enhance the linear tetrahedron method to eliminate systematic errors arising from overestimations and underestimations of integrals for convex and concave functions, respectively. Unlike the Bl\"ochl correction, which is limited to total energy and charge (spin) density calculations, our approach extends to a broader range of applications, including response functions and phonon frequencies. We validate the efficacy of this method through phonon calculations for MgB$_2$ and fcc lithium.

In recent years, there has been a resurgence of interest in commonsense representation and reasoning within natural language understanding. Central to these advancements has been the creation of new commonsense knowledge graphs (CSKGs), whose diverse facts enable machine learning models to address novel and difficult tasks. However, challenges persist regarding the quality and comprehensiveness of these resources, given the immense scale needed to fully capture general commonsense knowledge. This study posits that manually curated CSKGs will never achieve the coverage required for NLP agents to handle all real-world scenarios. Consequently, we introduce a novel evaluation framework that assesses the utility of knowledge graphs based on their ability to facilitate the learning of implicit knowledge representations. Aligned with this objective, we present ATOMIC 2020, a new CSKG containing general-purpose commonsense knowledge absent from pretrained language models. We evaluate its characteristics against other leading CSKGs, conducting the first large-scale pairwise analysis of commonsense resources. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ATOMIC 2020 is superior for training models that generate accurate, representative knowledge for unseen entities and events. Finally, human evaluation reveals that despite GPT-3 (175B parameters) showing impressive few-shot performance, it lags by approximately 12 absolute points compared to a BART-based model trained on ATOMIC 2020, even though the latter uses over 430 times fewer parameters.

Score-based generative models (SGMs) have recently become a promising category for generating high-quality images. Their core mechanism involves recurrently adding Gaussian noise and gradients to an initial sample until it converges to the target distribution, a process known as diffusion sampling. However, to ensure stable convergence and maintain generation quality, this sequential approach requires a small step size and a large number of iterations (e.g., 2000). While several acceleration techniques have been developed, they primarily focus on low-resolution generation. This work addresses the more challenging and critical issue of accelerating high-resolution generation with SGMs. We theoretically demonstrate that the slow convergence is mainly caused by neglecting the target distribution. To address this, we propose a novel Target Distribution Aware Sampling (TDAS) method that exploits structural priors in both spatial and frequency domains. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CelebA, LSUN, and FFHQ datasets confirm that TDAS consistently accelerates state-of-the-art SGMs, especially for demanding high-resolution (1024x1024) tasks, achieving up to an 18.4x speedup while largely preserving synthesis quality. TDAS maintains good image quality with fewer iterations, whereas existing methods often degrade significantly or fail entirely.

Ear-EEG has emerged as a promising option for wearable brain monitoring in real-world settings. Although experimental studies have validated its use in various scenarios, the relationship between sensors and sources for different neural origins remains undefined, and a comprehensive theoretical analysis of its sensitivity to artifacts is still lacking. This study establishes the sensitivity of various ear-EEG configurations to neural sources across diverse brain surface locations, as well as to ocular sources such as blinks, vertical saccades, and horizontal saccades, which generate EEG artifacts. The findings strongly support integrating ear-EEG into conventional EEG paradigms for monitoring neural activity originating in the temporal lobes, while also delineating its utility for sources located further away. The potential for using ear-EEG with distant sources is further substantiated by analyzing the prominence of ocular artifacts. These results provide valuable insights to support both current and future experimental ear-EEG studies and applications regarding sensitivity to neural and ocular artifacts.

This study investigates sodium isotopes ranging from $A = 20$ to $31$ by employing various microscopic effective interactions within the $sd$-shell. These interactions, generated via {\it ab initio} methods from microscopic nucleon-nucleon (NN) and three-nucleon (NNN) potentials for the $sd$-shell, are used to analyze ground-state binding energies, low-lying spectral levels, and electromagnetic properties, including reduced electric quadrupole transition strengths, as well as quadrupole and magnetic dipole moments of the sodium chain. The findings derived from these microscopic interactions are benchmarked against experimental data and compared with results obtained using the phenomenological USDB interaction. Furthermore, charge radii for the sodium isotopes are calculated utilizing shell model harmonic oscillator wave functions. The discussion also extends to matter radii and neutron skin thickness across the sodium chain, with particular emphasis placed on neutron-deficient isotopes.

We examine a two-dimensional autophoretic particle model featuring a circular shape that emits or absorbs a solute, which subsequently diffuses and moves with the surrounding fluid. When the emission or absorption rate exceeds a specific threshold (defined by the dimensionless Péclet number, $Pe$), the particle transitions from a stationary state to a motile one. As $Pe$ increases, the trajectory evolves from linear to circular and eventually to chaotic motion. By deriving a reduced closed model from the full system involving solute diffusion and advection, we obtain a framework dependent on only two time-varying amplitudes, $C_1(t)$ and $C_2(t)$, representing the first two Fourier modes of the solute concentration. This system comprises two coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations for $C_1$ and $C_2$, offering significant benefits: (i) it allows for complete analytical treatment of straight and circular motions; (ii) it enables highly efficient numerical analysis of complex behaviors like chaos, surpassing the computational cost of the full partial differential equation model; (iii) it adopts a universal structure governed solely by symmetries; and (iv) it is extensible to higher Fourier modes. Although the derivation is demonstrated for a 2D case for simplicity, it readily applies to 3D scenarios and various phoretic models where chemical activity drives locomotion, such as cell motility driven by acto-myosin kinetics. This approach provides a robust method for modeling swimmers using ordinary differential equations, balancing analytical solvability with efficient numerical computation.

This study examines whether a maximizer exists for the product of torsional rigidity and Newtonian capacity (or logarithmic capacity in the case of $d=2$) across open, bounded, convex sets in $\R^d$ where $d\ge 3$, subject to constraints defined by Lebesgue measure or a combination of Lebesgue measure and perimeter.

We introduce a data-driven method for building entropy-based closures for moment systems derived from kinetic equations. This approach learns the entropy function by modeling the relationship between moments and entropy, thereby remaining independent of space-time discretization and specific problem setups like initial or boundary conditions. By utilizing convex and $C^2$ approximations, the proposed closure retains key structural features of entropy-based methods, including entropy dissipation, hyperbolicity, and the H-Theorem. We developed convex approximations for Maxwell-Boltzmann entropy using both convex splines and neural networks, validated them on a plane source benchmark for linear transport in slab geometry, and compared their performance against standard optimization-based M$_N$ closures. The numerical results demonstrate that these data-driven closures achieve accurate solutions significantly faster than M$_N$ closures.

We present a cohomology theory for $n$-ary self-distributive objects within the tensor category of vector spaces, which serves to classify their infinitesimal deformations. For objects derived from $n$-Lie algebras, we demonstrate that ($n$-ary) Lie cohomology naturally embeds into the self-distributive cohomology; under mild additional conditions, this embedding becomes an isomorphism between the second cohomology groups. Consequently, the deformations of the self-distributive structure are fully determined by those of the Lie bracket. This framework offers significant applications in the analysis of Yang-Baxter operators, as self-distributive deformations yield nontrivial deformations of the associated operators. Specifically, we establish a homomorphism from the second self-distributive cohomology to the second cohomology of the corresponding Yang-Baxter operator, which becomes a monomorphism when the underlying Lie algebra has a trivial center. We also develop a deformation theory based on simultaneous modifications of both the coalgebra and self-distributive structures. Our results indicate that even when the Lie algebra possesses nontrivial cohomology (such as semi-simple algebras), simultaneous deformations can remain nontrivial, thereby generating corresponding Yang-Baxter operator deformations. Finally, we provide low-dimensional examples and computations, and we offer a complete characterization of $2$-cocycles for self-distributive objects arising from all nontrivial real Lie algebras of dimension $3$ (Bianchi types I–IX) and all nontrivial complex Lie algebras of dimension $3$.

Recent medical research has shown growing interest in applying deep learning techniques to model survival data. This paper introduces a Bayesian hierarchical deep neural network model designed for both modeling and predicting survival outcomes. Unlike prior methods, this new approach offers not only point estimates of survival probability but also quantifies the associated uncertainty, a feature that is vital for predictive modeling and informed decision-making. The statistical advantages of these point and uncertainty estimates were validated through simulation studies and analysis of real-world data. Additionally, Python code implementing the proposed methodology is made available.

Emotions offer a natural communication channel that enhances the existing multi-modal capabilities of social robots, such as text and speech, across various domains. To explore the advantages of incorporating emotions into Search and Rescue (SAR) robots, we conducted three online studies involving 112, 223, and 151 participants. The first experiment assessed the feasibility of transmitting SAR-related information through robotic emotions, establishing mappings between specific SAR scenarios and emotional states. The second study employed Affect Control Theory as a more adaptable alternative for generating these mappings, allowing for adjustments across different emotion sets and robot types. In the third experiment, we developed affective expressions for an appearance-constrained outdoor research robot using LEDs as the expressive medium. By applying these expressions in various simulated SAR scenarios, we evaluated their impact on the situational awareness of participants acting as rescue workers. Our findings and proposed methodologies yield (a) insights into how emotions can facilitate message conveyance within SAR contexts and (b) evidence supporting the effectiveness of integrating emotions as a communication modality in simulated SAR environments.

The total irregularity of a simple undirected graph $G$, represented by $irr_t(G)$, is defined as $irr_t(G) = \frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{u,v \in V(G)}|d(u) - d(v)|$. This paper introduces the concept of edge-transformation regarding the total irregularity of simple undirected graphs containing at least one cut edge. Additionally, we propose the notion of an edge-joint connecting two simple undirected graphs. Furthermore, we extend the definition of total irregularity to simple directed graphs based on in-degree and out-degree, designating these new invariants as total in-irregularity and total out-irregularity, respectively. The study initiates an investigation into these parameters for both simple undirected graphs and simple digraphs.

In the field of speech enhancement, complex neural networks have demonstrated significant potential because of their ability to effectively handle complex-valued spectra. While most recent methodologies primarily target wide-band signals at 16 kHz, research into super wide-band (32 kHz) or full-band (48 kHz) denoising remains scarce, largely due to the challenges in modeling extended frequency ranges, particularly high-frequency components. This paper presents a substantial extension of our prior deep complex convolution recurrent neural network (DCCRN) into a super wide-band variant, termed S-DCCRN, designed for 32 kHz speech denoising. To achieve this, we introduce a cascaded sub-band and full-band processing module comprising two lightweight DCCRNs: one processes sub-band signals while the other handles full-band signals, thereby leveraging both local and global frequency information. Furthermore, rather than relying solely on STFT features as input, we employ an end-to-end trained complex feature encoder to refine information across various frequency bands. A corresponding complex feature decoder then maps these features back to the time-frequency domain. Additionally, we implement a learnable spectrum compression technique to modulate the energy of different frequency bands, facilitating more efficient neural network learning. The proposed S-DCCRN model outperforms PercepNet and other competitive approaches, achieving state-of-the-art results in both speech quality and intelligibility. Ablation studies further validate the efficacy of each proposed contribution.

Supersymmetry typically results in a scalar condensate forming along the potential's flat directions following cosmological inflation. Since this condensate is generally unstable, it often breaks apart into non-topological solitons known as Q-balls. The gravitational waves generated during this fragmentation process are potentially detectable by observatories such as LISA, LIGO, and BBO, providing a valuable probe into the early universe and physics at extremely high energy scales.

We present a general bipartite-like framework and Schmidt decomposition for any pure state of $N$ indistinguishable fermions, utilizing states composed of $M<N$ and $(N-M)$ fermions. This approach is intrinsically linked to reduced $M$- and $(N-M)$-body density matrices (DMs), which share an identical spectrum in these states. Within this context, the notion of $M$-body entanglement arises naturally, extending the concept of one-body entanglement. We subsequently derive rigorous majorization relations for the normalized $M$-body DMs, demonstrating that the associated entropy does not increase on average under specific operations where these DMs serve as post-measurement states. Furthermore, this entropy acts as an upper limit for the average bipartite entanglement entropy produced by operations transforming the original state into a bipartite configuration of $M$ and $N-M$ effectively distinguishable fermions. Additionally, we provide analytic evaluations of the $M$-body DM spectra for certain strongly correlated fermionic states.

Utilizing archival Chandra X-ray data from a large sample of dwarf galaxies, we investigated the presence of accreting intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs), which are anticipated to reside in such environments and exhibit distinct luminosity and spectral characteristics. We announce the identification of an X-ray source linked to an Abell 85 dwarf galaxy that aligns with the IMBH profile. With an estimated stellar mass of $2 \times 10^8$ $M_\odot$, the host galaxy represents one of the least massive systems known to potentially harbor an accreting black hole. This source is visible in the soft X-ray band (below 1 keV) but remains undetected at higher energies. Its X-ray luminosity is approximately $10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$, rendering it nearly three orders of magnitude brighter than the most luminous stellar-mass supersoft sources. Based on the black hole mass–stellar mass correlation, the black hole's mass falls within the intermediate range. Additionally, the expectation that supersoft emission correlates with high accretion rates near the Eddington limit yields another estimate of an intermediate mass. We propose that the observed $\approx$ 1.8 kpc offset of the X-ray source from the galactic center stems from galaxy interactions, a hypothesis supported by literature linking black hole activity to such interactions.

The anomalous magnetic moment of the muon remains a focal point of research because of the growing discrepancy between experimental results [1,2] and Standard Model predictions [3]. The hadronic light-by-light scattering component is one of two diagrammatic structures currently limiting theoretical precision. To enhance accuracy in a data-driven framework based on dispersion theory [4,5], we have established several short-distance constraints on the correlation function involving four electromagnetic currents. This paper details our prior advances within the purely short-distance domain and outlines ongoing work in the Melnikov-Vainshtein limit.

This study introduces a stabilization technique for quantum Gaussian states using continuous measurement. The dynamics of the open quantum system are characterized via the quantum stochastic master equation. We establish necessary and sufficient criteria ensuring the existence of a unique stabilizing steady Gaussian state. These criteria are significantly less restrictive than those required by previous methods relying on environment engineering. Furthermore, we outline the parametric requirements for generating any arbitrary pure Gaussian state. Compared to dissipation-induced approaches, this method offers greater flexibility in selecting the system Hamiltonian and system-environment coupling operators. Additionally, we address stabilizing conditions applicable to scenarios with imperfect measurement efficiency. These findings are expected to facilitate the practical experimental realization of quantum Gaussian states.

RFID tags are widely deployed globally to provide cost-effective identification for numerous everyday items. A primary limitation of RFID technology is the inability of tags to support energy-intensive cryptographic methods. Consequently, Radio Fingerprinting (RFP) has emerged as a promising solution, utilizing inherent imperfections in a tag's wireless circuitry to detect large-scale RFID clones. However, recent studies indicate that fluctuating channel conditions can substantially reduce RFP accuracy. This paper presents the first extensive investigation into RFP under dynamic channel conditions. We conducted a massive data collection effort using a testbed comprising 200 identical, off-the-shelf RFID tags and a software-defined radio (SDR) reader. Data were gathered across various tag-reader distances in an over-the-air setup, and to simulate implanted tags, we also collected data with two types of porcine meat placed between the tag and the reader. Utilizing this comprehensive dataset, we trained and evaluated multiple convolutional neural network (CNN) classifiers across diverse channel scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that training and testing under mismatched channel conditions severely degrade classifier performance. To address this, we introduce a novel training framework combining federated machine learning (FML) and data augmentation (DAG) to enhance accuracy. Extensive experiments show that (i) our FML method increases accuracy by up to 48%, and (ii) our DAG approach further boosts FML performance by up to 31%. To our knowledge, this is the first study to experimentally validate the effectiveness of FML and DAG on a large-scale device population. We are making our fully labeled 200-GB RFID waveform dataset, along with all source code and trained models, available to the research community.

Utilizing data from the Michelson Doppler Imager (MDI) on the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO), we created a computational algorithm to automatically detect bipolar magnetic regions (BMRs) within active regions and analyze their statistical characteristics. A magnetic pole (positive or negative) is classified as part of a BMR if it exhibits an absolute strength exceeding 55 G and an area greater than 250 pixel² (495 Mm²); a BMR is then defined as a positive-negative pole pair separated by the shortest area-weighted distance. Applying this methodology to MDI synoptic magnetograms from Carrington Rotation 1909 (May 6, 1996) through Rotation 2104 (December 10, 2010), we identified 2,234 BMRs: 1,005 in the northern hemisphere and 1,229 in the southern. Our analysis reveals that BMR parameters, such as latitude, separation, fragmentation, and strength, closely resemble those of active regions (ARs). Furthermore, using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), we determined that the frequency distributions of BMR occurrences regarding area size and magnetic flux follow a power-law pattern. Additionally, orientation angles align with Hale's Polarity Laws but show a slight deviation toward the solar equator. Consistent with prior studies, we observed the dependence of orientation angles on latitude for normal BMRs during the 23rd solar cycle and confirmed the presence of north-south asymmetry in these regions.

Classifying functional data presents a significant challenge when attempting to leverage traditional classifiers, primarily because functional data are inherently infinite-dimensional. This intrinsic dimensionality prevents direct application of classical methods and often leads to poor performance due to the curse of dimensionality. To overcome this limitation, we suggest projecting functional data onto a specific direction and subsequently constructing a distance-weighted discrimination (DWD) classifier based on the resulting projection scores. The optimal projection direction is determined by minimizing an empirical risk function that incorporates the DWD-specific loss function within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This approach not only mitigates overfitting but also retains the advantageous characteristics of DWD classifiers. Furthermore, this framework is generalized to handle classification scenarios involving scalar covariates alongside functional data. Unlike prior studies, we derive a non-asymptotic bound for the estimation error of the relative misclassification rate. Additionally, simulation experiments and a real-world application demonstrate that, in finite samples, our proposed classifiers achieve superior prediction accuracy compared to several commonly used functional classification methods.

The LHC is preparing an upgrade initiative aimed at raising instantaneous luminosity to approximately $5-7.5\times10^{34}~\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ by 2028, with the potential to accumulate 3000–4500 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity by 2039. This High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) project necessitates a "Phase-2" upgrade for the detectors. Existing CMS components, specifically the Outer Tracker and the Phase-1 Pixel Detector, are already operating beyond their design limits and cannot withstand the intensified radiation of the HL-LHC era. Consequently, CMS must implement entirely new hardware to meet these stringent operational requirements and maximize data yield. The new Outer Tracker will additionally incorporate trigger functionalities. To realize these objectives, R&D efforts have explored various configurations for both the Outer Tracker and the Pixel Inner Tracker. The proposed solutions will enable the inclusion of tracking data at the Level-1 trigger stage. This discussion outlines the design selections for the tracker upgrades, highlighting key technological decisions and associated research activities.

This study investigates nonequilibrium electrons and holes in intrinsic graphene at low temperatures under far- and mid-infrared (IR) radiation across a broad spectrum of intensities. Carrier energy distributions are computed using a quasiclassic kinetic equation that incorporates energy relaxation via acoustic phonons and radiative generation-recombination processes driven by both thermal radiation and photoexcitation from incident light. Results indicate that nonequilibrium distributions arise from the competition between weak acoustic phonon relaxation and generation-recombination mechanisms, alongside pumping saturation effects. Consequently, at high intensities, carrier distribution functions display plateaus near the pumping region due to saturation. Furthermore, sufficiently strong mid-IR pumping can induce population inversion below the pumping energy. The DC conductivity of graphene versus pumping intensity shows significant nonlinearity, featuring a sub-linear regime at moderate intensities and saturation at high levels. However, even within a very wide intensity range, increases in pumping lead to only modest gains in carrier concentration and DC conductivity. Finally, graphene's conductivity under mid-IR irradiation demonstrates high sensitivity to the specific mechanisms governing carrier momentum relaxation.

This paper demonstrates the existence of equilibrium in choice for games in choice form, a concept recently introduced by A. Stefanescu, M. Ferrara, and M. V. Stefanescu. Our findings bridge recent developments with earlier methodologies concerning games in normal form or qualitative games.

The latitude where the ascending branch of the Hadley circulation reaches in the summer hemisphere is a key yet poorly understood feature of Earth's climate. This study introduces a predictive, analytical theory for that latitude, grounded in the concept of supercritical forcing. Supercriticality defines the minimum reach of a large-scale circulation by analyzing the angular momentum and absolute vorticity distributions of a hypothetical state where the circulation does not exist. We explicitly model this state using a latitude-by-latitude radiative-convective equilibrium (RCE) simulation. Its depth-averaged temperature profile is well-approximated by a simple analytical formula that rises linearly with $\sin\varphi$ (where $\varphi$ is latitude) from the winter to the summer pole. This relationship results in a one-third power-law scaling between the extent of supercritical forcing and the thermal Rossby number. Furthermore, moist and dry idealized General Circulation Model (GCM) simulations driven by solsticial forcing across various planetary rotation rates confirm that the ascending edge latitudes generally follow this scaling.

We are releasing a COVID-19 news dataset comprising over 10,000 links to Swiss media articles about the Coronavirus pandemic, dating from early January 2020. This collection is valuable for analyzing the Swiss media's response to the outbreak and extracting meaningful insights for future research. We aim for this dataset to assist both researchers and the public in producing findings that enhance our analysis of the pandemic and deepen our understanding of the unfolding events.

A convex polygon $Q$ is inscribed within a convex polygon $P$ when each side of $P$ includes at least one vertex from $Q$. We introduce algorithms to determine the minimum area and minimum perimeter convex polygon inscribed in any given convex $n$-gon, achieving $O(n)$ and $O(n^3)$ time complexities, respectively. Additionally, we explore other variations of this problem.

This paper introduces a Monte-Carlo approach to simulate fluid flow adjacent to a solid boundary. The proposed random vortex method utilizes reflection and perturbation techniques to model the dynamics of vortices. Building upon this framework, a Monte-Carlo simulation is implemented, followed by several computational experiments analyzing flows in the vicinity of the solid wall.

This study introduces a straightforward initialization strategy for word embeddings grounded in a dense, independent co-occurrence model. Preliminary findings indicate that this approach is competitive and merits deeper exploration. Specifically, using information-theoretic minimum description length (MDL) probing, we show that our method, EigenNoise, rivals the performance of empirically trained GloVe even without any pre-training data. We present these early results to highlight the potential of this competitive initialization in the absence of pre-training, while encouraging future research into smarter initialization schemes driven by harmonic linguistic structure theory. Furthermore, applying this theory offers a new and effective interpretation of recent findings that clarify the distributional information captured by linguistic representations and their contrastive distributions.

A significant portion of binary neutron star mergers is anticipated to produce long-lived neutron star remnants, substantially changing the multi-messenger signals of these events. This work expands upon current models of magnetar-driven kilonovae to investigate the variety of kilonovae and their afterglows. By examining the influence of magnetic field strength—currently uncertain—we analyze the resulting electromagnetic signatures based on external dipolar and internal toroidal fields. These two factors dictate the balance between magnetic-dipole spindown and gravitational-wave spindown (caused by magnetic-field deformation) in rapidly rotating remnants. Our findings indicate that even when gravitational-wave emission dominates, a kilonova powered by a magnetar will be markedly brighter than one without an engine, as a larger fraction of spin-down luminosity is thermalized in this regime. Conversely, systems with minimal gravitational-wave emission may yield kilonovae indistinguishable from standard ones without early-epoch data; however, since most energy in these cases accelerates ejecta, they generate brighter afterglows that peak sooner. To conceal the magnetar's presence in both the kilonova and afterglow, the rotational energy transferred to the ejecta must remain below $\lesssim 10^{-3}-10^{-2} E_{\rm rot}$. Finally, we outline diagnostic tools for identifying magnetar-driven kilonovae in serendipitous observations and compare them to other potential magnetar-driven explosions, including superluminous supernovae and broad-line supernovae Ic.

Non-orthogonal state discrimination is fundamental to key quantum information applications, including computing and cryptography, making the identification of optimal discrimination scenarios critical. We experimentally examine strategies for optimally distinguishing two non-orthogonal states under a fixed rate of inconclusive outcomes (FRIO). The primary benefit of the FRIO approach lies in its ability to bridge the gap between unambiguous and minimum error discrimination by simply varying the inconclusive outcome rate. We introduce a flexible experimental framework capable of executing optimal FRIO measurements for any pair of non-orthogonal states, regardless of their a priori probabilities or the chosen inconclusive rate. By adjusting free parameters within the FRIO protocol, we implemented the scheme using qubit states encoded in the polarization of single photons generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Furthermore, we utilized an innovative double-path Sagnac interferometer to carry out the necessary three-outcome non-projective measurement, achieving results that align closely with theoretical predictions. This work offers a practical toolkit for diverse quantum state discrimination strategies based on the FRIO scheme, promising significant advantages for both fundamental quantum theory research and practical quantum information applications.

We report our calculations of the leptonic decay constants fDs and fD+ using the MILC collaboration's 2+1 flavor asqtad gauge ensembles. Our methodology employs clover heavy quarks under the Fermilab interpretation alongside improved staggered light quarks. The simultaneous chiral and continuum extrapolation, used to derive both constants, incorporates partially-quenched lattice data at lattice spacings of approximately 0.09, 0.12, and 0.15 fm. We have implemented several recent refinements in our analysis: a) incorporating fit terms for leading-order heavy-quark discretization effects, b) adopting a more precise r1 value consistent with our previous D and B meson investigations, and c) retuning the input bare charm masses based on this updated r1. Our preliminary findings yield fDs = 260 +/- 10 MeV and fD+ = 217 +/- 10 MeV.

This study examines a highly complex plasma environment comprising Cairns nonthermal electrons, adiabatically warm inertial ions, and stationary positively charged dust (PCD) particles. Utilizing the pseudo-potential method, which accommodates arbitrary amplitude, time-independent ion-acoustic (IA) solitary waves (SWs) and double layers (DLs), the research investigates how PCD species, nonthermal electrons, and adiabatic ion temperature influence these structures. Findings indicate that the inclusion of PCD species lowers the phase speed of IA waves, thereby facilitating the formation of subsonic compressive SWs in such plasmas. Conversely, increasing either the adiabatic ion temperature or the population of nonthermal/fast electrons diminishes the likelihood of subsonic SWs, promoting a transition to supersonic ones. Furthermore, once the nonthermal parameter exceeds a specific threshold, both positive and negative potential supersonic SWs and DLs with exclusively negative potentials emerge. The paper concludes by briefly outlining applications of these findings in various space environments—such as Earth's mesosphere, cometary tails, and Jupiter's magnetosphere—as well as in laboratory settings where warm ions, nonthermal electrons, and PCD species are observed.

This work outlines the coordination of a decentralized swarm of rotary-wing UAV-relays designed to enhance the coverage and service capacity of a terrestrial base station. The primary objective is to minimize the average service latency for transmission requests from ground users, assuming Poisson arrivals, while adhering to an average power constraint for the UAVs. Utilizing rate adaptation to exploit the stochastic nature of air-to-ground channels, we first derive an optimal control policy for a single relay using a semi-Markov decision process framework combined with competitive swarm optimization for trajectory planning. This approach is structured through a multiscale decomposition: outer-layer decisions regarding radial wait velocities and final positions optimize the long-term trade-off between delay and power, while inner-layer decisions concerning angular velocities, service scheduling, and trajectories greedily minimize instantaneous delay-power costs. Extending this to UAV swarms through replication and consensus-driven command-and-control, the policy is integrated with heuristics for spread maximization and conflict resolution. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of average service latency and per-UAV power consumption: it achieves 11x faster data payload delivery compared to static UAV-relay deployments and 2x faster performance than a deep-Q network solution. Notably, a single relay utilizing our scheme surpasses three relays operating under a joint successive convex approximation policy by 62%.

This study presents the development of Generalized Rough Polyharmonic Splines (GRPS) within a Bayesian context, specifically targeting multiscale partial differential equations featuring rough coefficients. We establish that the optimal coarse basis can be automatically generated by randomizing the original PDEs using an appropriate prior distribution and computing the conditional expectation based on partial edge or derivative data. Furthermore, we demonstrate the quasi-optimal localization and approximation characteristics of these derived bases, substantiating our theoretical findings through numerical experiments.

Stellar flares are defined by sudden bursts of electromagnetic radiation within stellar atmospheres. While previous knowledge largely relied on photometric observations that failed to detect plasma motions, analysis of LAMOST DR7 spectroscopic data has revealed a specific flare on an M4-type star. This event featured an impulsive rise followed by a gradual decline in H$\alpha$ line intensity, with a total radiated energy via H$\alpha$ estimated at approximately $10^{33}$ erg. During the flare, the H$\alpha$ line exhibited a Voigt profile, likely resulting from Stark pressure broadening caused by a sharp increase in electron density and/or opacity broadening due to intense non-thermal heating. Notably, an enhancement was detected in the red wing of the H$\alpha$ profile following the initial intensity surge, indicating plasma receding from Earth at speeds of 100–200 km s$^{-1}$. Drawing parallels with solar flare mechanisms, this red wing enhancement may stem from flare-driven coronal rain, chromospheric condensation, or a filament/prominence eruption characterized by non-radial backward propagation or strong magnetic suppression. The estimated mass of this moving plasma is on the order of $10^{15}$ kg.

Robots operating in domestic or industrial settings must acquire the ability to utilize objects as tools for task execution, such as using a tray to transport items. This work addresses the challenge of learning commonsense knowledge regarding when a tool is applicable and how to combine multiple tools to achieve complex, human-directed goals. We present TANGO, a new neural architecture designed to forecast task-specific tool interactions, which is trained on demonstrations provided by human instructors guiding a virtual robot. TANGO employs a graph neural network to encode the world state, capturing both objects and their symbolic relationships. The model leverages goal information and action history to focus on relevant scene elements before decoding the symbolic actions required for execution. A key contribution is the model's capacity to generalize to unseen environments where familiar tools are absent but novel alternatives exist. By enriching the environmental representation with pre-trained embeddings from a knowledge base, TANGO achieves effective generalization to new settings. Experiments demonstrate that this approach yields an absolute improvement of 60.5% to 78.9% over baseline methods in predicting successful symbolic plans for a simulated mobile manipulator in unseen scenarios.

The proliferation of modern mobile devices and tracking sensors has generated massive daily data volumes, necessitating innovative methodologies to extract meaningful insights from this vast information. In response, researchers have created various trajectory classification algorithms to annotate tracking data. This study introduces a novel approach that leverages image-based representations of trajectories, termed TraClets, to classify paths using computer vision techniques in an intuitive, human-like manner. The proposed method was evaluated on several real-world datasets, comparing its performance against other state-of-the-art trajectory classification algorithms. Experimental results indicate that TraClets achieves classification accuracy comparable to, and often superior to, existing methods, establishing it as a universal, high-precision solution for trajectory classification.

Current audio-only hearing aids struggle significantly in environments dominated by overwhelming noise. In contrast, next-generation audio-visual (lip-reading driven) hearing aids offer a promising path toward greater audio intelligibility. However, their widespread adoption faces hurdles related to high data rates, low latency, minimal computational complexity, and privacy concerns. To overcome these obstacles, this work proposes a framework integrating 5G Cloud-Radio Access Networks, the Internet of Things (IoT), and robust privacy algorithms. This envisioned 5G IoT-enabled secure audio-visual hearing aid transmits encrypted, compressed visual and audio data and receives real-time, enhanced, reconstructed speech, thereby mitigating cybersecurity threats like location tracking and eavesdropping. Security is ensured through real-time, lightweight audio-visual encryption, while speech enhancement is achieved by processing received AV information in the cloud using a combination of deep learning and analytical acoustic modeling. To handle computational load and optimize performance in real-time, the heavy lifting of deep learning and big data optimization is offloaded to the cloud. Specifically, this study presents three key contributions: (1) a 5G IoT-based secure audio-visual hearing aid framework targeting a round-trip latency of 5ms and a data rate of 100 Mbps; (2) a real-time, lightweight audio-visual encryption method; and (3) a cloud-based, lip-reading-driven deep learning approach for speech enhancement. Critical analysis confirms the technology's potential to deliver high-quality speech reconstruction and secure mobile audio-visual hearing aid communication.

Van der Waerden's theorem asserts that for any positive integers $k$ and $r$, there is a minimal integer $n = w(k,r)$, known as the van der Waerden number, such that any $r$-coloring of the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ guarantees a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression. This work examines two related variants: the numbers $n = n(AP_D,k;r)$, representing the smallest $n$ ensuring a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression with a common difference from the set $D$ in any $r$-coloring of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, and the numbers $n = \Delta(D,k;r)$, the smallest $n$ where every $r$-coloring of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ yields a sequence $x_1 < \dots < x_k$ such that the gaps between consecutive terms belong to $D$. Focusing on the scenario where $D$ consists of Fibonacci numbers $F$, we provide tighter bounds for the maximum $r$ for which $n(AP_F,k;r)$ and $\Delta(F,k;r)$ are defined for all $k$. Additionally, we present computational findings regarding $\Delta(D,k;r)$ for various other sets $D$.

This study reports ALMA 870μm and JCMT SCUBA2 850μm dust continuum data for a sample of strongly lensed, optically dark galaxies within cluster environments. Achieving median rms sensitivities of approximately 0.11 mJy and 0.44 mJy respectively—with the latter nearing the confusion limit at 850μm—this work constitutes one of the most sensitive searches to date for dust emission in such galaxies. Dust emission was detected in 12 of the 15 galaxies at a significance level exceeding 3.8σ, yielding an 80% detection rate. Leveraging gravitational lensing, these observations attain a limiting flux three times deeper than previous surveys conducted in blank fields. De-lensed infrared luminosities are estimated between log(L_IR) = 11.5 and 12.7 L☉, corresponding to dust-obscured star formation rates (SFRs) ranging from 30 to 520 M☉/yr. Stellar population modeling of optical-to-NIR photometry indicates a median redshift of z = 4.26 and a de-lensed stellar mass of log(M_*) = 10.78 M☉. These galaxies contribute a lensing-corrected star-formation rate density at least ten times higher than that of equivalently massive UV-selected galaxies at z > 3. The findings imply a previously missing population of massive, star-forming galaxies in the early Universe, potentially dominating the SFR density at the high-mass end. Furthermore, five optically dark galaxies are found within r < 50 arcsec in a single cluster field, suggesting a physically significant overdensity structure with a confidence level >99.974% based on Poisson statistics. Future spectroscopic follow-up using ALMA and JWST is essential to verify if this structure is associated with a protocluster at similar redshifts.

We present a finite-dimensional extension of free probability tailored for rectangular matrices, which involves manipulating the singular values of polynomials. We demonstrate that this framework reproduces the standard transforms found in free probability and exhibits asymptotic convergence from the rectangular finite case to the rectangular free case. Furthermore, we establish that classical probabilistic results, including the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, can be explicitly formulated within this new setting where random variables are substituted by polynomials.

Although the supernova remnant (SNR) G35.6-0.4 exhibits a non-thermal radio shell, no X-ray or gamma-ray counterparts have been identified to date. A TeV source, HESS J1858+020, was discovered nearby and appears spatially linked to clouds located at 3.6 kpc. The objective of this study is to better understand the origin of HESS J1858+020 by investigating the connection between SNR cosmic rays (CRs) and clouds via Fermi-LAT analysis and hadronic modeling. The methodology involved performing a Fermi-LAT analysis to examine GeV emission within and surrounding the SNR, utilizing existing multi-wavelength data to explore SNR physics, and constructing a hadronic model based on runaway CRs to account for GeV-TeV observations. The results reveal a hard GeV source (SrcX2) spatially aligned with both HESS J1858+020 and a molecular cloud complex at 3.6 kpc, alongside a soft GeV source (SrcX1) at the SNR's northern edge. The GeV spectrum of SrcX2 seamlessly connects with the TeV spectrum of HESS J1858+020, forming a continuous gamma-ray spectrum spanning from several GeV to tens of TeV with a power-law index of approximately 2.15. Several observational pieces of evidence support the hypothesis that this is a middle-aged SNR. Furthermore, a hadronic model utilizing runaway CRs from the SNR successfully explains the GeV-TeV emission observed at HESS J1858+020, requiring a diffusion coefficient significantly lower than the Galactic average.

Motile organisms typically navigate and explore their habitats using a limited spatial perception of their environment. However, conventional search models generally rely exclusively on immediate, local sensory data. To understand how a restricted perceptual horizon influences ecological search, we introduce a framework for optimal navigation that integrates random walk concepts with optimal control theory. Our findings indicate that while local strategies remain optimal for both extremely short and very long search durations, finite perception accelerates convergence and boosts search efficiency during the transient time scales characteristic of biological systems. Searchers can sustain the advantages of a finite horizon by adjusting their response sensitivity to match the spatial scale of environmental stimuli, and these benefits are further amplified when agents interact through heightened consensus within subpopulations. Ultimately, this framework clarifies the significance of spatial perception and transient dynamics in search movements and collective environmental sensing.

V-shaped three-level atoms interacting with light can support dark states. We investigate such a system where the atoms are coherently coupled to the two quadratures of a dissipative cavity. The interaction between the atomic energy levels and dissipation causes the phase diagram of this open system to differ significantly from its closed counterpart. Specifically, this interplay stabilizes a continuous manifold of dark and nearly dark excited many-body states with inverted populations as steady states. These states exhibit multistability, which can be detected through their unique fluctuations and excitation spectra, as well as the system's Liouvillian dynamics that are highly responsive to ramp protocols. Experimentally, this model can be realized by mapping the two higher-energy modes onto orthogonal density-modulated states within a bosonic quantum gas. Such an implementation paves the way for applications including quantum optical random walks and microscopy with subwavelength spatial resolution.

It is generally anticipated that the emitting current density ($J$) in field emission (FE) will transition into space-charge-limited current (SCLC) when charge accumulates within a gap of spacing $D$ under a sufficiently high voltage $V$. However, this study identifies a unique phenomenon where the expected two-stage shift from FE to SCLC does not hold for emitters that do not follow the traditional Fowler-Nordheim (FN) law. This anomaly occurs because non-FN emitters cannot inject enough charge at high voltages to maintain SCLC. By utilizing a generalized FN scaling of $\ln\left(J/V^k\right) \propto - 1/V$, we identify a \emph{critical exponent} $k_c = 3/2$. When $k < k_c$, unusual behaviors emerge: (a) FE persists at small $D$ without transitioning to SCLC regardless of how large $V$ becomes, and (b) a three-stage transition occurs at large $D$, moving from FE to SCLC and then reverting to FE. Conversely, for any $k > k_c$, the standard two-stage transition from FE to SCLC is guaranteed for all $D$, a condition that also encompasses the conventional FN law where $k = 2$. We explicitly illustrate these distinct transitions using various unconventional FE models with $k \neq 2$. Furthermore, through normalized modeling, our results reveal the complex interaction between source-limited FE and bulk-limited SCLC across a broad spectrum of operating conditions.

Beginning with a specific topological invariant, we demonstrate the construction of a topological field theory characterized by a finite set of Feynman diagrams and an amplitude dependent on gauge-invariant objects that is a function of said invariant. This framework applies to cases such as the Gauss linking number and abelian BF models, which have proven effective in the statistical mechanics of polymers. In this study, we show that an appropriate generalization of the BF model extends its applicability to polymer dynamics, accounting for non-static polymer trajectories that evolve over time.

To identify the most probable failure scenarios within specific operational domains, critical-scenario-based testing is widely recognized as an effective strategy for guiding developers in refining algorithms. However, current state-of-the-art generation methods, which typically rely on random search or reinforcement learning, are computationally expensive and ill-suited for testing evolving development targets or real-time systems. This paper introduces a Real-Time Critical-Scenario-Generation (RTCSG) framework to overcome these limitations. Our approach employs an aggressive-driving algorithm to control virtual agent vehicles, utilizes a specialized cost function to steer scenarios toward critical states, and implements a self-adaptive coefficient iteration to ensure robust performance across varying conditions. This method allows for the direct generation of critical scenarios for black-box systems, making real-time critical-scenario testing a practical reality. Simulation results demonstrate that our approach yields a higher volume of critical scenarios and greater stability compared to existing methods under most conditions. Furthermore, for real-time testing applications, our method achieves an efficiency improvement of approximately 16-fold.

Accessing information within non-linear, high-dimensional probability distributions remains a fundamental challenge in contemporary statistics. Traditionally, estimators extending beyond point estimates fall into two categories: Variational Inference (VI) and Markov-Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC). Although MCMC methods have been developed to leverage the geometric properties of continuous distributions for enhanced efficiency, VI approaches typically ignore geometry. This study addresses that gap by introducing geometric Variational Inference (geoVI), a technique grounded in Riemannian geometry and the Fisher information metric. By constructing a coordinate transformation linking the Riemannian manifold defined by this metric to Euclidean space, the method renders the distribution in the induced coordinate system sufficiently simple to permit accurate approximation via a normal distribution. Additionally, the algorithmic framework enables efficient implementation, as demonstrated across various examples, from low-dimensional illustrations to complex, non-linear hierarchical Bayesian inverse problems involving thousands of dimensions.

The majority of massive stars reside in binary or higher-order systems, where the influence of a companion can fundamentally reshape their life cycles through binary interactions. These interacting pairs serve as crucial astrophysical sites for investigating compact objects. Over the past twenty years, binary population synthesis (BPS) has been widely employed to explain observations of compact-object binaries and unravel the physical mechanisms driving their formation. We introduce POSYDON, a new BPS code that integrates comprehensive stellar-structure and binary-evolution models—powered by the MESA code—across the entire evolutionary timeline of binaries. POSYDON facilitates a self-consistent analysis of physical phenomena in both stellar and binary evolution, encompassing realistic mass-transfer dynamics and stability assessments, internal angular-momentum transport and tidal effects, stellar core dimensions, mass-transfer rates, and orbital periods. This work outlines the detailed methodology and implementation of POSYDON, covering the underlying physics of stellar and binary evolution, extensive grids of detailed single- and binary-star models, and the post-processing, classification, and interpolation techniques developed for these grids. Additionally, it addresses the handling of evolutionary phases not covered by pre-calculated grids. The initial release of POSYDON focuses on binaries with massive primary stars (potential progenitors of neutron stars or black holes) at solar metallicity.

In numerous machine learning applications, data arrives sequentially in large batches over time, requiring practitioners to determine how to allocate their computational resources to maximize performance at any given moment. While online learning theory for convex optimization recommends using data immediately upon arrival, this approach may be suboptimal for deep non-linear networks, especially when multiple passes over each batch render the data distribution non-i.i.d. This paper formalizes this setting in the simplest case where each chunk originates from the same underlying distribution and empirically investigates key questions: how long should a learner delay training on new data, what architecture is most suitable, and whether model capacity should increase as more data is observed. We evaluate this framework using convolutional neural networks on standard computer vision benchmarks and a large-scale transformer model on a language modeling task. The code is available at \url{www.github.com/facebookresearch/ALMA}.

This work investigates the connection between classical cumulants and Koszul brackets, demonstrating that cumulants represent an exponential variant of the latter. Furthermore, subject to specific technical conditions, we establish that both frameworks align with standard homological perturbation theory in a meaningful way. Leveraging these findings, we offer novel proofs of the homotopy transfer Theorem for $L_\infty$ and $IBL_\infty$ algebras, utilizing the symmetrized tensor trick and the standard perturbation Lemma as done in typical $A_\infty$ contexts. Additionally, we present a new homotopy transfer Theorem for commutative $BV_\infty$ algebras, formulated according to Kravchenko's definition. In the process, we also propose a fresh definition for morphisms between commutative $BV_\infty$ algebras.

Data-driven, model-free analytics are well-suited for discovering and forecasting complex, nonlinear systems. Techniques functioning within the system's state-space must rely on either an explicit multidimensional framework or one approximated from observed data. Because observational data often contain noise, there is a risk that this noise corrupts the state-space representation, thereby reducing analytical performance. This study assesses the combination of empirical mode decomposition with empirical dynamic modeling, a method we call empirical mode modeling, to enhance the information content of state-space representations despite noisy conditions. Evaluations across a mathematical model and an ecologically significant geophysical application, utilizing three distinct state-space representations, indicate that empirical mode modeling could be a valuable approach for data-driven, model-free state-space analysis when noise is present.

Edge computing serves as a fundamental driver for enabling Beyond 5G (B5G) and 6G networks. Given the exponential growth in traffic and computational requirements anticipated in future networks, Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) is regarded as a vital solution to deliver cloud-computing capabilities directly within the Radio Access Network (RAN), thereby positioning services closer to end users. While extensive research exists regarding MEC and its applications, there is limited discussion on the critical factors necessary for deploying MEC to satisfy the diverse needs of future applications. This article outlines key considerations for edge deployment in B5G/6G environments, covering aspects such as edge architecture, server placement and capacity, user density, and security. Additionally, we review state-of-the-art edge-centric services expected in future networks. The paper includes an experimental evaluation of edge-based service deployments, specifically focusing on video transcoding and deep learning inference. Finally, we offer valuable insights and identify open research challenges concerning edge computing for 6G networks.

Symmetry breaking and restoration in translational and rotational contexts within condensed matter systems are intrinsically linked to exotic phenomena such as superconductivity, magnetism, spin density waves, and charge density waves. The complex interplay among various order parameters frequently generates significant scientific debate, particularly regarding the relationship between charge density waves and superconductivity. In the compound La1.875Ba0.125CuO4 (LBCO), charge density wave domains are observed to be pinned on a nanometer scale. By employing coherent X-ray diffraction techniques, researchers can directly visualize domain structures associated with these symmetry alterations. This study extends Bragg Coherent Diffractive Imaging (BCDI) to cryogenic temperatures, where most quantum material phase transitions occur. Using BCDI, we tracked the structural evolution of LBCO microcrystals during the transition from the high-temperature-tetragonal (HTT) to the low-temperature-orthorhombic (LTO) phase. Our findings reveal the emergence of LTO domains near the transition temperature and demonstrate how domain dimensions change with temperature. Specifically, LTO domain size decreases as temperature drops and is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the orthorhombic distortion. Furthermore, the domain count aligns with secondary order parameter (or orthorhombic strain) measurements, exhibiting a critical exponent consistent with the 3D universality class.

This work analyzes the excitation spectrum of a two-component quasi-two-dimensional Bose-Einstein Condensate. We investigate the evolution of excitation characteristics across the transition from miscible to immiscible phases. Our findings indicate that bulk excitations resemble those of a single-component BEC, supplemented by interface bending modes. Furthermore, we examine how these excitations vary with changes in interaction strength.

Machine learning, and more recently Deep Learning, has successfully unlocked the immense potential of the vast data volumes generated globally across networks. While Deep Learning has rapidly become the preferred framework for numerous applications, its widespread adoption has been hindered by the centralization of computing resources and the necessity for data aggregation. Edge Computing addresses these issues by leveraging previously unused processing capabilities at the network's edge, giving rise to Edge Intelligence (EI) as a potent alternative for distributed learning. Deep Edge Intelligence (DEI), which combines Deep Learning with Edge Computing, represents a key area within this rapidly evolving field. This article outlines the primary constraints in deploying DEI, consolidating major research directions into Federated Learning, Distributed Computation, Compression Schemes, and Conditional Computation. Additionally, we discuss existing challenges and identify promising future research avenues.

The known cases for $1$-factorizations of an infinite complete equipartite graph $K_m[n]$ (consisting of $m$ parts of size $n$) with a vertex-regular automorphism group $G$ are limited to the scenario where $n=1$, $m$ is countable (yielding countable complete graphs), and $G$ is a finitely generated abelian group of order $m$. This paper demonstrates that a vertex-regular $1$-factorization of $K_m[n]$ under group $G$ exists if and only if $G$ possesses a subgroup $H$ of order $n$ such that the index of $H$ in $G$ is $m$. Additionally, we establish a sufficient condition for an infinite Cayley graph to admit a regular $1$-factorization and construct $1$-factorizations that include a specified subfactorization, where both possess a vertex-regular automorphism group.

We introduce an axisymmetric angle-dependent gap (ADG) state characterized by broken rotational symmetry within isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter. In this configuration, the deformation of neutron and proton Fermi spheres enhances pairing probabilities along the symmetry-breaking axis near the average Fermi surface. Our findings indicate that at high isospin asymmetries, this state exhibits both a larger gap magnitude and lower free energy compared to the angle-averaged gap state. These characteristics primarily arise from the coupling of distinct $m_j$ components of the pairing gap. Additionally, we observe that the transition from the ADG state to the normal state is second-order, and the ADG state disappears at a critical isospin asymmetry where the angle-averaged gap also vanishes.

This study pioneers the adaptation of conditional generative adversarial networks (cGAN) for image-to-image translation to learn both forward and inverse solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs). Although the proposed framework could serve as a surrogate for solving any PDE, this research specifically targets steady-state solutions of coupled hydro-mechanical processes within heterogeneous porous media. Addressing strongly heterogeneous material properties—which manifest as discontinuous features and variable coefficients in PDEs—requires specialized techniques for both forward and inverse modeling, as standard reduced-order modeling struggles to parameterize spatial heterogeneity effectively. To overcome these hurdles, we employ image-to-image translation to learn the necessary solution operators using a U-Net generator and a patch-based discriminator. Our findings demonstrate that this data-driven reduced-order model offers competitive predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and training speed compared to state-of-the-art data-driven methods for both forward and inverse problems.

Although self-supervised pretraining has enabled few-shot learning across numerous NLP tasks, these pretraining objectives are rarely tailored specifically for in-context few-shot scenarios. This paper introduces an intermediate training phase utilizing self-supervision between standard pretraining and downstream few-shot application, designed to explicitly instruct models on performing in-context few-shot learning. We evaluate four distinct self-supervised objectives across two benchmarks and demonstrate that this intermediate stage yields models that surpass strong baselines. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that factors such as the volume of training data and the diversity of objectives significantly impact downstream performance. Since human-annotated cross-task supervision and self-supervision are complementary, qualitative analysis indicates that models trained via self-supervision excel at adhering to task requirements.

Cross-domain alignment is fundamental to various applications, including machine translation and transfer learning. Recently, purely unsupervised techniques leveraging monolingual embeddings have effectively constructed bilingual lexicons without supervision. However, existing state-of-the-art methods concentrate solely on point vectors, despite the fact that distributional embeddings capture richer semantic information. This paper introduces a stochastic optimization approach designed to align probabilistic embeddings. We evaluate our method on unsupervised word translation by aligning embeddings trained on monolingual data. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields strong performance across multiple language pairs in the bilingual lexicon induction task, outperforming traditional point-vector-based methods.

In their 2003 publication in *Designs, Codes and Cryptography* (Vol. 29, pp. 149-164), Gohar M. Kyureghyan and Alexander Pott established the linear feedback polynomials for certain special cases of Sidel'nikov-Lempel-Cohn-Eastman sequences. Upon reviewing this work, we identified errors in Corollary 4 and Theorem 2, noting that numerous counterexamples exist which invalidate these claims. This note presents specific counterexamples to refute Corollary 4 and Theorem 2 from their paper.

Magnetic reconnection must disconnect open magnetic flux to maintain equilibrium against the injection of such flux caused by Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) and other eruptions. Leveraging recent improvements in heliospheric background subtraction, we have captured numerous instances of abrupt disconnection. These occurrences generate dense plasma clouds with unique shapes that can now be tracked from the corona through the inner solar system using heliospheric imaging. The initial morphology of each event reflects magnetic reconnection across a current sheet, resulting in a newly disconnected "U"-shaped flux loop that travels outward while gathering coronal and solar wind material.

We examined a specific event occurring on December 18, 2008, as it formed and accelerated at 20 m/s² up to 320 km/s. The feature expanded self-similarly until it left our field of view at 1.2 AU from the Sun. Based on acceleration data and photometric mass estimates, we calculated the coronal magnetic field strength to be 8 µT at 6 solar radii above the photosphere, with an entrained flux of 1.6×10¹¹ Wb (1.6×10¹⁹ Mx). We modeled the feature's propagation by equating the inferred magnetic tension force with accretion drag; this model aligns with the observed behavior and established solar wind parameters.
