Additionally, by analyzing the effective potential exterior to the event horizon, we delineate the parameter regions governing superradiant stability for dyonic string-theoretic black holes.

The jet colour ring, a new observable designed as a colour tagger, effectively distinguishes between the decay of a colour-singlet into two jets and a two-jet background arising from a different colour configuration. Simulation studies focusing on the production of a boosted Higgs boson decaying into two b-quarks alongside an associated electroweak boson demonstrated that the jet colour ring exhibits significant discriminatory power compared to other observables. These findings suggest a broad range of opportunities for future research.

We restructure perturbation theory for neutrino oscillations in matter using an expansion parameter defined by the ratio of solar to atmospheric $\Delta m^2$ scales. Departing from prior studies, we employ a renormalized basis that incorporates specific first-order effects directly into the zeroth-order Hamiltonian. This novel framework yields an exceptional property: the neutrino oscillation probability in matter mirrors the vacuum structure up to first order in the expansion parameter. This approach not only streamlines the physical interpretation of the equations but also renders the oscillation probability expressions remarkably concise. For instance, the $\nu_e$ disappearance probability at this order adopts a straightforward two-flavor form with suitably redefined mixing angles and $\Delta m^2$. More broadly, all oscillation probabilities can be expressed in a universal format featuring channel-discrimination coefficients of $0$, $\pm1$, or simple functions of $\theta_{23}$. Although these formulas are compact, they encompass all-order effects of $\theta_{13}$ and the matter potential, accurate to first order in our expansion parameter.

This work revisits the rigorous mathematical underpinnings of density functional theory, incorporating infinitesimal (nonstandard) techniques. It provides a comprehensive analysis of fundamental properties regarding internal and ground-state energy functionals, alongside refinements and clarifications of established findings. A simple, metrizable topology is defined for the space of densities based on a hierarchy of spatial partitions; although inherently weak, this topology, when combined with constraints on internal energy, achieves a strength comparable to $L^1$ in a general sense. As a result, the internal energy functional $F$ demonstrates lower semicontinuity under this topology. By distinguishing between positive and negative components of external potentials, the framework can effectively manage severely irregular or infinite positive potentials, thereby allowing confining potentials to be integrated directly into the density functional formalism.

The limits on resonance production cross sections established by LHC searches for heavy particles beyond the Standard Model are not universal; they vary based on the specific properties of the resonance and are constrained by the assumptions and approximations used in their calculation. These bounds are commonly employed to determine mass exclusion limits for new resonances. This work examines specific challenges arising when deriving such limits for a strongly coupled composite $SU(2)_{L+R}$ vector resonance triplet that couples exclusively to the third quark generation. We demonstrate that including these direct interactions within the model can result in reduced mass exclusion limits.

Using operator theoretic techniques, we rigorously establish concentration properties for a specific observable `$r$' within a discrete-time Markov chain that possesses an invariant ergodic measure `$\mu_{\pi}$', even when the state space is unbounded. The primary advancement of this work lies in replacing cumbersome probabilistic approaches with an analysis of the composition of the Markov transition operator $P$ and a multiplication operator defined by $e^{r}$. We demonstrate that even for unbounded reward functions, if there exists a $q>2$ such that $\|e^{r}\|_{q \rightarrow 2} \propto \exp\big(\mu_{\pi}(r) +\frac{2q}{q-2}\big)$ and $P$ satisfies the hyperboundedness condition $\|P\|_{2 \rightarrow q }< e^{\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{q}]}$, then sharp non-asymptotic concentration bounds are achieved. The \emph{transport-entropy} inequality guarantees this upper bound on the multiplication operator for all $q>2$, thereby clarifying the role of \emph{reversibility} in concentration phenomena. These findings are especially valuable to reinforcement learning and control communities, as they provide concentration inequalities regarding standard unbounded observables and reward functions without requiring exact system knowledge or reversibility of the stationary measure.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are constructed through sequential linear and non-linear operations, where combining these procedures is essential for creating a sufficiently deep feature space. Most non-linear operators derive from activation or pooling functions, whereas mathematical morphology offers a distinct set of non-linear tools for diverse image processing tasks. This paper explores integrating these morphological operations into an end-to-end deep learning framework. DNNs aim to learn realistic representations for specific tasks, while morphological operators provide topological descriptors that capture salient shape information within images. We propose a meta-learning-based approach to embed these morphological operators into DNNs. Our results demonstrate that the resulting architecture leverages novel morphological operations to significantly enhance DNN performance across various applications, including image classification and edge detection.

The study of universal thermodynamic connections linking entropy corrections to extremality across various black hole solutions has been widely explored. In this context, we examine several distinct black brane configurations under perturbative corrections to general relativity, specifically analyzing black branes within Rastall AdS massive gravity, Einstein-Yang-Mills AdS massive gravity, and general anisotropic black branes in Horava-Lifshitz gravity. By introducing a small constant correction to the action, we compute both the entropy and the extremality bound. Surprisingly, our results indicate that black branes do not adhere to these universal thermodynamic relations, meaning that a universal connection between entropy and extremality corrections does not hold for black brane structures.

We examine and contrast several semilocal exchange potentials commonly used in density-functional theory (DFT) against their exact counterpart, the Optimized Effective Potential (OEP), specifically within the jellium-slab model of a metal-vacuum interface. Because these three semilocal potentials depend explicitly on the ground-state density, its gradient, and its kinetic-energy density, they reach their respective asymptotic limits more rapidly than the OEP. All three exhibit an asymptotic scaling of $-\alpha\,e^2/z + V_{\infty}$ where $\alpha < 1$. In this work, we derive the leading analytic asymptotics for these model potentials and determine that none matches the exact OEP slab asymptotics of $-\;e^2/z$. While the Becke-Roussel potential's leading term closely resembles its exact OEP equivalent, the other two potentials approach a material-dependent positive constant deep within the vacuum, leading to significantly overestimated ionization potentials.

We introduce a decentralized framework for recognizing view overlaps that functions across freely moving cameras without requiring a reference 3D map. In this system, each camera independently extracts and aggregates feature-point descriptors into a hierarchical structure, sharing them over time. View overlaps are identified through view matching and geometric validation to eliminate incorrect matches. The framework is versatile and compatible with various descriptors. We evaluate the system using both publicly available datasets and new sequences captured with handheld cameras. Our results demonstrate that Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF (ORB) features, combined with Bags of Binary Words within this framework, achieve higher precision and accuracy comparable to or exceeding that of NetVLAD, RootSIFT, and SuperGlue.

Achieving viable product designs often relies on product development processes that employ mathematical programming and numerical simulations. Among these, topology optimization stands out as a highly effective method for deriving insightful design decisions. However, topology optimization problems are classified as NP-hard combinatorial optimization challenges, specifically involving the determination of whether material exists or is absent at specific locations. This study investigates the application of quantum computers as a viable solution for such problems. The proposed approach utilizes two variational quantum algorithms (VQAs): the initial algorithm computes the state equilibrium equation across all potential material configurations, while the second algorithm enhances the probability of an optimal configuration within a quantum superposition by leveraging the state generated by the first VQA. Experimental results, including tests on actual quantum hardware, demonstrate that the method successfully identifies optimal configurations. These outcomes indicate that quantum computers hold significant promise for addressing topology optimization challenges, paving the way for advanced product designs in the near future.

With the increasing volume of vehicles, parking spaces in urban streets have become scarce. Furthermore, drivers' unfamiliarity with available spots forces them to circle blocks heuristically, which wastes time and fuel while exacerbating city congestion. Aligning with recent trends toward building convenient, green, and energy-efficient smart cities, we reevaluate traditional high-profile smart parking methods and introduce a user-engaged, crowdsourcing-based prototype utilizing sonar technology to detect on-street parking availability. This system comprises an ultrasonic sensor, a GPS receiver, and Arduino micro-controllers mounted on the passenger side of a vehicle to measure distances to roadside obstacles. Field tests conducted in Wheatley, Oxford, gathered data to simulate a crowdsourcing model. By analyzing vehicle features from these traces, a supervised learning algorithm was created to estimate parking occupancy and identify illegal parking. Additionally, a quantity estimation model was developed to determine the necessary number of sensing units for urban coverage, which was quantitatively compared against a fixed sensing solution. The findings demonstrate that the crowdsourcing approach requires significantly fewer sensors than a fixed sensing system.
This paper presents the concept of F-manifold color algebras and investigates their properties, thereby extending certain results previously established for F-manifold algebras.

Although the Pierre Auger Observatory is a highly effective tool for detecting ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), it is increasingly employed in diverse multi-messenger campaigns, contributing to the identification of air showers generated by atomic nuclei, neutrons, photons, and neutrinos. This overview details the Observatory's multi-messenger initiatives, including searches for ultra-high energy photons and neutrinos coincident with gravitational wave detections from LIGO and Virgo; investigations into correlations between UHECR arrival directions recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory and high-energy neutrinos from IceCube and ANTARES; efforts to detect Galactic neutrons; and the "Deeper, Wider, Faster" campaign designed to facilitate simultaneous observations across various complementary instruments. We also examine the methodologies and outcomes of these searches.

FEniCS Mechanics is a Python package designed to streamline computational mechanics simulations. It leverages the `dolfin` library from the FEniCS Project to formulate and numerically solve problems in their variational form. By utilizing general balance laws from continuum mechanics, it facilitates the rapid prototyping of various material models. Beyond its versatility, FEniCS Mechanics validates user inputs to ensure physical consistency in problem definitions. Consequently, this tool makes simulating custom mechanics problems more accessible to individuals with limited expertise in programming or mechanics.

Sentence embedding models are designed to generate general-purpose representations for sentences. Although many models examined in this study claim strong performance on Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) tasks, they rarely address their suitability for clustering. This paper evaluates four recent sentence embedding models: the Universal Sentence Encoder (Cer et al., 2018), Sentence-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), LASER (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019), and DeCLUTR (Giorgi et al., 2020), providing a brief overview of their underlying concepts. It then analyzes how well topic categories from two text classification datasets—the Amazon Reviews (Ni et al., 2019) and the News Category Dataset (Misra, 2018)—align with clusters within their respective embedding spaces. While the resulting unsupervised classification model does not achieve perfect accuracy, it outperforms random guessing. This finding is significant because it demonstrates that topic classes in real-world datasets can be partially reconstructed by clustering sentence embeddings without supervision.

Class imbalance is inherent when training and testing models across different domains. Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) enhances model performance by utilizing labeled data from the source domain and unlabeled data from the target domain. However, current state-of-the-art UDA techniques focus on learning domain-invariant representations and are primarily evaluated on class-balanced datasets. In this study, we introduce a reinforcement learning-based UDA approach that simultaneously exploits feature variations and imbalanced labels across domains. We evaluate our method on the text classification task, leveraging readily available datasets, and compare it against five baseline models. Experiments conducted on three datasets demonstrate that our approach effectively learns robust domain-invariant representations and successfully adapts text classifiers to handle class imbalance across domains. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/woqingdoua/ImbalanceClass.

We investigate potential variations in the electromagnetic fine structure constant ($\alpha \equiv e^2/\hbar c$) by analyzing a sample of 58 Sunyaev-Zel'dovich selected clusters within the redshift interval $0.2<z<1.5$, detected by the South Pole Telescope and observed via X-ray measurements from XMM-Newton. Our observable is the ratio of the integrated SZ Comptonization signal to its X-ray equivalent. First, we establish a model-independent constraint on $\alpha$ with an uncertainty of approximately 0.7%, based on the redshift independence of this ratio. Next, we examine a logarithmic variation of $\alpha$ with redshift, defined as $\Delta \alpha/\alpha = -\gamma \ln(1+z)$, a prediction of runaway dilaton models. Our results yield $\gamma$ = $-0.046 \pm 0.1$, indicating no significant logarithmic variation of $\alpha$ with redshift. Additionally, we search for a dipole variation of the fine structure constant using the same cluster dataset and find no evidence for such spatial variation.

This study investigates which function classes admit more efficient testing than learning within the standard distribution-free, sample-based PAC framework. Our primary finding demonstrates that while the VC dimension alone fails to always yield tight sample complexity bounds for testing, combining it with a related concept we term "lower VC" (LVC) dimension enables the derivation of robust lower bounds. Leveraging this insight, we establish strong and often nearly optimal lower bounds for testing unions of intervals, halfspaces, intersections of halfspaces, polynomial threshold functions, and decision trees. In contrast, we prove that testing juntas and monotone functions requires significantly fewer samples—specifically, a polynomially smaller number—than those needed for PAC learning. Additionally, by exploiting the relationship between VC dimension and property testing, we derive new lower bounds for testing radius clusterability and the feasibility of linear constraint systems.

Sunspot light bridges frequently display dynamic and enduring phenomena, such as surges and small-scale jets, within the chromosphere and transition region. Although magnetic reconnection is widely cited as the driver of this small-scale activity, sustained flaring events lasting several hours from a single location on a light bridge are seldom documented. By combining data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly and the Helioseismic Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we examined homologous flaring within a small light bridge situated in an emerging flux region. These flares consistently generated broad, collimated jets, with one reaching B6.4 class intensity. The jets ascended at approximately 200 km/s, attained projected heights of roughly 98 Mm, and originated from the same spot for nearly 14 hours before stopping entirely. A non-linear force-free extrapolation of the photospheric magnetic field revealed a low-lying flux rope linking the light bridge to a distant opposite-polarity network. The persistence of these flares resulted from the rapid horizontal motion of the leading sunspot, which induced reconnection between the relatively vertical magnetic fields in the adjacent umbra and the low-lying flux rope in the light bridge. Our findings suggest that the flaring activity ceases once the flux rope has sufficiently lost its twist through repeated reconnection events.

Human psychology significantly influences organizational success, yet comprehending employee behavior remains challenging due to psychological intricacies, volatile dynamics, and insufficient data. Drawing on evidence-based psychological principles, this paper introduces a hybrid framework combining machine learning with ontology-based reasoning to identify human psychological markers at scale. This distinctive architecture strikes an optimal balance between processing efficiency and interpretability. The resulting system outputs can be integrated with graph science and model management platforms to enhance business processes, analyze team interactions, forecast insider threats, optimize talent management, and support additional strategic initiatives.

This research establishes a verifiable condition for identifying the causal impact of a treatment on an outcome using observational data, dependent on two variable sets: observed covariates for control and a potential instrument. Within a causal framework typical of empirical work, the testable conditional independence between the suspected instrument and the outcome—given the treatment and covariates—yields two key conclusions. First, it validates the instrument by ensuring it does not directly influence the outcome (except via the treatment) and remains unconfounded once covariates are controlled. Second, it confirms that the treatment is unconfounded conditional on the covariates, thereby allowing for the identification of the treatment effect. We propose machine learning-based tests for this conditional independence that adaptively account for covariates, analyzing their asymptotic properties and finite sample performance through simulations. Furthermore, we apply this testing framework to assess the effect of fertility on female labor supply, utilizing the sibling sex ratio of the first two children as the instrument. Our analysis indicates a likely violation of the testable implication when considering a moderate range of socio-economic covariates.

This study investigates the production of prompt photons in conjunction with $Z$ bosons during proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. Utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$ gathered by the ATLAS detector at the LHC between 2015 and 2018, the analysis determines the cross-section for the process $pp \rightarrow \ell^+\ell^-\gamma+X$ (where $\ell$ represents electrons or muons). This measurement is conducted within a specific fiducial phase-space region constrained by kinematic criteria for the photon and leptons, as well as photon isolation requirements. The resulting experimental precision for the fiducial cross-section reaches 2.9%. Additionally, differential cross-sections are derived as functions of six distinct kinematic variables describing the $\ell^+\ell^-\gamma$ system. These findings are evaluated against theoretical predictions utilizing next-to-leading-order and next-to-next-to-leading-order perturbative QCD, with the influence of next-to-leading-order electroweak corrections also examined.

This work addresses the challenge of transferring a network trained on three-channel color images to a hyperspectral domain characterized by a high number of channels. To achieve this, we introduce domain adaptor networks designed to map inputs into a format compatible with models trained on extensive color image datasets like ImageNet. These adaptors facilitate effective learning on limited hyperspectral datasets where training from scratch often fails. We examine various architectural designs and training strategies for these adaptors, evaluating them across a benchmark of multiple hyperspectral datasets. Our findings indicate that straightforward methods, such as linear projection or subset selection, are frequently the most effective, although they can occasionally result in performance degradation. Additionally, we propose a novel multi-view adaptor that combines inputs in an intermediate network layer using an order-invariant approach to yield further improvements. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments by varying the number of training samples within the benchmark to analyze the accuracy and computational trade-offs provided by these adaptors.

The study examines the evolution of contact binary star systems within the coordinate of mass asymmetry (mass transfer). Changes in the orbital period are attributed to the system's evolution toward symmetry, a process termed symmetrization. It is predicted that decreasing and increasing orbital periods correspond, respectively, to the non-overlapping and overlapping phases of the binary system during this symmetrization. During symmetrization, a substantial amount of energy, approximately $\Delta U \approx 10^{41}$ J, is transformed from potential energy into the stars' internal energy. The analysis demonstrates that the merger of stars in binary systems, including KIC 9832227, is energetically unfavorable. Furthermore, the sensitivity of the calculated results to variations in total mass and orbital angular momentum is evaluated.

Session identification is a widely adopted approach for creating metrics in web analytics and analyzing user behavior. Previous research has suggested that using an inactivity threshold is inherently arbitrary, often recommending a standard of 30 minutes. This study, however, reveals a consistent pattern in the timing of user-initiated events across various online domains, including video gaming, search, page views, and volunteer contributions. We outline a method for detecting clusters of user activity and contend that the regularity of these clusters supports a more effective rule-of-thumb inactivity threshold of approximately one hour. Finally, we discuss how these observed temporal rhythms could influence system design, grounded in our theories and observations of goal-directed human activity.

We investigated the complex conductivity, $\sigma$, of FeSe$_{1-x}$Te$_x$ films ($x=0-0.5$) in their superconducting state, focusing on samples exhibiting a significant rise in superconducting transition temperature, $T_\textrm{c}$, upon the vanishing of nematic order. Given that the magnetic penetration depth, $\lambda$ (exceeding 400 nm), surpasses the typical film thickness ($\sim$100 nm), we utilized a combination of coplanar waveguide resonators and cavity perturbation methods to determine both the real and imaginary components of $\sigma$. Our measurements revealed that films possessing nematic order display distinct temperature dependencies in penetration depth and quasiparticle scattering time compared to those lacking such order, implying that nematicity affects the superconducting gap structure. However, a linear relationship between superfluid density, $n_\textrm{s}$ ($\propto\lambda^{-2}$), and $T_\textrm{c}$ persisted regardless of nematic order. This suggests that superfluid density exerts a more dominant influence on $T_\textrm{c}$ in Fe(Se,Te) than the mere presence or absence of nematic order. By integrating these findings with density functional theory band structure calculations, we propose that Fermi surface modifications driven by nematicity are the primary mechanism governing changes in both $T_\textrm{c}$ and the superconducting gap structure within Fe(Se,Te).

This study investigates the temperature dependence of Tan's contact parameter $C$ and its derivatives within spin gapped quantum magnets. Employing the Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) framework to model the low-temperature behavior of triplons, we utilize the $\mu VT$ ensemble to account for the variable particle number and condensate fraction in our thermodynamic calculations. Interactions are handled using the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov approximation. We derived the temperature profiles for $C$ and its derivatives with respect to both temperature and applied magnetic field, covering regions above and below the critical temperature $T_c$ of the transition from the normal phase to BEC. Our findings indicate that $C$ remains regular, whereas its derivatives exhibit discontinuities at $T_c$, consistent with Ehrenfest's classification of phase transitions. Additionally, a sign reversal in $\partial C/\partial T$ is observed near the critical temperature. Regarding the quantum critical point, both $C$ and its derivatives display regularity as a function of the control parameter $r$ driving the quantum phase transition. At very low temperatures, $C$ can be approximated using the expression $C=m^2\mu^2/{\bar a}^{4}$, requiring only the estimation of the quasiparticle effective mass. Finally, we propose a methodology for measuring Tan's contact in spin gapped dimerized magnets.

We introduce a novel family structure for Standard Model fermions that reassigns the muon to the third generation. This approach uncovers significant patterns in mass and mixing, offering specific and experimentally verifiable predictions.

We propose a new model for graphenic crystallites in disordered carbons that moves past the conventional view of randomly oriented graphitic platelets. Utilizing large atomistic simulations with one million atoms, we redefine the interpretation of the $L_a$ parameter derived from X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns. We employ two complementary methods to determine the size of these crystallites, which are defined as areas of regularly arranged hexagons: first, by directly calculating XRD patterns from atomic coordinates and analyzing them as in standard experiments; second, by identifying crystallites through a direct geometric analysis of the structure. By mapping the structure directly, we substitute the idealized crystallite concept with a more realistic material representation and offer a precise interpretation for $L_a$ measurements in disordered carbon. A critical finding is that the size distribution is strongly skewed toward small fragments, with over 75% of crystallites being smaller than half the value of $L_a$.

For artificial agents to achieve success and robustness in their tasks, they must learn to act based on observations. Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a prominent method for acquiring such policies; however, existing RL algorithms frequently struggle with reward shaping, lack the ability to generalize across different environments, and are typically sample inefficient. This paper investigates active inference and the free energy principle—a normative neuroscience framework that describes how self-organizing biological systems function by sustaining a world model and treating action selection as an inference task. We apply this concept to the mountain car problem, a classic challenge in the RL community, demonstrating that active inference unifies both reinforcement learning and learning from demonstrations.

Although reading comprehension models have recently reached near-human levels of performance on extensive English datasets like SQuAD, CoQA, MS Marco, and RACE—primarily thanks to fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embeddings such as BERT and ELMo—most research remains focused on English. This study investigates the efficacy of fine-tuning multilingual BERT on large-scale English reading comprehension data (e.g., RACE) to address Bulgarian multiple-choice reading tasks. We introduce a novel dataset comprising 2,221 questions from twelfth-grade matriculation exams across history, biology, geography, and philosophy, supplemented by 412 history questions from online quizzes. Since the original quiz authors provided no contextual information, we integrated Wikipedia knowledge by retrieving documents that match the question paired with each answer option. Additionally, we tested various indexing and pre-training strategies. The evaluation yielded an accuracy of 42.23%, significantly surpassing the baseline of 24.89%.

Current state-of-the-art self-supervised visual representation learning methods leverage multi-sensor data by aligning feature representations across different views and modalities. This study examines the impact of such alignment on visual features derived from cross-view and cross-modal contrastive learning applied to images and point clouds. We trained and evaluated 108 models based on four distinct pretraining strategies across five real-world datasets and five tasks. Our findings indicate that cross-modal representation alignment tends to discard complementary visual details like color and texture in favor of redundant depth cues, which subsequently enhance downstream depth prediction performance. Overall, cross-modal alignment produces more robust encoders than cross-view alignment, particularly for depth prediction, instance segmentation, and object detection.

Quantile regression, which relies on check loss, serves as a prevalent inferential framework in statistics and econometrics. It offers a robust alternative to traditional conditional means by enabling the quantification of predictive uncertainty with minimal distributional assumptions. This study extends the concept of check loss to binary classification, assuming that conditional quantiles are smooth functions learnable via Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Under certain regularity conditions, we demonstrate that the proposed loss possesses bounded curvature and a computable Lipschitz constant, thereby allowing the direct application of recent findings regarding DNN architectural complexity and error rates.

We measure uncertainty in class probabilities through prediction intervals and generate individualized confidence scores to assess prediction reliability at scoring time. By aggregating these scores across a dataset, we introduce two supplementary metrics—model confidence and retention rate—to enhance standard classifier summaries. Furthermore, we evaluate the robustness of this non-parametric binary quantile classification framework and illustrate how smoothed conditional quantiles can derive various univariate summary statistics, including conditional means, thus facilitating the use of explanation methods like Shapley for mean predictions. Finally, we present an efficient training approach utilizing Stochastic Gradient Descent with Lipschitz Adaptive Learning Rates (LALR) for this loss function.

This study demonstrates that numerous existing self-supervised learning algorithms can be unified and generalized when viewed through the perspective of equivariant representations. We propose a novel framework termed Homomorphic Self-Supervised Learning, which theoretically encompasses input augmentations when paired with an augmentation-homomorphic feature extractor. Experimental validation confirms this theory for basic augmentations, illustrating that the framework fails without representational structure. Furthermore, we empirically investigate the relationship between the parameters of this framework and those of conventional augmentation-based self-supervised learning, concluding with a discussion on the advantages offered by this new viewpoint.

We introduce an adaptive Intelligent Tutoring System that leverages model-based reinforcement learning, specifically contextual bandits, to allocate learning tasks to students. By training on the trajectories of thousands of learners, the model optimizes exercise completion rates and continuously adapts online to new activities through self-learning. Empirical results from a randomized controlled trial demonstrate that our approach outperforms alternative methods in both completion rates and student engagement. This fully automated method unlocks new possibilities for personalizing learning experiences.

For each affine Kac-Moody algebra $X_n^{(r)}$ with rank $\ell$ and $r \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, we select a vertex $c_m$ from the Dynkin diagram where $m \in \{0, \dots, \ell\}$. Utilizing the matrix-resolvent method, we construct a gauge-invariant tau-structure for the related Drinfeld-Sokolov hierarchy and provide explicit formulas for the generating series of the logarithmic derivatives of the tau-function expressed via matrix resolvents. This work extends findings from [Mosc. Math. J. 21 (2021), 233-270, arXiv:1610.07534] which covered the cases $r=1$ and $m=0$. Specifically, for $r=1$ and $m=0$, we confirm that the defined tau-structure satisfies the axioms of Hamiltonian tau-symmetry as outlined in [Adv. Math. 293 (2016), 382-435, arXiv:1409.4616] and [arXiv:math.DG/0108160].

The line-intensity mapping power spectrum and voxel intensity distribution (VID) are two primary summary statistics used to investigate line-intensity maps. By reformulating the VID derivation through local overdensities, we establish, for the first time, an analytic covariance between the VID and the line-intensity mapping power spectrum. We examine the characteristics of this covariance across various experimental configurations and demonstrate that our approach yields results comparable to those derived from simulations. Furthermore, this formalism enables the calculation of the cosmic variance contribution to VID uncertainty, which we determine to be negligible relative to the standard variance arising from Poisson sampling. Consequently, our findings facilitate comprehensive joint analyses of the VID and the line-intensity mapping power spectrum.

Spin qubits within semiconductor quantum dots offer significant potential for quantum information processing due to their scalability and extended coherence times. A pivotal system in this domain involves double quantum dots confining two electrons or holes, where spin states are utilized to represent either singlet-triplet qubits or two single-spin qubits interacting via exchange coupling. This article details advancements regarding spin dephasing in exchange-coupled pairs within double quantum dots. We begin by reviewing schemes for two-qubit gates and qubit encodings based on exchange interactions in both gate-defined quantum dots and donor atoms. Subsequently, we present findings on the dephasing of singlet-triplet qubits and two-qubit gates, followed by a discussion on strategies to mitigate spin dephasing. Gaining a deeper understanding of these dephasing mechanisms could yield critical insights for achieving high-fidelity quantum gates in spin-based quantum computing.

Undetected faults significantly compromise the reliability of the U.S. electrical grid. These hazards trigger protective device malfunctions and can induce multi-component outages, thereby substantially raising the probability of cascading failures. This paper offers a comprehensive examination of the origins and dangers associated with hidden failures, outlining strategies to pinpoint critical areas where such faults may precipitate cascading events. The primary objective is to determine effective mitigation techniques capable of preventing these failures within protective relays.

Origin semantics for transducers were introduced in 2014, yielding numerous characterization and decidability findings that diverge from classical semantics. This paper presents an additional decidability result concerning transducers that approximate one-way transducers within the origin semantics framework. Specifically, we demonstrate that it is decidable whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an origin-equivalent one-way transducer via resynchronization by a bounded, regular resynchronizer. This finding contrasts sharply with standard semantics, where determining if a non-deterministic two-way transducer is equivalent to any one-way transducer remains undecidable.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are commonly employed in advanced speech enhancement systems; however, standard CNN modules struggle with noise context modeling due to the dimensional constraints of their convolutional kernels. To address this, we integrate a recurrent component into the feature extraction layers of CNNs to create a robust, context-aware strategy for single-channel speech enhancement. This approach enables the capture of local noise statistics at the feature level, allowing the model to distinguish speech signals even in highly noisy environments. Compared to models using vanilla CNNs, our recurrent architecture achieves a Segmental Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SSNR) gain of up to 1.5 dB in unseen noise conditions, improves Mean Opinion Score (MOS) by 0.4, and reduces the number of optimized parameters by 25%.

Time Series Analysis (TSA) is a fundamental workload for consumer-facing devices, and accelerating it is essential across various domains to extract valuable insights and forecast future events. The current state-of-the-art method, subsequence Dynamic Time Warping (sDTW), suffers from quadratic computational complexity relative to time series length, leading to two major performance bottlenecks. First, commodity systems typically offer far fewer processing units than the high degree of data parallelism required by sDTW. Second, sDTW is memory-constrained due to its low arithmetic intensity and substantial memory footprint. To address these issues, we utilize Processing-using-Memory (PuM) to execute computations directly within memory cells where data resides. This approach mitigates data movement bottlenecks and unlocks significant parallelism.

This paper introduces MATSA, the first MRAM-based accelerator designed for Time Series Analysis. By leveraging magneto-resistive memory crossbars, MATSA achieves fast and energy-efficient time series computation in memory. Its primary advantages include exploiting column-wise arithmetic operations to harness high levels of parallelism within the memory substrate and drastically reducing data movement costs by performing calculations directly in the memory cells. We evaluated three versions of MATSA tailored to different environments—embedded, desktop, and high-performance computing (HPC)—in light of MRAM technology trends. Through design space exploration, we demonstrated that the HPC version of MATSA outperforms server CPUs, GPUs, and PNM architectures by 7.35x, 6.15x, and 6.31x in performance, and by 11.29x, 4.21x, and 2.65x in energy efficiency, respectively.

Coherent quantum phase slips are anticipated to suppress direct current conduction in narrow superconducting nanowires once a specific critical voltage threshold is reached. We report experimental data from NbN nanowires that not only exhibit this critical voltage but also demonstrate its tunability via a side-gate electrode, which induces periodic variations in the critical voltage. Although these findings align qualitatively with predictions regarding quantum interference among coherent phase slip components, the observed tuning period exceeds simple capacitance-based estimates by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, measurements on a single nanowire revealed two distinct, abrupt shifts in this periodicity, providing constraints for detailed theoretical models. We also evaluate the viability of an explanation attributing this behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowire.

A common approach to enhancing blockchain throughput involves operating smaller side chains that submit block hashes to a trusted main chain. However, these side chains face stalling attacks, where a node broadcasts a block's hash but withholds the actual data from other side chain participants. Recently, Sheng et al. addressed this issue by proposing a data availability oracle utilizing LDPC codes and a dispersal protocol; despite demonstrating improvements, their disjoint design of the code and protocol may not minimize the oracle's communication costs optimally. This paper introduces a tailored dispersal protocol and a specialized LDPC code construction based on the Progressive Edge Growth (PEG) algorithm, termed the dispersal-efficient PEG (DE-PEG) algorithm, specifically designed to lower communication expenses. Our proposed code construction not only reduces communication costs but also imposes fewer constraints on overall system architecture.

Recent technological progress has triggered a significant rise in online trading, intensifying worries regarding theft and fraud, particularly on anonymous platforms like Bitcoin OTC. To address these risks, it is crucial to evaluate user reputations derived from their trading histories. The signed network of "who trusts whom" effectively mirrors the positive and negative relationships between users, enabling the analysis of linkage patterns, strength, and resilience within such platforms. Given that interpersonal trust is dynamic, these networks are prone to link or node failures, underscoring the importance of understanding their stability. This paper addresses the challenge of quantifying the resilience of signed networks through trustworthy community structures. We introduce a metric to calculate the trustworthiness of a community structure and utilize scores from various structures to create a pipeline for assessing network resilience. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these generated resilience scores align accurately with the inherent characteristics of the network.

Due to the absence of empirical support for weakly interacting dark matter, it is logical to consider alternative candidates, such as a confining dark sector containing a particle count comparable to the Standard Model. One such framework is the Twin Higgs mirror matter model, which posits a twin sector where particle masses are 3 to 6 times greater than those in the Standard Model, thereby addressing the hierarchy problem. This model generically predicts the existence of mirror neutron stars—degenerate objects composed entirely of mirror nuclear matter. By employing a realistic equation of state that transitions from a crust of nuclei to a core described by a relativistic mean-field model, and scaling particle masses based on lattice QCD findings, we analyze their structure. Our results indicate that these mirror neutron stars possess distinctive signatures detectable through gravitational waves and binary pulsars, offering a promising avenue for investigating dark matter.

This study investigates compact stars featuring hybrid equations of state, which include a nuclear outer layer and two nested quark phases, each bounded by a strong first-order phase transition from the lower-density phase. We assess the stability of these models by computing their radial oscillation modes across various conversion rates between adjacent phases, thereby establishing the corresponding junction conditions at the phase boundaries. When the transition timescale is shorter than the oscillation period, we recover the standard stability criterion, requiring $\partial M/\partial\rho_c>0$ on stable branches, where $M$ represents mass and $\rho_c$ denotes central density. Conversely, in the limit of slow conversion, we identify stable stellar multiplets extending beyond triplets. These systems comprise stars stable under the conventional criterion alongside hybrid stars with $\partial M/\partial\rho_c<0$ that achieve stability through an alternative junction condition for the fluid displacement field at the interface, which accounts for the sluggish conversion rate. Furthermore, for the first time, we examine the reaction mode—a radial mode exclusive to stars with rapid (abbreviated as $r$) phase transitions—in configurations involving either two rapid transitions or alternating rapid and slow transitions. Finally, we analyze the consequences of these alternative junction conditions, finding that they generally yield stability characteristics comparable to those observed under slow conversion rates.

Determining the redshift of galaxies is a fundamental prerequisite for numerous cosmological studies. Since obtaining spectra for every observed galaxy is infeasible, estimating photometric redshifts (photo-z) remains a critical challenge. This study evaluates various deep learning techniques for deriving photo-z directly from images, contrasting them with conventional machine learning approaches that rely on photometric magnitudes. We assess both standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and those incorporating inception modules, while also proposing a new mixed-input architecture that integrates image data and magnitude information to enhance redshift accuracy. Furthermore, we conduct benchmarking to evaluate the performance and scalability of these algorithms. The research utilizes a dataset of one million galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), featuring five-filter (ugriz) images, complete photometry, and spectroscopic redshifts as ground truth. The novel mixed-input inception CNN achieved a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.009, representing a 30% improvement over the traditional Random Forest (RF) method. Performance was even more pronounced at lower redshifts (z < 0.3), where the MSE dropped to 0.0007, a 50% gain over RF. These findings suggest that this approach could significantly benefit future large-scale surveys, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), by enabling the rapid and precise generation of vast numbers of photo-z estimates.

The CHIME/FRB experiment, leveraging its sensitivity and wide field of view, has identified thousands of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs); however, its limited angular resolution hinders the localization of these events to their host galaxies. Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI), triggered by CHIME/FRB detections, offers a solution for localizing non-repeating events. Utilizing a refurbished 10-meter radio dish at the Algonquin Radio Observatory in Ontario, Canada, we established a testbed for a VLBI experiment capable of achieving theoretical precision better than 30 milliarcseconds. This overview details the 10-meter system, its refurbishment, data acquisition methods, and a fringe-fitting procedure that simultaneously calculates the geometric delay required for localization and the dispersive delay caused by the ionosphere. By analyzing single pulses from the Crab pulsar, we validated the system and localization protocol while assessing inter-site clock stability, a critical factor for phase-referencing FRB events. Our results indicate that the current system can achieve a localization accuracy of 50 milliarcseconds. Additionally, for sources with weak signals or limited bandwidth that prevent simultaneous measurement of both geometric and ionospheric delays, we demonstrate that the differential ionospheric contribution between sites must be measured with a precision of $1 \times 10^{-8}$ pc/cc to ensure reasonable localization within the 400–800 MHz band. Finally, we report the detection of an FRB observed simultaneously by both CHIME and the Algonquin 10-meter telescope, marking the first VLBI cross-correlation of an FRB in such a long baseline. This initiative serves as a testbed for the upcoming CHIME/FRB Outriggers project.

Young stellar groups serve as archives of historical star formation; by analyzing their dynamics and ages, we can reconstruct the complete timeline of these events. The Gaia mission has significantly increased the number of accessible stellar populations, recently highlighting Cepheus Far North (CFN). This association, which includes hundreds of members within a span exceeding 100 pc, offers a manageable yet complex case study due to its proximity (d $\lesssim$ 200 pc), visible substructure, and modest size. Leveraging Gaia's astrometry and photometry alongside spectroscopic data, we have identified more than 500 candidate CFN members distributed across seven subgroups. By integrating age estimates derived from isochrones, asteroseismology, dynamics, and lithium depletion, we have established precise ages for all seven subgroups, uncovering a largely continuous 10 Myr star formation history. Tracing current populations back to their origins reveals two distinct, spatially and dynamically separate formation sites: one linked to $\beta$ Cephei characterized by mostly co-spatial formation, and another associated with EE Draconis displaying a more dispersed star formation pattern. This comprehensive analysis illustrates the intricate nature of the star formation process, even within the smallest regions.

This paper establishes the almost sure values of $\Phi$-dimensions for random measures defined on random Moran sets that adhere to a uniform separation condition. As intermediate Assouad-like dimensions, these include the (quasi-)Assouad dimensions and the $\theta$-Assouad spectrum as specific instances. The resulting values vary according to the magnitude of $\Phi$, where specific magnitudes correspond to the Assouad and quasi-Assouad dimensions, respectively. We provide numerous applications, such as those concerning equicontractive self-similar measures and one-variable random Moran measures, including Cantor-like measures with uniformly distributed probabilities. Furthermore, we derive the $\Phi$-dimensions for the underlying random sets.

A $p$-centered coloring of a graph $G$, where $p$ is a positive integer, assigns colors to the vertices of $G$ so that every connected subgraph either includes a vertex with a unique color or exhibits more than $p$ distinct colors. We provide an explicit construction for a $p$-centered coloring of the planar grid that utilizes $O(p)$ colors.

Numerous practical scenarios, including autonomous vehicle coordination and network packet routing, can be modeled as multi-agent cooperation tasks. While deep reinforcement learning (DRL) offers a promising framework for enabling such cooperation through agent-environment interactions, traditional methods struggle with the high dimensionality arising from multiple agents with continuous action spaces during policy optimization. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of agent policies leads to non-stationary training environments. To address these challenges, we introduce a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that combines high-level decision-making with low-level individual control to facilitate efficient policy search. This design allows for efficient learning of multi-agent cooperation within a high-level discrete action space, while simultaneously reducing low-level control tasks to manageable single-agent reinforcement learning problems. Complementing this hierarchy, we propose an opponent modeling network to capture the policies of other agents throughout the learning process. Unlike end-to-end DRL methods, our approach mitigates learning complexity by decomposing the overall task into hierarchical sub-tasks. We validate the effectiveness of our method through a real-world case study on cooperative lane changing, where both simulation and physical experiments demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches in terms of collision reduction and faster convergence.

To capture behavioral and neural patterns of language understanding in natural settings, researchers increasingly utilize comprehensive natural language processing and machine learning tools. While previous studies focusing on explicit syntactic structure have largely depended on context-free grammars (CFGs), these formalisms lack the expressiveness required for human language. In contrast, Combinatory Categorial Grammars (CCGs) offer a directly compositional and sufficiently expressive modeling approach with flexible constituency that supports incremental interpretation. This study assesses whether a more expressive CCG outperforms a CFG in modeling human neural signals obtained via fMRI during audiobook listening. We also compare different CCG variants regarding their handling of optional adjuncts. These evaluations are benchmarked against a baseline incorporating next-word predictability estimates from a Transformer language model. The results highlight unique contributions of CCG structure-building, primarily localized in the left posterior temporal lobe, where CCG-derived measures provide a superior fit to neural data compared to CFG-derived ones. These effects are spatially distinct from bilateral superior temporal regions uniquely associated with predictability. Consequently, neural responses to structure-building can be separated from those to predictability during naturalistic listening, and the latter is best modeled by a grammar whose expressive power is grounded in independent linguistic principles.

The integration of deep learning with Earth observation holds great promise for advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Emerging innovations and diverse applications are transforming how humanity addresses planetary challenges. This paper examines current deep learning methodologies for analyzing Earth observation data, focusing on their role in monitoring and achieving the five SDGs most influenced by this technological surge: ending hunger, ensuring sustainable cities, securing land tenure, combating and adapting to climate change, and conserving biodiversity. The study reviews relevant case studies and highlights significant societal, economic, and environmental implications. We are entering an exciting era where algorithms and Earth data can jointly help tackle the climate crisis and foster more sustainable development.

We present a sophisticated information extraction pipeline designed to automatically process vast volumes of unstructured text for investigative journalism. This pipeline acts as a novel input handler for the upcoming major release of our New/s/leak 2.0 software, developed in partnership with a major German news organization. The primary use case involves journalists receiving massive file collections, ranging up to several gigabytes, with unknown contents. These collections may stem from official document disclosures, such as Freedom of Information Act requests, or unofficial data leaks. Our software facilitates a visually supported exploration of these datasets, enabling journalists to rapidly identify potential stories by automatically extracting entities and analyzing their co-occurrence within documents. Unlike similar projects, we prioritize three key requirements essential for cross-border investigative journalism: 1) integrating multiple state-of-the-art NLP tools for entity extraction, 2) supporting multi-lingual document sets comprising up to 40 languages, and 3) providing a fast, user-friendly method for extracting full text, metadata, and entities from diverse file formats.

Finding an exact solution for the Ising model on a simple cubic lattice remains a persistent, unresolved challenge in rigorous statistical mechanics. It is widely conjectured that resolving this issue would mark a methodological revolution, offering significant future applications much like Lars Onsager's solution to the two-dimensional model eight decades prior. Consequently, numerous efforts have been made to derive an analytic formula for the exact partition function $Z$, yet all have encountered insurmountable conceptual or mathematical barriers. Given the model's status as a fundamental yet simple paradigm, this work establishes rigorous, minimal plausibility criteria for any purported exact expression of $Z$. We introduce six necessary (though not sufficient) conditions that such a function must satisfy, enabling rapid validation of future claims. To demonstrate the utility of these criteria, we analyze previous erroneous "solutions," highlighting their specific deficiencies.

Recent years have seen the development and deployment of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) within intelligent vehicles. These systems execute various functions, including Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC), Lane Change Warning (LCW), Lane Departure Warning (LDW), and Lane Keeping Assistance (LKA). Among these, real-time Lane Detection and Tracking (LDT) is a pivotal component for enabling such operations. Video-derived images often contain noise and interfering elements like lighting variations and shadows from nearby objects, necessitating robust preprocessing for effective lane marking detection and tracking. This preprocessing stage is essential for maintaining real-time performance and facilitating subsequent steps by eliminating irrelevant image data and enhancing features of interest. This paper provides a survey of preprocessing techniques designed for real-time vision-based systems to detect lane markings and track lane boundaries.

The McMillan system offers a new approach to enhance beam tune spread without compromising dynamic aperture, leveraging its integrable nature. Although the theoretical model assumes an infinitely thin kick, practical implementation necessitates a thick electron lens equipped with a solenoid. Simulating particle transport through this lens is challenging due to the complex forces acting on the circulating beam. This study presents an accurate simulation of a thick McMillan lens within a solenoid by utilizing symplectic integrators based on Yoshida's method.

This study details findings derived from photometric and statistical-parallax analyses of 850 field RR Lyrae (RRL) variables. The dataset comprises spectroscopic data for 448 RRLs obtained via new observations with the Southern African Large Telescope (SALT), photometric data collected using the 1.0-m telescope at the South African Astronomical Observatory (SAAO), and additional information from existing literature. These measurements are integrated with precise proper motion data from the second Gaia data release (DR2). The research primarily aims to determine the velocity distribution of RRLs in the solar neighborhood while also calibrating the zero points for the visual V-band luminosity-metallicity (LZ or $M_V-$[\text{Fe/H}]) and period-luminosity-metallicity (PLZ) relations within the \textit{WISE} $W_1-$ and \textit{2MASS} $Ks-$bands. Utilizing these calibrated relations, the study estimates the distance to the Galactic Center and the distance modulus of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), yielding values of 7.99$\pm$0.49\,kpc and 18.46$\pm$0.09 \,mag, respectively. These results align excellently with prior statistical parallax studies but offer significantly greater accuracy and precision. Furthermore, the zero points of the calibrated PLZ and LZ relations remain consistent with outcomes from other methods, producing an LMC distance modulus that falls within 0.04\,mag of the current most precise estimate.

This paper presents a sketching algorithm designed to build a tensor train representation of a probability density using sample data. Unlike the conventional recursive SVD-based approach for constructing tensor trains, our method formulates and solves a series of small linear systems to determine each individual tensor train core. This strategy mitigates the curse of dimensionality, which otherwise impacts both the algorithmic and sample complexities of the recovery task. Specifically, for Markov models, we demonstrate that the tensor cores can be recovered with a sample complexity that remains constant regardless of the dimension. Additionally, we validate the method's performance through several numerical experiments.

Visualizing high-dimensional datasets, particularly those from critical application areas, is a core challenge in machine learning. This difficulty intensifies when dealing with large, imbalanced datasets. This study applies the t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) algorithm to reduce the dimensionality of an earthquake engineering dataset for visualization. To address the imbalanced nature of the data, which often hinders classifier accuracy, we utilize the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE). We present findings from both t-SNE and SMOTE, comparing them against baseline methods across multiple dimensions. By evaluating four options and six classification algorithms, we demonstrate that applying t-SNE to the imbalanced data and SMOTE to the training set allows neural network classifiers to achieve promising results without compromising accuracy. Consequently, the scientific data is transformed into a two-dimensional (2D) space, facilitating the visualization of classifiers and their decision boundaries via 2D plots.

We analyze a dataset of 9,739 early-type galaxies (ETGs) by cross-matching Galaxy Zoo 1 with MPA-JHU emission-line measurements from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7. We first determine the optimal divisor separating ETGs with and without star formation (SF), identifying $W2-W3=2.0$ as the best separator. By rejecting various ionization sources and applying this diagnostic line, we isolate 5,376 ETGs exhibiting SF and measure their metallicities using four different abundance calibrators. Our composite ETG sample displays $M_*$ and star formation rate (SFR) distributions comparable to those of star-forming galaxies (SFGs), with most residing on the "main sequence"; however, our derived slope is slightly steeper than that reported by Renzini & Peng. Comparing the four metallicity indicators, we find that the Courti17 method provides the most accurate calibration for composite ETGs. A weak positive correlation between SFR and metallicity emerges only when using the PP04, Curti17, and T04 indicators, contrasting with the negative correlation observed in SFGs. We attribute this weak correlation to the dilution effect caused by gas inflow driven by minor mergers.

Upcoming high-energy $e^+e^-$ colliders are poised to deliver some of the most rigorous tests of the Standard Model, with statistical uncertainties anticipated to decrease by orders of magnitude compared to existing measurements. This advancement introduces a significant new challenge: the need to accurately evaluate and reduce systematic uncertainties. Beam polarisation could offer a distinctive capability to isolate and quantify these systematic effects. The present study seeks to validate this hypothesis by constructing a combined fit that analyzes both systematic effects and electroweak observables, allowing for the examination of various beam polarisation and luminosity configurations. A framework for this fitting procedure is established. In an initial validation, luminosity and polarisation are fitted alongside external constraints applied to 2-fermion and 4-fermion differential distributions. The inclusion of a first systematic effect—specifically muon acceptance—demonstrates consistent behavior within this framework. These results provide a foundation for investigating how systematic and physical effects interact, both with and without the use of beam polarisation.

Argumentation has garnered significant interest within knowledge representation, reasoning, and multi-agent systems over the past two decades. Nevertheless, within dynamic multi-agent environments, the proliferation of arguments generated by agents leads to heightened representational complexity and computational expenses. This study explores the concept of abstraction through a model-checking lens, where multiple arguments supporting the same stance from different perspectives are consolidated. This approach aims to diminish the scale of the argumentation framework while maintaining the system's underlying semantic flow structure.

Depth estimation is a critical computer vision task, particularly valuable for autonomous vehicle navigation and robotic object manipulation. This work addresses the problem using an end-to-end neuromorphic strategy that integrates two event-based cameras with a Spiking Neural Network (SNN) featuring a slightly adapted U-Net-like encoder-decoder structure, termed StereoSpike. Training was conducted in a supervised fashion on the Multi Vehicle Stereo Event Camera Dataset (MVSEC) using surrogate gradient descent, leveraging its provided ground-truth depth data. We introduce a novel readout mechanism to generate dense analog depth predictions for each pixel directly from the decoder's spikes. Our results demonstrate that StereoSpike generalizes exceptionally well, outperforming non-spiking models and achieving state-of-the-art test accuracy. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance of a fully spiking network solving such a large-scale regression problem. Furthermore, we show that regularization enables low firing rates (under 10%) with negligible accuracy loss, indicating that StereoSpike can be efficiently deployed on neuromorphic hardware for low-power, real-time embedded applications.

RTNeural is a C++ neural inference library engineered for systems with stringent hard real-time requirements, prioritizing speed, flexibility, compactness, and ease of use. The text details the library's design philosophy and motivations, alongside real-world applications and performance benchmarks against other neural inference solutions.

We re-examine the Fisher-Shannon representation plane ${\mathcal H} \times {\mathcal F}$, which is assessed using the Bandt and Pompe method to derive a probability distribution for time series data. To demonstrate this methodology, we analyze various stochastic dynamical processes (noises characterized by $f^{-k}$ power spectra for $k \geq 0$) and chaotic systems (comprising 27 chaotic maps). Our primary contribution lies in revealing the informational characteristics associated with positions within this plane.

Kinetic methods are typically precise for microscale plasma physics but become computationally prohibitive when applied to large-scale or multiscale systems. A persistent challenge in the field is merging kinetic physics with fluid models, a task often accomplished via complex analytical closure terms. This study presents the successful development of a multi-moment fluid model that incorporates an implicit fluid closure within a neural network using machine learning techniques. The model was trained on a sparse dataset derived from kinetic simulations of Landau damping, employing both physics-informed neural networks (PINN) and gradient-enhanced physics-informed neural networks (gPINN). Both PINN and gPINN-based models effectively replicate the time evolution of electric field energy, including damping rates, and plasma dynamics observed in kinetic simulations. For the first time, we introduce a novel gPINN variant called gPINN$p$, designed specifically to capture the Landau damping process; unlike standard gPINN, which incorporates gradients of all equation residuals, gPINN$p$ applies only the gradient of the pressure equation residual as an additional constraint. Among the three approaches evaluated, the multi-moment fluid model built with gPINN$p$ yielded the most accurate results. This research provides new insights into creating accurate and efficient models for large-scale systems, with potential applications extending to complex multiscale problems in laboratory, space, and astrophysical plasma physics.

The stress-strain relationship for two-dimensional frictional dispersed grains interacting with a harmonic potential under finite strain, without accounting for dynamical slip, is derived through eigenvalue analysis of the Hessian matrix. Once the grain configuration is established, the stress-strain curve generated by this eigenvalue analysis aligns almost perfectly with simulation results, even in the presence of plastic deformation induced by stress avalanches. Contrary to initial expectations, the eigenvalues within this model fail to serve as precursors to stress-drop events.

Emergency data encompasses diverse formats, often characterized by high volume and velocity, necessitating rapid response times and robust analytical and management strategies. Knowledge graphs offer a rich, flexible, and consistent representation of this data, aligning effectively with emergency management requirements by leveraging existing standards, tools, and techniques for semantic computing. This chapter outlines key semantic technologies and their role in supporting knowledge graphs, followed by an examination of their advantages and challenges, along with examples of pertinent data sources and vocabularies. Additionally, it addresses the unique analytical difficulties posed by natural language text, particularly from social media platforms like Twitter, by providing an overview of relevant text processing techniques.

This study examines collinear magnets within honeycomb lattices subjected to time-dependent strains. By analyzing the regime of high-frequency periodic deformations, we establish an effective Floquet theory for the spin system, which gives rise to spin chirality. We observe that the interaction between magnons and spin chirality is sensitive to specific strain characteristics, including spatial distribution and orientation. Determining magnonic fluctuations around the ferromagnetic ground state reveals that spatially homogeneous strains induce topologically protected phases in the magnon system. Specifically, certain uniform strain fields emulate an out-of-plane next-neighbor Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Additionally, we investigate nonuniform strains, which result in the confinement of magnon states; for uniaxial strains, propagation occurs along the axis maintaining translational symmetry. Ultimately, this work highlights a direct and innovative method for manipulating the magnon spectrum via time-dependent strain engineering, offering significant potential for probing topological transitions in quantum magnonics.

This study addresses energy shaping for stochastic port-Hamiltonian systems. As a robust methodology, energy shaping enables the systematic derivation of feedback laws to modify a controlled system's Hamiltonian, ensuring convergence to or tracking of a target configuration under general passivity conditions. Although this approach has recently been extended to stochastic port-Hamiltonian systems, the resulting framework faces significant practical limitations, effectively excluding important scenarios like additive noise. This paper extends the investigation into a weak form of passivity for stochastic systems and the associated weak convergence for shaped systems, as previously proposed by the authors. This weak passivity concept is intrinsically linked to the existence and uniqueness of an invariant measure, imparting a distinctly probabilistic character to the developed theory. We demonstrate that all key results of energy shaping can be recovered within this weak framework. Furthermore, we illustrate how this weak passivity perspective establishes a meaningful connection between stochastic port-Hamiltonian systems and their infinite-dimensional counterparts.

Microscopic models of reaction-diffusion on cell membranes connect local spatiotemporal dynamics to the macroscopic self-organized patterns frequently observed there. Simulation frameworks utilizing the microscopic lattice method (MLM) represent these processes at the individual molecular level by tracking hard-sphere molecules on fine lattice voxels. While MLM is straightforward to implement and typically less computationally intensive than off-lattice methods, its precision and consistency in modeling surface reactions have remained unverified. By employing the Spatiocyte scheme, we evaluated the accuracy of MLM regarding diffusion-influenced surface reactions. We derived lattice-based bimolecular association rates for two-dimensional surface-surface interactions and one-dimensional volume-surface adsorption, grounded in the Smoluchowski-Collins-Kimball model and random walk theory. By aligning time-dependent lattice rates with their off-lattice equivalents, we established the correct expressions for MLM parameters using physical constants. These results indicate that for accurate simulation of surface reactions on triangular lattices, the voxel size must be at least 0.6% larger than the molecule; on square lattices, this minimum increases to 5%. Furthermore, we demonstrated that MLM-based schemes like Spatiocyte can effectively simulate reaction-diffusion models spanning all dimensions: three-dimensional cytoplasmic diffusion, two-dimensional membrane diffusion, and one-dimensional cytoplasm-membrane adsorption. Using this model, we analyzed how the 2D reaction pathway contributes to the overall reaction rate across varying levels of reactant diffusivity, reactivity, and concentration.

To effectively guide policy and resource distribution aimed at reducing maternal mortality globally, it is crucial to comprehend the root causes of these deaths across all regions. Yet, many nations suffer from a severe lack of data regarding maternal death causes, and available data often fail to represent the entire at-risk population. This study introduces a Bayesian hierarchical multinomial model designed to estimate global, regional, and national distributions of maternal causes of death. The methodology synthesizes information from diverse sources, such as civil registration and vital systems, smaller-scale surveys, and high-quality confidential enquiries or surveillance data. This framework accommodates variations in data quality and coverage, including scenarios where specific causes of death are unrecorded. Furthermore, the model's performance is demonstrated through three case studies representing countries with varying degrees of data availability.

OPAL-FEL is a newly created instrument designed for modeling particle accelerators that include wigglers or undulators. It builds upon the well-known 3D electrostatic particle-tracking code OPAL by integrating it with the MITHRA finite-difference time-domain electromagnetic solver. We present results from two benchmark cases where OPAL-FEL simulations are compared to experimental data. Both experiments involve electron beamlines where the longitudinal phase space is modulated using a short magnetic wiggler. In both the space charge and radiation-dominated regimes, the simulations showed strong agreement with the experimental results.

Recently, there has been growing interest in using neural networks to learn the distribution of non-dispatchable renewable energy sources, such as photovoltaics and wind, alongside load demands. Normalizing flow density models are especially advantageous for this purpose because they allow for direct log-likelihood maximization during training. However, research in image generation indicates that standard normalizing flows tend to learn only smeared versions of manifold distributions. Previous studies on scenario generation using normalizing flows have failed to address this limitation, resulting in the sampling of noisy time series due to these blurred distributions. In this paper, we leverage the isometry of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to configure the normalizing flow within a lower-dimensional space, thereby maintaining both direct and computationally efficient likelihood maximization. We trained the resulting Principal Component Flow (PCF) on data from Germany (2013–2015) regarding PV and wind power generation as well as load demand. The findings demonstrate that the PCF successfully preserves essential characteristics of the original distributions, including the probability density and temporal frequency patterns of the time series. Furthermore, the application of the PCF is not restricted to renewable energy; it is applicable to any dataset or time series that can be effectively reduced via PCA.

This study investigates $(m,\rho)$-quasi Einstein manifolds, demonstrating that a complete, connected Riemannian manifold satisfying specific conditions must be compact. We also establish an upper limit for the diameter of such manifolds and show that the potential function aligns with the Hodge-de Rham potential up to a real constant within this framework. Additionally, we derive triviality and integral conditions for non-compact, complete $(m,\rho)$-quasi Einstein manifolds of finite volume. Furthermore, we prove that under particular constraints, a complete Riemannian manifold possesses a finite fundamental group, and we deduce several criteria ensuring compactness.

This study systematically investigates one-dimensional and two-dimensional honeycomb structures of boron nitride (BN) using the first-principles plane wave approach. Two-dimensional BN, resembling graphene, exhibits ionic bonding and functions as a wide band gap semiconductor, with phonon dispersion curves confirming the stability of its flakes. Quasi-one-dimensional armchair BN nanoribbons act as nonmagnetic semiconductors featuring edge states; however, hydrogen passivation of these edges eliminates the states and widens the band gap. In contrast, bare zigzag BN nanoribbons are metallic but transform into ferromagnetic semiconductors upon hydrogen passivation of both edges. Notably, their magnetic ground state, electronic band structure, and band gap vary significantly depending on whether the boron or nitrogen edges are saturated with hydrogen. Additionally, vacancy defects in both armchair and zigzag nanoribbons influence the magnetic state and electronic structure. To highlight dimensionality effects, these findings are compared against various three-dimensional BN crystals and one-dimensional BN atomic chains.

The field of NLP has been transformed by pretrained Transformer models fine-tuned on domain-specific corpora. Typically, when addressing multiple tasks within a single dataset, practitioners either fine-tune separate models or employ task-specific adapters. This study demonstrates that a single multi-task model can match or surpass the performance of multiple BERT variants fine-tuned for distinct tasks, as well as BERT models augmented with task-specific adapters. We validated our approach using an internal dataset of cervical spine radiologist reports.
