We investigate the reconstruction of Faber–Schauder coefficients for a continuous function $f$ based on discrete samples of its antiderivative $F$. Our methodology begins by modeling the problem using piecewise quadratic spline interpolation, followed by the derivation of a closed-form solution and a detailed error analysis. These findings reveal counterintuitive insights into the classical domain of quadratic spline interpolation: specifically, the notorious instabilities of this method are confined entirely to the last generation of estimated Faber–Schauder coefficients, which exhibit non-locality and a strong reliance on both the initial value and the input data. In contrast, all preceding coefficients rely solely on local data, remain independent of the initial value, and possess uniform error bounds. Consequently, we conclude that a robust and stable estimator for this problem can be achieved by simply discarding the final-generation coefficients from the set of estimated Faber–Schauder coefficients.

We substantially enhance generalization bounds for VC classes by employing two core strategies. Initially, we apply hypergeometric tail inversion to establish a highly precise, non-uniform, distribution-independent upper bound on risk for VC classes. Subsequently, we refine the ghost sample technique to achieve an additional, significant improvement. Leveraging these advancements, we derive a relative deviation bound, a multiclass margin bound, and a lower bound. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that our new bound is almost never vacuous and remains tighter than existing VC bounds across all reasonable dataset sizes.

By generalizing DiNezza-Lu's method to the context of large cohomology classes, we establish that solutions to degenerate complex Monge-Ampère equations on compact Kähler manifolds remain continuous over a Zariski open subset. Consequently, we demonstrate that the potentials for singular Kähler-Einstein metrics on log canonical varieties of general type are continuous on the ample locus, excluding the non-klt portion.

We introduce a correction scheme for the coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) method, utilizing frozen natural orbitals (FNOs) and diagrammatically separated contributions that primarily drive basis set incompleteness error (BSIE). As noted in recent literature, the BSIE affecting CCSD correlation energy is chiefly governed by the second-order M{\o}ller-Plesset (MP2) perturbation energy and the particle-particle ladder term. In this work, we develop a straightforward approximation for the BSIE of the particle-particle ladder term, which effectively functions as a rescaled, pair-specific MP2 BSIE; the scaling factor is determined by the spatially averaged correlation hole depth found in both coupled-cluster and first-order pair wavefunctions. These derived expressions are easily implemented within any existing computational code. We validate the method's efficacy using the uniform electron gas and apply it to coupled-cluster calculations for atoms and molecules using FNOs. By employing the proposed correction alongside an increasing number of FNOs per occupied orbital, we demonstrate that rapidly convergent closed and open-shell reaction energies, atomization energies, electron affinities, and ionization potentials can be achieved for a test set. Additionally, we show that a comparable optimal balance between the size of the virtual orbital basis set and residual BSIEs can be attained for the perturbative triples contribution to CCSD(T) energy when using FNOs and the (T*) approximation.

Inbreeding homophily is a common characteristic of human social networks, carrying significant implications for individual and group health, economics, and social dynamics. While existing literature suggests numerous dimensions along which relationships can be categorized, it lacks a unified, empirically validated framework for sorting these attributes. This study utilizes comprehensive data on university freshmen with highly similar demographics—specifically age, race, and education level—to compare the influence of observable versus unobservable traits on friendship formation. By employing Bayesian Model Averaging, a technique specifically suited for addressing model uncertainty and evaluating the robustness of candidate attributes in predicting friendships, we demonstrate that while observable factors such as class sections, gender, and smoking habits are reliable determinants of friendship, unobservable attributes—including personality, cognitive skills, economic preferences, and socio-economic factors—are highly sensitive to model specification and do not serve as significant predictors.

This work establishes the precise large-time asymptotic behavior of the tail distribution for the extinction time of a self-similar fragmentation process characterized by a negative self-similarity index, thereby refining earlier findings regarding its logarithmic asymptotics. The resulting behavior is governed by two key elements: the self-similarity index and the distribution of the largest fragment at the moment of dislocation. As an application, we derive the asymptotic properties of all moments for the largest fragment and contrast them with those of a tagged fragment, noting that the latter's moments generally decay significantly more slowly. We demonstrate these findings through various examples, including fragmentations associated with random real trees. Specifically, we determine the large-time tail behavior for the height of stable Lévy trees (encompassing the Brownian tree of Aldous, as well as the models by Duquesne, Le Gall, and Le Jan), the alpha-model of Ford, and the beta-splitting model of Aldous.

This study proposes a method for analyzing the thermodynamics of rotating, non-linear, magnetic-charged black holes in the presence of quintessence. We calculate key thermodynamic properties, including mass, temperature, magnetic potential, and heat capacity. Furthermore, we investigate phase transitions by examining the heat capacity curve. Our findings indicate that the black hole mass decreases as the temperature rises from negative absolute values. Additionally, based on the heat capacity behavior, we conclude that the black hole experiences a second-order phase transition that shifts toward higher entropy values as either the rotation parameter $a$ or the magnetic charge parameter $Q$ increases.

This study examines the two-dimensional Schrödinger operator under a constant magnetic field, defined as $H(V)=(D_x-By)^2+D_y^2+V_h(x,y)$, where $V$ vanishes at infinity and $h$ represents a small positive parameter. The analysis focuses on two distinct regimes: the semi-classical limit, where $V_h(x,y)=V(h x,h y)$, and the large coupling constant limit, where $V_h(x,y)=h^{-\delta} V(x,y)$. We derive a full asymptotic expansion in powers of $h^2$ for ${\rm tr}(\Phi(H(V),h))$, with $\Phi(\cdot,h)$ being a smooth function with compact support in $\mathbb R$. Furthermore, we establish a Weyl-type asymptotic formula for the eigenvalue counting function of $H(V)$, accompanied by an optimal estimate for the remainder term.

Let $f$ be a smooth symplectic diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that possesses a non-split separatrix linked to a hyperbolic fixed point. We demonstrate that if $f$ arises as a perturbation of the time-1 map of a symplectic autonomous vector field, then this separatrix is approached by a set of invariant circles with positive measure. Conversely, we construct examples of smooth symplectic diffeomorphisms featuring a Lyapunov unstable non-split separatrix that are not approached by any invariant circles.

The revival of chat-based conversational systems in both consumer and enterprise sectors has led to significant advancements in data-driven and rule-based natural language models for interpreting user intent. However, because these models depend heavily on extensive data and domain-specific knowledge, expanding services into new markets is often hindered by language barriers that impede dialog automation. This paper introduces a user study assessing the effectiveness of ready-to-use machine translation technology to (1) quickly launch multilingual spoken dialog systems and (2) assist human analysts in comprehending utterances in foreign languages. Furthermore, we evaluate machine translation within human-assisted environments where some traffic is handled by analysts. Our experiments involving English-to-Spanish translation reveal substantial potential for dialog automation and demonstrate that human analysts can accurately process foreign language inputs.

Position emission tomography (PET) is extensively utilized in clinical and research settings because of its high sensitivity and quantitative capabilities, yet it is hindered by a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have recently been adopted to enhance PET image quality, their efficacy in extracting local features is limited by a restricted receptive field, which prevents them from effectively capturing long-range dependencies. Although global multi-head self-attention (MSA) is a favored method for addressing long-range information, applying it to 3D images incurs significant computational costs. To overcome this, we introduce the Spach Transformer, an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that integrates spatial and channel information through both local and global MSAs. The proposed framework was evaluated using datasets comprising various PET tracers, including $^{18}$F-FDG, $^{18}$F-ACBC, $^{18}$F-DCFPyL, and $^{68}$Ga-DOTATATE. Quantitative analysis demonstrates that the Spach Transformer outperforms other reference methods.

The Lasso is widely recognized as the Bayesian posterior mode estimate under a Laplacian prior. While the point estimate suffices for the standard Lasso, sampling from the full posterior distribution in the Bayesian Lasso framework offers significant performance improvements. Traditional implementations relying on Gibbs sampling face challenges such as poor scalability, undefined convergence rates, and the production of correlated samples. We introduce a measure transport method to generate independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) posterior samples by constructing a transport map that transforms samples from the Laplacian prior into posterior samples. This construction is decomposed into parallelizable modules that iteratively solve Lasso problems and execute closed-form linear algebra updates. Utilizing this sampling technique, we apply the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate the Lasso regularization parameter via maximum likelihood. We compare our approach to conventional Gibbs samplers using the diabetes dataset from Efron et al. Finally, we present a GPU-accelerated implementation that leverages parallelization, demonstrating an execution time with significantly reduced dependence on dimensionality compared to standard methods.

Consider a Schrödinger operator $\mathcal{L}=-\Delta+V$, where the nonnegative potential $V$ lies in the reverse Hölder class $B_{q}$. Utilizing the subordination formula, we derive estimates for the regularity properties of the fractional heat semigroup $\{e^{-t\mathcal{L}^{\alpha}}\}_{t>0}$ linked to $\mathcal{L}$. Consequently, we establish the $BMO^{\gamma}_{\mathcal{L}}$-boundedness of the maximal function and the Littlewood-Paley $g$-functions associated with $\mathcal{L}$ by applying the $T1$ theorem, respectively.

Utilizing approximation theory, we identify the absolute minima of potentials generated by spherical $(2m-3)$-designs possessing a non-trivial index $2m$, provided these designs are situated within a union of $m$ parallel hyperplanes ($m\geq 2$) that meet specific supplementary conditions. The interaction between points is governed by a function of the dot product featuring positive derivatives of orders $2m-2$, $2m-1$, and $2m$. This framework encompasses classical Coulomb, Riesz, and logarithmic potentials, as well as a completely monotone potential based on squared distance. We demonstrate this finding by proving that the absolute minimum of the potential for the icosahedron's vertices on the unit sphere $S^2$ in $\mathbb R^3$ occurs at the vertices of its dual dodecahedron, and conversely, the minimum for the dodecahedron's vertices is achieved at the dual icosahedron's vertices. Furthermore, we show that the absolute minimum of the potential for the configuration of $240$ minimal vectors of the $E_8$ root lattice, normalized to the unit sphere $S^7$ in $\mathbb R^8$, is realized at a specific set of $2160$ points on $S^7$, which we detail.

This study employs Stein's method to derive rates of normal approximation regarding total variation distance for a broad range of sums involving score functions from marked Poisson point processes on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Similar to investigations utilizing the weaker Kolmogorov distance, the score functions are required to meet stabilizing and moment criteria. While an extra non-singularity condition for the score functions is necessary, we demonstrate that the resulting rates align with those found under the Kolmogorov distance. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of these theorems through four examples: Voronoi tessellation, $k$-nearest neighbours, timber volume, and maximal layers.

Discovered in 1995 as the first T-dwarf, GJ 229B has been the subject of more extensive observations than most other brown dwarfs, yet it lacks a complete atmospheric analysis using modern methods. Its spectrum displays unique characteristics, and recent dynamical calculations regarding its mass and orbit have yielded conflicting results, both necessitating further study. Situated tens of AU from its host star, GJ 229B resides near the boundary between planetary and stellar formation zones, meaning its atmosphere may hold keys to understanding the origins of such intermediate bodies. To address these uncertainties, we applied the open-source APOLLO code to published spectra spanning 0.5–5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$ to perform atmospheric retrievals. Our results yield a refined mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an effective temperature of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K; these figures align better with brown dwarf evolutionary models and indicate a system age exceeding 1.0 Gyr. Additionally, we derived molecular abundances for the atmosphere, successfully reproducing the previously noted high CO levels, and explore their implications for the object's formation and evolution. This retrieval study offers valuable insights for analyzing other brown dwarfs and directly imaged planets, including those targeted by JWST and future telescopes.

We introduce a novel methodology grounded in information theory and entropy to address the dissemination of conspiracy theories. The process begins by representing an event, such as the 9/11 attacks, as a sequence of information strings encoded by two-state variables ($E_i = \pm 1$) for $i=1$ to $N$. By assigning these values, we establish an initial order parameter and entropy level. When conspiracy theorists comment on the report, they repeatedly target specific strings ($E_k$) and flip their interpretations from $-1$ to $+1$. This action renders the event's interpretation increasingly ambiguous, causing entropy to rise. Once entropy surpasses a chosen threshold—set at its maximum value of $N/2$ variables equal to $1$—doubt dominates the narrative, creating conditions for an alternative theory to emerge. Consequently, tracking the evolution of entropy serves as a metric for the penetration depth of a conspiracy theory. Our framework leverages online content voluntarily contributed by crowds in response to news agency reports or blog posts. We examine various aggregation levels, including individual comments, persons, and discussion threads, to analyze corresponding patterns in entropy fluctuations.

Monocular depth estimation has gained significant research attention over the years, particularly because self-supervised networks have effectively narrowed the performance gap with supervised and stereo-based approaches. Nevertheless, existing methods prioritize dense 3D reconstruction and often capture minute details that are unnecessary for autonomous navigation. To address this, we propose estimating a navigation map using a quadtree representation. Our goal is to generate an adaptive depth prediction that selectively extracts only the information crucial for obstacle avoidance, while representing other areas of the 3D space with approximate distances. Experiments on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that this approach substantially reduces the volume of output data without compromising accuracy.

We define an introverted Boolean algebra $\cal B$ consisting of clopen subsets of a topological group $G$, demonstrating that its associated Stone space $(\nu_{\cal B} G, \nu_{\cal B})$ constitutes a totally disconnected semigroup compactification of $G$, and proving that every such compactification arises in this manner. We examine and characterize the universal totally disconnected semigroup, semitopological semigroup, and group compactifications of $G$. Our primary findings are derived independently of Gelfand theory and established properties of the standard (typically non-totally disconnected) universal compactifications $G^{LUC}$, $G^{WAP}$, and $G^{AP}$, although we utilize Gelfand theory to elucidate the connections between these traditional compactifications and their totally disconnected analogues.

Hydrogen I (HI) gas is a fundamental component of galaxy evolution, yet studying it has historically been restricted to nearby galaxies because the 21-cm hyperfine transition is too faint to detect at greater cosmological distances. This study introduces a novel method to estimate the HI mass ($M_{\rm HI}$) of individual galaxies out to $z\approx 6$ by directly measuring the [CII]-to-HI conversion factor in star-forming systems at $z\gtrsim 2$ using $\gamma$-ray burst afterglows. By synthesizing recent [CII]-158 $\mu$m emission data, we quantify how HI content evolves across cosmic time. Our results indicate that HI mass surpasses stellar mass ($M_\star$) at $z\gtrsim 1$ and grows with increasing redshift. Consequently, the fraction of total baryonic mass comprised of HI rises from roughly 20% at $z=0$ to approximately 60% at $z\sim 6$. Additionally, we identify a universal correlation between the HI gas fraction ($M_{\rm HI}/M_\star$) and gas-phase metallicity that remains consistent from $z\approx 6$ down to $z=0$. At $z>2$, most galaxies exhibit HI depletion times ($t_{\rm dep,HI} = M_{\rm HI}/{\rm SFR}$) of less than 2 Gyr, which is significantly shorter than in local ($z\sim 0$) galaxies. Finally, applying the [CII]-to-HI conversion factor allows us to calculate the cosmic mass density of HI in galaxies ($\rho_{\rm HI}$) at three epochs: $z\approx 0$, $z\approx 2$, and $z\sim 4-6$. These findings align with prior estimates derived from local 21-cm observations and damped Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers (DLAs) at $z\gtrsim 2$, indicating that $\rho_{\rm HI}(z)$ has decreased by a factor of about 5 from the end of reionization to the present day.

Assume $\Gamma$ represents a conformal loop ensemble (CLE$_\kappa$) characterized by simple loops, where $\kappa$ lies in the interval $(8/3,4)$, situated within a simply connected domain $D \subseteq {\mathbf C}$ whose boundary is also formed by a CLE$_\kappa$ loop. Let $\Upsilon$ denote the carpet of $\Gamma$, defined as the subset of $D$ not encircled by any loop of $\Gamma$. We establish that specific approximations of the chemical distance metric within $\Upsilon$ are tight. Specifically, for any path $\omega \colon [0,1] \to \Upsilon$ and $\epsilon > 0$, we define ${\mathfrak N}_\epsilon(\omega)$ as the Lebesgue measure of the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $\omega$. For points $z,w \in \Upsilon$, we set ${\mathfrak d}_\epsilon(z,w;\Gamma) = \inf_\omega {\mathfrak N}_\epsilon(\omega)$, where the infimum ranges over all paths connecting $z$ to $w$ in $\Upsilon$. Furthermore, let ${\mathfrak m}_\epsilon$ represent the median of $\sup_{z,w \in \partial D} {\mathfrak d}_\epsilon(z,w;\Gamma)$. We demonstrate that the mapping $(z,w) \mapsto {\mathfrak m}_\epsilon^{-1} {\mathfrak d}_\epsilon(z,w;\Gamma)$ is tight, and that any subsequential limit yields a geodesic metric on $\Upsilon$ which is Hölder continuous relative to the Euclidean metric. We further conjecture that this subsequential limit is unique, possesses conformal covariance, and characterizes the scaling limit of the chemical distance metric for discrete loop models converging to CLE$_\kappa$ for $\kappa \in (8/3,4)$, such as the critical Ising model.

A truly versatile magnetometer must provide readable outputs across a broad spectrum of target field parameters. This study experimentally validates that pairing a $^{171}$Yb$^{+}$ atomic sensor with properly trained neural networks allows for the characterization of target fields in various difficult scenarios. Specifically, we estimate the parameters of radio frequency (RF) drives despite large shot noise, covering the extreme case of continuous data acquisition via single-shot measurements, as well as regimes where the magnetometer's response significantly deviates from standard harmonic behavior.

This paper addresses boundary stabilization and observation for the multidimensional unstable heat equation. Due to the general nature of the domain, standard partial differential equation back-stepping techniques are difficult to apply. Instead, the unstable dynamics are managed by integrating finite-dimensional spectral truncation with dynamics compensation. By incorporating additional finite-dimensional actuator and sensor dynamics, the problem of unbounded stabilization and observation is transformed into a bounded one, thereby simplifying the controller and observer design. The study presents designs for both full-state feedback stabilizers and state observers, achieving exponential stability in the closed-loop system and ensuring the well-posedness of the observer.

Existing methods for lexical simplification depend heavily on heuristics and corpus-level features that often fail to match human judgment. We have developed a human-annotated lexicon containing 15,000 English words and introduced a new neural readability ranking model. This model employs a Gaussian-based feature vectorization layer that leverages these human ratings to assess the complexity of individual words or phrases. Our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art systems across various lexical simplification tasks and evaluation datasets. Furthermore, we generated SimplePPDB++, a lexical resource comprising over 10 million simplifying paraphrase rules, by applying our model to the Paraphrase Database (PPDB).

Analyzing organ vessels is critical for computer-aided diagnosis and surgical planning, yet it remains a challenging task due to the fine, connected structures that introduce ambiguity in segmentation and sub-type identification, particularly within low-contrast capillaries. Additionally, recent two-stage methods often propagate and exacerbate errors from initial whole-vessel segmentation to subsequent pixel-wise sub-type classification. These difficulties are further compounded by a scarcity of manual annotations. To tackle these challenges, we introduce a hierarchical deep network utilizing an attention mechanism to localize low-contrast capillaries based on whole-vessel context, thereby enhancing spatial activation for sub-type vessel detection. Furthermore, we develop an uncertainty-aware semi-supervised training framework to mitigate the annotation dependency typical of deep models. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on benchmarks for retinal artery/vein segmentation in fundus images and liver portal/hepatic vessel segmentation in CT images.

To explain resonance within a linearly coupled system, the study analyzes the photosensitive CDIMA reaction-diffusion equation. It derives the conditions for Turing instability in the coupled reaction-diffusion framework and analytically investigates the critical diffusion coefficients required to exit resonance-type patterns. Furthermore, the impact of photosensitivity on $3:1$ resonance forcing is examined under both strong and weak coupling scenarios. Numerical simulations are conducted to verify these theoretical results.

Two recent studies by Pore et al. and Khuyagbaatar et al. announced the discovery of the new isotope Md-244, yet their reported decay data are inconsistent. Pore et al. identified two isomeric states undergoing alpha decay with energies of E(1)=8.66(2) MeV and a half-life of 0.4+0.4/-0.1 s, alongside E(2)=8.31(2) MeV and a half-life of approximately 6 s. In contrast, Khuyagbaatar et al. observed only a single transition characterized by a broad energy range of E=(8.73-8.86) MeV and a half-life of 0.30/-0.09 s. Given that the findings from Pore et al. closely resemble those previously published for Md-245 (E=8.64(2), 8.68(2) MeV; T_1/2=0.35+0.23/-0.16 s), we have compared the Md-244 data from Pore et al. with reports on Md-245 by both Ninov et al. and Khuyagbaatar et al.. Our conclusion is that the data attributed to Pore et al. actually correspond to Md-245, with minor contributions (one event each) from Fm-245 and likely Md-246.

Scene Graph Generation (SGG) seeks to construct a structured scene representation based on objects and their pairwise relations, which aids various downstream applications. However, existing SGG approaches often underperform due to the long-tailed distribution inherent in training data. To mitigate this, we introduce Resistance Training using Prior Bias (RTPB) for SGG. Specifically, RTPB employs a distributed prior bias to enhance the detection of infrequent relationships during training, thereby boosting the model's generalization on tail categories. Additionally, to better capture contextual information regarding objects and relations, we propose a contextual encoding backbone called the Dual Transformer (DTrans). Extensive experiments on the VG150 benchmark demonstrate the efficacy of our approach for unbiased scene graph generation. Notably, applying RTPB to current SGG methods yields over a 10% improvement in mean recall. Moreover, the combination of DTrans and RTPB surpasses nearly all state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.

The notion of a skew root within skew polynomials serves to define algebraic closedness for $\sigma$-fields, which are fields endowed with an endomorphism. It is demonstrated that any $\sigma$-field can be embedded into algebraically closed $\sigma$-fields of various types.

The atmospheric properties of exoplanets ranging from 2 to 10 Earth masses remain largely unclear; however, the sub-Neptune K2-18b, which receives Earth-like stellar radiation, provides a crucial opportunity to study such atmospheres. Prior studies utilizing transmission spectrum data from Kepler, Hubble (HST), and Spitzer, along with various retrieval and forward-modelling techniques, have indicated the presence of water vapor and an H$_2$--He envelope but failed to detect other species like methane (CH$_4$). This work presents Exo-REM simulations—a self-consistent 1D radiative-equilibrium model—applied to K2-18b across a broad parameter grid to constrain its chemical makeup. Our results suggest atmospheric metallicities between 40 and 500 times solar values and indicate the potential for H$_2$O-ice clouds, while ruling out liquid water clouds. We reaffirm our previous finding that methane absorption features should nominally dominate the HST spectral range. Comparing these simulations with retrieval algorithm results reveals that the interpretation of a water-dominated spectrum likely stems from either omitting methane absorptions or excessive overfitting. Furthermore, we explored scenarios permitting a methane-depleted atmosphere; while the data could be fitted under these conditions, a high internal temperature for K2-18b is deemed highly improbable. A low carbon-to-oxygen ratio (approximately 0.01–0.1) allows water to dominate the spectrum and fit the observations, yet this configuration currently lacks a physical basis. Conversely, simulations with a C/O ratio below 0.01 fail to satisfactorily match the data.

This work investigates the Witten-type topological field theory (W-TFT) framework applied to self-organized criticality (SOC) within stochastic neural networks. We derive the Parisi-Sourlas-Wu quantization for general stochastic differential equations (SDEs) governing these networks, along with the Becchi-Rouet-Stora-Tyutin (BRST) symmetry inherent in diffusion systems. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between spontaneous symmetry breaking and instantons that connect steady states in SDEs, and we determine both sufficient and necessary conditions for pseudo-supersymmetry in stochastic neural networks. Assuming neuronal avalanches serve as a mechanism for cortical information processing and storage, that the stochastic neural network model is accurate, and that SOC systems can be interpreted as W-TFTs with spontaneously broken BRST symmetry, we aim to recover these phenomena from the stochastic neural network model. Our findings indicate that, provided the drift coefficients exhibit small, non-constant divergence, the stochastic neural network model maintains BRST symmetry. Consequently, if SOC in brain neural networks is viewed as a W-TFT with spontaneously broken BRST symmetry, the general stochastic neural network model widely utilized in neuroscience is insufficient to describe such SOC. Additionally, utilizing the Fokker-Planck equation, we demonstrate the sufficient condition regarding diffusion required for the existence of a steady-state probability distribution in stochastic neural networks. This process gives rise to firing rate rhythms in neuronal networks while simultaneously conserving certain biological laws.

Game-theoretic motion planning offers a powerful approach for managing systems of highly interactive, multi-robot agents. However, most current planners rely on the unrealistic assumption that all agents possess prior knowledge of each other's objective functions. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a fault-tolerant receding horizon game-theoretic planner that utilizes inter-agent communication grounded in intention hypothesis likelihood. In this framework, robots exchange their objective functions alongside their intended goals. A discrete Bayesian filter is then employed to infer objectives in real-time by analyzing the divergence between communicated intentions and actual observed trajectories. Simulations across three safety-critical autonomous driving scenarios—overtaking, lane merging, and intersection crossing—demonstrate that the proposed planner effectively leverages alternative intention hypotheses to generate safe trajectories even when communication networks experience faults.

This paper begins by examining the "energy-peaks" initiative, a decade-old broad program in collider physics. We analyze the energy distribution of a massless daughter particle in the laboratory frame, originating from the unpolarized two-body decay of a heavy parent particle with an arbitrary boost profile. Notably, the peak of this daughter's energy distribution coincides exactly with its fixed energy value in the parent's rest frame, a value determined solely by the masses of the parent and the other decay product. We outline extensions to various decay modes and discuss diverse Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) applications. Furthermore, the energy-peak concept offers a robust method for measuring the top quark mass via the energy of the resulting bottom quark. Relying on "parent-boost-invariance," this approach minimizes sensitivity to the specific top quark production mechanism, addressing limitations in other methods that assume purely Standard Model production and are thus vulnerable to associated uncertainties, including potential BSM contributions. While the original proposal utilized $b$-jet energy as a proxy for bottom quark energy—a strategy successfully adopted by the CMS collaboration—this method suffers from jet-energy scale (JES) uncertainties. This limitation can be overcome by employing the decay length of a $B$-hadron within the $b$-jet as a proxy for the bottom quark energy. We propose a combined strategy that merges these two concepts to achieve an optimal top quark mass determination: leveraging $B$-hadron decay lengths while enhancing precision through the energy-peak principle. This hybrid approach eliminates JES uncertainty and remains largely independent of the top quark production model. We present the results of this analysis here, which are scheduled for publication in an upcoming paper.

We examine a Hamiltonian featuring cutoffs that models the weak decay of massive spin-one bosons into the complete lepton family. This Hamiltonian is defined as a self-adjoint operator within a suitable Fock space and possesses a unique ground state. We establish a Mourre estimate and a limiting absorption principle for energies lying above the ground state but below the first threshold, provided the coupling constant is sufficiently small. Consequently, we demonstrate that there are no eigenvalues and that the energy spectrum is absolutely continuous within this same spectral range.

Specific water arrangements within partially filled containers can drastically diminish their bounce. Through experiments involving containers filled to a volume fraction $\phi$, we demonstrate that rotation provides an efficient means to manipulate these distributions and thereby significantly alter the bounce. High-speed imaging captures the underlying physics, uncovering a complex series of fluid-dynamic processes that we have modeled to reflect our experimental observations.

Enterprise databases typically feature large and intricate schemas, making it difficult for programmers to manually author complete schema mapping queries without deep expertise in both source and target structures. While sample-driven schema mapping allows users to define mappings through data records, specifying actual data remains more challenging than conveying other insights about the desired mapping. This project introduces PRISM, a schema mapping system supporting multiresolution interactions. Users are no longer restricted to high-resolution constraints such as exact records; instead, they can provide constraints at various levels of detail, including incomplete records, value ranges, and data types. This enhanced interaction model offers greater flexibility in describing schema mappings, and this demonstration illustrates the practical application of PRISM for real database schema mapping.

The High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.) conducted an extensive survey of the Galactic plane, confirming approximately 78 TeV $\gamma$-ray sources, many of which remain unidentified. Among the 17 confirmed point-like sources in the H.E.S.S. Galactic Plane Survey (HGPS) catalog is HESS J1828-099, a source with a Gaussian standard deviation of less than 0.07$^{\circ}$. This object is distinct because it shows no apparent association with counterparts at other wavelengths. This study investigates the nature of HESS J1828-099 using multi-wavelength data. Previously, a high mass X-Ray binary (HMXB) consisting of pulsar XTE J1829-098 and a Be star companion was detected in X-ray and infrared bands at a distance of 14$'$ from HESS J1828-099. Utilizing 12 years of $\textit{Fermi}$-LAT $\gamma$-ray observations, we examine whether 4FGL J1830.2-1005 serves as the GeV counterpart to HESS J1828-099. Within the RXTE confidence region, existing radio surveys reveal a plausible counterpart exhibiting a steep spectrum ($\alpha_{radio}$ = - 0.746 $\pm$ 0.284). For the first time, this letter utilizes multi-wavelength data to determine if HESS J1828-099, 4FGL J1830.2-1005, and the HMXB system share a common origin. Our findings suggest that HESS J1828-099 may represent a TeV high mass $\gamma$-ray binary source.

(Ca$_{x}$Sr$_{1-x}$)$_3$Rh$_4$Sn$_{13}$ represents a unique system where structural quantum criticality and superconductivity interact in a fascinating manner. It is hypothesized that a structural quantum critical point, concealed beneath a wide superconducting dome, optimizes the material's superconducting performance. Nevertheless, the superconducting dome obstructs the investigation of this critical point via electrical transport, since transport coefficients disappear in the superconducting state. To address this, we utilized critical current density to probe the region within the superconducting dome. Our results demonstrate a significant increase in critical current density at the zero-temperature limit as the system approaches the structural quantum critical point.

Immediately following a disaster, high-resolution satellite imagery is vital for response planning, offering a comprehensive view of critical infrastructure conditions like building destruction, flooding, and blocked access routes. Creating damage maps at this resolution traditionally demands hundreds of hours of work by experts. Nevertheless, by combining crowdsourcing with recent deep learning advancements, this process can be reduced to mere hours in real time. Requiring volunteers to mark specific points rather than delineate the exact shapes of damaged areas significantly cuts down the analysis time needed for immediate response. However, volunteer markings often vary in consistency. This study introduces methods to aggregate these potentially inconsistent marks to train a neural network capable of detecting damage.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA) is a developing discipline focused on extracting hidden topological insights from datasets. While TDA tools have traditionally been employed to generate filters and descriptors that enhance Machine Learning (ML) performance, this paper introduces an algorithm that applies TDA directly to multi-class classification tasks, eliminating the need for subsequent ML stages. This approach demonstrates particular efficacy with imbalanced datasets. The method constructs a filtered simplicial complex and utilizes Persistent Homology (PH) to identify a sub-complex where unlabeled points are assigned labels based on majority voting from their labeled neighbors. The study evaluates the proposed TDABC algorithm across eight datasets varying in dimensionality, class overlap, and sample imbalance. On average, TDABC outperforms KNN and weighted-KNN. Furthermore, it matches the performance of baseline classifiers like Local SVM and Random Forest on balanced data while surpassing all baselines in classifying entangled and minority classes.

Over a span of more than three years, NASA's Kepler mission monitored background areas within its field of view using custom super-apertures known as EXBA masks. Because these masks target broad sky regions rather than individual objects, the standard Kepler Science Data Processing pipeline generated Target Pixel Files but omitted light curves for the sources inside them. This study generates light curves for 9,327 sources detected in the EXBA masks by employing aperture photometry based on the instrument's Pixel Response Function (PRF). The PRF models, derived from Kepler's full-frame images, allow for the creation of apertures that match the Point Spread Function (PSF) shapes and facilitate the calculation of flux completeness and contamination metrics. These light curves are accessible via the MAST archive as a High Level Science Product (kbonus-apexba). Accompanying this dataset is kepler-apertures, a Python library designed to compute PRF models and execute aperture photometry on Kepler-like data. Analysis of the EXBA mask light curves identified an exoplanet candidate orbiting Gaia EDR3 2077240046296834304, consistent with a large companion having a radius of $0.81 R_J$, and revealed a catalog of 69 eclipsing binaries. The authors invite the community to utilize this new dataset for advanced time-domain analyses, including the demographic study of eclipsing binaries.

Unobservable physiological signals can significantly strengthen biometric authentication systems. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is particularly convenient due to its ease of measurement and inherent protection against remote threats; however, any leakage of PPG data allows adversaries to compromise these systems. The emergence of remote PPG (rPPG) further enables attackers to recover PPG signals from video, posing a potential danger. Despite this risk, rPPG-based attacks have been largely ignored because previous methods relied on the victim's leaked PPG signals. This paper introduces a novel spoofing technique that utilizes rPPG waveforms extracted from video clips to deceive PPG-based authentication. We developed a new PPG restoration model capable of generating adversarial attacks without requiring leaked PPG data. Experimental results on state-of-the-art PPG-based authentication systems demonstrate that signals recovered via rPPG constitute a severe threat to the security of such systems.

Multiple intriguing scenarios extending beyond the Standard Model forecast signals characterized by atypical charged particle paths. When these unusual tracks constitute the most prominent feature, they present substantial experimental hurdles for the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), especially regarding trigger systems. This paper investigates track-based triggers for a representative selection of long-lived and non-standard signatures anticipated at the upcoming High Luminosity LHC. The examined scenarios encompass soft-unclustered-energy-pattern models yielding numerous low-momentum tracks, displaced leptons and anomalous prompt tracks from a Supersymmetry model featuring long-lived staus, and displaced hadrons arising from a Higgs portal scenario with long-lived scalars. The study quantifies trigger efficiency relative to baseline track trigger parameters, specifically transverse momentum and impact parameter, and offers recommendations for future hardware-based track triggers.

We examine the minimal seesaw model, which extends the Standard Model with two right-handed neutrinos to account for neutrino masses and mixing angles observed in oscillation experiments. If one of these right-handed neutrinos has a mass below the electroweak scale, it can make a substantial contribution to neutrinoless double beta ($0\nu \beta \beta$) decay. We demonstrate that the observation of $0\nu \beta \beta$ decay by upcoming experiments would have profound implications for the search for such light right-handed neutrinos.

We develop constructive geometric methods to identify when a domain is $L^s$-averaging and derive both upper and lower bounds for the $L^s$-integrals of quasihyperbolic distance. Additionally, we provide illustrative examples that clarify our geometric tools and the connection between $p$-Poincaré domains and $L^s$-averaging domains. Finally, we investigate finite unions of $L^s(\mu)$-averaging domains.

In 2017, the STAR Collaboration reported measurements of hyperon global polarization in heavy ion collisions, indicating that the subatomic fireball fluid generated in these events is the most vortical fluid known. An intriguing question remains: at what beam energy does this most vortical fluid exist? This study conducts a systematic investigation into the beam energy dependence of hyperon global polarization, focusing particularly on the $\hat{O}(1\sim 10)\ \rm GeV$ range. Our findings reveal a non-monotonic trend, where global polarization initially rises and then falls as beam energy decreases from $27~\rm GeV$ to $3~\rm GeV$. The peak polarization signal occurs near $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 7.7~\rm GeV$, suggesting that heavy ion collisions at this energy produce the most vortical fluid. Precise experimental measurements within the $\hat{O}(1\sim 10)\ \rm GeV$ beam energy region are anticipated to validate this prediction shortly.

In April 2021, the CONCERTO spectral-imaging instrument was deployed at the 12-meter Atacama Pathfinder EXperiment (APEX) telescope. Designed to detect radiation from ionised carbon atoms ([CII]) using the "Intensity Mapping" technique, it aims to establish the initial constraints on the power spectrum of dusty star-forming galaxies. The system comprises two arrays of 2,152 pixels built with Lumped Element Kinetic Inductance Detectors (LEKID), which function at cryogenic temperatures alongside cold optics and a Fast Fourier Transform Spectrometer (FTS). A newly engineered electronic system, housed in five microTCA crates and consisting of twelve readout boards plus two control boards, manages the instrument's operation and readout. This paper details the architecture and performance characteristics of the system.

We present a fixed point iteration method grounded in optimizing a linear function across a compact domain. We demonstrate that this process invariably converges to a fixed point and investigate the distribution of such points within diverse convex sets. Specifically, we analyze elliptopes and establish an algebraic definition for their fixed points. We further prove that the attractive fixed points of an elliptope correspond precisely to its vertices. Lastly, we examine the application of fixed point iteration in rounding solutions derived from semidefinite programming relaxations.

Gravitationally enhanced friction can decelerate the inflaton to facilitate ultra-slow-roll inflation, thereby amplifying curvature perturbations. These amplified perturbations can produce a substantial number of primordial black holes (PBHs) and concurrently generate significant background gravitational waves (SIGWs). This paper examines the primordial non-Gaussianity of curvature perturbations within the framework of inflation driven by gravitationally enhanced friction. Our findings indicate that when this mechanism influences inflationary dynamics, the resulting non-Gaussianity is significantly greater than that predicted by standard slow-roll inflation. Specifically, during the phase where the curvature perturbation power spectrum approaches its peak, the non-Gaussianity parameter transitions from negative to positive values. At the point of maximum power spectrum amplitude, the non-Gaussianity parameter is approximately zero ($\sim \mathcal{O}(0.01)$). Additionally, while primordial non-Gaussianity enhances PBH formation, its impact on SIGWs remains negligible.

As social media dominates information consumption, the rapid spread of fake news has created significant hurdles for platforms in identifying authentic versus false content. Detecting fake news remains a complex challenge due to the varied nature of news topics and the high costs associated with manual annotation. This study overcomes the shortcomings of current automated detection systems by integrating auxiliary data, such as user comments and interaction patterns, into a new reinforcement learning framework named \textbf{RE}inforced \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{L}earning \textbf{F}ake \textbf{N}ews \textbf{D}etection (REAL-FND). By leveraging both cross-domain and within-domain knowledge, REAL-FND demonstrates robustness in target domains even when trained on different source domains. Comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets confirm the model's efficacy, particularly in scenarios where labeled data in the target domain is scarce.

Flat electronic bands present a counterintuitive challenge because the vanishing electron velocity renders standard quasiparticle transport theories inapplicable. This study investigates quantum transport within generalized families of perfectly flat bands [PRB 105, L241102 (2022)], revealing that although conventional contributions disappear, a quantum-geometric term drives enhanced electronic transport. This term arises from Wannier orbital quantization specific to geometrically nontrivial flat bands, such as flat Chern bands. We derive analogous expressions for superfluid weight, thermal conductance, and thermoelectric response. Notably, we report an anomalous thermopower in flat topological bands that reaches the quantum unit of thermopower, $\frac{k_B}{e}\ln 2 \approx 60\ \mu\text{V/K}$, a magnitude not anticipated in standard dispersive bands.

In cybersecurity, detecting malicious or anomalous behavior often requires aggregating numerous weak indicators of compromise, none of which might trigger suspicion individually. Furthermore, the trajectory these indicators follow is frequently vital. This complexity makes cybersecurity data analysis particularly well-suited for Topological Data Analysis (TDA), a discipline that leverages algebraic topology to examine the high-level structure of data, serving both exploratory purposes and machine learning pipelines. By presenting TDA and reviewing its existing applications within cybersecurity, we aim to draw researchers' attention to a promising domain with significant potential to advance cybersecurity data science.

Although extensive research has examined the semantics of conditional sentences, formal models addressing their pragmatic interpretation and use remain underexplored. This study adopts a probabilistic framework for pragmatic reasoning regarding indicative conditionals, one that seamlessly incorporates gradient beliefs concerning complex world states. Specifically, we model how listeners revise their prior beliefs about causal structures and the joint probabilities of antecedents and consequents, grounded in assumptions regarding the speaker's production process. Our model successfully accounts for various empirically observed inferences—including epistemic inferences, conditional perfection, and the relationship between antecedents and consequents—when provided with natural contextual assumptions. Furthermore, we propose that this approach resolves three puzzles identified by Douven (2012) concerning belief updates with conditionals, demonstrating that a listener's confidence in the antecedent may rise, fall, or stay constant depending on the specific utterance context.

This paper introduces an enhanced mean-field inference algorithm designed for fully connected paired Conditional Random Fields (CRFs). The proposed method replaces the original linear convolution in the Message Passing operation with a graph attention mechanism, transforming the inference process into the forward pass of a Graph Attention Network (GAT). When integrated with the mean-field inferred label distribution, this approach yields results equivalent to a classifier relying solely on unary potentials. Consequently, we present a graph attention network model incorporating residual structures, which is versatile enough to address various sequence annotation tasks, including pixel-level image semantic segmentation and text annotation.

The Pigeonhole Principle (PHP) has been extensively examined within automated reasoning, encompassing both theoretical and practical dimensions. While the majority of solvers exhibit exponential growth in both runtime and proof length, certain specialized methods manage to achieve polynomial complexity. Decades ago, Cook manually engineered $O(n^4)$ extended resolution proofs, with $n$ representing the number of pigeons. Current automated approaches only outperform Cook's results in analogous proof systems when $n$ is large. We have developed the shortest known proofs of PHP using the DRAT format, which is standard for modern SAT solvers. By employing auxiliary variables and recursively decomposing the original problem into smaller instances, we manually constructed proofs with a length of $O(n^3)$ and a leading coefficient of $5/2$.

Within the context of bulk reconstruction, we clarify the connections among the action of CFT modular Hamiltonians on bulk operators, the potential equations of motion for these operators, and the asymptotic charge distributions associated with such bulk fields. Specifically, for scalar fields interacting with gravity or gauge fields, we demonstrate how CFT analyses of modular Hamiltonian actions restrict possible bulk equations of motion to ensure consistency with both gauge invariance and diffeomorphism invariance. Furthermore, we establish that demanding compatibility between the modular Hamiltonian's action on a dressed bulk scalar operator and a simple, albeit unspecified, equation of motion uniquely determines both the equation of motion and the modular Hamiltonian's action—provided the first-order $\frac{1}{N}$ terms are known and reasonable assumptions hold.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) enable the manipulation of wireless propagation environments by adjusting multiple reflecting elements. While RISs have traditionally relied on single-connected architectures modeled by diagonal scattering matrices, recently proposed Beyond Diagonal RISs (BD-RISs) utilize non-diagonal matrices to unlock new opportunities and advantages. These efficient BD-RIS designs are built upon group and fully connected reconfigurable impedance networks; however, a closed-form solution for their globally optimal scattering matrix has been lacking. This paper presents such a solution, demonstrating that theoretical performance upper bounds can be precisely achieved regardless of the channel conditions. We initially address received signal power maximization in single-user single-input single-output (SISO) systems assisted by a BD-RIS operating in either reflective or transmissive mode, subsequently extending the approach to single-user and multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed algorithm offers lower computational complexity than the iterative methods found in prior literature. Specifically, the complexity of our algorithm scales linearly with the number of RIS elements for group-connected architectures and cubically for fully-connected ones.

This paper presents GigaSpeech, an expanding, multi-domain English speech recognition corpus containing 10,000 hours of high-quality labeled audio for supervised learning and 40,000 hours of total audio for semi-supervised and unsupervised tasks. Approximately 40,000 hours of transcribed audio were initially gathered from sources including audiobooks, podcasts, and YouTube, encompassing both read and spontaneous speech across diverse topics like arts, science, and sports. A novel forced alignment and segmentation pipeline was developed to generate training-appropriate sentence segments and exclude low-quality transcriptions. For system training, GigaSpeech offers five subsets ranging from 10 hours to 10,000 hours. During the filtering and validation phase, the 10,000-hour XL subset maintains a word error rate cap of 4%, while all smaller subsets are capped at 0%. Conversely, the DEV and TEST evaluation sets underwent re-processing by professional human transcribers to guarantee high transcription quality. Baseline systems are also provided for widely used speech recognition toolkits, including Athena, ESPnet, Kaldi, and Pika.

Arabic, a widely spoken Semitic language with numerous dialects, has seen the emergence of various transformer models trained on both the language and its dialects, following the success of pre-trained language models. Although these models have been evaluated on downstream NLP tasks, no study has directly compared their internal representations. This work investigates how linguistic information is encoded in Arabic pre-trained models across different language varieties. By conducting a layer and neuron analysis using three intrinsic tasks—two morphological tagging tasks based on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), a dialectal part-of-speech tagging task, and a dialectal identification task—we uncover several key insights: (i) word morphology is acquired in the lower and middle layers; (ii) dialectal identification requires more knowledge, leading to its preservation even in the final layers; (iii) despite significant vocabulary overlap, MSA-based models fail to capture the nuances of Arabic dialects; and (iv) embedding layer neurons exhibit polysemy, whereas middle-layer neurons are specialized for specific properties.

Let $F_2$ denote the prime field with two elements, and let $GL_s := GL(s, F_2)$ represent the general linear group of rank $s$. We denote the Steenrod algebra over $F_2$ by $\mathscr A$. The (mod-2) Lambda algebra, $\Lambda$, serves as a key instrument for analyzing the elusive "Ext-groups." Furthermore, William Singer's $s$-th algebraic transfer is anticipated to be a valuable tool in this context. This transfer is defined as a homomorphism $Tr_s: F_2 \otimes_{GL_s}P_{\mathscr A}(H_{*}(B\mathbb V_s, F_2))\to {\rm Ext}_{\mathscr {A}}^{s,s+*}(F_2, F_2)$, where $\mathbb V_s$ is the elementary abelian $2$-group of rank $s$, $H_*(B\mathbb V_s)$ represents the homology of its classifying space, and $P_{\mathscr A}(H_{*}(B\mathbb V_s, F_2))$ signifies the primitive component of this homology under the $\mathscr A$ action. It has been established that $Tr_s$ is significantly non-trivial; specifically, it is an isomorphism for $s\leq 3$. Additionally, Singer demonstrated that $Tr_4$ is an isomorphism in certain internal degrees and investigated the image of the fifth transfer using invariant theory. In this note, we employ an alternative approach to examine the image of $Tr_5$. Specifically, through direct computations utilizing a representation of $Tr_5$ over the algebra $\Lambda$, we demonstrate that $Tr_5$ detects the non-zero elements $h_0d_0\in {\rm Ext}_{\mathscr A}^{5, 5+14}(F_2, F_2)$, $h_2e_0\in {\rm Ext}_{\mathscr A}^{5, 5+20}(F_2, F_2)$, and $h_1h_4c_0\in {\rm Ext}_{\mathscr A}^{5, 5+24}(F_2, F_2)$. This methodology can be extended to homological degrees $s\geq 6$ provided certain conditions are met.

We demonstrate that the gap between the measured muon anomalous moment and the standard model forecast can be resolved within nonlocal theoretical frameworks. By calculating the leading and next-to-leading order nonlocal corrections to the anomalous magnetic moment, denoted as $\alpha_{NL}$, we establish a dependence on the nonlocality scale $M_f$ and fermion mass $m_f$ given by $\alpha_{NL} \propto m_f^2/M_f^2$. This relationship explains, under a flavor-blind nonlocality scale, why the electron's anomalous magnetic moment aligns closely with standard model predictions, while simultaneously predicting a significant anomaly for the $\tau$ particle. Furthermore, we establish lower limits for the nonlocality scale in both flavor-blind and flavor-dependent scenarios.

This study presents a novel methodology for identifying an optimal penalty coefficient in functional regression. We assume that both dependent and independent variables, as well as regression coefficients, are time-dependent functions, and that error dynamics adhere to a stochastic differential equation. Initially, we formulate an objective function based on a time-dependent residual sum of squares and minimize it regarding the regression coefficients under various error dynamics, including LASSO, group LASSO, fused LASSO, and cubic smoothing splines. Subsequently, employing a Feynman-type path integral approach, we derive a Schrödinger-type equation that encapsulates the complete system information. Finally, applying first-order conditions with respect to these coefficients yields a closed-form solution.

Linearized Bregman iterations (LBreI) and their variants have garnered significant interest within compressed sensing and signal/image processing. Recently, LBreI has been adapted to a broader range of nonconvex functions, though several theoretical challenges remain. Notably, the standard requirement of gradient Lipschitz continuity limits its applicability in many practical scenarios. This study introduces a generalized algorithmic framework that unifies LBreI-type methods. A key finding is that the gradient Lipschitz continuity condition can be substituted with a Lipschitz-like convexity condition, applicable to both convex and nonconvex contexts. Consequently, the proposed framework and its theoretical underpinnings are utilized to address linear and quadratic inverse problems.

This work investigates the transmission probability of Dirac fermions in graphene as they encounter a triangular double-barrier potential under an external magnetic field. The system consists of two triangular barrier regions separated by a well with an energy gap. By solving the Dirac-like equation and matching boundary conditions, we derived the transmission and reflection coefficients using a transfer matrix approach. Our results demonstrate that transmission exhibits oscillation resonances indicative of the Klein tunneling effect. We found that the electrostatic field of the triangular barrier is crucial for controlling the peak of tunneling resistance; however, it only marginally alters resonances at oblique incidence and leaves the Klein paradox unchanged at normal incidence.

This paper details an implementation of the Schwerdtfeger-Fillmore-Springer-Cnops construction (SFSCc) and provides examples of its application. The SFSCc linearizes the linear-fractional action of the Möbius group within $\mathbb{R}^n$, offering significant benefits across various theoretical and practical domains, particularly in engineering. Our implementation leverages the Clifford algebra functionalities of the GiNaC computer algebra system (http://www.ginac.de/), as previously outlined in cs.MS/0410044. The core of this realization operates for arbitrary dimensions of $\mathbb{R}^n$ utilizing a metric defined by an arbitrary bilinear form. Additionally, we introduce a specialized subclass for two-dimensional cycles—specifically circles, parabolas, and hyperbolas—which incorporates dimension-specific routines and visualization capabilities exporting to PostScript files via the MetaPost (http://www.tug.org/metapost.html) or Asymptote (http://asymptote.sourceforge.net/) packages. This software serves as the foundation for numerous results published in math.CV/0512416, which are demonstrated here through its applications. The library is portable to other Computer Algebra Systems possessing similar Clifford algebra capabilities, though this may require varying degrees of modification. An ISO image of a Live Debian DVD is attached as an auxiliary file, with a duplicate also available on Google Drive.

The ultra-high sensitivity of Sagnac interferometers for parameter estimation, particularly in optical fiber sensing, stems from their non-reciprocity. This study investigates a novel form of non-reciprocity in optical fiber Sagnac interferometers that accounts for polarization-dependent loss. Distinct from previous research, this phenomenon arises from geometric phases induced by continuous weak measurements rather than the physical effects previously examined. Consequently, it exhibits a unique sudden phase transition, potentially offering a new avenue for designing future high-precision optical fiber sensors.

The $\mathsf{HYBRID}$ model was proposed to facilitate the theoretical analysis of distributed networks employing diverse communication mechanisms. Conceptually, it functions as a synchronous message-passing framework featuring two distinct modes: a local mode where every node transmits large messages to all adjacent nodes in a local graph during each round, and a global mode where each node possesses a limited (polylogarithmic) bandwidth per round for communicating with any node in the network. Previous research has frequently targeted shortest path problems within the local network, leveraging their global characteristics to demonstrate how combining communication modes in the $\mathsf{HYBRID}$ setting can surpass the individual lower bounds of either mode. This work addresses a related challenge: the computation of distance oracles and routing schemes. In the former, all nodes must generate local tables enabling them to retrieve distance estimates to any target node in the local network upon receiving its label. In the latter, nodes only need to identify the subsequent node on an (approximately) shortest path to the destination. Our objective is to minimize both the time required to compute these local tables and the size of the associated labels. We demonstrate that exact solutions can be achieved in $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/3})$ communication rounds using labels of size $\Theta(n^{2/3})$ bits. Furthermore, for constant-stretch approximations, we attain labels of size $O(\log n)$ within the same timeframe. Additionally, our primary technical contribution involves establishing computational lower bounds for various problem parameters. For example, we prove that obtaining solutions with a stretch below a specific constant necessitates $\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{1/3})$ rounds, even when utilizing labels of size $O(n^{2/3})$.

As we move toward deploying data-driven controllers for black-box cyberphysical systems, ensuring strict adherence to safety constraints is paramount. When input-output data are contaminated by noise, two critical questions arise: the level of uncertainty tolerable without endangering safety, and the resulting impact on control performance. By examining finite-horizon constrained linear-quadratic problems, we answer these questions based on the model mismatch generated during an initial identification stage. We introduce a control design approach utilizing a quasiconvex relaxation of the underlying robust optimization problem, demonstrating that if uncertainty remains sufficiently low, the resulting controller guarantees safety and near-optimality. Specifically, the suboptimality gap scales linearly with the magnitude of the model mismatch. Because this method does not depend on a specific identification technique, our findings apply alongside advanced behavioral estimators beyond standard least-squares. Numerical experiments confirm the validity of our primary theoretical results.

This study examines diffusion dynamics on metric graphs featuring semipermeable sticky membranes at every vertex. We demonstrate that the process is controlled by a Feller semigroup and determine its asymptotic behavior as the diffusion speed approaches infinity at the same rate that the permeability coefficients approach zero.

Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained popularity in graph representation learning under the assumption of homophily, where connected nodes share similar labels or features. However, these models often struggle to generalize in heterophilous graphs, particularly those with low to medium homophily. Current approaches attempt to overcome this by enhancing intra-class information extraction, either through improved GNN architectures or by restructuring graphs to include distant nodes with similar characteristics. Despite these successes, we identify two areas for further improvement: (a) prioritizing the extraction of a node's own features, which offers more reliable intra-class signals, and (b) developing node-wise GNNs to better accommodate varying homophily ratios across different nodes. This paper introduces IIE-GNN (Intra-class Information Enhanced Graph Neural Networks), a novel method addressing these issues. We propose a unified framework that extracts intra-class information from both a node itself and its neighbors using seven specifically designed blocks. Leveraging Neural Architecture Search (NAS), we establish a new search space and an architecture predictor to generate tailored GNNs for each node. Experimental results demonstrate that IIE-GNN improves model performance by utilizing node-wise designs to strengthen intra-class information extraction.

Hierarchical structures are frequently necessary in stochastic sequential decision-making, where high-level actions must be decomposed into primitive states and actions. Furthermore, real-world scenarios often demand plans that adhere to constraints on secondary costs, such as risk metrics or fuel usage. This paper introduces the hierarchical constrained stochastic shortest path problem (HC-SSP), a unified framework designed to address both requirements. While HC-SSP offers a robust modeling tool for various practical applications, its inherent complexity renders optimal solution discovery slow, thereby limiting its applicability to real-time and risk-sensitive contexts. To overcome this limitation, we propose an algorithm that utilizes a branch-and-bound scheme to iteratively distribute cost budgets to lower-level planning tasks. This approach rapidly identifies feasible solutions and incrementally refines the best-known solution. We validate the proposed method using an evacuation scenario, demonstrating its superiority over existing state-of-the-art mathematical programming approaches.

This research investigates learning-augmented predictive linear quadratic control, aiming to develop a controller that balances \textit{"consistency"—the competitive ratio under accurate predictions—with \textit{"robustness"—the bounded competitive ratio when predictions are flawed. We introduce a new $\lambda$-confident policy, offering a competitive ratio upper bound determined by a trust parameter $\lambda \in [0,1]$, which reflects confidence in predictions and a prediction error $\varepsilon$. Inspired by online learning techniques, we create a self-tuning policy that adaptively determines $\lambda$, achieving a competitive ratio dependent on $\varepsilon$, system perturbations, and prediction variations. We demonstrate that this ratio is bounded above by $1+{O(\varepsilon)}/({{\Theta(1)+\Theta(\varepsilon)}})+O(\mu_{\mathsf{Var}})$, where $\mu_\mathsf{Var}$ quantifies the variation in perturbations and predictions. Consequently, when these variations are minimal, the self-tuning mechanism ensures a competitive ratio that does not increase with the prediction error $\varepsilon$ by automatically adjusting $\lambda$ online.

The Dirac-Frenkel variational approach, utilizing a Davydov D2 trial wavefunction, has been expanded through the incorporation of a thermalization algorithm to model the dynamics of general open quantum systems. This method enables the regulation of temperature fluctuations within a finite harmonic bath interacting with the quantum system. Thermal equilibrium for the bath's vibrational modes is achieved via stochastic scattering, modeled as a discrete-time Bernoulli process governed by Poisson statistics. By guiding the evolution of these vibrational modes toward canonical thermal equilibrium, the algorithm controls the bath temperature. Numerical investigations into exciton relaxation within a small molecular cluster demonstrate that this thermalization mechanism significantly accelerates computations by reducing the number of vibrational modes required for convergence.

Reversible spreading processes, characterized by repeated infections, are prevalent in both natural systems and human society, exemplified by the propagation of gonorrhea and the dissemination of memes. Identifying key spreaders within the dynamics of reversible spreading on complex networks is a critical and widely studied challenge. Beyond structural centrality, a node's dynamical state significantly impacts its spreading influence. This study introduces a novel metric for identifying influential spreaders that integrates the count of outgoing edges with the infection risks posed by a node's neighbors into structural centrality, thereby accounting for the interplay between structural and dynamic factors. Specifically, the number of outgoing edges reflects the positive contribution of local structural features, while the infection risks from neighbors represent the negative influence of dynamical states. Our findings indicate that an optimal balance between these two characteristics substantially enhances the accuracy of identifying the most influential spreaders. Notably, the proposed measure achieves peak performance when the negative impact of dynamical states is slightly attenuated relative to the positive impact of local structural traits. Quantitatively elucidating the relative weights of structure and dynamics offers crucial insights into detecting influential nodes in reversible spreading scenarios.

This paper presents a case study of an embodied machine-learning (ML) agent that enhances its capabilities through interactions with crowd-workers. The agent comprises a combination of learned and heuristic modules. Although the agent is not "end-to-end" in the traditional ML sense, end-to-end interaction remains a crucial component of its learning process. We outline how the agent's architecture, alongside various annotation interfaces, enables crowd-workers to attribute credit for module errors based on end-to-end interactions and to label data for specific modules. Across multiple cycles of automated human-agent interaction, credit assignment, data annotation, and model re-training and redeployment, we demonstrate the agent's progressive improvement.

Current machine learning methods in particle physics often rely on generic architectures with excessive parameters that ignore fundamental physics principles, thereby restricting their utility as scientific models. This study introduces a novel architecture that utilizes inputs maximally reduced under full 6-dimensional Lorentz symmetry and maintains full permutation equivariance. We apply this network to top quark tagging, demonstrating that it surpasses all existing competitors despite significantly lower complexity. Furthermore, we present a Lorentz-covariant variant of the same network applied to a 4-momentum regression task.

Recent neutrino detections from blazars necessitate efficient interactions between relativistic protons and surrounding soft photon fields. However, these interactions also generate gamma-ray photons that interact with the same fields to create electron-positron pairs. The intensity of this cascade profoundly impacts photon spectra across various energy bands and imposes strict limits on pion and neutrino production. This study examines how external thermal photon fields (the accretion disk, broad-line region, and dusty torus) influence proton-photon interactions using a newly developed time-dependent one-zone hadro-leptonic code (OneHaLe). We analyze both steady-state scenarios and a time-dependent case where the emission region travels through the jet. Within the scope of this simplified model, external fields can alter the typical double-humped blazar spectrum, and a moving emission region may traverse significant portions of the jet without achieving the steady states previously identified.

This paper addresses the enduring challenge of automatically reconstructing 3D objects from single line drawings. While prior optimization-based techniques can produce compact and precise 3D models, their efficacy relies critically on (i) identifying a sufficient set of authentic geometric constraints and (ii) selecting an appropriate initial value for numerical optimization. To overcome these hurdles, we propose training deep neural networks to identify pairwise relationships between geometric entities (edges) and to forecast initial vertex depths. Experimental results on a extensive dataset of CAD models demonstrate that integrating deep learning into a geometric constraint solving pipeline substantially enhances the success rate of optimization-driven 3D reconstruction.

The Biermann battery offers a viable mechanism for generating seed magnetic fields throughout the universe. We introduce a novel driving force for this process within an inhomogeneous plasma containing a beam component. Specifically, an electron pressure gradient arises that is not aligned with the density gradient, caused by an inhomogeneous electron flow driven by return currents. This misalignment results in magnetic field generation via the Biermann battery. We validate this new magnetic field generation mechanism through three-fluid plasma simulations. According to this mechanism, initial cosmic rays can produce seed magnetic fields on astrophysical scales at a redshift of approximately 20.

In computational pathology, the challenge of limited annotations alongside abundant unlabeled data is often addressed through semi-supervised learning, which typically involves a self-supervised pretext task followed by model fine-tuning. We propose S5CL, a unified framework that consolidates this two-stage process into a single training phase capable of handling fully-supervised, self-supervised, and semi-supervised learning. By defining three distinct contrastive losses for labeled, unlabeled, and pseudo-labeled images, S5CL learns feature representations that capture a hierarchy of distance relationships: augmentations and similar images are embedded closest together, followed by visually distinct images of the same class, while images from different classes are separated by the largest distances. Additionally, the framework offers flexibility in combining these losses to suit various scenarios. Experiments on two public histopathological datasets demonstrate significant performance gains with sparse labels; specifically, accuracy on a H&E-stained colorectal cancer dataset improved by up to 9% over supervised cross-entropy loss, and the F1-score on a highly imbalanced dataset of leukemia white blood cells increased by up to 6%.

Although deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success, their training predominantly depends on manual experimentation to select architectures, hyperparameters, initializations, and training methods. This study investigates the efficacy of standard gradient descent across specific combinations of dataset, architecture, and initialization (DAI). By conducting comprehensive systematic experiments, we demonstrate that monitoring the evolution of singular values within the hidden layers of a DNN can predict the success of gradient descent training, even without access to validation labels. This insight enables early termination of training for models unlikely to generalize well, saving computational resources. Furthermore, our results across various datasets, architectures, and initializations indicate that these proposed singular value scores offer a more accurate prediction of DAI success compared to relying solely on validation accuracy at early training stages.

This study investigates asymmetric heat flow, or thermal rectification, in a one-dimensional mass-graded system comprising a coupled harmonic oscillator lattice (acting as a ballistic spacer) and two diffusive leads connected at the boundaries via nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) interactions. The inclusion of NNN interactions significantly improves the system's rectification capabilities, particularly its independence from system size. Rectification efficiency peaks at a specific value of the parameter governing NNN coupling strength, which varies depending on the device's operating temperature range. This peak arises from an asymmetric local heat flow response attributed to the NNN contribution on both sides of the lighter mass-loaded diffusive lead, as revealed by spectral properties. Furthermore, varying system parameters consistently demonstrates that device performance is enhanced when NNN interactions are present.

Graph signal processing (GSP) offers a framework for analyzing and manipulating data structured as graphs.
