This study examines the feasibility of generating mock galaxy catalogs using COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration (COLA) simulations within Modified Gravity (MG) frameworks that utilize the Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) approach. We specifically analyze two MG theories: $f(R)$ gravity featuring the chameleon mechanism and the nDGP braneworld model incorporating the Vainshtein mechanism. To validate the precision of COLA, we compare its outputs against a suite of full $N$-body simulations serving as a benchmark. Regarding Dark Matter (DM), our results indicate that COLA accurately reproduces the matter power spectrum up to $k \sim 1 h {\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, although its representation of the velocity field is less precise. For constructing halo catalogs, we observe that the ROCKSTAR halo-finder is ineffective with COLA data; however, employing a simple Friends-of-Friends (FoF) algorithm alongside an empirical conversion from FoF to spherical over-density masses yields halo catalogs that align well with $N$-body results. To account for the influence of the MG fifth force on halo profiles, we develop fitting formulae for concentration-mass and velocity dispersion-mass relations, calibrated using ROCKSTAR catalogs from $N$-body simulations. These findings allow us to extend the HOD formalism to COLA-based modified gravity simulations. Utilizing a five-parameter HOD model tuned for redshift-space galaxy catalogs, we demonstrate that despite the model's flexibility, Modified Gravity leaves distinct signatures in the redshift-space power spectrum multipoles, which are successfully captured by the COLA-generated galaxy catalogs.

Quantile serves as a critical metric for assessing the stochastic behaviors of a system. This paper examines a pooled quantile estimator, defined as the sample quantile derived from detailed simulation outputs after aggregating independent sample paths. We establish the asymptotic representation of this estimator and demonstrate its normality. Through both theoretical analysis and empirical comparison with the classical quantile estimator used in stochastic simulation, we show that the proposed method offers distinct advantages within the framework of parallel simulation.

Upon detecting an HIV-positive individual in Cuba, health authorities request a list of their sexual partners from the preceding two years, facilitating the collection of data on epidemic transmission. This research analyzes the temporal evolution of the sexual contact network among detected cases and the directed graph of HIV transmissions, covering the period from 1986 to 2004, building upon a prior investigation into the network's static properties at the end of 2004. Employing various advanced graph algorithms, the study examines network characteristics such as diameters, geodesic distances, community structure, and centrality to illustrate the epidemic's growth. The analysis compares the HIV network against other real-world networks and graphs generated via the configuration model. Findings indicate that the epidemic initially emerged within the heterosexual population before expanding primarily through Men who have Sex with Men (MSM) contacts. The network features a giant component characterized by degenerate chains of vertices; notably, after 1989, observed diameters exceeded those predicted by equivalent configuration model graphs. In 1997, a significant rise in detection rates—from 73 to 256 cases per year, predominantly involving MSM—triggered a rapid expansion of distances and diameters within the giant component.

Crowd counting from a drone perspective is a compelling area in computer vision, introducing unique difficulties like detecting small objects, dealing with cluttered backgrounds, and handling wide viewpoints. Nevertheless, algorithms specifically designed for drone-captured crowd data remain scarce due to the absence of extensive datasets. To address this gap, we assembled a large-scale dataset and organized the Vision Meets Drone Crowd Counting Challenge (VisDrone-CC2020) alongside the 16th European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV 2020) to foster advancements in this domain. The resulting dataset comprises 3,360 images, partitioned into 2,460 for training and 900 for testing. In each video frame, individuals are manually annotated with points. A total of 14 algorithms from 15 different institutions participated in the VisDrone-CC2020 Challenge. We present a comprehensive analysis of the evaluation outcomes to finalize the challenge. Further details are available at \url{http://www.aiskyeye.com/}.

This study reports findings from the inaugural deployment of compact, high-definition gas Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) featuring pixel chip readout within the BEAST II beam background measurement initiative at SuperKEKB. These TPCs deliver precise 3D imaging of ionization caused by neutron-induced nuclear recoils using a helium and carbon dioxide gas mixture under standard temperature and pressure conditions. Our results demonstrate superior electron background rejection, enabling background-free measurements of nuclear recoils exceeding 50 keVee even in this highly radioactive environment. We achieved an angular resolution superior to 20 degrees for recoil tracks longer than 1.7 mm, which corresponds to an average ionization energy of roughly 100 keVee. Furthermore, by analyzing charge profiles along the recoil axis, we determined the 3D vector direction of helium recoils with a head/tail assignment accuracy of approximately 80%. Leveraging this performance, we compared measured data against simulations regarding event rates, recoil energy spectra, and directional distributions stemming from beam-gas interactions and Touschek beam losses at SuperKEKB. Utilizing head/tail recognition, we distinguished neutron components moving with positive radial velocity from those with opposing directions within the Belle II coordinate system. Additionally, we introduced a new technique to differentiate beam-gas interactions from Touschek losses, potentially eliminating the requirement for dedicated accelerator runs for background characterization; although currently limited by statistics, future validation could allow neutron background analysis to occur symbiotically during normal Belle II operations. The demonstrated capabilities indicate that high-definition recoil imaging in gas TPCs is also suitable for low-energy, low-background experiments, such as directional dark matter searches.

This report details our progress in determining the decay constants f_B and f_Bs through lattice-QCD simulations conducted by the RBC-UKQCD Collaboration on 2+1 flavor domain-wall Iwasaki lattices. By employing domain-wall light quarks alongside relativistic b-quarks, we have analyzed data across multiple partially quenched light-quark masses at two distinct lattice spacings, approximately 0.11 fm and 0.08 fm.

This study examines the critical role of high-frequency damping within high-order conservative finite-difference methods used for viscous terms in the Navier-Stokes equations. Through an investigation into nonlinear instability arising in a high-resolution viscous shock-tube simulation, we found that correcting the viscous scheme, rather than the inviscid one, effectively eliminates spurious oscillations near shocks. This correction involves adding a damping term for high frequencies that is absent in standard conservative high-order viscous schemes. While the necessity of damping is well-established for unstructured grid schemes, it has often been overlooked in very high-order difference schemes, particularly those that are conservative. This paper explains why damping is frequently missed in such conservative frameworks and outlines how to enhance these schemes by incorporating an appropriately designed damping term.

This study employs a homogeneous curve-shifting analysis based on the difference-smoothing method applied to publicly available light curves from 24 gravitationally lensed quasars with reported time delays. Realistic simulated light curves were used to estimate the uncertainty of each measured delay, and we introduce a method for generating such simulations with known time delays within a plausible range. We identified 14 systems with high-quality light curves, allowing the measurement of at least one adjacent time delay (in arrival-time order) with a precision exceeding 20% (including systematic errors). For ten of these systems, which possess known lens redshifts, accurate astrometric data, and simple mass distributions, we utilized the publicly available PixeLens code to model the mass distribution. This modeling yielded a value of $H_0$ equal to 68.1 $\pm$ 5.9 km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ (1$\sigma$ uncertainty, 8.7% precision) for a spatially flat universe with $\Omega_m$ = 0.3 and $\Omega_\Lambda$ = 0.7. It is important to note that the lens modeling approach used here is relatively simple and does not account for subtle systematics, such as those arising from line-of-sight effects; consequently, our $H_0$ estimate should be viewed as indicative.

Although predictive policing is increasingly utilized to support criminal justice decisions, its application remains contentious. Certain deep learning tools suffer from inaccuracy (e.g., low F-1 scores), and a lack of transparency in decision-making processes fuels concerns regarding bias, including perceived racial and age disparities. This study tackles these bias issues by employing post-hoc explanations to generate trustworthy predictions of future criminal charges based on an individual's history, utilizing twenty years of temporal behavioral data. We utilize Bi-LSTM networks to mitigate the vanishing gradient problem, attentional mechanisms to interpret feature significance, and complex-valued networks inspired by quantum physics to enhance model transparency. Our method demonstrates consistent and reliable precision and recall on a real-world dataset. Furthermore, our analysis of input feature importance reveals the critical causal drivers of decision-making: while criminal history is a statistically significant factor, identifiers such as race and age are not. Finally, the algorithm suggests that crime severity tends to increase gradually over time rather than abruptly.

**Context:** Vela X-1 stands as one of the most extensively researched X-ray binaries, yet subsequent studies often rely on fixed parameter values without adequately exploring alternative possibilities. **Aims:** This work seeks to create a robust synthesis of existing knowledge regarding Vela X-1 to serve as a reliable foundation for future research and to pinpoint specific directions for upcoming investigations. **Methods:** We conducted a comprehensive review of the literature concerning Vela X-1 and associated modeling efforts to trace the evolution of system understanding, while also incorporating data from public sources, particularly the Gaia EDR3 release. **Results:** We have updated the distance to Vela X-1 and the spectral classification of HD 77518, suggesting the supergiant is nearly filling its Roche lobe. Constraints on stellar wind clumpiness have been refined; while the orbit is precisely determined, uncertainties in inclination limit constraints on the neutron star's mass. Stellar wind estimates have shifted toward lower velocities, supporting the hypothesis of transient, wind-captured disks around the neutron star. Furthermore, hydrodynamic models and observations align with the presence of an accretion wake trailing the neutron star. **Conclusions:** Although Vela X-1 serves as an ideal laboratory, significant improvements are still necessary. Future progress requires well-coordinated multi-wavelength campaigns to address intrinsic variability, alongside advancements in new instrumentation. Stellar wind models must incorporate orbital eccentricity and the non-spherical shape of HD 77581. Additionally, realistic, multi-dimensional radiative transfer models in UV and X-ray regimes are essential but remain challenging. Enhanced MHD models spanning a broad range of scales are needed to better understand plasma-magnetosphere coupling, and a complete characterization of the accretion column remains a critical open challenge. (Abbreviated for arXiv)

Distinguishing between colorectal polyps is a critical clinical task, necessitating computer-aided diagnosis systems to ensure accuracy from colonoscopy images. While prior research has primarily focused on developing models using Narrow-Band Imaging (NBI) or similar enhanced visuals, their clinical utility remains constrained by the slow evolution of imaging technologies. To address this, we introduce a novel framework utilizing a teacher-student architecture for precise colorectal polyp classification (CPC) that operates directly on standard white-light (WL) colonoscopy images. During the training phase, auxiliary NBI images are employed to train a teacher network, which guides the student network in learning richer feature representations from WL images. This feature transfer is achieved through domain alignment and contrastive learning, enabling the final student network to extract aligned features solely from WL images to optimize CPC performance. Additionally, we provide the first publicly available paired dataset containing WL-NBI images specifically designed for alignment training. Quantitative and qualitative assessments demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing approaches in CPC, achieving a 5.6% increase in accuracy with high computational efficiency.

This work introduces a pure state framework for the hydrodynamic dynamics of isolated quantum many-body systems. We construct a pure state representing local thermal equilibrium, termed a local thermal pure quantum ($\ell$TPQ) state. It is demonstrated that thermodynamic functionals and expectation values of local operators (including real-time correlation functions) derived from the $\ell$TPQ state converge to those of a local Gibbs ensemble in the limit of large fluid cells. As a numerical proof of concept, we examine a one-dimensional spin chain, revealing hydrodynamic relaxation that adheres to Fourier's law. Additionally, we establish the second law of thermodynamics and the quantum fluctuation theorem, both of which are confirmed through numerical simulations. The $\ell$TPQ formulation offers a robust theoretical foundation for describing emergent hydrodynamic behavior in quantum many-body systems, combining numerical efficiency with applicability across both non-relativistic and relativistic regimes.

Existing networking protocols are inefficient at addressing the two primary challenges of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks: connectivity loss and energy constraints. One potential solution involves learning-based routing protocols that enable nodes to make near-optimal local decisions, with Q-routing serving as a prominent example. However, current Q-routing implementations fall short in performance, primarily because they lack the adaptability required to handle continuous topology changes. This paper introduces a full-echo Q-routing algorithm featuring a self-adaptive learning rate. By employing Simulated Annealing (SA) optimization, the algorithm regulates its exploration rate through a temperature decline curve, which is dynamically adjusted based on the observed variation rate of Q-values. Experimental results demonstrate that this method effectively adapts to network dynamics without requiring manual re-initialization during abrupt topology shifts. Compared to state-of-the-art Q-routing protocols, our approach achieves an energy consumption reduction of 7% to 82% and a 2.6-fold increase in successful packet delivery rates.

This article introduces a robust color-edge feature extraction method utilizing the Quaternion Hardy filter, an emerging theory in edge detection. By integrating the Quaternion Hardy filter with Poisson and conjugate Poisson smoothing kernels, the approach effectively manages various noise types. The proposed color-edge feature detection algorithm combines the Quaternion Hardy filter with Jin's color gradient operator and Hough transform, specifically for lane marking detection. Experimental results validate the algorithm's accuracy and robustness in detecting lane markings within complex environments.

The precision of quantum dynamics simulations is typically assessed by the error of the unitary evolution operator within the operator norm, a metric reliant on specific norms of the Hamiltonian. For unbounded operators, discretization often results in an excessively large Hamiltonian norm, thereby substantially raising simulation expenses. However, while the operator norm captures worst-case simulation errors, practical applications are more concerned with errors relative to a specific initial state. We show that, under appropriate conditions regarding the Hamiltonian and initial vector, measuring error via the vector norm allows Trotter-type methods to maintain computational costs even as the Hamiltonian norm grows. In this regard, our findings surpass all prior error bounds in quantum simulation literature. Furthermore, we extend the work of [Jahnke, Lubich, BIT Numer. Math. 2000] to time-dependent scenarios and elucidate the existence and significance of commutator scalings in both standard and generalized Trotter methods for simulating time-dependent Hamiltonians.

A universally satisfactory classification for the tail behaviors of probability distributions remains elusive. Because data often lacks information beyond its observed range, describing distribution tails requires multiple characteristics. While the index of regular variation is useful, it groups distributions with markedly different tail behaviors into the same category; for instance, Pareto($\alpha$), Fréchet($\alpha$), and Hill-horror($\alpha$) distributions with a fixed parameter $\alpha > 0$ are lumped together. Furthermore, Value at Risk (VaR), expectiles, and hazard functions rely on the distribution's center and scaling factors, making them suitable for forecasting "big losses" but inadequate for characterizing the specific type of "payoff." When analyzing heavy-tailed distributions, where theoretical moments often do not exist and empirical moments fluctuate excessively, a characteristic independent of moments is essential. This paper demonstrates that probabilities associated with different types of extreme values serve as effective tail characteristics. Derived from the concept of Tukey's box plots, these metrics remain invariant under increasing affine transformations and do not require moment existence. They provide a consistent measure of tail behavior across the entire distributional type and address the question of how far one can observe "unexpected" values.

While image reconstruction, matrix completion, and link prediction are established areas within machine learning, this study applies a denoising autoencoder to reconstruct partial multiplication (Cayley) tables for finite semigroups. We introduce a new loss function tailored to the algebraic properties of semigroup data and release a software package to facilitate similar experiments. Results indicate that using just 10% of the data, the model can successfully reconstruct a complete Cayley table from a half-filled one in approximately 80% of instances.

We investigate automated intrusion prevention via reinforcement learning by framing the task as a novel optimal stopping problem. This perspective reveals that the optimal policies possess a threshold-based structure. Because dynamic programming is computationally infeasible for practical scenarios, we approximate these optimal policies using reinforcement learning within a simulation environment. To establish the simulation's dynamics, we emulate the target infrastructure and gather relevant measurements. Our evaluation results demonstrate that the learned policies closely approximate the optimal solution and successfully adhere to a threshold-based formulation.

We investigate how local decoherence impacts arbitrary quantum states. By adapting methods from quantum metrology, we demonstrate that even generic local noise processes, however minute, invariably produce states where the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) regarding local observables scales linearly with system size N, regardless of the initial state. This finding indicates that all macroscopic quantum states, defined by a QFI scaling quadratically with N, are inherently fragile under decoherence and cannot be sustained without perfect isolation. Furthermore, we derive analytical bounds on the effective system size, revealing that for small noise parameters p, this size scales inversely with p across all considered noise channels, thereby rendering the generation of macroscopic or even mesoscopic quantum states increasingly unfeasible. Finally, we establish that preparing a macroscopic quantum state relative to a conserved quantity necessitates a device possessing a QFI at least as large as that of the target state. Since such a preparation device is classical and cannot be a perfectly isolated macroscopic quantum state itself, it must be quadratically larger than the macroscopic state it aims to create.

Deep neural networks achieve state-of-the-art performance with abundant labeled data but are prone to overfitting when training examples are scarce. Generating vast amounts of labeled data is resource-intensive, time-consuming, and laborious. When acquiring new labels is impractical, semi-supervised learning offers superior generalization compared to purely supervised approaches by leveraging both labeled and unlabeled instances. This paper is driven by the insight that transfer learning can further enhance performance by utilizing models pretrained on related domains. Specifically, we investigate the application of transfer learning within semi-supervised self-learning frameworks. Our primary contribution is an empirical study evaluating transfer learning across various combinations of similarity metric learning methods and label propagation algorithms in semi-supervised settings. Our results demonstrate that transfer learning consistently and significantly boosts model accuracy when labeled data is limited, irrespective of the specific training loss function employed. These conclusions are drawn from extensive experiments on the SVHN, CIFAR10, and Plant Village image classification datasets, where pretrained weights from ImageNet were utilized for transfer learning.

This study evaluates the efficiency of weak lensing-selected galaxy cluster counts versus the weak lensing bispectrum in capturing non-Gaussian features within the dark matter distribution. Utilizing the halo model, we calculate the weak lensing power spectrum, bispectrum, and expected cluster detections to derive cosmological parameter constraints for a large-scale survey with minimal systematic errors. Our analysis focuses on the $\Omega_m$-$\sigma_8$ plane and the dark energy equation of state. We decompose the power spectrum into resolved (detected clusters) and unresolved (remaining field) components. Furthermore, we examine four distinct cluster count methods varying in information content: signal-to-noise ratio peaks, mass-dependent counts, redshift-dependent counts, and combined mass-redshift counts. Our results indicate that combining these four count types with the power spectrum yields comparable constraints, enabling the use of the most direct count methods to achieve percent-level precision on cosmological parameters. Additionally, we demonstrate that the weak lensing bispectrum offers constraints similar to those from the power spectrum, effectively capturing non-Gaussian features akin to cluster counts. When combined with the power spectrum, the bispectrum produces cosmological parameter errors comparable to, and potentially marginally smaller than, those from cluster counts. Finally, we emphasize that to fully realize the bispectrum's potential, calculations must incorporate all triangle configurations, as relying solely on equilateral triangles yields limited information.

This study investigates the large $n$-limit of random matrices with an external source featuring three distinct eigenvalues, specifically within the Hermite ensemble where these values are $-a$, $0$, and $a$. For the regime where $a^2 > 3$, we demonstrate that local eigenvalue correlations exhibit universal behavior as $n \to \infty$, consistent with findings in unitarily invariant random matrix models. Specifically, these correlations are described by the sine kernel in the bulk and the Airy kernel at the spectral edge. Our findings are derived through the analysis of a $4 \times 4$ Riemann-Hilbert problem utilizing the nonlinear steepest descent method.

This thesis focuses on the logical analysis of discrete processes, specifically those arising from gene regulatory networks. Concepts such as states, transitions, and operators from temporal logics are formulated within the framework of Formal Concept Analysis. Utilizing the attribute exploration algorithm, either an expert or a computer program can derive a minimal and complete set of implications, for instance, by comparing observed data against predictions found in literature. In this context, these rules capture temporal dependencies within gene regulatory networks, covering aspects like gene coexpression, state reachability, invariants, and potential causal links. This novel methodology is grounded in the theory of universal coalgebras, encompassing automata, Kripke structures, and Labelled Transition Systems. The work also includes a comparison regarding the temporal expressivity of Description Logics. Key theoretical contributions involve integrating background knowledge into the iterative exploration of defined data structures, known as formal contexts. The application of this method involves analyzing a Boolean network from existing literature that models the sporulation of *Bacillus subtilis*. Furthermore, an asynchronous Boolean network was developed to model extracellular matrix formation and degradation in the context of rheumatoid arthritis.

As the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) has escalated into a global pandemic, resulting in millions of infections and tens of thousands of fatalities, we have developed a comprehensive tracking and visualization platform to elucidate its worldwide dynamics. This system incorporates four key features: 1) a global map displaying confirmed cases and cumulative totals; 2) worldwide trend analysis across multiple granularities; 3) multi-view comparisons of metrics such as confirmed cases per million, mortality rates, and cumulative recovery rates; and 4) a detailed, multi-grained examination of the epidemic's progression and containment efforts within China.

This study explores the benefits of coherently superposing two distinct coded channels within quantum metrology. In a continuous variable framework, we demonstrate that the coherent superposition can surpass the Heisenberg limit of $1/N$ without relying on indefinite causal order. Furthermore, in the context of parameter estimation, we show that this superposition strategy outperforms the quantum switch approach, which generates indefinite causal order. We analytically derive the general expression for estimation precision using quantum Fisher information and prove that a nonlinear Hamiltonian enhances this precision, scaling the measurement uncertainty as $1/N^m$ where $m\geq2$. These findings can aid in developing high-precision measurement devices applicable to detecting coupling strengths, testing time dilation, and investigating modifications to the canonical commutation relation.

Auxiliary Learning represents a machine learning methodology where the model recognizes objects that fall outside of its known categories. This term was adopted because the approach introduces an auxiliary class. The paper emphasizes enhancing the generality of specialized neural networks and underscores the necessity of managing unknown objects, using a Cat & Dog binary classifier as a running example.

We propose a three-state framework to investigate how a neutral faction influences opinion dissemination. In this model, agents' propensity to align with neighbors can be adjusted to support either the neutral faction or two opposing polarized groups, with social agitation represented as temperature capable of disrupting this alignment. Using various analytical methods and Monte Carlo simulations across different network topologies—including fully-connected graphs, one-dimensional chains, and Erdős-Rényi random graphs—we examine the model's equilibrium phase diagram and non-equilibrium stochastic dynamics. Our findings reveal that, under mean-field approximation, the boundary between disordered and polarized phases features a tricritical point. Specifically, on fully-connected graphs without social agitation, kinetic barriers hinder the system from achieving optimal consensus. For one-dimensional chains, the primary outcome is that dynamics are driven by the expansion of opinion clusters. Lastly, in the Erdős-Rényi ensemble, a phase transition similar to that of the fully-connected graph occurs; however, the system can reach optimal consensus at low temperatures unless average connectivity is low, a condition that leads to dynamical traps caused by locally frozen configurations.

Liquid crystal properties are modeled using an order parameter that captures the variability in the local orientation of rod-like molecules. Defects within the director field can emerge due to external influences like electric or magnetic fields, or the geometric constraints of the container. Comprehending defect formation and dynamics is crucial for designing and controlling liquid crystal devices, yet it presents substantial challenges for numerical modeling. This paper addresses the numerical solution of a $\bf{Q}$-tensor model for nematic liquid crystals, where defects manifest as rapid variations in the $\bf{Q}$-tensor within a minute physical region relative to the device scale. Efficient resolution of the resulting six coupled partial differential equations is attained through a finite element-based adaptive moving mesh technique, which refines an unstructured triangular mesh toward high-activity zones, particularly around defects. Spatial convergence analyses, utilizing a stationary defect as a test case, demonstrate that the adaptive method achieves optimal convergence with quadratic triangular finite elements. The method's full efficacy is further illustrated by solving a demanding two-dimensional dynamic Pi-cell problem that involves the generation, migration, and elimination of defects.

Prostate cancer ranks as the second leading cause of cancer death among American men. Although Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is increasingly employed to guide targeted biopsies, its effectiveness is constrained by frequent false positives and negatives, along with inconsistent agreement among readers. Machine learning approaches designed to detect and localize prostate cancer on MRI could help standardize radiological interpretations; however, current methods differ not only in model architecture but also in the ground truth labeling strategies used for training. This study evaluates various labeling approaches, including radiologist-confirmed labels, pathologist annotations on whole-mount histopathology, and lesion- and pixel-level digital pathologist labels (derived from a validated deep learning algorithm predicting pixel-level Gleason patterns). We analyze how these different labels influence the performance of trained machine learning models. Our results demonstrate that: (1) radiologist labels and corresponding models may fail to detect cancers or underestimate their extent; (2) digital pathologist labels show high concordance with traditional pathologist annotations; and (3) models trained using digital pathologist labels achieve superior performance in prostate cancer detection across two distinct cohorts with varying disease distributions, regardless of the model architecture. Digital pathologist labels can mitigate challenges associated with human annotation, such as labor costs, time consumption, and reader variability, while also bridging the gap between prostate radiology and pathology by enabling the development of reliable machine learning models for detecting and localizing prostate cancer on MRI.

Numerical solutions for hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental across science and engineering. The method of lines is a favored technique for discretizing PDEs in spacetime by handling space and time independently. However, when applying explicit timesteppers to adaptive grids, relying on a global timestep determined by the finest grid resolution creates inefficiencies in coarser areas. Although adaptive spatial discretization is prevalent in computational sciences, temporal adaptivity remains rare due to its complexity. This paper introduces highly scalable algorithms to facilitate local timestepping (LTS) for explicit schemes on fully adaptive octrees. We validate both the accuracy of our methods and the framework's scalability across 16,000 cores on TACC's Frontera system. Additionally, we provide a speedup estimation model for LTS that predicts performance gains over global timestepping (GTS) with an average relative error of 0.1.

Recent studies have promoted the application of deep learning for power allocation in the downlink of massive MIMO (maMIMO) systems, yet these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. In this specific context, such attacks involve injecting carefully crafted, subtle perturbations into the input data during the inference phase (after training is complete) to compel the regression model to generate infeasible power allocation results. This paper introduces an autoencoder-based defense mechanism that enables deep learning power allocation models to function securely against adversaries without necessitating retraining. Specifically, we propose a denoising autoencoder (DAE) that establishes a mapping between perturbed inputs and their original, unperturbed counterparts. Our evaluations across various attack scenarios and threat models demonstrate that our approach: (i) effectively neutralizes adversarial impacts on power allocation networks utilizing two prevalent precoding schemes; (ii) surpasses existing benchmarks for mitigating regression-based adversarial attacks in maMIMO environments; (iii) maintains high accuracy when no attack is present; and (iv) functions with minimal computational overhead.

Recent years have seen major advancements in online display advertising, driven primarily by the Real-Time Bidding (RTB) mechanism for buying and selling ad space. RTB allows for the instantaneous purchase of individual ad impressions as they are generated during a user's session. Beyond simply scaling the acquisition process by consolidating vast inventories from numerous publishers, RTB's most critical contribution is the ability to target specific users directly. Consequently, this technology has radically transformed the digital marketing ecosystem. From a scientific perspective, the push for automation, integration, and optimization within RTB has opened new research avenues in information retrieval, data mining, machine learning, and related disciplines. This monograph provides a comprehensive overview of the foundational infrastructure, algorithms, and technical solutions underpinning this emerging field of computational advertising. Key subjects covered include user response prediction, forecasting the bidding landscape, bidding strategies, revenue optimization, statistical arbitrage, dynamic pricing, and the detection of ad fraud.

This paper presents a continuous-time, multi-stage stochastic optimization framework designed to schedule generating units, manage their commitment and reserve capacities, and define continuous-time generation profiles within the day-ahead wholesale electricity market. By approximating the solution to a variational problem where balance, generation capacity, and ramping constraints are modeled in continuous time, our approach captures ramping events with higher precision. This enhanced representation ultimately boosts system reliability and reduces real-time operational costs.

Novae are among the most frequently observed optical transients and offer significant insights into binary evolution. Although binary population synthesis codes are the primary tools for modeling these systems, they have historically relied on oversimplified nova physics, hindering detailed analysis. This study integrates a model that treats hydrogen (H) and helium (He) novae as discrete events within the \binaryc code, representing a major advancement over the conventional "averaging" approach. We examine the evolutionary routes to these events and provide nova occurrence rates alongside distributions of key physical parameters. Results indicate that most novae originate from massive white dwarfs, with roughly 70% of H novae and 55% of He novae occurring on oxygen/neon (O/Ne) white dwarfs. While only 15% of H-nova systems experience a common-envelope phase, these systems account for the bulk of H nova events. Conversely, all He-accreting He-nova systems are post-common-envelope and are destined to merge with their donor stars via gravitational-wave inspiral. We estimate the current annual nova rate in the Andromeda galaxy (M31) to be approximately $41 \pm 4$ for H novae, which falls below the observational estimate of $65^{+15}_{-16}$, and $0.14 \pm 0.015$ for He novae. Sensitivity tests varying common-envelope parameters reveal that the H nova rate could range from 20 to 80 events per year.

This study computes the low-lying glueball spectrum, various string tensions, topological characteristics, and the behavior of the running coupling within SU(N) lattice gauge theories in 3+1 dimensions. Calculations were performed for N ranging from 2 to 12 using Wilson plaquette action simulations. We analyzed glueball states across all representations of the cubic rotation group, covering both parity and charge conjugation values. Results were extrapolated to the continuum limit for each N and subsequently to the N=infinity limit. For several states, we successfully identified their continuum spins with minimal ambiguity. We determined the fundamental and k=2 string tensions to investigate the N-dependence of their ratio. By utilizing the string tension as a scale, we computed the lattice coupling's running and verified that g(a)**2 scales as 1/N to maintain constant physics as N approaches infinity. Our string tension values were fitted against the 3-loop beta-function to extract Lambda-MSbar (in units of string tension) for all tested N values, including SU(3). We calculated the topological charge Q for N=2 through 6, where sufficient fluctuations allowed for a reasonable estimate of the continuum topological susceptibility. Additionally, we computed the renormalization factor ZQ(beta) for the lattice topological charge across all SU(N) theories using a standard definition and provided interpolating formulae potentially useful for estimating the renormalization of the lattice theta parameter. Finally, we present quantitative findings on how topological charge freezes as lattice spacing decreases and N increases, demonstrating the methods used to address this issue in our computations.

Utilizing first-principles calculations and crystal structure searching techniques, we predict that a novel NaCaBi family compound crystallizing in the ZrBeSi-type structure ($P6_{3}/mmc$) exhibits strong topological insulator (STI) properties. Focusing on $P6_{3}/mmc$ NaCaBi, the computed band structure reveals a band inversion between two bands of opposite parity at the $\Gamma$ point. Unlike the established Bi$_2$Se$_3$ family, this band inversion in the NaCaBi family occurs even without spin-orbit coupling (SOC), resulting in a nodal ring surrounding $\Gamma$ within the $k_z=0$ plane, which is protected by $M_z$ symmetry. With both time reversal symmetry ($\cal T$) and inversion symmetry ($\cal I$), the spinless nodal-line metallic phase, protected by $[{\cal TI}]^2=1$, represents the weak-SOC limit of the spinful topological insulating phase. Once SOC is included, the nodal ring opens a gap, transforming the system into an STI. Beyond inversion symmetry, the nontrivial topology of NaCaBi is also characterized by $\bar{6}$ symmetry. Remarkably, the SOC-induced band gap in NaCaBi is approximately 0.34 eV, exceeding the energy scale of room temperature. Additionally, four other compounds in this family (KBaBi, KSrBi, RbBaBi, and RbSrBi) are thermodynamically and dynamically stable at ambient pressure, although their gaps are smaller than that of NaCaBi. Consequently, these materials offer promising platforms for investigating topological states through both theoretical and experimental studies.

This study addresses the Helmholtz equation within unbounded regions situated outside bounded 2D domains, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions and the Sommerfeld radiation condition at infinity. To facilitate a solution, the infinite domain is truncated into a bounded computational region enclosed by a curved, smooth artificial boundary, where a non-reflecting boundary integral condition is enforced. Within this finite domain, the curved virtual element method is employed in conjunction with a one-equation boundary element method on the artificial boundary. The paper provides a theoretical analysis of this methodology and establishes an optimal convergence error estimate in the energy norm. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

This study conducts an event-by-event intermittency analysis using Toy Monte Carlo simulations, specifically modeling high-multiplicity collisions typical of recent RHIC and LHC heavy-ion experiments. The analysis identifies self-similar fluctuations through the power-law behavior of Normalized Factorial Moments ($F_q$) relative to the number of bins ($M$). Furthermore, the investigation examines how detector efficiencies and inherent fluctuations influence these Normalized Factorial Moments. The findings established here serve as a reference for experimental data, offering clarity on implementing efficiency corrections.

Discrete Green's functions represent the inverse (or pseudoinverse) of a graph's Laplacian or its variants. This paper provides combinatorial interpretations of these functions by counting trees and forests within a graph, a method used to generate new formulas for various graph invariants. Specifically, we demonstrate that the trace of the Green's function $\mathbf{G}$, corresponding to the combinatorial Laplacian of a connected simple graph $\Gamma$ with $n$ vertices, is given by $\text{Tr}(\mathbf{G})=\sum_{\lambda_i \neq 0} \frac 1 {\lambda_i}= \frac{1}{n\tau}|\mathbb{F}^*_2|$. In this equation, $\lambda_i$ represents the eigenvalues of the Laplacian, $\tau$ is the count of spanning trees, and $\mathbb{F}^*_2$ denotes the set of rooted spanning 2-forests in $\Gamma$. We also establish forest-based formulas for discrete Green's functions in the context of directed and weighted graphs, applying these findings to analyze random walks on both graphs and digraphs. Furthermore, we derive a forest expression for the hitting time in digraphs, offering combinatorial proofs for both established and novel results concerning hitting times, traces of discrete Green's functions, and associated metrics.

The proliferation and widespread availability of shared instruments and observatories have made observational data a cornerstone of application workflows and a key driver of scientific discovery across various disciplines. However, the simultaneous surge in the number of users accessing these facilities, alongside the expanding scale and diversity of the data, presents significant challenges. These factors strain the cyberinfrastructure (CI) of such facilities, making it difficult to ensure timely access, integration, and analysis of data.

This paper introduces the design of a push-based data delivery framework that utilizes emerging in-network capabilities combined with data pre-fetching techniques grounded in a hybrid data management model. We analyze access traces from two large-scale observatories—the Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI) and the Geodetic Facility for the Advancement of Geoscience (GAGE)—to identify common user access patterns and develop a corresponding pre-fetching model. Additionally, we evaluate both the model and the proposed framework through simulations of the Virtual Data Collaboratory (VDC) platform, which offers in-network data staging and processing. The results demonstrate that the framework can significantly enhance data delivery performance and reduce network traffic at the observatories' facilities.

We introduce a class of associative algebras that extends the concept of "clannish algebras" (originally defined by the second author) by integrating semilinear structures, similar to those found in skew polynomial rings. Since clannish algebras themselves generalize the well-known "string algebras" developed by Butler and Ringel, our primary achievement is the classification of finite-dimensional indecomposable modules for these newly defined algebras.

Although existing research actively explores non-expert users' views on cybersecurity and privacy regarding both traditional and smart home devices, it frequently concentrates on modern gadgets like mobile phones and IoT units. Furthermore, much of this prior work relies on small-scale empirical methods, such as interviews and online surveys. This study aims to address those limitations by analyzing a large-scale, real-world dataset comprising 413,985 tweets from non-experts posted on Twitter over six months across three consecutive years (January and February of 2019, 2020, and 2021). We employed two machine learning classifiers to process this extensive dataset to examine non-expert perspectives on privacy and security, specifically tracking yearly trends and the influence of the COVID-19 pandemic. Utilizing topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and qualitative reviews of selected tweets, we uncovered several key insights. Notably, there was a 54% surge in cybersecurity and privacy-related tweets in 2021 compared to the pre-lockdown period (January 2019 to February 2020), alongside a rise in help-seeking behavior during the pandemic. The discussion topics among non-experts were diverse, spanning VPNs, Wi-Fi, smartphones, laptops, smart home equipment, financial security, and privacy concerns involving various stakeholders. Additionally, an overall negative sentiment was detected across nearly all discussed topics throughout the three-year period. These findings underscore the multifaceted nature of non-expert user perspectives, highlighting the need for more holistic, comprehensive, and nuanced research into these issues.

This work tackles novel view video prediction, where a network generates video from an unseen angle based on input clips from one or multiple existing views. Unlike recent methods that handle only minor viewpoint shifts, our prior-free approach successfully predicts videos across wider angular ranges, up to 45 degrees. Furthermore, the method utilizes solely RGB frames to learn a dual representation comprising both view-dependent and global components; the latter integrates complementary details to facilitate prediction from novel viewpoints. We validate the framework's efficacy on two real-world datasets, NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic. Comparative analysis against state-of-the-art techniques reveals significant improvements without relying on explicit priors from target views: a 26.1% gain in SSIM, a 13.6% increase in PSNR, and a 60% reduction in FVD scores.

This paper introduces a novel approach for designing suboptimal consensus protocols in a specific class of multiagent systems. The method relies on extending newly established sufficient conditions for suboptimal linear-quadratic optimal control, which are derived here through an explicit noniterative solution technique for the infinite-horizon linear quadratic regulation problem within the Krotov framework. For consensus protocol design, the structural constraints on the overall feedback gain matrix—naturally dictated by agent dynamics and interaction topology—are reformulated as conditions on a particular matrix within a suitably defined convex optimization problem. Consequently, it is no longer necessary to preassign identical feedback gain matrices to a network of homogeneous agents acting on relative state variables with respect to neighbors. The suboptimality of the resulting control laws is quantified by implicitly establishing an upper bound on the cost, expressed via the solution of a convex optimization problem and initial conditions, rather than being specified beforehand. Numerical examples are included to illustrate the implementation of the proposed methods and to compare them with existing approaches in the literature.

Minimizing the thermal conductivity of dielectrics through minimal structural changes, without compromising electrical properties, is crucial for enhancing thermoelectric efficiency in low-cost materials like silicon. We previously identified specific nanoscale pore arrangements in silicon that drastically reduce thermal conductivity while generating strongly anticorrelated heat current fluctuations—a phenomenon overlooked by standard diffuse adiabatic boundary conditions in numerical Boltzmann transport models. This manuscript utilizes molecular dynamics simulations and a Monte Carlo ray tracing model to dissect this effect, revealing that specialized pore layouts elastically backscatter long-wavelength heat-carrying phonons. Consequently, the heat transport initiated by a phonon before scattering is effectively cancelled by the scattered phonon, yielding an effective mean-free-path significantly shorter than the geometric line-of-sight to the pores. This impact is most pronounced for long-wavelength phonons with long mean-free-paths, whose transport is hindered far more severely than predicted by standard scattering models based on defect spacing. This "super-suppression" of the mean-free-path below the characteristic length scale of nanostructuring provides a pathway to minimize thermal conductivity with minimal structural disruption, while the preferential targeting of long wavelengths opens avenues for designing band-pass phonon filters. Furthermore, the ray tracing model developed herein demonstrates that various forms of correlated scattering leave a distinct signature in the heat current autocorrelation function, which could serve as a diagnostic tool for other nanostructured systems.

Identifying variation patterns within a dataset is crucial for exploratory data analysis and unsupervised learning. Techniques like contrastive principal component analysis (cPCA) isolate patterns specific to a target dataset by contrasting them against a background dataset designed to represent irrelevant variation. However, these methods usually depend on a tuning parameter to control the contrast level, making objective selection difficult. Additionally, existing approaches struggle to handle scenarios where multiple background datasets need to be contrasted. We introduce Unique Component Analysis (UCA), a parameter-free method that extracts low-dimensional representations of a target dataset relative to one or more comparison sets. UCA remains computationally efficient even when dealing with a vast number of features. Experimental results demonstrate that UCA using a single background dataset yields performance comparable to cPCA across various tuning settings, while UCA utilizing multiple individual backgrounds outperforms both cPCA with a single background and cPCA with a pooled background.

We demonstrate that moduli spaces of parabolic symplectic and orthogonal bundles over a smooth curve are of globally $F$-regular type. This result implies the vanishing of all higher cohomology for theta line bundles. Furthermore, our proof introduces a technique for estimating codimension and examines infinite Grassmannians associated with parabolic $G$-bundles.

Leveraging the bulk-boundary correspondence in topological matter, disclinations have recently been utilized to trap fractionally quantized densities of states (DoS) within classical wave systems. However, because these fractional DoS states are localized at the disclination core without chiral symmetry protection, they remain vulnerable to deconfinement. This typically results in resonances with finite lifetimes and suboptimal confinement. In this study, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate within acoustic lattices a new approach where topological states bind to disclinations without exhibiting a fractional DoS, yet still maintaining chiral symmetry. By preserving this symmetry, the states are pinned at the mid-gap, ensuring protected maximal confinement. The integer DoS at the defect creates two-fold degenerate states that remain un-gapped due to symmetry constraints. Our work offers a novel viewpoint on the relationship between symmetry-protected topological phases and topological defects, with potential implications for both classical and quantum systems.

Beginning with vector multipliers, this approach defines the inner product, norm, distance, and the addition of vectors across different dimensions, thereby establishing a topological vector space known as the Euclidean Space of Different Dimensions (ESDD). An equivalence relation based on distance is derived, leading to the construction of dimension-free Euclidean spaces (DFESs) and dimension-free manifolds (DFMs) as quotient spaces of ESDDs. These new structures feature bundled vector spaces as tangent spaces at every point. By applying natural projections from ESDDs to DFESs, a fiber bundle structure emerges, where the ESDD serves as the total space and the DFES as the base space. Classical differential geometry concepts, including smooth functions, (co-)vector fields, and tensor fields, are extended to DFMs utilizing projections between Euclidean spaces of varying dimensions. Consequently, dimension-varying dynamic systems (DVDSs) and control systems (DVCSs) are introduced, with DFMs acting as their state spaces. The study further examines the realization of these systems as lifts from DFMs into ESDDs, as well as their projection from ESDDs back onto DFMs.

Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) involves adapting a model trained on labeled source data to unlabeled target data without access to the source during the adaptation phase. Current SFDA approaches typically employ entropy-minimization, which is limited to classification tasks, degrades model calibration, and depends heavily on the source model already achieving strong feature-space class separation in the target domain. We address these limitations for measurement shift, a common type of domain shift, by restoring source features instead of extracting new ones. Specifically, we introduce Feature Restoration (FR), which involves storing a lightweight, flexible approximation of the source feature distribution and adjusting the feature extractor so that the target data's approximate distribution realigns with the saved source distribution. Additionally, we propose Bottom-Up Feature Restoration (BUFR), a bottom-up training scheme that enhances performance. Experiments on both real and synthetic datasets show that BUFR surpasses existing SFDA methods in accuracy, calibration, and data efficiency, while reducing reliance on the source model's initial performance in the target domain.

This research investigates phase transformations in pure thermoelastic fluids using the continuum thermodynamics framework. To analyze the kinetics of these transformations, the study prioritizes the jump condition derived from the entropy inequality axiom. This approach recovers the standard finding that stable phase equilibrium requires the continuity of temperature, pressure, and free enthalpy across the phase boundary. Furthermore, this jump condition enables the derivation of a constitutive equation for the phase transformation mass flux, expressed as $-\left[\left[\frac{1}{T}\mathbf{q}\right]\right]\cdot\mathbf{n}^{\Gamma}/\left[\left[s\right]\right]$. In this formula, the numerator represents the normal jump in entropy flux across the interface $\Gamma$, while the denominator denotes the corresponding entropy jump. The resulting relation indicates that phase transformations inherently involve a temperature discontinuity at the phase boundary. While preliminary experimental data shows promising agreement with this formula, additional evidence is required to fully validate the proposed constitutive model. Additionally, this continuum framework is highly compatible with computational implementations, such as the finite element method.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are widely adopted deep learning models that extend CNNs to irregular domains by substituting standard convolutions with Graph Filters (GFs). Nevertheless, conventional GFs are susceptible to numerical inaccuracies because they rely on high-order polynomials. This vulnerability becomes more severe when multiple filters are stacked in sequence, thereby restricting the feasible depth of GCNNs. To address this limitation, we introduce Neighborhood Graph Filters (NGFs), a class of GFs that substitutes powers of the graph shift operator with $k$-hop neighborhood adjacency matrices. NGFs mitigate the numerical instability inherent in traditional GFs, facilitate the construction of deeper GCNN architectures, and improve resilience against topological errors in the graph. To demonstrate their superiority in practical scenarios, we employed NGFs within deep neighborhood GCNNs for graph signal denoising and node classification tasks using both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We examine the contribution of $c \bar c g$-Fock states to the diffractive photoproduction of $J/\psi$ mesons. This work extends our previous analysis within the color-dipole framework, which incorporated the rescattering of $c \bar c$ pairs via a Glauber-Gribov formulation of the dipole-nucleus amplitude. Our calculated results are compared against recent experimental data from the ALICE and LHCb collaborations concerning $J/\psi$ photoproduction.

PHENIX presents findings on electromagnetic and hadronic observables derived from extensive datasets of p+p, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions across various center-of-mass energies. Centrality-dependent measurements of $\pi^0$, $\eta$, reconstructed jets, and $\psi\prime$ are utilized to quantify initial state effects within cold nuclear matter. Leveraging the inaugural run of the new EBIS ion source at RHIC, we provide initial results regarding particle flow ($v_1$ and $v_2$) and quarkonium production in U+U and Cu+Au collisions. The hot matter generated in Au+Au collisions is analyzed through event-plane dependent HBT and dielectron studies. Furthermore, interactions between partons and the medium are examined using high $p_T$ single hadrons, $\gamma$-hadron correlations, and heavy flavor decay electrons, the latter identified by the recently installed VTX detector.

Self-propelled particles exhibit complex dynamics arising from various bulk and surface interactions. When a particle is embedded within a host solid near its bulk melting point, interfacial premelting may occur, causing the host material to melt at the particle's surface. The resulting melt film's thickness is governed by temperature, impurities, material properties, and geometry. A temperature gradient induces a thermomolecular pressure gradient that drives the interfacial liquid—and consequently the particle—from lower to higher temperatures, a mechanism known as thermal regelation. If the host is ice and the embedded particle is biological, this system represents a unique form of active matter, bridging issues ranging from terrestrial and extraterrestrial extremophiles to ecological dynamics within Earth's cryosphere. Central to these scenarios is the combined impact of biological activity and thermal regelation on the redistribution of bioparticles. Consequently, we reformulate this class of regelation phenomena using the stochastic framework of active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics to generate predictions relevant to biological and geophysical challenges. We specifically investigate how thermal regelation affects paleoclimate research in ice core dating, discovering that biological activity alters particle dynamics during regelation by increasing the effective diffusion coefficient. Thus, precise dating necessitates a quantitative approach that accounts for both effects.

Foundation Models (FMs) are systems trained on extensive datasets that can generalize to novel tasks at a massive scale without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. As these models expand in size, ongoing innovations continue to expand their capabilities in language and image processing. This paper investigates an underexplored domain of FMs: traditional data operations such as cleaning and integration. Using a proof-of-concept approach, we reformulated five data cleaning and integration tasks as prompting exercises and assessed FM performance on them. Our findings indicate that large FMs successfully generalize and achieve state-of-the-art results on these data tasks, despite lacking specific training for them. We also outline specific research challenges and opportunities presented by these models, including issues related to private and domain-specific data, as well as the potential to make data management systems more accessible to non-experts. Our code and experimental results are publicly available at: https://github.com/HazyResearch/fm_data_tasks.

We investigate the capabilities of Hamiltonian cycle powers within randomly augmented Dirac graphs, defined as $n$-vertex graphs $G$ where the minimum degree is at least $(1/2+\varepsilon)n$ for some $\varepsilon>0$. For any graph of this type and every integer $m\ge2$, we provide a highly precise estimate of the threshold probability $p=p(n)$ required for the random augmentation $G\cup G(n,p)$ to contain the $m$-th power of a Hamiltonian cycle.

This study examines two $L^2$ hypocoercivity techniques utilizing Fourier decomposition and mode-by-mode analysis, applied to convergence and decay rates in kinetic equations across the torus and Euclidean space. The core approach involves perturbing the standard $L^2$ norm via a twist derived from either a nonlocal perturbation rooted in diffusive macroscopic dynamics or a scalar product modification grounded in Lyapunov matrix inequalities. The work investigates various estimates for equations featuring Fokker-Planck and linear relaxation operators, reviewing simple cases to emphasize the precision of rate estimations. Finally, the two methodologies are compared within the context of the one-dimensional Goldstein-Taylor model.

This work introduces an end-to-end design for compact, lossless, and passive metasurface (MTS) antennas featuring integrated feeds. The resulting low-profile system comprises a single-layer reactive impedance MTS printed on a grounded dielectric substrate, excited by sources embedded within that substrate. We develop a precise and efficient volume-surface integral equation model to serve as the foundation for rapidly optimizing the device's performance. These optimized designs utilize specially tailored auxiliary surface waves supported by the impedance MTS to spread localized source power across the aperture. This approach enables extreme field transformations, such as wide-angle or shared-aperture beam-forming, achieving nearly 100% aperture efficiency. Furthermore, the method supports arbitrary beam shaping with full control over the main beam and side lobes. We also establish several feasibility constraints that can significantly improve power efficiency and bandwidth in practical implementations. Full-wave numerical simulations validate the effectiveness of this approach and demonstrate the extreme field transformation capabilities of the synthesized designs.
We examine the row sequences of vector-valued Padé-Faber approximants (which are simultaneous Padé-Faber approximants) and establish a theorem analogous to Montessus de Ballore's.

We present a novel approach to multimodal sensor fusion that operates through a two-stage framework. Initially, a multimodal generative model is built using unlabelled training data. In the subsequent stage, this model functions as both a reconstruction prior and a search manifold for executing sensor fusion tasks. Furthermore, the method accommodates scenarios where observations are available only through subsampling, akin to compressed sensing. Our evaluations across various multimodal fusion applications—including multisensory classification, denoising, and recovery from subsampled data—demonstrate the technique's efficacy and superior performance.

This study investigates the kick dynamics of periodically driven quantum systems, deriving a time-independent effective Hamiltonian with an analytical form that accurately captures long-timescale dynamics. We observe that within certain parameter regimes, the effective coupling strength significantly exceeds that of the original system, a phenomenon attributed to the instantaneous nature of the kicks. Additionally, distinct dynamical regimes within a three-level system can be interconverted solely by adjusting the kick period. Notably, we demonstrate that population in excited states can be selectively suppressed in periodic kicks by leveraging the large detuning regime of the original system. Finally, we outline practical applications and physical implementations of these periodic kicks. These distinctive characteristics position periodic kicks as a potent instrument for manipulating quantum states.

Regarding the standard metric on the six-dimensional sphere equipped with the Levi-Civita connection $
abla$, we demonstrate that no almost complex structure $J$ exists where $
abla_X J$ and $
abla_{JX} J$ commute for all $X$, nor does there exist an integrable $J$ satisfying $
abla_{JX} J = J 
abla_X J$ for all $X$. The latter finding extends a prior result concerning the absence of integrable orthogonal almost complex structures on the six-sphere. Furthermore, refined versions of these statements are formulated as intrinsic first-order differential inequalities involving only $J$ and the metric. The novel methods utilized involve an almost-complex counterpart to the Gauss map, which is defined for any almost complex manifold embedded in Euclidean space.

We describe the detection of spin-polarized superconductivity in Bernal bilayer graphene doped to a saddle-point van Hove singularity induced by a strong perpendicular electric field. Our findings reveal a sequence of electrostatic gate-controlled transitions between electronic phases characterized by their polarization within the isospin space, which combines spin and momentum-space valley degrees of freedom. Although these phases remain metallic in zero magnetic fields, we identify a transition to a superconducting state under a finite parallel magnetic field of approximately 150 mT. This superconductivity emerges near a symmetry-breaking transition and is found exclusively above the $B_\parallel$ limit predicted for a paramagnetic superconductor with an observed critical temperature of roughly 30 mK, indicating a spin-triplet order parameter.

Based on proton-proton collision data from the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb^{-1}, the ratio of branching fractions for the decays B0 -> D*- pi+ pi- pi+ and B0 -> D*- pi+ is determined to be 2.64 \pm 0.04 (stat.) \pm 0.13 (syst.). For the first time, the Cabibbo-suppressed decay B0 -> D*- K+ pi- pi+ is observed, yielding a branching fraction ratio relative to B0 -> D*- pi+ pi- pi+ of (6.47 \pm 0.37 (stat.) \pm 0.35 (syst.)) x 10^{-2}. Additionally, a search for orbital excitations of charm mesons within the B0 -> D*- pi+ pi- pi+ final state leads to the first observation of the B0 -> Dbar_{1}(2420)^0 pi+ pi- decay. The corresponding ratio of branching fractions, defined as B(B0 -> (Dbar_{1}(2420)^0 -> D*- pi+) pi- pi+) / B(B0 -> D*- pi+ pi- pi+), is measured to be (2.04 \pm 0.42 (stat.) \pm 0.22 (syst.)) x 10^{-2}, where the numerator denotes the product of B(B0 -> Dbar_{1}(2420)^0 pi- pi+) and B(Dbar_{1}(2420)^0 -> D*- pi+).

If individuals with greater wealth enjoy higher returns than those with less, inequality will inevitably rise; however, can equal opportunity alone stop this? According to various models in economics and econophysics, the answer is no. These models consistently show wealth concentration as an inherent characteristic of the system's dynamics, even when no single agent possesses a repeating advantage in gains. By extending these specific models, we offer a rigorous analytical proof using the master equation formalism, demonstrating that any fair market where every agent receives the same expected return will ultimately drive the system toward maximum inequality.

We examine the conditions required to translate the geometric framework of particle kinematics, which probes a specific Hamiltonian in phase space, into a formulation based on Finsler geometry (and the reverse mapping).

A primary objective of the LHCb experiment is to measure the mixing-induced $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and the decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ arising from $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. Given the Standard Model's precise prediction for $\phi_{s}$, these observables serve as a powerful tool for detecting new physics. This review summarizes the LHCb measurements of $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ based on the 3.0~fb$^{-1}$ dataset collected between 2011 and 2012. Future enhancements in measurement precision are anticipated through the incorporation of results from decay channels with lower branching fractions.

We have examined the scaling behaviors near the quantum critical point separating the extended and critical phases in the Aubry-Andr\'{e}-Harper model with p-wave pairing, a regime that has been underexplored compared to the more commonly studied transition from the critical to the localized phase. Our findings reveal that the spectrum-averaged entanglement entropy and the generalized fidelity susceptibility serve as prominent universal order parameters for this critical point, even in the absence of a spectral gap closing. By introducing a Widom scaling ansatz for these indicators, we constructed a unified framework for critical exponents and scaling functions. Utilizing finite-size scaling with system sizes following the Fibonacci sequence, we determined the correlation-length exponent $\nu$ and the dynamical exponent $z$. The resulting values of $\nu \simeq 1.000$ and $z \simeq 3.610$ demonstrate that the transition from the extended to the critical phase belongs to a distinct universality class compared to the localization transition. This methodology provides a foundation for investigating unconventional quantum criticality and its universal properties in quasiperiodic systems using advanced quantum simulation experiments.

This study introduces a multi-scale recurrent encoder-decoder framework designed to forecast organ deformation caused by breathing in subsequent frames. The model was trained end-to-end using input images to generate a sequence of motion labels, where target data were derived by quantizing displacement fields from deformable image registration. Results are presented based on free-breathing MRI scans from 12 participants. The experiments focused on evaluating the proposed multi-scale design and analyzing how increasing the number of predicted frames impacts overall accuracy. The model successfully predicted vessel positions in the next temporal image with a mean accuracy of 2.07 (2.95) mm, demonstrating improved performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

This study presents a feature-based registration algorithm designed to align multi-source remote sensing images within a geometric space for fusion purposes. By addressing the distinct characteristics and variations inherent in these image types, the proposed approach integrates three core technologies: image scale-space to handle multi-scale properties, Harris corner detection for keypoint extraction, and a partial intensity invariant feature descriptor (PIIFD) for describing keypoints. Consequently, a comprehensive multi-scale Harris-PIIFD registration framework is established. Experimental evaluations using four sets of representative real-world data demonstrate that the algorithm delivers excellent and stable performance in registering multi-source remote sensing imagery, achieving precise spatial alignment with significant practical application value and robust generalization capabilities.

Considering a sequence of Markov chains $(\mathfrak{X}_i, \mathscr{K}_i)_{i=1}^\infty$, the cut-off phenomenon refers to a rapid transition to stationarity that occurs on a timescale asymptotically smaller than the mixing time. This analysis examines mixing times and the presence of cut-off in the total variation metric for random walks on cyclic groups $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ (where $p$ is prime), driven by a uniform measure on a symmetric generating set $A_p$.

This study addresses model efficiency by leveraging redundancy within the \textit{implicit structure} of convolutional neural network building blocks. We begin by defining \textit{Composite Kernel} structures, which facilitate convolution operations through efficient, scaled, sum-pooling components. Specifically, we introduce \textit{Structured Convolutions}, a special case that decomposes convolutions into a sum-pooling step followed by a low-complexity convolution with reduced weight count. This decomposition is applicable to 2D and 3D kernels as well as fully-connected layers. Additionally, we propose a Structural Regularization loss that encourages neural networks to adopt this structure during training, enabling decomposition with minimal performance degradation. Applied across various CNN architectures, our approach yields ResNets up to 2$\times$ smaller and a novel Structured-MobileNetV2 that maintains an accuracy loss of under 1% on ImageNet and CIFAR-10. We also demonstrate structured variants of EfficientNet on ImageNet and HRNet for semantic segmentation on Cityscapes. Compared to existing tensor decomposition and channel pruning techniques, our method achieves equal or superior complexity reduction.

An operator $T$ on a Banach space $X$ is defined as recurrent if, for every nonempty open subset $U$ of $X$, there exists a natural number $n$ such that $T^n(U)$ intersects $U$. This work extends the concept of recurrence from a single operator to a collection $\Gamma$ of operators. As an application, we investigate the recurrence properties of $C$-regularized groups of operators.

Patience Sort organizes a sequence of numbers using the minimum number of queues, which operate on a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) basis. Specifically, if the input sequence contains a longest decreasing subsequence of length $L$, Patience Sort requires exactly $L$ queues. This study investigates the potential for improving sortedness when constrained to $k$ queues, where $k$ is less than $L$. We examine this question using two metrics for sortedness: the count of down-steps and the length of the longest decreasing subsequence. For the down-steps metric, we present an optimal algorithm, whereas for the longest decreasing subsequence metric, we provide partial results. The research originated from a challenge encountered in the car manufacturing industry.

To meet the demands for long-range, self-sustaining communication in Internet of Things (IoT) devices, we propose a Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT) system utilizing a resonant beam equipped with an internal telescope modulator within a cavity to mitigate diffraction losses. Our theoretical analysis examines power transfer in the Telescope Internal Modulator-Resonant Beam System (TIM-RBS), focusing on electromagnetic field propagation, end-to-end power delivery, and the reception of both power and information. Numerical results indicate that the telescope modulator effectively compresses the beam spot, enabling the TIM-RBS to transmit energy twice as far as a standard Resonant Beam System (RBS) without the modulator when operating at higher power levels. Furthermore, both the maximum transmission distance and output power scale proportionally with input power; specifically, an input of 200W yields a transmission range of approximately 34 meters, 4W of electric power, and a spectral efficiency of 12 bps/Hz. Consequently, the TIM-RBS emerges as a viable solution for achieving long-range, high-power, and high-rate SWIPT applications.

Since its initial proposal in 1996, the relational interpretation of quantum mechanics (RQM) has garnered increasing attention. Typically framed as a philosophical overlay on standard quantum formalism lacking specific mathematical foundations, this approach has contributed to misunderstandings and imprecise discourse within the scientific community. To address these issues, this paper introduces a radical restructuring of quantum mechanics from the outset, termed "fact-nets." The central concept posits that all worldly facts are binary relations between two systems, where the roles of observer and observed are symmetric. This work initiates an investigation into the fact-nets formalism and demonstrates how it can provide fresh relational insights into well-known quantum phenomena.

This study investigates how ionized outflows from Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) influence star formation in high-redshift host galaxies by integrating Near-Infrared Integral Field Spectroscopy (NIR IFS) data—mapping H$\alpha$ and [OIII] outflows—with matched-resolution rest-frame Far-Infrared (FIR) observations. We present high-resolution ALMA Band 7 data for eight X-ray-selected AGN at z~2 from the SUPER sample, focusing on the ~260 $\mu$m continuum at a resolution of approximately 2 kpc (0.2''). Six of the eight targets were detected in the ALMA maps with a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10, exhibiting continuum flux densities between 0.27 and 2.58 mJy and FIR half-light radii ($R_e$) ranging from 0.8 to 2.1 kpc. These $R_e$ values are consistent with those of other AGN and star-forming galaxies at similar redshifts found in the literature. However, our analysis reveals that the mean FIR size in X-ray AGN ($R_e = 1.16 \pm 0.11$ kpc) is marginally smaller than in non-AGN systems ($R_e = 1.69 \pm 0.13$ kpc). Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) fitting indicates that dust heated by star formation dominates the 260 $\mu$m flux density, with contributions from AGN-heated dust and synchrotron emission accounting for less than 4% and 1%, respectively. Most of our sample displays distinct morphologies for FIR emission (primarily reprocessed stellar light) and ionized gas emission (H$\alpha$ and [OIII], primarily AGN-driven), likely due to spatial segregation of dust and gas, different emission sources, or dust obscuration effects.
