We failed to detect any residual H$\alpha$ emission attributable to star formation above the AGN-dominated baseline. Assuming FIR emission reliably traces obscured star formation, our results suggest that obscured star formation activity in these AGN hosts is not significantly impacted by ionized outflows. Nevertheless, we cannot exclude the possibility that star formation suppression occurs on spatial scales smaller than our 2 kpc resolution or on different timescales.

Attaching an external starshade to the {\it Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope} will facilitate the direct imaging of Earth-sized planets located approximately 1 AU away. To classify these detected worlds as Earth-like, scientists must employ spectroscopy for atmospheric analysis and multi-epoch imaging to map their trajectories. This study evaluates the Starshade Rendezvous Probe's capacity to determine the orbits of directly imaged, Earth-analog planets. The mission targets the 16 nearest stars most favorable for direct imaging. Due to solar exclusion constraints, the starshade's field of regard is limited to four observing windows over a two-year period. Our results indicate that for habitable-zone planets detected at least three times across these four opportunities, semi-major axes are measured with a median precision of 7 mas, corresponding to a fractional precision of 3%. Under these conditions, habitable-zone planets are correctly identified 96.7% of the time, with a false positive rate of 2.8%. However, applying a more conservative classification criterion (requiring a 95% probability) reduces the false positive rate to nearly zero, though it lowers the detection rate of genuine Earth-like planets to 81%.

Over the last few years, parameterized quantum circuits have emerged as a primary method for constructing quantum algorithms aimed at solving optimization tasks. The primary difficulty in maximizing the utility of these circuit families involves identifying an optimal set of parameters within a non-convex search space that can expand exponentially with the number of parameters. We present a novel framework for optimizing such circuits by rounding solutions derived from Semidefinite Programming (SDP) to circuit parameters. Within this approach, we detail an algorithm that yields approximate solutions for the Quantum Max Cut problem. Notably, this rounding procedure operates in polynomial time relative to the number of parameters, irrespective of the structure of the underlying interaction graph. Consequently, our method achieves a 0.562-approximation ratio for generic Quantum Max Cut instances, surpassing the performance of prior best algorithms, which were limited to approximation ratios below 0.54.

Pre-trained programming language (PL) models, including CodeT5, CodeBERT, and GraphCodeBERT, offer the capability to automate software engineering tasks related to code comprehension and generation. Nevertheless, these models function primarily within the natural channel, focusing on human readability rather than code semantics, which renders them fragile to input variations and vulnerable to adversarial attacks. We introduce CodeAttack, a straightforward yet powerful black-box attack framework that leverages code structure to create adversarial samples that are effective, efficient, and imperceptible, thereby exposing the weaknesses of current state-of-the-art PL models against code-specific adversarial threats. Our evaluation assesses the transferability of CodeAttack across various code-to-code (translation and repair) and code-to-NL (summarization) tasks spanning multiple programming languages. CodeAttack surpasses existing state-of-the-art adversarial NLP attack models by achieving superior performance drops while maintaining greater efficiency, imperceptibility, consistency, and fluency. The implementation is available at https://github.com/reddy-lab-code-research/CodeAttack.

The carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour on an electricity grid fluctuate throughout the day and differ significantly by location, depending on the generation mix. Consequently, hyperscale computing networks—collections of warehouse-scale computers—generate excess carbon if they operate without accounting for these temporal and spatial variations in carbon intensity. This paper presents Google's Carbon-Intelligent Compute Management system, which reduces both the electricity-related carbon footprint and power infrastructure costs by postponing workloads that are temporally flexible. The system's core consists of analytical pipelines that collect next-day carbon intensity forecasts, train day-ahead demand prediction models, and employ risk-aware optimization to produce carbon-aware Virtual Capacity Curves (VCCs) for every datacenter cluster in Google's fleet. These VCCs enforce hourly resource limits on flexible workloads while maintaining total daily capacity, ensuring all such tasks finish within a single day. Operational data demonstrates that VCCs successfully restrict hourly capacity during periods of high-carbon energy supply and shift the execution of flexible workloads to "greener" time slots.

When interacting with chatbots, users often express multiple intents within a single dialogue utterance. Rather than developing a specialized multi-intent detection model, we introduce DialogUSR, a task focused on splitting and reformulating dialogue utterances. This approach first divides complex user queries into individual single-intent sub-queries and then restores all coreferential and omitted information within them. DialogUSR functions as a plug-in, domain-agnostic module that enhances multi-intent detection capabilities in existing chatbots with minimal effort. We have assembled a high-quality, naturally occurring dataset spanning 23 domains using a multi-step crowdsourcing process. To evaluate this dataset, we developed several action-based generative models involving both end-to-end and two-stage training, followed by a comprehensive analysis of the strengths and limitations of these proposed baselines.
This paper introduces a characterization of finite simple involutive non-degenerate set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation using left braces and presents several notable examples.

For any dynamical system $(X,\varphi)$ on a totally disconnected compact space, we construct an associated left-orderable group, $T(\varphi)$. This group consists of homeomorphisms acting on the suspension of $(X,\varphi)$ that leave every orbit of the suspension flow invariant and function as dyadic piecewise linear maps along the flow direction. We demonstrate that if the system is minimal, $T(\varphi)$ is simple, and if the system is a subshift, the group is finitely generated. These results are established through concise and elementary proofs, yielding direct examples of finitely generated simple left-orderable groups. Furthermore, for minimal systems, every action of $T(\varphi)$ on the circle possesses a fixed point; these represent the inaugural examples of finitely generated left-orderable groups exhibiting this fixed point property. Additionally, we prove that $T(\varphi)$ contains no infinite subgroups with Kazhdan's property $(T)$ for any system $(X,\varphi)$. We also show that for every minimal subshift, the corresponding group fails to be finitely presentable. Finally, if $(X,\varphi)$ admits a dense orbit, the isomorphism class of $T(\varphi)$ serves as a complete invariant for the flow equivalence of the pair $\{\varphi, \varphi^{-1}\}$. The appendix details a Polish group into which $T(\varphi)$ embeds densely.

This study revisits recent advancements in one-dimensional discrete Hardy's inequality, proving an extended version that establishes its optimality. Additionally, we examine one-dimensional discrete Copson's inequality, achieving an improvement for a specific case. Furthermore, we investigate fundamental properties—including completeness, K\"{o}the-Toeplitz duality, and separability—of the sequence spaces derived from these improved discrete Hardy and Copson inequalities.

In an optimal visiting problem, the objective is to steer a trajectory that minimizes the distance to a set of target points or regions. We propose a hybrid control methodology for this classic challenge, where the path can transition between discrete states associated with the targets. Furthermore, we adapt this model into a mean-field framework to investigate viability and crowd fluxes, thereby representing a large number of indistinguishable agents.

This paper demonstrates that for appropriately selected Dwork motives, the local Galois representation derived from the middle cohomology of fibers at a point possessing a $p$-adic valuation less than zero on the base is both regular and ordinary. This finding will be pivotal for the upcoming work on Potential Automorphy for $GL_n$. The proof is established through the construction of a semistable blowup and the application of Hyodo-Kato's log crystalline cohomology framework.

Generating code comments involves creating high-level natural language descriptions for specific code methods or functions. While prior research has explored various automatic generation techniques, previous approaches have primarily focused on representing code tokens solely through their semantic forms (often using language models), treating other code properties, such as tree structures, merely as auxiliary inputs. This approach faces two main limitations: first, representing a code token in its entirety may fail to capture source code information succinctly, and second, these tokens inherently lack syntactic information, which is crucial in programming languages. To address these issues, this paper introduces LAMNER (LAnguage Model and Named Entity Recognition), a code comment generator designed to effectively encode code constructs and capture token structural properties. LAMNER utilizes a character-level language model to derive semantic representations for code tokens and a Named Entity Recognition model to identify different token types, thereby capturing structural properties. These representations are then input into an encoder-decoder architecture to generate comments. Evaluated on a widely used Java dataset using four standard metrics, LAMNER's generated comments outperformed baseline models across all measures: BLEU-1, BLEU-2, BLEU-3, and BLEU-4 improved by 14.34%, 18.98%, 21.55%, and 23.00% respectively; ROUGE-L by 10.52%; METEOR by 1.44%; and CIDEr by 25.86%. Furthermore, fusing LAMNER's code representations with baseline models resulted in consistent improvements over non-fused versions. Human evaluation confirms that LAMNER produces high-quality code comments.

This study investigates how a central transport barrier is destroyed within a dynamical model of geophysical zonal jets in the ocean or atmosphere, featuring two propagating Rossby waves. We introduce a computational approach to determine a central invariant curve, which signals the presence of this barrier. The barrier collapses and chaotic cross-jet transport initiates when variations in Rossby wave amplitudes trigger specific resonances that generate stochastic layers within the central jet. The primary finding is that these resonances can dismantle the transport barrier at surprisingly low amplitude values, potentially significantly affecting mixing and transport processes in both the ocean and atmosphere. These theoretical predictions can be validated through laboratory experiments involving azimuthal jets and Rossby waves in rotating tanks, provided specific wave numbers are met.

We examine the challenge of simulating correlations generated by arbitrary local projective measurements on the two-qubit Werner state $\rho = v |\psi_- > <\psi_- | + (1- v ) \frac{1}{4}$ using a local hidden variable (LHV) model, with $|\psi_- >$ representing the singlet state. Analytically, we demonstrate that these correlations exhibit locality at $v = 999\times689\times{10^{-6}} \cos^4(\pi/50) \simeq 0.6829$. Since this issue connects closely to a mathematical problem posed by Grothendieck, our findings establish a novel upper bound for the Grothendieck constant: $K_G(3) \leq 1/v \simeq 1.4644$. Additionally, we provide an LHV model capable of reproducing the statistics of arbitrary POVMs on the Werner state for $v \simeq 0.4553$. The methodologies developed here can be extended to construct LHV models for various other entangled states and to derive bounds for additional Grothendieck constants.

Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) offers the potential for ultra-long-distance secure key exchange, exceeding the rate-distance limit and reducing the need for trusted nodes in extensive quantum networks. Significant progress has been made in implementing TF-QKD, with finite-size analysis already enabling secure distribution over 500 km in both laboratory and field settings. In this study, we experimentally demonstrate the sending-or-not-sending TF-QKD protocol, achieving a secure key rate with finite-size analysis over 658 km of ultra-low-loss optical fiber, thereby improving the secure distance record by approximately 100 km. Furthermore, since phase fluctuations caused by temperature and environmental changes in a TF-QKD system must be tracked and compensated, this phase data can be leveraged to detect channel vibrations. Using our QKD system, we successfully recovered and localized artificial vibrational perturbations on the fiber generated by a vibroseis with a resolution superior to 1 km. These findings not only establish a new distance record for QKD but also highlight that the redundant information in TF-QKD enables remote sensing of channel vibrations, with potential applications in earthquake detection and landslide monitoring alongside secure communications.

Thermostatically controlled loads (TCLs), including air conditioners and water heaters, can adjust their power usage within specific bounds to assist power grid balancing authorities in maintaining supply-demand equilibrium. Achieving this requires coordinating on/off switching decisions so that the collective power profile follows a grid-provided reference signal, all while preserving each consumer's quality of service (QoS). Although extensive research exists on TCL coordination, it faces notable limitations: existing methods often fail to guarantee reference tracking performance and QoS adherence, and they lack mechanisms to calculate an appropriate reference signal for TCL power demand. This study introduces a framework that overcomes these shortcomings. The proposed approach coordinates any number of TCLs by being computationally efficient, implementable via local feedback with minimal communication, and capable of ensuring reference tracking while strictly satisfying temperature and cycling constraints for every unit at all times. Built upon a Markov model derived from discretizing a pair of Fokker-Planck equations previously developed by Malhame and Chong [21], the framework designs randomized policies for TCLs. The balancing authority disseminates a uniform policy to all devices, allowing each TCL to make on/off decisions based solely on local measurements. Simulation results are presented to validate these assertions.

Shape priors have historically proven highly effective for reconstructing 3D shapes from noisy or incomplete data. When employing deep-learning-based representations, this typically requires learning a latent vector, either as a single global entity or a set of local ones. While local representations offer greater flexibility, they are susceptible to overfitting. This paper proposes a hybrid method that represents shapes using 3D meshes, assigning a distinct latent vector to each vertex. During training, these vectors are constrained to share identical values to mitigate overfitting; however, during inference, they are updated independently under spatial regularization constraints. We demonstrate that this approach achieves a balance of flexibility and generalization, validated across various medical image processing applications.

Recent studies by the ALICE and STAR collaborations have detected notable increases in J/$\psi$ production at very low transverse momenta during peripheral hadronic nucleus-nucleus (A+A) collisions. These anomalies suggest coherent photon-nucleus interactions, a phenomenon traditionally restricted to ultra-peripheral collisions, are occurring even in violent heavy-ion impacts. Assuming coherent photoproduction drives these excesses in peripheral A+A collisions, it becomes crucial to evaluate its role in proton-proton (p+p) collisions involving nuclear overlap, specifically non-single-diffractive events. This paper presents a calculation of exclusive J/$\psi$ photoproduction in such non-single-diffractive p+p collisions at RHIC and LHC energies, utilizing a parametrization based on pQCD and global experimental data. This approach aims to refine the precision of phenomenological models for photoproduction in A+A systems. We also report the differential rapidity and transverse momentum distributions of J/$\psi$ produced via photoproduction. When compared to J/$\psi$ production from hadronic interactions, our findings indicate that the photoproduction contribution is negligible.

Prior studies have shown that infectious disease characteristics can be deduced from online search patterns. This study leverages temporal data on search query frequencies to assess COVID-19 prevalence across several nations. Initially, we created unsupervised models grounded in symptom categories defined by the UK's National Health Service and Public Health England. Subsequently, we addressed potential biases in these signals stemming from public interest rather than actual infections by using the share of news coverage dedicated to COVID-19 as a proxy. Our findings reveal that search-based models predict confirmed cases and deaths 16.7 (95% CI: 10.2–23.2) and 22.1 (95% CI: 17.4–26.9) days ahead, respectively. Additionally, we explored transfer learning to adapt supervised models from nations with advanced epidemic stages to those in earlier phases. We also analyzed multi-country time series of search activity versus confirmed cases or deaths, identifying distinct querying patterns, such as the superior predictive power of rarer symptoms compared to common ones. Finally, we demonstrated that incorporating web searches enhances the short-term forecasting accuracy of autoregressive models for COVID-19 mortality. Overall, this research supports the use of online search data as a complementary public health surveillance tool to aid the COVID-19 response alongside traditional methods.

The long-time asymptotic behavior of solutions to the fifth-order modified Korteweg-de Vries equation on the line, for initial data within specific weighted Sobolev spaces, is investigated using the Dbar method and Deift and Zhou's nonlinear steepest descent technique for oscillatory Riemann--Hilbert problems. By applying Fourier analysis and the $I$-method, we establish global well-posedness in lower regularity Sobolev spaces and subsequently derive the asymptotic behavior within these weighted settings.

This paper presents a family of online algorithms designed for the classical coloring problem concerning intersection graphs of discs with bounded diameter. Leveraging a geometric representation of these graphs, our approach draws inspiration from an algorithm by Fiala et al. but achieves superior competitive ratios. This enhancement results from employing two vertex partitioning techniques prior to coloring; notably, one technique utilizes b-fold coloring of the plane. The proposed method is more versatile, demonstrating its applicability to coloring other planar shapes and adapting effectively for online L(2, 1)-labeling.

The widespread use of the Finch-Skea ansatz in modeling relativistic stars has motivated our investigation into the analytic solutions of the Einstein field equations. We derived a set of exact solutions by examining two distinct scenarios: (i) a positive anisotropic parameter and (ii) a state of zero anisotropy. By ensuring a smooth transition between our interior solutions and the Schwarzschild exterior metric, we successfully determined the relevant constants. The physical characteristics of these solutions were analyzed both numerically and graphically, specifically applying them to the pulsar $4U~1608-52$ (Mass = $1.57^{+0.30}_{-0.29}~M_\odot$, Radius = $9.8\pm 1.8~km$). Furthermore, we evaluated the stability criteria for the model, concluding that it remains stable only in the case of zero anisotropy.

We examine dynamical black holes within Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet (EGB) gravity alongside stationary black holes in the recently identified 4-dimensional novel Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet framework\cite{Glavan}. In the context of dynamical EGB black holes under fully local conditions, we compute the horizon temperature. Conversely, for stationary black holes in 4-dimensional novel EGB theory, we investigate thermodynamic characteristics, specifically determining both entropy and temperature.

Data frequently employed for analysis or forecasting often exhibits a hierarchical organization, such as observations from multiple individuals executing identical tasks. Capturing this structural complexity can enhance both the reliability of derived conclusions and the predictive accuracy for unseen data. While Bayesian modeling offers a framework for constructing such hierarchical models, the Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques typically used for parameter estimation are computationally intensive, often limiting their practicality in many scenarios. In contrast, variational Bayesian methods enable the derivation of approximations with significantly reduced computational costs. This document outlines the derivation of a variational approximation for hierarchical linear Bayesian regression and illustrates its application through data analysis.

Previous EEG-based emotion recognition systems typically employ single-task learning, a method prone to overfitting and resulting in emotion features with limited generalization. This paper introduces a graph-based multi-task self-supervised learning framework, termed GMSS, designed for EEG emotion recognition. By simultaneously integrating multiple self-supervised tasks—specifically spatial and frequency jigsaw puzzles alongside contrastive learning—GMSS acquires more generalized representations. This multi-task approach reduces the risk of overfitting on the primary emotion recognition task by learning a unified representation that satisfies all associated objectives. The spatial jigsaw puzzle task specifically targets the intrinsic spatial correlations among different brain regions, while the frequency jigsaw puzzle task focuses on identifying critical frequency bands essential for emotional signal analysis. Furthermore, a contrastive learning task is incorporated to map transformed data into a shared feature space, thereby regularizing learned features and promoting the extraction of inherent representations. Comparative experiments against various supervised and unsupervised methods on the SEED, SEED-IV, and MPED datasets demonstrate that GMSS significantly outperforms existing approaches in learning discriminative and generalizable features for EEG emotional signals.

The Relevance Vector Machine (RVM) is a supervised learning technique derived from Support Vector Machines (SVM) utilizing a Bayesian sparsity model. Unlike regression tasks, RVM classification is more challenging due to the absence of a closed-form solution for the weight parameter posterior. The original RVM classification method employed Newton's method to find the mode of this posterior and subsequently approximated it using Laplace's method, effectively applying frequency-based techniques within a Bayesian framework. This paper introduces a Generic Bayesian approach for RVM classification, hypothesizing that it yields convergent estimates for key quantities, in contrast to the nonconvergent results of the original algorithm. Additionally, we propose a Fully Bayesian approach featuring a hierarchical hyperprior structure, which enhances classification performance, particularly when dealing with imbalanced data. Numerical studies demonstrate that our proposed algorithms achieve high classification accuracy, with the Fully Bayesian hierarchical hyperprior method surpassing the Generic approach in imbalanced data scenarios.

This paper investigates mid-cap firms, defined as publicly traded entities with a market capitalization under US $10 billion. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset of US mid-cap companies spanning three decades, we aim to forecast the medium-term default probability term structure and identify which data sources—fundamental, market, or pricing—most significantly influence default risk. Unlike conventional methods that aggregate data across different time periods to create cross-sectional features, we formulate the task as a multi-label time-series classification problem. We adapt transformer models, a cutting-edge deep learning architecture originally developed for natural language processing, to the domain of credit risk modeling. Furthermore, we utilize attention heat maps to interpret model predictions. To enhance performance, we introduce a custom loss function tailored for multi-label classification and a novel multi-channel architecture featuring differential training, enabling the model to efficiently process all input data. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed deep learning framework outperforms traditional models, achieving a 13% improvement in AUC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve). Additionally, we illustrate how to generate importance rankings for various data sources and temporal relationships using a Shapley approach designed specifically for these models.

Spin-polarized atomic ensembles interrogated via light through the Faraday effect serve as a flexible platform for various applications in quantum information processing and metrology. This study examines an ensemble of alkali atoms that undergo continuous optical pumping and probing. Because of collective photon scattering at high optical depths, the atomic steady state does not match the typically assumed uncorrelated tensor-product state. We present a self-consistent approach to approximate this steady state while incorporating pair correlations and accounting for the atoms' multilevel structure. Our analysis identifies and characterizes regimes of Raman lasing, similar to superradiant lasers. Furthermore, we determine the spectrum of collectively scattered photons, which defines the coherence time of collective spin excitations superimposed on the stationary correlated mean-field state, a factor critical for metrology and quantum information applications.

This article provides a concise overview of the Dino programming language to contextualize its position among other dynamic languages. It details the current implementation, the tools employed, and key architectural choices, specifically focusing on the development of a stable, portable, and straightforward Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler. We evaluate how these critical design decisions impact Dino's performance across x86-64, AARCH64, and Powerpc64 architectures. Specifically, benchmarks on x86-64 show a performance gain of approximately 3.1x after transitioning from a stack-based virtual machine to a register-transfer architecture. Subsequent optimizations yielded further improvements: byte code combining added another 1.5x speedup, the JIT compiler contributed an additional 2.3x, and type inference combined with byte code specialization delivered a final 4.4x boost, resulting in an overall performance increase of roughly 47 times. To provide context, we compare Dino's performance against established implementations of Ruby, Python 3, PyPy, and JavaScript on these three platforms. The primary objective of this work is to share the lessons learned from Dino's development with other dynamic language creators, aiming to assist them in building faster, more portable languages with fewer resources while avoiding pitfalls encountered during Dino's creation.

One-class classifiers are trained exclusively using samples from the target class. Intuitively, their conservative modeling of class descriptions could enhance traditional classification tasks where classes are challenging to distinguish due to overlap and data imbalance. This study introduces three methods that utilize the combination of one-class classifiers based on non-parametric models, N-ary Trees, and Minimum Spanning Tree class descriptors (MST-CD) to address binary classification issues. These approaches manage inconsistencies resulting from merging multiple classifiers and resolve spurious connections generated by MST-CD in multi-modal class distributions. Experimental results across various datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach is viable and performs comparably to state-of-the-art algorithms.

The indistinguishability of independent single photons is demonstrated by representing each pulse as a mixed state of various transform-limited pulses. Entanglement with external environments or other photons causes a distribution in the center frequencies of these pulses, rendering the photons distinguishable; consequently, only photons sharing the identical transform-limited form remain indistinguishable. Specifically, the indistinguishability of single photons generated by solid-state quantum emitters and spontaneous parametric down-conversion is investigated using a two-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer. Furthermore, experimental techniques for improving indistinguishability are explored, with particular emphasis on the application of spectral filtering.

A fundamental feature of topological phases of matter is the presence of Wilson loop operators that preserve the ground state subspace. In this work, we introduce and execute an \it unbiased \rm numerical optimization framework designed to systematically identify these Wilson loop operators using only a single ground state wave function of a gapped Hamiltonian defined on a disk. We demonstrate that these operators can be further optimized to be cut and glued, resulting in constructs capable of creating, transporting, and annihilating anyon excitations. Leveraging these tools, we determine the braiding statistics and topological twists of the anyons, thereby establishing a method to completely extract topological order from a solitary wave function. We apply this technique to the ground states of perturbed toric code and doubled semion models under magnetic fields reaching up to half the critical value. From a modern viewpoint, this represents a machine learning strategy for uncovering emergent 1-form symmetries within a ground state wave function, while from a practical standpoint, it offers a pathway to identify Wilson loop operators in existing quantum simulators.

Due to their unique spectral characteristics, synthetic crystals constructed on non-Euclidean lattices, including hyperbolic and fractal structures, have garnered significant renewed interest, particularly within materials and metamaterials research. These systems can be analyzed through the lens of quantum dynamics defined on the Cayley graphs of finitely generated groups. This study examines the numerical dimensions of such quantum dynamics. By employing an algebraic framework for "periodic boundary conditions" attributed to Lueck [Geom. Funct. Anal. 4, 455-481 (1994)], we developed a practical and convergent numerical approach capable of determining the true bulk spectrum of the associated Hamiltonians. Furthermore, exact calculations of the resolvent's matrix elements, derived from the combinatorial properties of the Cayley graphs, serve to validate our algorithms and yield novel combinatorial insights. Consequently, our findings facilitate the systematic investigation of quantum dynamics across a broad spectrum of finitely generated groups, encompassing free and Fuchsian groups.

Byte-addressable persistent memory (B-APM) offers a novel solution to narrow the performance divide between main memory and storage. This paper explores usage scenarios for this emerging technology, grounded in the capabilities of Intel's DCPMM. We detail fundamental performance traits of DCPMM and describe how its configuration can meet the demands of memory- and I/O-intensive applications within high-performance computing (HPC) and data-centric environments. Two decision trees are provided to guide B-APM configuration choices, accompanied by two illustrative examples. We demonstrate that the technology's flexibility holds disruptive potential, driven not only by significant performance gains but also by its ability to support a broader spectrum of applications on uniform hardware.

A full construction of the AFLT states is presented, and for every case examined, the AGT conjecture—asserting the equivalence between Nekrasov Instanton Counting and the $Vir\oplus u(1)$ conformal block—has been confirmed.

This paper aims to derive several qualitative uncertainty principles concerning the windowed Opdam-Cherednik transform on weighted modulation spaces linked to this transform. Specifically, we establish the Cowling-Price, Hardy, and Morgan uncertainty principles within this framework. The proofs rely on Phragmén-Lindlöf type results for several complex variables adapted to weighted modulation spaces, alongside the properties of the Gaussian kernel associated with the Jacobi-Cherednik operator.

This study introduces the Fashion Intelligence System, leveraging the visual-semantic embedding (VSE) model to quantify abstract fashion descriptors like "casual," "adult-casual," and "office-casual," thereby aiding user comprehension. While standard VSE models struggle with images containing multiple components—such as hair, tops, pants, skirts, and shoes—we propose Partial VSE, which facilitates sensitive learning for each specific fashion coordinate. By partially learning embedded representations, this approach maintains existing practical functionalities while enabling new image-retrieval tasks that modify only designated parts and reordering tasks focused on specific elements, capabilities absent in conventional models. Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms traditional approaches without increasing computational complexity.

The identification of atypical ferroelectricity in twisted bilayers has led to the exploration of moiré heterostructures as polar materials. Nevertheless, misunderstandings regarding the fundamental nature and source of this observed ferroelectricity suggest a deeper theoretical comprehension of their polar characteristics is required. This study proposes, and confirms through first-principles calculations, that every moiré heterostructure possesses an out-of-plane moiré polar domain (MPD) structure. In transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers, variations in stacking configurations across the moiré superlattice induce interlayer charge transfer, generating local out-of-plane dipole moments whose magnitude and morphology are primarily governed by chalcogen atoms. Although MPDs in all heterostructures respond to changes in the moiré period, only homo-bilayers allow for tuning via an out-of-plane electric field. The text addresses prevailing misconceptions about ferroelectricity in these systems, positing that MPDs can be classified as ferroelectric domains only when a global van der Waals sliding occurs by one-third of a unit cell in a homo-bilayer. The paper concludes with a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the polar properties of moiré heterostructures.

Entity linking, also known as normalization, is a critical component of text mining that connects entity mentions in medical documents to standardized entries within a specific Knowledge Base (KB). This process holds significant value for the medical field and facilitates the integration of various medical and clinical ontologies. This paper focuses specifically on disease linking or normalization, a two-stage process involving candidate generation and candidate scoring. We propose a method to rank potential KB entries by evaluating their similarity to disease mentions, utilizing a Triplet Network for this ranking. Although previous approaches relied on manually crafted sieves and external resources for generating candidates, we introduce a robust, portable generation scheme that eliminates the need for hand-crafted rules. Experimental evaluations on the standard NCBI disease benchmark demonstrate that our system significantly outperforms prior methods.

Although CuTe is a two-dimensional layered material, it exhibits a quasi-one-dimensional charge-density-wave (CDW) state along the a-axis within the ab-plane, with a high transition temperature of $T_{CDW}=335$ K, yet its anisotropic characteristics have not been fully investigated. We employed a combination of transport measurements, polarized infrared reflectivity, and ultrafast pump-probe spectroscopy to elucidate the fundamental CDW physics in CuTe. Polarized optical data demonstrate that an energy gap develops progressively along the a-axis during cooling, whereas no corresponding gap signature appears along the b-axis, indicating significant electronic anisotropy in this quasi-2D system. Furthermore, time-resolved optical reflectivity shows that both the amplitude and relaxation time of photo-excited quasiparticles undergo drastic changes across the CDW phase transition. By applying fast Fourier transformation to oscillation signals derived from collective excitations, we identified a 1.65-THz mode as the CDW amplitude mode, which softens gradually at higher temperatures. Ultimately, these findings provide additional support for the existence of a fully anisotropic CDW order in CuTe, a phenomenon that is uncommon in quasi-2D materials.

Inter-orbital coupling denotes the ability to excite orbital states through otherwise orthogonal, non-interacting modes—a process typically forbidden in photonic lattices due to intrinsic propagation constant detuning. In this study, we experimentally demonstrate using femtosecond laser writing that fundamental and excited orbital states can couple when situated at distinct spatial locations. We provide a comprehensive characterization of an asymmetric double-well-like potential and employ a scanning method to effectively map dynamics along the propagation axis. This key observation directly addresses the need for a spatial mode converter device, which can be integrated anywhere within a photonic glass chip. Leveraging the phase structure of higher-order photonic modes and the effective negative coupling generated, we propose a trimer configuration functioning as a phase beam splitter ($\pi$-BS), offering significant potential for multiplexing and interference-based photonic concatenated operations.

We establish a theorem connecting the decomposition of parabolically induced representations with the Bushnell--Kutzko theory of typical representations. As a consequence, we demonstrate the existence of a well-defined inertial Langlands correspondence that preserves the monodromy action of L-parameters, assuming standard conjectures about the local Langlands correspondence hold true. Furthermore, to facilitate future applications of this inertial Langlands correspondence, we present a full construction of the set of typical representations, parametrizing them via the structure of the Bruhat--Tits building of $G$.

Continual learning enables agents to progressively enhance their capabilities across a sequence of tasks. Although recent literature on this topic has predominantly concentrated on specific loss functions or specialized neural network architectures—such as those modeling episodic memory or neural plasticity—this study examines continual learning through the lens of the training mechanism itself. We introduce the COnitnual Match BAsed Training (COMBAT) framework to train a population of advantage-actor-critic (A2C) agents within Pommerman, a partially observable multi-agent environment that prohibits communication. Adhering to this framework, we developed an agent named Navocado, which secured the top position in the NeurIPS 2018 Pommerman Competition. Two key attributes of Navocado are its reliance on no demonstrations for learning and its high reproducibility. As a technical report, we detail the design of the state space, action space, and reward structure, with a primary focus on the COMBAT framework. Experimental results demonstrate that Pommerman serves as an ideal setting for investigating continual learning, allowing the agent to acquire new skills without forgetting previous ones. Furthermore, the competition outcomes validate the agent's robustness against diverse opponents.

This study pursues two primary objectives. First, it establishes a second main theorem for meromorphic functions defined on the complex disc $\Delta (R_0)\subset\mathbb C$ that possess a finite growth index and small functions, featuring counting functions truncated at level $1$ and a more refined estimation of the small term. Second, it demonstrates a generalization and enhancement of Nevanlinna's five values theorem, specifically addressing the scenario involving five small functions within the complex disc $\Delta (R_0)$.

Designing distributed optimal controllers under communication constraints is inherently challenging unless specific structural assumptions—such as sparsity, delay, or spatial invariance—are applied to the system dynamics and information exchange patterns. This paper introduces Graph Symmetric Systems (GSSs), a new class of systems defined by their symmetry relative to an underlying graph topology, drawing inspiration from graph signal processing. We demonstrate that for linear quadratic problems governed by GSS dynamics, the optimal centralized controller corresponds to a novel type of graph filter characterized by transfer function-valued taps, which can be executed through distributed message passing. Subsequently, we propose multiple strategies to approximate this optimal centralized filter with a distributed controller that communicates only with a limited subset of neighboring subsystems. We also establish stability and suboptimality guarantees for these distributed solutions. Empirical results confirm that our method enables a principled balance between communication costs and performance while ensuring stability. Ultimately, these findings represent an initial step toward unifying the domains of distributed optimal control and graph signal processing.

Simulations of many-body quantum systems are currently computationally prohibitive for classical computers because the required time and memory scale exponentially with the particle count $N$. While classical approximations offer an efficient alternative, they tend to overestimate spin fluctuations at low temperatures, leading to exaggerated thermal effects; thus, evaluating the validity of this approximation is crucial. This study addresses that need by comparing numerical results for small Mn$^{3+}$ magnetic clusters in GaN, contrasting a classical treatment of Mn spins with a quantum-mechanical approach based on a crystal field model. In the classical scenario, spin precessional dynamics are modeled using the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) equation with spins represented as classical vectors. Conversely, the quantum model characterizes the Mn$^{3+}$ ion ($d^4$ configuration, $S=2$, $L=2$) using orbital and spin quantum numbers $|m_s,m_L>$. Special care is taken to ensure identical single-ion magnetic anisotropy parameters in both frameworks. The work concludes with a comprehensive comparison of magnetization $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{H}, T)$ as a function of magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$, temperature $T$, cluster size $N$, and super-exchange interaction strength $J$ derived from each method.

We report the accidental identification of a previously unknown galaxy group at $z\sim0.044$ within the XMM-LSS field using MIGHTEE Early Science data. Twenty galaxies were detected in neutral hydrogen (HI), achieved with a $3\sigma$ column density sensitivity of $N_\mathrm{HI} = 1.6\times10^{20}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. Despite the field being a well-known extragalactic legacy target, this group had not been recognized prior to this study. We provide spatially-resolved HI total intensity and velocity maps for all objects, which show disturbed morphologies indicative of environmental interactions. The group possesses a dynamical mass of $\log_{10}(M_\mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{M}_\odot) = 12.32$ and is notably gas-rich, exhibiting an HI-to-stellar mass ratio of $\log_{10}(f_\mathrm{HI}^\mathrm{*}) = -0.2$, which exceeds expectations by 0.7 dex. The specific distributions of the group's HI content, spatial configuration, velocity, and galaxy types strongly imply it is in the early phases of assembly. This discovery underscores the value of mapping spatially-resolved HI across diverse environments, particularly galaxy groups. The MeerKAT telescope's high sensitivity, extensive field of view, and broad instantaneous bandwidth have significantly advanced this scientific objective.

This study introduces two methods that significantly enhance the performance of tensor-network-based quantum circuit simulations. Implemented within the QTensor package, these techniques were evaluated using Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) circuits. As a result, the maximum simulatable depth and size of QAOA circuits were expanded; specifically, the depth was raised from 2 to 5, and the circuit size grew from 180 to 244 qubits. Additionally, simulation speeds improved by up to ten million-fold. This work offers valuable insights into how various strategies can dramatically accelerate quantum circuit simulations.

Introducing a massive graviton to alter gravity over vast distances could account for the universe's observed acceleration without invoking Dark Energy. While the Fierz-Pauli theory represents the standard framework for Massive Gravity, it suffers from significant issues when approaching the massless limit, most notably the vDVZ discontinuity. This phenomenon creates a discrepancy between the massless limit of the Fierz-Pauli theory and General Relativity. Our method employs a field-theoretic perspective on Massive Gravity, treating General Relativity in the weak-field regime as a gauge theory of a symmetric rank-2 tensor field. This approach yields an alternative formulation of linearized Massive Gravity that maintains five degrees of freedom for the graviton, successfully resolves the vDVZ discontinuity, and ensures a consistent massless limit. Furthermore, this theory relies on a single mass parameter, remaining consistent with the Fierz-Pauli model.

We introduce AutoProf, an automated non-parametric pipeline designed for extracting light profiles. By encompassing all steps required for surface brightness (SB) profile extraction, AutoProf facilitates efficient analysis of galaxy images. It enhances existing non-parametric ellipse fitting methods through fit-stabilization procedures derived from machine learning. This flexible pipeline also incorporates advanced analysis capabilities, such as extracting brightness profiles along radial or axial slices, generating smooth axisymmetric models, and utilizing decision trees for complex workflows. The authors present detailed comparisons against established photometry tools like photutils, XVISTA, and GALFIT, utilizing a substantial dataset of late-type galaxy images from the PROBES survey. Results indicate that AutoProf reliably detects fainter isophotes than competing methods, often exceeding a difference of >2 mag/arcsec^2. Furthermore, contrasting non-parametric elliptical fitting with simple parametric models reveals that two-component fits (e.g., S\'ersic plus exponential) fail to accurately describe late-type galaxies. Consequently, elliptical isophote fitting, and AutoProf specifically, are deemed ideal for a wide array of automated isophotal analysis tasks. AutoProf is freely accessible to the community at: https://github.com/ConnorStoneAstro/AutoProf

Vision-and-language pretraining (VLP) seeks to derive general multimodal representations from vast collections of image-text pairs. Although numerous successful methods have been developed, achieving fine-grained semantic alignment between images and text remains central to their success. However, most current VLP approaches fail to fully leverage the inherent knowledge contained within these pairs, which constrains the quality of learned alignments and limits overall model performance. To address this, we propose ROSITA, a novel VLP framework that unifies cross-modal and intra-modal knowledge within a single scene graph to strengthen semantic alignments. Specifically, we introduce a Structural Knowledge Masking (SKM) strategy that utilizes the scene graph structure as prior information for masked language and region modeling, thereby improving semantic alignment by filtering out interfering information from both within and across modalities. Extensive ablation studies and comprehensive analysis confirm the efficacy of ROSITA in enhancing semantic alignments. When pretrained on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, ROSITA significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art VLP methods across three standard vision-and-language tasks on six benchmark datasets.

Using the finite-temperature Lanczos method (FTLM), we examine the ground state of an anisotropic Kitaev model featuring antiferromagnetic (AFM) coupling under a $[001]$ magnetic field. Specifically, we analyze the case where $K_{X}=K_{Y}$, $K_{X}+K_{Y}+K_{Z}=-3K$, and $K_{Z}<-K$. As the magnetic field strength increases, the initial gapped quantum spin liquid (QSL) undergoes a series of transitions: first to a gapless QSL at $h_{c1}=g\mu_{B}H_{z1}/K$, then to a distinct gapless QSL possessing $C_{6}$ rotational symmetry at $h_{c2}$, and finally to a new $U(1)$ gapless QSL within the range of $h_{c3}$ and $h_{c4}$. These findings suggest that the magnetic field initially restores anisotropic gapped or gapless QSLs to an isotropic $C_{6}$ gapless state, after which they evolve similarly to their isotropic counterparts. Furthermore, the critical fields $h_{c1}$ through $h_{c4}$ increase monotonically with the Kitaev coupling, indicating that magnetic fields can effectively modulate anisotropic Kitaev materials.

Text encoders utilizing C-DSSM or transformer architectures have proven highly effective across numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. To meet the rigorous computational demands of sponsored search, low-latency versions of these models have been engineered. Nevertheless, relying solely on pure semantic data within these encoders is insufficient to fully resolve all Natural Language Understanding (NLU) challenges, particularly in accurately identifying user intent. We introduce the TextGNN model, which augments robust twin-tower encoders with complementary graph-derived information from user historical behaviors. This graph data acts as a guiding mechanism to enhance intent comprehension and improve language representation quality. By inheriting the advantages of twin-tower structures like C-DSSM and TwinBERT, TextGNN maintains suitability for low-latency environments while outperforming strong encoder-only baselines in both offline evaluations and online production systems. Specifically, offline experiments revealed a 0.14% rise in overall ROC-AUC and a 1% accuracy boost for long-tail, low-frequency ads. Furthermore, online A/B testing demonstrated a 2.03% increase in Revenue Per Mille alongside a 2.32% reduction in the ad defect rate.

Hyperspherical embeddings have become a leading approach for face and voice recognition, where Euclidean vectors are trained to represent individual identity through direction while disregarding magnitude. However, emerging research suggests that the magnitudes of embeddings produced by deep neural networks can reflect input quality. This study investigates how embedding magnitudes relate to quality assessment and out-of-distribution detection. We introduce a novel probabilistic speaker extractor that utilizes magnitude-encoded information within the speaker verification framework and develop multiple quality-aware diarization methods that integrate these magnitudes. Our findings demonstrate substantial performance gains over magnitude-agnostic baselines in both speaker verification and diarization tasks.

Stress presents a complex challenge with profound physical and psychological effects on daily human performance, making acute stress detection a significant area for contextual understanding. While subject-dependent training yields the highest accuracy for stress detection models, subject-independent methods offer a more practical and cost-effective solution, enabling the deployment of detection and management systems on consumer wearables without needing end-user training data. To enhance the performance of subject-independent models, this paper proposes a bio-signal processing pipeline utilizing a simple neural network architecture. This architecture leverages statistical features derived from multimodal contextual sensing sources—specifically Electrodermal Activity (EDA), Blood Volume Pulse (BVP), and Skin Temperature (ST)—captured by a consumer-grade wearable device. We evaluate the proposed model by comparing stress detection accuracy between models using individual signal sources and those employing the fusion of multiple sensors. Extensive experiments on the public WESAD dataset demonstrate that our model surpasses conventional methods and achieves a 1.63% higher mean accuracy score than the state-of-the-art model, all while maintaining a low standard deviation. Furthermore, our results indicate that integrating features from multiple sensor sources yields more accurate predictions than relying on any single source in isolation.

The flip processes, originally presented in [Garbe, Hladk\'y, \v{S}ileikis, Skerman: From flip processes to dynamical systems on graphons], constitute a category of random graph processes governed by a rule $\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{H}_k\rightarrow \mathcal{H}_k$ that maps every labelled graph of order $k$ to itself. Initiated with an arbitrary $n$-vertex graph $G_0$, the evolution proceeds by selecting $k$ random vertices $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ from the current graph $G_{i-1}$ and substituting the induced subgraph $G_{i-1}[v_1,\ldots,v_k]$ with $\mathcal{R}(G_{i-1}[v_1,\ldots,v_k])$ to form $G_i$. Leveraging the framework of dynamical systems on graphons established in the aforementioned work, we investigate various specific instances of these processes. These include the triangle removal process and its extensions, such as "extremist flip processes" where $\mathcal{R}(H)$ yields either a clique or an independent set based on whether the edge density of $H$ falls below or exceeds half of its potential edges, and "ignorant flip processes" where the output $\mathcal{R}(H)$ remains independent of the input $H$.

The $\Omega^{-}$ baryon, composed of three strange quarks (sss), has rarely been detected experimentally and has instead been the subject of extensive theoretical investigation. This study employs the hypercentral Constituent Quark Model (hCQM) featuring a linear confining potential to examine its properties. Resonance mass spectra were calculated for the 1S-4S, 1P-4P, 1D-3D, and 1F-2F states. Furthermore, the magnetic moment was analyzed alongside Regge trajectories to explore the linear nature of the system based on the computed data. Finally, these results were benchmarked against existing experimental data and other theoretical approaches.

This study presents a novel approach for real-time detection and recognition of underwater objects within sidescan sonar imagery streams, illustrated through case studies in underwater archaeology and the recovery of abandoned fishing gear. The methodology involves synthesizing images from raw sonar data, followed by geometric and radiometric corrections. Subsequently, 2D feature detection algorithms are employed to locate point clouds of visual microfeatures, such as corners and edges. A clustering algorithm is then applied to these feature point clouds to organize them into regions of interest, filter out false positives, and produce a georeferenced inventory of detected objects.

We introduce a memory-driven framework designed for real-time, data-efficient target analysis within forward-looking-sonar (FLS) imagery. The approach begins by employing a compact DenseNet-inspired network to strip non-discriminative details, thereby streamlining subsequent analysis and enabling generalization from limited labeled data. This filtered imagery is then fed into a novel NeuralRAM-based convolutional matching network (NRMN) for low-shot target recognition. Additionally, a small-scale FlowNet (LFN) aligns and registers FLS imagery across local temporal scales, facilitating target label consensus voting and enhancing both detection and recognition rates. Evaluation using real-world FLS imagery featuring diverse target classes with high intra-class variability and complex sub-class structures demonstrates that few-shot learning, utilizing only ten to thirty class-specific exemplars, achieves performance comparable to supervised deep networks trained on hundreds of samples per class. Furthermore, effective zero-shot learning is attainable. The framework's high performance stems from the inductive-transfer capabilities of NRMNs once distractor elements are eliminated.

This paper presents a probabilistic polynomial time algorithm that successfully reduces the complete factorization of any squarefree integer $n$ to the task of counting points on elliptic curves modulo $n$, with a success probability of $1-\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

This paper aims to explore the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for a semilinear parabolic equation featuring double nonlocality in both spatial and temporal dimensions, a model that emerges from the chaotic dynamics of a polymer chain within a biological nano-sensor. Specifically, the problem incorporates a symmetric Lévy-type integrodifferential operator and an interaction potential term dependent on the time-integral of the solution across the entire solution interval. By employing the Galerkin approximation method, the study establishes the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution to this nonlocal complement value problem for small time intervals, subject to specific conditions on the interaction potential.

This paper employs Euler's function to derive an explicit formula for all integral solutions of the linear indeterminate equation $a_1x_1+a_2x_2+...+a_sx_s=n$ with $s$ variables. The formula is expressed explicitly in terms of the coefficients $a_1, a_2, ..., a_s$ and the constant term $n$.

The pursuit of formalizing knowledge within a specific domain has drawn researchers from diverse fields into the area of ontology learning. This overview emphasizes classical machine learning and data mining techniques designed to semi-automate the construction of description logic (DL) ontologies. These methods rely on association rule mining, formal concept analysis, inductive logic programming, computational learning theory, and neural networks. We examine each approach individually, detailing how they have been modified to address DL ontologies. Furthermore, we analyze the respective advantages and constraints of these techniques when applied to learning DL ontologies.

This study enhances the Lieb-Thirring type inequalities established by Demuth, Hansmann, and Katriel (J. Funct. Anal. 2009) for Schrödinger operators featuring complex-valued potentials. Our findings incorporate a positive, integrable function. Specifically, in the one-dimensional scenario, we demonstrate that the result is sharp; that is, substituting a non-integrable function renders an analogous inequality invalid.

Current methods for joint image-text understanding typically assume that both modalities can be universally represented by a single implicit model. However, since co-occurring images and text can exhibit qualitatively diverse relationships, explicitly modeling these connections could enhance the performance of existing joint understanding systems. In this paper, we introduce a Cross-Modal Coherence Model designed for text-to-image retrieval. Our analysis demonstrates that models trained to recognize image-text coherence relations successfully retrieve images originally paired with the target text more frequently than coherence-agnostic models. Furthermore, human evaluations reveal that images retrieved by our proposed coherence-aware model are preferred over coherence-agnostic baselines by a significant margin. These findings offer valuable insights into how different modalities interact and highlight the role of coherence relations in capturing commonsense inferences within text and imagery.

A hollow matrix defined by a graph $G$ is a real symmetric matrix with zero diagonal entries, where off-diagonal elements correspond to the adjacencies in $G$. For a specific graph $G$, the task of identifying all feasible spectra of matrices linked to $G$ constitutes the hollow inverse eigenvalue problem for $G$. This paper provides solutions for the hollow inverse eigenvalue problem concerning paths and complete bipartite graphs. Furthermore, findings regarding related subproblems—such as achievable ordered multiplicity lists, the maximum multiplicity of an eigenvalue, and the minimum count of distinct eigenvalues—are presented for other graph families.

This paper presents the winning solution for Shared Task 3 of SwissText 2021, a public challenge focused on translating Swiss German speech into Standard German text. Swiss German encompasses various Alemannic dialects spoken in the German-speaking regions of Switzerland, which differ markedly from standard German in pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar, often rendering them unintelligible to native German speakers. Additionally, the dialect lacks a standardized written form. To address this difficult problem, we developed a hybrid automatic speech recognition system featuring a translation-enriched lexicon, a first-pass language model tailored to Swiss German nuances, a transfer-learned acoustic model, and a robust neural language model for second-pass rescoring. Our submission achieved a BLEU score of 46.04% on a blind conversational test set, surpassing the runner-up by a 12% relative margin.

This note addresses Question 16 from http://cubics.wikidot.com, specifically investigating which configurations of 15 points in projective 3-space correspond to the eigenpoints of a cubic surface. We demonstrate that a general eigenscheme within projective n-space constitutes the complete intersection of two appropriate smooth determinantal curves situated on a smooth determinantal surface. Furthermore, we establish that the converse is true when n=3, thereby offering a resolution to the cited question for any degree. Additionally, we show that any arbitrary general collection of points in projective 3-space can be extended to form an eigenscheme of a partially symmetric tensor.

Expressive reading, which serves as the hallmark of oral reading fluency, involves the prosodic articulation of phrasing and emphasis. In the assessment of oral reading, this element aids in verifying the speaker's grasp of the text. This study utilizes a labeled dataset of children's reading recordings to detect prominent words through speaker-independent methods, leveraging both acoustic-prosodic and lexico-syntactic features. A previously optimized random forest ensemble model is substituted with an RNN sequence classifier to capture contextual dependencies spanning longer utterances. Additionally, deep learning techniques are employed to extract word-level features from low-level acoustic contours—including fundamental frequency, intensity, and spectral shape—in an end-to-end manner. Comparative performance analyses are provided across various feature types and learning architectures for prominent word prediction to derive meaningful insights.

Although Neural Networks (NNs) significantly enhance the empirical performance of closed-loop systems, they complicate the formal verification of safety properties. This study addresses the estimation of forward reachable sets for neural feedback loops. While existing methods offer bounds, computationally efficient approaches produce overly conservative results that hinder verification, whereas methods providing tighter bounds are too resource-intensive for online use. This work bridges that divide by formulating a convex optimization problem for reachability analysis in NN-controlled closed-loop systems. Although these solutions are less precise than prior semidefinite programming techniques, they are markedly faster to compute. Furthermore, a portion of these time savings enables the application of novel input set partitioning strategies to refine bounds, substantially narrowing the gap in tightness. The proposed framework accommodates real-world complexities, including uncertainty (such as measurement and process noise) and nonlinearities (such as polynomial dynamics). Additionally, a new backward reachability algorithm is introduced to determine initial state sets that guarantee reaching a specified target set when only the target is known. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach, utilizing linear relaxations and partitioning, achieves a $5\times$ reduction in conservatism with $150\times$ less computation time compared to state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, tests on quadrotors, a 270-state system, and polynomial dynamics confirm the method's efficacy in managing uncertainty, high dimensionality, and nonlinear behavior.

Previous studies have employed indices such as CKA and CCA variants to assess similarity among cross-lingual representations within multilingual language models. However, this paper contends that the underlying assumptions of CKA/CCA are misaligned with a primary objective of cross-lingual learning analysis: elucidating zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. We identify critical aspects of cross-lingual similarity that these indices overlook and present an empirical case study \textit{demonstrating this limitation}. Subsequently, we propose \textit{Average Neuron-Wise Correlation (ANC)} as a simple alternative that avoids the pitfalls of CKA/CCA and is particularly suited for cross-lingual scenarios. Furthermore, we utilize ANC to provide evidence that the "first align, then predict" paradigm occurs not only in masked language models (MLMs) but also in multilingual models employing \textit{causal language modeling} (CLM) objectives. Additionally, we demonstrate that this pattern holds for \textit{scaled versions} of both MLMs and CLMs, extending up to 85 times the size of the original mBERT model.\footnote{Our code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/TartuNLP/xsim}}

Traditional beamforming relies on channel estimation, a process that becomes both computationally demanding and prone to inaccuracies as antenna arrays grow larger. This paper investigates the outage probability within positioning-assisted beamforming frameworks. By accounting for positioning errors, link distances, and beamwidths, we derive closed-form bounds for outage probability. Leveraging these analytical findings, we demonstrate that optimizing beamwidth based on link distance and transmit power markedly reduces outage probability.

Science and society are inextricably linked, evolving in tandem. Analyzing scientific trends allows researchers to identify pivotal topics and formulate more effective funding policies. Scholarly organizations, such as the Korean Physics Society (KPS), have historically played a crucial role in the development of science; understanding their impact motivates our research, as these societies actively strive to enhance society. While previous studies have attempted to map scientific trends using academic outputs like papers and patents, they often confined their scope to the academic realm, overlooking societal interactions. This study aims to analyze the co-evolution of science and society by examining the public magazine "Physics and High Technology," published by the KPS. We constructed keyword co-occurrence networks for various time periods and applied community detection to map and track the evolution of keyword structures. Our analysis reveals that research-related clusters consistently dominate the networks, with sub-clusters branching into diverse physics fields, indicating increasing specialization within the discipline. Additionally, the persistent appearance of education and policy clusters highlights the KPS's contribution to broader societal issues. Furthermore, we utilized the PageRank algorithm to assess the temporal shifts in the significance of selected keywords, such as "semiconductor," "woman," and "evading." For instance, the rising prominence of the keyword "woman" over time suggests that academia is increasingly addressing gender issues, mirroring recent social movements.
We provide a proof of the Moon in a puddle theorem and apply its central lemma to establish a generalization of the four-vertex theorem.

Shape metrics for high-dimensional objects remain scarce; existing measures, such as hyper-volume, are restricted to well-understood forms like Platonic solids and $n$-cubes. Furthermore, characterizing objects with ill-defined shapes in higher dimensions is inherently ambiguous. Previous approaches fail to provide a single scalar value for qualitative object assessment; for instance, principal component analysis yields $n$ separate metrics rather than one. Consequently, there is a need for a unified metric capable of distinguishing between objects of varying shapes. While prior research has focused on shape metrics for two or three dimensions, there is significant potential to develop metrics applicable to any dimension. To address this, we introduce two novel metrics for objects in arbitrary dimensions: hyper-Sphericity and hyper-Shape Proportion (SP). We examine the properties of these metrics across various shapes, including $n$-balls, and demonstrate their utility in analyzing multidimensional data, such as the Iris dataset.

We present a novel method for separating trends (drift) from changepoints (shifts) in time series data. This locally adaptive, model-based strategy robustly decouples these elements by integrating Bayesian trend filtering with machine learning regularization. The process begins by applying an over-parameterized Bayesian dynamic linear model (DLM) to characterize drift, followed by the use of a weighted penalized likelihood estimator paired with the DLM's posterior distribution to detect shifts. We demonstrate that Bayesian DLMs utilizing shrinkage priors yield smooth trend estimates even amidst complex noise; however, their inability to shrink coefficients exactly to zero prevents direct changepoint detection. Conversely, while penalized likelihood methods excel at locating changepoints, they are limited to data with simple signal and noise patterns. Our proposed decoupling approach merges the advantages of both: the flexibility of Bayesian DLMs and the hard thresholding capability of penalized likelihood estimators, enabling effective changepoint analysis in complex, modern environments. This framework is robust to outliers and capable of identifying various changes, such as shifts in mean and slope. Furthermore, it is easily extendable to analyze parameter shifts in time-varying parameter models, including dynamic regressions. We evaluate the flexibility, performance, and robustness of this approach against several alternative methods through extensive simulations and real-world applications.

We introduce a novel approach for individually addressing trapped ion qubits by selecting them based on their motional frequencies. Our findings demonstrate that geometric phase gates can execute single-qubit rotations through the coherent interference of spin-independent and global spin-dependent forces. These spin-independent forces, achievable through localized electric fields, accelerate gate operations and diminish sensitivity to motional decoherence, a conclusion supported by both analytical and numerical analyses. Although this scheme is broadly applicable to various trapped ion experimental configurations, we also present a numerical simulation of a specific laser-free implementation, revealing cross-talk errors under $10^{-6}$ for feasible parameters.

While traditional human-computer interaction depends on keyboards, mice/touchpads, and screens, new tools have emerged that engage multiple senses including sound, smell, tactile feedback, muscular resistance, voice commands, balance, and simultaneous multi-sensory input. How could these advancements influence the practice of statistics and data science? Individuals with low vision might gain enhanced capabilities to comprehend and investigate data. More broadly, techniques designed to facilitate this multi-sensory engagement could enable sighted analysts to utilize additional senses, thereby improving their analytical skills. We aim to adapt a variety of existing computer and sensory input/output technologies to revolutionize data science workflows. The following outlines a vision of the potential achievements of this synthesis.

During the 10th International Workshop on Top Quark Physics (TOP2017), the field of top quark research was experiencing rapid growth. The unprecedented surge in high-energy data at the LHC during Run 2 has largely eliminated statistical limitations for traditional top-quark analyses, shifting the primary challenge to overcoming "Systematics Wall" and optimizing data utility. Researchers are now investigating novel top-quark processes for the first time, while also exploring established pair-production mechanisms in unique environments, such as heavy-ion collisions or low center-of-mass energy "reference data" collected by the LHC. The conference included 37 presentations by experimentalists, featuring seven talks in the "Young Scientists Forum" that allowed emerging researchers to present their work in greater depth than usual. Given the vast number of experimental results presented, this document offers a highly selective and somewhat biased overview, reflecting primarily the author's personal preferences.

Unlike simultaneous Bayesian predictive classifiers (sBpc), marginal Bayesian predictive classifiers (mBpc) process data points individually, implicitly assuming observation independence. However, the detrimental impact of this false assumption on mBpc accuracy diminishes as training data volume increases, due to the saturation of generative model parameter learning; this ensures the convergence of both classifiers under de Finetti-type exchangeability. This finding is non-trivial for sequences governed by Partition exchangeability (PE), where even extensive training data cannot entirely eliminate the possibility of unobserved outcomes. We present a computational framework for generating PE sequences and demonstrate, through controlled increases in training data, the convergence of sBpc and mBpc. These results support the preference for simpler, computationally efficient marginal classifiers over simultaneous ones. Additionally, we offer parameter estimation for the generative model underlying PE sequences and a testing protocol for parameter equality across samples. The PEkit package, available on CRAN and GitHub, implements Bayesian predictive supervised classification, parameter estimation, and hypothesis testing for the Ewens Sampling formula generative model.

Although deep convolutional neural networks excel at removing synthetic, spatially invariant noise, their effectiveness diminishes with real-world noisy images unless they employ multi-stage architectures. To enhance the practical application of denoising techniques, this paper introduces RIDNet, a novel single-stage blind real image denoising network built on a modular design. By incorporating a residual-on-residual structure to facilitate low-frequency information flow and utilizing feature attention to capture channel dependencies, the model achieves superior results. Comprehensive evaluations across three synthetic and four real noisy datasets, measured through quantitative metrics and visual quality against 19 state-of-the-art methods, confirm the outstanding performance of RIDNet.

Image copy detection and retrieval from large databases rely on two key components: a neural network that converts images into transformation-robust vector representations, and an efficient yet approximate similarity search algorithm that balances scalability with search quality, often introducing errors. This paper enhances the robustness of image copy detection through active indexing, which optimizes the interaction between these two elements. By applying imperceptible modifications to images prior to their release, we reduce quantization loss in their vector representations. These adjustments are determined by back-propagating the loss through the deep neural network while adhering to perceptual constraints, thereby making the images more easily retrievable. Experimental results demonstrate a significant improvement in both retrieval and copy detection for activated images; specifically, Recall@1 increases by 40% across various image transformations and for several popular indexing structures based on product quantization and locality-sensitive hashing.

The paper derives the explicit construction of local observable algebras within quasi-Hermitian quantum theories using both the tensor product model of locality and free fermion models. This construction is specifically applied to various instances of a $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric toy model involving particle-conserving free fermions on a one-dimensional lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions and open boundaries. Although the Hamiltonian exhibits locality, local observables are absent in generic site collections within the lattice. The existence of nontrivial observables in specific site configurations is highly dependent on the nature of the complex potential.

A primary challenge in video-language (VidL) modeling stems from the gap between static video representations derived from standard image/video models and the dynamic nature of downstream VidL data. While recent efforts attempt to bridge this divide through end-to-end training, existing methods often rely on computationally efficient strategies that "imagify" video inputs. These approaches typically process a sparse subset of frames using 2D CNNs, followed by simple pooling or concatenation to generate video representations. Although effective to some degree, these simplified techniques risk discarding crucial temporal information necessary for successful VidL tasks. To address this, we introduce VIOLET, a fully end-to-end VIdeO-LanguagE Transformer that leverages a video transformer to explicitly capture temporal dynamics. Furthermore, contrasting with prior findings that pre-training tasks like masked frame modeling are suboptimal, we propose a novel pre-training objective called Masked Visual-token Modeling (MVM).
