The results cover the Polyakov loop, multiple susceptibilities, the chiral condensate and its susceptibility, as well as the emergence of parity doubling within the light and strange baryonic sectors.

Inspired by current experimental efforts, including those at the Helmholtz International Beamline for Extreme Fields (HIBEF) within the European X-ray Free-Electron Laser (XFEL) facility, we compute x-ray birefringent scattering occurring in the combined field of two optical or near-optical lasers, evaluating multiple scenarios. To aid the experimental observation of quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence, our analysis prioritizes cases where the initial and final x-ray photons exhibit differences not only in polarization but also in propagation direction—corresponding to scattering angles within the milliradian range—and potentially in energy.

A tiling of a topological disc using topological discs is termed monohedral when all constituent tiles are congruent. Maltby (J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 66: 40-52, 1994) provided a characterization of monohedral tilings of a square using three topological discs, while Kurusa, Lángi, and Vigh (Mediterr. J. Math. 17: article number 156, 2020) did the same for a circular disc. This note aims to bridge these two findings by characterizing monohedral tilings of any regular $n$-gon (for $n \geq 5$) utilizing at most three tiles.

We introduce Masked Siamese Networks (MSN), a self-supervised learning framework designed for image representation learning. The method aligns the representation of an image with randomly masked patches against that of the original, unmasked image. This pre-training strategy offers significant scalability when applied to Vision Transformers, as the network processes only the unmasked patches. Consequently, MSNs enhance the scalability of joint-embedding architectures and generate high-level semantic representations that excel in low-shot image classification. For example, on ImageNet-1K, our base MSN model reaches 72.4% top-1 accuracy with just 5,000 annotated images and achieves 75.7% top-1 accuracy with only 1% of the labels, establishing a new state-of-the-art for self-supervised learning on this benchmark. The code is publicly accessible.

Identifying buildings and other structures in aerial imagery holds significant value for urban planning and cartography. However, automated building detection from such images remains a difficult challenge due to factors like inconsistent lighting, shadows, and occlusions. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) offer some resilience against these variations, they often struggle to differentiate between easy and hard cases. This study trains a detection algorithm using RGB-D images to generate segmented masks via the DenseNet architecture. First, we enhance the model's performance by employing a statistical re-sampling method known as Bootstrapping, which ensures the retention of more informative examples. Second, the proposed approach surpasses the non-bootstrapped version by achieving superior results with only one-sixth of the original training data, reaching a precision-recall break-even point of 95.10% on our aerial imagery dataset.

We introduce weighted Sobolev spaces and establish a corresponding trace theorem for them. As an application, we examine non-zero boundary value problems for parabolic equations. The weighted parabolic Sobolev spaces considered here are specifically tailored for the regularity theory of stochastic partial differential equations on bounded domains.

Recently, fine-tuning pre-trained language models has become a standard approach for developing NLP models across various tasks, particularly in few-shot scenarios. We contend that aligning fine-tuning objectives more closely with pre-training goals can maximize the potential of these models. This study focuses on few-shot named entity recognition (NER) as a pilot investigation, noting that current fine-tuning methods diverge significantly from pre-training strategies. We introduce FFF-NER, a novel framework for few-shot NER, which incorporates three specialized token types: "is-entity," "which-type," and "bracket." These tokens allow us to reframe NER fine-tuning as either masked token prediction or generation, contingent on the specific pre-trained language model used. Experimental results demonstrate that applying FFF-NER to fine-tune both BERT and BART on multiple benchmark datasets yields substantial improvements over existing methods, including sequence labeling, prototype meta-learning, and prompt-based techniques. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal a strong correlation between few-shot NER performance and the degree of similarity between fine-tuning and pre-training objectives.

Drought presents a severe risk to the fragile economies of Sub-Saharan Africa. This research examines how large-scale ocean oscillations affect drought patterns in West Africa. The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) was calculated using monthly precipitation records from the Climate Research Unit covering the 1961–1990 period. The study employed linear correlation, co-integration testing, mutual information, and nonlinear synchronization techniques to analyze the relationship between the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and regional drought. Results indicated a predominantly positive correlation between the SOI and drought, whereas the PDO and NAO exhibited negative correlations, a finding supported by co-integration tests. However, nonlinear analyses revealed more intricate dynamics among these variables. Furthermore, the PDO demonstrated a weaker influence on drought in coastal areas compared to the Sahel region of West Africa.

The scarcity of medical expertise in image annotation has made developing label-efficient methods for segmentation a prominent research area. Current advancements aim to leverage weak annotations alongside a small number of strong labels to achieve segmentation quality comparable to professional scenarios. However, existing methods primarily address the inconsistency between strong and weak supervision while overlooking inconsistencies within the weakly-annotated instances themselves, which inevitably causes performance decline. To resolve this, we introduce a novel hybrid-supervised framework that evaluates each weakly-annotated instance individually. This framework learns instance weights guided by the gradient direction of strong annotations, thereby better exploiting high-quality priors and depicting weak instances more accurately. Specifically, our proposed Dynamic Instance Indicator (DII) fulfills these goals and is integrated into a Dynamic Co-regularization (DCR) framework to mitigate performance degradation caused by weak annotation distortions. Extensive experiments on two hybrid-supervised medical segmentation datasets show that with only 10% strong labels, the proposed framework efficiently utilizes weak labels to achieve competitive performance against scenarios using 100% strong labels.

Limited Discrepancy Search (LDS) is a widely used algorithm for exploring a state space using a heuristic to prioritize actions, while Nested Search (NS) employs the same heuristic approach for state space exploration. However, NS allocates more computational effort to the move linked to the highest heuristic playout value, whereas LDS focuses its additional time on the single best heuristic move. Despite these differences, both algorithms consume comparable amounts of time at equivalent search depths. This paper argues that prioritizing the move associated with the best heuristic playout, as NS does, is frequently superior to the strategy of following the heuristic directly, as seen in LDS.

This study seeks to decompose higher-dimensional functions in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ into sums of non-tangential boundary limits derived from corresponding Hardy space functions on tubes, specifically for the range $0<p<1$. In the one-dimensional setting, Deng and Qian \cite{DQ} recently established such a decomposition: for any $f\in L^p(\mathbb{R})$ with $0<p<1$, one can find $f_1$ and $f_2$ such that $f=f_1+f_2$, where $f_1$ and $f_2$ represent the non-tangential boundary limits of Hardy space functions in the upper and lower half-planes, respectively. This paper extends the aforementioned one-dimensional Hardy space decomposition result to higher dimensions and investigates the uniqueness of such decompositions.

The Zwicky Transient Facility has recently identified an optical transient, AT2020blt, located at a redshift of $z=2.9$, which aligns with the afterglow of an on-axis gamma-ray burst despite the absence of observed prompt emission. By applying detailed modeling, we demonstrate that the data most strongly support the classification of AT2020blt as the afterglow of an on-axis long gamma-ray burst, thereby excluding alternative explanations such as a cocoon or a low-Lorentz factor jet. Furthermore, our search of \textit{Fermi} data establishes stricter upper limits on the prompt emission than those reported in the initial discovery paper. Combining these findings with KONUS-\textit{Wind} observations, we determine that the gamma-ray efficiency of AT2020blt is likely between $0.3\%$ and $4.5\%$. We hypothesize that both AT2020blt and AT2021any represent the low-efficiency end of the long gamma-ray burst distribution, a population now becoming increasingly accessible for observation thanks to advanced facilities like the Zwicky Transient Facility.

Using an efficient single-cluster growth algorithm, we investigate bond percolation across various four-dimensional (4D) lattices, specifically the simple (hyper) cubic (SC), the SC lattice incorporating both nearest and second nearest neighbors (SC-NN+2NN), the body-centered cubic (BCC), and the face-centered cubic (FCC) structures. For the SC lattice, our calculation yields $p_c = 0.1601312(2)$, aligning with prior findings derived from alternative methods. Additionally, we determine a novel critical probability of $p_c = 0.035827(1)$ for the SC-NN+2NN lattice, a case not previously examined in bond percolation studies. Regarding the 4D BCC and FCC lattices, we derive $p_c = 0.074212(1)$ and $p_c = 0.049517(1)$, respectively, offering significantly improved precision over earlier estimates. Furthermore, our results for the critical exponents $\tau = 2.3135(5)$ and $\Omega = 0.40(3)$ agree with previous numerical data and the recent four-loop series expansion by Gracey [Phys. Rev. D 92, 025012, (2015)].

This study presents three analytical solutions for the linearized modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation within the framework of bulk electrolyte theory, alongside a comparison to mean spherical approximation outcomes. The linear models forecast a shift in the mean electrostatic potential from a Debye-Hückel-style damped exponential decay to a damped oscillatory pattern as electrolyte concentration surpasses a specific threshold. Furthermore, in the regime of damped oscillatory potential, the screening length diminishes with rising concentration. These findings are contrasted with recent experimental data regarding screening in aqueous NaCl solutions.

While data augmentation techniques like simple transformations or mixed samples can significantly enhance the generalization performance of deep learning models trained via Empirical Risk Minimization, our empirical analysis reveals a negative impact on distillation. Specifically, when a teacher model is trained using mixed sample strategies such as MixUp or CutMix, the student model distilled from it exhibits impaired generalization. We hypothesize that these strategies restrict a model's ability to learn example-specific features, thereby degrading the quality of the supervision signal during the distillation process. To quantify this performance dichotomy, we introduce a novel Class-Discrimination metric, which links these outcomes to the discriminative capacity induced by various strategies within a network's latent space.

The Distance Geometry Problem seeks to realize a weighted graph within $\mathbb{R}^K$. Two variants, rooted in protein conformation, rely on a specified vertex order representing the protein backbone. Both require a discrete choice when placing the next vertex relative to the $K$ already realized predecessors. The distinction lies in whether these $K$ predecessors must be contiguous; this constraint enables a combinatorial counting proof that establishes the realization algorithm's fixed-parameter tractability. Conversely, without this constraint, one can efficiently construct the vertex order directly from the graph. Consequently, developing a combinatorial counting method that does not depend on contiguity would be beneficial. However, this paper demonstrates that such a method is generally unattainable.

This paper introduces a scalable, multi-sensor adaptive track initiation method designed for labeled random finite set filters. While a straightforward approach to constructing the multi-sensor adaptive birth set distribution results in an exponential growth of newborn components relative to the number of sensors, this study establishes a truncation criterion for the labeled multi-Bernoulli birth density. It is demonstrated that this criterion ensures a bounded L1 error within the generalized labeled multi-Bernoulli posterior density. Leveraging this criterion, the authors develop a Gibbs sampler capable of generating a truncated, measurement-generated labeled multi-Bernoulli birth distribution with complexity scaling quadratically with the number of sensors. Furthermore, the paper presents both a closed-form solution and an approximate Monte Carlo importance sampling solution for the conditional sampling distribution under linear Gaussian likelihoods. Finally, multiple simulation results validate the effectiveness of the truncation criterion and confirm the achieved reduction in computational complexity.

The CMS experiment measured the transverse momentum ($p_\mathrm{T}$) distributions for $\Lambda$, $\Xi^-$, and $\Omega^-$ baryons, their antiparticles, and K$^0_\mathrm{S}$ mesons in proton-proton (pp) and proton-lead (pPb) collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, covering a wide rapidity interval. Data collection involved integrated luminosities of 40.2 nb$^{-1}$ for pp and 15.6 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ for pPb. For each particle type, the nuclear modification factor $R_\mathrm{pPb}$—defined as the ratio of particle yield in pPb collisions to a scaled pp reference—was determined. A distinct species dependence emerges in the $p_\mathrm{T}$ range of 2 to 7 GeV: $R_\mathrm{pPb}$ for K$^0_\mathrm{S}$ aligns with unity, whereas the three baryon species exhibit an enhancement ordered by strangeness content and/or mass. Additionally, strange hadron production in pPb collisions displays asymmetry around the nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass rapidity, with particle-type-dependent enhancements observed in the direction of the lead beam. These findings were compared against EPOS LHC model predictions, which incorporate parametrized radial flow. While the model qualitatively matches the $R_\mathrm{pPb}$ data, it fails to accurately describe the particle-species dependence in yield asymmetries away from mid-rapidity in pPb collisions.

For decades, the Faraday rotation of linearly polarized synchrotron emission within magneto-ionized media has been a well-established topic. However, because the direction of rotation is often irrelevant in many applications, conflicting interpretations have emerged in the literature regarding this specific detail. In this work, we derive the correct orientation of Faraday rotation by applying fundamental plasma theory to model the propagation of polarized emission from a radio source through a magnetized, ionized environment. We provide clear visual aids to demonstrate the breakdown of a linearly polarized wave into right- and left-circular modes, the evolution of their phases over time and space, and the consequent physical rotation of the polarization angle. Furthermore, we revisit scenarios where a medium both rotates polarization and emits polarized radiation, illustrating how helical magnetic fields can either enhance or diminish Faraday rotation. Ultimately, this paper seeks to clarify a point of contention between plasma physicists and radio astronomers and to prevent common errors associated with this counterintuitive phenomenon.

In April 2021, muon physics experts convened to define the scientific rationale for the new High-Intensity Muon Beams (HIMB) initiative at PSI, which aims to supply approximately $10^{10}$\,s$^{-1}$ surface muons for experimental use. Over the subsequent months, these concepts were refined and consolidated into this document. The proposed high intensities will enable entirely new experiments with significant discovery potential and unique sensitivities. The scientific case is exceptional and diverse, spanning fundamental particle physics, chemistry, condensed matter research, and applications in energy research and elemental analysis. In all these areas, HIMB will ensure that PSI's S$\mu$S and CHRISP facilities, part of the High Intensity Proton Accelerator complex (HIPA), maintain their world-leading status despite competition from other global muon facilities.

Real-world knowledge graphs (KGs) are typically incomplete, making the recovery of missing relations, known as KG completion, a prominent research focus. KG embedding, which represents entities and relations in a low-dimensional space, serves as a pivotal technique for this task. Recent advancements have been driven by convolutional neural networks in models like ConvE, SACN, InteractE, and RGCN. This paper introduces ComDensE, adopting a distinct architectural perspective that integrates relation-aware and common features through dense neural networks. Specifically, the relation-aware feature extraction employs a unique encoding function for each relation to induce relational biases, while the common feature extraction utilizes a shared encoding function across all input embeddings; both are realized via dense layers within ComDensE. The model achieves state-of-the-art results in link prediction, surpassing previous baselines in MRR and HIT@1 metrics on the FB15k-237 and WN18RR datasets. Furthermore, an extensive ablation study assesses the contributions of the relation-aware and common layers, with experimental outcomes confirming that the combined dense architecture of ComDensE yields superior performance.

Although crystal inversion symmetry in Dirac semimetals is expected to suppress the circular photogalvanic effect (CPGE), we have observed this phenomenon in Cd3As2 nanobelt field-effect transistors when photoexcitation is localized near metal contacts at room temperature. We attribute this CPGE to symmetry breaking caused by the Schottky electric field, which enables photocurrent modulation through circularly polarized light via spin-momentum locking. This hypothesis is validated by comprehensive experiments, including spatially and angularly resolved helicity-dependent photocurrent measurements, Kelvin probe force microscopy, and gate voltage studies. Furthermore, first-principles calculations demonstrate that field-induced structural distortion triggers a topological phase transition. These findings offer critical insights into electrically controlled, helicity-dependent optoelectronics within Dirac materials.

Numerous practical applications of language models (LMs), including code completion and writing support, rely on human-LM interaction. Yet, standard LM benchmarks remain non-interactive, generating output without human participation. To assess human-LM interaction, we introduce HALIE (Human-AI Language-based Interaction Evaluation), a framework that extends non-interactive evaluation across three dimensions: (i) the interactive process rather than just the final output, (ii) first-person subjective experience alongside third-party assessment, and (iii) preference criteria beyond mere quality. We designed five tasks spanning goal-oriented to open-ended scenarios to represent various interaction types. Evaluations on four state-of-the-art LMs (three GPT-3 variants and AI21's J1-Jumbo) reveal that high non-interactive performance does not guarantee superior human-LM interaction, and that first-person and third-party metrics may diverge, highlighting the need to examine the nuances of human-LM engagement.

Typological knowledge bases like WALS (Dryer and Haspelmath, 2013) store data on the linguistic characteristics of global languages and have proven valuable for applications such as cross-lingual transfer learning and linguistic probing. However, their widespread use is hindered by two main issues: they are sparsely populated, as most languages lack annotations for many features, and skewed, since only a limited number of features have extensive coverage. Because typological features often correlate, they can be predicted to automatically fill these gaps, which is the central aim of this shared task. The event received 8 submissions from 5 teams, with the top-performing methods leveraging feature correlations. Nevertheless, our error analysis indicates that even the most advanced systems face significant difficulties predicting feature values for languages with very little known information.

Recent studies employing deep models have yielded superior outcomes across diverse image restoration tasks. However, these supervised methods necessitate training datasets with distributions matching the target images. Conversely, shallow, typically unsupervised methods continue to show promise in numerous inverse problems, such as image compressive sensing (CS), by effectively exploiting non-local self-similarity priors inherent in natural images. Nevertheless, many of these shallow approaches rely on patch-based techniques, which often result in ringing artifacts due to simplistic patch aggregation. Relying exclusively on either deep or shallow strategies frequently restricts performance and generalizability in image restoration. To address this, we introduce a joint low-rank and deep (LRD) image model integrating three complementary pairs of priors: external/internal, deep/shallow, and local/non-local. We further develop a novel hybrid plug-and-play (H-PnP) framework grounded in the LRD model specifically for image CS. To ensure optimization tractability, we propose a straightforward yet efficient algorithm to solve the H-PnP based CS problem. Comprehensive experiments indicate that our proposed H-PnP algorithm substantially outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, including SCSNet and WNNM, for image CS recovery.

We analyze the phase-dependent Helfrich energy to derive an Euler-Lagrange equation along the phase separation boundary. While this finding was previously noted by researchers such as Jülicher-Lipowski and later Elliot-Stinner, our work reduces the required regularity condition for this boundary to $C^{1,1}$. The proof relies on a strategically selected test function based on the signed distance function.

Accurate semantic access to textual data depends on identifying toponyms and linking them to their actual-world counterparts, a process frequently complicated by significant toponym variation. The task of candidate selection involves pinpointing potential entities that a recognized toponym might refer to. Although this area has historically been underexplored, research indicates that candidate selection critically influences downstream tasks, particularly entity resolution, especially when dealing with noisy or non-standard text. This paper presents a flexible deep learning approach for toponym matching and candidate selection, leveraging state-of-the-art neural architectures. We evaluate this method intrinsically using several novel, realistic datasets that address diverse challenges, including cross-lingual and regional variations as well as OCR errors. Furthermore, we assess the method's performance on candidate selection within the downstream toponym resolution task, testing it against both existing datasets and a newly created, manually annotated corpus of nineteenth-century English OCR text.

The Galactic object G2.4$+$1.4 is an optical and radio nebula hosting an extreme Wolf--Rayet star. Initially, limited observations of its apparent non-thermal radio spectrum led some to classify it as a supernova remnant. However, further data revealed a flat, optically thin thermal radio spectrum, reclassifying the source as a photoionized, mass-loss bubble rather than a remnant. Despite this, recent claims suggest the source possesses a non-thermal integrated radio spectrum. This paper examines integrated radio flux densities from various surveys for G2.4$+$1.4, demonstrating that it exhibits a flat spectrum at gigahertz frequencies. Specifically, the spectral index is $\alpha = 0.02 \pm 0.08$, indicating that flux density $S$ scales with frequency $\nu$ according to $S \propto \nu^{-\alpha}$.

This study investigates information processing within neural networks by employing logistic regression probes \cite{probes} and the saturation metric \cite{featurespace_saturation}. We demonstrate that problem difficulty and network capacity exert an antagonistic influence on predictive performance, thereby offering a method to detect over- and under-parameterization relative to specific tasks. Furthermore, we establish that these observed effects are independent of previously documented pathological patterns, such as the "tail pattern" detailed in \cite{featurespace_saturation}. Finally, we show that saturation patterns stabilize early in the training process, facilitating a more efficient analysis cycle.

We examine the application of discrete time crystals, formed within a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of ultracold atoms bouncing resonantly on an oscillating mirror, to explore condensed matter phenomena across the time dimension. This bouncing BEC system demonstrates significant breaking of time-translation symmetry, enabling the formation of discrete time crystals with up to approximately 100 temporal lattice sites, thereby providing a platform for diverse temporal condensed matter effects. First, we analyze single-particle phenomena in time, such as Anderson localization caused by temporal disorder, topological time crystals, and quasi-crystalline structures in time. Next, we address many-body temporal condensed matter phenomena, including Mott insulator phases in time, many-body localization in time, many-body topological time crystals, and time crystals characterized by long-range exotic interactions. Additionally, we cover the construction of two- and three-dimensional time lattices, achieved by bouncing a BEC between two or three orthogonal oscillating mirrors or between two mirrors oriented at 45 degrees. The latter setup supports a versatile M\"obius strip geometry capable of hosting various two-dimensional time lattices, such as honeycomb and Lieb square time lattices. Finally, we discuss the creation of a six-dimensional time-space lattice based on periodically driven BECs confined in a three-dimensional optical lattice.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are commonly employed to anonymize human figures, yet existing state-of-the-art methods restrict this capability to facial anonymization only. This paper introduces DeepPrivacy2, a novel framework designed for realistic anonymization of both human figures and faces. We present a new, extensive, and diverse dataset for synthesizing human figures, which substantially enhances the quality and variety of generated images. Additionally, we develop a style-based GAN capable of producing high-quality, diverse, and editable anonymizations. Our results demonstrate that the proposed full-body anonymization framework offers superior privacy protections compared to previously established methods.
This paper investigates generalized $\phi$-recurrent generalized $(k,\mu)$-contact metric manifolds and demonstrates the existence of this concept through a specific example.

By incorporating the phase into the state, an autonomized system is constructed for periodic linear control systems subject to bounded control constraints. Within this framework, a unique control set—defined as a maximal set of approximate controllability with a nonempty interior—is established, characterized by the spectral subspaces of the associated periodic linear homogeneous differential equation. Employing the Poincaré sphere facilitates a compactification of the state space, thereby enabling the analysis of the original system's behavior at infinity. Additionally, applying these concepts to quasi-affine systems results in the existence of a unique control set possessing a nonempty interior.

In gauge-Higgs unification (GHU), the dynamical breaking of gauge symmetry arises from an Aharonov-Bohm (AB) phase, $\theta_H$, associated with the fifth dimension. We investigate $SU(2)$ GHU models containing an $SU(2)$ doublet fermion, examining both flat $M^4 \times (S^1/Z_2)$ spacetime and the Randall-Sundrum (RS) warped geometry. Under orbifold boundary conditions, the $U(1)$ component of the gauge symmetry stays unbroken at $\theta_H = 0$ and $\pi$. At $\theta_H = 0$, the fermion multiplet exhibits chiral zero modes that acquire mass at $\theta_H = \pi$. Consequently, the AB phase $\theta_H$ transforms chiral fermions into vectorlike ones. The chiral anomaly, which exists at $\theta_H = 0$, changes continuously with $\theta_H$ and disappears at $\theta_H = \pi$. We illustrate this remarkable behavior within the RS framework, where the mass spectrum avoids level crossing, allowing all quantities to vary smoothly. Conversely, the flat spacetime limit becomes singular as the AdS curvature of the RS space vanishes, ultimately recovering the flat spacetime results. Anomalies also emerge for various combinations of Kaluza-Klein excitation modes of gauge fields. While the magnitude of these anomalies relies on $\theta_H$ and the RS warp factor, it remains independent of the fermion bulk mass parameter—which dictates the field's mass and wave function—at general values of $\theta_H$.

For a fixed positive $x$, the modified Bessel function of the second kind $K_{i
u}(x)$ with imaginary order features a countably infinite set of real zeros. Recent findings indicate that the $n$th zero approximates $
u_n\sim \pi n/\log\,n$ as $n$ grows large. This note provides a more refined asymptotic estimate for these zeros by leveraging the established expansion of $K_{i
u}(x)$ for large $
u$, and numerical examples are included to demonstrate the precision of the derived formula.

This paper introduces a comprehensive theoretical approach to analyzing risk bounds when adversaries are present. Specifically, we aim to frame adversarial learning within the minimax framework. First, we demonstrate that the original adversarial learning challenge can be transformed into a minimax statistical learning problem by establishing a transport map between distributions. Subsequently, we derive a novel risk bound for this minimax formulation based on covering numbers, assuming a relaxed Lipschitz condition. This methodology is applicable to multi-class classification tasks and standard loss functions, including hinge and ramp losses. As illustrative applications, we calculate adversarial risk bounds for Support Vector Machines (SVMs), deep neural networks, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Our derived bounds incorporate two data-dependent terms that can be optimized to enhance adversarial robustness.

Bertotti-Robinson spacetimes, which are topologically equivalent to $AdS_2 \times S^2$ and defined by a conformally flat metric, form a class of static, geodetically complete Einstein-Maxwell solutions when combined with a Coulomb electric potential. This study demonstrates that incorporating Wu-Yang magnetic pole potentials into the Bertotti-Robinson metric yields a set of static solutions to non-minimally coupled Einstein-Yang-Mills equations. These solutions are significant for exploring vacuum polarization effects within a first-order perturbative framework for quantum fields.

This paper investigates Higgs boson production through vector boson fusion and in association with a vector boson, specifically examining their decays into two vector bosons, with a particular emphasis on managing virtual loops and virtual photons. Utilizing the JHU generator framework, our analysis compares results against several other frameworks and expresses findings within an effective field theory context. Key innovations in this study include a proposed method for resolving singularities related to Higgs decays into light fermions via photons, the calculation of partial Higgs widths under anomalous photon couplings, a comparison of next-to-leading-order electroweak corrections against effective coupling effects, and phenomenological insights into the unique role of intermediate photons in LHC data analysis using effective field theory. These aspects are demonstrated through projections for future experimental measurements using full datasets from both the LHC and HL-LHC.

A theoretical study examined a five-layer nanorod-mediated surface plasmon sensor featuring an inhomogeneous liquid crystal (LC) layer. Reflectance curves as a function of incident angle were computed for various analyte refractive indices across different applied voltages. By adjusting the LC director orientation, researchers can shift the positions of reflective dips to select the one offering maximum sensitivity to the analyte's refractive index. Once an optimal incident angle is established, the analyte's refractive index can be determined from the corresponding reflectance value. The reorientation effect of the director is most pronounced when the prism's refractive index lies between the ordinary and extraordinary indices of the LC; under these conditions, increasing the voltage and decreasing the prism's refractive index produce analogous impacts on the reflectance characteristics.

NEUT is a simulation tool designed for neutrino-nucleus interactions, capable of modeling events where neutrinos possess energies ranging from 100 MeV up to several TeV. Beyond neutrino processes, it also simulates hadron interactions within nuclei, serving to model nucleon decay and hadron-nucleus collisions for particle propagation in detector studies. This article outlines the various interaction types modeled by NEUT and details their implementation methods.

Bloom and cuckoo filters offer rapid approximate set membership with minimal memory usage, making them valuable for engineers seeking to reduce costly disk and network operations. Although recently introduced xor filters are smaller and faster than these traditional methods, they still require 44% more storage than the theoretical lower bound compared to the 23% required by Bloom filters. Drawing inspiration from Dietzfelbinger and Walzer, we developed binary fuse filters—probabilistic structures that achieve storage efficiency within 13% of the theoretical limit without compromising query speed. Furthermore, constructing binary fuse filters takes more than twice as long as building xor filters. By accepting a slight reduction in query speed, we can further optimize storage to just 8% above the lower bound. When evaluated against a broad spectrum of competitors, including blocked Bloom filters, vector quotient filters, cuckoo filters, and ribbon filters, our experimental results indicate that binary fuse filters outperform xor filters.

Electronic flat bands serve as a fundamental system for studying strongly correlated matter, driven by their divergent density of states. Typically, introducing electron-electron interactions in these systems triggers magnetic instabilities under repulsive conditions and superconductivity under attractive ones. However, Kondo-type interactions within flat band systems have seen limited investigation. This study examines the formation of interacting states arising from a Kondo lattice coupled to a flat band. By integrating dynamical mean-field theory with tensor network methods to solve flat band Kondo lattice models in one and two dimensions, we demonstrate the emergence of a robust underscreened regime that results in magnetic ordering within the flat band. These findings establish flat band Kondo lattice models as a valuable framework for investigating the authentic interaction between flat band physics and many-body Kondo screening.

We propose a new framework for the Multi-Goal Path Finding (MGPF) problem by integrating concepts from uni-directional and bi-directional heuristic search with approximation algorithms for the Traveling Salesman Problem. This approach ensures a 2-approximation guarantee for finding a minimum-cost path from a start point to an end point that visits every node in a specified goal set at least once. Numerical results demonstrate that our method outperforms conventional alternatives by reducing both the number of expanded nodes and execution time.

This study introduces a generalization of the bondage number known as the \textit{$k\,$-synchronous bondage number}, defined as the minimum number of edges whose removal raises a graph's dominating number by $k$. We begin by examining the 2-synchronous case before extending the concept to arbitrary $k$. Our work derives specific values for various graph families and establishes bounds applicable to general graphs. Furthermore, we suggest that this parameter serves as a useful metric for assessing graph connectivity, with potential applications in network design and optimization.

This paper presents a framework for multivariate spatio-temporal functional data, specifically introducing a mixture model designed for spatio-temporal prediction (cokriging) where both the response variable and covariates are functional. Addressing the methodological and computational hurdles associated with expansive datasets, we develop a novel Monte Carlo Expectation Maximization algorithm utilizing importance sampling for parameter estimation. Our approach is validated through simulation studies and benchmarked against existing functional clustering techniques. To overcome computational barriers, we outline several advancements that facilitate the analysis of large-scale spatio-temporal data. The proposed method is applied to Argo oceanographic data from the Southern Ocean to forecast oxygen concentration—a metric vital for ocean biodiversity and indicative of the carbon cycle. Our model and implementation deliver comprehensive oxygen predictions with associated uncertainty estimates while successfully recovering known oceanographic fronts.

Contemporary biomedical data mining demands feature selection techniques capable of handling massive feature spaces (such as `omics` datasets), operating effectively in noisy environments, identifying intricate association patterns (like gene-gene interactions), adapting flexibly to diverse domains and data types (including genetic variants, expression levels, and clinical records), and maintaining computational efficiency. In response, this study investigates a collection of filter-based algorithms inspired by the `Relief` method, known as Relief-Based Algorithms (RBAs). We have implemented and extended these RBAs within an open-source platform named ReBATE (Relief-Based Algorithm Training Environment). Through a thorough genetic simulation study, we compared various existing RBAs, a newly proposed method called MultiSURF, and other standard feature selection approaches across multiple problem scenarios. The findings indicate that: (1) RBAs are highly flexible, efficient, and potent methods capable of distinguishing features with univariate, multivariate, epistatic, or heterogeneous relationships; (2) proposed enhancements effectively improve performance for both classification and regression tasks, as well as for handling discrete versus continuous features, missing data, multiple classes, and class imbalance; (3) certain specific limitations of particular RBAs were identified; and (4) while MultiSURF excels at explicitly detecting pure 2-way interactions, it delivers the most consistent and reliable feature selection performance across a broad spectrum of problem types.

We develop a model in which two superpowers engage in a Stackelberg game to select locations for club goods that generate production externalities. Production costs are determined by the number of small countries willing to join the club. By merging non-cooperative and cooperative game theories into a unified framework where two groups of heterogeneous players have interrelated objectives, we analyze how these superpowers compete to establish their clubs. Furthermore, we simulate the game using data from 2006 to 2019 for the US and China, alongside projections spanning from 2030 to 2100.

This study demonstrates that the pressures exerted on the healthcare system by the COVID-19 pandemic have generated significant negative ripple effects on the accessibility and quality of non-COVID care. Our observations reveal persistently deteriorating performance and extended waiting times in A&E, severely restricted access to specialist services, notably delayed or unavailable diagnostic procedures, and a sharply compromised access to and quality of cancer treatment. We find that healthcare providers facing COVID-related pressures experienced significantly higher excess mortality among non-COVID hospital episodes, such as heart attack treatments. Our estimates indicate at least one non-COVID-related excess death for every 30 COVID-19 deaths attributable to care disruptions. In total, this resulted in 4,003 non-COVID excess deaths between March 2020 and February 2021. Furthermore, at least 32,189 cancer patients who should have begun treatment are missing, suggesting that delayed access to care will likely lead to continued increases in excess deaths in the future.

The Wavelength-shifting Optical Module (WOM) represents a new photosensor concept designed for equipping large detector volumes with single-photon sensitivity. Its primary goal is to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio by separating the sensor's photosensitive region from the cathode area of its photomultiplier tube (PMT). The WOM is constructed as a transparent tube with PMTs attached to both ends; the tube is coated with wavelength-shifting paint that absorbs ultraviolet photons with nearly 100% efficiency. Depending on the environment, such as air or ice, up to 73% (41%) of the subsequently emitted optical photons can be captured via total internal reflection and guided toward the PMTs for recording. The paint's optical properties, the tube's geometry, and the coupling to the PMTs have been optimized for maximum sensitivity through both theoretical analysis and experimental testing. Prototypes were developed to validate the technique and establish a reproducible manufacturing process. Key measurable characteristics of the WOM include its wavelength-dependent effective area, the transit time spread of detected photons, and the signal-to-noise ratio. The WOM significantly outperforms bare PMTs, particularly regarding the signal-to-noise ratio, achieving an improvement factor of up to 8.9 in air (5.2 in ice). Since the sensitivity gain is primarily in the UV regime, the WOM is an ideal sensor for Cherenkov and scintillation detectors.

Experimental investigations into the electron transport characteristics of molecular junctions frequently utilize solvents, where solvent-molecule coupling and inherent solvent properties serve as external stimuli to regulate electric current. This study introduces a model incorporating the dynamical aspects of solvent-molecule interactions within non-equilibrium Green's function calculations for current flow. In this framework, the solvent is modeled as a macroscopic dipole moment undergoing stochastic reorientation and interacting with tunneling electrons. The Keldysh-Kadanoff-Baym equations governing electronic Green's functions are solved in the time domain, followed by averaging over random rotational variables using the Furutsu-Novikov method to achieve an exact closure of the infinite hierarchy of stochastic correlation functions. This theoretical approach necessitates a wide-band approximation and a classical treatment of solvent degrees of freedom. Applied to a model molecular junction, the theory demonstrates that both the electrostatic interaction between the junction and solvent and solvent viscosity can modulate the junction's electrical properties. Specifically, the alignment of the rotating dipole moment disrupts the particle-hole symmetry of the transmission spectrum, thereby favoring either hole or electron transport channels contingent upon the aligning potential.

We examine the transverse field Ising model augmented with global all-to-all spin interactions. We demonstrate that a mean-field approach becomes exact in the thermodynamic limit, even with the inclusion of 1D short-range couplings. This result is derived by identifying eigenstates as coherent states with amplitudes varying across the Hilbert space. Subsequently, we analyze the model's thermodynamics to distinguish its various phases. Notably, this 1D system exhibits a second-order phase transition at finite temperature and displays inverse melting.

This work presents exact analytical solutions to the symmetron field theory equations for configurations involving one or two mirrors, covering both spontaneously broken phases in vacuum and matter. These findings complement a prior study [1] that addressed the symmetron in a broken vacuum phase but a symmetric matter phase. In this analysis, the one-dimensional equations of motion are solved exactly for both setups, with results expressed using Jacobi elliptic functions. For the two parallel mirror system, the equations of motion yield a discrete spectrum of solutions characterized by an increasing number of nodes and energies. The derived solutions are applicable to qBOUNCE experiments and neutron interferometry, facilitate the calculation of the symmetron-induced "Casimir force" in the Cannex experiment, and enable exploration of previously inaccessible regions within the symmetron parameter space.

The potential return on investment is heavily influenced by stock market efficiency. An efficient market removes opportunities for arbitrage and unexploited profits. This research evaluates the weak-form efficiency of the Indian stock market, focusing on the two primary exchanges, BSE and NSE. Using daily closing figures for the Sensex and Nifty indices from April 2010 to March 2019, the study employs the Runs, Autocorrelation, and Autoregression tests. The findings indicate that the Indian stock market is weak-form inefficient, suggesting it is possible to achieve outperformance.

Let $M^n$ denote a connected, closed, smooth manifold with $n \geq 2$. In this article, we adapt techniques from Micheletti and Pistoia (2009) and Ghimenti and Micheletti (2011) to establish the generic nondegeneracy of solutions to the Van der Waals-Allen-Cahn-Hilliard equation subject to a volume constraint on $M$.

This thesis introduces the concept of spaces with upper-bounded curvature and explores its applications within Combinatorial Algebra. The work is divided into two sections: a theoretical component and an applied one. Specifically, we examine applications to $CAT(0)$-spaces and Gromov's Theorem regarding cubical complexes. In the concluding section, we introduce a new class of discrete groups that extend well-known right-angled Artin groups. We construct a cubical $CAT(0)$-complex upon which these groups act, thereby deriving certain algebraic properties of them.

We establish the Kakeya set conjecture for $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ for arbitrary $N$, as formulated by Hickman and Wright [HW18]. This achievement involves generalizing and merging the methods developed by Arsovski [Ars21a] for $N=p^k$ with those of the author and Dvir [DD21] for square-free $N$. Furthermore, we derive tighter lower bounds for the cardinality of $(m,\epsilon)$-Kakeya sets over $\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z}$ by adapting the techniques from [Ars21a] through the use of multiplicities, following the approach of [SS08, DKSS13]. Finally, we demonstrate that our bounds are nearly optimal by presenting a novel construction of Kakeya sets for both $\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$.

Stars influence their planetary systems via gravity, radiation, and magnetic fields. While magnetic activity wanes over time—diminishing high-energy outputs like coronal XUV emission and flares—stellar winds endure throughout the system's entire lifecycle. These persistent winds exert a cumulative force that significantly impacts both the star and any orbiting exoplanets, thereby shaping potential habitability. However, observational data on stellar winds from low-mass main sequence stars remains scarce, necessitating the use of models to investigate wind characteristics and behavior. This study presents results from a comprehensive grid of 3D, state-of-the-art stellar wind models designed for cool stars (spectral types F to M). We analyze how various stellar properties—specifically mass, radius, rotation, and magnetic field strength—dictate the features of the resulting magnetized winds, including mass and angular momentum loss, terminal velocities, and wind topology, while identifying the most critical parameter dependencies. Ultimately, these findings aim to establish scaling laws that can fill the gaps left by the current lack of observational constraints.

Evaluating speech intelligibility is crucial for treating patients with pathological speech disorders. There is a need for automatic, objective metrics to support therapists who currently rely on subjective and time-consuming evaluations. This study explores a new method to generate such a metric by measuring the divergence between disentangled latent speech representations of paired utterances from a healthy reference and a pathological speaker. Experiments conducted on an English database of Cerebral Palsy patients, utilizing every available utterance per speaker, revealed a strong and significant correlation (R = -0.9) with subjective intelligibility ratings, alongside minimal variance (+-0.01) across four different reference speaker pairs. Furthermore, we established the method's robustness (R = -0.89 with +-0.02 deviation over 1000 iterations) by testing it with a significantly reduced number of utterances per speaker. These findings represent some of the first demonstrations that disentangled speech representations can facilitate automatic assessment of pathological speech intelligibility, offering a solution that remains invariant to the choice of reference speaker pair and functions effectively even with limited data.

Sliding mode control research predominantly relies on robust methodologies, where expanding the parameter space often compromises performance. Recently, data-driven sliding mode control has gained significant attention for its ability to enhance controllers using data, yet most existing studies depend on identification techniques that restrict online application due to stringent data requirements. This paper integrates an input-mapping technique into the sliding mode control framework to counteract the effects of unknown system dynamics. The primary innovation of the proposed input-mapping sliding mode control strategy is the co-design of the sliding mode surface and controller through online learning from historical input-output data to minimize an objective function. Consequently, this approach significantly improves the system's convergence rate. Finally, simulations are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

We present the initial direct determination of the inclusive branching fraction ${\mathcal B}(B_s \rightarrow D_s X)$ by utilizing $B_s$ tagging within $e^+e^-\to\Upsilon$(5S) collisions. The tagging method involves partially reconstructing semileptonic decays of the form $B_s \rightarrow D_s X \ell \nu$, where $X$ represents unreconstructed extra hadrons or photons and $\ell$ refers to either an electron or a muon. Based on 121.4 fb$^{-1}$ of data recorded at the $\Upsilon$(5S) resonance by the Belle detector at the KEKB asymmetric-energy $e^+ e^-$ collider, we measure ${\mathcal B}(B_s \rightarrow D_s X)$ to be $(60.2 \pm 5.8 \pm 2.3)$\%, with the first uncertainty being statistical and the second systematic.

Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian ring with a non-zero identity, $\fa$ an ideal of $R$, and $X$ an $R$--module. This paper investigates, for fixed integers $s$ and $t$ and a finite $\fa$--torsion $R$--module $N$, the membership of $\Ext^{s+t}_{R}(N, X)$ and $\Ext^{s}_{R}(N, H^{t}_{\fa}(X))$ within Serre subcategories of the category of $R$--modules. We subsequently establish conditions guaranteeing an isomorphism between these two objects. Finally, we define Serre cofiniteness as an extension of cofiniteness and examine this property in relation to specific local cohomology modules.

We examine random graphs where edges may exhibit dependence, utilizing a model termed the $p$-robust random graph. In this framework, edge dependence is highly general, defined by the condition that each edge exists with a probability of at least $p$, irrespective of the states of other edges. This approach extends beyond the standard case of independent edges with probability $p$, a distinction demonstrated through various examples. Our primary finding establishes that for any monotone graph property, the likelihood of occurrence in a $p$-robust random graph is at least as great as that in an Erdős-Rényi random graph with edge probability $p$. This result is particularly valuable because it enables the extension of numerous classical results from Erdős-Rényi models to non-independent settings, serving as effective lower bounds.

This study introduces a novel, fully automated technique for extracting yarn geometrical features within woven composites, enabling direct parametrization of textile reinforcement (such as for FE meshes). Our objective extends beyond merely segmenting yarns from tomographic images; it aims to deliver a comprehensive descriptive model of the fabric. Consequently, this direct method surpasses earlier techniques that rely on voxel-wise masks as intermediate steps, followed by re-meshing processes to estimate yarn envelopes. The proposed framework utilizes two deep neural network architectures: U-Net and Mask R-CNN. Initially, U-Net is trained to synthesize CT images from corresponding finite element (FE) simulations, thereby generating vast amounts of annotated data without the need for expensive manual labeling. This synthetic data subsequently trains the Mask R-CNN to predict contour points surrounding individual yarns. Experimental findings demonstrate that our method is both accurate and robust for yarn instance segmentation on CT images, a conclusion supported by both quantitative and qualitative analyses.

Quantum complexity quantifies the minimum number of basic operations needed to approximately construct a specific state or unitary channel. Beyond quantum computing, this metric is increasingly utilized to investigate the dynamics of quantum many-body systems and the long-term characteristics of AdS black holes. Within this framework, Brown and Susskind proposed that chaotic quantum systems exhibit linear growth in complexity over time, persisting up to durations exponential in system size, before saturating at a maximum and maintaining that state until recurrences occur at doubly-exponential intervals. This study demonstrates the saturation and recurrence of complexity for both quantum states and unitaries within a chaotic time-evolution model utilizing random quantum circuits, where local random unitary transformations are applied at each step. Notably, these conclusions apply broadly to various random circuit models, regardless of the specific gate set or qubit interaction geometry. These findings enhance the comprehension of long-term behaviors in chaotic quantum systems and may provide insights into black hole interior physics. Technically, the results rely on novel quantitative links between the Haar measure and high-degree approximate designs, alongside the principle that random quantum circuits of adequate depth converge to such designs.

This study examines normalized solutions to the Schrödinger equation featuring a combination of Hartree-type and power nonlinearities, defined by the system:
\begin{equation*}
\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} -\Delta u+\lambda u=\gamma (I_{\alpha }\ast
\left\vert u\right\vert ^{p})|u|^{p-2}u+\mu |u|^{q-2}u & \quad \text{in}\quad
\mathbb{R}^{N}, \\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}|u|^{2}dx=c, & \end{array}% \right.
\end{equation*}
where $N\geq 2$ and $c>0$ represents a fixed real constant. Based on varying conditions regarding $\gamma$, $\mu$, $p$, and $q$, we establish multiple findings concerning existence, nonexistence, and multiplicity. Our primary focus lies on scenarios involving the competition between Hartree and power nonlinearities, specifically when $\gamma \mu <0$, covering both $\gamma <0,\mu >0$ and $\gamma >0,\mu <0$. Given the distinct "strengths" of these two nonlinearity types, we observe significant variations in both the outcomes and the geometric properties of the associated functionals between these two cases.

Double-sided auctions are a staple in financial markets for aligning supply with demand. While previous research has largely concentrated on single-quantity trade requests, we broaden the scope of double-sided auctions to accommodate multiple quantity requests. We introduce fully formalized matching algorithms for these auctions, complete with correctness proofs, and derive new uniqueness theorems that allow for the automatic identification of violations in exchange programs by contrasting their outputs against a verified baseline. All proofs are rigorously formalized within the Coq proof assistant without relying on any additional axioms. Furthermore, we generate verified implementations in OCaml and Haskell suitable for use by both market exchanges and regulators. Finally, we validate the practical utility of our approach by executing the verified program on real-world exchange data to automatically detect algorithmic violations.

Protoplanetary disks arise from the conservation of angular momentum during the collapse of dense cores. This study presents the first high-resolution simulations of disk formation, extending down to 1 astronomical unit (au) via the collapse of 1,000 solar mass clumps. We self-consistently model non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics featuring ambipolar diffusion and radiative transfer using the flux-limited diffusion approximation, while also accounting for stellar feedback. Utilizing the RAMSES adaptive mesh-refinement code, we examine three scenarios to assess the magnetic field's impact on disk properties. Our results indicate that simulations without magnetic fields produce a population dominated by large disks, which contradicts observational data for Class 0 disks. However, incorporating magnetic fields alters the evolution significantly through magnetic braking; in these runs, disks smaller than 50 au constitute roughly half the population, while approximately 70% of stars remain diskless, suggesting our resolution may still be too coarse to retain the smallest disks. With ambipolar diffusion included, small disks remain prevalent, yielding a flat mass distribution between 0.01 and 0.1 solar masses and disk-to-star mass ratios of ~0.01–0.1. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that the magnetic field and its temporal evolution are critical in determining the initial characteristics of disk populations.

We introduce a streamlined framework for generating the Universe's baryon ($B$) asymmetry, where the Affleck-Dine (AD) mechanism produces this asymmetry within a complex inflaton condensate through $B$-violating quadratic terms in the inflaton potential. Our analysis demonstrates that these quadratic mass terms induce an oscillating asymmetry in the complex inflaton condensate at later stages. During reheating, the transfer of this asymmetry to the Standard Model sector is naturally suppressed to the level of the observed $B$ asymmetry due to averaging effects over the $B$ oscillations. This method of baryogenesis is readily applicable across a broad spectrum of inflation models. Furthermore, we establish that AD baryogenesis driven by inflaton mass terms avoids the fine-tuning of field dynamics typically required by the conventional AD mechanism.

In the field of mode connectivity, it is generally acknowledged that similarly trained neural networks on identical data are linked by a path in parameter space where test accuracy remains stable. While such paths are often assumed to be linear—particularly in transfer learning scenarios—our research on text classifiers (trained on MNLI, QQP, and CoLA) reveals that some finetuned model pairs exhibit significant barriers causing loss increases along linear trajectories between them. For each task, we identified distinct clusters of models that are linearly connected within their own groups but disconnected from models in other groups, effectively occupying separate basins on the loss surface. Through performance evaluation on specially designed diagnostic datasets, we determined that these clusters reflect different generalization strategies: one group behaves like a bag-of-words model during domain shifts, whereas the other relies on syntactic heuristics. Our findings illustrate how the geometry of the loss surface can direct models toward distinct heuristic functions.

Keyphrase extraction is a fundamental task in document understanding within NLP. Although most existing research focuses on formal texts like books, news articles, and web blogs, informal content such as video transcripts remains underexplored. To address this gap, this study introduces a new corpus and methodology for extracting keyphrases from transcripts of videos hosted on the Behance platform. Specifically, we propose a novel data augmentation technique to enhance the model by incorporating background knowledge from other domains regarding keyphrase extraction. Extensive experiments conducted on the proposed dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the introduced approach.

Interactions between two two-level emitters, such as atoms, can be significantly improved through nonreciprocal photonic media, offering advantages across diverse fields including quantum information and biological sensing. This study presents a thorough analysis explaining how nonreciprocal photon-mediated coupling boosts the efficiency of inter-atomic excitation transport. We examine a setup with two two-level emitters within a general photonic environment and demonstrate analytically, by contrasting symmetric and asymmetric photon exchange, that violating electromagnetic reciprocity allows the cooperative decay rate to surpass the spontaneous decay rate, even in a homogeneous, translation-invariant system. Consequently, an emitter's excitation preferentially decays into the other emitter rather than leaking into reservoir photonic modes. Furthermore, we illustrate a scenario involving a chain of two-level emitters interacting primarily through reciprocal modes of a plasmonic waveguide. We show that introducing nonreciprocity in this arrangement by driving a DC current through the plasmonic material can dramatically raise the probability of photon transfer from one emitter to another, resulting in a tenfold increase in quantum energy-transport efficiency.

This paper investigates specific toric Gorenstein varieties featuring isolated singularities, which arise as quotient spaces of generic unimodular representations acted upon by a one-dimensional torus or by the product of such a torus with a finite abelian group. Drawing upon the research of \v{S}penko and Van den Bergh [Invent. Math. 210 (2017), no. 1, 3-67] and Mori and Ueyama [Adv. Math. 297 (2016), 54-92], we demonstrate that the singularity categories of these varieties contain tilting objects. Consequently, these categories are triangle equivalent to the perfect categories of certain finite-dimensional algebras.

We compared the radial specific star formation rate (sSFR) profiles of 169 star-forming galaxies in close pairs against mass-matched controls from the SDSS-IV MaNGA survey. Our analysis reveals that interacting galaxies exhibit a central sSFR enhancement of approximately 0.3 dex within one effective radius, alongside a weak suppression of about 0.1 dex in their outer regions. By stacking difference profiles across five stellar mass bins ranging from log(M/M$_\star$) = 9.0 to 11.5, we determined that this sSFR enhancement is independent of stellar mass. This conclusion holds even when control galaxies are matched to their paired counterparts by both stellar mass and redshift. Furthermore, we observed that the sSFR enhancement is stronger in pairs with similar masses and smaller projected separations, consistent with prior single-fiber spectroscopy studies. Additionally, we found that outer-region sSFR offsets depend on the companion's mass status: more massive companions show zero to positive enhancement, whereas less massive companions experience suppression. These findings highlight the intricate tidal influences on star formation in closely paired galaxies.

We propose a straightforward ansatz for investigating velocity autocorrelation functions (VAFs) across various timescales in fluids. This approach relies on effectively summing an infinite continued fraction, predicated on the assumption that the relaxation times of higher-order memory functions—which stem purely from kinetic origins—converge reasonably. We compare the VAFs derived using this method against those obtained via the Markovian approximation for memory kernels. Our findings indicate that while both methods align closely during initial and intermediate stages of system evolution within the "overdamped" regime, our formalism produces a power-law relaxation of the VAFs that is absent when describing the system with a finite number of collective modes. Furthermore, explicit formulas for the transition times between kinetic and hydrodynamic regimes are derived by analyzing singularities in the spectral functions within the complex frequency plane.

We present the Poisson bracket operator, an alternative quantum counterpart to the classical Poisson bracket. Defined via the operator derivative from quantum analysis, this operator converges to the standard Poisson bracket in the classical limit. Leveraging this framework, we derive the quantum canonical equation, which governs the time evolution of operators. While equivalent to the Heisenberg equation in standard quantum mechanics, the quantum canonical equation also applies to c-number canonical variables, thereby recovering the classical canonical equation. Consequently, the Poisson bracket operator facilitates a unified description of both classical and quantum dynamics. Furthermore, this equation extends to non-standard systems where the Heisenberg equation is undefined; for instance, we examine a system containing coexisting c-number and q-number particles. The resulting dynamics adhere to the Ehrenfest theorem and ensure the conservation of energy and momentum.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a prevalent non-invasive tool for diagnosing brain tumors. Nevertheless, manually segmenting tumors from 3D MRI volumes is labor-intensive and demands skilled radiologists, often leading to low inter-rater reliability and diagnostic inconsistencies due to human subjectivity. Given that effective treatment relies heavily on early intervention, prompt detection is critical. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a fully automated segmentation method that offers both efficiency and reliability for tumor detection and quantification. This study introduces an end-to-end approach for brain tumor segmentation based on a modified QuickNAT architecture, a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for brain tissue segmentation. Evaluated on a dataset of 233 T1-weighted images from patients with annotated meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, our proposed model, QuickTumorNet, demonstrates rapid, accurate, and reliable segmentation capabilities. These results indicate that QuickTumorNet can effectively support clinicians in diagnosis and treatment planning.

We investigate imaginary-time relaxation dynamics near quantum critical points using semi-ordered initial states. Unlike homogeneous ordered initial states, where the order parameter $M$ decays uniformly as $M\propto 	au^{- eta/
u z}$, in the semi-ordered case, $M$ varies with position $x$, exhibiting complex scaling behaviors. Analogous to classical Model A critical dynamics featuring an initial domain wall, the imaginary-time evolution causes the domain wall to expand into an interfacial region of increasing size. Within this interfacial region, the local order parameter decays as $M\propto 	au^{- eta_1/
u z}$, where $ eta_1$ represents an additional dynamic critical exponent. Far from the interfacial region, the local order parameter initially decays as $M\propto 	au^{- eta/
u z}$ during the short-time regime before crossing over to the $M\propto 	au^{- eta_1/
u z}$ scaling once the location $x$ becomes absorbed into the interfacial region. We develop a comprehensive scaling form to characterize these properties and validate the scaling theory using the quantum Ising model in one and two dimensions. Furthermore, for the quantum Ising model, we determine that the scaling function is analytical and that $ eta_1$ is not an independent exponent.

For the Research Topic on Data Assimilation and Control in Life Sciences, we begin by reviewing the statistical data assimilation (SDA) formulation and examining algorithms designed to approximate the conditional expected values of biophysical properties within functional neural circuits. Subsequently, we present applications of SDA to: (1) investigate the characteristics of individual neurons in the avian song system's HVC nucleus, and (2) model individual neurons as very large-scale integration (VLSI) analog circuits, aiming to construct functional, biophysically realistic VLSI representations of nervous systems. Given that neural networks present a significantly greater challenge, we also discuss the design of experiments to probe properties—particularly functional connectivity—within the song command circuits of HVC.

Although authorship attribution (AA) and authorship verification (AV) have been studied for decades, the field struggles to evaluate current performance due to inconsistent data splits, filtering criteria, and mismatched evaluation protocols. This paper surveys these domains to clarify ambiguities, introduces Valla—a framework designed to standardize and benchmark AA/AV datasets and metrics—and offers a large-scale empirical evaluation with direct comparisons between existing methods. We tested eight promising approaches across fifteen datasets (including distribution-shifted challenge sets) and released a new large-scale dataset derived from Project Gutenberg archives. Contrary to expectations, traditional N-gram models outperformed BERT-based models on five of seven AA tasks, achieving a mean macro-accuracy of 76.50% compared to 66.71% for BERT. However, BERT models proved superior on AA datasets with larger per-author text volumes and on AV datasets. While AV methods are readily applicable to AA tasks, they are rarely used as baselines in AA literature; we demonstrate that incorporating hard-negative mining makes AV methods competitive alternatives to traditional AA approaches. All code for Valla and the experiments is available at: https://github.com/JacobTyo/Valla

We provide a complete characterization of mean ergodic composition operators on $H^\infty(\mathbb{B}_n)$. Specifically, we demonstrate that a composition operator on this space is mean ergodic if and only if it is uniformly mean ergodic.

Introductory physics students frequently encounter difficulties with vector algebra, often linked to the contextual and representational aspects of the problems. Performance on tasks involving the direction of a cross product is notably weak, with some research attributing this largely to the incorrect application of the right-hand rule. However, detailed investigations into student usage of this rule have been limited due to a lack of resolution in previous studies. This research synthesizes literature across multiple disciplines, including spatial cognition, to pinpoint ten contextual and representational features most likely to affect performance on problems requiring a right-hand rule. The study employed four assessment methods: two quantitative measures (accuracy and response time) and two qualitative measures (strategies employed and error types) to examine how these features influence student outcomes. Quantitative findings align with existing theoretical expectations but indicate that certain factors—specifically the type of reasoning needed and the physical awkwardness of using the rule—exert a stronger influence than others, such as whether vectors are positioned together or apart. Furthermore, the qualitative analysis provided deeper insights by uncovering previously unaddressed sources of difficulty and demonstrating that supplemental techniques, like physically rotating the paper, can help reduce errors associated with specific problem features.

Reviews offer valuable insights into product attributes and user preferences, making them a common asset for enhancing recommender systems. Prior research indicates that jointly learning review generation can improve rating prediction, with the synthesized reviews serving as explanations that help users understand the predicted scores. However, despite existing models producing fluent, human-like reviews, it remains uncertain how thoroughly these outputs reveal the underlying rationale for the predicted ratings. This study evaluates state-of-the-art models and their review generation components, demonstrating that the resulting explanations are fragile and require further scrutiny before they can be trusted as literal justifications for the estimated ratings.

The origin of nematicity in FeSe remains unclear, though elastoresistivity studies suggest it arises from an electronic instability. Previous investigations were limited to small strains exhibiting linear responses; this study instead applies large elastic strains to FeSe using two distinct measurement approaches. First, nematic resistive anisotropy below the transition temperature ($T_s$) is quantified by using strain to manipulate twinning. Second, resistive anisotropy is tracked as strain induces nematicity at temperatures above $T_s$. In both scenarios, resistive anisotropy peaks at approximately 7% as nematicity strengthens before declining. Notably, below roughly 40 K, the nematic resistive anisotropy reverses sign, prompting a discussion of its theoretical implications. Additionally, we report that: (1) under experimentally accessible conditions in bulk crystals, stress—not strain—acts as the conjugate field for FeSe nematicity; (2) at low temperatures, twin boundary resistance accounts for about 10% of the total sample resistance and must be subtracted to determine intrinsic resistivity; and (3) biaxial in-plane compression simultaneously increases in-plane resistivity and the superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$), supporting the significance of the $y_z$ orbital in electronic correlations.

Reinforcement learning (RL) stands as a highly active area of research within machine learning and has recently been utilized to address numerous difficult challenges. This paper centers on off-policy evaluation (OPE), a foundational concept in RL. Over the past few years, various OPE techniques have emerged in both statistics and computer science fields. We examine the efficiency bounds of OPE, review leading current methods, analyze their statistical characteristics, and highlight other related research avenues that are currently under active investigation.

This study introduces an algorithm that leverages backpropagation gradients to identify feature importance throughout various training phases, alongside a proposed method for qualitatively representing the learning trajectory. Experimental validation using the Wisconsin cancer dataset from sklearn demonstrated a notable convergence of "learning gradients" toward the most critical features. Similarly, the Spanish text describes an algorithm utilizing learning gradients to uncover input significance in neural networks, proposing a framework to evaluate importance and depict the learning process across training stages. Results derived from the Wisconsin dataset on malignant and benign tumors revealed patterns in the model's most influential variables and their temporal evolution.

The exploration/exploitation (E&E) dilemma is central to interactive systems like online advertising, leading to the development of contextual bandit algorithms. While Bayesian methods offer principled uncertainty estimation to guide exploration, their utility is often constrained by overly simplified assumptions. Conversely, non-Bayesian bootstrap techniques can handle complex scenarios using deep reward models but lack clear directives for exploration strategies. Consequently, creating a practical solution for complex deep contextual bandits remains largely unsolved.

This paper presents Guided Bootstrap (GuideBoot), which merges the strengths of both approaches. GuideBoot directs exploration behavior by training multiple models on a combination of real data and noisy samples with fabricated labels, where the noise injection is proportional to predictive uncertainty. The method is efficient because it enables real-time decision-making using a single randomly selected model, yet it remains effective as it functions as a non-Bayesian approximation of Thompson sampling. Furthermore, we extend the approach to an online variant capable of learning exclusively from streaming data, a feature highly valued in practical applications. Extensive experiments on both synthetic tasks and large-scale advertising environments demonstrate that GuideBoot yields significant performance gains over previous state-of-the-art methods.

We investigate the forward scattering of two-dimensional massless Dirac electrons at positive Fermi energy ($\varepsilon > 0$) within single-layer graphene, passing through a one-dimensional rectangular barrier of height $u_0$ under uniform Rashba spin-orbit coupling (strength $\lambda$). This study highlights the significance of the Klein paradox in graphene spintronics. Our findings reveal that: (1) Partial Klein tunneling occurs when $u_0$ lies between $\varepsilon - 2\lambda$ and $\varepsilon + 2\lambda$; notably, for small $\lambda > \lambda_0 \approx 0.1$ meV, transmission approaches zero when the scattering energy matches the barrier height ($\varepsilon = u_0$). (2) Spin density and spin-current density exhibit distinct behaviors compared to those predicted for bulk single-layer graphene, showing strong sensitivity to both $\lambda$ and $u_0$.
