(3) The spatial dependence of spin current densities indicates the presence of non-zero spin torque density. Consequently, this system could function as a graphene-based spintronic device operating without external magnetic fields or magnetic materials.

This article investigates how altering boundary conditions in an elliptic boundary value problem affects its solution. Focusing on the conductivity equation, we examine a reference scenario featuring mixed homogeneous Dirichlet and Neumann conditions. We analyze two distinct perturbations of this baseline: (i) replacing the homogeneous Neumann condition with a homogeneous Dirichlet condition on a "small" subset $\omega_\varepsilon$ of the Neumann boundary, and (ii) replacing the homogeneous Dirichlet condition with a homogeneous Neumann condition on a "small" subset $\omega_\varepsilon$ of the Dirichlet boundary. The metric defining the "smallness" of $\omega_\varepsilon$ varies between these cases; harmonic capacity applies to the first scenario, whereas we define a "Neumann capacity" for the second. In the initial section, we establish representation formulas capturing the structure of the first non-trivial term in the asymptotic expansion of the voltage potential for a general $\omega_\varepsilon$, provided it is sufficiently small in the relevant sense. In the final section, we explicitly compute this first non-trivial term for the specific geometric case where $\omega_\varepsilon$ is a vanishing surface ball.

We demonstrate two key results: first, that for any subset $A\subseteq \{0, 1\}^n$, there exists a polytope $P\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $P \cap \{0, 1\}^n = A$ and its extension complexity is $O(2^{n/2})$; second, that there exists a specific subset $A\subseteq \{0, 1\}^n$ for which any polytope $P$ satisfying $P\cap \{0, 1\}^n = A$ requires an extension complexity of at least $2^{\frac{n}{3}(1-o(1))}$. Additionally, we note that the extension complexity of any 0/1-polytope in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is bounded above by $O(2^n/n)$ and raise the question of whether this upper bound can be tightened to $O(2^{cn})$ for some constant $c<1$.

Concurrent with the swift integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), driven by research breakthroughs, there has been a rising consciousness and apprehension regarding data privacy. Significant recent advancements in data regulation have triggered a major pivot in focus toward privacy-preserving AI, thereby boosting the prominence of Federated Learning (FL) as the primary framework for training machine learning models on isolated data sources while maintaining privacy. This survey investigates the realm of Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) to tackle the core obstacles FL faces when dealing with heterogeneous data, a trait ubiquitous in all real-world datasets. We examine the primary drivers behind PFL and introduce a distinctive taxonomy of PFL methods, organized by the central challenges and personalization strategies involved. Furthermore, we underscore their fundamental concepts, associated hurdles, and potential, while outlining promising future research directions aimed at novel PFL architectures, practical benchmarking, and trustworthy PFL methodologies.

Creating high-speed nanodevices for magnonic information processing demands the use of short spin-wave pulses; however, shorter pulses suffer greater information loss from dispersion and broadening. Engineering these pulses and managing their propagation offers a solution to this challenge. This study presents an inverse design method to generate linear spin-wave pulses with specific spatial-temporal profiles within magnonic waveguides. Theoretically, we demonstrate that narrow stripline antennas can produce both rectangular and self-compressing pulses in advanced waveguides with fidelities exceeding 96%. This approach is computationally efficient, universal—applicable to any targeted pulse shape, wave type (exchange or dipolar), material, and geometry—and extensible to more complex magnonic architectures. Consequently, these findings may facilitate the deployment of large-scale magnonic circuits for both classical and quantum information processing.

This study operates within the domain of blackbox optimization, addressing scenarios where objective functions are costly to evaluate and derivative information is inaccessible. A common strategy in this field involves constructing surrogate models for both the objective and constraints to reduce computational expenses. This research introduces novel uncertainty quantification methods tailored for ensembles of surrogates. By integrating these uncertainty measures with an ensemble framework, the approach functions as a stochastic model, thereby enabling the application of efficient Bayesian optimization techniques. Specifically, the method is embedded within the search phase of the Mesh Adaptive Direct Search (MADS) algorithm to enhance search space exploration. Empirical evaluations across seven analytical problems, two multi-disciplinary cases, and two simulation-based tasks demonstrate that the proposed technique achieves higher precision and lower computational costs compared to existing stochastic models when solving expensive simulation-driven optimization problems.

u_{	au}[\gamma] ight) / \Gamma \left(P	o \mu 
u_{\mu}[\gamma]ight)$ for $P=\pi,K$ offer an ideal framework for testing lepton universality, verifying CKM unitarity, and probing non-standard interactions in $	au$ decays. Furthermore, prior theoretical predictions for these observables date back over twenty-five years and rely on several unrealistic assumptions. Consequently, an updated calculation of $R_{	au / P}$ was necessary. We computed one-loop radiative corrections using an expansion of Chiral Perturbation Theory that incorporates the lightest spin-one resonances while adhering to short-distance constraints imposed by QCD. Our results yield $\delta R_{	au/\pi}=(0.18\pm 0.57 )\%$ and $\delta R_{	au/K}=(0.97\pm 0.58 )\%$, with uncertainties primarily stemming from the estimation of counterterms. Using these values, we examined lepton universality and CKM unitarity and searched for evidence of new physics in $	au$ decays. Additionally, as a secondary outcome, we derived the theoretical radiative corrections for the $	au 	o P 
u_{	au}[\gamma]$ decay rates, finding $\delta_{	au \pi} = -(0.24 \pm 0.56) \%$ and $\delta_{	au K} = -(0.15 \pm 0.57) \%$.

Addressing severely imbalanced binary classification tasks often involves training models on bootstrapped data where class frequencies are adjusted to a more equitable ratio, such as one-to-one. We examine algorithmic inequity by framing it as an imbalanced classification issue: to ensure a classifier performs consistently across different groups, we can bootstrap training sets to balance both labels and group identities. Using the prediction of suicide death from administrative patient records as a case of extreme class imbalance, we demonstrate how an equity-focused bootstrap approach can significantly align test set sensitivities and specificities with the equal odds criterion. Furthermore, within the frameworks of naive Bayes and logistic regression, we analyze this method, showing that it functions by driving odds ratios toward unity and connecting it to techniques involving intercept adjustment, thresholding, and weighting.

This note outlines the algorithm developed by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris for producing all fully transitive polyhedra in $\mathbb{E}^d$. Additionally, we utilize this method to construct a novel polyhedron within the Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^3$.

By applying Quantum Field Theory techniques, we calculate the bulk polarization tensor and dielectric functions for Dirac materials under conditions of a mass gap, chemical potential, and finite temperature. Leveraging these findings while disregarding boundary effects, we investigate the Casimir interaction within these materials. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the distinctive properties of the dielectric functions and examine how they impact the Casimir pressure.

This paper tackles the challenges of achieving scalable, interoperable, and prompt information dissemination within resource-constrained IoT environments. Scalability is achieved through a publish-subscribe architecture, while interoperability and timeliness are addressed by proposing an HTTP/3 (H3) solution that leverages significant advancements over HTTP/2. We evaluated this approach by benchmarking it against MQTT-over-QUIC, a state-of-the-art alternative. Given that both QUIC and H3 have been standardized simultaneously, we hypothesized that H3 would utilize the QUIC transport more effectively than an MQTT mapping. Our analysis examined performance, network overhead, and device overhead for both protocols. Our H3-based solution met the timeliness requirement by reducing publish message arrival time at the broker by one RoundTrip Time (RTT), a substantial improvement in IoT networks characterized by high RTTs. Conversely, we observed that MQTT-over-QUIC imposed slightly less strain on the network.

This study presents initial findings on a fully-digital direct-conversion array receiver operating at 28 GHz, which leverages commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) electronics for its receiver chain. The architecture features a custom 28 GHz patch antenna sub-array that provides elevation gain, while azimuthal beamforming is achieved through real-time digital signal processing (DSP) algorithms executed on a Xilinx RF System on Chip (RF SoC). Utilizing element-wise fully-digital processing, the receiver supports analog-to-digital converter (ADC) sample rates of up to 2 GS/s and an operating bandwidth of 1 GHz per antenna. All RF mixed-signal data conversion and DSP operations are handled by a single-chip RF SoC integrated onto the Xilinx ZCU1275 prototyping platform.

We introduce a modified Kerr-Schild approach that leverages the mapping between Ricci-based Gravity (RBG) and General Relativity (GR). The process involves constructing known GR solutions from a canonical metric and subsequently deriving their corresponding configurations within the $f(R)$ gravity framework. This novel technique enables the perturbation of a GR metric using a null geodetic vector; however, rather than yielding a new solution governed by Einstein's sector, it facilitates the realization of this solution within the context of RBG.

Multi-task learning (MTL) involves training a single model to perform predictions across multiple tasks concurrently. While joint training offers benefits such as reduced computational costs and enhanced data efficiency, conflicting gradients from different tasks often result in performance that lags behind individual single-task models. To address this, common strategies combine per-task gradients into a unified update direction using heuristics. This paper reframes the gradient combination process as a bargaining game where tasks negotiate to determine an optimal joint parameter update direction. Assuming certain conditions, we propose utilizing the Nash Bargaining Solution—a unique resolution to this bargaining problem—as a rigorous framework for MTL. We introduce Nash-MTL, a novel optimization method grounded in this approach, and establish theoretical convergence guarantees. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Nash-MTL attains state-of-the-art performance across various domains on multiple MTL benchmarks.

Neural networks (NNs) utilizing linear layers and trained via gradient descent can be reinterpreted as key-value memory systems that retain all training data and initial weights, generating outputs through unnormalized dot attention across the complete training history. Although this mathematical equivalence has been recognized since the 1960s, it has not been effectively analyzed, likely due to prohibitive computational costs and impractical model sizes that scale linearly with the number of training examples. Despite these challenges, this dual perspective enables the direct visualization of how NNs leverage training patterns during inference by inspecting attention weights. We present experiments on small-scale supervised image classification tasks across single-task, multi-task, and continual learning scenarios, as well as on language modeling, to explore the benefits and constraints of this viewpoint for interpreting neural network behavior. Our code is publicly available.

The Kochen-Specker (KS) theorem demonstrates the incompatibility between quantum mechanics and any underlying model adhering to KS-noncontextuality. A logical proof of this theorem relies exclusively on the compatibility relations within a specific set of projectors (a KS set) to expose this contradiction. These relations are visualized as a hypergraph known as a contextuality scenario. This paper focuses on scenarios termed "KS-uncolourable," such as those utilized in logical KS proofs. We propose a hypergraph-based method to derive noise-resilient contextuality witnesses from these scenarios. Our methodology extends the findings of Kunjwal and Spekkens (Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 110403, 2015) by offering novel perspectives on how the structure of a contextuality scenario correlates with the noise-robust noncontextuality inequalities that detect it. Furthermore, this work serves as a complementary counterpart to the framework established by Kunjwal (Quantum 3, 184, 2019), which is limited to KS-colourable scenarios—those that allow statistical rather than logical KS proofs. Our approach utilizes a single hypergraph invariant, the weighted max-predictability defined in Kunjwal (2019), which features prominently in our contextuality witnesses. Consequently, this study can also be interpreted as an investigation into this invariant. Notably, unlike the approach in Kunjwal (2019), none of the graph invariants from the Cabello, Severini, and Winter (CSW) framework (Phys. Rev. Lett. 112, 040401, 2014) are applicable to our noise-robust noncontextuality inequalities.

We present SeCaV, a sequent calculus verifier for first-order logic implemented in Isabelle/HOL, alongside the SeCaV Unshortener, an online utility that converts concise derivations into full SeCaV syntax. By utilizing Isabelle/HOL as a proof checker, we ensure the verification of SeCaV derivations. The interactive capabilities of Isabelle/HOL enhance system transparency; for example, users can click on any side condition to view its precise definition. Our formalized proofs of soundness and completeness apply directly to the calculus presented to the user, rather than merely to an internal model of the tool. Additionally, users can compose derivations in the SeCaV Unshortener using a streamlined syntax before expanding them for verification. Both tools have been effectively utilized in our educational settings.

A phylogenetic variety represents an algebraic structure defined by statistical models describing the evolution of biological sequences along a tree. Analyzing these varieties is a key challenge in algebraic statistics, particularly for reconstructing phylogenies. While significant theoretical progress has been made in computing invariants for algebraic varieties in this field—extending beyond standard measures like dimension and degree to include algebraic degrees such as the maximum likelihood degree and Euclidean distance degree—explicit calculations for phylogenetic varieties remain absent from the current literature. This study addresses that deficiency by determining these invariants for phylogenetic varieties derived from the most basic group-based nucleotide substitution models: the Cavender-Farris-Neyman, Jukes-Cantor, Kimura 2-parameter, and Kimura 3-parameter models, specifically for small trees containing up to five leaves.

This paper investigates the characteristics of certain sums derived from the sequence $\{Z[t_\nu(\tau)]\}$. Our findings demonstrate the critical role of the Lindelöf hypothesis in validating the associated formulae. Specifically, sections 1 through 6 present the English translation of our previous work \cite{6}, whereas section 7 introduces new results, offering a fresh set of transformations of the primary multiform discussed in our earlier publication \cite{7}.

Generating high-fidelity videos from real-world multi-view inputs remains difficult due to environmental complexity and highly dynamic movements. Although prior neural radiance field approaches have achieved high-quality reconstructions of dynamic scenes, training them on real-world data is often prohibitively slow, requiring days or weeks. This paper introduces MixVoxels, a novel method designed to represent dynamic scenes efficiently with rapid training and competitive rendering performance. MixVoxels models 4D dynamic scenes as a combination of static and dynamic voxels, processed by distinct networks. By utilizing a lightweight model for the computation-intensive static voxel modalities, the method significantly reduces computational load, particularly for scenes where the background remains largely static. To distinguish between these voxel types, we introduce a new variation field that estimates the temporal variance of each voxel. Furthermore, for dynamic voxels, we employ an inner-product time query mechanism to efficiently access multiple time steps, which is crucial for capturing high-dynamic motion. Consequently, MixVoxels achieves superior PSNR compared to previous methods, training dynamic scenes with 300-frame inputs in just 15 minutes. The code and trained models are accessible at https://github.com/fengres/mixvoxels.

This paper investigates subgeometric ergodicity in univariate nonlinear autoregressions featuring autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH). First introduced in the Markov chain literature during the 1980s, subgeometric ergodicity describes a scenario where transition probabilities converge to a stationary measure at a rate slower than geometric, a speed closely tied to the convergence of $\beta$-mixing coefficients. Although prior research on subgeometrically ergodic autoregressions typically assumes homoskedastic errors, this study extends the framework to accommodate conditionally heteroskedastic ARCH-type errors, thereby significantly broadening its applicability. We examine suitably defined higher-order nonlinear autoregressions with potentially nonlinear ARCH errors and demonstrate that, under specific conditions, they exhibit subgeometric ergodicity at a polynomial rate. Furthermore, an empirical application utilizing energy sector volatility index data highlights the utility of subgeometrically ergodic AR-ARCH models.

Currently, the off-shell production of Higgs bosons in pp → ZZ collisions at the LHC offers the most direct method to measure the Higgs width without contributions from beyond the Standard Model. This analysis examines how anomalous Z couplings to fermions influence the determination of the Higgs width. We demonstrate that, although these couplings are tightly restricted by existing electroweak precision data, they can significantly impact Higgs width measurements during LHC Runs 2 and 3. However, in future runs with higher integrated luminosities, such as those planned for the High-Luminosity LHC and the High-Energy LHC, the influence of these anomalous interactions on the Higgs width measurement becomes negligible.

While sentiment analysis benefits from diverse corpora across many languages, emotion analysis remains constrained, thereby limiting cross-lingual research and the creation of predictive models for non-English languages. This study addresses that specific gap for German by developing deISEAR, a corpus modeled after the established English ISEAR emotion dataset. Drawing on Scherer's appraisal theory, we conducted a two-phase crowdsourcing experiment: first, participants generated descriptions of emotional events associated with specific emotions, and second, five annotators evaluated the emotion conveyed in those texts. Our findings demonstrate that transferring an emotion classification model from the original English ISEAR to the German deISEAR corpus via machine translation does not, on average, result in a decline in performance.

This study investigates the collision and coalescence dynamics of drops in the Leidenfrost state using liquids with varying physicochemical properties. While identical liquid drops deposited on a hot concave surface merge immediately upon contact, collisions between different liquids result in multiple bounces before eventual coalescence. This occurs when the drop with the higher evaporation rate reaches a critical size, roughly equivalent to the capillary length. The bouncing behavior arises because the drops are not only in the Leidenfrost state relative to the substrate but also experience a Leidenfrost effect between themselves during impact. This inter-drop effect is driven by their differing boiling points, causing the hotter drop to act as a hot surface for the cooler one and creating three simultaneous Leidenfrost contact zones. We have termed this phenomenon the triple Leidenfrost effect.

Coherent noise frequently disrupts seismic recordings, introducing artifacts and uncertainties into downstream processing and imaging results. The exceptional denoising performance of deep learning in natural and medical imaging has recently inspired numerous neural network applications for seismic data. However, most existing approaches rely on supervised learning, necessitating clean, noise-free target data for training. To address this, blind-spot networks were recently introduced, enabling direct training on noisy field data as an effective random noise suppressor. By carefully adapting this methodology, we extend it to handle coherent noise suppression. This work presents a blind-trace network that successfully eliminates trace-wise coherent noise. Extensive synthetic analyses demonstrate the method's robustness across varying noise levels and proportions of noisy traces within shot gathers, showing the network can accurately suppress noise even when up to 60% of the original traces are corrupted. Additionally, the approach was applied to the Stratton 3D field dataset, where it successfully restored previously distorted direct arrivals. This self-supervised adaptation for trace-wise noise removal holds potential for other applications, such as mitigating coherent noise caused by wellsite operations, passing vessels, or nearby industrial activities.

De Graaf et al. (2019) project that groundwater extraction could render 42–79% of global watersheds environmentally exhausted by 2050. We question the validity of these estimates, citing their reliance on non-unique assumptions regarding irrigation water requirements and a superficial examination of model uncertainty. Furthermore, their sensitivity analysis demonstrates a broad absence of fundamental design of experiments principles among the modelers, thereby failing to substantiate the robustness of their conclusions.

Do current state-of-the-art language models possess, or can they readily acquire, competencies like boolean coordination, quantification, conditionals, comparatives, and monotonicity reasoning? Although these phenomena are integral to natural language inference (NLI) and exceed basic linguistic comprehension, their presence in existing NLI benchmarks and their learnability by models remain uncertain. To address this, we introduce semantic fragments—systematically generated datasets targeting specific semantic phenomena—to probe and efficiently enhance such capabilities in linguistic models. This methodology offers precise control over the semantic diversity and complexity of the targeted phenomena, enabling a more accurate assessment of a model's linguistic behavior. Experiments utilizing a library of eight semantic fragments yield two striking insights: (a) Leading models, including BERT pre-trained on standard NLI benchmarks, perform poorly on these fragments despite the probed phenomena being central to NLI tasks. (b) Conversely, a BERT-based model can master all logic and monotonicity fragments with just minutes of additional fine-tuning using a carefully tuned learning rate and a novel "inoculation" variation, all while maintaining performance on established NLI benchmarks.

Message-passing Graph Neural Networks (MP-GNNs) typically construct node representations by exchanging information only among immediate 1-hop neighbors, which inherently restricts their ability to model long-range interactions (LRIs) essential for certain graph tasks. While Transformer-based approaches have recently gained traction for their capacity to leverage full node connectivity and capture LRIs beyond sparse structures, MP-GNNs often outperform them on standard benchmarks when enhanced with positional encodings and other innovations, thereby diminishing the apparent advantage of Transformer-like architectures. To address this, we introduce the Long Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB), comprising five datasets—PascalVOC-SP, COCO-SP, PCQM-Contact, Peptides-func, and Peptides-struct—that necessitate LRI reasoning for high performance. Our evaluation of both baseline GNNs and Graph Transformers confirms that models capable of capturing long-range dependencies achieve significantly superior results on these tasks. Consequently, the LRGB serves as an appropriate platform for assessing and exploring both MP-GNNs and Graph Transformer designs aimed at modeling long-range dependencies.

The emergence of a novel coronavirus, subsequently identified as COVID-19, has ushered in a new global reality shaped by numerous direct and indirect factors. These influences range from human-controllable elements, such as intervention policies, mobility restrictions, and vaccination efforts, to uncontrollable variables like weather conditions. This study investigates how adjustments to these controllable factors impact two key metrics: daily case counts and economic consequences. By utilizing current data and precise measurement, policymakers can design targeted interventions and accurately assess their costs. The primary objective is to establish a predictive analytics framework capable of modeling, forecasting, and simulating the spread of the virus alongside the socio-economic repercussions of mitigation strategies, including policies and vaccines. This tool empowers government officials, business leaders, and policymakers to make more informed decisions through forward-looking scenario planning regarding the potential outcomes of various interventions. The research leverages a newly available open-source COVID-19 big data platform, drawing on published studies to identify relevant variables. Rigorous data quality checks and analytical methods were employed for feature selection and prediction. Furthermore, an advanced machine learning pipeline featuring a self-evolving model has been developed and deployed on a modern architecture. This system demonstrates high accuracy in trend forecasting, validated through back-testing with r-squared metrics, and includes interpretability features to provide deeper insights.

Traditional object detection systems typically rely on a backbone derived from image recognition to extract deep features, which are then fused by a neck module to capture multi-scale information. However, because object detection operates at higher resolutions than image recognition, the backbone's computational burden often dominates the total inference cost. This "heavy-backbone" approach stems largely from historical adaptations of recognition models rather than being optimized end-to-end for detection. Our research demonstrates that this paradigm results in sub-optimal detection performance. To address this, we introduce GiraffeDet, a novel "heavy-neck" architecture designed for efficient object detection. GiraffeDet employs an extremely lightweight backbone paired with a deep, expansive neck module that facilitates dense information exchange across various spatial scales and semantic levels simultaneously. This design ensures that both high-level semantics and low-level spatial details are processed with equal priority from the network's early stages, enhancing detection effectiveness. Extensive evaluations on multiple benchmarks confirm that GiraffeDet consistently surpasses previous state-of-the-art models across diverse resource constraints. The source code can be found at https://github.com/jyqi/GiraffeDet.

Applications analyzing damping effects necessitate solving quadratic eigenvalue problems (QEPs), a task addressed here using refined isogeometric analysis (rIGA). Although rIGA maintains the high continuity benefits of standard isogeometric analysis (IGA), it incorporates lower-continuity basis functions to reduce the coupling between degrees of freedom. This reduction in algebraic connectivity accelerates LU factorizations within multifrontal direct solvers. We evaluate the computational efficiency of rIGA against IGA for 2D vector-valued multifield QEPs using Krylov eigensolvers. In large-scale scenarios, the dominant cost is the LU factorization, followed by matrix and vector operations required for Krylov projections. To minimize expenses, we introduce C⁰ and C¹ separators at element interfaces for rIGA extensions of Nedelec and Raviart-Thomas finite elements. With a polynomial degree of $p$, rIGA achieves an asymptotic LU factorization speedup of up to $O((p-1)^2)$ over IGA, theoretically reducing total eigencomputation costs by the same factor for sufficiently large problems. However, for moderate-sized eigenproblems, this improvement rate diminishes as the number of computed eigenvalues grows due to the cumulative cost of multiple matrix and vector operations. Numerical experiments indicate that for moderately sized problems where a reasonable number of eigenvalues are sought, rIGA accelerates QEP solutions by a factor of $O(p-1)$.

We utilized the Immersion GRating Infrared Spectrometer (IGRINS) to derive fundamental parameters for 61 young stellar objects (YSOs) of K- and M-type within the Ophiuchus and Upper Scorpius star-forming regions. By fitting specific K-band spectral regions with synthetic spectra and a Markov chain Monte Carlo method, we measured photospheric temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$), surface gravity ($\log$ g), magnetic field strength (B), projected rotational velocity ($v \sin i$), and K-band veiling ($r_{\rm K}$). Magnetic fields were successfully determined for approximately 46% of the sample. These results were compared to findings from the Taurus-Auriga and TW Hydrae Association (TWA) presented in Paper I of this series. All YSOs in the IGRINS survey were classified using infrared spectral indices from 2MASS and WISE photometry spanning 2 to 24~$\mu$m. Our analysis reveals that Class II YSOs generally exhibit lower $\log$ g and $v\sin i$, comparable magnetic field strengths, and higher K-band veiling relative to Class III YSOs. Furthermore, we derived stellar parameters for a sample of K and M field stars also observed by IGRINS, identifying intrinsic similarities and differences across various evolutionary stages through our homogeneous parameter determination. Using $\log$ g as an age indicator, we concluded that the Ophiuchus and Taurus samples share similar ages, whereas Upper Scorpius and TWA YSOs are of comparable age to each other but more evolved than those in Ophiuchus and Taurus.

We experimentally present a multi-mode interferometer utilizing a Bose-Einstein condensate of $^{39}$K atoms confined within a harmonic trap, where interatomic interactions are nullified via Feshbach resonances. By employing Kapitza-Dirac diffraction from an optical lattice, the BEC is coherently divided into multiple momentum components separated equally, establishing distinct interferometric paths that are closed by the harmonic confinement. We examine two distinct interferometric configurations, applying the recombination pulse following either a full or half oscillation within the trapping potential. Our results indicate that the relative amplitudes of the momentum components at the output are sensitive to external forces, mediated by the displacement of the harmonic potential relative to the optical lattice. Furthermore, we detail the calibration and full characterization of the interferometer's output, alongside a discussion of potential future enhancements.

The ASHRAE Great Energy Predictor III (GEPIII) competition, organized in late 2019, stands as one of the most significant machine learning contests dedicated to building performance. Hosted on Kaggle, the event generated 39,402 prediction submissions, with the top five teams sharing a $25,000 prize pool. This paper synthesizes key takeaways from participants, particularly those achieving results within the top 5%, by analyzing publicly shared notebooks, submissions, winning team documentation, and responses to an online survey. The highest-performing solutions predominantly relied on ensemble Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) tree models, with LightGBM being the most frequently utilized package. Survey data highlighted that preprocessing and feature extraction were the most critical components of successful modeling approaches. Furthermore, all respondents employed Python as their primary language and commonly utilized Jupyter-style Notebooks for development. These findings provide essential guidance for future research and practical applications in building energy meter prediction.

When an expert maneuvers a dangerous dynamic system, the optimal constraint information is implicitly embedded within their demonstrated paths and control inputs. Given the system dynamics and task goals, one can calculate the probability of these demonstrations and identify the most likely constraints. Previous research on inferring constraints has primarily centered on deterministic models; however, stochastic models are better suited to represent the uncertainty and risk preferences inherent in many real-world systems. This paper broadens maximum likelihood constraint inference to stochastic contexts by employing maximum causal entropy likelihoods. Additionally, we introduce an efficient algorithm that calculates both constraint likelihood and risk tolerance within a single Bellman backup step, enabling generalization to stochastic systems without escalating computational costs.

Although the data privacy community has focused heavily on generating synthetic data under differential privacy (DP), the analysis of such data has been largely overlooked. Prior research indicates that treating DP synthetic data as real data leads to invalid population-level inferences; for instance, confidence intervals become overly narrow, a finding illustrated by a simple experiment. To address this, we integrate synthetic data analysis techniques from multiple imputation (MI) with noise-aware (NA) Bayesian modeling for data generation, creating an NA+MI pipeline that yields accurate uncertainty estimates for population metrics. Specifically, for discrete data generation via marginal queries, we introduce a novel algorithm called NAPSU-MQ, which utilizes the maximum entropy principle. Our experiments confirm that the NA+MI pipeline successfully generates precise confidence intervals from DP synthetic data, with interval widths increasing appropriately under stricter privacy constraints to account for the additional uncertainty introduced by DP noise.

Color images are intuitive to interpret and rich in details like texture and color, making them prevalent in tasks such as segmentation. However, privacy concerns necessitate alternative data collection methods for indoor person segmentation. To address this, we introduce a novel approach for human segmentation using invisible airborne ultrasound. Initially, ultrasound waves are transformed into directional ultrasound images to facilitate segmentation based on non-visual data. While these images can roughly locate a person, their detailed shapes remain ambiguous. To resolve this, we propose a collaborative learning probabilistic U-Net that jointly trains on both ultrasound and segmentation images, aligning the latent space parameters to bridge the distribution gap between them. During inference, segmentation results are derived solely from ultrasound inputs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves more accurate human segmentation estimates compared to conventional probabilistic U-Nets and other variational autoencoder models.

Statistical modeling and data-driven learning are two critical domains that have garnered significant attention. While statistical models aim to capture and interpret relationships between variables, data-driven learning seeks to extract information directly from raw data, bypassing the need for complex pre-processing models. Despite extensive research in both areas, a key challenge remains: effectively integrating data-driven methods with existing knowledge or models. This paper addresses this issue using time series data by proposing two distinct integration strategies: a decomposition-based approach and a method leveraging statistical feature extraction. The first approach decomposes data into linear stable, nonlinear stable, and unstable components; statistical models are applied to the stable parts, while machine learning tools handle the unstable parts. The second approach utilizes statistical models to extract data features, which are then fed as additional inputs into a machine learning platform for training. The core challenge lies in identifying and extracting valuable information from mathematical or statistical models to enhance machine learning performance. Evaluations using time series data with varying stability levels demonstrate that both proposed methods outperform existing schemes that use models and learning separately, achieving improvements of over 60%. These results indicate that both approaches offer promising solutions for bridging the gap between model-based and data-driven techniques, ultimately delivering superior overall learning performance.

This paper investigates the exact solutions for two types of generalized Fokker-Planck equations, characterized by integral kernels defined as either the distributed order function $k_{1}(t) = \int_{0}^{1} t^{-\mu}/\Gamma(1- \mu) d\mu$ or the distributed order Prabhakar function $k_{2}(\alpha, \gamma; \lambda; t) = \int_{0}^{1} e^{-\gamma}_{\alpha, 1 - \mu}(\lambda; t) d\mu$, where the latter is denoted by $e^{-\gamma}_{\alpha, 1 - \mu}(\lambda; t)$. Both kernels are identified as Stieltjes functions and represent fading memory functions. The study demonstrates that their Stieltjes property guarantees the non-negativity of mean square values and higher even moments, while odd moments are zero; consequently, the solutions to these generalized Fokker-Planck equations qualify as probability density functions. Furthermore, the Volterra-Prabhakar function and its generalization, which underpin the definition of $k_{2}(\alpha, \gamma; \lambda; t)$, are introduced as generators of the probability density function $p_2(x, t)$.

This article calculates the linear mass density of vertically suspended heavy springs for two distinct scenarios: first, for a spring of constant length fixed at the bottom and suspended from the top, and second, for a hanging heavy spring supporting an additional load. Both problems are resolved by minimizing the total energy, defined as the sum of potential energy and energy resulting from deformation.

Psychological research has extensively examined human personality dimensions, including extroversion, agreeableness, and emotional stability, often utilizing frameworks like the "Big Five" for assessment and diagnosis. This study investigates whether language models display consistent perceived personalities during text generation; specifically, it examines if models like GPT-2 respond uniformly to prompts such as attending a party. Furthermore, we explore the controllability of these traits. Our findings demonstrate that when exposed to various contexts—such as personality descriptions or responses to diagnostic queries—models like BERT and GPT-2 can reliably identify and mirror personality markers. This indicates a capacity for predictable manipulation, positioning these models as effective tools for detecting personality traits and managing personas in applications like dialogue systems. Additionally, we introduce two datasets: one containing crowd-sourced personality descriptions of human subjects paired with their "Big Five" assessments, and another comprising personality descriptions aggregated from Reddit.

Research into quantum Hall physics centers on both natural matter and engineered systems, such as cold atomic gases, which exhibit non-trivial topological order. This study reports the detection of a chiral edge current within a synthetic quantum Hall system characterized by separate bulk and edge dynamics. This system is realized in a two-dimensional state space comprising one spatial dimension and one synthetic dimension, which is encoded in the J = 6 electronic spin of erbium atoms. To characterize the setup, the Hall drift of the atomic Bose-Einstein condensate in the lowest Landau level was measured. Topological properties were confirmed by calculating the local Chern marker, and through system excitations, both cyclotron orbits in the bulk and skipping orbits at the edge were observed. Future directions involve investigating new topological phases within cold atom platforms.

This study investigates the long-term dynamics of strong solutions within the 2-D compressible Oldroyd-B and Hall-MHD frameworks. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique alongside time-weighted energy estimates, we derive an $L^2$ decay rate of $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Furthermore, applying Littlewood-Paley theory, we establish that the solutions reside in a critical Besov space characterized by a negative index. Finally, we demonstrate the optimal decay rate within the $H^2$ setting.

Malware creators employ various obfuscation methods on generic malware features, such as unique signatures, to generate new variants and evade detection. Current Siamese Neural Network (SNN) approaches struggle to distinguish between different malware families when these generic features overlap across variants, leading to elevated false-positive rates. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel Task-Aware Meta Learning-based Siamese Neural Network designed to withstand obfuscated malware while functioning effectively with only one or a few training samples. By integrating entropy features of malware signatures with image features as task inputs, our task-aware meta learner dynamically adjusts parameters for feature layers, enabling more precise feature embedding adaptation for diverse malware families. Furthermore, the model leverages meta-learning with features from a pre-trained network (e.g., VGG-16) to eliminate biases common in models trained on limited datasets. Our approach demonstrates high efficacy in identifying unique malware signatures, ensuring accurate classification of samples within the same family despite applied obfuscation. Experimental validation using N-way N-shot learning confirms that our model achieves superior classification accuracy compared to existing similar methods.

Efficient and eco-friendly solid-state cooling can be achieved through high-entropy order-disorder phase transitions, a barocaloric effect demonstrated in the plastic crystal adamantane. Adamantane exhibits a massive, isothermally reversible entropy change of 106 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹ with extremely low hysteresis, allowing operation at pressure differences under 200 bar. While configurational entropy accounts for only roughly 40% of the total change, the remainder stems from vibrational effects. Neutron spectroscopy and supercell lattice dynamics calculations reveal that this vibrational contribution arises primarily from the softening of acoustic modes linked to molecular rotations in the high-entropy phase. This behavior is attributed to the shift from an 'interlocked' state in the low-entropy phase to sphere-like behavior in the high-entropy phase. Despite adamantane being a simple van der Waals solid with near-spherical molecules, this methodology offers a pathway to design more intricate barocaloric molecular crystals. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that supercell lattice dynamics calculations can precisely model how orientational disorder influences the phonon spectrum, facilitating future investigations into vibrational entropy, thermal conductivity, and other thermodynamic properties in complex materials.

In biopharmaceutical manufacturing, fermentation is vital for ensuring productivity and profitability. Because these processes involve living cells with intricate biological mechanisms, they often exhibit high variability in their outputs. To address this, we developed a stochastic model that characterizes the accumulation of proteins and impurities by leveraging their underlying biological growth patterns. However, a significant industry hurdle is the scarcity of data, particularly during development and early production phases. This data limitation introduces "model risk," an additional layer of uncertainty arising from the difficulty of accurately estimating model parameters. This paper investigates harvesting decisions for fermentation processes under such model risk. Specifically, we employ a Bayesian approach to update unknown parameters of growth-rate distributions, utilizing the resulting posterior distributions to quantify how model risk affects output variability. We formulate the harvesting problem as a Markov decision process where knowledge states encapsulate these posterior distributions, thereby integrating model risk into the decision-making framework. The model is solved using a reinforcement learning algorithm based on Bayesian sparse sampling. We derive analytical insights into the structure of the optimal policy and its objective function, while explicitly examining how model risk influences harvesting choices. Case studies conducted at MSD Animal Health demonstrate that our proposed model and solution methodology enhance real-world harvesting decisions, yielding substantially higher average batch outputs alongside reduced batch-to-batch variability.

In recent years, magnon-phonon coupling has garnered significant interest because of its pivotal role in spin caloritronics and the nascent field of acoustic spintronics. While this magnetoelastic interaction drives the creation of magnon polarons at resonance—phenomena responsible for exotic effects like magnonic heat currents and phononic spin—it has largely been studied only through mesoscopic spin-lattice models, with only a few recent exceptions. Driven by the goal of embedding magnon-phonon coupling within first-principles many-body electronic structure theory, we derived the non-relativistic exchange contribution. This contribution is more nuanced than the spin-orbit term and was calculated using Schwinger's method of functional derivatives. To bypass the need for self-consistently solving the well-known Hedin-Baym equations, phonons were treated as a perturbation to the electronic structure. We developed a formalism based on imposing crossing symmetry on the interaction, allowing charge and spin to be treated equally. Through an iterative approach, we determined that the spin-flip component of the collective four-point interaction, $\mathcal{V}$, used to compute the magnon spectrum, comprises a first-order "screened T matrix" term and a second-order term that is arguably more significant. In the limit of local spins, this second-order term describes the same phonon emission and absorption processes found in phenomenological magnetoelastic models. In this context, "order" refers to the screened collective four-point interaction, $\mathcal{W}$, which serves as the crossing-symmetric counterpart to Hedin's $W$. Finally, proof-of-principle calculations were conducted at various temperatures for the isotropic magnon spectrum in three dimensions, considering a flat optical phonon branch.

Recently, in-memory computing has emerged as a favored architecture for deep-learning hardware accelerators, driven by its high parallelism, energy efficiency, and compact footprint. Nevertheless, In-RRAM computing (IRC) faces significant challenges due to substantial device variability and various hardware imperfections. While prior methods that incorporated these effects into model training enhanced tolerance to variation, they addressed only a subset of nonidealities and were limited to simpler classification problems. This paper introduces a co-design strategy optimizing both hardware and software to create a robust IRC macro tailored for object detection. By employing a low word-line voltage to reduce cell current, we facilitate full convolution calculations in a single step, thereby mitigating the impact of nonlinear addition errors. Furthermore, we adopt ternary weight mapping and eliminate batch normalization to improve resilience against device and sense amplifier variations, as well as IR drop issues. An additional bias term is integrated to address limitations in current sensing ranges. When applied to a complex object detection task, this approach achieves only a 3.85% drop in mAP, whereas a naive design experiences catastrophic failure under the same nonideal conditions.

This study employs the periodic Schur process, as detailed in arXiv:math/0601019v1, to analyze the random height function associated with lozenge tilings (or equivalently, dimers) on an infinite cylinder subject to two distinct $q^{\operatorname{vol}}$ measure distributions. The first distribution corresponds to random cylindric partitions, where the height function converges to a deterministic limit shape, and the surrounding fluctuations conform to the Gaussian free field within the conformal structure anticipated by the Kenyon-Okounkov conjecture. The second distribution represents an unrestricted dimer model on the cylinder, exhibiting fluctuations characterized by the same Gaussian free field augmented by a discrete Gaussian shift. This latter type of fluctuation has previously been conjectured for dimer models defined on planar domains containing holes.

The operation of Superconducting Radio Frequency (SRF) cavities with high loaded quality factors is gaining prominence for low beam loading applications, such as Energy Recovery Linacs (ERL). However, vibration-induced microphonics detuning represents a significant operational hurdle in these low-bandwidth systems, compromising field stability. Beyond passive vibration mitigation, modern SRF cavities are increasingly equipped with fast tuners utilizing piezo-electric actuators. This work demonstrates a narrow-band active noise control algorithm for active resonance management and proposes a modification grounded in the Least Mean Square approach to adaptively tune control parameters, analyzing both stability and performance. We also share insights from employing passive mitigation strategies during the commissioning of the Main Linac Cryomodule for the Cornell-BNL ERL Test Accelerator (CBETA), reporting a net decrease in peak detuning by over a factor of two in unstiffened cavities. Finally, we showcase the stable operation of our resonance control system, achieving a consistent reduction in peak microphonics detuning by nearly a factor of two across multiple cavities.

This chapter provides an overview of discrete choice models, a specific type of limited dependent variable model where the outcome is discrete, inherently ordered, and derived from an underlying continuous latent variable. These models address scenarios where the dependent variable assumes only two values (yielding binary models like probit and logit) or multiple ordered values ($j=1, 2, \ldots, J$), resulting in ordinal models such as ordinal probit and logit. The central objective is to estimate the probability of specific outcomes conditional on covariates. The discussion links discrete choice models to the economic random utility framework, covers estimation methods, explains how to calculate covariate effects, and outlines measures for model fit assessment. Recent advancements in modeling discrete data are also reviewed. Following this theoretical foundation, the chapter applies binary and ordinal models to examine public sentiment regarding marijuana legalization and its scope in the United States, a socially significant yet contentious issue. Key findings indicate that past usage, attitudes toward legalization, and political affiliation are significant determinants of public opinion.

The Hall-D Online Skim System (HOSS) was created to address two key challenges for the high-intensity GlueX experiment: parallelizing raw data file writes to disk to enhance bandwidth and distributing raw data across multiple compute nodes to generate online calibration skims. This highly configurable architecture utilizes Python-driven zeroMQ, RDMA, and RAM disks to concurrently process and store the complete high-intensity GlueX data stream.

This study examines theoretical approaches to path planning within Traveling Salesman Problems (TSP) characterized by non-probabilistic uncertainty. Specifically, the uncertainty pertains to the edges connecting cities, where multiple routes may exist between nodes, yet the traversal time for any given path remains imprecise. Such indeterminacy can arise from various factors, including environmental congestion during peak hours, battery levels, weather conditions, or safety considerations. The paper analyzes two distinct advanced uncertainty frameworks: a probabilistic-precise model utilizing probability distributions and a non-probabilistic-imprecise model based on intervals. Furthermore, the research investigates the theoretical outcomes achievable under two specific optimality criteria, namely maximality and maximinity, within the context of the TSP.

Unclonable encryption, first introduced by Broadbent and Lord (TQC'20), is an encryption scheme characterized by the property that an adversary, given a ciphertext, cannot generate two distinct ciphertexts that both decrypt to the same original message. This work revisits that concept and establishes the following results:

*   **Reusability:** The original constructions by Broadbent and Lord suffer from limitations: they either ensure one-time security (where the key is usable only once) in the plain model or rely on the random oracle model for security. We propose unclonable encryption schemes that achieve semantic security. Specifically, we offer two constructions—one for public-key and one for private-key settings—based on minimal cryptographic assumptions.
*   **Lower Bound and Generalized Construction:** We re-examine the information-theoretic one-time secure scheme by Broadbent and Lord. In their construction, the adversary's success probability was bounded at $0.85^n$, where $n$ denotes the message length. We investigated whether the theoretical ideal success probability of approximately $0.5^n$ was unattainable. By generalizing their approach to a wider range of monogamy of entanglement games, we demonstrate a cloning attack with a success probability of $0.71^n$ against a class of schemes that includes theirs. Furthermore, we present a specific cloning attack with a $0.75^n$ success rate targeting their scheme exclusively.
*   **Implication to Copy-Protection:** We demonstrate that unclonable encryption, when satisfying a stronger property termed unclonable-indistinguishability (as defined by Broadbent and Lord), implies copy-protection for a specific class of unlearnable functions. Although encryption schemes meeting this stronger criterion are not yet known to exist, this result highlights a novel pathway for constructing copy-protection mechanisms.

This editorial introduces the algorithmic trading community to the launch of the new open-access journal, "Algorithmic Trading and Controls" (ATC), which features original research on trading algorithms and their control methods. In this inaugural piece, we outline nine significant challenges currently facing modern algorithmic trading. While the number nine holds no mystical significance, it serves as a convenient framework. These hurdles span various levels, ranging from strategy issues like executing trades in illiquid markets or optimizing portfolio performance, to risk management and control concerns such as developing automated systems and conducting simulations. Although our perspectives may inevitably reflect personal biases, they are offered with the sincere aim of advancing this critical domain within modern financial services and technology.

Electron cooling, utilized for generating high-intensity ion beams, faces a practical ceiling regarding the maximum achievable peak phase space density. We outline a novel experiment designed to investigate the electron cooling of 2.5 MeV protons at this intensity threshold within the Integrable Optics Test Accelerator (IOTA), a Fermilab storage ring dedicated to beam physics. This setup facilitates the examination of magnetized electron cooling in proton beams experiencing transverse incoherent tune shifts nearing -0.5, driven by strong space-charge forces. The project overview includes details on the hardware design, simulations, and the specific experiments planned for execution.

The insideness problem, a core component of image segmentation, involves distinguishing which pixels lie inside versus outside a specific region. Although Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) achieve high performance on segmentation benchmarks, their capacity to address the insideness problem remains uncertain due to the need to evaluate long-range spatial dependencies. This study isolates the insideness problem by excluding texture and semantic information to prevent interference from other segmentation factors. We find that DNNs with limited units possess sufficient complexity to solve the insideness problem for any curve; however, they struggle significantly to learn generalized solutions. In contrast, recurrent networks trained on small images successfully learn solutions that generalize effectively across nearly all curves. This success is attributed to the ability of recurrent networks to break down long-range dependency evaluation into sequential local operations, while training on small images mitigates the typical challenges associated with training recurrent networks over many unrolling steps.

Recent research in biometric identification indicates that deep learning approaches yield superior performance by typically extracting global features to represent images. However, these methods struggle with fine-grained biometric tasks because a single image descriptor often lacks sufficient detail to fully characterize an image. To address this, we introduce a dual global descriptor model that integrates multiple global descriptors to leverage multi-level image features. Additionally, we employ a contrastive loss function to maximize the distance between representations of confusing classes. Our framework secured the top-2 position in the CVPR2022 Biometrics Workshop Pet Biometric Challenge. The source code and trained models are accessible at: https://github.com/flyingsheepbin/pet-biometrics

Daily sunspot group area records maintained by the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, spanning from May 1874 to 1976, reveal an intriguing pattern regarding the penumbral areas of smaller sunspot groups. Generally, as the total area of a sunspot group grows from 100 to 2000 microHems (where one microHem equals one-millionth of a solar hemisphere's area), the ratio of penumbral to umbral area rises steadily from approximately 5 to 6. This trend remains consistent regardless of the group's latitude or the specific phase of the sunspot cycle. In contrast, sunspot groups smaller than 100 microHems exhibit a distinct and systematic evolution over this historical period. For these smallest spots, the ratio hovered near 5.5 between 1874 and 1900, surged rapidly to exceed 7 by 1905, declined smoothly to below 3 by 1930, climbed again to surpass 7 in 1961, and settled back near 5.5 from 1965 through 1976. The continuous variation observed between 1905 and 1961 displays no abrupt shifts that could be linked to changes in observational equipment or staff. Notably, this period coincided with a monotonic increase in overall solar activity, yet the penumbra-to-umbra ratio dropped to less than half its peak before recovering. If corroborated by data from other observatories such as Mt. Wilson or Kodaikanal, these findings could significantly influence our comprehension of penumbra formation, dynamo models, and historical estimates of solar irradiance variations.

Current state-of-the-art pretrained contextualized models (PCMs), such as BERT, are typically evaluated using lexical tasks like WiC and WSD, with the implicit assumption that performance on these tasks accurately reflects a model's ability to represent coupled word and context semantics. We challenge this premise by conducting the first quantitative analysis of the context-word interactions tested in major contextual lexical semantic tasks. To accomplish this, we apply probing baselines to masked inputs and introduce metrics to quantify and visualize context versus word biases within existing datasets. This analysis was conducted across both models and human participants. Our results reveal that models are not assessed for word-in-context semantics in the same manner as humans; this discrepancy offers new insights into the model-human gap. Specifically, for PCMs, most existing datasets skew toward extreme biases: retrieval-based tasks demonstrate strong target word bias, whereas WiC-style tasks and WSD exhibit strong context bias. In contrast, humans display less bias and achieve significantly better performance when both the word and context are available compared to when input is masked. We advocate for our framework as a tool to understand and control these biases, aiding in model interpretation and the design of future tasks.

Deep learning object detectors have achieved significant advancements. Nevertheless, supervised methods struggle when training and testing data exhibit different distributions. To overcome this, domain adaptation transfers knowledge from a label-rich source domain to a label-scarce target domain. Self-training is a potent technique for domain adaptation, particularly for class-wise adaptation; however, naive approaches relying on pseudo-labels as ground truth often degrade performance due to label errors. This paper proposes a Weak Self-Training (WST) method combined with Adversarial Background Score Regularization (BSR) for unsupervised domain adaptive one-stage object detection. WST mitigates the negative impact of inaccurate pseudo-labels to stabilize training, while BSR aids the network in extracting discriminative features for target backgrounds to minimize domain shift. These two components are complementary: BSR enhances the distinction between foregrounds and backgrounds, whereas WST strengthens class-wise discrimination. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively boosts one-stage object detection performance in unsupervised domain adaptation scenarios.

Given a locally finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a coloring $\chi: A \to \{0,1,\ldots,s\}$, we define the chromatic Delaunay mosaic of $\chi$. This structure, a Delaunay mosaic within $\mathbb{R}^{s+d}$, illustrates the interaction between points of varying colors. Assuming $d$ and $s$ are constant, our primary findings establish bounds on the size of this mosaic. For instance, if $A$ is finite with $n$ points and the coloring is random, the expected number of cells in the chromatic Delaunay mosaic is $O(n^{\lceil{d/2}\rceil})$. Conversely, for Delone sets and Poisson point processes in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the expected cell count within any closed ball is proportional to the number of points in that ball. Additionally, in $\mathbb{R}^2$, every coloring of a dense set of $n$ points yields a chromatic Delaunay mosaic of size $O(n)$. These results suggest that chromatic Delaunay mosaics are valuable for practical applications.

We demonstrate that spin squeezing indicates entanglement in tripartite quantum systems where the bipartite subsystem is identical. This study examines the connection between spin squeezing parameters and entanglement via quantum entropy, considering a system starting in a pure state within a binomial cavity. We find that spin squeezing offers valuable insights into the entanglement dynamics of subsystems interacting simultaneously with a cavity field, particularly during off-resonant interactions, both with and without a nonlinear medium inside the cavity. Specifically, in scenarios involving large off-resonance interactions, spin squeezing effectively clarifies entanglement properties; however, this does not hold universally when the cavity contains a nonlinear medium. In such cases, insights into entanglement dynamics are more pronounced in weak nonlinear regimes compared to strong ones. Additionally, we investigate the role of phase space distributions in quantifying entanglement. Numerical analysis of the Husimi $Q$-function reveals that integer strengths of the nonlinear medium generate Schrödinger cat states, which are essential for quantum entanglement.

We conduct a thorough new Monte Carlo analysis of high-energy scattering data involving lepton-lepton, lepton-hadron, and hadron-hadron interactions to simultaneously extract proton parton distribution functions (PDFs) and parton-to-hadron fragmentation functions (FFs). This study incorporates all existing semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering and single-inclusive $e^+ e^-$ annihilation data for pions, kaons, and unidentified charged hadrons, thereby enabling constraints on the flavor dependence of fragmentation functions. By utilizing a novel multi-step fitting approach and more flexible parametrizations for both PDFs and FFs, we evaluate how various data sets influence sea quark densities and reaffirm the previously noted suppression of the strange quark distribution. The resulting fit, designated "JAM20-SIDIS," will facilitate enhanced investigations into the universality of parton correlation functions, including transverse momentum dependent (TMD) distributions, across diverse processes, as well as the matching between collinear and TMD factorization frameworks.

Experimental studies have examined the photodisintegration cross sections for the $^{94}\text{Mo}(\gamma,n)$ and $^{90}\text{Zr}(\gamma,n)$ reactions using quasi-monochromatic photon beams at the High Intensity $\gamma$-ray Source (HI$\gamma$S) within the Triangle Universities Nuclear Laboratory (TUNL). With high precision, the energy dependence of these photoneutron cross sections was measured from the specific neutron emission thresholds up to 13.5 MeV. These findings support a wider effort to understand nuclear reactions essential to the p-process nucleosynthesis. The data were contrasted with predictions from Hauser-Feshbach statistical model calculations employing two distinct dipole $\gamma$-ray strength function models. Consequently, the calculated stellar reaction rates for both isotopes, plotted against temperature in the range typical for the p-process, demonstrate the significant sensitivity of these rates to experimental measurements near the neutron threshold.

This article examines the material characteristics necessary to achieve peak optical responses. We emphasize theoretical findings that allow for shape-independent quantification of material "figures of merit," spanning from traditional sum rules to newer single-frequency scattering limits. A crucial distinction at optical frequencies lies between polaritonic materials, which facilitate highly subwavelength resonances, and dielectric materials capable of exhibiting negligible loss rates. We explore the primary metrics used to compare materials both within these categories and across them. Additionally, we address analogous metrics for two-dimensional materials and identify applications where rigorous comparisons between bulk and 2D material strategies are feasible. These results underscore the synergy between materials discovery and theoretical nanophotonic constraints, highlighting prospects for reaching new extremes in light-matter interactions.

This study demonstrates that information-theoretic authentication is feasible at the physical layer within additive white Gaussian noise channels, provided the adversary lacks omniscience. The framework involves an encoder, a decoder, and an adversary who possesses the message, a non-causal noisy view of the transmission, and unlimited transmission power; conversely, the decoder receives a noisy observation of the sum of the encoder's and adversary's outputs. The authors propose a technique to adapt generic existing channel codes for authentication purposes. They prove that this adaptation incurs an asymptotically negligible reduction in coding rate and ensures authentication as long as the adversary's observation is not noiseless. Notably, this modification does not depend asymptotically on the statistical properties of the adversary's channel and requires no secret key, thereby facilitating robust practical deployment. Based on these findings, the channel-authenticated capacity is computed and found to match the capacity of the non-adversarial channel. Although this modular approach is tailored for the specified channel model, it remains applicable across a broad spectrum of scenarios.

Human pose estimation, defined as identifying the positions and orientations of body limbs within video footage, serves critical roles in surveillance, diagnosing movement disorders, and computer animation. Although deep learning has driven significant progress in 2D and 3D pose estimation from single video sources, estimating 3D poses from multiple overlapping cameras has received comparatively less attention. When multiple cameras are available, fusing multi-view pose estimates and observing limbs that are occluded in certain views can substantially enhance 3D reconstruction accuracy. Previous methods for multi-view 3D pose estimation have relied on probabilistic graphical models to reason over constraints such as per-image estimates, temporal smoothness, and limb length. This paper introduces a pipeline for estimating the 3D poses of multiple individuals that integrates a state-of-the-art 2D pose detector with a factor graph of 3D limb constraints optimized via belief propagation. We evaluate our approach on the TUM-Campus and Shelf datasets for multi-person 3D pose estimation, demonstrating that our system significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods using a more simplified model of limb dependency.

This study reports state-resolved measurements of rotational excitation and cooling rates for CH$^+$ molecular ions resulting from inelastic electron collisions. Conducted at the Cryogenic Storage Ring, the experiments utilize a monoenergetic electron beam with matched velocities alongside state-sensitive laser-dissociation techniques to simultaneously track rotational level populations. By employing storage times as long as 600 seconds, we establish conditions where electron-induced cooling to the $J = 0$ ground state surpasses radiative relaxation, enabling the precise determination of inelastic electron collision rates to validate current theoretical models. More broadly, these experiments lay the foundation for investigating inelastic electron collisions across a range of molecular ions significant to diverse plasma environments.

In economic network analysis, econometric methods treat the traditional Gravity Model as an expected link weight derived from an arbitrarily chosen probability distribution, whereas statistical-physics methods build maximum-entropy distributions for weighted graphs that adhere to specific measurable network constraints. A recent companion study merged these two frameworks and applied them to the World Trade Web; however, that work was limited to discrete link weights. This paper extends the theoretical framework to accommodate continuous-valued link weights. Specifically, we develop two broad categories of maximum-entropy models: integrated and conditional. These are distinguished by how they derive and combine probabilistic rules for link placement and weight assignment. In integrated models, both rules emerge from a single constrained optimization of the continuous Kullback-Leibler divergence. Conversely, in conditional models, the rules are separated, with the weight distribution's functional form resulting from a distinct conditional optimization process. Following the derivation of the general functional forms for both classes, we transform them into proper econometric model families by identifying the specific function that relates expected link weights to macroeconomic factors. Finally, after testing these model classes against World Trade Web data, we evaluate their respective strengths and limitations.

We provide experimental evidence of both a predicted spontaneous symmetry breaking and an unforeseen explicit symmetry breaking near the Hopf bifurcation in a nominally symmetric annular combustor; this bifurcation marks the transition between linearly stable azimuthal thermoacoustic modes and self-oscillating ones. By deriving and solving a multidimensional Fokker-Planck equation, we establish a unified understanding of the phase space topology. We show that symmetric probability density functions for the thermoacoustic state vector are difficult to achieve, as even negligible asymmetries are significantly amplified in the vicinity of the bifurcation.

Privacy regulations impact not only legal adherence but also user satisfaction. The surge in App reviews offers a rich repository for requirement knowledge. While existing research has focused on automatically extracting requirement-related data—such as feature requests, bug reports, and user opinions—from these reviews, there has been insufficient attention given to refining privacy requirements through this mining process, a step crucial for addressing privacy concerns. This study aims to detect privacy-related features within App reviews to support software maintenance. We propose a semi-automatic framework that identifies privacy-related reviews, extracts App features from them, and maps these to features listed in App descriptions. The process begins by combining information retrieval with supervised text classification to pinpoint privacy-related reviews. Next, a dependency parsing method is employed to extract App features from these specific reviews. Finally, the automatically extracted features are matched against manually annotated ones in App descriptions using phrase similarity. We quantitatively evaluated the three components of our framework using reviews from diverse App categories. For identifying privacy-related reviews, the Gradient Boosting classifier achieved the highest F1 score of 93.77%, outperforming other competitive algorithms, including deep learning models. Regarding App feature extraction, our dependency parsing method attained an 85.63% recall, exceeding the baseline by more than 20%. For feature matching, phrase embedding cosine similarity yielded the best results among four tested methods, achieving an average accuracy of 57%. We conclude by discussing the framework's potential applications in detecting feature issues that could lead to privacy threats.

Shared autonomy involves strategies that allow autonomous agents to collaborate with humans to enhance their performance. Beyond performance gains, it is often advantageous for these agents to simultaneously prioritize the user's satisfaction and overall collaboration experience. To address this dual objective, we investigate methods for enhancing user experience by limiting the frequency of autonomous interventions. We introduce two model-free reinforcement learning techniques capable of managing both hard and soft constraints on intervention counts. Our results demonstrate that these methods not only surpass existing baselines but also remove the necessity for manually tuning opaque hyperparameters to regulate assistance levels. Furthermore, we offer a detailed analysis of intervention scenarios to deepen the understanding of the system.

For positive integers $r$ and $t$, the hypergraph matching Ramsey number $R_r(s_1,\ldots,s_t)$ represents the smallest integer $n$ such that every $t$-hyperedge coloring of the complete $r$-uniform hypergraph $K_n^r$ guarantees a matching of size $s_j$ within the subhypergraph formed by edges of color $j$, for some $j \in \{1,2,\ldots,t\}$. This value was fully determined by Alon, Frankl, and Lovász in 1986. In 2015, the first author and Hossein Hajiabolhassan derived a sharp lower bound for the chromatic number of general Kneser hypergraphs using the concept of the alternation number of hypergraphs. In this paper, we first develop a theory that extends that result. As our second contribution, we characterize $R_r(s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_t)$. Finally, we introduce a generalization of the $\mathbf{\mathbb{Z}_p}$-Tucker Lemma and apply it to determine the matching Ramsey number $R_r(s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_t)$.

Twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides serve as excellent systems for investigating flat-band phenomena. This study examines flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer MoS$_2$ (tb-MoS$_2$) using a comprehensive tight-binding model combined with the random phase approximation. When lattice relaxations are accounted for in tb-MoS$_2$, the flat band remains distinct from remote valence bands, leading to a significantly different contribution from interband transitions to plasmon dispersion and energy. Specifically, considering only intraband transitions within the doped flat band yields low-damped, quasi-flat plasmons, while including interband transitions between the flat band and remote bands results in a $\sqrt q$ plasmon dispersion. Additionally, plasmon energies can be tuned via twist angles and doping concentrations. Conversely, in rigid samples without lattice relaxations, lower-energy quasi-flat plasmons and higher-energy interband plasmons may coexist; however, in highly doped rigid tb-MoS$_2$, strongly enhanced interband transitions suppress the quasi-flat plasmons. Based on the influences of lattice relaxation and doping, we conclude that observing the low-damped, quasi-flat plasmon mode in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides requires two key conditions: an isolated flat band and an appropriate level of hole doping. We anticipate that our findings on flat-band plasmons will provide valuable insights into the potential for plasmon-mediated superconductivity in these materials.

Digital Twins are a cornerstone of the Industry 4.0 vision, designed to represent, manage, forecast, and optimize Cyber-Physical Production Systems (CPPSs). These long-lived, complex systems are deployed and configured across varied environments, yet their behavior may drift from intended performance over time due to factors like specific deployments, configurations, wear, tear, or environmental influences. Consequently, adjusting CPPS configurations often depends on the specialized knowledge of human operators.
