By encapsulating this expertise and learning from it to tackle unexpected challenges, Digital Twins can greatly enhance self-adaptive manufacturing, particularly in scenarios where experience is highly specific and unsuitable for deep learning methods. This work utilizes case-based reasoning to explicitly model domain expertise, thereby boosting Digital Twin capabilities in such contexts. We introduce a modeling framework for self-adaptive manufacturing that enables the representation of domain-specific cases, defines rules for case similarity, and executes case-based reasoning within a modular Digital Twin. Leveraging explicitly modeled domain expertise to automatically configure Digital Twins can shorten manufacturing times, minimize waste, and ultimately advance sustainable manufacturing practices.

We re-examine the azimuthal decorrelation $\delta\phi$ between a jet and a $Z$ boson at hadron colliders. Utilizing various jet recombination schemes yields markedly different next-to-leading-logarithmic (NLL) resummed predictions for this distribution. Specifically, reconstructing jets using the $E$-scheme (four-momentum addition) within $k_t$ or anti-$k_t$ algorithms renders the resummation highly complex due to non-global and/or clustering logarithms. We calculate these logarithms analytically at two-loop order and numerically to all orders in the large-$\mathrm{N_c}$ limit, providing a complete NLL resummation of $\delta\phi$. Furthermore, we enhance the fixed-order accuracy of the perturbative expansion of the resummed distribution to next-to-next-to-leading-logarithmic (NNLL) precision by incorporating $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s)$ next-to-leading-order (NLO) corrections generated via MadGraph5_aMC@NLO. Finally, we contrast our results with predictions from multiple Monte Carlo event generators and experimental data from the CMS collaboration.

Generating squeezed light within semiconductor materials enables the development of on-chip devices functioning at the quantum level. This study theoretically investigates a squeezed light source based on polariton dark solitons confined in a geometric potential well of semiconductor microcavities under strong coupling conditions. We demonstrate that dark solitons with odd and even parities can be generated by adjusting the potential depth. Furthermore, linearly varying the potential depth induces bistability between solitons of these two different parities. Significant intensity squeezing is achieved near the bistability's turning point, resulting from substantial nonlinear interactions that are controllable via Feshbach resonance. Large-scale numerical simulations were used to map the phase diagram of both the bistability and the squeezing of the dark solitons. This research advances ongoing efforts to implement topological excitations and squeezed light sources using solid-state devices.

Generalized Zero-Shot Learning (GZSL) seeks to identify both observed and novel classes using only training data from the observed set, though instances of the novel classes often exhibit a bias toward the observed ones. To address this, we introduce the Cluster-based Contrastive Disentangling (CCD) method, designed to mitigate semantic gaps and domain shifts within GZSL. Our approach begins by clustering batch data into groups of similar classes. Subsequently, we decompose visual features into semantic-unspecific and semantic-matched components, further splitting the latter into class-shared and class-unique variables based on the clustering. This disentangled learning module, enhanced by random swapping and semantic-visual alignment, effectively bridges the semantic gap. Additionally, we apply contrastive learning to the semantic-matched and class-unique variables to foster high similarity within sets and classes while maximizing discrimination between them. The resulting visual features align with the intrinsic characteristics of general images and possess robust discriminative power, significantly reducing the domain shift issue. Experiments on four datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both conventional and generalized scenarios.

A primary obstacle to applying modern machine learning techniques for feedback control is the absence of methods capable of analyzing long-term dynamics, specifically regarding robustness guarantees. This challenge stems from the curse of dimensionality and the opaque, black-box nature of learned policies. This paper addresses the issue of dimensionality. While system state spaces may be high-dimensional, model-based control methods often yield closed-loop systems with dominant dynamics that quickly converge to a lower-dimensional subspace. We propose that fractal geometry, particularly concepts of fractional dimension, effectively characterizes this subspace. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dimensionality of trajectories generated by model-free reinforcement learning agents can be reduced by incorporating a post-processing function into their reward signal. We verify that this dimensionality reduction remains robust against system noise and show that the modified agents exhibit enhanced robustness to noise and disturbances across the systems studied.

Social media platforms like Twitter serve as a primary source of user-generated information. During the ongoing Covid-19 pandemic, these platforms have generated a vast amount of data, which can be categorized as either informative or uninformative. This paper details our approach to identifying informative English tweets related to Covid-19 using the RoBERTa model as a contribution to the W-NUT workshop 2020. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model on a public dataset, achieving an F1-score of 0.89 on the validation set and 0.87 on the leaderboard.

Magnetic reconnection, defined as the breaking and reconfiguration of magnetic field topology, serves as a fundamental mechanism for the rapid release of magnetic energy into plasma particles across the universe. In most natural settings, the plasma conditions on either side of the reconnection layer are asymmetric; specifically, collision rates—which depend on both density and temperature—critically govern the reconnection mechanism. To date, laboratory experiments on magnetic reconnection have been restricted to either purely collisional or purely collisionless regimes. This study reports a well-designed experimental investigation into asymmetric magnetic reconnection within a novel hybrid collisional-collisionless regime, achieved through interactions between laser-ablated copper and methane plasmas. We demonstrate that the growth rate of the tearing instability in this hybrid regime remains extremely high, leading to the rapid formation of multiple plasmoids at a rate lower than in the purely collisionless case but significantly higher than in the collisional case. Furthermore, utilizing highly resolved proton radiography, we present the first direct observation of the topological evolution throughout the entire process of plasmoid-dominated magnetic reconnection.

This paper characterizes the potential function $f$ of an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold using the non-dynamical scalar field $p$, derives the necessary conditions for $f$ to remain constant, and establishes a relationship between $\lambda$ and $f$. Additionally, we prove a sufficient condition for an almost conformal Ricci soliton to qualify as an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton and provide a classification of such solitons based on whether they are shrinking, steady, or expanding.

This paper investigates how different transmitter and receiver parameters influence the quantum bit error rate (QBER) in underwater quantum key distribution systems. We employ a Monte Carlo method to simulate photon trajectories traveling through water from the transmitter to the receiver. First, using propagation delay data, we establish an appropriate bit period to prevent intersymbol interference caused by multiple scattering. Next, we define a suitable field-of-view based on the angle of arrival of received photons to minimize average background noise. Finally, we identify the optimal single photon avalanche diode (SPAD) gate time that minimizes QBER for the chosen system parameters and specific propagation conditions.

Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a crucial approach for cyberthreat detection (CTD) in recent years, prompting significant research into specialized algorithms for this purpose. However, from an operational standpoint, the advancement of ML-based CTD is constrained by the challenge of acquiring large volumes of labeled data required to train these detectors. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) offers a promising solution by leveraging a combination of limited labeled data and extensive unlabeled datasets. This paper seeks to systematize existing SSL research within the context of CTD, with a specific focus on understanding the value of unlabeled data. To achieve this, we evaluate the costs associated with labeling across various CTD tasks and establish a formal cost model for SSL in this domain. Building on this foundation, we define a set of requirements for assessing SSL methods, clarifying the specific contributions of unlabeled data. Our review of current state-of-the-art approaches reveals that no existing work fully satisfies these requirements. Consequently, we propose a new framework for evaluating the benefits of unlabeled data in SSL. We demonstrate the application of this framework through the first benchmark evaluation, which examines the tradeoffs of nine SSL methods across nine public datasets. Our results indicate that, in certain scenarios, unlabeled data yields a small yet statistically significant performance improvement. Ultimately, this study underscores the substantial potential for improvement in SSL for CTD, aiming to inspire further research in this area.

In recent years, federated machine learning has garnered significant attention as a method to extract insights from data while safeguarding provider privacy. A primary barrier to its widespread adoption remains the absence of universally accepted, transparent, and equitable incentive mechanisms for rewarding contributors. Blockchain-based smart contracts offer a solution by providing immutable, transparent, and independently verifiable records of all network participants. We exploit the inherent openness of smart contracts to establish incentivization rules grounded in a novel metric called "federated contribution." This blockchain-driven, reward-based model holds the potential to transform enterprise adoption of federated learning. Our work presents two key contributions: first, demonstrating how smart contracts serve as a natural communication channel for federated learning; and second, illustrating how to construct an intuitive measure of individual agent contributions and integrate it into the training and reward lifecycle.

Numerous proteins can form amyloid fibrils, structures linked to various human ailments such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Unlike the thermodynamic stability of folded proteins, that of amyloid fibrils remains unclear, particularly regarding the balance of entropic and enthalpic factors like chain entropy and the hydrophobic effect. By employing simulations of a coarse-grained protein model, we mapped the enthalpic and entropic contributions driving fibril elongation and predicted a distinct temperature-dependent enthalpic signature. This thermodynamic profile was validated through calorimetric experiments and a meta-analysis of existing literature. Furthermore, these findings clarify the conditions required to observe cold denaturation in amyloid fibrils. In summary, we demonstrate that amyloid fibril elongation is characterized by a negative heat capacity; the magnitude of this value strongly correlates with the hydrophobic surface area buried during fibril formation, underscoring the critical role of hydrophobicity in maintaining fibril stability.

Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) are extensively utilized for material handling in flexible manufacturing environments, where specific products require diverse raw materials to complete their assembly. AGVs facilitate the automated transport of these materials across various locations, and an efficient task allocation strategy is crucial for lowering transportation costs and enhancing distribution efficiency. However, traditional centralized methods impose significant demands on the control center's computing resources and real-time processing capabilities. This paper introduces decentralized solutions to enable flexible and self-organized AGV task allocation. Specifically, we propose two enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms, MADDPG-IPF (Information Potential Field) and BiCNet-IPF, to achieve AGV coordination across different scenarios. To mitigate the problem of sparse rewards, we develop a reward shaping strategy grounded in the information potential field, which offers stepwise rewards and implicitly directs AGVs toward their respective material targets. Experiments conducted under varying configurations (3 and 6 AGVs) demonstrate that our approach achieves up to a 47% improvement in task response and a 22% reduction in training iterations compared to baseline methods.

The energy flux method is an acoustic propagation framework that determines locally averaged intensity without relying on explicit eigenvalue calculations or ray tracing. Historically, this approach has been limited to two-dimensional scenarios where the third dimension is collapsed through rotational or translational symmetry. This report details the derivation and implementation of a three-dimensional ocean acoustic model that integrates normal modes with the energy flux method, specifically designed for a wedge environment featuring a radial sound speed front at a distance from the shore. The results from this hybrid model are compared against a normal-mode-only propagation model for the same setting. Observations show general agreement regarding the shape, position, and amplitude of caustic features, though discrepancies exist, likely due to differences in the underlying model derivations. This study acts as a foundational step toward creating a more generalized three-dimensional energy flux model.

We explore energy transfer pathways between velocity and magnetic fields in a rotating plane layer dynamo driven by Rayleigh-Bénard convection through direct numerical simulations. By partitioning kinetic and magnetic energies into mean and turbulent components, we examine the production, transport, and dissipation linked to both large- and small-scale dynamos. This energy balance analysis uncovers distinct mechanisms for generating large- and small-scale magnetic fields, which vary according to the velocity field characteristics and boundary conditions.

We examine the Poincaré method for calculating 3D gravity partition functions dual to Rational CFTs. For a single genus-1 boundary, we demonstrate that for specific infinite level sets, SU(2)$_k$ WZW models offer unitary instances where the Poincaré series forms a positive linear combination of two modular-invariant partition functions. This finding bolsters the view that the bulk gravitational theory (specifically a topological Chern-Simons theory here) corresponds to an average of distinct CFTs sharing the same Kac-Moody algebra. We determine the weights of this average for every seed primary and all relevant $k$ values. Subsequently, we analyze other WZW models, including SU($N$)$_1$ and SU(3)$_k$, observing that each class exhibits notably different characteristics. Finally, we explore scenarios with multiple genus-1 boundaries, identifying a class of seed functions for the Poincaré sum that accounts for both disconnected and connected contributions—the latter representing analogues of 3-manifold "wormholes"—thereby accurately reproducing the anticipated average.

This work introduces the Multimodal Fiber Array Snapshot Technique (M-FAST), a system utilizing an array of 96 compact cameras positioned behind a primary objective lens and a fiber bundle array to achieve large-area, high-resolution, multi-channel video capture. The design offers two significant advancements over previous cascaded imaging methods: a unique optical configuration that supports planar camera arrays and the capacity to acquire multi-modal image data. As a scalable, multi-modal imaging platform, M-FAST is capable of capturing snapshot dual-channel fluorescence images alongside phase contrast measurements across an 8x10mm² field of view with a full-pitch resolution of 2.2µm.

An analysis of the decays $B_c^+ \to J/\psi D^{(*)0} K^+$ and $B_c^+ \to J/\psi D^{(*)+} K^{*0}$ was conducted using 3 fb$^{-1}$ of data from the LHCb experiment. For the first time, the decays $B_c^+ \to J/\psi D^0 K^+$ and $B_c^+ \to J/\psi D^{*0} K^+$ are observed, while first evidence is presented for the $B_c^+ \to J/\psi D^{*+} K^{*0}$ and $B_c^+ \to J/\psi D^+ K^{*0}$ modes. The branching fractions for these processes are calculated relative to the $B_c^+ \to J/\psi \pi^+$ decay. Using the $J/\psi D^0 K^+$ final state, the $B_c^+$ mass is measured as $6274.28 \pm 1.40 (stat) \pm 0.32 (syst)$ MeV/$c^2$, representing the most precise single determination of this mass to date.

Solving linear systems stands as a cornerstone challenge in computer science. Specifically, for a satisfiable system defined by $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the goal is to determine a vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying $Ax = b$. Existing state-of-the-art algorithms for dense systems rely on matrix multiplication, achieving a runtime of $O(n^{\omega})$. This work investigates the task of locating $\varepsilon$-approximate solutions under the $L_2$-norm, meaning finding an $x$ where $||Ax - b||_2 \leq \varepsilon||b||_2$. Our primary contribution is a fine-grained reduction from matrix rank computation to finding such approximate solutions. Consequently, if the current $O(n^\omega)$ algorithm for computing the rank of $n \times O(n)$ matrices is optimal—a conjecture we support—then obtaining an $\varepsilon$-approximate solution for dense systems also necessitates $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{\omega})$ time, even when $\varepsilon$ is relatively large, such as $(1 - 1/\text{poly}(n))$. Furthermore, based on adjusted conjectures regarding rank determination, we establish optimal hardness of approximation for sparse systems, systems involving positive semidefinite matrices, well-conditioned systems, and $L_p$-norm approximations for $p \geq 1$. Central to these findings is a new reduction from the rank problem to the decision variant of the approximate linear systems problem, a method that maintains critical attributes like matrix sparsity and bit complexity.

This study examines the $P_{cs}$ states arising from the interaction of $\bar{D}^{(*)} \Xi^{(\prime*)}_c$ coupled channels. By analyzing pseudoscalar-baryon ($\frac{1}{2}^+, \frac{3}{2}^+$) and vector-baryon ($\frac{1}{2}^+, \frac{3}{2}^+$) blocks, we identify 10 resonant states that predominantly couple to $\bar{D} \Xi_c, \bar{D}^* \Xi_c, \bar{D} \Xi'_c, \bar{D}^* \Xi'_c, \bar{D} \Xi^*_c$, and $\bar{D}^* \Xi^*_c$. A key finding is that the $\bar{D} \Xi_c/\bar{D}_s\Lambda_c$ and $\bar{D}^* \Xi_c/\bar{D}^*_s\Lambda_c$ channels, driven by a strong transition potential, generate greater attraction than their strangenessless counterparts ($\bar{D} \Sigma_c/\bar{D}\Lambda_c$ or $\bar{D}^* \Sigma_c/\bar{D}^*\Lambda_c$), where the transition potential vanishes. This enhanced attraction in the $\bar{D} \Xi_c/\bar{D}^* \Xi_c$ systems rules out their association with the $P_{cs}(4338)$ and $P_{cs}(4459)$ states, respectively. Instead, the $P_{cs}(4338)$ naturally corresponds to the state coupling primarily to $\bar{D}^* \Xi_c$, while $P_{cs}(4459)$ aligns with the state dominated by $\bar{D} \Xi'_c$ coupling. Additionally, four further states emerge, including some with degenerate spins. In total, 10 distinct spin states are predicted, which may be observable in the near future.

Offering personalized rationales for recommendations enables users to grasp the core insights behind suggestions, thereby enhancing the effectiveness, transparency, persuasiveness, and trustworthiness of recommender systems. Although current explainable models typically produce textual explanations using pre-defined sentence templates, these methods are constrained by limited expressiveness and demand substantial manual effort to define templates. Addressing these limitations, we introduce a framework for generating free-text natural language explanations tailored to personalized recommendations. Specifically, we develop a hierarchical sequence-to-sequence model (HSS) for this purpose. Unlike standard NLP sentence generation tasks, a key challenge in e-commerce recommendation is that not every phrase in user reviews serves an explanatory function. To tackle this, we propose an auto-denoising mechanism leveraging topical item feature words to refine sentence generation. Empirical evaluations across multiple e-commerce domains demonstrate that our approach improves both recommendation accuracy and explanation quality, as measured by offline metrics and feature word coverage. This study represents an initial step toward equipping intelligent agents with the capability to articulate their reasoning through natural language.

Recognizing emotions automatically in real-world scenarios presents a significant challenge, as human emotional expressions are often subtle and can involve a blend of multiple emotions. While most current studies classify entire utterances or video clips as a whole, this coarse-grained approach often fails to capture the nuanced temporal dynamics within them. Typically, a single clip contains only a few emotion-salient segments amidst many neutral ones. To address this, we propose utilizing attention mechanisms within deep recurrent neural networks to identify Regions-of-Interest (ROIs) that are highly emotionally salient in speech and video, and then estimate temporal emotion dynamics by aggregating these specific regions. We compare the ROIs derived from audio and video sources and analyze their characteristics. Additionally, we evaluate the proposed attention-based networks against state-of-the-art LSTM models on a multi-class classification task involving six basic human emotions. Our results demonstrate that the attention models achieve significantly superior performance. Furthermore, the distribution of attention weights offers interpretability by revealing how an utterance can be understood as a mixture of various possible emotions.

Research into nanomaterials remains a vibrant field, driving both fundamental scientific inquiry and technological innovation. While aerodynamic lenses are frequently used to generate isolated nanoparticle beams for in-vacuum analysis, characterizing these beams has historically been challenging because conventional light scattering methods struggle with particles exceeding the diffraction limit. This work introduces a novel characterization approach based on strong-field ionization. By directing an ultrafast, millijoule-level laser into the particle beam, individual nanoparticles within the focal region are ionized, allowing for detection via their ejected electrons. This technique provides immediate access to nanoparticle density at the focal point; by scanning this focus across the beam's transverse and longitudinal dimensions, a full three-dimensional density map can be constructed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that strong-field ionization successfully detects spherical nanoparticles as small as 10 nm in diameter. Beyond detection, this method serves as a powerful tool for optimizing particle beams for specific applications. For instance, we show that manipulating gas flow into the aerodynamic lens allows for precise control over both the beam's density and width.

This paper introduces CTNet, a hybrid deep learning framework that integrates convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers for detecting COVID-19 using 3D chest CT images. The architecture employs a CNN feature extractor enhanced with SE attention mechanisms to capture essential characteristics from CT scans, complemented by a transformer model to identify discriminative patterns within the 3D data. By incorporating a data resampling strategy, CTNet offers an effective and efficient solution for COVID-19 diagnosis. The proposed model achieved advanced performance on the large, public COV19-CT-DB benchmark, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline approach developed alongside the dataset.

High-power operation during extreme fast charging significantly elevates the risk of internal faults in electric vehicle batteries, potentially accelerating their failure. Early identification of these faults is vital for ensuring battery safety and facilitating the widespread adoption of fast charging technologies. In this context, we introduce a real-time framework designed to detect voltage and thermal anomalies. A primary challenge in this domain stems from uncertainties caused by sensor errors, nominal aging, and unmodeled dynamics. Drawing inspiration from physics-based learning, we propose a detection paradigm that integrates physics-based models, model-based observers, and data-driven learning methods to overcome these hurdles. Specifically, we develop detection observers grounded in an experimentally derived electrochemical-thermal model, with observer tuning parameters optimized according to Lyapunov stability theory. Additionally, we employ Gaussian Process Regression to learn both model and measurement uncertainties, thereby assisting the observers in differentiating between actual faults and noise. This uncertainty learning effectively mitigates the impact of these variables, potentially enabling earlier fault detection. We validate the proposed fault detection scheme through simulation and experimental case studies, demonstrating the efficacy of physics-based learning in the early identification of battery faults.

The European XFEL (EuXFEL) serves as a user-accessible X-ray free-electron laser, prioritizing high availability as a core operational feature. By 2022, the facility had completed its sixth year of operation. Its linear accelerator utilizes TESLA superconducting RF technology, functioning at 1.3 GHz with RF pulses lasting 650 $\mu$s and a 10 Hz repetition rate. The Low-Level Radio Frequency (LLRF) system adheres to the MicroTCA standard and operates with extensive automation. This paper reviews the LLRF operations at the EuXFEL and outlines the development of new tools and features designed to enhance system monitoring and expand its usability.

This research examines neutrino propagation from compact astrophysical sources with intense magnetic fields, such as magnetars. We incorporate both neutrino spin rotation and oscillations within a realistic three-flavor framework, solving the evolution equation in the magnetic field near the source to determine probabilities for all spin-flavor transitions. Assuming neutrinos are generated inside the star in a left-handed, electron-flavor state, we apply these transition probabilities to estimate the fraction that undergo helicity reversal during travel to Earth, rendering them unobservable. By modeling the magnetar with a dipolar magnetic field, we illustrate anisotropy in the fluxes of left-handed versus right-handed neutrinos emitted from these objects.

Custom gas cells filled with ammonia and methane at atmospheric pressure were fabricated in our chemical lab, and their low-resolution near-infrared spectra were acquired in our optical facility. These measurements were compared against simulations from the high-resolution HITRAN database at 300 K and 500 K, as well as against near-infrared data from late-T and Y dwarfs, Jupiter, and Saturn. We focused on the 1.5 to 1.7 micron (H-band) region because it is accessible via the Euclid red grism, offers high sensitivity to ammonia and methane opacity variations, and lacks significant interference from other major molecules like water vapor. Our laboratory results revealed that the ammonia and methane features predicted by the HITRAN simulations are incomplete. Consequently, we proposed an updated NH3-H spectral ratio with broader integration limits, which enhances the index's variation across different spectral types. By combining our laboratory spectra and treating the ammonia-to-methane absorption ratio as a free parameter, we identified optimal fits for observed spectra. This analysis established a relationship between effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$) and the ammonia-to-methane ratio for spectral classes T5 through Y2 (1100 K to 350 K), showing reasonable qualitative agreement with theoretical models for high-gravity objects between 1100 K and 500 K. Furthermore, the ammonia-to-methane ratios in late-T and Y dwarfs resemble those of Jupiter, implying comparable chemical compositions. Finally, simulations of Euclid's spectroscopic capabilities suggest the mission will determine $T_{\rm eff}$ and ammonia-to-methane ratios for more than 10$^3$ late T dwarfs across its entire survey.

Using the linear sigma model, we determine the transport coefficients of hadronic matter under conditions of temperature and magnetic field. Within the framework of the relaxation time approximation, we estimate the ratio of shear viscosity to entropy density, $\eta/s$. By employing the $S$-matrix approach, we calculate point-like interaction rates for hadrons in a magnetic field to derive a relaxation time that varies with both temperature and magnetic field strength. Our results indicate that transport coefficients exhibit anisotropy when a magnetic field is present. Incorporating the calculated relaxation time allows us to compute temperature- and magnetic field-dependent anisotropic shear viscosity coefficients. We find that the viscosity-to-entropy density ratio is reduced in a magnetic field compared to a purely thermal medium, and we also analyze the behavior of the perpendicular components of the shear viscosity. Furthermore, this study accounts for temperature-dependent hadron masses arising from mean-field effects.

Stifle joint problems are a primary cause of lameness in dogs and serve as a significant indicator of various injuries or diseases. Utilizing a known Tibial Plateau Angle (TPA) can significantly shorten the time required for diagnosis. This paper explores the use of the state-of-the-art YOLO object detection algorithm and its variants to identify joints, their centroids, and other regions of interest. By drawing multiple line axes from these identified points, the study calculates the TPA. The investigated methods successfully predict the TPA within the normal range for 80 percent of the analyzed images.

The Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) has identified numerous gamma-ray sources emitting significantly above 100 TeV, suggesting they could be PeVatrons. To determine if their gamma-ray emission is of hadronic or leptonic origin, neutrino data analysis is essential. Using a Bayesian approach on ten years of IceCube data (2008–2018), we have constrained the hadronic gamma-ray components in these LHAASO sources. Current neutrino observations indicate that the hadronic gamma-ray flux from the Crab Nebula is less than 86% of the total observed flux at 90% confidence, ruling out a purely hadronic origin for emissions below tens of TeV. However, existing neutrino data do not yet provide meaningful constraints on the radiation mechanisms for the other LHAASO sources. Accounting for source extension uncertainties reveals that upper limits on hadronic flux rise with increased extension; yet, sources such as LHAASO J2032+4102, J1929+1745, and J1908+0621 exhibit statistically significant neutrino signals if their extension is smaller than 0.6 degrees. Finally, we project future detection capabilities using proposed neutrino telescopes: if the PeV gamma-rays detected by LHAASO are indeed hadronic, the Crab Nebula could be detected above 100 TeV at a 3-sigma confidence level within 20 years by a detector possessing an effective area 30 times greater than that of IceCube.

De novo peptide sequencing via mass spectrometry is a crucial technique for protein identification. While various deep learning methods have been employed for this task, with DeepNovoV2 being a prominent example, this study introduces an improved model called DePS. DePS enhances sequencing accuracy even when tandem mass spectrometry data contains missing signal peaks or excessive noise. Evaluation on the same test set used by DeepNovoV2 demonstrates that DePS achieves superior performance with an amino acid recall of 74.22%, amino acid precision of 74.21%, and peptide recall of 41.68%. Additionally, results indicate that DePS surpasses DeepNovoV2 when tested on cross-species datasets.

This study examines the task of predicting core-stable coalition structures in hedonic games under agents' noisy preferences, analyzing both complete information (where all agents' noisy preferences are known) and partial information (where only specific coalition preferences are known). We propose a noise model that probabilistically scales coalition valuations, using the probability of a correct prediction based on available noisy preferences as the performance metric. Our findings indicate that this prediction probability is generally low, often approaching zero and rarely reaching one. In a complete information two-agent model where agents either retain or inflate coalition values, we derive prediction probability expressions as functions of the noise probability and determine the noise intervals ensuring predictions meet a specified threshold. Notably, for certain noisy games, no such noise interval exists even for a low threshold of 0.1481, further confirming the generally low prediction rates. Regarding partial information, we analyze $n$-agent games with $l$ support levels for noise values available for only some coalitions, establishing bounds on the prediction probability of a partition being $\epsilon$-PAC stable in a noise-free setting, contingent on whether the realized noisy game possesses or lacks such a stable outcome.

Bayesian approaches are increasingly favored for embedding prior knowledge and uncertainty quantification into machine learning frameworks. However, the intricacy of contemporary models hinders the ability to interpret their reasoning and formally articulate specific prior assumptions. Although our primary focus lies on interpretability, advancements in transparent machine learning could simultaneously expand the types of prior information applicable to complex Bayesian systems. Drawing inspiration from self-explaining models, we propose a similar concept for variational Gaussian Processes. This contribution not only enhances the transparency of such models but also enables the integration of both global prior knowledge regarding the target function and specific priors concerning the influence of individual features through our proposed self-explaining variational posterior distribution.

Heteroscedasticity frequently occurs in practical applications and is typically managed by integrating case weights into modeling frameworks. Intuitively, the complexity of models fitted with varying weight schemes differs based on how closely the weights approximate the inverse of error variances. However, prevailing statistical theories regarding model complexity, or degrees of freedom, were largely developed under the assumption of homoscedasticity. This study examines linear regression procedures and aims to generalize existing complexity measures to accommodate heteroscedastic settings. Our investigation into weighted least squares uncovers notable characteristics of these extended measures; specifically, they rely on both the weights applied during model fitting and those used for evaluation. Furthermore, employing optimal weights to model heteroscedastic data generally yields fewer degrees of freedom compared to using equal weights, with the magnitude of this reduction contingent upon the degree of variance heterogeneity. These findings offer valuable insights for weighted modeling approaches, particularly in the contexts of risk estimation and model selection.

String and M theories necessitate extending standard differential geometry, typically by broadening the tangent bundle into larger vector bundles endowed with diverse algebroid structures. While the most comprehensive geometric framework remains unclear, a unifying theory for these structures is required. This paper proposes such a framework by adapting the hierarchical axiomatic approach of Courant algebroids—progressing from almost-Courant to metric, pre-Courant, and finally Courant algebroids. We specifically address the symmetric component of the bracket and metric invariance, seeking the most general interpretation possible. This inquiry leads to the definition of novel structures termed Bourbaki and metric-Bourbaki algebroids. By analyzing a specific case of exact pre-metric-Bourbaki algebroids through a reverse-mathematical examination of Severa's classification of exact Courant algebroids, we construct maps that extend the Cartan calculus of exterior derivatives, Lie derivatives, and interior products. Abstracting the essential traits of these maps, we introduce the concept of Bourbaki pre-calculus. Conversely, given a Bourbaki pre-calculus, we build a pre-metric-Bourbaki algebroid featuring a standard bracket akin to the Dorfman bracket. We demonstrate that any exact pre-metric-Bourbaki algebroid meeting specific criteria must possess a bracket that is a twisted variant of the standard one, and we show that numerous algebroids found in existing literature fit within this new category. Furthermore, our constructions can be straightforwardly generalized by substituting the tangent bundle with a Lie algebroid $A$, thereby defining $A$-Bourbaki algebroids and $A$-Bourbaki pre-calculus; this extension accommodates many other known algebroids within the proposed framework.

Although computer vision has achieved notable recent advancements, numerous opportunities for exploration persist. This study introduces TEOS (The Effect of Self-Occlusion), a novel 3D blocks world dataset designed to examine how self-occlusion impacts deep neural networks. Focusing on the geometric properties of 3D objects and the pervasive issue of self-occlusion, TEOS aims to clarify the role of self-occlusion in object classification. Despite significant progress in this field, self-occlusion remains a formidable hurdle for deep learning methods in real-world scenarios, whereas humans typically overcome it through complex strategies like altering viewpoints or manipulating scenes. TEOS comprises two difficulty levels (L1 and L2) featuring 36 and 12 objects, respectively. For each object, the dataset provides 738 uniformly sampled views along with corresponding masks, object and camera positions and orientations, quantified self-occlusion levels, and CAD models. Baseline evaluations using five established classification deep neural networks demonstrate that TEOS presents a substantial challenge to all of them. Both the dataset and pre-trained models are publicly accessible to the scientific community at https://nvision2.data.eecs.yorku.ca/TEOS.

Model-based control typically depends on precise models derived from CAD and actuator specifications, where higher accuracy yields superior control performance. However, in agile bipedal robots performing actions like running or hopping, environmental impacts cause deformations in vulnerable components, rendering predefined models invalid. Consequently, an adaptable kinematic structure capable of accounting for such deformation is essential. To address this, we propose a method that models all robotic joints as 6-DOF units and develops an algorithm to identify the kinematic structure from motion capture data. We evaluated this approach in both simulation using a three-link pendulum and on the physical ATRIAS bipedal robot. In the simulation, the algorithm achieved a 3.6% error relative to the ground truth, while testing on the real robot confirmed our hypothesis regarding out-of-plane joint deformations. Furthermore, the algorithm successfully predicts torques and forces based on the reconstructed joint modes.

This work addresses polynomial ordinary differential equations derived from chemical reaction network models. Given that these systems often involve high dimensions and numerous parameters, reducing the dimensionality within specific parameter ranges is frequently desirable. Singular perturbation theory, pioneered by Tikhonov and Fenichel, offers a framework for achieving such reductions. This paper examines parameter values that enable Tikhonov-Fenichel reductions, known as TFPVs. While an algorithmic method exists, it is currently limited to small-scale systems. Instead, we establish conditions under which TFPVs occur for specific classes of reaction networks, either by deactivating reactions (setting rate constants to zero) or eliminating certain species, a strategy related to the classical quasi-steady-state approach to model reduction. Specifically, we provide conclusive findings for complex balanced reaction networks with zero deficiency and for first-order reaction networks.

While automatic documentation generation tools, commonly known as auto docs, are extensively employed to visualize API data, every tool adopts a distinct format for presenting this information. This paper leverages an information visualization analysis of auto docs to derive design principles aimed at enhancing their usability. Developers typically utilize these tools to locate specific API primitives based on partial clues regarding the name, type, or behavior of the function. The discussion explores ways to improve search and scanning capabilities for these clues, such as by implementing more information-dense visualizations of method signatures.

This paper presents a novel approach to learning transferable content within multi-task imitation learning. Drawing from the human ability to flexibly apply skills—such as using cycling for commuting and driving for shopping—we propose that a policy network's latent memory can be disentangled into two distinct components: one representing task-specific environmental context and the other encompassing generalizable skills. This separation enhances training efficiency and improves generalization to unseen combinations of skills within the same environment, as well as to the same task across different environments. We validated this method by training a disentangled agent in two distinct multi-task imitation learning scenarios, achieving a 30% higher task success rate compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we successfully demonstrated the approach's efficacy in real-world robot navigation.

Mastering functions with high-dimensional outputs is vital for various fields, including engineering design and physical simulation. Nevertheless, gathering training data for these tasks is frequently expensive, often requiring costly numerical solvers. Recent research (Li et al., 2022) introduced the first multi-fidelity active learning strategy for such outputs, capable of acquiring data at varying fidelity levels to lower costs and enhance learning performance. However, this prior approach queries only a single pair of input and fidelity simultaneously, risking the selection of highly correlated examples that diminish learning efficiency. In this paper, we introduce Batch Multi-Fidelity Active Learning with Budget Constraints (BMFAL-BC), a method designed to increase the diversity of training samples to optimize the benefit-cost ratio while adhering to specific budget limits for batch queries, thereby enhancing practical utility. Specifically, we develop a new batch acquisition function that quantifies the mutual information between a set of multi-fidelity queries and the target function, penalizing correlated queries to foster diversity. Optimizing this function is difficult due to the combinatorial nature of searching across multiple fidelities under budget constraints. To overcome this, we propose a weighted greedy algorithm that sequentially selects each (fidelity, input) pair, achieving a near $(1 - 1/e)$-approximation of the optimal solution. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through several applications in computational physics and engineering.

A longstanding open issue in complexity theory involves determining the minimal degree of a polynomial that represents the $n$-bit OR function modulo a composite integer $m$. This inquiry connects to analyzing the capabilities of circuits equipped with $\text{MOD}_m$ gates when $m$ is composite. The OR function stands out as the most basic function for which communication complexity bounds fail. Tardos and Barrington demonstrated a lower bound of $\Omega((\log n)^{O_m(1)})$, while Barrington, Beigel, and Rudich proved an upper bound of $n^{O_m(1)}$. Despite twenty years of effort, no advancement has narrowed this gap, suggesting that novel methods are necessary.

We advance this line of inquiry by adopting a complementary viewpoint: instead of fixing the modulus $m$ to bound the degree $d$ relative to $n$, we fix the degree $d$ and constrain $n$ in terms of $m$. Specifically, for $d=2$, we establish a quasipolynomial bound of $n \le m^{O(d)} \le m^{O(\log m)}$, which surpasses the prior best bound of $2^{O(m)}$ derived from Tardos and Barrington's general result.

To elucidate the computational strength of quadratic polynomials modulo $m$, we introduce a dichotomy of independent significance. We define the boolean rank of a quadratic polynomial $f$ and link it to diagonal rigidity. Leveraging additive combinatorics, we demonstrate that low rank implies $f(\mathbf x)=0$ possesses numerous solutions, whereas techniques from exponential sums show that high rank implies $f$ is nearly equidistributed. In both scenarios, $f$ is incapable of representing the OR function across many variables.

Stars and planets alike can shed mass via expansive winds, often guided by surrounding magnetospheres formed by magnetic fields. The powerful outflows from massive stars are believed to be powered by the line-scattering of radiative momentum, whereas the Sun and lower-mass stars experience significantly weaker mass loss driven by the thermal expansion of a mechanically heated corona. For exoplanets orbiting these low-mass stars, the interaction between radiative heating and stellar winds can cause their atmospheres to expand thermally or undergo mechanical ablation. While stellar magnetospheres arise from the internal trapping of wind outflow, planetary magnetospheres are generally shaped by the external pressure of the stellar wind. In both scenarios, this stress can trigger magnetic reconnection, producing observable phenomena such as X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review provides an overview of the underlying physics of these mechanisms, focusing on both their commonalities and differences between stars and planets.

We examine a Lorentz invariant action that is quadratic in two rank-2 symmetric tensor fields within Minkowski spacetime. Utilizing the three-dimensional rotation invariance of this spacetime, we perform a scalar-vector-tensor decomposition on both tensor fields and categorize theories possessing seven degrees of freedom through Hamiltonian analysis. Our investigation identifies two novel theories that cannot be derived from the linearized Hassan-Rosen bigravity; in these models, new mass interactions become permissible due to the action's transverse diffeomorphism invariance.

Complex socio-environmental interdependencies drive biological invasions, resulting in damage across vast spatial scales. For widespread invasions, management strategies relying on optimization approaches often fail due to computational or data limitations. This study evaluates an alternative method that acknowledges complexity by modeling invasions as networks and using network structure to guide management site selection. We compare optimal versus network-guided invasive species management at a landscape scale, specifically analyzing the placement of boat decontamination stations to address 1.6 million boater movements across 9,182 lakes in Minnesota, USA. Assessing performance across 58 counties, we found that when full information regarding invasion status and boater movements is available, the best network-guided metric achieves a median and lower quartile performance equal to 100% of the optimal solution. Furthermore, performance remains relatively high even with varying network metrics or reduced information (median above 80% and lower quartile above 60% of optimal for most metrics), though it exhibits greater variability, particularly at the lower quartile. Additionally, performance remains generally stable across counties with differing numbers of lakes, indicating the viability of this approach for large-scale invasion management.

A Coxeter group is defined as \emph{$\mathbf{a}(2)$-finite} when it contains a finite number of elements with an $\mathbf{a}$-value of 2, according to Lusztig's definition. This paper provides explicit combinatorial characterizations of the left, right, and two-sided Kazhdan--Lusztig cells corresponding to this $\mathbf{a}$-value within irreducible $\mathbf{a}(2)$-finite Coxeter groups. Specifically, we define new elements termed \emph{stubs} to parameterize the one-sided cells and describe these cells using both star operations and weak Bruhat orders. Additionally, we determine the cardinalities of all one-sided and two-sided cells.

We present an elementary and novel proof of a classical theorem by Cheeger, asserting that for a metric-measure space $X$ satisfying a $p$-Poincaré inequality, the Sobolev space $N^{1,p}(X)$ is both reflexive and separable for any $p \in (1,\infty)$. Additionally, we establish separability for the case $p=1$. Our approach relies on constructing an equivalent norm on $N^{1,p}(X)$ for $p \in [1,\infty)$ in a direct manner, which is uniformly convex when $p \in (1,\infty)$. Furthermore, we explicitly define a functional that is pointwise comparable to the minimal $p$-weak upper gradient for $p \in (1,\infty)$.

The virtual detector is a widely used simulation method for characterizing wavefunction properties. One variant measures probability density and current at specific locations over time, enabling instantaneous momentum determination at boundaries, which can serve as the interface between classical and quantum simulations. However, when used for spectral analysis, this incoherent approach suffers from inherent limitations. An alternative coherent virtual detector samples the complex wavefunction value at a fixed real-space position over time and applies Fourier analysis to generate an energy spectrum. While this yields exact results for unidirectional propagation, it introduces nonphysical interference between forward- and backward-moving wavepackets when bidirectional flow occurs. We propose a new bi-directional virtual detector that retains the advantages of the coherent method while resolving propagation direction and eliminating such interference through a dual measurement point. In the continuum limit with a globally constant potential, this detector reproduces an equivalent wavefunction, making it functionally identical to the exact spectrum.

Periodically driven quantum many-body systems display unique nonequilibrium phenomena, including prethermalization, discrete time crystals, and many-body localization. Recently, a general mechanism involving fractional resonances was introduced, which decelerates many-body dynamics in systems possessing both $U(1)$ and parity symmetries. This study demonstrates that such fractional resonances remain stable even under local noise models. To validate this conclusion, we performed numerical simulations on a small-scale Bose-Hubbard model, which is compatible with current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. These results indicate a viable route to achieving stable nonequilibrium states of matter, offering potential applications in quantum information processing through robust quantum memories.

The formation mechanism of supermassive black holes ($\gtrsim\!10^9\,M_{\odot}$) in the early universe (at redshift $z \sim 7$) is currently unclear. While the gravitational collapse of massive primordial gas clouds is a leading hypothesis, existing theories struggle to explain how these black holes grow rapidly enough. This study examines the influence of magnetism on star formation within atomic-cooling gas clouds. Employing three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations with varying initial magnetic field strengths, we analyzed the star formation dynamics in magnetized clouds. Our results indicate that a primordial magnetic seed field can be rapidly amplified during the initial accretion phase following the birth of the first protostar. Strong magnetic fields efficiently extract angular momentum from the infalling gas, thereby boosting the accretion rate and leading to a high fragmentation rate in gravitationally unstable disk regions. Conversely, the magnetic-induced transfer of angular momentum also enhances the coalescence rate of these fragments. Since nearly all fragments merge into the primary star, the magnetic effects significantly accelerate the mass growth of the massive star. Consequently, we conclude that magnetic effects provide support for the direct collapse scenario in supermassive star formation.

Computational topology faces significant challenges when processing large filtered geometric complexes derived from point cloud data, such as Vietoris-Rips filtrations. Consequently, researchers have developed parallel computation and compression schemes that limit simplices to reside within open sets of a data cover. This work extends the concept of acyclic carriers to persistent homology, providing precise bounds on the relationship between Vietoris-Rips filtrations restricted to specific covers and their complete construction. We illustrate how these restricted complexes facilitate the analysis of data over a base space and utilize our findings to inform the selection of appropriate data covers. Furthermore, we apply these techniques across various cover types, demonstrating their effectiveness in exploring higher-order homology within a model of high-dimensional image patches.

Time series data are essential across numerous domains, including financial markets and energy systems. Consequently, the volume and intricacy of analytical tools and methodologies have been steadily growing. Nevertheless, researchers often face difficulties integrating these resources into their projects and replicating findings due to ambiguous application programming interfaces (APIs) and insufficient documentation. Furthermore, the field is rife with repetitive tasks that are frequently re-implemented for every new project, resulting in wasted time. To address these challenges, we introduce \texttt{pyWATTS}, an open-source, Python-based, non-sequential workflow automation package designed for time series analysis. \texttt{pyWATTS} features modules with well-defined interfaces to facilitate the seamless incorporation of new or existing methods, supports subpipelining to streamline the reproduction of recurring tasks, offers load and save capabilities for easy result replication, and provides native compatibility with major Python machine learning libraries such as scikit-learn, PyTorch, and Keras.

This paper investigates the geometry of iterated variations, demonstrating that the Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV) Laplacian does not inherently contain sources of divergence. Consequently, there is no requirement to impose arbitrary conventions, such as setting $\delta(0)=0$ or $\log\delta(0)=0$, within the BV framework for quantizing gauge systems. Notably, this geometric approach to iterated variations operates independently of constructing Dirac's $\delta$-function as a limit of smooth kernels. We substantiate these arguments by rigorously re-deriving, rather than merely formally postulating, the standard properties of the BV-Laplacian and the Schouten bracket, while verifying their fundamental interrelations, including the preservation of cohomology by gauge symmetries of the quantum master equation.

Enhancing the prediction of molecular properties in ab initio simulations is crucial for advancing material discovery. Although machine learning has recently made strides, applying deep neural networks to refine quantum chemistry models is still constrained by the lack of diverse and sufficient experimental data. This study demonstrates that training a neural network to substitute the exchange-correlation functional within a fully differentiable three-dimensional Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) framework can significantly boost simulation precision. Remarkably, using just eight experimental data points from diatomic molecules, the resulting exchange-correlation networks achieve superior accuracy in predicting atomization energies for a set of 104 molecules, including those with novel bonds and atoms absent from the training set.

We provide a concise summary of the initial flavour physics findings from the LHC. Multiple experiments have measured the cross-sections for charm and beauty production, and the first competitive results regarding D and B decays are now presented.

Intrinsic charge trap capacitive non-volatile flash memories currently hold a substantial portion of the semiconductor electronics market. A key challenge lies in generating intrinsic traps within the dielectric layer without employing high-temperature processing. Although low-temperature polymer-based memory devices have been developed as an alternative, their performance deteriorates quickly after only a few operational cycles. Furthermore, traditional memory devices require tunneling and blocking layers because the memory dielectric or polymer alone cannot prevent leakage. The primary objective in memory device design is to simultaneously optimize intrinsic trap density and leakage current. This study presents a tunable flash memory device that eliminates the need for tunneling and blocking layers by leveraging solution-derived, inorganic, spin-coated dielectric films heated at 200°C or lower. These films exhibit high intrinsic charge trap densities (>$10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$) alongside low leakage currents (<$10^{-7}$ A.cm$^{-2}$). Additionally, memory storage can be systematically adjusted up to 96% by modulating trap density through varying heating temperatures.

Modern applications require system scale-out and semiconductor downscaling, both of which negatively impact hardware reliability. Beyond causing system crashes, this unreliability frequently results in silent data corruptions (SDCs) that degrade application outputs. Consequently, there is a demand for cost-effective, low-effort solutions to mitigate the frequency and impact of SDCs. This work proposes utilizing Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) for online error detection, trained via software fault injection. Our results indicate that the average overhead of this approach, combined with costly re-execution for error correction, amounts to 6.45% in CPU cycles. Furthermore, ANNs detect 94.85% of faults, leading to minimal degradation in output quality. To validate our method, we overclocked ARM Cortex A53 CPUs, ran benchmarks, and analyzed the resulting program outputs. ANNs demonstrated superior efficiency as an error detection mechanism compared to the state-of-the-art approximate method, Topaz, achieving lower CPU overhead (6.45% vs. 12.81%) and higher detection coverage (94.85% vs. 94.11%).

This dissertation tackles various challenging tasks within computer vision and pattern recognition by reframing them as clustering problems. Leveraging a unified framework based on dominant set clustering and its extensions, we introduce novel methods to address multi-target tracking, visual geo-localization, and outlier detection. These proposed approaches yield superior performance compared to several state-of-the-art techniques.

This study utilizes three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations alongside analytical methods to demonstrate the generation of intense, high-order plasma surface harmonics endowed with a time-varying orbital angular momentum (OAM), known as self-torque. We find that obliquely irradiating an overdense plasma target with two laser beams possessing distinct OAMs ($l_1$ and $l_2$) and a specific temporal delay yields harmonics exhibiting OAM values ranging from $nl_1$ to $nl_2$, where $n$ denotes the harmonic order. These powerful self-torqued harmonics present novel opportunities for advancements in ultrafast spectroscopy.

We present 2D blind spot estimation as a vital task for comprehending road scenes. By automatically identifying occluded areas from the vehicle's perspective, we can proactively warn both manual drivers and autonomous systems about potential accident triggers, such as a child emerging from a hidden zone. While performing this reasoning in full 3D is difficult and computationally costly—even with LiDAR—we propose learning to estimate blind spots in 2D using only a monocular camera. Our approach involves two stages: first, we develop an automated method to generate "ground-truth" blind spot training data for any driving video by combining monocular depth estimation, semantic segmentation, and SLAM. The core concept is to reason in 3D from 2D inputs by defining blind spots as road regions currently invisible but expected to become visible soon. Using this offline process, we created a large-scale dataset named the Road Blind Spot (RBS) dataset. Second, we introduce BlindSpotNet (BSN), a streamlined network that utilizes this dataset to automatically produce frame-wise blind spot probability maps for arbitrary driving footage. Comprehensive experiments validate both the RBS dataset and the efficacy of our BSN model.

This study presents a novel penalized synthetic control approach designed for policy evaluation. By penalizing the count of predictors employed to construct the counterfactual, the proposed sparse synthetic control method enhances pre-treatment fit and identifies the most relevant variables. Within a linear factor model framework, the theoretical motivation for this method includes a proof of model selection consistency and a derivation of the mean squared error convergence rate. A simulation study subsequently demonstrates that the sparse synthetic control yields lower bias and superior post-treatment fit compared to the unpenalized version. Finally, the method is applied to analyze the impact of California's Proposition 99 in a context characterized by a high dimensionality of predictors.

Although random flux is generally thought unable to drive complete metal-insulator transitions in non-interacting systems, we demonstrate that it can indeed induce a full metal-to-band insulator transition in the two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Notably, the resulting insulator is not a standard Anderson insulator but rather an extrinsic higher-order topological insulator featuring zero-energy corner modes within specific parameter regimes. Using both level statistics and finite-size scaling analysis, we characterize this transition and numerically determine its critical exponent to be $\nu=2.48\pm0.08$. To uncover the physical mechanism behind this phenomenon, we propose an effective band structure framework based on the random flux-averaged Green's function.

Like the rest of the world, Mexico is grappling with the COVID-19 pandemic. Due to the country's vast territory, containment efforts have required both national and regional strategies. This study compared daily new case curves for each municipality reported by the federal government. Our analysis revealed that 114 municipalities constitute a large network of statistically dependent epidemic phenomena. Leveraging the modular structure of this network, we identified four distinct communities of coordinated epidemic activity. Notably, these clusters are not defined by geographical proximity. These insights can assist public health officials in evaluating past strategies and designing new, targeted interventions.

Emergent language stands out within machine learning due to its open-ended nature, which often lacks clearly defined problems. Consequently, current research has primarily been exploratory, aimed at identifying new challenges, methods, and phenomena. However, once these issues are established, future advancements must demonstrate measurable improvements over previous approaches through what we term systematic research. In this paper, we exemplify this systematic approach specifically for emergent language. We begin by outlining the primary goals of this field, classifying them as either scientific or engineering endeavors. Based on this distinction, we examine the fundamental methodological components of both science and engineering, evaluate their current application in emergent language research, and offer recommendations for their effective implementation.

Calibrating inertial sensors is becoming increasingly critical across various research fields, particularly in navigation engineering. Achieving accurate calibration significantly enhances overall navigation performance by effectively filtering out both deterministic and stochastic measurement errors inherent to these devices. Although numerous techniques exist for modeling and eliminating deterministic errors, substantial recent research has focused on characterizing the complex structures of stochastic errors. Typically, multiple replicates of these error signals are gathered, and a model is identified based on a single replicate. While this method has improved navigation, it fails to utilize the data from the other collected replicates. It is often observed that error behaviors differ between replicates, likely due to varying external conditions during data collection. Regardless of the cause, the underlying model structure appears consistent across replicates, though the parameter values change. Consequently, this study examines and analyzes different approaches to integrate information from all replicates while accounting for parameter variations, validating these methods through both simulations and real-world inertial sensor data. By considering parameter shifts between replicates, this work demonstrates how such approaches can enhance average navigation precision and yield reliable uncertainty estimates for the navigation solution.

This paper introduces the Structured Context Transformer (SC-Transformer), an end-to-end trainable model designed to solve the Generic Event Boundary Detection (GEBD) task, which identifies points where humans naturally perceive event boundaries. The architecture utilizes a backbone convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from individual video frames. To capture temporal context, the SC-Transformer re-partitions the input sequence of frames, maintaining a computational complexity that scales linearly with video length. Subsequently, the model calculates group similarities to discern differences between frames. These grouped similarity maps are then processed by a lightweight fully convolutional network to pinpoint event boundaries. Additionally, to mitigate ambiguities in boundary annotations, the ground-truth labels are preprocessed using a Gaussian kernel to enhance accuracy. Extensive evaluations on the challenging Kinetics-GEBD and TAPOS datasets confirm that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

The Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes (CHNS) system describes the evolution of two isothermal, incompressible, and immiscible fluids within a bounded domain. This study investigates the well-posedness of the CHNS system under nonhomogeneous boundary conditions for the velocity equation. Using semi-Galerkin approximation in a two-dimensional bounded domain, we establish the existence of global weak solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the continuous dependence of solutions on initial conditions and boundary data, thereby proving the uniqueness of the weak solution. Additionally, this work confirms the existence of strong solutions.

This study examines Bayesian finite mixture models (MFMs) and Dirichlet process mixture models (DPMs) for clustering purposes. Although recent asymptotic theory indicates that DPMs tend to overestimate cluster counts in large samples and that estimators from both model classes are inconsistent regarding cluster numbers under misspecification, the effects on finite sample analyses remain ambiguous. Typically, the final output of these models is a single representative clustering derived via MCMC summarization, yet the accuracy of such summaries in estimating the number of clusters is uncertain. Through simulations and an analysis of gene expression data, we explore these practical issues and conclude that: (i) DPMs still overestimate cluster numbers in finite samples, but only slightly, a bias that may be mitigated with suitable summaries; and (ii) misspecification can cause substantial overestimation in both DPMs and MFMs, though the resulting findings often remain interpretable. We offer guidance on MCMC summarization techniques and suggest that despite the theoretical advantages of MFMs' asymptotic properties, which provide a strong rationale for their preference, practical results from both MFMs and DPMs are frequently quite comparable.

This paper extends the Cantor function to two-dimensional cubes and establishes a cyclic 2-cocycle on Cantor dust. While this cocycle is non-trivial when applied to the pullback of smooth functions on the 2-torus via the generalized Cantor function, it vanishes on Lipschitz functions defined on the Cantor dust. The calculation of this cocycle is achieved by integrating 2-forms on the torus, employing a combinatorial Fredholm module.

This study reexamines the phase diagram of the $(1 + 1)$-dimensional Gross-Neveu model under conditions of varying chemical potential and temperature using the mean-field approximation. By analyzing the momentum dependence of the bosonic two-point function, we identify the established second-order phase transition from the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetric phase to an inhomogeneous phase. In this latter state, the chiral condensate exhibits spatial periodicity, thereby breaking translational invariance. Serving as a proof of concept, this work demonstrates that stability analysis of the homogeneous phase can accurately delineate second-order phase transition lines between non-condensed phases and those characterized by spatially inhomogeneous condensation. To supplement existing literature utilizing this method, we provide a detailed explanation of the stability analysis, discussing its limitations and successes specifically within the context of the Gross-Neveu model. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical results for bosonic wave-function renormalization from the two-point function within the mean-field framework. Our findings reveal a "moat regime" where the wave-function renormalization becomes negative, a feature that accompanies the inhomogeneous phase as anticipated.

Text-to-image generation models have recently garnered significant attention due to their transformative potential across various sectors. However, training these models necessitates vast datasets that may harbor privacy-sensitive data, such as facial identities. Although privacy vulnerabilities have been well-documented in image classification and GAN domains, they remain largely unexamined within text-to-image generation. This study presents the inaugural privacy analysis of these models using membership inference attacks. We introduce three core insights regarding membership information and develop four corresponding attack strategies. Our comprehensive evaluation covers two prominent architectures: sequence-to-sequence and diffusion-based models. The empirical findings reveal that all proposed attacks yield substantial performance, occasionally nearing 100% accuracy, indicating a severity of risk far exceeding that of previous membership inference attacks. Furthermore, an extensive ablation study identifies factors influencing attack efficacy, offering developers and researchers guidance on mitigating vulnerabilities. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the proposed attacks constitute a genuine and serious privacy threat to text-to-image generation systems.

Neural transmission occurs at synapses via a chemical mechanism involving the fusion of pre- and post-synaptic terminals. Presynaptic terminals release neurotransmitters either in response to action potentials or spontaneously, independent of such activity. However, the specific mechanisms driving evoked and spontaneous transmission that activate postsynaptic terminals remain unclear. To investigate this, we utilized mathematical simulations to explore spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission, aiming to determine the biophysical constraints that govern the independent activation of NMDA receptor-mediated currents following the release of evoked and spontaneous glutamate. We analyzed quantitative factors—including synapse size, diffusion mobility inhomogeneity, synaptic cleft geometry, and neurotransmitter release rates—to identify spatial relationships between these release events. Simulation results indicate that smaller synapses with a more cohesive peripheral cleft space compared to the center are more likely to exhibit crosstalk between signals released from the center and edges. Conversely, larger synapses with a central cleft space having higher affinity than the periphery, combined with a narrower fusion geometry, increase the likelihood of independence between currents released from the center and edges. These computational findings align well with existing experimental data and provide a roadmap for future research into the independence of evoked and spontaneous release mechanisms.

Recent studies demonstrate that quantum computers can calculate scattering probabilities in large quantum field theories with a runtime polynomial in the number of particles, their energy, and the required precision. In this work, we investigate a related quantum field theory problem: estimating the vacuum-to-vacuum transition amplitude for a massive scalar field in (1+1) dimensions, subject to spacetime-dependent classical sources. We prove that this task is BQP-hard, meaning solving it allows any problem solvable by a quantum computer in polynomial time to be solved as well. Consequently, no efficient classical algorithm can accurately estimate this amplitude, even in weakly coupled regimes, unless BQP equals BPP. Additionally, the associated decision problem can be solved by a quantum computer in time polynomial with respect to the number of bits required to define the classical source fields, rendering it BQP-complete. Our framework can be viewed as an idealized architecture for a universal quantum computer implemented within a laboratory system modeled by massive $\phi^4$ theory coupled to classical, spacetime-varying sources.

This lecture series explores cosmology through the lens of particle physics. Consequently, the focus lies on the empirical evidence for new physics found in cosmological and astrophysical data, utilizing only the essential theoretical frameworks required to comprehend and value this evidence. I will examine the argument for non-baryonic dark matter and outline prevalent models that integrate it. Simultaneously, the narrative of dark energy will be presented, encompassing the Universe's current accelerated expansion, its origin in the Big Bang, and the backing for the Inflationary theory provided by CMBR observations.

The Hayden-Preskill recovery problem offers valuable perspectives on quantum black hole physics and the dynamics of quantum many-body systems through the lens of quantum error-correcting codes. Although constructing an efficient, universal method for information recovery appears difficult, specific classes of dynamical systems may support such algorithms. This work introduces straightforward deterministic recovery protocols for the Hayden-Preskill scenario where unitary evolution is governed by Clifford operators. These protocols employ generalized Bell measurements and implement feedback actions contingent upon the measurement outcomes. By examining operator growth, one can determine both the recovery fidelity and the required feedback operations. Furthermore, these methods function as a decoding strategy for entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Additionally, we outline a variant utilizing local Pauli basis measurements, interpretable as a fault-tolerant, many-body extension of quantum teleportation. Finally, we explore a connection between out-of-time-order correlation functions and discrete Wigner functions, a relationship that holds independent significance.

A prevalent heuristic in semi-supervised deep learning (SSDL) involves selecting unlabeled data based on its semantic similarity to labeled examples, such as pairing unlabeled images of numbers with labeled ones rather than cars. We term this approach semantic dataset matching. This paper investigates the limitations of this strategy, demonstrating that it can occasionally degrade the performance of state-of-the-art SSDL algorithms. We introduce and provide access to non-IID-SSDL, a comprehensive simulation environment designed to stress-test SSDL algorithms across varying degrees of distributional mismatch between labeled and unlabeled datasets. Furthermore, we show that simple density-based dissimilarity measures within the feature space of a generic classifier offer a more reliable and promising quantitative criterion for selecting unlabeled data prior to SSDL training.

This research expands the EULAG-MHD computational framework to incorporate Hall magnetohydrodynamics (HMHD), a capability essential for investigating rapid magnetic reconnection events occurring at the ion inertial length scale. Applications span solar transients, magnetospheric and magnetotail reconnections, and laboratory plasma experiments. The study presents results from two separate sets of implicit large-eddy simulations, one including and one excluding the Hall forcing term, both initialized with a unidirectional sinusoidal magnetic field. While the HMHD simulation serves to benchmark the code, it also highlights the intricate nature of three-dimensional (3D) evolution compared to two-dimensional (2D) models. In HMHD, magnetic reconnection initiates significantly sooner; notably, the magnetic field generated by the Hall term disrupts inherent symmetry, driving the system into 3D. These 3D reconnection events produce magnetic flux ropes and tubes, which, when projected onto the reconnection plane, manifest as magnetic islands. These islands subsequently fragment into secondary islands before merging to form an X-type neutral point. These outcomes align with current HMHD theories and simulations, validating the model extension.
