Initial empirical studies on the MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and CIFAR10 datasets validate the efficiency of this proposed strategy.

Determining the fundamental mechanisms behind optically driven spin dynamics is crucial for understanding ultrafast light-matter interactions and advancing the development of smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient technologies. Central to this goal is the capacity to utilize experimental spectroscopic techniques to reveal energy- and spin-resolved dynamics within non-equilibrium electron distributions. This combined theoretical and experimental study demonstrates that ultrafast helicity-dependent soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy (HXAS) provides access to state occupations that are specific to spin, time, and energy following optical excitation. Applying this technique to cobalt, a prototype transition metal ferromagnet, we observe strong agreement between our theoretical models and experimental data. The resulting energy-resolved spin dynamics expose the complex interplay and characteristic time scales between optical excitation and spin-orbit induced spin-flip transitions in the material: specifically, the spin moment integrated below the Fermi level initially rises ultrafast due to the excitation of minority carriers by the laser pulse, before decreasing as spin-flip processes in highly localized, low-energy states become dominant. These findings highlight the potential of element-specific transient HXAS as a powerful new tool for identifying and elucidating the roles of fundamental processes in optically driven spin dynamics within magnetic materials.

We introduce a framework designed to benchmark quantum computers by integrating quantum algorithms, an architecture-specific noise model, and an ideal simulator. This approach measures the divergence between actual quantum computer evolution and both simulated noisy and ideal scenarios. We applied this framework to evaluate three IBMQ systems, employing a variety of benchmark algorithms—including continuous-time variants—to stress-test the hardware across diverse circuit types. Our findings indicate that circuit complexity directly impacts efficiency, as larger circuits tend to exhibit increased noise. Additionally, utilizing continuous-time algorithms alongside their Hamiltonian decomposition yields insightful comparisons of the efficiency between these two methods. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that our benchmarks deliver comprehensive and robust insights into the performance characteristics of each quantum computer.

We investigate the large $N$ sign oscillations in twisted indices for 3D theories of class $\mathcal{R}$ derived from M5-branes wrapped on hyperbolic 3-manifolds. From a holographic perspective, this oscillatory behavior arises from the imaginary components of on-shell actions associated with two Euclidean supergravity solutions, Bolt$_{\pm}$ (where $p=0$), which represent Wick rotations of magnetically charged AdS$_4$ black holes. These two solutions exhibit identical imaginary parts but with opposite signs. This imaginary component originates from the $F\wedge F$-term in the supergravity action, with a coefficient proportional to the Chern-Simons invariant of the 3-manifold. By integrating the holographic calculation with the 3D-3D relation for twisted indices, we propose a non-trivial mathematical conjecture concerning the phase factor of twisted Reidemeister-Ray-Singer torsion on hyperbolic 3-manifolds.

This study presents measurements of fiducial integrated and differential cross sections for inclusive production of $W^+$, $W^-$, and $Z$ bosons. The analysis utilizes $25.0 \pm 0.5$ pb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at $\sqrt{s} = 5.02$ TeV using the ATLAS detector at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. Results from both electron and muon decay channels are combined to yield integrated cross sections of $\sigma_{W^+}$ = 2266 $\pm$ 9 (stat) $\pm$ 29 (syst) $\pm$ 43 (lumi) pb, $\sigma_{W^-}$ = 1401 $\pm$ 7 (stat) $\pm$ 18 (syst) $\pm$ 27 (lumi) pb, and $\sigma_Z$ = 374.5 $\pm$ 3.4 (stat) $\pm$ 3.6 (syst) $\pm$ 7.0 (lumi) pb. These findings align well with next-to-next-to-leading-order QCD predictions and provide reference values for Pb+Pb interactions at the LHC corresponding to this nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy.

We introduce the Momentum Re-identification (MoReID) framework, designed to harness a vast quantity of negative samples for general re-identification tasks. Inspired by Momentum Contrast (MoCo), which utilizes a dictionary to archive current and historical batches for constructing an extensive set of encoded samples, MoReID diverges by relying exclusively on a large pool of negative samples rather than past positive samples, which often exhibit inconsistency with the current positive feature encoding. However, conventional Triplet loss, which relies on single representative samples for positive and negative sets, fails to effectively exploit the expanded negative dataset generated by MoReID. To fully capitalize on this scaled-up negative sample set, we propose the Hard-distance Elastic loss (HE loss), a novel mechanism capable of utilizing multiple hard samples to represent large groups. Our experiments confirm that the MoReID framework achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the VeRi-776, Market-1501, and VeRi-Wild benchmarks only when paired with the HE loss, thereby enabling the complete utilization of the abundant negative samples.

This study introduces SigVM, an innovative blockchain virtual machine featuring an event-driven execution model that empowers developers to create autonomous smart contracts. Within SigVM, contracts can emit signal events that other contracts may monitor; upon triggering, designated handler functions automatically execute as signal transactions. To actualize SigVM's capabilities, we developed SigChain, an end-to-end blockchain platform, and SigSolid, a compiler for the contract language. Experimental findings demonstrate that benchmark applications can be autonomously reimplemented using SigVM, removing reliance on unstable off-chain relay servers. Furthermore, the effort required for this reimplemention is minimal, with an average code modification rate of just 2.6%.

We have developed a genome-scale metabolic network reconstruction for Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells. By enhancing annotation standards, we improved upon existing reconstructions to support their application in dynamic modeling. The resulting network can be accessed via ChoNet (http://cho.sf.net/).

We expand our algorithm for automating the computation of two-loop dijet soft functions to cover observables that violate the non-Abelian exponentiation theorem, specifically those necessitating a separate calculation for uncorrelated-emission contributions. Given that the singularity structure of uncorrelated double emissions differs significantly from correlated emissions, we develop a new phase-space parametrisation to isolate these divergences. The resulting integrals are incorporated into SoftSERVE 1.0, which we release with this paper and enhance with a regulator compatible with the rapidity renormalisation group framework. Employing this automated framework, we validate existing results for several jet-veto observables and present a new prediction for the soft-drop jet-grooming algorithm.
